rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy from voluntary relocation for study to relocation compelled by benefit conditions; the analogy is offered without addressing the disanalogy that was the point of the question (no guaranteed housing or support).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let’s be clear: the Labour-Greens Government had a 3.5 percent unemployment rate and still put 60,000 people on the jobseeker benefit. It’s because they don’t care about young people in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: infers a motive ('they don't care') directly from a benefit statistic. Nothing offered connects the caseload figure to the claim about intent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The economy is recovering from a period of economic management in which the previous Government engaged in reckless increases to Government spending, which drove inflation sky high, which in turn required huge hikes in interest rates, and which then in turn caused a deep, protracted economic downturn.
rigor.explanation: A coherent four-step causal chain, but a single-cause explanation: no evidence is offered against the obvious alternative that the inflation and rate cycle was substantially global.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, these comparisons are interesting; however, I note that the member did not make those comparisons in the first quarter of the year when New Zealand’s growth rate was three times the rate of Australia’s.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the questioner's past silence is offered as the answer to a present comparison, which does not bear on whether the comparison is apt.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The way that we do that is we get a grip on spending, which the previous Labour-Greens Government didn’t do; we make sure that we lower inflation, which the previous Labour-Greens Government didn’t do; we lower interest rates; we get our economy growing, and that creates jobs for people.
focus.explanation: A real fiscal and monetary mechanism is described, but it is repeatedly wrapped in a contrast with 'the previous Labour-Greens Government' rather than left to stand on its own.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Families that are below $66,000 will be exempted from this scheme. But any parental income of $66,000 or above, they will take responsibility for their 18- to 19-year-olds, to make sure they get connected to work, training, or education.
focus.explanation: Answers squarely on the design of the measure at issue — the threshold and its effect — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he expect young people in regional Aotearoa to be in “jobs, education, or training”, as he says, when there are an average of four times as many job seekers for every job vacancy, and when polytechs are cutting courses, staff, and campuses across regional Aotearoa because of his Government’s cuts?
focus.explanation: Names the policy expectation, a labour-market ratio and a specific consequence in the tertiary sector. Scrutiny of a named commitment against named outcomes.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How exactly does he reconcile his statement to young people “The world doesn’t owe you a living.” with his $3 billion tax cut to landlords?
focus.explanation: Juxtaposes a named ministerial statement with a named, costed tax measure — a policy contrast rather than party characterisation, though the framing is rhetorical.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he understand that removing Work and Income support for young people and directing them to move away from their communities and people they love, without any guarantee of housing and support, into seasonal, short-term work will adversely impact on their wellbeing?
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the measure directly — what is removed, what is required, and the gap in housing support — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The work they have done over successive generations, despite the efforts of the last Government to tie them up in red tape, regulation, and farmer bashing, is extraordinary and will help drive New Zealand’s economic recovery.
focus.explanation: A gesture at regulation, but no measure, cost or mechanism is named; the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of the previous government ('farmer bashing').
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How is it fair to scapegoat young people as being “lazy, sitting on the couch playing PlayStation” when there are far more job seekers than jobs in almost every region in the country, and when they are competing for those jobs with people more experienced than they are?
civility.explanation: 'Scapegoat' imputes a motive to the Prime Minister rather than addressing the policy alone, edging toward the person without landing a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: As is always the case with that member, I’d have to see the context of the statistic and what it’s actually referring to before I commented on it.
civility.explanation: 'As is always the case with that member' is a condescending aside about the questioner personally, attached to what would otherwise be an unobjectionable refusal to comment.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she agree with one business leader, who said, “Willis’ so-called growth agenda is spin without substance. She excels at bashing business for non-issues like butter prices, but has not shown any genuine thought leadership.”?
civility.explanation: The quoted material attacks the Minister's personal credibility and 'thought leadership' rather than the policy; putting it to her makes it the questioner's own sneer, not just a report.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So if the member wants to go blow for blow on mood of the boardroom, she’s welcome to do so, but it won’t reflect well on her, her leader, or her colleagues.
civility.explanation: A taunt aimed at the questioner and her colleagues personally rather than at any argument — needling how they will 'reflect', not what they claimed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member can sit opposite me and critique, but given the only policy she’s talked about so far is a higher target for inflation and more tax, I’d suggest she’s got more homework to do.
civility.explanation: 'She's got more homework to do' is condescension directed at the member personally, treating her as unprepared rather than answering the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The current system has the best of intentions but has placed a heavy financial burden on property owners, leaving 5,800 buildings currently still awaiting either remediation or demolition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 5,800 buildings remain on the earthquake-prone buildings system awaiting remediation or demolition as at October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's EPB register / national earthquake-prone building statistics as at October 2025; true if the count of buildings still awaiting remediation or demolition is approximately 5,800, false if materially different (e.g. under 4,000 or over 8,000).

veracity.statement: Out in the real world, Tararua District Mayor Tracy Collis says that the changes indicate the survival of rural New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to the Tararua District Mayor about what the announced changes mean for rural New Zealand; what is being asserted is that Collis made this characterisation.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, media releases or news reports from Tararua District Mayor Tracy Collis in the week to 7 October 2025; true if she publicly characterised the changes in these terms, false if no such statement exists or she said something materially different.

veracity.statement: What costs has New Zealand incurred in the nine years since the earthquake-prone building rules came into place, and was ACT right, in hindsight, to be the only party opposed to the 2016 bill?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as the premise of the question, that ACT was the only party to oppose the 2016 earthquake-prone buildings legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record for the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill's third reading in 2016; true if ACT was the sole party recorded against, false if it voted for it or if any other party also voted against.

rigor.statement: New Zealand’s known as the Shaky Isles for a good reason, but the latest science does indicate that seismic risk varies greatly across the country. That’s why the Government’s removing Auckland, Northland, and the Chatham Islands from the earthquake-prone building system.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: variation in seismic hazard is offered as the reason for exempting three regions. The direction follows, but there is a gap between 'risk varies greatly' and 'these three regions can be removed entirely' — no threshold or figure is given to bridge it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Under the new system, unreinforced masonry or brick buildings under three storeys in small and rural towns will no longer require mandatory remediation or warning notices, as the risk from falling facades is lower in towns with fewer people.
rigor.explanation: Premise (fewer people passing beneath a facade means fewer people exposed to falling masonry) genuinely supports the conclusion of dropping mandatory remediation for that class of building. The inference is sound, though nothing is offered to show the residual risk is acceptable rather than merely lower.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Dannevirke, Pahiatua, and Woodville will save, respectively, $68 million, $29 million, and $22 million.
specificity.explanation: Named towns with a distinct dollar figure attached to each — precise enough that anyone could check the costing behind it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s difficult to quantify the cost exactly, not least of all because the opportunity cost and the chilling effect of regulations that were well intended, admittedly, but have proven difficult to implement in the intervening eight years, have meant a focus on those particular risks, as opposed to other risks in the built environment.
specificity.explanation: Asked directly what the costs have been, the answer supplies no figure, no range and no mechanism for estimating one — 'opportunity cost' and 'chilling effect' are gestured at in the abstract. He is trying to convey substance, so it is eligible; he simply conveys very little.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The purpose of this bill is to contribute to the restoration of the health, the mauri, the wellbeing of the Hauraki Gulf and to acknowledge customary rights within various areas. It provides modern marine protection tools that reflect the needs of both the taiao—the environment—and the people.
specificity.explanation: Introducing a bill at third reading, so substance is expected, but the description stays at the level of purpose: 'modern marine protection tools' names no instrument, no area, no threshold and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In relation to political parties’ positions, I think, as I’ve acknowledged, the intent of all parties at the time following the tragedy that was the Canterbury earthquakes was right, but lived experience has indicated in the intervening period that it has been appropriate first to pause the enforcement of the current rules, as we’ve legislated, but also to take another look, which is what we’re pleased now to have done.
civility.explanation: Invited by the question to say that every other party got the 2016 law wrong, which was a genuine opening to disparage opponents. He credits all parties' intent and confines the criticism to how the rules worked in practice.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What costs has New Zealand incurred in the nine years since the earthquake-prone building rules came into place, and was ACT right, in hindsight, to be the only party opposed to the 2016 bill?
focus.explanation: The first half names a specific policy and asks a legitimate question about its costs. The second half asks the Minister to certify his own party's past voting record, which carries no policy content — a real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For example, removing the ability for the bill to regulate customary non-commercial fishing, something that other parties were willing to preserve. But I, as a Māori, am not willing to enable the department or others to dictate to iwi and Māori what customary rights happen to be.
focus.explanation: Names a specific amendment to the bill (removing its power to regulate customary non-commercial fishing) and gives the reason for it. The passing reference to what 'other parties were willing to preserve' is party framing, but the weight of the statement is squarely on the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: For example, removing the ability for the bill to regulate customary non-commercial fishing, something that other parties were willing to preserve. But I, as a Māori, am not willing to enable the department or others to dictate to iwi and Māori what customary rights happen to be.
rigor.explanation: There is a real inference about a real policy: the department should not define customary rights, therefore the bill should not regulate customary non-commercial fishing. The premise is offered, but the support leans on the speaker's own standing ('I, as a Māori, am not willing') rather than on an argument about the mechanism — an appeal to the speaker's authority in place of a reason a listener could weigh.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There are 19 marine protection areas that have been created and there is further investment of putea, time, effort, and energy that will be announced in short course.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 19 marine protection areas have been created — a count attributable to the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana marine protection legislation being progressed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Hauraki Gulf Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill as reported back from select committee, and the accompanying Department of Conservation / Ministry for the Environment material; true if the number of marine protection areas established or extended by the bill is 19, false if the count is materially different.

specificity.statement: There are 19 marine protection areas that have been created and there is further investment of putea, time, effort, and energy that will be announced in short course.
specificity.explanation: Carries one hard, checkable figure (19 areas), but the second half — 'further investment of putea, time, effort, and energy' — names no amount, no programme and no date beyond 'in short course'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are a number of efforts that have been taken in the past. Sometimes they’ve been successful, sometimes they haven’t been, but there’s a serious and significant intention to make sure that this special place is further supported.
specificity.explanation: Genuinely attempting to convey substance about the record of past interventions, but names no effort, no measure of success or failure, and no figure or mechanism behind the stated 'intention'. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They can support their young person by encouraging them to get connected to employment, training, or work.
specificity.explanation: Asked what evidence supports the affordability assumption behind the $65,529 threshold, the answer offers a general exhortation with no mechanism, figure or named support — nothing checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re making sure they’ll get a job.
specificity.explanation: Answering a question about what measures will be put in place for 4,300 young people, this names no measure, no agency, no funding and no timeframe — a bare assurance committing to nothing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, at just over 5 percent, our unemployment rate is actually below what it has been, on average, over the last 15 years or so.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a figure and an explicit comparison base, so the claim can be checked, though the comparison period is left loose ('15 years or so').
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
specificity.explanation: Carries the policy threshold figure, a derived income comparison, and the specific costs the threshold is said to ignore — precise enough for the Minister to answer or rebut directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What measures, if any, will the Prime Minister put in place to stop the 4,300 young people expected to lose jobseeker support next year from falling into poverty, homelessness, or leaving Aotearoa entirely?
specificity.explanation: Names a benefit, a numerical population affected, and a timeframe, so the question sets a checkable bar for the answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What does the Prime Minister say to Carlos, an 18-year-old building apprentice in Whanganui who has applied for 22 jobs and is now moving to Australia?
specificity.explanation: Concrete in its particulars — named person, age, trade, location, number of applications — though the detail is a single case rather than a mechanism or aggregate that could be acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re also introducing $1,000 bonus payment from October next year for a young person aged 18 to 24 who has worked with a community job coach, moved into employment, and stayed in a job for at least 12 months.
specificity.explanation: Amount, start date, age band and the full eligibility conditions are all stated — someone could check the policy against this or determine whether they qualify.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The parental support gap test will determine if a young person can reasonably be expected to rely on their parents for support. This would need to be verified through a third party—for example, through evidence from a doctor, counsellor, or other agency.
specificity.explanation: Describes the actual mechanism of the second limb of the test and who would verify it, though it leaves the threshold for 'reasonably be expected' undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she accept that cutting almost $1 billion of Kāinga Ora’s building spend has contributed to the 20,000 jobs lost in the construction sector; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Two concrete figures tied to a named agency and a named sector, precise enough to be confirmed or refuted from published data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Let me step you through the numbers: in the last 23 months under this Government, we have delivered over 7,000 new-build social homes. By comparison, under the entire past three years under the last Labour Government, only 6,000 homes were delivered, so I’ll take our record over your record any day.
specificity.explanation: Two delivery totals with explicit and comparable time periods and a defined unit (new-build social homes), which is enough for someone to check the comparison.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s why we’ve got fast track—which that member and Labour oppose—and that’s why we’re opening up mining and oil and gas. Because there are opportunities for young people in those sectors in Australia but not here in New Zealand, because the Opposition opposes those.
focus.explanation: Names specific policies (the fast-track regime, mining, oil and gas) and ties them to the employment question, so there is real policy content, but a substantial share of the weight is party framing about what the Opposition opposes.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the Parental Assistance Test — the income threshold and whether it reflects household costs. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy parameter, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can the Prime Minister justify cutting jobseeker access for our rangatahi when it is the Government, not our young people, that created the conditions of poverty and unemployment that they are now being punished for?
focus.explanation: Names the policy at issue (cutting jobseeker access for 18- and 19-year-olds), but the framing widens into a general charge about the Government having created poverty and unemployment rather than a specific measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How many construction jobs were lost when the Government cancelled 3,500 Kāinga Ora homes?
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision and a specific number of homes and asks for the consequence — scrutiny of a government decision, which is squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When we ask the private sector what stops them making those investments, they highlight two key factors: (1) high interest rates—that’s why it’s important we bring them down—and (2) consenting issues, which is why we have introduced the fast-track Act, which is already working to get major infrastructure developments off the ground.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance directly: identifies the constraints on private infrastructure investment and links each to a named policy response. No party framing carries the point.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s why we’ve got fast track—which that member and Labour oppose—and that’s why we’re opening up mining and oil and gas. Because there are opportunities for young people in those sectors in Australia but not here in New Zealand, because the Opposition opposes those.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur in the causal chain: the conclusion that the opportunities do not exist in New Zealand 'because the Opposition opposes those' does not follow, since an opposition party does not control whether the governing parties' policies take effect. The inference is about a real policy, so it is assessable here rather than merely a jibe.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can the Prime Minister justify cutting jobseeker access for our rangatahi when it is the Government, not our young people, that created the conditions of poverty and unemployment that they are now being punished for?
rigor.explanation: The premise that the Government 'created the conditions of poverty and unemployment' is asserted rather than supported, and is built into the question so that any answer concedes it — a loaded question resting on an unestablished causal claim. The argument is about the policy, so the defect is one of inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does she now regret slashing infrastructure projects when we can all see it has directly contributed to 20,000 job losses in the construction sector?
rigor.explanation: The causal link is asserted by appeal to obviousness — 'we can all see' — with nothing offered to connect the funding decisions to the sector-wide job losses, and 'directly contributed' is stronger than anything established. The claim is about the policy, so this is a genuine inference failure rather than a swipe.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If that member is so wrong-headed to think that every single construction job in New Zealand is dependent on public infrastructure, then perhaps she needs to get a little bit more reading done, because, as is actually the case, the construction sector relies heavily on private sector development—things like housing development, which tends to be funded also by the private sector, Member Andersen, and things like the Auckland Port development, which is being funded by that organisation.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the member claimed public building spend contributed to construction job losses, not that every construction job depends on public infrastructure. The substantive point about private-sector funding is sound but refutes a position nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, at just over 5 percent, our unemployment rate is actually below what it has been, on average, over the last 15 years or so.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things: that the current unemployment rate is just over 5 percent, and that this is below the average rate over roughly the preceding 15 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate for the quarter current at 7 October 2025, compared with the arithmetic mean of the quarterly HLFS unemployment rate over the 15 years to that date. True if the current rate is at or just above 5% AND is lower than that 15-year mean; false if the current rate is materially different from 'just over 5 percent' or is at or above the 15-year mean.

veracity.statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two parents both earning the minimum wage have a combined income roughly $33,000 above the parental income threshold of just over $65,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ adult minimum wage in force on 7 October 2025, multiplied by two full-time (40-hour) earners over 52 weeks, compared with the stated parental income threshold of $65,529. True if the excess is approximately $33,000 (within a few thousand dollars); false if the excess is materially different.

veracity.statement: What measures, if any, will the Prime Minister put in place to stop the 4,300 young people expected to lose jobseeker support next year from falling into poverty, homelessness, or leaving Aotearoa entirely?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 4,300 young people are expected (on official projections) to lose jobseeker support in the following year as a result of the announced changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD advice, the Regulatory Impact Statement, or Ministerial announcements for the Parental Assistance Test / youth jobseeker changes, for the projected number of young people losing jobseeker support in 2026. True if the official projection is approximately 4,300; false if the published projection is materially different or no such projection exists.

veracity.statement: Evidence shows us that if a young person goes on to welfare before the age of 25, they can spend, on average, another 18 years on benefit over their lifetime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an empirical finding: that people entering the benefit system before age 25 spend, on average, a further 18 years on a benefit over their lifetime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MSD benefit system actuarial valuation (Taylor Fry) figures for average future years on benefit for clients entering the system under age 25. True if the published average is approximately 18 years; false if the published figure is materially different or measures something other than lifetime years on benefit.

veracity.statement: How many construction jobs were lost when the Government cancelled 3,500 Kāinga Ora homes?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government cancelled 3,500 Kāinga Ora homes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora build programme documents, Budget 2024/2025 papers, or Ministerial announcements recording the number of planned Kāinga Ora homes stopped or removed from the programme. True if approximately 3,500 planned homes were cancelled or descoped; false if the number is materially different or the homes were never funded/committed.

veracity.statement: Does she accept that cutting almost $1 billion of Kāinga Ora’s building spend has contributed to the 20,000 jobs lost in the construction sector; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts: that almost $1 billion was cut from Kāinga Ora's building spend, and that 20,000 jobs have been lost in the construction sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget appropriations for Kāinga Ora capital/building programmes before and after the 2024 and 2025 Budgets, and Stats NZ employment data (HLFS or filled jobs) for the construction sector between 2023 and the September 2025 quarter. True if the reduction approaches $1 billion AND construction employment has fallen by roughly 20,000; false if either figure is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: Was Kāinga Ora wrong when they advised that $1 billion of building spend supports approximately 5,200 Kiwi jobs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kāinga Ora gave advice stating that $1 billion of building spend supports approximately 5,200 jobs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora briefings or advice released under the OIA containing a jobs-per-billion estimate for building spend. True if such advice states approximately 5,200 jobs per $1 billion; false if no such advice exists or it gives a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: Let me step you through the numbers: in the last 23 months under this Government, we have delivered over 7,000 new-build social homes. By comparison, under the entire past three years under the last Labour Government, only 6,000 homes were delivered, so I’ll take our record over your record any day.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over 7,000 new-build social homes were delivered in the 23 months to October 2025, against 6,000 delivered across the final three years of the previous Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora and HUD public housing supply reporting on new-build social home completions, for the 23 months to October 2025 and for the three years to October 2023. True if both totals match on a like-for-like definition of new builds; false if either total is materially overstated or understated, or if the two figures use different counting definitions.

civility.statement: I’m afraid this question highlights the importance of the work being done by my colleague Erica Stanford on structured literacy.
civility.explanation: An implied jibe that the questioner cannot read properly, aimed at the member rather than the substance of the infrastructure question. Short of a direct insult, but it is mockery of the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She’s as bad at maths as she is at structured literacy.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the member's competence — numeracy and literacy — rather than on anything she claimed. Nothing about the housing figures is engaged in the remark itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m grateful to the advice from my colleague Minister Stanford, who advises that some children require repeated instruction in order to grasp concepts.
civility.explanation: Compares the questioner to a slow-learning child — sustained condescension aimed at the member's intelligence rather than at the substance of the Kāinga Ora funding question.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Crayfish and scallops have become functionally extinct.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that crayfish and scallop populations in the Hauraki Gulf have collapsed to the point of functional extinction — an ecological status claim about the present state of the gulf, not a prediction or a value judgement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of Our Gulf' reporting and Fisheries NZ stock assessments for CRA 2 rock lobster and Coromandel/Hauraki scallops; true if those assessments describe gulf crayfish and scallop populations as functionally extinct or at a comparably collapsed level, false if they report populations at or near sustainable biomass targets.

veracity.statement: There are around 2 million - odd people who live in the area around where the Hauraki Gulf marine protected areas are going to be established, in Auckland, Waikato, and the Bay of Plenty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a population figure of roughly 2 million for the Auckland, Waikato and Bay of Plenty areas surrounding the new marine protected areas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Auckland, Waikato and Bay of Plenty regions as at the date of the statement; true if the combined gulf-adjacent population is in the region of 2 million, false if materially different (e.g. below 1.5 million or above 3.5 million).

veracity.statement: You actually can’t even kill Caulerpa or treat pests and other invasive species in a marine reserve.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the legal regime governing marine reserves prohibits killing the invasive seaweed Caulerpa or otherwise controlling pests and invasive species inside a reserve.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Marine Reserves Act 1971 and DOC's permitting practice for marine reserves; true if the Act and DOC policy bar pest or invasive-species control (including Caulerpa treatment) within a marine reserve, false if DOC can and does authorise such control inside reserves.

specificity.statement: Now, the bill sets some time frames: 25 years will be the milestone where the first comprehensive assessment of biodiversity and improvement in the gulf will be carried out.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete statutory mechanism and a precise timeframe — a first comprehensive biodiversity assessment at 25 years — which anyone could check against the bill text and act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s very important that as soon as is practical, we establish a biodiversity baseline for these places we intend to protect in the gulf and that there is regular monitoring and reporting back, so all of those who doubt whether this is going to work can actually have their fears and concerns addressed.
specificity.explanation: Names a real action (a biodiversity baseline plus regular monitoring and reporting) but supplies no timing beyond 'as soon as is practical', no measures, no frequency and no cost — a direction with partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it points the way for how New Zealanders feel about their environment and they actually want to get involved in enhancing and protecting it and not just having to leave it to nature to heal itself, because quite often it’s degraded to a point where it can’t heal itself without human helping hands.
rigor.explanation: Infers a nationwide public attitude from the fact that a bill permits active management — a non sequitur, since the content of legislation is not evidence of what the public wants. The supporting clause (that degraded environments cannot self-heal) argues for active management but not for the claim about how New Zealanders feel.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it makes sense that local commercial vessels can continue to fish in a sustainable way under the fisheries regulations and supply the people with good quality and affordable food.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from a stated premise — most people buy their fish rather than catching it — to the conclusion that small local commercial vessels should retain access. The premise supports continued commercial supply generally, but there is a gap between that and the specific conclusion that these vessels must fish inside the gulf's protected areas.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it makes sense that local commercial vessels can continue to fish in a sustainable way under the fisheries regulations and supply the people with good quality and affordable food.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the measure before the House: who is affected by the access rules, the regulatory regime they would operate under, and the consequence for food supply. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That is what we expect: abundance; that these structures, these protected areas, will actually allow the gulf to be restored to a place where if we do want to go for a fish, if we want to go and catch a crayfish or collect some scallops outside these areas, they’ll be available to all of us.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the protected areas established by this legislation will restore gulf abundance to the point where crayfish and scallops are available for recreational harvest outside the protected areas. This is an outcome of the policy, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Monitoring under the Act (the five-yearly reviews and the statutory comprehensive assessment) together with Fisheries NZ stock assessments and Hauraki Gulf Forum reporting; true if crayfish and scallop abundance in the gulf recovers sufficiently that recreational take outside the protected areas is open and viable, false if those populations remain collapsed or harvest closures remain in place.

specificity.statement: Overfishing, habitat loss, pollution, sedimentation, and the effects of poorly planned urban development have led to what we see today in the gulf: a 57 percent decline in key fish stocks in the Hauraki Gulf, a 67 percent decline in seabirds, and a 97 percent decline in whales and dolphins.
specificity.explanation: Three named ecological indicators with percentage figures attached to a named place; directly checkable against the State of our Gulf reports.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Delayed it to this point, passed eleventh-hour amendments that enable some commercial ring-net fishing in two of the high protection areas, which weakens the intent of this bill and has alarmed environmentalists and recreational fishers alike.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (commercial ring-net fishing), the scope (two high protection areas) and the timing (eleventh-hour amendments), though no figures or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So given that more than 30,000 people signed an open letter to the Prime Minister, urging this Government to reverse this particular change which allows ring-net fishing in the high protection areas, and more than 5,000 emails were sent by concerned members of the public to the relevant Ministers, and they—this Government—have chosen not to make those changes, Labour, in Government, will reverse the change that allows ring-net fishing in those HPAs.
specificity.explanation: Two petition/correspondence figures plus a precisely bounded commitment: reversing the named ring-net fishing provision in the high protection areas. Someone could check whether it was done.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just to take a step back and to reflect on the very core purpose ostensibly of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act, which is 20-odd years old now at this point, what that did was establish an entity that has the power to report on the health of the Hauraki every three years yet did not meaningfully give that entity the teeth to enforce the protections that communities so desperately wanted and deserved for our ocean, for our moana.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, its approximate age and the concrete mechanism it created (three-yearly reporting) along with the gap identified (no enforcement power), but supplies no figures or particular provisions.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: While we have ended up with a situation that is far better than the status quo, and we can and should celebrate the consensus that this House has come to with increasing protection to 6 percent, it is nowhere near the 30 percent that is necessary, that scientists tell us is necessary, but more so that our communities so desperately want, nor does it even touch the sides on the need to ban bottom trawling, for which we have so much evidence and which research tells us releases immense amounts of carbon and poses serious risks, therefore, for us with regard to climate changing emissions.
specificity.explanation: Gives the protection level the bill achieves (6 percent), the target advocated (30 percent) and a named further measure (banning bottom trawling); the evidence base behind them is gestured at rather than cited.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Overfishing, habitat loss, pollution, sedimentation, and the effects of poorly planned urban development have led to what we see today in the gulf: a 57 percent decline in key fish stocks in the Hauraki Gulf, a 67 percent decline in seabirds, and a 97 percent decline in whales and dolphins.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific magnitudes of decline in the Hauraki Gulf, sourced by the speaker to successive State of our Gulf reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of our Gulf' report series (and the underlying Sea Change / NIWA baseline work): true if those reports give declines of approximately 57% in key fish stocks, 67% in seabirds and 97% in whales and dolphins for the gulf; false if the reported declines differ materially from those figures.

veracity.statement: In fact, crayfish and scallop populations are now functionally extinct in parts of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that crayfish and scallop populations have collapsed to functional extinction in some areas of the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed surveys of Hauraki Gulf rock lobster (e.g. the University of Auckland/Leigh surveys) and Fisheries New Zealand scallop (SCA CS) stock assessments and closure notices: true if published assessments describe these populations as functionally extinct in parts of the gulf; false if surveys show populations at ecologically functional levels throughout.

veracity.statement: All they have done is to also remove all reference to whānau and hapū in this bill, although both play a significant role in the restoration work of the gulf, and, again, they have been sidelined, although they have led much of that restoration as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the late amendments deleted every reference to whānau and hapū from the bill — a total claim about the enacted text, not merely that some references were removed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the bill as reported back by the Environment Committee with the version as passed (and the Amendment Paper): true if every occurrence of 'whānau' and 'hapū' was struck out, false if either word survives anywhere in the enacted text.

veracity.statement: His own Cabinet paper stated, quite clearly, that that fishing could occur elsewhere in the gulf, but he chose to ignore that, sadly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific content of the responsible Minister's own Cabinet paper — that the affected fishing could be carried out outside the high protection areas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The proactively released Cabinet paper on the amendments to the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana marine protection bill: true if it states that the ring-net fishing in question could take place elsewhere in the gulf, false if it contains no such statement or says the opposite.

veracity.statement: Here, I would just make the comparison that we have seen, when we have seen threats to our livestock, and we have seen Governments pour in close to a billion dollars to try and prevent the spread of Mycoplasma bovis but nowhere near the equivalent when it comes to eradicating the threat that is Caulerpa brachypus.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that government spending on the M. bovis eradication approached a billion dollars and vastly exceeds what has been spent on eradicating exotic Caulerpa.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI / Treasury reporting on the total cost of the Mycoplasma bovis eradication programme, and MPI/Biosecurity NZ budgets for the Caulerpa brachypus response: true if M. bovis spend approaches $1 billion and the Caulerpa response is an order of magnitude smaller, false if the figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: We did not need New Zealand First’s support to pass this legislation. We could have passed it in its original format with members of the Opposition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a majority for the unamended bill was available from the governing parties plus the Opposition, so New Zealand First's votes were not required.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Party seat counts in the 54th Parliament and the division record for the bill: true if the combined votes of National, ACT and the Opposition parties reach a majority (61) without New Zealand First's members, false if New Zealand First's votes were arithmetically necessary.

focus.statement: But sadly, despite the Environment Committee unanimously recommending to this House that the bill be passed with no substantive change, at the eleventh hour, because of some active lobbying of the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, we saw this Government cave to that pressure, and they have chosen to water-down the protections in the original bill.
focus.explanation: Names the select committee recommendation, the amendment stage and the specific outcome (weakened protections in a named bill). This is scrutiny of a government decision, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: While this bill is a step in the right direction, it is no thanks to the current Government, even though the Minister responsible—Minister Potaka—has, in the past, continuously tried to take credit for it.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point (who authored and progressed the bill) but the weight of the sentence is on which side deserves credit rather than on the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Delayed it to this point, passed eleventh-hour amendments that enable some commercial ring-net fishing in two of the high protection areas, which weakens the intent of this bill and has alarmed environmentalists and recreational fishers alike.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: names the amendment, the activity permitted, the number of areas affected and the consequence for the bill's intent.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But sadly, despite the Environment Committee unanimously recommending to this House that the bill be passed with no substantive change, at the eleventh hour, because of some active lobbying of the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, we saw this Government cave to that pressure, and they have chosen to water-down the protections in the original bill.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of a decision and of the Government's response to lobbying. No individual's character or competence is attacked; 'cave to that pressure' is pointed about the choice rather than the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: While this bill is a step in the right direction, it is no thanks to the current Government, even though the Minister responsible—Minister Potaka—has, in the past, continuously tried to take credit for it.
civility.explanation: Imputes credit-grabbing to a named Minister — a suggestion of bad faith about the person rather than the policy, but short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In fact, the New Zealand Sport Fishing Council and the environmental group LegaSea wrote to Ministers Potaka and Jones, and they, basically, alluded to the fact, and said, that their behaviour—both those Ministers—is, quite frankly, embarrassing, that they are deeply disappointed in their lack of judgment, in permitting gillnetting within two of the HPAs in the gulf, and then went on to say that their lack of common sense and good judgment will be remembered.
civility.explanation: The speaker puts on the record, without distancing herself, a characterisation of two named Ministers as embarrassing and lacking common sense and judgment. Relaying an attack on individuals' judgment is still the speaker choosing to make it; the target is the men, not the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We interrogated this abject ridiculousness at the committee of the whole House stage, and the Minister could not provide us with any evidence whatsoever for those fundamentally baseless assertions, nor was the Minister willing to engage in the many amendments that we put forward as members of the Opposition to try and actually work with—if we were to take in good faith—the rationale from the Minister to protect high-protected areas: to do what it says on the tin.
civility.explanation: 'Abject ridiculousness', 'fundamentally baseless' and the pointed conditional 'if we were to take in good faith' shade from criticising the Minister's rationale into mockery of it and a suggestion of bad faith on his part.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Here, I would just make the comparison that we have seen, when we have seen threats to our livestock, and we have seen Governments pour in close to a billion dollars to try and prevent the spread of Mycoplasma bovis but nowhere near the equivalent when it comes to eradicating the threat that is Caulerpa brachypus.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: differential spending on two biosecurity incursions is offered as evidence that marine biodiversity threats are under-resourced. The comparison is apt but the analogy alone does not establish that the two incursions are comparable in tractability or cost, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: While we have ended up with a situation that is far better than the status quo, and we can and should celebrate the consensus that this House has come to with increasing protection to 6 percent, it is nowhere near the 30 percent that is necessary, that scientists tell us is necessary, but more so that our communities so desperately want, nor does it even touch the sides on the need to ban bottom trawling, for which we have so much evidence and which research tells us releases immense amounts of carbon and poses serious risks, therefore, for us with regard to climate changing emissions.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that 30 percent is necessary and that trawling must be banned rests on bare appeals to authority — 'scientists tell us', 'research tells us', 'so much evidence' — with none of that evidence stated. A reasonable position, but the support offered is an appeal rather than an argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You’re kind of undermining those so-called high-protected areas if you are providing for, explicitly in legislation, carve-outs. That sets a seriously dangerous precedent.
rigor.explanation: The first inference is sound on its own terms: legislating exceptions to a protection does reduce the protection. The 'dangerous precedent' conclusion is a step further with nothing offered to connect this carve-out to future ones — a mild slippery slope grafted onto an otherwise valid point.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s been a rare occurrence under this Government, unfortunately.
focus.explanation: A general jab at the Government's overall legislative record with no policy, measure or figure named — the statement is about the other team rather than the bill before the House. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched; there is no inference to assess, so nothing is emitted for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When you have an ocean, any part of ocean that is 99 percent exploited, compromise does not look like protecting 6 percent and still allowing commercial fishing in the high-protection areas.
specificity.explanation: Carries two concrete proportions (99 percent exploited, 6 percent protected) and names a specific mechanism in the bill — commercial fishing permitted inside high-protection areas. Checkable against the bill and the gulf's protection statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Everyone can be proud of the huge environmental achievement where we see this bill delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf, nearly tripling the protected area in the Hauraki Gulf, establishing high-protection areas for 800 square kilometres of the gulf.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named area figure (800 square kilometres of high-protection areas) and a quantified change (nearly tripling the protected area). Held short of the top because 'highest ever level of protection' is a superlative rather than a measure, and no timeframe or mechanism is supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When you have an ocean, any part of ocean that is 99 percent exploited, compromise does not look like protecting 6 percent and still allowing commercial fishing in the high-protection areas.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure: from the premise that the gulf is almost wholly exploited, she concludes that the protected share on offer does not amount to a compromise. The reasoning tracks the premise, but the gap is an unstated benchmark for what proportion would constitute compromise, so the conclusion is partly definitional rather than derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When you have an ocean, any part of ocean that is 99 percent exploited, compromise does not look like protecting 6 percent and still allowing commercial fishing in the high-protection areas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the gulf is 99 percent exploited, that the bill protects only about 6 percent of it, and that commercial fishing remains permitted inside the areas designated as high-protection.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Two separable factual claims. (a) Extent of protection: the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill as passed, plus DOC's published figures for the total area of the high-protection areas against the total area of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park — true if the high-protection areas amount to roughly 6 percent of the gulf, false if materially higher or lower. (b) Whether commercial fishing is permitted in high-protection areas: the text of the Act as enacted, including the late-stage Supplementary Order Paper — true if any commercial fishing method is authorised to continue within a high-protection area, false if all commercial fishing is excluded. The '99 percent exploited' figure resolves against the pre-Act share of the gulf open to fishing.

veracity.statement: Everyone can be proud of the huge environmental achievement where we see this bill delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf, nearly tripling the protected area in the Hauraki Gulf, establishing high-protection areas for 800 square kilometres of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three quantitative facts about what the bill does: that it sets the highest level of protection the Hauraki Gulf has ever had, that it nearly triples the protected area, and that the high-protection areas it creates total 800 square kilometres.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Act as enacted plus DOC's published marine protection figures for the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park. (a) 'Nearly tripling' — true if the total protected area after commencement is between roughly 2.5 and 3 times the pre-Act protected area, false if materially outside that. (b) '800 square kilometres' — true if the combined area of the high-protection areas created by the Act is approximately 800 km², false if materially different. (c) 'Highest ever level of protection' — true if the post-Act protected proportion of the gulf exceeds every previous level recorded by DOC, false if any earlier regime protected more.

civility.statement: There’s been a lot of talk about compromise, with this bill, and I do want to challenge that because, quite frankly, it’s a load of fishmeal.
civility.explanation: A blunt, colourful dismissal aimed at the characterisation of the bill as a compromise, not at any member. Under the re-anchored scale, hard criticism of a position sits near the top; it comes down slightly from 1.0 because the phrasing is a flat dismissal of others' framing rather than engagement with it, edging toward the people making the argument without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’ll expand the protected area from currently 6.7 percent to over 18 percent of the gulf.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures for the before-and-after extent of protection; directly checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That flows out into the ocean, into the harbour, the Mahurangi Harbour, and so far just this year alone, the Mahurangi oyster farmers have had closures for 158 days due to sewage contamination being spilled by Watercare—a total of 4 million litres of sewage contamination being spilled into the Mahurangi River.
specificity.explanation: Names the affected industry, a day count, a volume and the responsible operator — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’ll expand the protected area from currently 6.7 percent to over 18 percent of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill lifts protected area from 6.7% to over 18% of the gulf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's regulatory impact statement / DOC's published figures for marine protection in the Hauraki Gulf before and after the Act; true if the pre-Act figure is ~6.7% and the post-Act figure exceeds 18%, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Government has already noted, and I note Matua Shane, Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, the Hon Shane Jones, has already taken steps to help protect the Hauraki Gulf and restore its mauri by having special permits available to go and smash up the kina.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries has made special permits available for kina removal in the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Fisheries New Zealand / ministerial announcements and the special permit register under the Fisheries Act; true if special permits for kina removal in the Hauraki Gulf were issued or made available under Shane Jones as Minister, false if no such permit regime exists.

veracity.statement: So that has been done, and $15 million has already been put forward to deal with Caulerpa, which is that exotic invasive species which is causing a great concern right around the gulf and also up into Northland and down into the top of the Coromandel as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a government funding figure of $15 million allocated to the exotic Caulerpa response.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget documents and Biosecurity New Zealand / ministerial announcements on exotic Caulerpa funding; true if cumulative committed funding as at October 2025 is ~$15m, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Today, eight of those beaches are currently closed due to waste-water overflows.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that eight of the named Auckland beaches were closed on 7 October 2025 because of waste-water overflows.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Safeswim / Auckland Council beach status records for 7 October 2025; true if eight of the beaches she names were flagged closed for waste-water contamination that day, false if fewer or the cause was different.

veracity.statement: If I just go back a few months to 11 May, 64 beaches were either black or red flagged for waste contamination.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 64 beaches carried black or red water-quality flags for waste contamination on 11 May 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Safeswim historical records for 11 May 2025; true if 64 beaches were black- or red-flagged for waste contamination that day, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: They were normally around two per annum and they’re now up to 200 discharges that Watercare can make into the Mahurangi River.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the 2022 alternative discharge frequency consent raised permitted discharges into the Mahurangi River from about two a year to up to 200.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auckland Council resource consent granted to Watercare in 2022 (alternative discharge frequency) and the prior consent conditions; true if permitted discharge frequency for the Mahurangi River rose from ~2 to ~200 per annum, false if the consented numbers differ materially.

veracity.statement: That flows out into the ocean, into the harbour, the Mahurangi Harbour, and so far just this year alone, the Mahurangi oyster farmers have had closures for 158 days due to sewage contamination being spilled by Watercare—a total of 4 million litres of sewage contamination being spilled into the Mahurangi River.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 158 days of Mahurangi shellfish harvesting closures in 2025 and 4 million litres of sewage spilled into the Mahurangi River.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI/NZ Food Safety shellfish harvest closure notices for Mahurangi in 2025 and Watercare's reported overflow volumes for the Mahurangi River; true if closures total ~158 days and spill volume ~4 million litres, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: The most recent spill was 50 cubic metres on 24 September.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific 50 cubic metre wastewater spill on 24 September 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Watercare / Auckland Council overflow incident reports for September 2025; true if a spill of ~50 m³ is recorded on 24 September 2025 at the Mahurangi site, false if no such incident or a materially different volume.

veracity.statement: It was in 1975 that Cape Rodney-Okakari Point was set up as a marine reserve, so this year we celebrate 50 years of this marine reserve, and I would be very pleased to receive an invitation from Ngāti Manuhiri as they conduct the celebrations in November.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Cape Rodney-Okakari Point marine reserve was established in 1975, making 2025 its fiftieth year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Gazette notice and DOC records for the Cape Rodney-Okakari Point Marine Reserve; true if established/gazetted in 1975, false if a different year.

veracity.statement: During the committee of the whole House, Te Pāti Māori tabled amendments aimed at ensuring that there is a mandatory consultation process when giving permits, ensuring that the process requires consultation with mana whenua.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pāti Māori tabled amendments requiring mandatory consultation with mana whenua on permits during the committee of the whole House stage of this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and the Supplementary Order Papers for the committee of the whole House stage of the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill; true if Te Pāti Māori tabled amendments of that effect, false if none appear.

civility.statement: We need to take a look, and Watercare absolutely must take a look at their practices, because the degradation of the water quality due to Watercare’s infrastructure failures is unacceptable and totally objectionable, and it’s happening all around the Hauraki Gulf.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation aimed entirely at an organisation's infrastructure and practices; no individual is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need to take a look, and Watercare absolutely must take a look at their practices, because the degradation of the water quality due to Watercare’s infrastructure failures is unacceptable and totally objectionable, and it’s happening all around the Hauraki Gulf.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named operator's discharge practices and their effect on gulf water quality — a concrete accountability point, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Te Pāti Māori knows for a fact that whānau who go for a dive or fish to gather kai or kai moana for kai for tangihanga—they will be the ones who will be criminalised and fined, rather than the big corporate commercial fishing companies who exploit our taonga and kai.
focus.explanation: Directed at a concrete predicted effect of the bill's permit and protection regime on customary gatherers versus commercial operators; the swipe at 'big corporate' fishers is framing around a real policy point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We support the Hauraki Māori Trust Board’s statement that placing further limitations on the exercise of tino rangatiratanga by Hauraki / Tīkapa Moana iwi over their taonga and territories—which has never been extinguished or annihilated—is counter-productive to achieving the purpose of this bill.
focus.explanation: Engages the bill's own purpose clause and the mechanism by which it restricts iwi authority — entirely on the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We need to take a look, and Watercare absolutely must take a look at their practices, because the degradation of the water quality due to Watercare’s infrastructure failures is unacceptable and totally objectionable, and it’s happening all around the Hauraki Gulf.
rigor.explanation: The call for a review is grounded in the spill counts, closure days and volumes she has just set out; the inference from repeated overflows to a need to review practices tracks the evidence, though the causal step from 'infrastructure failures' to the observed degradation is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We support the Hauraki Māori Trust Board’s statement that placing further limitations on the exercise of tino rangatiratanga by Hauraki / Tīkapa Moana iwi over their taonga and territories—which has never been extinguished or annihilated—is counter-productive to achieving the purpose of this bill.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the conclusion that the limitations are counter-productive rests on the Trust Board's statement, with no mechanism offered for how restricting rangatiratanga would worsen restoration of the gulf.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Te Pāti Māori knows for a fact that whānau who go for a dive or fish to gather kai or kai moana for kai for tangihanga—they will be the ones who will be criminalised and fined, rather than the big corporate commercial fishing companies who exploit our taonga and kai.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that enforcement under the new protection regime will fall on whānau gathering kai rather than on commercial fishing companies.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Enforcement records under the Act (Fisheries NZ/DOC prosecutions and infringement notices for breaches of the new high protection areas and marine reserves) in the first years after commencement; true if the large majority of penalties are imposed on individual customary or recreational gatherers and none or almost none on commercial operators, false if commercial operators are a substantial share of enforcement action.

focus.statement: I had to look up what ring-net fishing was and I was worried about what I saw in terms of catching a particular amount of fish and a particular type of fish and that it might not be a very good move.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — she engages a specific amendment mechanism (ring-net fishing) rather than the party that lodged it.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I had to look up what ring-net fishing was and I was worried about what I saw in terms of catching a particular amount of fish and a particular type of fish and that it might not be a very good move.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the amendment 'might not be a very good move' rests on her own first impression after looking the term up; no evidence about catch effects is offered. Argument from personal impression.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we’re going to have industries like oysters in that area, which bring fish which would allow a lot of the things we are wanting, we’re going to have to accept that Government’s got a role there, that we need to look after those places, that we need to know the effluent’s going in because we’ve pushed and pushed and pushed on people’s resources.
rigor.explanation: A genuine conditional argument — wanting an oyster industry implies a government role in wastewater — but the linking step, that under-resourcing is what puts effluent in the harbour, is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I had to look up what ring-net fishing was and I was worried about what I saw in terms of catching a particular amount of fish and a particular type of fish and that it might not be a very good move.
specificity.explanation: Names ring-net fishing but supplies no quantity, species, area or consequence — 'a particular amount' and 'a particular type' carry no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I take the point that the member who raised that issue is totally genuine about it, but I’d like to see this particular piece of legislation be one that fosters a real interest in Government getting in, boots and all, and looking after places like the Hauraki Gulf, looking at the connected issues of things like effluent coming into the sea.
civility.explanation: Disagreeing with another member's point while crediting their good faith; the disagreement is entirely about what the legislation should do, with nothing aimed at the person.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So we have a situation where we know that the gulf was lined with mussels.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Hauraki Gulf historically held extensive mussel beds, prior to their loss.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical fisheries records and NIWA/peer-reviewed studies of the pre-1960s extent of green-lipped mussel beds in the Hauraki Gulf and Firth of Thames; true if extensive subtidal mussel beds are documented across the gulf before the dredge fishery, false if the beds were localised or absent.

veracity.statement: There was already overflow from Warkworth and we didn’t do enough about it.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Watercare and Auckland Council consent-compliance and overflow records for the Warkworth wastewater treatment plant and network over the 2010s; true if recorded wastewater overflows into the Mahurangi catchment predate the statement by roughly a decade, false if no such overflows are on record.

divination.statement: My area is going to grow more than most because a lot of the building is going to happen in those areas.

divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates and Auckland Council dwelling-consent counts for the Mount Albert / Albert-Eden area; true if population and dwelling growth rates there exceed the Auckland regional average over the years following 2025, false if they are at or below the regional average.

veracity.statement: Now, those changes actually stipulated in the Minister of Conservation’s very own words, in his own Cabinet paper, that the ring-net fishers, who will still be able to fish in two of the high protection areas, could have fished in other parts, with minimal impact on them.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister of Conservation's Cabinet paper on the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill amendments (proactively released on the DOC/Cabinet Office website); true if the paper states that the affected ring-net fishers could fish in other areas with minimal or low impact on them, false if it contains no such assessment or states the opposite.

veracity.statement: They promised to accelerate it; instead, it has sat here on the Order Paper for two years while eleventh hour changes were made.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things: that the Government promised to accelerate this bill, and that it then sat on the Order Paper for about two years before late amendments were made.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Parliament bill-progress record for the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill (introduction, first reading, select committee report-back and third reading dates) plus ministerial statements on progressing the bill; true if a ministerial/coalition commitment to accelerate it exists and the elapsed time between report-back or first reading and this debate is around two years, false if no such commitment exists or the delay is materially shorter.

rigor.statement: Now, those changes actually stipulated in the Minister of Conservation’s very own words, in his own Cabinet paper, that the ring-net fishers, who will still be able to fish in two of the high protection areas, could have fished in other parts, with minimal impact on them. The gap is that 'undermine and weaken' is asserted rather than shown — the cited advice speaks to impact on fishers, not to the protection lost — so the conclusion runs slightly ahead of the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Despite the Minister’s own Cabinet paper saying that, unfortunately, the Government has chosen to proceed with amendments that will undermine and weaken this bill.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested point where an attack on the Minister was available, but the criticism lands entirely on the amendments and the Government's decision. No imputation of bad faith or attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They promised to accelerate it; instead, it has sat here on the Order Paper for two years while eleventh hour changes were made.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named commitment against a named outcome — the promise to accelerate this bill versus its two years on the Order Paper. Specific policy content, not party characterisation.

divination.statement: We will see the health of the ocean improve, and I’m looking forward to having visits in future years where we can actually point to real examples of where we are seeing fishery stocks grow back again in abundance.

divination.falsification_criterion: Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of Our Gulf' reporting and DOC/Fisheries NZ monitoring of the new high protection areas; true if post-implementation monitoring shows increases in fish biomass or abundance inside the protected areas relative to the pre-implementation baseline, false if monitoring shows no improvement or continued decline.

specificity.statement: But we will repeal those changes because they were the wrong thing to do—and we will continue to say that—so that we can protect the Hauraki Gulf for generations and years to come.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete action (repealing the late amendments that let ring-net fishers into two high protection areas) and the target is identifiable from the surrounding sentences, but gives no timeframe, no mechanism and no detail on what the restored protection would look like.
specificity.subject: speaker

Marked down only because the mechanism is asserted on 'we know' with no source or evidence offered for the link.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The answer was no, we can’t use either of those different tools, and that is, in part, because the Marine Reserves Act 1971 is very much about protection and being very, very focused on that protection only, and these reports had identified that there needed to be more than protection.

Valid inference from the premises given; no fallacy or gap of consequence.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The answer was no, we can’t use either of those different tools, and that is, in part, because the Marine Reserves Act 1971 is very much about protection and being very, very focused on that protection only, and these reports had identified that there needed to be more than protection.

specificity.statement: This is a major win for the environment, a major win for Auckland, and it’s this Government that’s delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf.

veracity.statement: I want to remind the House, while the Minister is here, that, as far as I am aware, the Gazette notices to finalise that South-East Marine Protection areas has not yet been undertaken, and, and I hope that it is very soon.

veracity.statement: That fisheries plan was looking at excluding from bottom trawling 74 percent to 89 percent of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Hauraki Gulf fisheries plan announced alongside the bill in 2023 proposed excluding between 74% and 89% of the gulf from bottom trawling.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 Fisheries New Zealand / MPI Hauraki Gulf fisheries plan and bottom-trawling consultation documents; true if the proposed exclusion options span roughly 74–89% of the gulf area, false if the documented options give materially different percentages.

veracity.statement: In May of this year, the current Minister for Oceans and Fisheries shelved those plans, and I want the other side of the House to really think about that, because we’ve heard in a number of these speeches and we see from all these reports that the Hauraki Gulf is protecting bits of the Hauraki Gulf.

veracity.statement: This has been a decade in the making—in fact, I would argue, at least 25 years in the making, when you reflect back on the landmark legislation that was the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000, which among other things created the Hauraki Gulf Forum, of course affectionately known as the “Guardians of the Gulf”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000 established the Hauraki Gulf Forum.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000 on legislation.govt.nz; true if the Act constitutes the Hauraki Gulf Forum, false if the Forum was created by some other instrument or predates the Act.

veracity.statement: This is a major win for the environment, a major win for Auckland, and it’s this Government that’s delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf.
