specificity.statement: So spending three days in secure is one thing, but the 22 previous days is really where I’d want to understand in a more thorough way, Minister, as to what that actually does look like and what is the model of care.
specificity.explanation: Carries two concrete figures (three days, 22 days) but the ask itself, 'what the model of care looks like', is broad: no named document, standard or metric is asked for.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question is, really: why wasn’t that explicit wording included in 384AC, and what was the intent of the removal of some of that language in section 384G, as well?
specificity.explanation: Names two specific sections and the exact wording at issue; the Minister could not mistake what is being asked, and anyone could check the clauses. A precise question, not an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So if you know you are going to be in a unit with young people that have weapons on them, that have the potential to stab you or kill you, you are not feeling safe. So what I would say is this is a valid response to making sure that young people in our care are safe.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: young people say they want to feel safe; weapons in the unit undermine that; therefore the item-restriction power is justified. The premises support the conclusion in general terms, but there is a gap between 'some items can be weaponised' and 'this particular regulation-making power is a valid response', and the framing leans on an appeal to fear of stabbing rather than on any evidence about how often it occurs.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I just want to make sure that people have an understanding that nobody goes to work to try and torture or break the rules and have a young person repeatedly in secure care—just to bring a bit of balance to it.
rigor.explanation: Answers a question about what safeguards prevent repeated use of secure care by appealing to the good intentions of staff. The conclusion does not follow: an argument from motive: abuse of a power is not ruled out by the absence of intent to abuse it, which is precisely why safeguards were being asked about.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve heard words like “de-escalation” from my colleagues on the right as a being a smart and good idea, but that takes real, solid, enduring training and monitoring and assessment as to whether people are up for that.
rigor.explanation: A sound conditional inference: if de-escalation is to be relied on as the alternative to force, it depends on sustained training, monitoring and assessment, so the adequacy of those is the relevant question. Not higher because nothing is offered on what level of training would suffice or where the current programme falls short.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It just feels to me like the appropriate people—like, (3)(a)(ii) is worded so broadly “another authorised person:”, I can’t imagine who might be included under regulation who sits outside being an authorised person.
rigor.explanation: Argues that the regulation-making power is redundant because the existing category is already drafted broadly. The premise is grounded in the clause text, but the conclusion rests on the speaker's inability to imagine a case, which is an argument from personal incredulity rather than a demonstration that no such case exists.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So spending three days in secure is one thing, but the 22 previous days is really where I’d want to understand in a more thorough way, Minister, as to what that actually does look like and what is the model of care.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the periods around a secure-care placement and the model of care that applies to them. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question is, really: why wasn’t that explicit wording included in 384AC, and what was the intent of the removal of some of that language in section 384G, as well?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the text of the bill: the drafting of two named sections and the intent behind a wording change. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: From what I’m hearing this morning, I can hear intention, but I don’t hear deep conviction in that way, and I’d like to understand that better.
civility.explanation: Pointed: it questions the depth of the Minister's personal commitment rather than the content of her answers, which edges toward the person. Mitigated by being framed as the speaker's own impression and by an explicit invitation to be persuaded, so it stops well short of imputing bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s also justified in light of news stories—last year, I think—around Korowai Manaaki, where contraband was being brought in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that there were reports in the preceding year concerning contraband being brought into the Korowai Manaaki youth justice residence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reporting and Oranga Tamariki / Independent Children's Monitor / Children's Commissioner reports on Korowai Manaaki youth justice residence dated 2024–2025; true if any document or news report of that period records contraband (including vapes) being brought into the residence, false if no such reporting or finding exists for that period.

veracity.statement: Some of us might recall—a couple of years ago, I believe—there was this kind of big drama about police taking lots of images of young Māori on the street and not storing those images securely, and the Privacy Commissioner found that there were tens of thousands of unauthorised, unsecure photos of young Māori children just floating around and being stored on these devices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Privacy Commissioner found tens of thousands of unauthorised, insecurely stored police photographs of young Māori. Two checkable parts: that an official finding was made about unlawful/unauthorised police photography of rangatahi, and that the quantity found was in the tens of thousands.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2022 joint inquiry by the Independent Police Conduct Authority and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner into Police photographing members of the public, and any subsequent OPC compliance notice; true if that inquiry found unauthorised, insecurely held photographs of young Māori numbering in the tens of thousands, false if the finding records a materially smaller number or does not support the quantity or the 'unauthorised/unsecure' characterisation.

specificity.statement: How will we know and monitor that those images have been deleted within that 24-hour window? Who has access to those images? Does that include third-party contractors?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory mechanism at issue (the 24-hour deletion window), the monitoring question, and a named category of possible data-holder (third-party contractors). A precise question the Minister could answer or fail to answer checkably.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of those is the clear plastic bags so that we can see what staff are bringing into residences, and holding the staff to the same level of accountability as any other visitor that comes into residence.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete operational practice (clear plastic bags for staff belongings) and the standard being applied (staff held to the same level as visitors). Checkable against residence procedure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If something is found, through either the scanning process or the pat-down process, if it is not an illegal item, then they will be given the option to take that back to their vehicle and then come back again.
specificity.explanation: A precise procedural answer: the trigger (item found by scan or pat-down), the qualifying condition (not illegal), and the consequence (return it to the vehicle and re-enter). Someone could check practice against it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d seek the Minister’s assurance that people would be given appropriate interventions in terms of things like nicotine patches, etc., because they’re undergoing huge amounts of stress and they’re being asked to, basically, detox at the same time, quite often.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete intervention (nicotine patches) and the substances at issue, but leaves the mechanism, threshold and who provides it unstated — a direction with partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How will we know and monitor that those images have been deleted within that 24-hour window? Who has access to those images? Does that include third-party contractors?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the operation of the bill's scanner-search provisions in Part 3 — mechanism, retention, access. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But what I would like to say is it's not as uncommon as we think. You walk through an airport; you get scanned at an airport, if you want to catch a flight. You often can come to these restrictions when going to court. There are multiple places where you walk through a scanner and nothing to see here and not a problem.
focus.explanation: Entirely engaged with the scanner provisions of the bill before the committee; the argument is weak but it is an argument about the measure, not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One thing I have heard from rangatahi who have been in youth justice residences is that the family visits can make a big different to the care they’re being provided, or maybe the counselling they’re getting in there or the programmes they’re doing.
rigor.explanation: Offers reported first-hand testimony as the premise for the conclusion that search regimes must not deter family visits. The inference is relevant and the testimony is on point, but it rests on anecdote — no data on visit frequency or rehabilitation outcomes is offered to support the generalisation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But what I would like to say is it's not as uncommon as we think. You walk through an airport; you get scanned at an airport, if you want to catch a flight. You often can come to these restrictions when going to court. There are multiple places where you walk through a scanner and nothing to see here and not a problem.
rigor.explanation: Weak analogy. The conclusion that image scanning here is unproblematic rests on the commonness of airport and court scanning, but the disanalogies are exactly the ones raised: those are adults choosing to enter a public facility, and the objection put was about storage, access and deletion of intimate images of children in State custody, which the analogy does not touch. Also carries an implicit appeal to common practice.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I remember I had a case where there was equipment for the use of marijuana and there was equipment for the use of P. In fact, it’s very hard to link that to the person who’s driving the car because so many people are in the car.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single remembered case to a general attribution problem with vehicle searches. The underlying point — that shared use of a vehicle weakens the link between a find and the driver — does support the conclusion independently of the anecdote, which keeps this above a bare appeal to anecdote, but no more than the one case is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One the challenges that many of us who’ve had dogs face is they’re not, actually, entirely in our control.
rigor.explanation: False analogy: the premise is about ordinary pet dogs and the conclusion is a risk claim about professionally trained detector dogs working under handler protocols. The two classes differ in exactly the respect the argument turns on, and nothing is offered to bridge them.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the bill removes the current requirement that pat-down searches only be carried out by a person of the same sex as the child or young person. This is done because it would completely contradict the new section that it’s being replaced by, which would require search plans under new section 384AA, inserted by, clause 1, where a child or young person can express the gender or sex of the staff member they prefer to be searched by.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the committee: premise (the new search-plan provision lets the young person nominate the sex/gender of the searcher), conclusion (the old same-sex-only requirement must go or the two provisions conflict). The conclusion tracks the premise; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They might be bringing items in for kitchen, they might be bringing anything in, and it just gives us the ability to be able to make sure that contractors aren’t bringing in unauthorised items, because they will be skipping the process of going through the scanner in the initial entrance to residence.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason for the vehicle-search power: contractor vehicles entering through the secure perimeter bypass the entrance scanner, so the scanner regime leaves a gap. The conclusion follows from the stated premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The question would just be that my read is also if someone were to go through a scanner and then the security were alerted for a need for a pat-down, the person could refuse a pat-down but still not fall within the section—so they’ve complied with one or the other and, therefore, this section wouldn’t prevent their entry.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference from the statutory scheme: if either search satisfies the entry obligation, then refusing the second cannot trigger the consequences provision. Valid on its stated premise, but the premise (that either alone suffices in all cases) is assumed rather than established — the Minister's answer indicates both may be required — so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the bill removes the current requirement that pat-down searches only be carried out by a person of the same sex as the child or young person. This is done because it would completely contradict the new section that it’s being replaced by, which would require search plans under new section 384AA, inserted by, clause 1, where a child or young person can express the gender or sex of the staff member they prefer to be searched by.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific provisions (section 384G, new section 384AA, clause 1) and the exact mechanism being changed — someone could check this against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s only to be used in shared spaces, and the dogs will be controlled by Police or Corrections handlers, not youth justice staff.
specificity.explanation: Concrete operational limits — where dogs may be used and who must handle them, with the excluded group named. Falls short of 1.0 because no threshold, frequency or authorisation process is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I just also wanted to raise our Amendment Paper 371, which talks about, within Part 3, the amendments that specify that an authorised person is able to use force.
specificity.explanation: Names the amendment paper by number and the Part it amends, and identifies the power at issue; no figures or thresholds, and the question that follows is broader than the citation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I wondered whether it would be useful to prioritise obscuring the genitals as opposed to making it an alternative, and that way, saying that the preference by far is for that to be used as an option instead of making them not easily distinguishable, which feels to me quite invasive.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a precise drafting change (make obscuring the primary requirement rather than one of two alternatives) tied to a named subsection, though no wording is proposed.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They might be bringing items in for kitchen, they might be bringing anything in, and it just gives us the ability to be able to make sure that contractors aren’t bringing in unauthorised items, because they will be skipping the process of going through the scanner in the initial entrance to residence.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the clause under question — who is searched, where, and why — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just also wanted to raise our Amendment Paper 371, which talks about, within Part 3, the amendments that specify that an authorised person is able to use force.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named amendment paper and a named Part of the bill, pursuing who may use force. This is scrutiny of the measure itself, not of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wondered whether it would be useful to prioritise obscuring the genitals as opposed to making it an alternative, and that way, saying that the preference by far is for that to be used as an option instead of making them not easily distinguishable, which feels to me quite invasive.
focus.explanation: Engages the drafting of a specific subsection governing imaging-technology searches — the exact wording, the ordering of the two options, and the effect on the person searched. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s the secure perimeter, so it wouldn’t be the car park that a visitor comes in to visit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a present fact that the new vehicle-search power in the bill is confined to vehicles brought inside the secure perimeter and does not reach visitors' vehicles in the car park — offered as reassurance in answer to Tamatha Paul's concern about families being deterred.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of new section 384KG ("Search of vehicles entering youth justice residence") as it stands in the version of the Oranga Tamariki amendment bill before the Committee: true if the search power is limited on its face to vehicles brought within the secure perimeter of a youth justice residence; false if it extends to vehicles in the visitor car park or elsewhere on the grounds outside the secure perimeter.

focus.statement: Because I talked so much about it earlier, in terms of that, I wanted to ask about that regulation-making power and what was envisaged in terms of time frames on making new objects, and what happens in a situation where a new object is presented which isn’t in the scope so far but would come into this regulating-making power—what will happen to that object at that time?
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the mechanism of the bill — the regulation-making power for harmful items, its timeframes, and the gap for unclassified objects. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It looks to me as if it’s balanced towards risk rather than benefit, and in most areas of the law we’ve moved to balancing those two things in our words as well, saying we need to actually look at the benefit as well as the risk when we decide whether to prohibit such an object.
focus.explanation: Entirely about how the provision is drafted and what test it applies. No reference to any party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: After a use of force, it’s reviewed by a team leader and would also be able to be escalated internally to Oranga Tamariki around any concerns of appropriateness of the use of force. If it is found that that use of force is questionable, I would assume and expect that that would be a disciplinary and that would actually be a matter when it comes to their contract.
focus.explanation: A direct answer about the operation of the use-of-force provisions; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So Part 4 deals with amendments to the Public Records Act 2005. Whilst this may seem like a small change, the change is to allow the chief archivist to audit an agency more frequently where required and allow the chief archivist to work with agencies to put in place action plans and to issue performance notices to improve practice.
focus.explanation: Explains the mechanism of the amendment before the committee. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just want to seek clarity from the Minister, who did comment on clause 17(4), which is amending section 384A. It was about the amendment of the Hon Willow-Jean Prime, which was around the definition of “authorised person” and the request in our amendment around adding the words “a person who has received training in de-escalation methods appropriate for children and young people”.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the text of a named amendment to a named clause.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question is really about what is appropriately placed in primary legislation versus secondary legislation, because those sections taken together and the broadness of the section as it’s currently drafted mean that regulations would set out how long an item that was seized from a visitor to a facility could be potentially held for and under what circumstances they could be released.
focus.explanation: Engages a precise drafting question — the primary/secondary legislation boundary for seizure of visitors' property — with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Because I talked so much about it earlier, in terms of that, I wanted to ask about that regulation-making power and what was envisaged in terms of time frames on making new objects, and what happens in a situation where a new object is presented which isn’t in the scope so far but would come into this regulating-making power—what will happen to that object at that time?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific power and the precise gap being probed (timeframes, unlisted objects), but carries no figures or proposed wording. A precise question, short of full detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: After a use of force, it’s reviewed by a team leader and would also be able to be escalated internally to Oranga Tamariki around any concerns of appropriateness of the use of force. If it is found that that use of force is questionable, I would assume and expect that that would be a disciplinary and that would actually be a matter when it comes to their contract.
specificity.explanation: Describes a real mechanism (team leader review, internal escalation) but the consequence is hedged into indefiniteness — 'I would assume and expect' — with no timeframe, threshold or named process for the disciplinary step.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So Part 4 deals with amendments to the Public Records Act 2005. Whilst this may seem like a small change, the change is to allow the chief archivist to audit an agency more frequently where required and allow the chief archivist to work with agencies to put in place action plans and to issue performance notices to improve practice.
specificity.explanation: Names the Part, the Act amended, the office affected and three concrete new powers (more frequent audits, action plans, performance notices). Someone could check the clauses against this description. Missing only amounts and commencement timing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So anything that we can do to improve this, bring some more accountability into this space, speed up the process, and actually make sure that we’re doing the right thing to help people reflect on their history, heal in their present, and empower their future is a good thing.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — improve, more accountability, speed up, do the right thing — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named step. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I just want to seek clarity from the Minister, who did comment on clause 17(4), which is amending section 384A. It was about the amendment of the Hon Willow-Jean Prime, which was around the definition of “authorised person” and the request in our amendment around adding the words “a person who has received training in de-escalation methods appropriate for children and young people”.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the section amended, the amendment's sponsor, the definition at issue and the exact words proposed. Fully checkable against the bill and the amendment paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question is really about what is appropriately placed in primary legislation versus secondary legislation, because those sections taken together and the broadness of the section as it’s currently drafted mean that regulations would set out how long an item that was seized from a visitor to a facility could be potentially held for and under what circumstances they could be released.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact matters left to regulation (retention period, conditions of release) and the class of person affected (visitors, not residents). No timeframes or figures proposed, which is what holds it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It looks to me as if it’s balanced towards risk rather than benefit, and in most areas of the law we’ve moved to balancing those two things in our words as well, saying we need to actually look at the benefit as well as the risk when we decide whether to prohibit such an object.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the drafting weighs risk only, comparable law weighs risk against benefit, therefore this should too. The analogy to 'most areas of the law' is asserted rather than evidenced, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I just need clarification that there is a description of what an authorised person is in order to make sure that they have the skills, because we know that we’re dealing with young people who have trauma and young people who are in escalated situations.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered — the population is traumatised and situations escalate, so the people handling them need skills. But the step from 'the Act describes who an authorised person is' to 'they therefore have the skills' is assumed; a definition of a role does not by itself establish a training requirement, which is the very gap the amendment addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I couldn’t imagine circumstances where anyone but an authorised person would be the person who was there for a pat-down search.
rigor.explanation: Argument from personal incredulity: the inability to imagine a case is offered as the reason no secondary power to prescribe other persons is needed. It reasons about the real provision, but the absence of an imagined counter-example does not establish the absence of one.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If I have understood your questions around harmful objects, I actually think I’ve been very thorough in my explanations, a couple of times now, and have gone through the process of “It must go through a process to be added to the list or taken off the list”. So, I will just leave that one because I think I’ve explained that one a couple of times.
civility.explanation: Pointed — declining to answer on the basis of her own thoroughness carries an implication that the questioner was not listening — but it lands on the exchange rather than on the member. No insult, no imputation of bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When it comes to the oversight of a youth justice facility, the Ombudsman does have access to that information. Mana Mokopuna does regular reviews of our youth justice facilities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two present-tense facts about oversight arrangements: that the Ombudsman has access to youth justice facility information (including use-of-force records), and that Mana Mokopuna conducts regular reviews of youth justice residences.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ombudsman's designation as a National Preventive Mechanism for youth justice residences under the Crimes of Torture Act 1989 and the access/information powers in the Ombudsmen Act and Oranga Tamariki Act; and Mana Mokopuna (Children and Young People's Commission) published monitoring/visit reports on youth justice residences. True if both bodies hold the stated access and Mana Mokopuna's reviews are recurring rather than one-off; false if either body lacks that access or does not conduct regular reviews.

rigor.statement: I would say that we continue to believe that transformation is needed in this space. It’s certainly what we are hearing from those who’ve been through the system this far and from those who represent them, that more needs to be done.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that transformation is needed rests entirely on reported testimony from unnamed people who have been through the system and their representatives — an appeal to anecdote/authority with no data, mechanism or comparison offered to connect what is being heard to what should change.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Section 33 in the current Act specifies that the archivist must carry the budget for those audits, and I wonder, if by making this change, we’re solving a budget problem but potentially not the independence issue, which the legislation, as it is currently drafted, protects.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: the current provision ties both funding and independence to the Chief Archivist, so allowing a departmental employee to conduct the audit could relieve the cost while weakening the independence. The gap is that the budget motive is inferred rather than shown — nothing offered establishes that cost is the driver, so the conclusion runs ahead of the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Following the Supreme Court’s December judgment, the High Court issued a decision that has made extensive findings of CMT, illustrating that the Supreme Court’s test has not altered the approach of the courts in practice.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: a single High Court decision is offered as proof of what 'the courts in practice' do, and the inference also assumes the extent of the findings is attributable to the test rather than to the merits of the applications before that court. One data point cannot establish that a new appellate test made no difference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Parliament, clearly, did not intend CMT would be available at that scale, so to resolve Parliament’s intent, legislative clarification is still required.
rigor.explanation: Question-begging: the disputed point is precisely what the 2011 Parliament intended the CMT threshold to be, and 'clearly' is asserted in place of evidence — no extrinsic material, debate record or statutory text is offered. The conclusion that clarification is required is then derived from the premise it was meant to support.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The amendment removes that time period and changes the language so that it’s just “as directed by the Chief Archivist”. I am wondering what the rationale was for removing that time period?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact change (removal of a statutory audit interval), quotes the replacement wording, and asks a question that can only be answered with a concrete rationale. A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I know that at one stage a young person received what was their Child, Youth and Family information back in the day, but a lot of it was hard to understand. Is there any ability to ensure that plain language can be included in this piece of legislation?
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete deficiency (records supplied in language the recipient could not understand) and a concrete remedy (a plain-language requirement in the Act), but supplies no drafting, standard or threshold for what plain language would require.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The advice here is that this allows for faster re-audits to check up on agency record-keeping.
specificity.explanation: Gives the mechanism — removing the minimum interval permits re-auditing sooner — but no timeframe, trigger or threshold for when a faster re-audit would be directed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill provides the necessary clarification because it goes further than the Supreme Court in crucial ways, including more tightly defining what “exclusive use and occupation” means, requiring the courts to base any inferences on firm physical evidence, not on cultural association alone, and placing the burden of proof more squarely on applicants.
specificity.explanation: Three named, checkable mechanisms — a tightened statutory definition, an evidential standard for inferences, and a reallocation of the burden of proof — each of which can be read against the bill's text. No figures, but the operative changes are identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Recognising the impact this will have for the affected applicants, the Government has approved $15 million to help meet their rehearing costs.
specificity.explanation: A named figure attached to a named purpose and an identified group — the funding decision and its use can be checked against Cabinet papers and appropriations.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The amendment removes that time period and changes the language so that it’s just “as directed by the Chief Archivist”. I am wondering what the rationale was for removing that time period?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — a named clause of the bill and the operative wording it substitutes. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know that at one stage a young person received what was their Child, Youth and Family information back in the day, but a lot of it was hard to understand. Is there any ability to ensure that plain language can be included in this piece of legislation?
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of Part 4 — what a care-experienced person actually receives when they request their records — and proposes a drafting change to the bill. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The advice here is that this allows for faster re-audits to check up on agency record-keeping.
focus.explanation: A direct engagement with the clause put to her, giving the operational rationale for removing the fixed interval.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bill provides the necessary clarification because it goes further than the Supreme Court in crucial ways, including more tightly defining what “exclusive use and occupation” means, requiring the courts to base any inferences on firm physical evidence, not on cultural association alone, and placing the burden of proof more squarely on applicants.
focus.explanation: Entirely on what the measure does and how it differs from the case law it responds to.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The current section 33 of the Act, which is the “Independent audits of public offices”, requires that audits of the data kept “must be conducted at an interval of not less than five years and not more than 10 years”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that section 33 of the Public Records Act 2005, as it currently stands, mandates independent audits of public offices at intervals of not less than five and not more than ten years, and that this is the wording of the provision.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 33 of the Public Records Act 2005 as in force on 8 October 2025 (NZ Legislation website); true if the section is titled 'Independent audits of public offices' and contains the interval requirement of not less than five years and not more than ten years, false if it carries no such interval or different figures.

veracity.statement: The Chief Archivist is statutorily independent as to looking at those audits, and the budget available for the audits is not changing.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the Chief Archivist's role in relation to these audits is protected by a statutory independence provision, and that the funding available for the audits is unchanged by the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Public Records Act 2005 independence provision governing the Chief Archivist's functions, plus the bill's clause 34 and its departmental disclosure statement/regulatory impact statement on funding; true if the Chief Archivist's audit function is covered by a statutory independence provision and no reduction to the audit appropriation accompanies the change, false if the independence provision does not extend to these audits or the audit funding is being reduced.

veracity.statement: However, in 2023, the Court of Appeal interpreted the CMT test in a way that significantly reduced the need for continuity and exclusivity in the scope of what can constitute a substantial interruption.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Court of Appeal's 2023 Re Edwards decision materially lowered the continuity and exclusivity requirements of the customary marine title test by narrowing what counts as a substantial interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Court of Appeal's 2023 Re Edwards judgment (Whakatōhea) and legal commentary on it; true if the judgment narrows the circumstances amounting to substantial interruption and reads down continuity/exclusivity relative to the prior interpretation, false if it left those requirements materially unchanged.

veracity.statement: The Supreme Court confirmed that the Government was right to have concerns about how the 2023 Court of Appeal Re Edwards decision approached the customary marine title test.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court's December 2024 Re Edwards judgment endorsed the Government's criticism of the Court of Appeal's approach to the CMT test — i.e. that the Supreme Court found the Court of Appeal to have erred in the way the Government contended.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court's December 2024 Re Edwards judgment; true if it holds the Court of Appeal erred in its approach to the CMT test in the respects the Government had raised, false if it upheld the Court of Appeal's approach or departed from it on unrelated grounds.

veracity.statement: Following the Supreme Court’s December judgment, the High Court issued a decision that has made extensive findings of CMT, illustrating that the Supreme Court’s test has not altered the approach of the courts in practice.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that a High Court decision issued after the Supreme Court's December 2024 judgment made extensive findings of customary marine title.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court customary marine title judgments delivered between December 2024 and October 2025; true if at least one such decision awards CMT over a substantial area or to numerous applicant groups, false if no post-judgment High Court CMT decision issued or the awards made were narrow.

veracity.statement: This will require rehearing seven cases, including four where customary marine title has already been recognised.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a precise count of the consequences of the bill's retrospective schedule: seven CMT cases decided since 25 July 2024 must be reheard, four of them having resulted in recognition of customary marine title.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The record of CMT determinations made between 25 July 2024 and the bill's enactment (High Court judgments and Ministry of Justice/departmental advice on the bill); true if seven determinations fall within the interim period and four of them recognised CMT, false if the counts differ materially.

civility.statement: I respect the role of the courts as one decisionmaker under this regime and the challenge in interpreting the CMT test in the context of the wider Act, but for this regime to work as Parliament intended, a rigorous test for CMT needs to be maintained.
civility.explanation: Contested ground where a minister overriding judicial decisions had every opportunity to disparage the judges; instead the disagreement stays on the interpretation and the statutory test, and explicitly acknowledges the difficulty of the task. No person is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If anyone knows where Waimahana is in the Far North, when you get to the ridge before you look down to the left on Waimahana, have a look to the right. There’s a place called Paradise Bay, where you can’t get to.
specificity.explanation: Names a real, locatable place as an instance of blocked beach access, so someone could go and check it — but supplies no mechanism, figures or extent of the problem beyond the one example.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Minister Finlayson—former Minister Finlayson, sorry—was very clear to this Government that what they’re doing to this bill is abhorrent, and it actually isn’t what he did when he passed this bill in 2011.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Christopher Finlayson, the Minister who carried the 2011 Act, has publicly told the present Government that this amendment bill is abhorrent and departs from what the 2011 Act was intended to do.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, select committee submissions, opinion pieces or interviews by Christopher Finlayson on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill; true if he has publicly opposed it in those terms, false if he has not commented or has supported the bill.

veracity.statement: I want to remind the House that that bill was carefully negotiated between the Māori Party and the National Party of the day.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 was the product of negotiation between the National Government and the Māori Party, its confidence-and-supply partner.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2010–2011 legislative history of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill — the National–Māori Party confidence and supply agreement, the ministerial review of the Foreshore and Seabed Act, and the parties' voting record; true if the Māori Party negotiated the bill's terms with National, false if it was drafted and passed without their involvement.

rigor.statement: We’ve got to ask ourselves, are there other pieces of legislation that the Government might look at simply because they don’t agree with a judgment from the court?
rigor.explanation: A slippery slope: from one instance of Parliament legislating over a court decision, it invites the inference of a general practice, without offering anything that connects this bill to any other legislation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That member sits there and shakes his head, but he is incorrect when he thinks we are the ultimate lawmaker here. Yes, we are—however, the courts have the opportunity to define that.
rigor.explanation: Self-contradictory: the member is declared incorrect for thinking Parliament is the ultimate lawmaker, and the very next clause concedes that it is. The intended point about judicial interpretation never gets connected to the denial.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That member can chirp all he wants—and I look forward to hearing what he has to say when it comes to his party’s call on this bill, because I can tell that member that when the ACT Party get up in this House and talk about Treaty settlement bills, we’re all going to sit here and go: “Two-faced.”.
civility.explanation: Belittles the interjecting member's contribution as chirping and brands his party two-faced — an imputation of bad faith that edges into a personal jibe rather than engaging what was said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That member doesn’t know what he’s talking about.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on another member's competence rather than on anything he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is unjust and it is unfair—it is grossly unfair that the Government, at the will of their policies—at the will, dare I say it, of many of their backers—push a bill like this through the House simply because they are unhappy with a judgment from the court.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that the bill is being advanced at the behest of the Government's financial backers — which is a motive allegation rather than an argument about the bill, though it lands on the Government collectively and insults no individual.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That member can chirp all he wants—and I look forward to hearing what he has to say when it comes to his party’s call on this bill, because I can tell that member that when the ACT Party get up in this House and talk about Treaty settlement bills, we’re all going to sit here and go: “Two-faced.”.
focus.explanation: Once the characterisation of ACT's future conduct on other bills is removed, nothing about this bill's content remains; it is about the other party rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Labour opposes this bill, for the matters of retrospectivity, for the matters that the Minister has raised about their push and their policy to exploit the minerals at the Government’s will.
focus.explanation: States the grounds of opposition in terms of the bill's own content — its retrospective effect and the minerals policy the Minister described — rather than the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Now the Minister is saying that it’s going to pass again, it will still pass before Christmas, a year after it was first introduced in this House.
divination.explanation: Relays the Minister's forecast that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill will complete its passage through the House before Christmas 2025, roughly a year after introduction.
divination.subject: other
divination.subject_name: the Minister in charge of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill
divination.falsification_criterion: The Parliament bill page and Hansard record for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill; true if the third reading is passed on or before 25 December 2025, false if the bill has not completed its third reading by that date.

veracity.statement: It is a 700-year-old sailing waka found on a beach at the top of the South Island.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the age (700 years) and find location (a beach at the top of the South Island) of the Anaweka waka.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published radiocarbon dating and archaeological reports on the Anaweka waka (e.g. Johns, Irwin & Sung, PNAS 2014) and DOC/Te Papa records of the find site; true if the hull is dated to roughly the 14th century (~700 years before the statement) and was recovered from the coastal Anaweka area at the northwest top of the South Island, false if the dating or the location is materially different.

veracity.statement: The 2011 correction of the confiscation of the foreshore and seabed that was affected by the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, was achieved by agreement across the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 was passed by cross-party agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the third reading of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill in March 2011; true if it passed with support spanning the major parties and no significant party opposed, false if it passed on a divided vote with major parties voting against.

veracity.statement: Even the ACT Party at the time thought it was a travesty that that right had ever been removed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ACT, at the time of the 2004 Foreshore and Seabed Act, opposed the removal of Māori access to the courts to have customary title determined.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ACT MPs' recorded speeches and votes on the Foreshore and Seabed Bill 2004 in Hansard, plus contemporaneous ACT statements; true if ACT voted against the 2004 Act and objected specifically to the extinguishment of the right to go to court, false if ACT supported the Act or objected on unrelated grounds.

veracity.statement: But this bill retrospectively cancels that right for all the claimants who’ve already been or are in the process of going to court.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the amendment bill retrospectively removes the right of existing and in-progress claimants to have customary marine title determined by a court.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The transitional/application provisions of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill as reported back by the Justice Committee; true if the new test applies retrospectively to applications already filed or already determined, false if pending applications are preserved under the pre-existing test or if determined claims are unaffected.

veracity.statement: Mr Christopher Finlayson, who wrote this bill, the former Attorney-General, put it plainly, “these amendments do not restore the original intent of Parliament, they undermine them”.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Christopher Finlayson: that the amendments undermine rather than restore Parliament's original intent. The checkable core is whether Finlayson made that statement in those terms.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Finlayson's public statements, op-eds or submissions on the Customary Marine Title Amendment Bill during 2025; true if he is on record saying the amendments do not restore and instead undermine Parliament's original intent, false if no such statement exists or he said the opposite.

veracity.statement: In fact, the Supreme Court agreed that the Court of Appeal got that wrong.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court held the Court of Appeal erred in its interpretation of the customary marine title test.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court's judgment in Whakatōhea Kotahitanga Waka (Edwards) [2024] NZSC; true if the Court held the Court of Appeal's interpretation of the s 58 test was wrong and substituted a different test, false if it upheld the Court of Appeal's approach.

veracity.statement: The Justice Committee—and I acknowledge the chair, the Hon James Meager—received and considered submissions from 6,692 interested groups and individuals and heard oral evidence from 69 submitters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific submission counts for the select committee stage: 6,692 written submissions and 69 oral submitters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill; true if the report records 6,692 submissions and 69 oral submitters, false if the recorded figures materially differ.

veracity.statement: A customary marine title cannot be sold, and public access is maintained.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two legal properties of customary marine title under the 2011 Act: that it is inalienable and that public access rights are preserved.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Sections 11, 26 and 27 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011; true if customary marine title is expressly inalienable and rights of public access to the common marine and coastal area are preserved, false if either can be defeated by a title order.

veracity.statement: In 2023, the Court of Appeal interpreted provisions of the Act about the requirements for recognising customary marine title which materially reduced the threshold of the continuous exclusive use.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Court of Appeal's 2023 decision lowered the statutory threshold for exclusive use and occupation without substantial interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Court of Appeal's 2023 judgment in Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) and commentary on the s 58(1)(b)(i) test; true if the Court's interpretation lowered the evidential threshold relative to the previously applied reading, false if it left the threshold unchanged or raised it.

veracity.statement: This bill fulfils a coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that amending the customary marine title test is a commitment in the National–NZ First coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement of November 2023; true if it contains a commitment to amend the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act to restore the intended customary marine title test, false if no such commitment appears.

veracity.statement: My colleague the Hon Shane Jones has stated that recent court decisions have made the test for customary marine title too easy, and that rights creep—rights creep—could enable iwi to obstruct critical development projects such as ports.
veracity.explanation: Relays claims attributed to Shane Jones — that court decisions made the customary marine title test too easy and that resulting 'rights creep' could let iwi block development such as ports. The checkable core is whether Jones made those statements.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, press releases and interviews by Shane Jones during 2024–2025 on customary marine title; true if he is on record saying the court-set test is too easy and that rights creep could obstruct port or similar infrastructure development, false if no such statement exists.

civility.statement: Anyone who thinks there can be a cohesion, or a lasting contentment, in our nation, for any of us, without upholding and making good on the dignity and the intent of that founding agreement— Te Tiriti o Waitangi—is a fool, frankly.
civility.explanation: Calls anyone holding the opposing view a fool. The target is the people who disagree rather than the argument they make — a clear, if generalised, personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister resurrects the darkest tradition of Crown betrayal, evokes the tradition of colonial theft, and should we be surprised, because that particular Minister believes colonisation was a good thing for iwi Māori, so surely doing more colonisations would be good in his estimations?
civility.explanation: Turns from the bill to the Minister himself — imputing a belief to him and using it to cast him as personally in the tradition of colonial theft. This lands on the person, not the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But this bill retrospectively cancels that right for all the claimants who’ve already been or are in the process of going to court.
focus.explanation: Names the specific mechanism of the measure before the House — the effect of the bill on existing court applications. Squarely on the policy, not on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They don’t really believe in property rights. They believe in the right to accumulation of capital of those who would exploit nature.
focus.explanation: Characterises what the governing parties are 'really' motivated by rather than engaging the measure. No policy, figure or outcome is named — strip out the claim about the other side's true beliefs and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It will amend the 2011 Act to provide much more clarity and certainty around how customary marine titles are determined, particularly in response to recent legal judgments re Edwards that have created some confusion, some ambiguity about Parliament’s original intent.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure directly — what the bill amends, and the specific judgment it responds to. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The idea that Parliament intent is being restored by this is absolute garbage, and if you have any doubt, you could simply ask the author of the original Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the policy, but the conclusion rests on an appeal to authority — the drafter's say-so is offered as settling what Parliament's intent was. The appeal is relevant rather than empty (the author is unusually well-placed on this question), so it is a weak inference rather than a fallacious one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is the Parliament of New Zealand that sets the laws of this land, and this inserts a statutory declaration that overturns the court’s reasoning and ensures the intent of this House is clear.
rigor.explanation: A valid enough appeal to parliamentary sovereignty — Parliament can indeed override a court's statutory interpretation — but there is a gap between that and the conclusion actually needed, that the declaration states what the 2011 Parliament originally intended rather than what this one now prefers. The premise establishes the power, not the claim about original intent.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This wretched bill will be the first bill on the repeal list of things that we will do to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi when there is a change of Government in one year’s time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a change of Government roughly a year from the statement — i.e. that the 2026 general election produces a government not led by the current governing parties. (The repeal undertaking itself is a promise about the speaker's own party and is not scored here.)
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The result of the New Zealand general election due in 2026 and the government formed after it; true if a government excluding the current National-led coalition takes office within about a year of October 2025, false if the incumbent coalition is returned.

specificity.statement: So what we are simply doing is making sure it’s very clear what the customary title test should be.
specificity.explanation: Conveys a direction — clarifying the test — but supplies no content on what the clarified test is, which limb it changes, or how. The detail is not supplied elsewhere in his call.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It will amend the 2011 Act to provide much more clarity and certainty around how customary marine titles are determined, particularly in response to recent legal judgments re Edwards that have created some confusion, some ambiguity about Parliament’s original intent.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act and the Edwards litigation, but describes the effect only as 'clarity and certainty' — no statement of what the amended test actually requires.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: All told, Government contracts are worth more than $50 billion a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the annual total value of New Zealand government contracts for goods and services exceeds $50 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / Treasury figures on total annual government procurement spend at the time of the statement; true if total government contracting spend is above $50b a year, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned by Crown Law’s own assessment that altering the powers of the tribunal could breach the principle of separation powers and the principle of responsible Government?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about the content of Crown Law advice — that altering the tribunal's powers could breach the separation of powers and responsible government.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown Law advice on the Waitangi Tribunal review (as released under the OIA or tabled/reported); true if that advice contains an assessment that altering the tribunal's powers could breach those constitutional principles, false if no such assessment exists.

veracity.statement: The IMF’s latest world economic outlook shows that in 2023, out of all the world’s advanced economies, New Zealand had the largest positive output gap.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the IMF's most recent World Economic Outlook ranks New Zealand's 2023 output gap as the largest positive one among advanced economies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The output gap table in the IMF World Economic Outlook current as at October 2025; true if New Zealand's 2023 output gap is the largest positive value among the advanced-economy group, false if any advanced economy has a larger positive gap.

veracity.statement: I’m pleased to report to the House that today’s Financial Statements of Government shows that debt, for the first time in five years, has not increased as a proportion of GDP.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Financial Statements of the Government released that day show debt flat or falling as a share of GDP, and that this is the first such year in five.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2025 and the four preceding years; true if the debt-to-GDP ratio did not rise in 2024/25 and rose in each of the previous four years, false if it rose in 2024/25 or if a prior year in that window was also flat/falling.

veracity.statement: It’s approximately $8 billion that we are paying to service the interest on our debt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual Crown finance costs (debt servicing) of approximately $8 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Finance costs line in the Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2025; true if around $8b, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I’m proud that, unlike the last Government, we’re actually funding Dunedin Hospital, that we’re rebuilding Nelson Hospital, that we’re building more classrooms every year than they ever managed, and that we built more social homes in the past 23 months than they did in three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a set of comparative delivery claims against the previous government, the sharpest being that more social homes were built in the past 23 months than the previous government built in three years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD public housing delivery statistics (net additional public homes placed in service) for the 23 months to October 2025 compared with any three-year window of the 2017–2023 government; true if the recent 23-month total exceeds the three-year comparator, false if it does not.

specificity.statement: When considering tender applications, Government agencies will now be required to give a weighting of at least 10 percent to benefits to New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (weighting in tender evaluation), the threshold (10 percent) and who it binds (Government agencies). Someone could check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government continues to be responsible in this space and is progressing the review announced, in a very timely manner.
specificity.explanation: A content-free reassurance: no timeframe, no stage of the review, no named change. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is an annual growth rate of negative 1.1 percent, three percentage points lower than forecast before the election, the result of her economic plan; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise figure and a precise comparison against a pre-election forecast — the checkable question, not a general complaint about the economy.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Let me count the ways: tax relief for more than a million working New Zealanders; Investment Boost to encourage investment in our businesses so that they can grow; delivering fast-track infrastructure projects; investing in structured literacy in our schools; overhauling the Overseas Investment Act to welcome capital into this country.
specificity.explanation: Names five identifiable policies and one scale figure, but gives no amounts, timeframes or delivery measures for most of them — a list of named actions rather than checkable detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If she understands numbers, then does she understand that the Government reduction in capital asset spending of $2.9 billion less has played a role in the decline of the construction sector and a loss of 20,000 construction sector jobs?
specificity.explanation: Two hard figures — a $2.9 billion capital spending reduction and 20,000 construction jobs — tied to a named sector, all of which could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This provision does not breach international trade agreements, because overseas companies have the same opportunity to demonstrate wider value to New Zealand, and similar provisions exist in many of our trading partners’ procurement rules.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: non-discrimination (equal opportunity to demonstrate value) plus comparator practice is offered as the reason the rule is compliant. The conclusion largely tracks the premises, though comparator practice is a weaker support than the non-discrimination point.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Inflation was far above the target band, and the Reserve Bank had to the raise the official cash rate (OCR) to 5.5 percent—the highest rate since 2008. That’s why the economy went into a long, painful downturn.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain with its premises stated: above-band inflation forced tightening, tightening caused the downturn. The mechanism is standard and the conclusion follows, though 'that's why' asserts a monocausal explanation without ruling out other contributors.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The member might think that spending more, taxing more, and borrowing more is an alternative plan, but I disagree with it and so do most New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity — 'most New Zealanders agree with me' is offered in place of any reason the alternative would fail. Also attributes a position to the member that she has not stated, so the thing rebutted is a construct.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can he confirm that the proposed name change would erode the independence of the tribunal, creating a system where Ministers decide what claims can be heard?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure — a named proposal and its claimed institutional consequence. Legitimate scrutiny of a specific policy, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would also point out that those who are suddenly concerned about deficits might want to ask why they said that every time we made a spending reduction, whether it was pay equity, reducing the number of bureaucrats, reversing stupid programmes, that we shouldn’t be cutting spending—get consistent.
focus.explanation: A hypocrisy charge against the opposition. It does anchor on named savings decisions (pay equity, headcount), so there is some policy content, but the weight of the remark is what the other side is like rather than the deficit question asked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, it is not, but I think that those who commit arson and then blame the firefighter should not repeat the same mistake.
focus.explanation: Beyond the bare 'no', the content is a metaphor about the previous government having caused the damage. No policy, figure or outcome is named — it is a characterisation of the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she agree with Christopher Luxon that, “Nicola Willis and myself understand economics. We understand Budgets. We understand numbers.”; if so, is that why, under, even her own measure of OBEGALx, the deficit is higher now than it was it in 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024?
civility.explanation: Sets a named person's claim to understand economics against the deficit figures in order to mock it. The substance is real, but the framing targets the Minister's and Prime Minister's personal competence rather than the fiscal argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is her idea of an economic plan to deliver more unemployment, a shrinking economy, an inflation that is on the rise, and to blame everyone else except Nicola Willis?
civility.explanation: The economic content is legitimate, but the closing clause imputes bad faith to a named Minister — that she deliberately deflects responsibility — rather than contesting her account.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Every opportunity that I have in this House, I will remind Government members of the bad choices that they have made for our country and for Māori alike: repealing Te Aka Whai Ora, taking us backwards on Māori wards, removing Te Tiriti from legislation.
focus.explanation: Names three specific measures — the repeal of Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori wards changes, and the removal of Treaty clauses from legislation. This is scrutiny of named policy decisions, which is the job of an opposition MP, not content-free party-bashing. Marked down slightly because the framing ('bad choices that they have made') carries some general party attack alongside the named policies.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But again, the backbench is reflective of their leadership, and that leadership is cynical. It is cynical, it is mean-spirited, and it continues the punch-down of our indigenous people in this country.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is like — their backbench, their leadership, their motives. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. Strip out the characterisation of opponents and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a terrible, terrible sleight on this Parliament, that we are moving this piece of legislation before the House as we celebrate 50 years of the Waitangi Tribunal.
focus.explanation: The named legislation is the subject, so this is not tribalism, but the objection is to the timing and symbolism of the reading rather than to any provision, cost, mechanism or outcome of the bill. A real policy point wrapped in occasion framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And this Minister in the House today, he has not consulted adequately with Māori. That, in itself, is a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy process for the bill before the House — whether consultation with Māori was undertaken. Names a specific procedural failing rather than characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As has been traversed by the Minister in charge and some of my colleagues already, the bill is amending the test for recognising customary marine titles, noting the decision of the Court of Appeal last year. We’re setting it in a place where we can seek some clarity around the intention of the legislation so that we can make it crystal clear.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the measure before the House does — the test being amended and the court decision prompting it. No reference to the other party at all. An ordinary, unremarkable contribution, included because routine on-policy speech counts as much as memorable attacks.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What’s happened since then is a court judgment has decided to go way above and beyond what the intention of this House was when we were restoring things in 2011; they went above and beyond what the intention was.
focus.explanation: Directly on the substantive rationale for the bill — the relationship between the 2011 Act's purpose and the court's interpretation of it. Names the legislation and the year and engages why the amendment is said to be needed.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Every opportunity that I have in this House, I will remind Government members of the bad choices that they have made for our country and for Māori alike: repealing Te Aka Whai Ora, taking us backwards on Māori wards, removing Te Tiriti from legislation.
specificity.explanation: Names three identifiable policies, so someone could go and check each one, but supplies no figures, dates, mechanisms or detail about what each change did.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As has been traversed by the Minister in charge and some of my colleagues already, the bill is amending the test for recognising customary marine titles, noting the decision of the Court of Appeal last year. We’re setting it in a place where we can seek some clarity around the intention of the legislation so that we can make it crystal clear.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the mechanism (amending the recognition test) and the triggering event (last year's Court of Appeal decision), but gives no detail of what the old or new test requires, and 'setting it in a place where we can seek some clarity' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister protests, but he doth protest too much, because he knows as much as anyone that the bill as it stood, the original piece of legislation, was carefully crafted, and it makes it very clear that, to establish customary title, the burden is high—that, in fact, you have to show that, across generations since 1840, you have exercised those rights, because customary rights can be lost through a failure to use them.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual content of the statutory test: a high burden, exercise of the rights across generations since 1840, and loss of customary rights through non-use. Concrete enough that a reader could go to the Act and check it. Short of 1.0 only because no section is named.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But again, the backbench is reflective of their leadership, and that leadership is cynical. It is cynical, it is mean-spirited, and it continues the punch-down of our indigenous people in this country.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith and ill intent — 'cynical', 'mean-spirited' — to the Government's leadership rather than engaging what the bill does. This is a character judgement about people, short of a direct insult but past the point of civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There is no reason for it, no reason other than keeping their crony mates happy so that they can get the consent they want to exploit coastal areas, whether it be for sandmining, for fishing, for wind farming—for whatever it might be.
civility.explanation: Imputes corruption as the sole motive for the bill — that it exists to keep 'crony mates' happy. This goes past bad faith to alleging that Government members are acting for the benefit of their associates, which is an attack on integrity rather than on the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s a terrible bill, and I can’t believe Jenny Marcroft, who usually is so sensible on things affecting Māori, spoke in support of it, either.
civility.explanation: The verdict on the bill itself is fine — brutal criticism of a measure is civil. What costs is the backhanded aside about a named member, using her supposed usual good sense to mark this as a personal lapse in judgement. Condescension aimed at a person, though mild and not abusive.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When we’re talking about cynical—someone from the other side of the House spoke about cynicism—it’s cynicism to work people up into a frenzy when they’re not saying what the actual truth is.
civility.explanation: Accuses opposition members of deliberately inflaming people while knowingly withholding the truth. That is an imputation of bad faith and dishonesty against the people opposite, not a criticism of anything they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And this Minister in the House today, he has not consulted adequately with Māori. That, in itself, is a breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: inadequate consultation, therefore a Treaty breach. The step is supported if the Crown's duty to consult is accepted, which is a standard premise here, but nothing is offered to establish what threshold 'adequate' consultation would meet, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded. Not fact-checking whether consultation actually occurred — that is Veracity's question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I want to recognise that customary and marine title is, essentially, a property right. Yet, the ACT Party, for all of its pro-property rhetoric, doesn’t believe in protecting the property rights for Māori that are enshrined in customary title.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inconsistency argument with a stated premise: customary marine title is a property right, ACT promotes a bill protecting property rights against uncompensated impairment, therefore ACT's support for this bill is inconsistent with its stated principle. The conclusion tracks the premises. Marked down because the leap from 'supports this bill' to 'doesn't believe in protecting property rights for Māori' overstates what the inconsistency shows, and the classification of customary title as a property right is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What’s happened since then is a court judgment has decided to go way above and beyond what the intention of this House was when we were restoring things in 2011; they went above and beyond what the intention was.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion restates the premise rather than supporting it: nothing is offered to establish what the House's 2011 intention actually was, and the second clause simply repeats the first in different words. Without an independent account of the intent, 'the court went beyond the intent' is a bare assertion. Whether the claim is factually right is Veracity's question, not this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, yes, I do know. And I do know because I’ve had members, elders, of Māoridom talk to me about what happened back then in 2004 and how it broke their hearts.
rigor.explanation: The knowledge claim rests entirely on personal anecdote — conversations she has had — offered as sufficient grounding for understanding the 2004 legislation and its effects. Personal testimony is evidence of a kind, so this is not empty, but an appeal to anecdote cannot carry the weight the conclusion places on it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Minister, Paul Goldsmith, in one of his speeches said this legislation creates and confers property rights, and that’s not true.
