rigor.explanation: The intermittency premise is sound, but the conclusion jumps from "firming is needed" to "that firming is thermal coal" — a false dichotomy that silently excludes gas, geothermal, hydro storage and batteries. Valid up to the last clause, which does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve already seen, from the Opposition’s gas and oil ban, how economic growth in this country was stifled under that announcement.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: a policy is named and an economic outcome asserted to follow from it, with nothing offered to establish the link — no figures, no counterfactual, no source. The conclusion rests on the sequence alone.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Opposition is shouting out, but you want to shut us down, you want to close our businesses down, and you want to skyrocket residential power prices just on an ideology that, for some reason, we are going to save the planet by not having some coal mines here in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the bill's proponents are given aims they have not stated — closing businesses and raising power prices — and their actual position is reduced to a caricature ("we are going to save the planet by not having some coal mines"). The argument is then made against that substitute rather than the bill.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, interestingly, we don’t actually need coal for thermal power in this country. We could easily do it with renewables if we went and built them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that coal-fired thermal generation is not needed for New Zealand's electricity supply and that renewables could readily substitute for it. The claim is about present system capability, not a forecast.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE electricity statistics and Transpower/Electricity Authority security-of-supply assessments for 2024–25 on whether New Zealand's electricity system can meet peak and dry-year demand without coal-fired thermal generation: true if those bodies find consented-but-unbuilt renewables plus existing firming could displace Huntly's coal burn, false if they identify a residual thermal firming requirement.

veracity.statement: The first is that, if we are to meet net zero emissions by 2050, we simply must have no new coal mines or extensions of existing ones.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to the IEA the specific position that reaching net zero by 2050 requires no new coal mines and no extensions of existing ones. What is checkable is whether the IEA said this.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the International Energy Agency's Net Zero by 2050 roadmap: true if it states that no new coal mines or mine extensions are required/approved in the net-zero pathway, false if it contains no such statement or states something materially different.

veracity.statement: That’s why we export millions of tons of it to India, South Korea, and Japan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a scale (millions of tonnes) and a set of destination countries for New Zealand West Coast coking coal exports. Both the volume and the destination list are checkable against trade statistics.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MBIE coal export statistics by tonnage and destination for recent years: true if annual coking coal exports run to millions of tonnes and India, South Korea and Japan are the destinations, false if annual export volumes are around or below one million tonnes or the named destinations are materially wrong.

veracity.statement: We’ve given coal- and gas-fired power stations the same one-year priority as renewables under the amended Resource Management Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific legislative change: that thermal generation now receives the same one-year consenting priority as renewables under the amended RMA.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the 2025 Resource Management Act amendments and associated national direction on electricity generation consenting: true if thermal (coal and gas) generation is given the same one-year consent-processing timeframe as renewable generation, false if that timeframe applies to renewables only or if no such timeframe exists.

veracity.statement: We also don’t talk enough about the fact that 0.17 percent is our emissions—0.17 percent is the emissions that we are producing here in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure for New Zealand's share of global greenhouse gas emissions. Checkable against the national inventory and global emissions totals.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand's gross greenhouse gas emissions as reported in the national inventory (MfE) expressed as a share of global emissions per UNFCCC / Global Carbon Project totals: true if the share is approximately 0.17%, false if it is materially different (e.g. below 0.1% or above 0.25%).

specificity.statement: Now, people talk in terms of the “just transition”, but let’s cash out what that actually means: it means protections for workers; it means training for workers; it means ensuring that there are good, well-paying jobs that people who currently work in coal mines can transition to, very much preferably in the places where they already live.
specificity.explanation: Explicitly promises to "cash out" the term and then supplies categories rather than content — protections, training and good jobs, with no mechanism, funding, agency, timeframe or number of workers. A direction with some shape but nothing checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve given coal- and gas-fired power stations the same one-year priority as renewables under the amended Resource Management Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (consenting priority), the timeframe (one year), the instrument (the amended Resource Management Act) and the classes of generation affected. Someone could go and check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New Zealand First believes we should be open for business.
specificity.explanation: A slogan offered as a position on the bill: no measure, mechanism, figure or timeframe. Commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And now they’ve all gone quiet on the Opposition benches, haven’t they.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the demeanour of the other side; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. Strip out the reference to the Opposition benches and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s absolutely farcical. People are laughing at that type of ideology that is coming from the Opposition parties.
focus.explanation: Content-free characterisation of the other parties' ideology and how it is received; no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome named. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility passes it — this is the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Unfortunately, it’s going to have a short life.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Julie Anne Genter's coal mining member's bill will be voted down rather than proceed past its first reading.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the first reading of the member's bill debated on 22 October 2025; true if the bill was defeated at first reading, false if it passed and was referred to select committee.

civility.statement: He’s certainly got a more pragmatic future than you, Mr Abel, I think, because his feet are grounded, let’s put it that way.
civility.explanation: A jibe aimed at a named member personally — the implication is that Steve Abel is not grounded and has no pragmatic future. It is directed at the person rather than any policy, though it stops short of outright abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’re full of dingbats on the other side—I knew you’d find that funny, Madam Speaker.
civility.explanation: A direct insult to the intelligence of the members opposite, with no argument attached. Contempt aimed at people rather than at any policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Tonight, I want to mihi to Julie Anne Genter and to my good friend Jacinda Ardern, because she was brave and she was courageous, unlike this useless lot on the other side, who keep embarrassing themselves and going down in the polls.
civility.explanation: 'This useless lot' and 'keep embarrassing themselves' disparage the members opposite personally rather than engaging anything they have argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In Horowhenua we were less a fan of your transport policy, in all fairness; we quite like our new expressways and we’re looking forward to having one built.
civility.explanation: Disagrees pointedly with an opponent's transport policy and its effect on his electorate while attacking nobody; the criticism stays entirely on the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When all the ideology of the last administration talked about shutting coal down and shutting fossil fuels down, and then all of a sudden we were left with these rising power prices, who do we turn to in the time of need?
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning about a real energy policy: the previous government's fossil-fuel settings are asserted to have caused rising power prices purely from sequence, with no mechanism, generation data or alternative causes (hydrology, gas field decline, demand) addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What it means is we’re going to keep importing that Indonesian coal, the same coal that members on that side of the House say that they hate and it’s a terrible thing and we shouldn’t have this. It doesn’t stop us using coal. It doesn’t lower our emissions.
rigor.explanation: A genuine carbon-leakage inference about the measure before the House: banning extraction but not use implies substitution by imports, so emissions need not fall. The conclusion broadly follows, but the step to 'doesn't lower our emissions' is asserted rather than shown — no import volumes, emissions factors or shipping figures are offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just by note, there’s something like 12 coal mining companies in New Zealand operating right now, and they’re employing people; they’re producing economic growth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 12 coal mining companies are currently operating in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Petroleum and Minerals / MBIE coal permit and production statistics for 2025 — the count of distinct companies holding active coal mining permits and reporting production; true if approximately 12, false if materially different (e.g. under 6 or over 20).

veracity.statement: Here’s the other thing: Winston Peters, the man who should still be Deputy Prime Minister, he supported the ban on oil and gas exploration in 2018.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Winston Peters personally supported the 2018 ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration permits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The April 2018 Cabinet decision announcing the end of new offshore exploration permits, and Winston Peters' and New Zealand First's contemporaneous public statements and Hansard contributions; true if Peters publicly endorsed or defended the ban at the time, false if he opposed it or publicly dissented.

veracity.statement: The reality is you opposed the Paris Agreement, repealed the zero carbon Act, and abolished our Climate Change Commission.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three completed actions by the ACT Party: opposition to the Paris Agreement, repeal of the zero carbon Act, and abolition of the Climate Change Commission.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ statute book as at October 2025 for whether the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act 2019 has been repealed; the status of He Pou a Rangi Climate Change Commission; and ACT's published policy on the Paris Agreement. True only if all three are borne out as accomplished; false if the zero carbon provisions and the Commission remain in force, in which case the claim states party policy positions as if they were completed acts.

veracity.statement: They certainly didn’t want to talk about the oil and gas ban when we had energy spot prices over $800, did they?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand wholesale electricity spot prices exceeded $800 (per MWh) during the recent energy shortage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electricity Authority wholesale market spot price data for 2024–2025; true if half-hourly spot prices at major nodes exceeded $800/MWh during the period referred to, false if the peak stayed materially below that.

veracity.statement: We don’t hear from them in question time asking about the environment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Green Party MPs do not use oral questions to raise environmental matters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard oral question record for 2024–2025; true if Green MPs lodged no or almost no oral questions to environment, conservation or climate change portfolio ministers, false if they did so regularly.

specificity.statement: I think what we could do is we could, potentially, support this if we changed “2025” to “2045”, or to “2055”, just to give us more of a runway to get there.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision at issue (the commencement date) and proposes concrete replacement years, so the amendment could be drafted from the statement as it stands. It stops short of full precision by offering two alternative dates rather than one.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We too care about our mokopuna, but we want to do it in a pragmatic way, not one that’s cooked up in ideology, where we burn papers in a bin on the steps of Parliament.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or figure is named. The weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the other party as ideological, capped with a reference to their protest theatrics; 'a pragmatic way' carries no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We know there’s a move going on in terms of the leadership. Louise Upston is a candidate, and I congratulate Louise Upston.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal leadership politics during a debate on a coal mining bill. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What it means is we’re going to keep importing that Indonesian coal, the same coal that members on that side of the House say that they hate and it’s a terrible thing and we shouldn’t have this. It doesn’t stop us using coal. It doesn’t lower our emissions.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill itself — what it bans, what it does not ban, and the consequence for supply. Legitimate engagement with the measure, not with the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’ve stuck with the green name because it sort of tries to work for their branding, but we never really hear from them.
focus.explanation: About the other party's branding and general visibility rather than any policy, measure or outcome. No policy content survives once the characterisation of the Greens is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No one wants to burn down the planet, but people on that side of the House seem to want to burn down our economy in the pursuit of it.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the motives of the other side of the House; no measure, cost or outcome is named. Aimed at a bloc rather than an individual, so Civility is not engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Fast track is going to be used to destroy a living museum, a national treasure, the Denniston Plateau, because of this Government, in order for Bathurst to expand coal mining operations that will not be used, will not have anything to do with electricity generation, which will cost the country more than they will pay in royalties, more than we will earn in having those jobs.
focus.explanation: Names a specific statute (fast track), a specific site, a specific company and a specific claimed outcome, and weighs royalties and jobs against costs. This is scrutiny of a named policy, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the Government members, when they say things are ideological, they're talking about themselves.
focus.explanation: A tu quoque about what the Government members are really like; no policy, measure or outcome is named. Once the characterisation of the other side is removed nothing is left, so Rigor is not scored.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The members in the National Party and the New Zealand First Party and the ACT Party have always said that the Greens were away with the fairies, because they're ignorant bullies.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what members of three other parties are like; no policy content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The reason that poor countries have higher emissions is because they can’t afford it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that poorer countries emit more than wealthier ones, with affordability of alternatives as the cause.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: World Bank / Our World in Data CO2 emissions per capita grouped by World Bank income classification: true if low- and lower-middle-income countries show higher emissions per capita than high-income countries; false if high-income countries emit more per capita.

veracity.statement: The International Energy Agency concluded in 2021—so that was four years ago—that no new coal mines, mine extensions, or unabated coal plants should be developed in order for us to achieve net zero by 2050.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to the IEA a 2021 conclusion that no new coal mines, mine extensions or unabated coal plants should be developed on a net-zero-by-2050 pathway.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IEA's 'Net Zero by 2050: A Roadmap for the Global Energy Sector' (May 2021): true if it states no new coal mines or mine extensions and no new unabated coal plants are required/approved in the Net Zero Emissions pathway; false if no such finding appears or the date/body is wrong.

veracity.statement: The coal is the most expensive kilowatt hours to generate electricity, and the overall price is all priced at the marginal price.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions about the New Zealand electricity market: that coal-fired generation is the highest-cost source per kWh, and that the wholesale market clears at the marginal price.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electricity Authority / MBIE documentation of the New Zealand wholesale market: true if the market is confirmed to clear at the marginal offer price and if published generation cost data (e.g. MBIE or Concept Consulting cost stacks) show coal-fired thermal as the highest short-run marginal cost source in the stack; false if the market is not marginal-priced or another source is dearer per kWh.

veracity.statement: We've got a whole lot of public servants and publicly funded roles: doctors, nurses, teachers, firefighters going on strike because they're not being paid sufficiently.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that doctors, nurses, teachers and firefighters were taking strike action over pay in New Zealand at the time of speaking (October 2025).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Employment Relations Authority strike notices and contemporaneous reporting for 2025: true if each of senior/resident doctors, nurses, teachers and firefighters took or notified strike action over pay in 2025; false if the occupations named did not strike or the disputes were not about pay.

rigor.statement: Banning coal would be like just banning petrol in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: A false analogy offered as a reductio: nothing is supplied to establish that restricting new coal mining is relevantly like a blanket ban on petrol (scale, substitutability and the fact the bill addresses new extraction rather than use are all left unaddressed).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So everybody's paying more for cheap hydroelectricity, for cheap wind power because of the coal peaking plants.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premise supplied immediately before it: if the market clears at the marginal price and coal peaking sets that margin, then cheap hydro and wind are indeed paid the coal-set price. A real inference, validly drawn from its stated assumptions.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They’re going to need a new one tomorrow, because this one’s not going to make it through.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the bill before the House will be defeated at this reading.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the bill's reading on or about 22 October 2025: true if the bill was voted down, false if it proceeded to the next stage.

divination.statement: I'm sorry, you're going to get voted out.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the parties forming the current Government will lose office at the next general election.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official result of the 2026 New Zealand general election declared by the Electoral Commission, and the government formed afterwards: true if National, ACT and New Zealand First do not together form the incoming government; false if they return to government.

specificity.statement: It kind of sounds nice, it doesn’t do what it says, and it creates more problems, and that’s why we’re not supporting the bill.
specificity.explanation: States the bill fails to do what it claims and creates problems, but names no clause, no mechanism, no cost and no example of a problem created. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The International Energy Agency concluded in 2021—so that was four years ago—that no new coal mines, mine extensions, or unabated coal plants should be developed in order for us to achieve net zero by 2050.
specificity.explanation: Names the body, the year, the precise scope of the finding (new mines, extensions, unabated plants) and the target it relates to. Directly checkable against a named document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Fast track is going to be used to destroy a living museum, a national treasure, the Denniston Plateau, because of this Government, in order for Bathurst to expand coal mining operations that will not be used, will not have anything to do with electricity generation, which will cost the country more than they will pay in royalties, more than we will earn in having those jobs.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named location, named consent holder and a named comparison (royalties and jobs against cost to the country), but supplies no figures for any side of that comparison and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I'm sure many of the members opposite have never heard of the International Energy Agency, but it's a very mainstream body.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the members themselves rather than their argument — a sneer at their ignorance, not a criticism of a position. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The members in the National Party and the New Zealand First Party and the ACT Party have always said that the Greens were away with the fairies, because they're ignorant bullies.
civility.explanation: A direct insult to the members themselves — 'ignorant bullies' attacks their character and intelligence, not any argument they have made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They're stuck in the past, and as of next year, this country has well and truly seen what a bunch of dinosaurs you are.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at the members opposite — calling them dinosaurs disparages the people rather than any policy or argument.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It takes too long, and it is too expensive to build in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A substantive diagnosis of the problem the bill addresses, but with no figure, timeframe, comparison or mechanism — nothing here is checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To ensure consent-exempt granny flats are simple, lower-risk buildings, the bill provides that they must be new, stand-alone, single-storey dwellings of 70 square metres or less.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact eligibility conditions and the 70 square metre threshold; anyone could check this against the bill or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Any small thing that will enable the building of new structures that are of a higher standard and that can get people into better-quality housing at an affordable rate, and make some kind of measure on the supply side to address the real needs in our communities, that is a good thing.
specificity.explanation: Attempting to convey a position on the bill's value, but it commits to no standard, no figure, no mechanism and no threshold — 'a higher standard', 'an affordable rate' and 'some kind of measure' are all unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Before getting into the detail of the bill itself, it’s worth noting that this bill is widely supported by the public and across the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two present facts: that the bill enjoys broad public support, and that support for it extends across parties in the House.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill (balance of submissions supporting vs opposing) and the division/voice-vote record for its readings. True if the majority of submissions supported the bill and it was supported at its readings by parties outside the coalition; false if submissions were predominantly opposed or if opposition parties voted against.

veracity.statement: This is a change of the supply side which will make a small movement of the dial to make housing more affordable, at a time when rents continue to rise and when people in New Zealand are still facing a housing stock which has significant challenges of dampness, of thermal inefficiency, and—particularly for those more vulnerable communities—real issues in terms of affordability.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a present fact that rents in New Zealand are continuing to rise as at October 2025, and that a significant share of the housing stock is damp and thermally inefficient.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index and MBIE tenancy bond median rent data for the quarters up to October 2025, plus the Stats NZ Housing Survey / General Social Survey measures of dampness and mould. True if rents were rising year-on-year at the time of the statement; false if the series were flat or falling.

focus.statement: It creates a new system for councils to be able to notify people of any risks associated with that, and that remains something that the Labour Party will continue to watch and determine whether that works because, as I have noted along the way in this process, there are systems in this which have been designed quickly; we do not know the full impact of them.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the council risk-notification mechanism the bill creates — and on whether that mechanism will work. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It creates a new system for councils to be able to notify people of any risks associated with that, and that remains something that the Labour Party will continue to watch and determine whether that works because, as I have noted along the way in this process, there are systems in this which have been designed quickly; we do not know the full impact of them.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: the notification system was designed quickly, therefore its effects are not yet known, therefore it warrants monitoring. That follows, but the only premise offered is the speed of design; no evidence is given about which parts of the system are untested.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Successive Governments from the 1940s, those were Labour Governments, absolutely changed the picture for housing ownership. Rates rose over those two decades that were post-war years to increase housing ownership from about half to about two thirds.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's home-ownership rate rose from roughly 50% to roughly two-thirds across the two post-war decades from the 1940s, under Labour governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ census / Stats NZ owner-occupied dwelling series for 1945 through the mid-1960s; true if the home-ownership rate rose from approximately one half to approximately two thirds over that period, false if the starting or ending levels or the direction of change are materially different.

veracity.statement: Some people saw their rents of State houses go up 300 percent in six months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the 1990s National Government's state-housing rent reforms, some state-house tenants faced rent increases of 300 percent within a six-month period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Records of the market-rents policy introduced under the Housing Restructuring Act 1992 (Housing New Zealand rent notices, contemporaneous reporting, select committee and Hansard evidence); true if documented individual state-house rents rose by around 300 percent within six months, false if the largest documented increases over such a period were materially smaller.

veracity.statement: The legislation was developed quickly. The regulatory impact statement says it was rushed due to the coalition agreement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's own regulatory impact statement records that policy development was rushed, and attributes that compression to a coalition agreement commitment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement published with the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill; true if it states that the policy development timeframe was compressed or constrained in order to meet a coalition agreement commitment, false if it contains no such statement.

veracity.statement: The previous Government built over 13,000 public homes, the most since the 1970s.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a delivery figure for the 2017–2023 Labour-led Government (more than 13,000 public homes) and a comparative record claim (the largest such delivery since the 1970s).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / Ministry of Housing and Urban Development public housing delivery statistics for 2017–2023, compared against delivery totals for each government since 1970; true if net public homes delivered exceeded 13,000 and no intervening government delivered more, false if either limb fails.

veracity.statement: This Government has cancelled 3,479 homes, cut $1.5 billion from Kainga Ora, and is selling off existing stock.
veracity.explanation: A compound factual claim: a specific count of cancelled public homes, a specific funding reduction to Kāinga Ora, and an ongoing disposal of existing state housing stock.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora build-programme decisions and asset disposal reporting, plus Budget 2024/2025 appropriations for Kāinga Ora; true if approximately 3,479 planned homes were cancelled, funding was reduced by about $1.5 billion, and Kāinga Ora is selling existing stock; false if any of the three figures or facts is materially different.

veracity.statement: This Government was warned that their policy changes would increase homelessness, and it happened.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things: that officials warned the Government its housing policy changes (notably emergency housing eligibility) would increase homelessness, and that homelessness subsequently rose.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official advice to Ministers on the emergency housing eligibility changes (MSD/HUD regulatory impact statements and briefings), plus subsequent homelessness measures (HUD homelessness insights reporting, emergency housing exit data, rough-sleeping counts); true if such a warning is documented and measured homelessness rose afterwards, false if no warning was given or homelessness did not rise.

rigor.statement: That is, I think, the point here: that we are missing a trick if we think that these measures will make the difference that we need to radically increase not only home ownership but the quality of housing in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is drawn from a historical analogy laid out immediately before: that post-war gains in ownership and quality came from the State acting on both supply and demand, whereas this bill acts only on supply. The inference is coherent and the premises are offered, but it rests on an analogy across very different eras and does not establish that demand-side support is necessary now.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But, you know, we can't hold councils responsible on one hand and remove their oversight on the other.
rigor.explanation: A valid consistency argument: the premise established in the preceding sentences is that the bill replaces consenting with PIMs and reduces council oversight, from which it follows that councils cannot simultaneously be held to account for the bill's intent. The conclusion tracks the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Most critically, this bill does absolutely nothing for social housing or addressing homelessness. It doesn't help people, whether they're grannies or solo parents on the public housing wait-list or sleeping rough. These dwellings require existing land and existing money, so to some extent they will help people who are already better off.
rigor.explanation: The distributional conclusion follows from the premise offered: if building one of these dwellings requires you already to own land and to have capital, the benefit accrues to existing property owners rather than to those on the wait-list. The reasoning is sound; the overstated 'absolutely nothing' is a factual matter, not an inferential one.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to see that commitment being bipartisan and being widely agreed as important to New Zealand because it increases our productivity overall. It increases our economic resilience; it increases resilience at the household and family level. It gives people something to be proud of and to hope for and a connection into their communities, which is unparalleled.
specificity.explanation: A chain of generic benefits — productivity, resilience, pride, connection — with no figures, no mechanism, and no named policy or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has cancelled 3,479 homes, cut $1.5 billion from Kainga Ora, and is selling off existing stock.
specificity.explanation: Three checkable particulars in one sentence — a precise home count, a dollar figure, and a named agency. Anyone could go and verify each.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These also became larger during the process of our consideration of the bill; up to 70 square metres. That is also something that we will watch closely because the intention here is—I think, in most Kiwis’ minds—that they will be small, but these will be larger buildings, so we need to make sure that the system is working for everyone.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific change made to the measure before the House — the size threshold rising to 70 square metres — and what it implies for how the system will work. Entirely about the policy, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it would be interesting to hear from the Minister in his closing speech what resources might be provided to councils for this new system? What training is council staff going to receive? How will the public know what they can and can't do? What support will licensed builders get for any changed responsibilities?
focus.explanation: Four questions directed squarely at the implementation mechanics of the measure — council funding, staff training, public guidance, builder responsibilities. Scrutiny of the policy itself, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, they want applause for enabling a few thousand granny flats over a decade.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath — the modest scale of the measure relative to the housing need — but it is delivered as a characterisation of the Government's posture rather than an engagement with the policy, so the weight sits in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It would have been good if the previous speaker Celia Wade-Brown had actually been on the committee, because a whole lot of the questions and issues that she raised were actually answered.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly condescending toward a named member — the implication is that she raised objections she would not have raised had she done the work — but it stops at her committee attendance rather than her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I wish to apologise for the previous speaker, Scott Willis, because I think he’s a bit upset that we didn’t get to debate the Consumer Guarantees (Right to Repair) Amendment Bill yesterday—his party’s bill. I have one message for the member, which is: you’ve got to show up to this House on time.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at a named member: it attributes his argument to personal pique and scolds him for punctuality rather than engaging anything he said.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We do not need any more demand-side intervention like KiwiBuild and other flops that did nothing but drive up the cost of housing in New Zealand and make the other side of the House ungovernable.
focus.explanation: A real policy point — demand-side versus supply-side intervention, with a named programme (KiwiBuild) — but the closing clause about the other side of the House is party framing carrying no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, unfortunately, just about everything this Government has done has made things worse for Kiwis.
focus.explanation: A blanket verdict on the other side's record with no policy, measure or figure named — the sweep of 'just about everything' is what makes it party framing rather than scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill’s regulatory impact statement tells us that there's going to be something like 7,800 new buildings in the next decade. Kāinga Ora was building 5,000 homes a year. The Green Party has put forward a proposal to build 7,000 homes a year.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: it compares the bill's own projected output against named alternative supply pathways.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We do not have housing in Port Chalmers in Ōtepoti Dunedin because of the failure to build the homes that were ready to be built.
focus.explanation: Names a specific site and a specific outcome — the cancelled Albertson Avenue build — which is accountability for a named housing decision rather than party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wish to apologise for the previous speaker, Scott Willis, because I think he’s a bit upset that we didn’t get to debate the Consumer Guarantees (Right to Repair) Amendment Bill yesterday—his party’s bill. I have one message for the member, which is: you’ve got to show up to this House on time.
focus.explanation: Nothing about the bill or any policy survives once the remarks about the other member and his party's bill are removed.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We do not need any more demand-side intervention like KiwiBuild and other flops that did nothing but drive up the cost of housing in New Zealand and make the other side of the House ungovernable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that KiwiBuild achieved nothing and that its effect was to raise New Zealand housing costs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MHUD/Kāinga Ora reporting on the number of homes completed under KiwiBuild, plus any independent evaluation (Treasury, MHUD review, academic) of KiwiBuild's effect on house prices. False if KiwiBuild delivered a material number of dwellings, or if no evidence attributes a rise in housing costs to it; true only if delivery was negligible and evidence links the programme to higher prices.

veracity.statement: There was a lot of support for the bill, unanimity in the Transport and Infrastructure Committee, which was chaired by none other than Andy Foster.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Transport and Infrastructure Committee reported the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill unanimously, and that Andy Foster chaired that committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report on the bill (does it record a unanimous recommendation or any minority/differing views?) and the Parliament record of the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's chair in 2025. True if the report is unanimous and Foster is the listed chair; false if either fails.

veracity.statement: We have seen many examples, during this process, for less than $250,000, which is well under the average building cost for New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that compliant small dwellings have been costed below $250,000 in evidence to the committee, and that this is well below the average New Zealand building cost.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Submissions/evidence to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee for costed examples under $250,000, and Stats NZ building consent values or the CoreLogic Cordell construction cost index for the average cost of a new NZ dwelling. False if the average build cost is at or below $250,000, or if no such costed examples appear in the evidence.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora was building 5,000 homes a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kāinga Ora's annual new-build delivery rate was about 5,000 homes per year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual reports / MHUD public housing delivery statistics for new homes completed per year. True if annual completions were around 5,000; false if materially lower (e.g. in the 2,000–3,000 range).

specificity.statement: What they are required to do is provide upfront the project information memorandum, as the Minister mentioned; identify any hazards; keep records of the finished dwelling; and levy any development contributions towards infrastructure, which addresses the Green Party member’s concerns earlier.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the precise duties the bill leaves with councils — PIM, hazard identification, record-keeping, development contributions — each of which can be checked against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill’s regulatory impact statement tells us that there's going to be something like 7,800 new buildings in the next decade. Kāinga Ora was building 5,000 homes a year. The Green Party has put forward a proposal to build 7,000 homes a year.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete, sourced-and-checkable numbers set against each other — the RIS projection, a stated Kāinga Ora build rate and his own party's proposed rate.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Getting more houses built faster creates jobs, creates housing where it’s of need, mostly, so we commend this bill to the Parliament.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but a thin one: the benefits are asserted rather than shown, and the step from 'more houses faster' to 'housing where it's needed' is hedged with 'mostly' and left unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There's not a great difference between the poor quality of those homes, and this is where we see a real risk, because if we don't have an understanding of what sometimes happens with builders, or plumbers, or electricians when they decided they’ve had enough—they’ve got too many risks—where does that liability fall?
rigor.explanation: Argues about the policy, but the inference rests on personal anecdote about homes in his own community, and the leap from 'consented and unconsented homes in my area are similarly poor' to 'this bill carries a liability risk' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It looks like an election slogan without a lot of work done, because we saw in the regulatory impact statement that it was done in a rushed manner because it’s part of the coalition agreement.
rigor.explanation: Evidence is actually offered — the regulatory impact statement's own account of the timeframe — but the conclusion that the policy is a slogan does not follow from the process being rushed; a rushed policy can still be substantive.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s always interesting to see my colleague Dan Bidois comment on other actions and showing up to the House on time, when, in fact, I think his own party has issues in getting votes right and practices in this House. But I’ll leave that for him to discuss with his own colleagues—foot-in-mouth syndrome, I think.
civility.explanation: A named member is mocked personally — "foot-in-mouth syndrome" is a jibe at Dan Bidois himself rather than at any argument or policy position he holds.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s always interesting to see my colleague Dan Bidois comment on other actions and showing up to the House on time, when, in fact, I think his own party has issues in getting votes right and practices in this House. But I’ll leave that for him to discuss with his own colleagues—foot-in-mouth syndrome, I think.
focus.explanation: Opens a third-reading speech on a housing bill entirely on the other party's conduct in the House and their vote-handling; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. Strip out the material about the other side and nothing remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Those conditions are that the granny flat must be simple in its design; it must be meets the building code, that building work must be carried out by authorised professionals—that’s an important one, of course, because there are some people that DIY at home and quality is important there—and thirdly, that councils must be notified prior to and on completion of building work.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the House — what the consent exemption requires — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For many ethnic communities in New Zealand, including the Pacific and Asian families, multiple-generation living is not just practical; it is culture. These families value being close while also respecting each other's needs for privacy and independence. This bill allows the development of small stand-alone dwellings that support this way of living.
focus.explanation: Entirely about who the measure affects and why the dwelling type suits them — a substantive point about the bill's beneficiaries with no reference to any other party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Those conditions are that the granny flat must be simple in its design; it must be meets the building code, that building work must be carried out by authorised professionals—that’s an important one, of course, because there are some people that DIY at home and quality is important there—and thirdly, that councils must be notified prior to and on completion of building work.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the three named statutory conditions in the bill — design specification, building code compliance, authorised professionals, and council notification before and after work. Checkable against the bill text, though no figures or dates beyond that.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That member will, of course, know that Glenfield Salvation Army is reporting a homelessness list—as he moves around the House uncomfortably—of 150 people, who are sitting on that register in our own community. That’s the highest that Salvation Army Glenfield have ever reported.
specificity.explanation: A named organisation, a named locality, a specific count (150) and a stated comparison to its own historical maximum. Someone could ring Glenfield and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As Labour’s tertiary spokesperson, I’m very clear that in the last two years, we’ve graduated 9,000 fewer apprentices in this country. That’s on top of the 20,000 - odd that have headed offshore.
specificity.explanation: Two figures with a stated timeframe and a named cohort — apprenticeship graduations and departures offshore. Directly checkable against TEC and migration data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The cost of living challenges are pretty heavy, and we aren’t seeing any solutions there.
specificity.explanation: A policy claim carrying no content — no measure, no figure, no timeframe, and no indication of which solutions are absent or what would count as one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That was a concern that we took through into the select committee stage and were able to traverse that and have that conversation, and we’re pleased that the select committee made some sensible changes in that report as well, and that has been said here this morning in this debate.
specificity.explanation: Reports that the select committee made changes without naming a single one, nor which clause or concern was addressed. "Some sensible changes" commits to nothing checkable, in a passage where the actual amendments were available to cite.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That member will, of course, know that Glenfield Salvation Army is reporting a homelessness list—as he moves around the House uncomfortably—of 150 people, who are sitting on that register in our own community. That’s the highest that Salvation Army Glenfield have ever reported.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts about the present: that the Salvation Army's Glenfield centre currently has 150 people on its homelessness register, and that this is the highest number that centre has ever reported.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Salvation Army Glenfield centre's own reported housing/homelessness register figures as at October 2025: true if the register stands at approximately 150 people and that is the highest figure that centre has recorded, false if the count is materially different or if a higher figure has previously been reported.

veracity.statement: We know that under this Government, over the last two years, the construction sector has gone backwards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that construction sector activity in New Zealand has contracted over the two years to October 2025, i.e. under the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction industry GDP and construction sector employment/filled-jobs series for the two years to October 2025: true if both (or the headline activity measure) show contraction over that period, false if the sector grew.

veracity.statement: As Labour’s tertiary spokesperson, I’m very clear that in the last two years, we’ve graduated 9,000 fewer apprentices in this country. That’s on top of the 20,000 - odd that have headed offshore.
veracity.explanation: Two numeric claims: that apprenticeship graduations have fallen by 9,000 over the last two years, and that a further ~20,000 (workers in the sector) have emigrated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission / Ministry of Education apprenticeship completion data for 2023–2025 compared with the preceding two years: true if completions fell by approximately 9,000; and Stats NZ migration data on construction-trades departures, true if roughly 20,000 left. False if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Labour Government, despite doing the largest public housing build since the 1970s, particularly, has been criticised for transitional housing options and using motels as an alternative.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the last Labour Government delivered the largest public housing build since the 1970s. The second half (that it was criticised over transitional housing and motels) is not in dispute; the build claim is the checkable one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD / Kāinga Ora public housing place delivery figures by term: true if net public housing places added under the 2017–2023 Labour Government exceed those added in any government term since the 1970s, false if an intervening term delivered more.

veracity.statement: It is great to hear that this bill received unanimous support from the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill passed through the House without any party opposing it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division/voting record for the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill's readings: true if every party voted in favour at each reading, false if any party recorded a vote against.

rigor.statement: He’ll be aware that De Paul House in Northcote are seeing the highest number of single kaumātua, kuia—seniors—accessing their support, so by no way is this a practical solution to our housing needs.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure, with a real gap: evidence that demand on emergency housing providers is at a record high shows the housing need is large, but it does not establish that the granny-flat exemption is not a practical contribution to meeting it. Absence of sufficiency is treated as absence of usefulness.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It wouldn’t have been compliant, because my father built it and he was not a certified personnel member, in this particular case, but that’s what happened back in those days.
rigor.explanation: A small but valid inference: the bill requires building work to be carried out by authorised professionals, her father was not one, therefore the dwelling would not have qualified. The conclusion follows directly from the stated condition.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I say that because I’ve had knowledge, just this year, of a couple of families in my area around me who were in social housing; they had family—not even extended family, but direct family—a 16-year-old young woman who had a child and was wanting to put a granny flat on that particular social housing property, and that had been declined. Unfortunately, there was no emergency housing for that young person and her baby, and she had to live in a tent on the grounds of that house.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and its gap: whether the small-dwellings regime reaches social housing land. Names a concrete policy interaction (granny flat consent on a Housing NZ/social housing property, emergency housing availability) rather than characterising another party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of the barriers—which I accept that this bill removes a lot of barriers and that's why we support it—when building on whenua Māori, especially, there are enough barriers you have to go through. First of all, to get your whānau together to look at the land block and then to go to get the consent from the shareholders; and then to get your ducks in a row to finally get to Te Kooti Whenua Māori; and then go through that process to get your occupation order or your license to occupy. That can take years.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism and its limits — the sequence of legal steps that will still bind whānau building on Māori land after this bill. No party framing at all; she credits the bill for what it does remove.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I say that because I’ve had knowledge, just this year, of a couple of families in my area around me who were in social housing; they had family—not even extended family, but direct family—a 16-year-old young woman who had a child and was wanting to put a granny flat on that particular social housing property, and that had been declined. Unfortunately, there was no emergency housing for that young person and her baby, and she had to live in a tent on the grounds of that house.
specificity.explanation: Carries real detail — the tenure type, the applicant's age and circumstances, the decision made, the fallback outcome — but no figures, no named provider or policy instrument, and no proposed mechanism for changing it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Again, those are questions for review down the track, but, overall, I think this is a really good change; it’s a pragmatic change; it won’t solve some of the big issues that we have as a country, but it will help certain demographics within the country.
specificity.explanation: A summing-up that is trying to convey a judgement about the bill's effect but commits to nothing checkable: 'certain demographics', 'some of the big issues', no numbers, no timeframe, no named group. She had just supplied concrete detail and did not carry any of it into the conclusion.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The other thing I’ll mention is we’ve already seen up to 29 percent of real estate sales going to first-home buyers in New Zealand. That’s the highest on record. This Government is serious about getting houses to New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A named metric, a percentage, and a superlative that can be looked up. Precisely the kind of claim someone could go and check — which is what this attribute rewards, independently of whether it turns out to be right.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the barriers—which I accept that this bill removes a lot of barriers and that's why we support it—when building on whenua Māori, especially, there are enough barriers you have to go through. First of all, to get your whānau together to look at the land block and then to go to get the consent from the shareholders; and then to get your ducks in a row to finally get to Te Kooti Whenua Māori; and then go through that process to get your occupation order or your license to occupy. That can take years.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual steps and the institution (shareholder consent, Te Kooti Whenua Māori, occupation order or licence to occupy) and gives a rough duration ('years'). Short of full marks only because there are no figures on how long or how many are affected.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Some of the criteria is such that I know of one person who couldn't get access to a $50,000 mortgage to renovate a family home on Māori land, but he could get a loan to buy a $77,000 vehicle.
specificity.explanation: Two figures, the tenure type, and the exact contrast being drawn — the finance barrier is made concrete rather than gestured at. Not full marks because the lender and the criteria in question are not named, so the barrier itself cannot be located in any particular policy.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill will go a long way to solving some of the issues some of my constituents have building on their land.
specificity.explanation: Offers a judgement about the bill's effect with no content behind it — 'some of the issues', 'some of my constituents', no barrier named, no figure, no mechanism. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The other thing I’ll mention is we’ve already seen up to 29 percent of real estate sales going to first-home buyers in New Zealand. That’s the highest on record. This Government is serious about getting houses to New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that first-home buyers have accounted for up to 29 percent of residential property sales in New Zealand, and that this is the highest share ever recorded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: CoreLogic NZ Buyer Classification data (the standard series for first-home buyer share of residential purchases), cross-checked against REINZ/Treasury commentary for the period to October 2025. True if the FHB share of purchases reached approximately 29% and that reading is the highest in the series; false if the recorded peak is materially below 29%, or if a higher share appears earlier in the series.

veracity.statement: I think of Toitū Tairāwhiti, who—referencing Willie Te Aho, who's one of their senior advisors—has already stated that they have the ability to build these, so they come pre-built to your whenua, within around two to three months.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Willie Te Aho of Toitū Tairāwhiti: that the organisation can already deliver these small dwellings pre-built to a site within roughly two to three months. She is reporting someone else's statement of capability, not asserting it on her own authority.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, media coverage or organisational records from Toitū Tairāwhiti or Willie Te Aho on prefabricated small-dwelling delivery timeframes, plus their documented post-Cyclone Gabrielle build record. True if such a statement is on record and the two-to-three-month delivery capability is corroborated by completed builds; false if no such statement exists or the documented delivery times are materially longer.

rigor.statement: The other thing I’ll mention is we’ve already seen up to 29 percent of real estate sales going to first-home buyers in New Zealand. That’s the highest on record. This Government is serious about getting houses to New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: The inference is the weak part: a market outcome (first-home buyers' share of sales) is offered as establishing the Government's seriousness, with nothing connecting the share to any action this Government took. A share of sales can rise because prices fell or investors withdrew. This is on-policy reasoning, not a jibe, but the conclusion outruns the evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Whānau who don't have access to resources to build their dream home are going to see this as an opportunity to whack up what they will see as housing options, as permanent full-time housing.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that dwellings enabled by the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill will in practice be occupied as permanent primary housing by whānau without the means to build a conventional home, rather than as the ancillary/secondary dwellings the bill contemplates.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE and territorial authority reporting on small stand-alone dwellings built under the Act (consent/notification volumes and occupancy), together with Stats NZ dwelling and household statistics for Tairāwhiti and Ikaroa-Rāwhiti. True if such dwellings are documented as being occupied as households' primary permanent residences at a non-trivial rate; false if the records show them used overwhelmingly as ancillary dwellings on properties whose main house is separately occupied.

specificity.statement: Out of those 705 submissions, 620 submitters opposed the bill, 34 supported it, and the remaining 51 were either unclear or did not take a position on this bill.
specificity.explanation: Exact submission counts broken down by position — fully checkable against the select committee record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are three things I want to touch on in terms of amendments that came through the Justice Committee: replacing “enemy alien” with “citizen of a State at war with New Zealand”, just to make that really clear what that reference related to; secondly, making it a question of law whether a person owes allegiance to New Zealand, so a judge will make that decision instead of a jury—that was a suggestion of the New Zealand Law Society—and, finally, a safeguard for protesters to ensure that engaging in protest, advocacy, or industrial action would not, by itself, be criminalised.
specificity.explanation: Three named amendments with the actual drafting change, the legal mechanism (question of law for a judge rather than a jury) and the source of the recommendation.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Out of those 705 submissions, 620 submitters opposed the bill, 34 supported it, and the remaining 51 were either unclear or did not take a position on this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the submission tally on the Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Bill: 705 total, 620 opposed, 34 in support, 51 neutral/unclear.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Bill and its published submissions list; true if the totals match 705/620/34/51, false if the breakdown materially differs.

veracity.statement: It took everyone by surprise, especially the trade Minister Todd McClay, because the very next day we got pinged with 50 percent tariffs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the day after the FBI office announcement, New Zealand was subjected to 50 percent United States tariffs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The US tariff rate applied to New Zealand goods under the 2025 executive orders (USTR/Federal Register schedules), and its effective date relative to the FBI Wellington office announcement; true if a 50 percent rate applied to New Zealand the following day, false if the rate was materially lower or not so timed.

veracity.statement: We’ve had Ministers say that this wasn’t about China, but then the person who came over to open the office, Kash Patel, reiterated that it actually is about countering China.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that New Zealand Ministers denied the new FBI Wellington office was about China and that Kash Patel, who opened it, said it was about countering China.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and transcripts of NZ ministerial statements on the FBI Wellington office, plus Kash Patel's remarks at or around the opening; true if Ministers denied a China focus and Patel affirmed one, false if either half is not on the record.

veracity.statement: There are three things I want to touch on in terms of amendments that came through the Justice Committee: replacing “enemy alien” with “citizen of a State at war with New Zealand”, just to make that really clear what that reference related to; secondly, making it a question of law whether a person owes allegiance to New Zealand, so a judge will make that decision instead of a jury—that was a suggestion of the New Zealand Law Society—and, finally, a safeguard for protesters to ensure that engaging in protest, advocacy, or industrial action would not, by itself, be criminalised.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Justice Committee made these three specific amendments to the bill, and that the judge-not-jury change was recommended by the New Zealand Law Society.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Bill and the New Zealand Law Society's submission on it; true if all three amendments appear as described and the allegiance change is attributed to the Law Society, false if any is absent or differently sourced.

rigor.statement: But if the Filipino Embassy had contacted me and asked me to share posts related to Filipino Restaurant Week, under the really vaguely defined provisions of the legislation, my posting that and encouraging people to celebrate Filipino Restaurant Week could potentially constitute a crime, if you interpret that under this legislation.
rigor.explanation: A reductio against the bill's drafting, but the inference skips the other elements the offence requires (covert conduct, deception, harm), so the absurd conclusion does not follow from the vagueness premise alone. Hedged throughout with 'could potentially', which weakens rather than supports it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Crown’s record in this regard is not good. We only have to look at the Urewera raids and the history of espionage, in a domestic way, to see that.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single named episode to a conclusion about the Crown's record overall — an argument from anecdote, with 'the history of espionage' gestured at rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It took everyone by surprise, especially the trade Minister Todd McClay, because the very next day we got pinged with 50 percent tariffs.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly mocking toward a named Minister ('especially the trade Minister Todd McClay'), but the target is his being caught out by events rather than his character.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This appears to step over successive Governments’ claims on independent foreign policy and continues with the trend that we’ve seen, under this Government, of being aligned to the United States rather than with other partners and our neighbours in the Pacific.
focus.explanation: A genuine foreign-policy point — independent foreign policy versus US alignment — but carried largely as a characterisation of 'this Government's' trend rather than a named measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are three things I want to touch on in terms of amendments that came through the Justice Committee: replacing “enemy alien” with “citizen of a State at war with New Zealand”, just to make that really clear what that reference related to; secondly, making it a question of law whether a person owes allegiance to New Zealand, so a judge will make that decision instead of a jury—that was a suggestion of the New Zealand Law Society—and, finally, a safeguard for protesters to ensure that engaging in protest, advocacy, or industrial action would not, by itself, be criminalised.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the content of the bill's amendments; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Russians have been identified often as one of the worst culprits in this respect.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Russia is frequently identified as among the worst state actors conducting covert foreign interference, including in elections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published threat assessments and official attributions (NZSIS Security Threat Environment reports, EU DisinfoLab/EEAS FIMI reports, US ODNI election-threat assessments): true if Russia is repeatedly named among the leading foreign-interference actors; false if such assessments do not name Russia in that tier.

veracity.statement: Think of the Government of Sid Holland, the National Party Prime Minister from 1949 in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Sid Holland was a National Party Prime Minister of New Zealand whose government dates from 1949.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Parliament / Te Ara records of prime ministerial terms: true if Sidney Holland took office as National Party Prime Minister in 1949; false if he led a different party or took office in a different year.

veracity.statement: It’s also, in my view, unacceptable that that the Chinese Government, through its United Front Works Department, deploys resources of the State to influence the behaviour and the publicly expressed opinions of the diaspora communities in New Zealand by controlling and influencing Chinese language media outlets who serve the diaspora communities in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Chinese state, via the United Front Work Department, controls or influences Chinese-language media outlets serving New Zealand diaspora communities. The "in my view" hedge attaches to the unacceptability, not to the underlying factual claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZSIS Security Threat Environment reports and peer-reviewed research on PRC influence activity in New Zealand (e.g. Brady, 'Magic Weapons'), plus documented ownership/content-sharing arrangements of NZ Chinese-language outlets: true if official or peer-reviewed sources document United Front Work Department direction or funding of those outlets; false if no such documentation exists and ownership is independent of PRC state bodies.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen occasions of that, where we know, on a regular basis, that our public institutions are constantly under attack in those spaces, all for access to data—to public and to private information.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand public institutions are subject to regular, ongoing cyber attacks aimed at obtaining public and private data.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NCSC/GCSB annual Cyber Threat Report incident counts for the period: true if the reports record recurring (dozens or more per year) malicious cyber incidents against nationally significant organisations and public agencies involving data access; false if recorded incidents against public institutions are rare or isolated.

veracity.statement: It’s rather fitting that we continue to speak and discuss this bill on a day when New Zealanders look towards taking to the streets to prove their point in the industrial action space, rallying against the moves by this Government with respect to their pay.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on the day of the debate (22 October 2025) New Zealanders were taking part in nationwide industrial action and street rallies over pay, in response to government pay decisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous news reporting and union (PSA/NZEI/NZNO) strike notices for 22–23 October 2025: true if nationwide public-sector strike action and public rallies over pay occurred on or about that date; false if no such industrial action took place then.

civility.statement: In fact, I regard myself as a principled critic of this Government’s headlong rush into the arms of the United Military Alliance, effectively with the United States, to counter China’s growing strength in the Asia-Pacific region.
civility.explanation: Sharp, contested criticism of the Government's foreign and defence policy direction ("headlong rush"), aimed entirely at the policy choice rather than at any person's character or competence. Under the re-anchored scale, hard criticism of a policy sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think it’s naive for many of our people out in New Zealand, who often sit in ignorance of many of the challenges that they face and of many of the challenges that this country faces—I think of some recent examples, whether it’s what seems like a benign kind of cyber attack or phishing, if we will, or whether it’s something far more sinister.
civility.explanation: Not an attack on any individual, but a condescending characterisation of the public as naive and sitting "in ignorance" rather than as under-informed about a genuinely obscure threat. Short of a personal insult, but it talks down at the people rather than about the risk.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have an enormous amount at stake not just in economic terms and trade, but China is already a great power in our region, and we need to conduct our relationship with China in a way that’s calm and thoughtful, and mature.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: two premises (large economic stake; China's existing great-power status in the region) are offered in support of a conclusion about how the relationship should be conducted. The conclusion tracks the premises, but the connecting step is asserted rather than shown — "calm and mature" is not derived from the stakes, it is presumed from them.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s also, in my view, unacceptable that that the Chinese Government, through its United Front Works Department, deploys resources of the State to influence the behaviour and the publicly expressed opinions of the diaspora communities in New Zealand by controlling and influencing Chinese language media outlets who serve the diaspora communities in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific state body (the United Front Work Department), a specific target (Chinese-language media serving NZ diaspora communities) and a specific mechanism (state resources deployed to control and influence those outlets). No figures or timeframe, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are some foreign States that try to influence what people in other countries do, and this is simply providing a means to better hold people accountable for undertaking foreign interference.
specificity.explanation: Attempting to convey substance about the bill but carries almost none: "some foreign States", "influence what people do", "a means to better hold people accountable". No offence defined, no threshold, no penalty, no named actor — a restatement of the bill's title in general terms.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to talk about the elephant in the room in this debate, and that is the quite well publicised activities of operatives from the Chinese Government who have been engaging in, I think, foreign interference, in the way that it is defined in this bill—their activities would qualify as foreign interference.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly, testing named real-world conduct against the bill's own statutory definition of foreign interference. Entirely about the policy; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Let’s just be really clear about what the legislation is intending to do here: it’s about strengthening the criminal law, and providing a means to better hold people accountable for undertaking foreign interference.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the purpose of the bill before the House. He had an open opportunity in a contested second reading to attack opponents and did not; no party content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this legislation will help to ensure that our criminal law is fit for purpose to address what we see as a harmful activity and will better equip the relevant agencies to hold people to account.
