specificity.explanation: Four named policies, which is real checkable content, but no design, cost, eligibility or timeframe for any of them — a direction rather than a proposal.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We had the $750 million walking and cycling bridge across Auckland Harbour, which, for that amount of money, didn’t even include a bus lane.
specificity.explanation: A named project, a dollar figure and a concrete design claim (no bus lane). Someone could go and check both.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are good reasons why this Government will soon begin work on a national infrastructure agency, one of the measures set down in the coalition agreement, and institute long-term city and regional infrastructure-deals, allowing public-private partnerships, tolling and value capture, and other innovative measures to generate revenues to pay for infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Names an institution to be created and four concrete funding mechanisms, but attaches no amounts, no dates and no scope beyond 'soon'.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s because it’s not good enough just to pick projects from some ideological bucket and announce them on a campaign trail; you actually have to consider how individual projects and programmes of work deliver economic and social benefits for the regions where they’re to be delivered.
rigor.explanation: A genuine premise (projects should be selected on assessed economic and social benefit) offered as the reason for the measures just announced. The inference has a real gap: nothing offered connects that premise to the specific remedies of an infrastructure agency, tolling and public-private partnerships, so the conclusion outruns the support.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The coalition Government also intends to introduce financial incentives for councils to enable more housing, including considering sharing a proportion of the GST revenue collected on new residential building with councils because local government has all of the costs of delivering local infrastructure, but, apart from some very basic rating tools, does not have the ability to access revenue to deliver those big pieces of bulk infrastructure which are needed to allow cities to grow up as well as out.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (sharing a proportion of GST collected on new residential building with councils) but gives no proportion, no dollar figure and no timeframe, and it is framed as something under consideration rather than settled.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will repeal those two pieces of legislation—the Spatial Planning and the Natural Built Environment Acts—in the first 100 days.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutes, the exact action (repeal) and a bounded deadline. Anyone can check on day 101 whether it happened.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The coalition Government also intends to introduce financial incentives for councils to enable more housing, including considering sharing a proportion of the GST revenue collected on new residential building with councils because local government has all of the costs of delivering local infrastructure, but, apart from some very basic rating tools, does not have the ability to access revenue to deliver those big pieces of bulk infrastructure which are needed to allow cities to grow up as well as out.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference with a stated reason: councils carry the cost of local infrastructure but have only rating tools for revenue, therefore a revenue-sharing incentive. The premise supports the conclusion; the gap is that no link is shown between council revenue and the volume of housing actually consented.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How is anybody supposed to get a consent to build infrastructure—roads, bridges, waste-water treatment plants, let alone a housing subdivision anywhere if you don’t even know what the terms in the bill mean?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: undefined statutory terms make consenting harder. But the leap from 'a term is contested' to 'nobody can get any consent for any infrastructure' is unsupported — consenting proceeds under many partly-litigated terms, and nothing is offered to bridge that gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve had successive governments run into activist judges and poorly thought-out environmental legislation.
civility.explanation: Criticising the legislation is fully civil, but 'activist judges' imputes political motive to the judiciary rather than engaging with any ruling's reasoning. No individual is named, so this is a failure of the imputing-bad-faith kind rather than a direct personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Imagine that: being able to use your land to build or grow what you want without the risk of having people come out of the woodwork, come from far and wide, bring their homemade signs to protest and oppose what you want to do with your own land.
civility.explanation: 'Come out of the woodwork' and the jibe about homemade signs mock those who make submissions or protest rather than engaging their objections. No individual is named, so it stops short of a personal attack, but it is sneering rather than substantive.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Think about projects like the Mt Messenger bypass in Taranaki; stymied by objectors who in the end were found to not have a case but who held the project up for years and have cost the Government and taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable things about the Mt Messenger bypass: that the objectors' case was ultimately rejected, and that the resulting delay cost the Crown and taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Environment Court, High Court and Court of Appeal decisions on the Mt Messenger bypass (Te Ara o Te Ata) consent appeals, plus NZTA/Waka Kotahi project cost and business-case documents. True if the appeals were dismissed AND documented delay-attributable cost escalation reaches $200m or more; false if the objections succeeded in part, or if the delay-attributable cost is materially below that figure.

veracity.statement: Or the objectors to seabed mining off the coast of Taranaki who—it turns out, all of the environmental considerations were addressed, and yet that project is still stuck dealing with the Supreme Court directions to consider tikanga, an esoteric concept that cannot be readily defined by applicants or lawyers or the Environment Court.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the Taranaki seabed mining (Trans-Tasman Resources) litigation the environmental considerations were all satisfied, and that what remains outstanding is a Supreme Court direction to consider tikanga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court judgment in Trans-Tasman Resources Ltd v Taranaki-Whanganui Conservation Board (2021) and the subsequent Environment Court/EPA process. True if the Court's remittal rested only on tikanga; false if the Court also found the environmental conditions or the treatment of environmental effects legally inadequate.

veracity.statement: They introduced new novel terms like “te oranga o te taiao”, which submitters told the Environment Committee could take a decade to litigate, to work out what they even meant.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that submitters to the Environment Committee on the Natural and Built Environment Bill told the committee that the term 'te oranga o te taiao' could take about a decade of litigation to define.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Written and oral submissions and the departmental report on the Natural and Built Environment Bill held by the Environment Committee. True if one or more submitters stated a roughly decade-long litigation horizon for defining te oranga o te taiao; false if no submission makes a claim of that kind.

focus.statement: Well, I heard for three years, sitting on the Environment Committee, all kinds of ways the previous Government was going to deal with that. However, the former Labour Government’s Spatial Planning Act, and Natural and Built Environment Act didn’t address it.
focus.explanation: Names two specific Acts and a specific claimed shortcoming in them. This is scrutiny of a named legislative outcome, not general party-bashing; the only party framing is the label identifying whose legislation it was.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is the topic I’d like to talk about a little bit today: after six years in the wilderness, after six years of directionless ambling around, directionless travel, economic hard times, we are back.
focus.explanation: Characterises the previous government's six years in wholly general terms — 'wilderness', 'directionless ambling' — without naming a single policy, measure, figure or outcome. Party framing carrying no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The coalition Government has done and will continue to do what the previous Government could not do, and that was to listen.
focus.explanation: Entirely a contrast between the two parties' general character. No policy, mechanism or named commitment is at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have been bombarded with regulations, with rules, and with restrictions that are not fit for purpose and that have not been based in scientific evidence of best practice.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the regulatory settings applying to farmers — the policy itself, not the other party's character. It stops short of 1.0 only because no particular regulation is identified.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want to establish stability again, we want to grow economic prosperity, we want to restore national unity and national pride.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goals offered as the Government's programme: no figures, no mechanisms, no timeframes, nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to reverse the ban on live animal exports, but New Zealand will become a world leader in ensuring the highest standards of animal welfare.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific, identifiable policy change (reversing the live animal export ban), but the accompanying welfare commitment carries no standard, mechanism or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management. We’re going to make it fit for purpose. We’re going to go catchment by catchment, and region by region. We’re not going to allow this top-down, nonsensical, unscientific approach to continue.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument to be replaced (the NPS for Freshwater Management) and the intended approach (catchment by catchment, region by region), but supplies no content for the replacement, no cost and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We understand that there are about $10 billion in non-tariff barriers sitting on the table that that previous Government ignored for six years.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete, checkable figure attached to a named problem (non-tariff barriers). Missing only which markets or barriers make up the total.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: At 16 percent, it is making life miserable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on-farm inflation — the rise in farm input costs, as distinct from consumer inflation — is running at 16 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Beef + Lamb New Zealand Economic Service / Stats NZ farm expenses price index for on-farm inflation in the year to March 2023 (the most recent figure available when this was said). True if the published on-farm inflation rate is approximately 16 percent; false if materially different (e.g. below 12 or above 20 percent).

veracity.statement: We understand that there are about $10 billion in non-tariff barriers sitting on the table that that previous Government ignored for six years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific dollar value — about $10 billion — for the non-tariff barriers facing New Zealand exports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT / NZIER published estimates of the value to New Zealand exporters of non-tariff barriers in key markets. True if an official or commissioned estimate puts the figure at roughly $10 billion; false if the best available estimates are of a materially different order (e.g. a few billion, or tens of billions).

veracity.statement: We are on track to meet those targets, and I know that every farmer in New Zealand is on board with that and is thoroughly incentivised to get going with it.
veracity.explanation: Two present-tense factual assertions: that New Zealand is currently on track for its 2050 carbon zero targets, and that every farmer in the country supports and is incentivised by them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Climate Change Commission's most recent monitoring advice as at December 2023 on whether existing policy puts New Zealand on track for the emissions budgets and the 2050 net zero target, plus published farmer surveys (e.g. Federated Farmers) on support for agricultural emissions targets. True if the Commission assessed the trajectory as on track and surveys show near-universal farmer support; false if the Commission found current policy insufficient or if a material share of farmers are recorded as opposed.

civility.statement: We’re going to replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management. We’re going to make it fit for purpose. We’re going to go catchment by catchment, and region by region. We’re not going to allow this top-down, nonsensical, unscientific approach to continue.
civility.explanation: 'Nonsensical' and 'unscientific' are harsh, but the target is a national policy statement and its design. No person is impugned, so this is fierce criticism of a policy — the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We are going to meet our carbon zero 2050 goals.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a national emissions outcome three decades out — an economy-wide result, not merely an action of the speaker's government.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand's greenhouse gas inventory measured against the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act 2019 target: net zero for long-lived gases and a 24–47 percent reduction in biogenic methane on 2017 levels by 2050. True if the reported 2050 position meets the statutory target; false if it does not.

focus.statement: New Zealand First is back, and we can thank a lot of people for this, but I think the people we really need to thank are the Labour Party for their increasingly authoritarian stances, for their attack on our very democracy, for being out of touch with the working New Zealanders that they purport to represent, for trying to centralise almost everything, and for running our economy into the rocks to where our economic outlook is sitting at 159th in the world by IMF measures, sitting only just above Equatorial Guinea, which actually happens to be in the middle of a coup at the moment.
focus.explanation: The weight of the passage is a general characterisation of the other party — 'authoritarian', 'out of touch', 'attack on our very democracy' — with no measure named. It is lifted above zero by two real policy points: centralisation of services and a specific IMF ranking for the economic outlook. A policy claim wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: New Zealand First is back, and we can thank a lot of people for this, but I think the people we really need to thank are the Labour Party for their increasingly authoritarian stances, for their attack on our very democracy, for being out of touch with the working New Zealanders that they purport to represent, for trying to centralise almost everything, and for running our economy into the rocks to where our economic outlook is sitting at 159th in the world by IMF measures, sitting only just above Equatorial Guinea, which actually happens to be in the middle of a coup at the moment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the IMF ranks New Zealand's economic outlook 159th in the world, immediately above Equatorial Guinea. Also asserts Equatorial Guinea was undergoing a coup at the time of speaking (December 2023).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IMF World Economic Outlook (October 2023) projections: New Zealand's rank among the ~190 economies covered on the relevant growth measure, and Equatorial Guinea's rank on the same measure. True if NZ sits at or near 159th and Equatorial Guinea sits just below it; false if NZ's rank is materially different, or if no IMF series produces that ordering.

veracity.statement: In fact, my decision to stand again for this House was not one that was taken lightly, but when the Labour Party announced that they were prepared to sacrifice 21 percent of the sheep and beef sector at the altar of the climate change policy, I just could not sit by and take that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour Government's agricultural emissions pricing proposal was projected to cut the sheep and beef sector by 21 percent, and that Labour advanced it knowing that.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official modelling published alongside the previous Government's agricultural emissions pricing proposal (He Waka Eke Noa / the October 2022 Government response), from MPI, the Ministry for the Environment or the Climate Change Commission. True if that modelling projected a reduction in sheep and beef production or land area of around 21 percent under the proposed pricing, and the Government proceeded with the proposal; false if the projected reduction was materially smaller or no such figure appears in the modelling.

veracity.statement: The numbers get thrown around time and time again to the point where they seem to not mean anything: $57 billion or $58 billion of foreign exchange to an economy that is running a current account deficit could not be more critical; 350,000 New Zealanders directly employed; it is 82 percent—82 percent—of New Zealand’s merchandise export trade.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three figures for the primary sector: $57–58 billion in export earnings, 350,000 New Zealanders directly employed, and 82 percent of merchandise export trade. Also asserts the economy is running a current account deficit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for the Primary Industries (December 2023 edition) for food and fibre export revenue and employment, and Stats NZ goods exports for the share of merchandise exports. True if export revenue is approximately $57–58 billion, direct employment approximately 350,000, and primary sector exports approximately 82 percent of merchandise exports; false if any figure is materially outside those values.

veracity.statement: Rural confidence was at a 20-year low; it didn’t come before in the nick of time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rural or farmer confidence had fallen to its lowest level in twenty years in the period before the 2023 election. The second clause is a live-speech stumble and carries no separate claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Federated Farmers Farm Confidence Survey and/or the Rabobank Rural Confidence Survey time series. True if a 2022 or 2023 reading was the lowest recorded in roughly twenty years; false if the series shows a lower reading within that period, or if the series does not extend back twenty years and no comparable measure supports the claim.

specificity.statement: In fact, my decision to stand again for this House was not one that was taken lightly, but when the Labour Party announced that they were prepared to sacrifice 21 percent of the sheep and beef sector at the altar of the climate change policy, I just could not sit by and take that.
specificity.explanation: Names a sector, a figure (21 percent) and the policy area driving it. Falls short of 1.0 because the specific instrument — the emissions pricing proposal — is referred to only as 'the climate change policy', and no date or document is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The numbers get thrown around time and time again to the point where they seem to not mean anything: $57 billion or $58 billion of foreign exchange to an economy that is running a current account deficit could not be more critical; 350,000 New Zealanders directly employed; it is 82 percent—82 percent—of New Zealand’s merchandise export trade.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete, checkable quantities: export revenue in dollars, direct employment headcount, and a share of merchandise exports. Anyone could look each one up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to turn New Zealand around. We need to be lifting our growth. We need to be providing more opportunities, and that is just what we intend to do as a coalition.
specificity.explanation: A statement of intent with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named policy. 'Lifting our growth' and 'more opportunities' commit to nothing checkable, and unlike his primary-sector passage the surrounding text supplies no detail to credit here.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In only a couple of weeks, in only 14 days, this Government has attacked my whole world from every corner. Health, taiao, wai, whenua, natural resources, Māori wards, reo, tamariki, and the right of me and you to be in this country under Te Tiriti. How can I not take anything personally when it feels like these policies were made about me?
civility.explanation: Genuinely contested political ground with a real opportunity to be uncivil, and she takes none of it: the criticism is aimed at a Government's policy programme, not at any individual member. 'These policies were made about me' imputes intent to a government rather than sneering at a person, which keeps this near the expected standard rather than at the 0.5 failure band.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In only a couple of weeks, in only 14 days, this Government has attacked my whole world from every corner. Health, taiao, wai, whenua, natural resources, Māori wards, reo, tamariki, and the right of me and you to be in this country under Te Tiriti. How can I not take anything personally when it feels like these policies were made about me?
focus.explanation: The weight of the statement is a list of policy domains — health, water, land, Māori wards, te reo, Te Tiriti rights — and a named timeframe, so it is directed at the Government's measures rather than at what the other parties are 'really like'. It falls short of 1.0 because the domains are named without naming the measures within them, so a share of the force comes from framing rather than from a specific policy.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In only a couple of weeks, in only 14 days, this Government has attacked my whole world from every corner. Health, taiao, wai, whenua, natural resources, Māori wards, reo, tamariki, and the right of me and you to be in this country under Te Tiriti. How can I not take anything personally when it feels like these policies were made about me?
specificity.explanation: Carries one hard figure (14 days) and one identifiable policy (Māori wards), but the central claim — 'attacked my whole world from every corner' — supplies no mechanism, no figures and no named legislation across the other eight domains listed. A direction with a little detail, well short of anything a reader could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Last time this meteor showered was in 1972, when te Petihana was brought to Pāremata from our grandparents.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the meteor shower visible over Aotearoa on the night of the speech is the same one last seen in 1972, and dates the delivery of the te reo Māori petition to Parliament to that year. Part (b) is the well-documented 14 September 1972 petition; the checkable weight sits on part (a), the identification of the shower and its 51-year interval. Scored by the resolver, not here.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Two separable parts. (a) Astronomical records for comet 46P/Wirtanen and December meteor activity: TRUE if a meteor display attributable to 46P was recorded in 1972 and recurred on 12 December 2023; FALSE if 46P has no recorded associated meteor shower, or if its apparitions do not fall in 1972 and 2023 given its ~5.4-year orbital period, or if the December 2023 activity over New Zealand was the Geminids (parent body 3200 Phaethon). (b) Parliamentary/NZHistory record of te Petihana, the Māori language petition: TRUE if it was presented to Parliament in 1972, FALSE if in another year.

veracity.statement: If we go back to what people were focused on during the election campaign; certainly, when I was up and down the country talking to people, the number one issue was the cost of living.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that cost of living ranked first among voters' concerns during the 2023 general election campaign.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published NZ public-opinion issue polling covering the 2023 election campaign (e.g. Ipsos NZ Issues Monitor 2023, 1News-Verian issue polling); true if cost of living/inflation ranked as the most important issue facing the country, false if another issue (health, crime, housing) ranked first.

veracity.statement: So an important part of our overall justice priority is to deal with those—half of the prisoners who are in prison right now are remand prisoners who are awaiting their trial.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that remand prisoners awaiting trial made up half the New Zealand prison population as at December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics (quarterly muster, remand vs sentenced) for the quarter to December 2023; true if the remand share was approximately 50%, false if materially lower (e.g. below 45%) or higher.

veracity.statement: After six years where truancy got out of control, our Government will be focused on dealing with some of those long-term drivers of crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that school truancy worsened substantially over the six years to 2023. The overstated wording ('out of control') is still checkable as a claim of substantial deterioration.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education attendance data — the regular attendance rate (students present more than 90% of a term) for 2017 through 2023; true if the rate fell substantially across that period, false if it was flat or improved.

veracity.statement: But it was Sir Douglas Graham that kicked things off with Prime Minister Jim Bolger, who got the Ngāi Tahu settlement sorted and one with Tainui, which set the benchmark that that got things going.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Tainui and Ngāi Tahu Treaty settlements were concluded under Jim Bolger's government with Doug Graham as the responsible Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waikato Raupatu Claims Settlement Act 1995 and the Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998, plus Office of Treaty Settlements records of the Minister in Charge of Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations at the time; true if both settlements were concluded under Bolger as Prime Minister with Graham as the responsible Minister, false if either was concluded under a different government or Minister.

rigor.statement: Well, because there have not been any adjustments to the tax rates over a long period of time during inflation, people are paying more and more tax.
rigor.explanation: A valid fiscal-drag inference: if income tax thresholds are not indexed and nominal incomes rise with inflation, a larger share of income falls into higher brackets, so tax paid rises. The conclusion follows from the premise offered. Whether thresholds were in fact frozen (and his use of 'rates' where 'thresholds' is meant) is a Veracity matter, not an inference defect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, that, I’m afraid, is not the truth. People see what’s going on in their communities, and they raised it with us over and over again.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts the charge that talking up crime is fearmongering by appealing to what people report seeing and raising on the doorstep. Public perception of crime is not evidence of the crime rate, so this is an appeal to anecdote and popular belief; the premise offered cannot support the conclusion that the fearmongering charge is false.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I was just talking to an architect in Auckland last week who was talking about the latest home insulation requirements in Auckland, and the extremely thick insulation required in a pretty warm part of the country, and the additional costs that that’s adding to building houses, and ultimately to the cost of housing, which flows through to every household in Auckland trying to get affordable housing.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a single conversation with one architect is generalised to a conclusion about build costs and about the housing costs of 'every household in Auckland'. No data, no cost estimate and no mechanism connecting the regulation to the aggregate outcome is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, that, I’m afraid, is not the truth. People see what’s going on in their communities, and they raised it with us over and over again.
civility.explanation: Contradicts named critics (former Ministers of Justice, academics) squarely on the substance of their claim. Flatly calling their characterisation untrue is pointed but lands on the argument, not on them personally.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I was just talking to an architect in Auckland last week who was talking about the latest home insulation requirements in Auckland, and the extremely thick insulation required in a pretty warm part of the country, and the additional costs that that’s adding to building houses, and ultimately to the cost of housing, which flows through to every household in Auckland trying to get affordable housing.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages a named regulatory measure — the current home insulation requirements in the Building Code — and its claimed cost effect. Entirely about the policy, with no party content; the weak inference is Rigor's problem, not this one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m very conscious of the fact that I stand in a proud tradition in the National Party of a party that has actually delivered in that space, because there’s a lot of talk on the other side.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy area at issue (Treaty settlements delivery), but the sentence is built as a party-versus-party contrast and the clause about opponents — 'a lot of talk on the other side' — names no policy, measure or outcome. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to be restricting the ability of judges to significantly reduce sentences so that people actually do face real consequences for crime. Then we’ll be giving the police the powers that they need in order to deal with gangs in our communities. So whether that’s banning gang patches in public places or whether it’s giving the police powers to disperse gangs when they’re taking over a township like Ōpōtiki, as we saw in the past, and also dealing with firearms that have become a real issue in our communities.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete mechanisms — capping sentence discounts, a public gang-patch ban, police dispersal powers — which is more than a direction of travel. But there are no figures (no cap on the discount), no timeframe, and no detail on the firearms element, so it stops short of something checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I regard that as actually quite an important economic portfolio, because the creative sector is significant in our economy. It’s actually a big export earner. The film industry is a big export earner. The music industry is a big export owner.
specificity.explanation: Four sentences that repeat the same unquantified assertion. No export value, no share of GDP, no employment figure, no named scheme — nothing anyone could check or act on, despite the claim being about measurable economic quantities.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If that chubby 14-year-old kid can go on to run a few marathons, join the air force and deploy on operations all around the world, then there must be hope for everyone.
rigor.explanation: Explicit if-then inference, but it generalises from a single case (the speaker's own life) to a universal conclusion about everyone. Hasty generalisation from anecdote; nothing is offered to connect one person's outcome to everyone else's prospects.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why I love National’s social investment approach: because it’s about outcomes; it’s about targeted results for those that would otherwise be left behind.
specificity.explanation: Names a real policy approach (social investment), which lifts it above a pure slogan, but supplies no mechanism, no cohort, no funding figure and no timeframe — 'outcomes' and 'targeted results' are generic virtues rather than anything checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Can I also acknowledge the previous 12 MPs for Ōtaki since 1893, in particular the Hon Nathan Guy, and I’d also like to acknowledge the Hon Roger Sowry and the Rt Hon Jim Bolger.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that exactly 12 members have represented the Ōtaki electorate before him, counting from 1893.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Parliament / Parliamentary Library electorate record for Ōtaki listing every member returned for the seat from 1893 up to the 2023 general election; true if that list contains 12 members preceding Costley, false if the count is materially different.

civility.statement: It is a highly symbolic and important act that we take today because we are remedying one of the greatest stains of the outgoing Government, and that is the stain of the cost of living crisis they have left behind them.
civility.explanation: A contested first-reading debate with ample opportunity to go personal. The criticism is brutal but aimed at the outgoing Government's record on the cost of living, not at any individual's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Under the watch of the previous Government, inflation was allowed to ramp on unchecked, out of target, for 2½ years and that is far too long and has left New Zealanders suffering.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual CPI inflation sat outside the Reserve Bank's target band continuously for about two and a half years during the previous Government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual inflation series and the RBNZ 1–3% target band: true if the annual rate was above 3% continuously for roughly 30 months up to December 2023; false if the out-of-band period was materially shorter or interrupted.

veracity.statement: When the dual mandate was added in 2019 it undid success in the past and, as we’ve seen, inflation in recent years has been consistently well above the Reserve Bank’s target of achieving and maintaining annual inflation between 1 and 3 percent over the medium term, as measured by the Consumers Price Index.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the dual mandate was added in 2019, and that the Reserve Bank's target is 1–3% annual CPI inflation over the medium term, which inflation has consistently exceeded in recent years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Monetary Policy) Amendment Act commencement date, the Monetary Policy Remit's stated target band, and the Stats NZ CPI annual series 2021–2023: true if the employment objective took effect in 2019, the band is 1–3%, and annual CPI was above 3% for most of that period; false on any of the three.

rigor.statement: When the dual mandate was added in 2019 it undid success in the past and, as we’ve seen, inflation in recent years has been consistently well above the Reserve Bank’s target of achieving and maintaining annual inflation between 1 and 3 percent over the medium term, as measured by the Consumers Price Index.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the inference that the 2019 mandate change 'undid success' rests on nothing but the sequence of the change and the later inflation. No mechanism is offered, and the obvious rival explanation (the global pandemic-era inflation shock, which hit single-mandate central banks too) is not addressed. Judged on the inference only — the factual premises are Veracity's business.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is perhaps characteristic of the outgoing administration that where there could be one priority they tended to pick nine; that where there were three things that could have been achieved, they tried nine and achieved none.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of what the previous Government was generally like. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — strip out the part about the other side and nothing remains. Note this insults no individual, so Civility passes it cleanly; Focus is the attribute that catches it, and no Rigor score is emitted because a jibe is not an argument.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have committed to introducing this legislation within our first 100 days in Government, to make our intentions crystal clear, and I intend for this bill to be passed under urgency to amend the Act before Christmas.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument, the process (urgency), and two checkable deadlines — within the first 100 days, and passage before Christmas. Anyone could verify whether it happened by that date.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Let the message be very simple and very clear, let there be no confusion: ours is a Government which is going to get inflation under control.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an economic outcome — that inflation will be brought back under control under this Government. Not a promise about a specific legislative action but a claim about where the inflation rate will end up.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation: true if the annual rate returns to and holds within the Reserve Bank's 1–3% target band during this parliamentary term; false if it remains above 3% throughout.

civility.statement: This is an unnecessary, short-sighted bill. It is not evidence based. It won’t do the things that the National Party are telling New Zealanders it will do.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation aimed entirely at the bill and at what the party is claiming for it; no person is attacked, imputed bad faith or sneered at. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a measure is the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In a rare burst of honesty, we just heard a Green member finish her speech by saying this is a waste of time. I completely agree with her and that was a good description of the speech she gave.
civility.explanation: 'A rare burst of honesty' imputes habitual dishonesty to the member, and the follow-up turns her own words into mockery of her personally rather than engaging anything she argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We heard from Grant Robertson, and the most interesting thing in his speech was that he said he made it to seventh form—not something I would have guessed—but I think we can be pretty sure that he didn’t do maths or economics, because he tried to argue that because Australia has a dual mandate and England doesn’t, and England had higher inflation than Australia at one point, the argument of removing the dual mandate is wrong.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the person: sneering at Robertson's schooling and asserting he lacks the numeracy for the office he held. The substantive point about two data points could have been made without it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That, Madam Speaker, is why the people of New Zealand have put the empty rhetoric of the Chlöe Swarbricks and the Grant Robertsons over there and put the Government over here.
civility.explanation: Pluralising named members into 'the Chlöe Swarbricks and the Grant Robertsons' and dismissing them as 'empty rhetoric' is sneering at individuals, though it stops short of a direct insult to character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is an unnecessary, short-sighted bill. It is not evidence based. It won’t do the things that the National Party are telling New Zealanders it will do.
focus.explanation: Directed at the measure before the House and the specific claim made for it (that it will reduce the cost of living), but carried mostly as assertion with party framing rather than named mechanism or figures.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That, Madam Speaker, is why the people of New Zealand have put the empty rhetoric of the Chlöe Swarbricks and the Grant Robertsons over there and put the Government over here.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome appears — it is entirely about who the electorate rejected, framed around named opponents as types. This is the tribalism case rather than scrutiny of a commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: For New Zealand and Australia, who both have dual mandates, our inflation peaked at either 7.2 percent or 7.8 percent, but in the UK, which has got a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, inflation peaked at 11.1 percent. So there’s no correlation there, as the member opposite might like to say.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific peak inflation rates for New Zealand and/or Australia (7.2 or 7.8 percent) and for the United Kingdom (11.1 percent) during the recent inflation episode, and that NZ and Australia have dual central bank mandates while the UK has a primary price stability mandate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI, ABS CPI and UK ONS CPI peak annual rates for the 2022 inflation episode, plus the statutory objectives of the RBNZ, RBA and Bank of England. True if the peak prints match the figures quoted (within rounding) and the mandate descriptions are correct; false if any quoted peak is materially different or a mandate is mischaracterised.

veracity.statement: It was also, in large part, a response to the actions of the then just-departed National Party Prime Minister Sir Robert Muldoon, who ran riot as both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance and put New Zealand in a position where we almost went broke, where the Reserve Bank was required to make sure that it went to ambassadors overseas and asked them to draw down foreign currency on their credit cards because New Zealand’s foreign reserves had been drawn down so badly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Muldoon simultaneously held the offices of Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, that New Zealand's foreign reserves were exhausted to the point of near-insolvency, and that the Reserve Bank had overseas ambassadors draw down foreign currency on personal credit cards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary and Cabinet records of Muldoon's portfolios 1975-84, RBNZ and Treasury accounts of the 1984 foreign exchange crisis, and published histories/oral accounts of the reserves drawdown. True if Muldoon held both offices and contemporaneous records confirm reserves were effectively exhausted with the ambassador credit-card expedient used; false if either the portfolio claim or the credit-card episode is unsupported by the record.

veracity.statement: When we made the change to go the other way, we had a full public consultation process run by an independent panel and then we came back and then we put it through the House and put it through a select committee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government's change adding the employment objective to the Reserve Bank Act was preceded by public consultation conducted by an independent panel, and that the resulting bill went through a select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Reserve Bank Act Review Phase 1 documents (terms of reference, independent expert advisory panel membership, consultation submissions) and the parliamentary stages of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Monetary Policy) Amendment Bill. True if an independent panel ran a public consultation and the bill was referred to a select committee; false if either step is absent from the record.

rigor.statement: For New Zealand and Australia, who both have dual mandates, our inflation peaked at either 7.2 percent or 7.8 percent, but in the UK, which has got a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, inflation peaked at 11.1 percent. So there’s no correlation there, as the member opposite might like to say.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: 'no correlation' is inferred from a handful of country-episodes, with no control for the size of the shock, fiscal stance or energy exposure. Offering counterexamples does bear on a claimed universal relationship, which is why this is not lower, but the conclusion drawn is far stronger than the evidence supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know that some of the most horrific events of the 20th century were in part precipitated by hyperinflation across Europe. We know that when the Governments around the world went overboard with hyperinflation, or at least excessive money printing after the global financial crisis (GFC), we saw political instability. We know that when Governments printed too much money and created stagflation in the 1970s, we had economic and political instability that led to the reforms of the late 1970s and 1980s.
rigor.explanation: False analogy stacked on bare assertion: Weimar hyperinflation, post-GFC quantitative easing and 1970s stagflation are treated as one phenomenon and offered as grounds for removing a dual mandate, with nothing connecting those episodes to the statutory objective actually at issue. The repeated 'we know' asserts the premises rather than evidencing them.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For New Zealand and Australia, who both have dual mandates, our inflation peaked at either 7.2 percent or 7.8 percent, but in the UK, which has got a central bank with a primary price stability mandate, inflation peaked at 11.1 percent. So there’s no correlation there, as the member opposite might like to say.
specificity.explanation: Named countries, named mandate types and three precise inflation figures — someone could go and check every element of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Māori unemployment has risen to 7.6 percent in the year to 30 September 2023—up 1.2 percentage points.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific Stats NZ labour-market figure for Māori unemployment and a specific year-on-year change, as at 30 September 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey, Māori unemployment rate for the September 2023 quarter (year to 30 September 2023); true if the rate is 7.6% ± rounding and the annual change is approximately +1.2 percentage points, false if materially different on either number.

veracity.statement: Our economy is driven by agriculture and horticulture, but our farmers are dealing with the highest level of on-farm inflation in 40 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on-farm input cost inflation in the period referenced is the highest recorded in four decades.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published on-farm inflation series for 2022/23 (Beef + Lamb New Zealand Economic Service / Stats NZ Farm Expenses Price Index); true if the measured on-farm inflation rate for that year is the highest in the series going back roughly 40 years, false if a higher rate is recorded within that window.

specificity.statement: Māori unemployment has risen to 7.6 percent in the year to 30 September 2023—up 1.2 percentage points.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named population, a precise rate, a dated reference period and a quantified change — anyone could look it up and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The commitment to beating inflation starts with ensuring the Reserve Bank is returning to a single mandate of keeping down inflation.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism before the House — reverting the Reserve Bank to a single inflation mandate — but attaches no target, timeframe or expected magnitude to it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is a solid start to tackling inflation and reducing the cost of living for everyday Kiwis and businesses and strengthening our economy.
specificity.explanation: A summing-up claim with no figure, mechanism or timeframe — no stated expectation of how much inflation falls or by when, so there is nothing here to check against later.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know this change will disproportionately impact tangata whenua. Why? Because members opposite, in regard to this legislation and the looming Order Paper are taking us backwards, having no regard at all for vulnerable populations.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is a policy-effect claim (removing the employment mandate will fall hardest on Māori) but the reason offered — that members opposite have no regard for vulnerable populations — is an appeal to motive, not a mechanism connecting the mandate change to Māori employment outcomes. Non sequitur. The speaker supplies real supporting evidence elsewhere in the speech, but not here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At the moment, it’s costing so much more to grow and export a box of apples—the costs of the trees, the cost of the fertiliser, the cost of the petrol, the labour costs, the shipping costs, the logistics costs; they’ve all gone up because inflation is so high, but growers aren’t getting more for that box of apples in the market.
rigor.explanation: The inference from rising input costs plus flat output prices to a margin squeeze on growers is sound. The weak link is explanatory: 'they've all gone up because inflation is so high' explains rising prices by invoking the aggregate of rising prices, which is close to circular rather than identifying a cause.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is one thing to argue the cost and benefits of legislation; it is another thing to merely repeal it to pay back a few billionaires who will do well under neoliberal economics.
civility.explanation: Imputes a corrupt motive — that the repeal is a payback to wealthy donors rather than a policy judgement. Bad faith attributed to those advancing the bill, which is a civility failure rather than criticism of the measure itself.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Not only will this adversely affect Māori, but you can spray a fire hose across this House and not hit any Pasifika whānau. The Government benches are a disgrace in not having the voice of our Pasifika whānau endeavouring to blunt the brutal legislation.
focus.explanation: Turns from the bill to the composition and character of the Government benches. There is a thread back to representation in the debate, but no policy mechanism, figure or outcome is named — the weight of the passage is on who the other side is rather than what the measure does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: While the members opposite might be out of touch with what people around New Zealand are dealing with, this Government will be laser-focused on getting the cost of living under control and inflation under control, and we cannot do that by having a dual mandate.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — the dual mandate is named as the obstacle to controlling inflation — but it is wrapped in a content-free characterisation of the other side as 'out of touch'. Real substance carried inside party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, members opposite need to make up their minds; is the bill bad or does it do nothing? Because it can’t be both and the confusion apparent on the opposite benches is, I think, indicative of the kind of Government we had over the past six years—it couldn’t really decide if it was coming or going or what it was doing from one day to the next.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the other party: their alleged confusion, and from that a general characterisation of six years of their government as indecisive. No policy, figure, mechanism or named outcome is engaged. Scored on Focus only — strip out the material about the other side and no argument about the bill remains, so this is not a Rigor item.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, let me spell it out clearly: without amending the Act, the monetary policy committee would still be required to have regard to two separate objectives. As well as price stability they would also be having to weigh maximum sustainable employment.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what the legislation does and why the remit alone would not achieve it. No party framing in this passage.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I met a family months ago that said that despite everything they are doing—working harder than they’ve ever worked—despite the odd wage increase, they are going backwards. That is because inflation is out of control.
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote: a single reported family's experience is offered, and the causal conclusion ('that is because inflation is out of control') is asserted from it with no data and no ruling out of other causes. The inference reaches well past what one case can support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No matter what we do to focus on jobs, if people earn more but inflation is getting higher, that wage increase means nothing.
rigor.explanation: A real conditional inference about real wages: nominal gains offset by price rises. The logic holds in outline, but the conclusion is overstated — a wage increase outpaced by inflation is diminished, not literally worth nothing, and no threshold is given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And as the regulatory impact statement notes, there is value in amending the Act to signal a greater focus on price stability than that which could be achieved through mere tweaks to the remit alone.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but it rests on the authority of the official advice rather than on a reason given in the House: the RIS's judgement that legislative change signals more than a remit change is cited, not argued. There is also a gap between 'there is value in' and the conclusion that the amendment is needed.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to help these people, and we cannot keep going like we are, where people cannot afford to meet their mortgage payments.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the case for the bill but carries no checkable content: no figure, no mechanism, no timeframe, no named measure. 'Help these people' and 'we cannot keep going like we are' commit to nothing anyone could act on or verify.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, let me spell it out clearly: without amending the Act, the monetary policy committee would still be required to have regard to two separate objectives. As well as price stability they would also be having to weigh maximum sustainable employment.
specificity.explanation: Names the statutory mechanism precisely — what the Act requires of the monetary policy committee, which two objectives are in play, and what changes without amendment. Checkable against the Reserve Bank Act as it stood; no figures or dates, which is why it is not at the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So some questions have been asked and I am prepared to educate the members opposite.
civility.explanation: Condescension: casting opposing members as needing education rather than as making arguments to be answered. Short of a direct insult, but it is a posture toward the members rather than engagement with what they said, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine failure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We had a comment from the member Chlöe Swarbrick that the remit would still have reference to having regard to employment, and I want to clarify for that member that that is incorrect.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of fact that the incoming remit will contain no reference to having regard to employment, and that a contrary statement by another member is wrong. The assertion is the speaker's own, not relayed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Monetary Policy Remit issued by the Minister of Finance to the Reserve Bank following this Bill (December 2023). True if that remit contains a single operational objective of price stability and no requirement to have regard to maximum sustainable employment; false if the remit retains any 'have regard to' reference to employment.

veracity.statement: And I point to the data and the data shows that it was on the watch of the members opposite with their new experiment that we have had 2½ years of inflation outside the band.
veracity.explanation: A quantified claim about how long annual inflation ran outside the Reserve Bank's target band during the previous government's term. The 'new experiment' refers to the dual mandate introduced in 2018; the checkable content is the duration outside the band.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series against the Reserve Bank's 1–3% target band, over the previous Labour government's term. True if annual CPI inflation sat above 3% for approximately two and a half continuous years up to December 2023; false if the continuous period outside the band is materially shorter.

divination.statement: But this bill will not put a single cent more in people’s pockets by Christmas. It simply won’t happen.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill will produce no increase in household income before Christmas 2023.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The enacted text of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill and any associated fiscal measure: true if the bill contains no provision transferring money to households and no household payment or tax change attributable to it takes effect before 25 December 2023; false if any such provision took effect by that date.

veracity.statement: The Treasury’s forecast predicts that it will be back within the 1 to 3 percent range—which has been our range for a long time now—in a few months, within a few months in 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Treasury's then-current forecast said about when annual CPI inflation returns to the 1–3 percent target band.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update published December 2023, CPI inflation track: true if that forecast has annual CPI inside 1–3 percent within the first few months of 2024; false if it forecasts the return to band later in 2024 or beyond.

veracity.statement: If we look at the regulatory impact statement, because at least this bill has one, it says that Treasury itself, while it could support this approach, would prefer to do it through the monetary policy remit, through the Reserve Bank remit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of the regulatory impact statement for this bill — specifically that Treasury recorded a preference for changing the monetary policy remit rather than amending the Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement published with the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill: true if it records Treasury preferring to achieve the change via the monetary policy remit; false if it records no such preference or a preference for the legislative route.

veracity.statement: The second requirement of the Reserve Bank was introduced back in 2019, right before the country was about to hit its highest level of inflation in decades.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the Reserve Bank's second (employment) objective took effect in 2019, and that New Zealand subsequently reached its highest inflation in decades.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement date of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Monetary Policy) Amendment Act 2018, plus the Stats NZ CPI series: true if the maximum sustainable employment objective commenced in 2019 and the annual CPI peak that followed was the highest in at least two decades; false if either fails.

veracity.statement: The first three pieces of legislation we’re seeing in this period of urgency are about removing a focus on jobs and wages for ordinary New Zealanders and rolling back action on climate change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the first three bills taken in the December 2023 urgency motion were about.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Order Paper and Hansard record for the urgency motion of 12–14 December 2023: true if the first three bills taken were the Reserve Bank (Economic Objective) Amendment Bill plus bills repealing an employment/wages measure and a climate measure; false if the first three include bills that do neither.

veracity.statement: I will put that against our first package of legislation where we brought in a healthy homes guarantee, a winter energy payment, a Best Start payment, and paid parental leave—all before Christmas in 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that four named measures were legislated by her own government before Christmas 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Dates of enactment on the New Zealand legislation register for the Healthy Homes Guarantee Act (No 2) 2017, the Families Package (Income Tax and Benefits) Act 2017 (Winter Energy Payment and Best Start) and the Parental Leave and Employment Protection Amendment Act: true if all four passed before 25 December 2017; false if any passed later.

rigor.statement: The need for lower inflation has already been met. That particular target is being met and it will be achieved. So this bill is not needed for that purpose, and that is because inflation worldwide is trending down.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the current inflation trajectory says nothing about whether a permanent change to the Reserve Bank's statutory objective is warranted, and the argument also assumes what it needs to show — that a falling series proves the framework is adequate.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In other words, on the advice of the Minister of Finance, the monetary policy committee could set aside one or more of its economic goals for a short period of time in order to achieve a short-term objective. This objective of saying that maximum sustainable employment should rank differently from price stability could have been achieved through section 125 of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from a stated statutory premise, but with a gap she does not close: section 125 as she describes it gives a temporary power capped at 12 months, which does not establish that a permanent change to the statutory objective could have been achieved by that route.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: High inflation is the tyranny of any country. Milton Friedman said inflation is one of the forms of taxation that can be imposed without legislation. So it should not come as a surprise that a reasonable Government such as this National-led coalition Government has this bill as the first piece of legislation being introduced to the House in this term.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to authority: a Friedman aphorism about inflation being a hidden tax is offered as the support for the conclusion that this particular bill should be the Government's first legislative priority, and nothing connects the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Labour’s experiment of including an additional focus for the Reserve Bank has failed and we’re all paying for it—literally. Cost of living is out of control, everybody knows that.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc plus appeal to common knowledge: the dual mandate is blamed for the cost of living purely because one followed the other, and the only support offered for the premise is that 'everybody knows' it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is no evidence that these two things do not work in alignment. There is simply no evidence, and the regulatory impact statement that the Minister saw made that incredibly clear.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: the compatibility of price stability and employment objectives is asserted on the ground that nothing shows otherwise, which supports no conclusion either way.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And the interesting thing about section 125 of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act is it enables the Governor-General, by Order in Council, to direct the monetary policy committee to formulate and implement monetary policy for one or more economic objectives for a period not exceeding 12 months.
specificity.explanation: Names the section, the instrument, the decision-maker and the statutory time limit — a reader can go to the Act and check the mechanism described.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There was another mechanism available to do this, but that Government, banking on symbolism and on empty symbolism at that, has chosen to put this ridiculous bill into the House.
civility.explanation: Scathing about the bill and about the Government's motive collectively, but no individual member is attacked — the target throughout is the legislation and the choice to bring it, which is the expected standard for contested debate.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bill removes the Labour Party’s introduced target of maximum sustainable employment. It’s an applaudable target, but clearly trying to deliver it via the Reserve Bank is the wrong place and it needs to be corrected.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — names the provision being removed and argues about the right institutional vehicle for the objective, rather than about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can only but feel for members on the Government benches—that they’re coming down with the excitement of being in Government to pass legislation, and all it is to do is to repeal; to undo. Not to put forward a vision, not to put forward a positive change that they want to see for New Zealand, but to say what they’re going to undo and not what they’re going to do.
focus.explanation: Anchored loosely to the legislative programme, but the weight is a characterisation of the other side's outlook and lack of vision rather than any provision, cost or effect of the bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a Government that has said it will not do the analysis; it will not put itself through the scrutiny required by a regulatory impact statement.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny aimed at a named process — the regulatory impact statement requirement — rather than at the other party's character; a specific accountability mechanism is identified.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It really began for me in 2014 when the then Governor of the Reserve Bank, Graeme Wheeler, began hiking the official cash rate (OCR) even though at that point in time inflation was actually only running at 1.5 percent and unemployment was 5.6 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific macroeconomic readings at the time the RBNZ began raising the OCR in 2014: annual inflation of 1.5 percent and unemployment of 5.6 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ annual CPI inflation and HLFS unemployment rate for the quarters spanning the RBNZ's OCR increases from March 2014; true if annual CPI was about 1.5% and unemployment about 5.6% over that period, false if either figure was materially different (e.g. unemployment above 6% throughout).

veracity.statement: There is no relationship between the speed at which central banks have responded to rising inflation and their monetary policy mandate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an empirical cross-country regularity: how fast a central bank tightened during the post-2021 inflation surge is unrelated to whether it holds a single or dual mandate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cross-country comparison of policy-rate tightening start dates and cumulative pace over 2021-2023 (BIS policy rate database) against each central bank's statutory mandate; true if single-mandate and dual-mandate banks show no systematic difference in timing or pace, false if dual-mandate banks tightened materially later or more slowly.

veracity.statement: Also, long-term inflation expectations, which the member opposite, Nicola Willis, mentioned just before she sat down, haven’t actually changed significantly since the dual mandate came in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that long-horizon inflation expectations are essentially unchanged between the introduction of the employment objective in 2018 and December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Survey of Expectations five-year and ten-year ahead inflation expectation series, comparing readings around 2018 with those in late 2023; true if the two are within roughly 0.2 percentage points, false if long-horizon expectations shifted materially.

veracity.statement: As we went through COVID, one of the things that I am the most proud of is that we kept New Zealanders in work; that when we were faced with forecasts of unemployment up into the double digits, we worked hard across Government, across all the parts of Government, in making sure we did the things we needed to to keep them in work—the fiscal measures like the wage subsidy scheme and so on—but also what was done in terms of the monetary policy response.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official forecasts during COVID projected unemployment above 10 percent and that it did not eventuate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's 2020 COVID economic scenarios and Budget Economic and Fiscal Update forecasts, against the Stats NZ HLFS outturn for 2020-21; true if published official forecasts projected unemployment of 10% or more and the actual rate stayed well below that, false if no official forecast reached double digits.

veracity.statement: We also know that right now, we are the only country in the OECD that does not have a capital gains tax, a stamp duty, an inheritance tax, a ghost house tax, or any other form of taxation which is explicitly focused on addressing those inequities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand is unique among OECD members in having none of a listed set of capital, property-transfer, inheritance or vacant-property taxes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD Revenue Statistics and the OECD tax database for all member countries; true if no other OECD member lacks all of capital gains tax, stamp duty, inheritance/estate tax and a vacant-property tax, false if at least one other member also lacks the full set.

veracity.statement: We knew, because we ended up with an Official Information Act request back from the Government with advice both from the RBNZ and Treasury, that if those unconventional monetary policy means were pursued, we would end up with what they called distributional impacts—that is, an increase in or an exacerbation of inequality.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that RBNZ and Treasury advice released under the OIA warned that unconventional monetary policy (large-scale asset purchases) would have distributional impacts amounting to increased inequality.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RBNZ and Treasury advice on unconventional monetary policy released under the OIA in 2020; true if that advice identifies distributional impacts increasing inequality and recommends fiscal policy as the mitigation, false if no such advice was released or it reached the opposite conclusion.

specificity.statement: It really began for me in 2014 when the then Governor of the Reserve Bank, Graeme Wheeler, began hiking the official cash rate (OCR) even though at that point in time inflation was actually only running at 1.5 percent and unemployment was 5.6 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names the official, the year, the instrument and two numeric readings — anyone could go and check it against the published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We also know that right now, we are the only country in the OECD that does not have a capital gains tax, a stamp duty, an inheritance tax, a ghost house tax, or any other form of taxation which is explicitly focused on addressing those inequities.
specificity.explanation: Names four distinct tax instruments and a defined comparator group, so the claim can be checked instrument by instrument against OECD data.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He ended up increasing over that period of time the OCR from 2.5 to 3.5 percent and in doing so, given how low inflation was, all he actually achieved was unemployment going up.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal inference: the OCR rose and unemployment rose, so the rate rises are treated as the sole cause ('all he actually achieved'). No counterfactual, no other drivers considered, and no evidence linking the two beyond sequence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, I’ve heard from members opposite that this is a particularly dangerous thing to have these two objectives, that somehow or other, the perfectly capable people that we employ at Reserve Bank and on the monetary policy committee couldn’t possibly handle two thoughts in their head at one time.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opposing argument is that a dual mandate blurs the policy hierarchy when objectives conflict, not that MPC members are incapable of holding two thoughts. Restating it in an absurd form and then rebutting the absurd form does not defeat the actual claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, again, as we’ve heard and as is laid out in the regulatory impact statement, this bill is not necessary.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, grounded in a cited document rather than assertion, but it leans on the authority of the regulatory impact statement: a RIS assesses options and their costs, it does not itself conclude that legislation is unnecessary, so there is a gap between the source and the conclusion drawn from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I do think it’s worthwhile spending some time reflecting on the point from the Minister about why perceptions do matter, because I think that’s a really important and salient point, and, actually, it goes some way to some broader reflections that some members may like to make on the fact that so much of this stuff that we do inside of the economy is largely driven by perception and, therefore, is kind of made up, and that maybe talking down our economy or certain industries has real-world impacts.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: that economic outcomes are heavily influenced by expectations does not entail that they are 'kind of made up'. The concluding clause about real-world impacts in fact cuts against the inference it is offered to support.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We modernised this legislation to put it right up there with what was going on around the rest of the world in modern monetary policy, and this is the Government that wants to take it backwards.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath — international alignment of the mandate — but the sentence resolves into a party-versus-party framing ('this is the Government that wants to take it backwards') rather than naming a mechanism or an outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It won’t do a thing before Christmas, and actually, the main thing it is likely to do is cause damage over the long run in terms of how monetary policy operates.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the repeal of the employment objective will produce no cost-of-living effect before Christmas 2023, contrary to the Government member's stated rationale for urgency.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: RBNZ monetary policy decisions and Stats NZ CPI/cost-of-living measures between the bill's passage and 25 December 2023; true if no change in monetary policy settings or measured cost of living is attributable to the Act in that window, false if an identifiable cost-of-living effect followed before Christmas.

civility.statement: He’s living in the past.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the speaker himself as out of date rather than engaging the argument about the 1989 Act — condescending, but a mild jibe rather than an attack on character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When that Act came into force in 1989—in fact, in February of 1990—New Zealand was the first country to have this formally adopted inflation target as we know it, and it worked.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand was the first country in the world to formally adopt an inflation target, dating this to the commencement of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1989 in February 1990.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Central-bank and economic-history sources on the origin of inflation targeting (RBNZ history, Bank for International Settlements / IMF surveys of inflation-targeting regimes). True if New Zealand's 1990 Policy Targets Agreement is the first formal numerical inflation target adopted by any central bank; false if another country (e.g. Canada 1991, UK 1992, or an earlier regime) preceded it.

veracity.statement: I would note, actually, that when the first policy targets agreement was signed by the Government in 1990, inflation was running at 7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual CPI inflation was around 7 percent at the time the first Policy Targets Agreement was signed in 1990.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI series for the quarters around the signing of the first Policy Targets Agreement (March 1990). True if annual CPI inflation was approximately 7 percent; false if materially different (e.g. below 5 or above 9 percent).
