focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the policy, the spend and the outcome. This is scrutiny of a specific commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I suspect, had they not done what they’d done, they may not be where they are now—on that side of the House.
focus.explanation: Nothing about the measure before the House — it is about the other party's electoral defeat and where they now sit. No policy, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if that was the problem, then we close our roads down tomorrow, but we don’t do that either, do we.
rigor.explanation: False analogy. Road deaths and a drinking-water contamination outbreak are offered as equivalent, so that regulating one implies shutting the other; nothing is offered to establish the parallel, and the disanalogy (roads are not a preventable failure of a single supply system) is what the argument needs to overcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And we heard the Hon Kieran McAnulty talk about all the savings that were going to be made. Well, the reality was that if you put in massive gains in efficiency into one model but you don’t put them into any other, of course you’re going to make it look as though it’s cheaper.
rigor.explanation: A genuine methodological objection: if efficiency gains are applied only to the counterfactual you favour, the comparison is rigged. The conclusion (the savings are an artefact of the modelling) tracks the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: By and large, those are exactly the same people as were paying for it already: the ratepayers. So there was nothing free.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference: if the ultimate payers under the new model are the same population as the ratepayers under the old, the cost has been relabelled rather than removed. The conclusion follows from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It became a hugely divisive policy after a great big race war centred around Te Tiriti o Waitangi, Māori rights, and co-governance was propagated around the country.
rigor.explanation: A causal claim — the policy was not inherently divisive, it was made so by a campaign — offered with nothing to connect the two. The inference rests on assertion alone, though it is a claim about the policy's reception rather than a jibe at opponents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s Gareth Morgan, one of the leading economic minds of this country, describing Māori rights to water. And I’ll just summarise it by saying he concludes by saying this: “Māori own the water”.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority, and to an authority outside the relevant field: an economist's standing is offered as the support for a conclusion about Treaty and property rights in water. No reasoning from Morgan's case is reproduced — only that he reached it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And we heard the Hon Kieran McAnulty talk about all the savings that were going to be made. Well, the reality was that if you put in massive gains in efficiency into one model but you don’t put them into any other, of course you’re going to make it look as though it’s cheaper.
civility.explanation: Names a minister and attacks his modelling and its assumptions, not the man. Robust criticism of substance is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I guess my friends on this side of the House wouldn’t understand a concept like te mauri o te taiao, but I can give you a quick little example.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at other members personally — an assertion that they are incapable of grasping a concept, followed by an offer to explain it simply. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the members rather than their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Having endured the 88,000 submissions through a long period on the Finance and Expenditure Committee that some of us endured—and I’m looking at the other side of the House here at Ingrid Leary who also had to endure that dreadful thing—it is an absolute pleasure to be talking today about repealing it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Finance and Expenditure Committee received 88,000 submissions on the water services legislation it considered last term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Finance and Expenditure Committee's report on the Water Services Entities Bill and the associated Parliament submission tallies; true if the recorded number of submissions is approximately 88,000, false if materially different (e.g. an order of magnitude out).

veracity.statement: Well, actually, we’ve been doing a lot, and if you look at the Department of Internal Affairs website, you will see that there was a royal commission of inquiry into the Havelock North affair, which started in mid-2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the inquiry into the Havelock North drinking water contamination was a royal commission of inquiry and that it began in mid-2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The inquiry's own terms of reference and the DIA/Government Inquiry record: true if it was constituted as a royal commission and commenced around mid-2017; false if it was a different form of inquiry (e.g. a Government Inquiry under the Inquiries Act) or was established at a materially different date.

veracity.statement: I do remember the other instance of déjà vu I had was while sitting on that side of the House, watching the Hon Matt Doocey on this side saying, “When we become Government, we’re going to co-invest.”—that is on Hansard—and yet there is nothing in this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Matt Doocey stated in the House, while in opposition, that a National-led government would co-invest with councils on water infrastructure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of Matt Doocey's speeches during the previous parliamentary term on the three waters legislation; true if he is recorded committing a future National government to co-investment with councils, false if no such statement appears.

veracity.statement: Standard & Poor’s have basically said that you need to have balance sheet separation in order for councils to be able to borrow more.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the credit rating agency Standard & Poor's has stated that balance sheet separation of water entities is required for councils to increase borrowing capacity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published Standard & Poor's commentary or ratings reports on New Zealand local government and the three waters reforms; true if S&P is on record linking balance sheet separation to increased borrowing headroom for councils, false if no such published position exists or if S&P's stated position is contrary.

veracity.statement: There is insufficient detail here for any devil to be able to have a look at, and so it’s going to be really interesting to see how this Government comes up with a plan to save ratepayers’ moneys, because the Minister today said that rates are not going to go up—nevertheless that Far North District Council’s looking at 33 percent rate increases, the West Coast council’s at 30 percent, Hamilton at 25.5 percent, and the Mayor of Porirua just said today 18 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Far North District Council is contemplating a 33 percent rates increase, the West Coast council 30 percent, Hamilton 25.5 percent, and that the Mayor of Porirua stated 18 percent on the day of the speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2024/25 draft annual plan or long-term plan consultation documents for Far North District Council, the relevant West Coast council and Hamilton City Council, plus reported remarks by the Mayor of Porirua on 13 February 2024; true if the proposed average rates increases match the figures within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: No communities of interest were considered when these boundaries were set up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that communities of interest played no part in how the water services entity boundaries were drawn.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Water Services Entities Act and the Department of Internal Affairs boundary design papers and cabinet papers setting out the criteria used for the four-entity model; true if communities of interest appear nowhere among the stated criteria, false if they are among the factors recorded as considered.

rigor.statement: The big issue with the previous economic efficiency and consumer bill was that it assumes that these entities were all about making profit and ripping off New Zealanders; that, of course, was the wrong approach and that’s why the overzealous economic regulations were totally inappropriate.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the conclusion that the regulations were 'totally inappropriate' rests entirely on the premise that the bill assumed the entities were profit-seeking. Economic regulation of monopoly infrastructure is normally justified by the absence of competition rather than by an assumption of profiteering, and no support is offered for the attributed assumption before it is used to carry the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Minister of Local Government earlier today said there is a pressing need to move on these water reforms, and yet the bill that is tabled by the other side of the House is just the repeal of the previous Government’s bill, of the previous Government’s work.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: an asserted urgency is set against the content of the bill actually before the House, and the tension follows. Small gap — a repeal can be the first step of a staged programme, which the argument does not address.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I mean, as the great President of Argentina, Javier Milei, says, collectivism does not work. This was a great example of collectivism that would have spiralled out of control, and it needs to be repealed.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority — a foreign leader's slogan is offered as the premise — followed by a slippery slope: nothing is supplied to connect the legislation to 'spiralled out of control', and the label 'collectivism' does the work of an argument about the entity model.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The big issue with the previous economic efficiency and consumer bill was that it assumes that these entities were all about making profit and ripping off New Zealanders; that, of course, was the wrong approach and that’s why the overzealous economic regulations were totally inappropriate.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: names the specific bill and the regulatory design at issue, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Minister of Local Government earlier today said there is a pressing need to move on these water reforms, and yet the bill that is tabled by the other side of the House is just the repeal of the previous Government’s bill, of the previous Government’s work.
focus.explanation: Names the measure before the House and what it does and does not contain. Legitimate scrutiny of a stated government commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These are increases that are going on to ratepayers, that this Government has done none of the work on in order to be able to provide that pressing need, that pressing solution, except for removing an actual policy solution that has Standard & Poor’s stated approval, which allows a balance sheet separation so that those entities can borrow more to bring down the cost of that infrastructure project across the time so that it’s cheaper for our ratepayers.
focus.explanation: Engages the financing mechanism itself: balance sheet separation, borrowing capacity, and the effect on rates over the life of the infrastructure. Named policy, named consequence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, it divided up Marlborough, and Marlborough ratepayers were going to be either on one side of the border and be in one entity or the other.
focus.explanation: A concrete consequence of the repealed legislation — entity boundaries splitting a named district — rather than a comment about the party that passed it.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we want to ensure is that New Zealanders do get access to high quality water, but we want to make sure that the decision making for that occurs at a local level.
specificity.explanation: Names one mechanism — decision making retained at local level — but gives no standard, threshold, funding figure or timeframe; 'high quality water' is left undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There is insufficient detail here for any devil to be able to have a look at, and so it’s going to be really interesting to see how this Government comes up with a plan to save ratepayers’ moneys, because the Minister today said that rates are not going to go up—nevertheless that Far North District Council’s looking at 33 percent rate increases, the West Coast council’s at 30 percent, Hamilton at 25.5 percent, and the Mayor of Porirua just said today 18 percent.
specificity.explanation: Four named councils each with a numbered proposed rates increase, tied to a dated statement by the Minister. Directly checkable against council planning documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: These are increases that are going on to ratepayers, that this Government has done none of the work on in order to be able to provide that pressing need, that pressing solution, except for removing an actual policy solution that has Standard & Poor’s stated approval, which allows a balance sheet separation so that those entities can borrow more to bring down the cost of that infrastructure project across the time so that it’s cheaper for our ratepayers.
civility.explanation: A hard charge — that the Government has done none of the work and is removing the only funded solution — aimed entirely at the policy and the record. No person is attacked, no bad faith imputed to anyone personally.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In Gore, 13,000 residents face $435 million worth of infrastructure costs with the peel back of the affordable water.
specificity.explanation: Named town, population figure, dollar figure and the policy change it is attributed to. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is an assault on homeowners, it’s an assault on ratepayers, it’s an assault on renters, who will have costs passed on to them, and it doesn’t do anything to assure people that this Government has a plan for affordable water.
specificity.explanation: A rhetorical triad with no figure, mechanism or timeframe; the repeated 'assault' framing commits to nothing checkable, even though the surrounding speech was detailed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The first bill, which we’ll be passing by the middle of 2024, will set out provisions relating to council service delivery plans and transitional economic regulations.
specificity.explanation: Names the legislative vehicle, its content (council service delivery plans, transitional economic regulation) and a passage date. No dollar figures, but concrete and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In Gore, 13,000 residents face $435 million worth of infrastructure costs with the peel back of the affordable water.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Gore's water infrastructure liability under the repeal is $435 million for a population of about 13,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Gore District Council's long-term plan / three waters infrastructure cost estimates and Stats NZ population for Gore district: true if the district's stated water infrastructure cost is ~$435m against a population of ~13,000, false if the figure is materially different or covers something other than water infrastructure.

veracity.statement: The last Labour Government, while they were in Government and in power, had all the time and resources and votes to do something, and they did not.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2017–2023 Labour Government took no action on water infrastructure despite having the time, resources and parliamentary majority to do so.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Legislative record for the 2017–2023 term and DIA reporting on the Three Waters / Affordable Water Reforms programme: true if no water reform legislation was enacted and no delivery entities or funding programmes were established, false if the Water Services Entities Act 2022 and associated Acts were passed and reform funding was allocated to councils.

veracity.statement: The previous Government’s lack of trust in local councils led to the imposition of a mandatory and centralised co-governed 10-entity water model—a model that spent $1.25 billion without even implementing their policy approach.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts: that the previous Government's model was a mandatory, centralised, co-governed 10-entity structure, and that $1.25 billion was spent on it before any of it was implemented.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Water Services Entities Act 2022 (as amended in 2023) for the entity count and governance structure, and Treasury/DIA/Auditor-General reporting on cumulative spend on the Three Waters reform programme to December 2023: true if the reported spend is ~$1.25b and no entity had begun delivering services, false if the reported spend is materially lower or entities had commenced operation.

rigor.statement: This is why southern mayors have been pleading for the affordable water reforms to stay. It’s because what is needed is scale and efficiency, and what the Government has said to date provides neither of those.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy — scale and efficiency are needed, the Government's plan supplies neither — but the key premise is asserted rather than shown, and the support offered is an appeal to the mayors' authority.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I support this bill because many voters have openly called out for the last Labour Government to stop the mega-merge into the three—and then later, 10—services entities.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity: the stated reason for supporting the repeal is that many voters called for it, which offers nothing about whether the merge was a good or bad way to deliver water services.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Council-controlled organisations can help make those long-term decisions and raise that long-term debt and spread that cost over the life of those assets rather than upon ratepayers today.
rigor.explanation: A genuine mechanism argument: separate borrowing capacity allows the cost of long-lived assets to be matched to their life rather than funded from current rates. The inference tracks; it is only weakened by not addressing whether debt-constrained councils can in fact raise that debt.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government’s solution does not respond to the question of who is going to pay, and what the Minister has said is that there will be some kind of regulatory solution. That is a wholly inadequate answer.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: identifies a specific gap in the Government's proposal (funding responsibility) and the Minister's stated answer to it. Scrutiny of a named policy, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill serves as a decisive step in stopping Labour’s unpopular and divisive three waters regime.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy regime and the bill's effect on it, but the weight of the sentence is party framing ('Labour's unpopular and divisive') rather than the mechanism or the outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I feel sorry for the mayors who are sitting in the gallery today, because I don’t think they’ll be around very long once they have to implement the rates hikes that they will be implementing in their councils.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the sitting mayors present — including the Otago and Southland mayors she has named — will lose office as a consequence of the rates rises they must impose. Not a promise about her own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Results of the October 2025 New Zealand local body elections for the Otago/Southland mayors referenced (Clutha, Central Otago, Gore, Dunedin): true if a clear majority of the incumbent mayors named are voted out or do not return to office, false if most are returned.

civility.statement: This is an assault on homeowners, it’s an assault on ratepayers, it’s an assault on renters, who will have costs passed on to them, and it doesn’t do anything to assure people that this Government has a plan for affordable water.
civility.explanation: Fierce language aimed entirely at the Government's policy and its effects. No individual is attacked, no bad faith imputed to a person — under the re-anchored scale this is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I wanted to make a mention, when the member talks about the visitors that we have in the gallery—our mayors—about watching their back and no longer having a job, that she should probably look up. Because the mayors are really shaking their head and disagreeing with the member’s comments.
civility.explanation: A pointed rebuttal that edges toward the person — 'she should probably look up' is a mild condescension aimed at the member rather than at her argument — but stops well short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The first point that I would make is that if this was such a crowning glory for the Government, wouldn’t the Minister of Local Government want to use the whole time that he has—10 minutes—to explain why?
focus.explanation: A measure is before the House, but this engages the Minister's use of his speaking time rather than any provision, cost or mechanism of the repeal. No policy content is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And this touches on this Government’s priorities; they’re more than happy to give money away to landlords but won’t invest in core, key infrastructure.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy contrast underneath (interest deductibility for landlords versus water infrastructure funding), but it is carried as a general charge about the Government's character and priorities rather than a named measure or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This will cost ratepayers more and it will not lead to more affordable water services that meet the regulatory requirements. That’s not just us saying that; it is the Minister’s own advice.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister's own departmental advice concluded the repeal would raise ratepayer costs and fail to deliver affordable, compliant water services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Department of Internal Affairs regulatory impact statement and Ministerial advice on the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill (Dec 2023 – Feb 2024); true if that advice states repeal will increase ratepayer costs or fail the affordability/regulatory-compliance objective, false if the advice contains no such assessment.

veracity.statement: It is quite clear that the only way to achieve the level of expenditure across all councils—noting that there are a very small number of councils that are in a particular position, unique to themselves, but on the whole, across the board, $185 billion needs to be spent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a national three-waters investment requirement of $185 billion across all councils.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The DIA / Water Industry Commission for Scotland estimate of national three-waters infrastructure investment need to 2050-51 cited in the reform documents; true if the published figure is approximately $185b, false if the official estimate is materially lower (e.g. the $120b–$185b range's lower bound is the operative figure).

veracity.statement: The Tararua District Council, which is part of northern Wairarapa and southern Hawke’s Bay, has 12,000 ratepayers. Obviously, there are more people living there, but there are 12,000 rating units in that area. They need to find $600 million over the next 30 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Tararua District Council has 12,000 rating units and faces $600 million of water infrastructure cost over 30 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tararua District Council's rating-unit count in its 2021-31 long-term plan / annual report, and its stated water infrastructure investment requirement to ~2054; true if both figures match within rounding, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: They have broken a promise. They stood here in the House—they went to every single district council in the country and said, “If you back us, we’ll back you.” They said, “We will help fund your infrastructure.” It’s not true. There’s been no announcement of funding.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming Government undertook to help fund council water infrastructure and that, as at 13 February 2024, no such funding had been announced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government and coalition-party statements to councils/LGNZ before the 2023 election, plus the record of Ministerial funding announcements between 27 November 2023 and 13 February 2024; true if a funding undertaking was given and no funding announcement had been made by that date, false if any council water infrastructure funding had been announced.

veracity.statement: The National Party started this process under the Hon Anne Tolley. Anne Tolley recognised that there was a problem and started this work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the three waters reform process was begun by a National-led government with Anne Tolley as the responsible Minister.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: DIA records and Cabinet papers for the Three Waters Review; true if the review was initiated 2016-17 while Anne Tolley held the Local Government portfolio, false if it was initiated under a different government or minister.

rigor.statement: I’ve heard nothing to suggest that the Government has a solution to that other than allowing them to do council-controlled organisations. They already can and it hasn’t worked. Look at Auckland; that’s unaffordable. Look at Wellington; that has not worked.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy, and a weak one: it rests on an argument from absence of evidence ('I've heard nothing to suggest') and generalises from two anecdotal cases (Auckland, Wellington) to every council in the country.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I absolutely oppose the language being used by the Minister, saying that this will force councils to spend money on the necessities rather than the nice-to-haves. How offensive is that to hard-working councillors and mayors who are trying their hardest to make sure that they are investing in infrastructure with the limited means that they have?
civility.explanation: Sharp and indignant, but the target is the Minister's framing of council spending, not the Minister himself. Pointed enough to edge toward the person without landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This repeal is unnecessary, it is irresponsible, and it is lazy. It is lazy because, in politics, you need to show leadership even when things aren’t popular. What they are trying to do is cynical.
civility.explanation: Harsh words about the repeal itself would pass cleanly, but 'lazy' and 'cynical' impute motive rather than describe the measure — a charge of bad faith against those promoting it, short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Tararua District Council, which is part of northern Wairarapa and southern Hawke’s Bay, has 12,000 ratepayers. Obviously, there are more people living there, but there are 12,000 rating units in that area. They need to find $600 million over the next 30 years.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific council, a rating-unit count, a dollar figure and a timeframe; someone could go and check every element against the council's long-term plan.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can imagine that Christchurch, Selwyn, and Waimakariri might join together, but why the hell would they voluntarily accept Ashburton, where, without reform, each individual ratepayer is facing $8,690 each year, by 2051, just for water?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific councils, a per-ratepayer annual dollar figure and the year it applies to — fully checkable against the reform modelling.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We’ll either have councils going bankrupt or councils not meeting their regulatory requirements in terms of water standards.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that under the repealed settings councils will end up either insolvent or in breach of the water regulator's standards.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Whether, by the resolve-by date, any New Zealand territorial authority becomes insolvent or is placed under Crown/statutory intervention for inability to fund water services, OR Taumata Arowai formally records councils failing drinking-water or wastewater standards on funding grounds. True if either occurs; false if all councils remain solvent and compliant.

civility.statement: So I guess I am not sure if I’m old enough to make this speech according to the last member, Julie Anne Genter.
civility.explanation: A light riposte to another member's remark about his age; it names her but lands no attack on her character or competence. He had a clear opening to hit back and did not take it.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But, look, the repeal of three waters is not just a relief to many New Zealanders, it’s symbolic of the broader change in direction away from centralised instincts of Labour and back towards empowering local communities.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the Three Waters repeal), but most of the sentence is directional party framing about Labour's 'instincts' rather than the policy's mechanism or effects.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There was no requirement for councils to reduce rates, reflecting the fact that they will no longer be supplying total water services.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Water Services Entities Act 2022 and the Water Services Legislation Bill: true if no provision required territorial authorities to reduce rates on transfer of water services to a water services entity; false if any such requirement or mandated rates adjustment existed.

veracity.statement: The ACT-National coalition agreement delivered stopwork notices to the three waters work stream.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition agreement resulted in stop-work notices being served on the Three Waters programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–ACT coalition agreement and Department of Internal Affairs / National Transition Unit records: true if stop-work notices were issued to the Three Waters work programme following that agreement, false if no stop-work instruction was issued.

veracity.statement: There was an interesting one from the Hon McAnulty which, in the end, exposed the $1.2 billion already spent on three waters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $1.2 billion had already been spent on the Three Waters programme, per a question-time answer that day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Internal Affairs / Treasury reported expenditure on the Three Waters (Affordable Water Reform) programme as at February 2024, and the Hansard record of the Minister of Local Government's answer that day: true if roughly $1.2 billion had been spent, false if the reported figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: I would also say to the previous member’s comment, New Zealand actually has one of the OECD’s most centralised tax systems.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's tax system is among the most centralised in the OECD, i.e. that local government raises an unusually small share of total tax revenue.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD Revenue Statistics, share of total tax revenue collected by sub-central (state/local) government: true if New Zealand ranks among the lowest few OECD members on that share, false if it sits mid-range or higher.

rigor.statement: We all know the status quo isn’t up to scratch, but Labour’s bureaucratic co-governed regime was never the answer.
rigor.explanation: Engages a named policy but the conclusion rests on an appeal to common assent ('we all know') and a bare assertion; nothing is offered to connect co-governance to the claimed failure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is the sort of thing that means that a place like Tauranga doesn’t have leaks running down the street, and it’s somewhere that is working well with its water infrastructure.
rigor.explanation: Argument from a single personal anecdote: one leak fixed on his own property is generalised to a city-wide conclusion about Tauranga's water infrastructure performance. No data connects the metering incentive to the outcome claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Three waters would have been great for middle-managers but a disaster for water users, with layers and layers of bureaucracy separating decision makers from the people.
specificity.explanation: Characterises the effect of a policy without a single figure, mechanism or named provision; 'layers and layers of bureaucracy' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But this Government will introduce fiscal incentives for councils to enable more housing, including looking at sharing with councils a proportion of GST collected on new residential builds to help fund infrastructure like pipes and encourage councils to get more houses built.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (sharing GST on new residential builds with councils), but gives no proportion, no threshold and no date, and hedges it as 'looking at'.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It has stirred up absolute hysteria and fear and made it divisive, despite it being a relatively sensible proposal, because, when those parties were in Opposition, they were desperate to do anything to get people to vote for them and to attack the Government of the day.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the governing parties' motives — that they whipped up fear to win votes. The only policy touch is the bare assertion that the reform was 'relatively sensible'; no mechanism, cost, figure or named provision. Party framing carries the whole statement.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There’s still huge opportunities to do things better; we maintain that stormwater should rest with councils, not the independent entities.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the legislation before the House — which body should hold stormwater responsibility. A named institutional design question, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister of Local Government, the Minister of Transport, Simeon Brown, is an absolute ideological extremist who would fit in with the Republicans in the United States, campaigning against access to reproductive health for women at university.
civility.explanation: A sustained attack on a named member's character and motives — 'absolute ideological extremist' — rather than on any policy he is responsible for. The comparison to US Republicans is used as a slur on the person, not an argument about transport or water policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s coming from a Minister who is extremely inexperienced in life, and who, frankly, believes his own hysterical rhetoric because he is an extremist.
civility.explanation: Attacks the Minister personally — his life experience, his sincerity, his character — rather than the transport priorities being disputed. 'Extremely inexperienced in life' goes to the man, not the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Minister of Local Government, the Minister of Transport, Simeon Brown, is an absolute ideological extremist who would fit in with the Republicans in the United States, campaigning against access to reproductive health for women at university.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Simeon Brown, while a university student, campaigned against women's access to reproductive health services. The 'ideological extremist' part is opinion; only the campaigning claim is checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary records of Simeon Brown's student politics at the University of Auckland — AUSA minutes/referendum records and student-press or news reporting from that period. True if he publicly campaigned or voted against the students' association providing or referring for abortion or contraception services; false if no such record exists.

veracity.statement: Now, in Aotearoa New Zealand, one of the lowest share of national revenue gathered is actually gathered by and spent by local government.
veracity.explanation: A comparative claim about the present: that local government in New Zealand collects and spends an unusually small share of total public revenue by international standards. The sentence is garbled in delivery but the intended comparison is plain.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD/IMF general government finance statistics (or Stats NZ local authority financial statistics) on the subnational share of total public revenue and expenditure. True if New Zealand's local-government share sits among the lowest in the OECD; false if it is at or above the OECD median.

veracity.statement: They have capital gains taxes, they have inheritance taxes.
veracity.explanation: Asserted of 'the countries we like to compare ourselves to' two sentences earlier. Two distinct claims: that those comparators tax capital gains, and that they also levy inheritance taxes. Both must hold for the sentence to stand as stated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD tax database entries for the countries New Zealand conventionally compares itself to (Australia, the UK, Canada, Ireland). True only if those comparators levy both a capital gains tax and an inheritance/estate tax; false if prominent comparators lack an inheritance tax.

veracity.statement: Because what you will find is that the National Party, the National-led Government, is spending the vast majority of the money on highways in the cities, in the very places where they are the most counter-productive.
veracity.explanation: A claim about current allocation: that most transport capital spending under this Government goes to urban highway building. 'Counter-productive' is opinion; only the share-of-spending claim is checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2024 Government Policy Statement on land transport and NZTA's National Land Transport Programme allocations. True if a majority of the transport capital budget is allocated to state-highway projects in urban areas; false if the majority goes to other modes, maintenance, or non-urban routes.

rigor.statement: To say that speed bumps and speed management and red-light cameras and bike lanes are the cause of all our problems is just utter, absurd nonsense.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: no opponent claims traffic-calming measures cause 'all our problems'. She inflates the opposing position to an absurdity and then dismisses it by assertion, offering nothing to rebut the narrower claim actually made. This is a real inference about a real policy, so it belongs here rather than to Focus.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is an absurd statement, because it is the lowest cost, highest value transport investments we can make, and we know this from many, many economic evaluations.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument about the policy, but the conclusion leans on an appeal to unnamed authority — 'many, many economic evaluations' — with no study, agency or benefit-cost ratio identified. The inference would hold if the evaluations said what she says, but nothing is offered to show that.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve lived in other countries, so I can speak to this with particular lived experience; it’s possible to do things much better.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote: having lived abroad is offered as the warrant for the conclusion that New Zealand could do far better on tax and infrastructure funding. Personal residence is not evidence about fiscal settings, and no observation from that experience is actually supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re comparing maybe $10 million on bike lanes with $10 billion needed on pipes.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete figures set against each other, enough for someone to check the order-of-magnitude claim. Marked down from the top because 'maybe' hedges the first number and neither figure is tied to a named budget, agency or period.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There’s still huge opportunities to do things better; we maintain that stormwater should rest with councils, not the independent entities.
specificity.explanation: Names a definite, checkable policy position (stormwater with councils rather than the water services entities), which is well past a slogan. Short of the top because no cost, timeframe or drafting change is attached to it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It was subsequent central governments pushing more and more responsibility on to local councils without ever offering the proper funding for them to carry out those responsibilities.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a real mechanism — devolution of responsibilities to councils unmatched by funding — which is more than a platitude, but no statute, transfer, period or dollar figure is named, so nobody could go and check which shifts she means.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the event in 2016 in Havelock North, four people died and up to 5,000 people became ill from drinking contaminated water.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific death toll (four) and illness figure (up to 5,000) for the 2016 Havelock North campylobacter outbreak.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government Inquiry into Havelock North Drinking Water (2017) Stage 1 report and Hawke's Bay DHB outbreak figures: true if the report attributes around four deaths to the outbreak and estimates illness at or above roughly 5,000 people; false if the recorded death toll or illness estimate is materially lower.

specificity.statement: In the event in 2016 in Havelock North, four people died and up to 5,000 people became ill from drinking contaminated water.
specificity.explanation: A named event, a year, a death count and an illness count — fully checkable, and she could easily have said only that people got sick from bad water.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government’s approach of scrapping the reforms—scrapping the Natural and Built Environment Act, scrapping the Spatial Planning Act, and now scrapping the water services Acts—is a huge missed opportunity to build on the work that has been done so far and is now leaving councils and communities facing years of uncertainty.
specificity.explanation: Three named Acts give it real checkable content, but the harm is left as 'years of uncertainty' — no duration, cost or mechanism attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Councils need sustainable funding mechanisms, and central government should be listening not only to local government but to the wider recommendations of the Future for Local Government review that has many improvements that would have aided us in our water services challenges ahead.
specificity.explanation: Points at a named source of proposals (the Future for Local Government review) but names none of them, and 'sustainable funding mechanisms' carries no amount, instrument or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we really need is Local Water Done Well, and we will deliver that.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, which is more than a slogan, but supplies no mechanism, funding, or delivery date — nothing here that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Simply put, the infrastructure of our water is not sustainable and it is a human failing, not an environment failing.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premise she has just offered — an inquiry finding systemic failure across services, provision, regulation and source protection does support 'human failing, not environment failing'. The small gap is generalising from one outbreak to the sustainability of the whole system.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I really want to use councils as an example here, because councils are typically made up of people from very diverse backgrounds, with different views, and despite these differences in opinion, councils ultimately figure out how to work together. And it prompts me to beg the question: why is it so hard for this Government to work constructively?
rigor.explanation: A weak analogy plus a loaded question: nothing is offered to show councils and central government face comparable incentives, and the closing question presupposes its own answer rather than establishing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Every 500 metres we would see a “stop three waters” sign, and the disgusting race division that was not perpetrated by Māori but was from white right-wing fragility.
focus.explanation: Characterises the motives of the reform's opponents rather than engaging the measure before the House. No mechanism, cost, figure or outcome is named; strip out the claim about who the other side really are and no policy content remains. (No individual is attacked, so Civility is untouched; and with no argument left once the party-directed part is removed, Rigor is not scored.)
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I had the privilege of serving on Canterbury Regional Council for two terms, and it was rather disconcerting over that time to see the misinformation and deliberate drumming up of race-based rhetoric not only from our current Government now but from local government elected members too.
focus.explanation: Aimed at what the Government and other elected members are like rather than at the repeal itself; no policy, figure or outcome is named. The council-service detail is biographical framing, not policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government’s approach of scrapping the reforms—scrapping the Natural and Built Environment Act, scrapping the Spatial Planning Act, and now scrapping the water services Acts—is a huge missed opportunity to build on the work that has been done so far and is now leaving councils and communities facing years of uncertainty.
focus.explanation: Names three specific statutes and a specific claimed consequence for councils. Legitimate scrutiny of a named government programme — the job of an opposition MP, and squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As I said when I spoke earlier, what we actually saw—and the High Court agreed—is that the last Government was going through a process which the courts said was expropriation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the High Court characterised the previous Government's water reform process as expropriation of council assets — a claim about what a court actually held, not about whether the reform was wise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court judgments in the judicial review proceedings brought by councils against the Three Waters / Water Services Entities reforms (e.g. the 2023 NZHC council challenges); true if a judgment describes the transfer of council water assets as expropriation, false if no judgment makes such a finding or if the courts expressly declined to so characterise it.

veracity.statement: You wouldn’t get 88,000 submissions—the vast majority of them against it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a submission count (88,000) on the water services legislation and that most of those submissions opposed it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Finance and Expenditure Committee's report on the Water Services Entities Bill and the associated departmental submission analysis; true if roughly 88,000 submissions were received and a clear majority were recorded as opposed, false if the count or the opposed proportion is materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, we’ve heard that the leader of the Labour Party has acknowledged that people weren’t taken with them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Labour leader has publicly conceded the previous Government failed to bring the public along on the water reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements and interviews by the Labour leader (Chris Hipkins) on the Three Waters / Affordable Water reforms; true if he has stated the reforms did not carry public support or that the public was not brought along, false if no such acknowledgement exists.

veracity.statement: And one of those areas where you can be more efficient is the previous legislation—the legislation which is being repealed—went all the way down to two houses constituted a local water scheme; two houses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the water legislation being repealed captured supplies serving as few as two houses. Note the ambiguity to be resolved: the two-dwelling threshold appears in the drinking-water regulation regime, which may not be among the statutes repealed by this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The definition of a drinking water supply / water supplier in the statutes repealed by this bill and in the Water Services Act 2021; true if the repealed legislation applies to supplies serving two or more dwellings, false if that threshold sits only in legislation not being repealed or if the threshold is higher.

rigor.statement: I think, by and large, the power bill is paid for by the tenant. So who do you think was going to pay the water bill when it’s separated out and it’s charged on a meter? I don’t think it was going to be the landlord; I think it was going to be the renter.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy from electricity billing to metered water billing, answering the objection that the reforms protected renters. The inference is plausible and the mechanism (separate metered charge, as with power) does track, but it rests on the analogy alone and on 'I don't think' rather than on tenancy or billing evidence, so there is a real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, basically, what we’re hearing from the Opposition benches there is that some of the councils which are in better condition wouldn’t do it of their own volition, so we’ll force them to do it.
rigor.explanation: Engages a real policy feature (the four-entity structure and its cross-subsidies) but restates the Opposition's position in a form they did not advance — a strawman. The conclusion attributed to them ('so we'll force them') is Foster's own inference from the amalgamation design, presented as what they said.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That’s not good faith, but the process of the legislation that we are getting rid of today and over this week did exactly that.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith, but to a legislative process and the previous Government collectively rather than to any individual member. Pointed and edging toward motive, without landing on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And one of those areas where you can be more efficient is the previous legislation—the legislation which is being repealed—went all the way down to two houses constituted a local water scheme; two houses.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete statutory threshold — a supply serving two dwellings counting as a scheme — which someone could go and look up in the Act. Falls short of 1.0 because no provision or statute is cited and no figure is attached to the claimed inefficiency.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And it makes much more sense to say, “Look, we’re going to get rid of that so you know where you are at the moment—you know that there’s reform coming.” So that gives them some certainty to be able to plan and to budget.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and its timing: why repeal now, and the effect on councils' long-term plans and budgets. Names a specific affected process rather than characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I predict that in three years’ time, when we come back to an election again, we won’t have updated legislation that’s working. We won’t have any new council-controlled organisations. We won’t have the investment that we needed, but we would have seen ratepayers having a significant increase in the cost of their rates.
divination.explanation: A four-part forecast about the state of water reform by the next election: no working replacement legislation, no new council-controlled organisations, no investment, and materially higher rates.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: As at the 2026 general election: (a) whether replacement water services legislation has been enacted and is in force; (b) whether any new water council-controlled organisations have been established under it; (c) whether territorial authority average rates increases since 2024 exceed the pre-reform trend on LGNZ/Stats NZ local authority financial statistics. True if all four hold, false if the legislation is in force and new water CCOs exist.

veracity.statement: In the Tāhunanui Hills, there is none—like, zero, no stormwater infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Tāhunanui Hills area of her Nelson electorate has no stormwater infrastructure at all.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nelson City Council stormwater asset register and network maps for the Tāhunanui Hills catchment; true if no reticulated stormwater assets are recorded there, false if piped or engineered stormwater assets exist.

veracity.statement: Because it was an election promise from National to help fund this infrastructure, yet now they’re saying they’re not going to do it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National made a 2023 election commitment to help fund Tāhunanui Hills stormwater infrastructure and has since resiled from it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 campaign policy documents and Nelson candidate/leader announcements on Tāhunanui stormwater or flood-recovery funding, plus subsequent ministerial statements; true if a funding commitment was made and later declined, false if no such commitment is on record or the funding is still being provided.

veracity.statement: The unbelievable defence of three waters reminds me of the belligerent, grumpy old man driving up the wrong side of the motorway blaming everyone else: 26 percent of people supported, at its peak, three waters, just as 26 percent supported the Labour Party.
veracity.explanation: Two numerical claims: that public support for three waters peaked at 26 percent, and that Labour's support was also 26 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published NZ polling on three waters/Affordable Water Reforms support (Curia/Taxpayers' Union, Talbot Mills, 1News-Verian) for the highest recorded support level, and Labour's 2023 general election party vote per the Electoral Commission; true if peak polled support was approximately 26% and Labour's vote approximately 26%, false if either figure is materially different.

focus.statement: So my question to the Minister of Local Government when we get into the committee of the whole House stage is: is he going to front up and actually support the money that’s needed for the Tāhunanui Hills?
focus.explanation: Names a specific infrastructure need in a specific place and puts a funding question directly to the responsible Minister — scrutiny of a named commitment, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But there was a smokescreen put up by the new Government—when they were in Opposition—because they just wanted to go after votes. They just wanted to go after votes rather than have an adult conversation about what was best for New Zealand.
focus.explanation: No policy content once the characterisation of the other party's motives is removed: the claim is about why opponents campaigned as they did, not about the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because, as my colleague Phil Twyford so accurately pointed out, the balance sheet separation that would have allowed councils to group together to borrow at a lower rate to invest earlier, therefore saving money—there’s tools out there that you study if you do accounting at university, you can learn about net present value.
rigor.explanation: A real mechanism is offered — balance-sheet separation lets councils aggregate and borrow more cheaply, so investing earlier costs less in present-value terms — but the chain is asserted rather than completed, and the support leans on an appeal to authority (a colleague's assertion, and 'you study this at university') in place of the figures.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It was a lightning rod during the election, three waters—the hoardings were up all around the country for two years. They rebranded; the hoardings stayed up. People could see; people did not want to give up those locally funded, locally owned assets. That was the driving point.
rigor.explanation: Infers what the public wanted from the fact that campaign hoardings — his own side's advertising — stayed up for two years. The evidence offered is the campaign, not any measure of opinion, so the conclusion about public will does not follow; it is an appeal to popularity resting on a premise the speaker's party supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, I sat on the Finance and Expenditure Committee that looked at the third piece of legislation where we made some changes, where we elected to turn four entities into 10.
specificity.explanation: Names the select committee, the stage of legislation and the concrete structural change with figures (four entities to 10); checkable against the committee record, though no cost or timing is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The unbelievable defence of three waters reminds me of the belligerent, grumpy old man driving up the wrong side of the motorway blaming everyone else: 26 percent of people supported, at its peak, three waters, just as 26 percent supported the Labour Party.
civility.explanation: Ridicules the previous speaker's defence by likening her to a 'belligerent, grumpy old man' driving the wrong way — mockery aimed past the argument at the person making it, not at the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’re really good at destroying things and kicking things down and not great at coming up with solutions to the big challenges this country faces, and, my goodness, New Zealand has a massive water infrastructure problem.
focus.explanation: Characterises the governing parties as destroyers rather than builders; it gestures at a real policy area (water infrastructure) but names no measure, figure or outcome — the weight of the sentence is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Far from being a genuine effort to fix the problem for the benefit of future generations, this bit of legislation from the National-led coalition is pure partisan politics. It is theatre.
focus.explanation: Names the bill, but the content is an attribution of motive to the other side rather than any engagement with what the bill does. Once the claim about partisan intent is removed, no policy point remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If the member’s opposite have emphasised so much on what they see locally, I wonder why nothing was delivered in the six years that they had the power and the time and the funding and, apparently, the solution to do anything.
focus.explanation: A general challenge to the previous government's whole six-year record. It names no policy, project, target or figure, which is what separates accountability from party framing — contrast the specific named projects the following speaker uses to answer it.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The bill to get New Zealand’s water infrastructure up to scratch is estimated to be $185 billion, and at least—at least—this Government is leaving Taumata Arowai in place, which is the regulator that our Government set up to set environmental standards and standards for clean, safe drinking water for our people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the estimated cost of bringing New Zealand's water infrastructure up to standard is $185 billion, and that Taumata Arowai was established as a regulator by the previous Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Department of Internal Affairs / Water Industry Commission for Scotland investment-need estimates published for the Three Waters programme: true if an official published estimate of around $185 billion (over the stated horizon) exists, false if the published estimates are materially different. Taumata Arowai's founding statute (Taumata Arowai—the Water Services Regulator Act 2020) settles the second limb.

veracity.statement: Well, newsflash: councils already have the ability to set up council-controlled organisations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the power for territorial authorities to establish council-controlled organisations pre-exists this bill, so the bill's CCO provision confers nothing new.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Part 5 of the Local Government Act 2002 (the CCO provisions) as in force before the Water Services Acts Repeal Bill: true if councils could already establish CCOs, including for water services, under existing law; false if that power is created or materially extended by this bill.

veracity.statement: My city—Auckland—is a case study of a city that simply hasn’t invested in the water infrastructure that it has needed for several decades as it has grown, and we saw that in the floods a year ago, when an extreme weather event saw whole communities, whole suburbs, experiencing catastrophic flooding because Auckland Council has not invested in stormwater ever.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as an absolute, that Auckland Council has never invested in stormwater infrastructure. Hyperbole of this kind is treated as an accuracy question, not a rhetoric question.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council long-term plan and annual report stormwater capital expenditure lines (Healthy Waters programme) for the years since amalgamation: false if any material stormwater capex is recorded, true only if stormwater investment is effectively absent from the record.

veracity.statement: Our waterways—our streams, our creeks, our harbours—are polluted with waste water, with sewage, and this summer, every time there has been a significant rain event, dozens of Auckland beaches have been off limits because they are polluted by raw sewage running into our waters, as well as run-off with heavy metals and contaminants from our streets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during the 2023/24 summer, every significant rain event put dozens of Auckland beaches off limits due to sewage contamination and street run-off.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's Safeswim monitoring data and public health warnings for summer 2023/24: true if rainfall events were routinely followed by no-swim alerts at dozens of sites, false if such alerts affected only a handful of beaches or did not follow rain events consistently.

veracity.statement: If the member’s opposite have emphasised so much on what they see locally, I wonder why nothing was delivered in the six years that they had the power and the time and the funding and, apparently, the solution to do anything.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Labour government delivered nothing on water infrastructure across its six years in office. Stated as an absolute rather than as a shortfall against a target.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Records of water-infrastructure delivery and funding under the 2017–2023 government — the Three Waters Reform stimulus package, 'Better Off' funding allocations, and completed council water projects funded through them: false if any material projects were funded and completed, true only if the record shows no delivery.

veracity.statement: An example in Nelson is the Saxton Creek upgrade which is about to be completed—a $30 million project that was needed because the stormwater was so deplorable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Saxton Creek upgrade in Nelson is a $30 million project nearing completion as at February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nelson City Council project pages, long-term plan and annual report figures for the Saxton Creek upgrade stages: true if the total project cost is around $30 million and the works were near completion in early 2024, false if the recorded cost or timing is materially different.

veracity.statement: It was such a small culvert in a significant industrial area that when it flooded a few years ago it caused millions of dollars’ worth of damage, and the Labour Government invested $7.5 million dollars to bring that project forward and it’s about to be completed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2017–2023 government contributed $7.5 million specifically to accelerate the Saxton Creek upgrade, and that earlier flooding at that culvert caused damage in the millions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown Infrastructure Partners 'shovel-ready' funding allocation records and Nelson City Council reporting on the Saxton Creek upgrade: true if a $7.5 million central-government contribution to that project is recorded, false if no such allocation exists or the amount differs materially.

rigor.statement: But the effect of taking away the affordable water reforms and leaving the regulator in place with no other significant intervention proposed to allow the infrastructure to be funded and financed—the infrastructure that this country desperately needs—can only mean one thing, and that is that the ratepayers are going to pay through the nose. There is no other way for it to happen.
rigor.explanation: The chain — repeal the funding mechanism, keep the regulatory standards, therefore ratepayers bear the cost — is a real and partly sound inference. But 'can only mean one thing' and 'there is no other way' is a false dichotomy: it forecloses the council-controlled-organisation financing route the bill offers, which he acknowledges exists later in the same speech before dismissing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So by separating out the balance sheets of the water entities from those of the councils and reassuring the rating agencies that the councils will not bail out a water entity were it to get into financial trouble, the water entities would have higher debt limits.
rigor.explanation: A properly constructed mechanism argument: the stated premise (rating agencies treat consumer water revenue as more bankable than general rates, and apply covenants accordingly) supports the stated conclusion (separated entities carry higher debt limits) without a gap. Whether the premise about rating-agency behaviour holds is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The point I want to put on record is it wasn’t about council members not wanting to do that; it was that the system was not designed to enable them to do that, because we all know that councils that put up rates to pay for infrastructure, they do get turfed out.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that under-investment is a structural constraint rather than a matter of council will — rests entirely on an appeal to common knowledge ('we all know') about councillors losing office after rates rises. No electoral evidence is offered for the pivotal premise, and the argument would also need to rule out councils that raised rates and survived.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is setting up a massive liability for ratepayers. It will come at a cost—a huge cost—and the ratepayers of New Zealand should be afraid. They should be very afraid.
specificity.explanation: Asserts a large cost with no figure, no mechanism, no timeframe and no affected group beyond 'ratepayers'. 'A huge cost' and 'very afraid' carry no checkable content, which is notable given he cited a precise $185 billion figure moments earlier.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They would be able to borrow more to invest in the pipes at a lower cost to their organisation, and that would, effectively, in the case of Auckland and the new water entity that would have been in place there, have allowed Watercare to borrow two to three times more to invest in the water infrastructure that the city needs than it currently can, because its balance sheet is, effectively, integrated or consolidated into Auckland Council’s balance sheet.
specificity.explanation: Names the entity (Watercare), the quantified effect (two to three times the borrowing capacity) and the causal mechanism (balance-sheet consolidation into Auckland Council). Someone could go and check it. Short of 1.0 only because no dollar amounts or dates are attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our Government, with our plan—the Local Water Done Well plan—will give local decisions and the ability to fix where things are really broken, where things really need to be built, where water infrastructure is really required.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy but supplies no mechanism, funding source, figure or timeframe. 'Where things are really broken, where things really need to be built, where water infrastructure is really required' is a string of generic restatements of the problem, not detail about the solution.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: An example in Nelson is the Saxton Creek upgrade which is about to be completed—a $30 million project that was needed because the stormwater was so deplorable.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific project, its location, its cost and its status. Concrete and checkable, offered directly in answer to a general claim that nothing was delivered.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The bill repeals all of the work that was done to set up a new, financially and environmentally sustainable water system for New Zealand, and it puts nothing in place except the bland assurance that councils will have the ability to set up council-controlled organisations.
civility.explanation: A dismissive, hard-hitting assessment ('nothing in place', 'bland assurance') aimed entirely at the legislation. No person is impugned and no bad faith is attributed to any individual — this is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It will mean the road where that culvert exists does not have to close when we have heavy rain in Nelson, and it will mean that the businesses in that area, like our meatworks, won’t suffer economic loss if we have a heavy rain event.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that once the Saxton Creek upgrade is complete, heavy rain will no longer force closure of the affected road or cause economic loss to nearby businesses in that industrial area.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Nelson City Council and local road-closure records for the road crossing the Saxton Creek culvert after the upgrade is commissioned: true if no flood-related closures or reported business flood losses occur at that site during subsequent significant rain events, false if the road closes or those businesses report flood damage in a comparable rain event.

rigor.statement: Some say the definition of “insanity” or “stupidity” is doing the same thing over and over and expecting a different outcome. This incoming coalition Government is going to hand back to councils and expect them to solve an issue they’ve not been able to solve for decades.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: councils failed for decades, therefore returning water to councils repeats a failure. The gap is that the premise 'the same thing' is asserted rather than shown — the repeal package is not identical to the pre-2020 arrangements, so the analogy is assumed, not established. Reasoning about the measure, weakly.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, he’s either going to sell the assets or allow the councils to increase their rates.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy. The two options are presented as exhaustive with nothing offered to rule out the alternatives the Government has actually proposed (new financing tools, council-controlled organisations, debt limits). Squarely on the policy, but the inference is closed off by construction.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I’m glad to follow the previous speaker Cameron Brewer, who sat on a council that has incompetently overseen the water assets of Auckland, where we’ve had billions of dollars of destruction to private assets—the assets that he would say he protects; those homeowners who, through stormwater non-management, have seen their assets destroyed, and beaches that can’t be swum at after a rain event.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the council's record would be a 1.0, but this ties a named member personally to 'incompetently overseen' and adds a hypocrisy jab ('the assets that he would say he protects'). Imputing bad faith to an individual member is the 0.5 band.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We had a proposal to do something different, and that naive Minister of Local Government sits in his seat now with all these wonderful empty promises and says that it won’t cost more.
civility.explanation: 'Naive' attacks the Minister's judgement personally and 'wonderful empty promises' is sneering; the target is the man, not the repeal. A clear personal attack rather than robust criticism of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It dribbles out of the Minister’s mouth—“The councils will have to come to us with financial reports that ensure sustainability”.
civility.explanation: 'Dribbles out of the Minister's mouth' is contemptuous physical imagery aimed at the person rather than any engagement with what he said. Mockery of an individual member.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: First of all, I just want to say that communities across New Zealand—there are some councils that are actually doing a particularly good job in this space, so it’s not every council that we’re trying to find a solution for.
civility.explanation: Directly rebuts the preceding speaker's blanket criticism of councils and does it entirely on the substance, immediately after a speech that named and criticised a member of his own side. Real opportunity to retaliate, taken up civilly.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Far North District Council: 33 percent rates increase required; Hamilton, 25 percent; Buller District, looking at 30 percent; Porirua, up to 50 percent.
specificity.explanation: Four named councils with a percentage attached to each — anyone can go to the councils' plans and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But we’re also trying to do this in a way that maintains local ownership, local control, and local delivery, and for that reason, I commend this bill to the House.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic principles — 'local ownership, local control, local delivery' — with no mechanism, funding tool, figure or timeframe attached. High focus, low specificity: policy-directed but nothing here anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Far North District Council: 33 percent rates increase required; Hamilton, 25 percent; Buller District, looking at 30 percent; Porirua, up to 50 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that these four specific councils are proposing or require rates increases of the stated magnitudes. Several councils did consult on very large increases in early 2024, but whether these four match these particular numbers is what needs checking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2024–34 draft long-term plan / annual plan consultation documents for Far North District Council, Hamilton City Council, Buller District Council and Porirua City Council as at February 2024. True if each council's proposed average rates increase matches the figure given (33%, 25%, 30%, up to 50%) within a couple of percentage points; false if the proposed increases are materially lower.

veracity.statement: The iconic destinations of Queenstown, Fox Glacier in the Speaker’s electorate, and Punakaiki—they have boil-water notices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a present-tense fact: that three named tourist destinations were all under boil-water notices at the time of the speech. Fox Glacier had a long-standing notice; Queenstown's cryptosporidium notice was lifted in late 2023, which is the part most likely to fail.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Taumata Arowai / Queenstown Lakes, Westland and Buller district council records of boil-water notices in force on 13 February 2024. True if all three of Queenstown, Fox Glacier and Punakaiki were under a boil-water notice on that date; false if any of the three was not.

veracity.statement: Literally hundreds of billions of dollars are needed to bring everything back up to speed, and it’s significant because as a result of it we can’t use the normal rating system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the scale of the national investment shortfall as 'literally hundreds of billions'. The word 'literally' rules out reading it as loose rhetoric, so it stands or falls against the published 30-year estimates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published estimates of New Zealand's three waters infrastructure investment need over 30 years — the Department of Internal Affairs / Water Industry Commission for Scotland modelling and successor Local Water Done Well analyses.
