veracity.statement: Our families package helped 330,000 Kiwi families in its first year, increasing the accommodation supplement and through the family tax credit, and by also introducing the Best Start payment and also the winter energy payment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a first-year reach figure for the Families Package, and that it comprised the accommodation supplement increase, family tax credit, Best Start and the winter energy payment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/MSD reporting on the Families Package: true if approximately 330,000 families received a Families Package entitlement in its first year of operation, false if the first-year recipient count is materially different.

veracity.statement: Because what’s shameful is the woeful record in child poverty that happened in the last six years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that child poverty worsened over the previous Government's six years in office. She asserts it herself rather than relaying it, so it is her own claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics releases covering 2017/18 to 2022/23 on the primary measures (before-housing-costs 50%, after-housing-costs 50%, material hardship): true if child poverty rates rose or were flat across those measures over the period, false if they fell materially.

specificity.statement: When we look at the regulatory impact statement from their own officials, who have provided the information for this bill, they say that changing the indexation will have a direct benefit and it will in fact disproportionately affect people who identify with population groups such as women, Māori, Pasifika, and disabled people; people who are already overrepresented in the main benefit population.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document, the mechanism (changing the indexation) and the specific groups affected. Someone could pull the RIS and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a first step of the review of Working for Families, we implemented changes that meant 346,000 families were better off by an average of $20 a week.
specificity.explanation: A named programme, a named review, a count of families and an average dollar amount. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The fact that they can sit there and laugh about it, draw a ring around those people and say that they can fill up a football stadium and find that amusing shows just how out of touch this Government is.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's demeanour and what they are 'really like'. No policy, figure or outcome is named; strip out the characterisation of the Government and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we’re seeing is those people who do it tough, those people who only get a 2 percent increase on the minimum wage, those people who are on unemployment benefits, those mums who are struggling to pay for childcare, those people who want to get their free prescriptions; all those people do worse under National.
focus.explanation: Names real policies — the minimum wage rise, free prescriptions, benefit levels — but the weight of the sentence lands on a general party verdict ('worse under National') rather than on the effect of any one of them.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We all look forward to this Budget to see what kind of disaster will be wreaked upon the rest of New Zealand, what times of deep Public Service cuts we will see with a 6.5 to 7.5 percent cut right across all our public services.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the forthcoming Budget will impose public service cuts of 6.5 to 7.5 percent across the board. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — it predicts the Government's Budget.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and agency baseline-savings decisions: true if the Budget applies savings targets in the 6.5–7.5 percent range broadly across public service agencies and delivers substantial reductions in public service spending/staffing; false if the Budget applies no such range, or if cuts are confined to a small number of agencies.

divination.statement: And mark me, this will probably be the next thing to go; we’ll see abatement thresholds come down as a way of decreasing and getting more money carved off to the side to fund tax cuts that were unaffordable when they first did their numbers.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government will reduce main benefit abatement thresholds as a further saving. A prediction about another party's future action, not a promise about her own.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Legislation, regulation or Budget decisions affecting main benefit abatement thresholds: true if the thresholds are lowered before the end of the parliamentary term, false if they are left unchanged or increased.

veracity.statement: It makes really clear that in the forecast period, we could be looking at an estimated increase of 7,000 children under the AHC50 poverty measure, and an estimated increase of 7,000 children under the BHC50 poverty measure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the supplementary analysis report 'Indexing Main Benefits to Inflation' (paragraphs 30-32) models an increase of about 7,000 children in poverty on each of the AHC50 and BHC50 measures over the forecast period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published supplementary analysis report 'Indexing Main Benefits to Inflation' for the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill, paragraphs 30-32: true if it estimates approximately 7,000 additional children in poverty under both the AHC50 and the BHC50 measures across the forecast period; false if the modelled figures, or the measures they attach to, differ materially.

veracity.statement: The Minister has, in the House, stood up and told us that they will be better off this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of record that the Minister for Social Development told the House that beneficiaries would be better off this year under the change to CPI indexation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record for the readings of the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill and related question time up to 13 February 2024: true if the Minister for Social Development stated in the House that beneficiaries would be better off this year; false if no such statement appears in the record.

veracity.statement: Now, building on what my colleague Carmel Sepuloni said, my understanding is that the figure that was being used with the change that our previous Government made was a figure on, net of tax and ACC earner levies, the average ordinary time weekly earnings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous Government's wage-indexation change, main benefits were adjusted by the movement in average ordinary time weekly earnings measured net of tax and ACC earner levies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The indexation provisions of the Social Security Act 2018 as amended to link main benefit rates to wage growth, together with MSD's published annual general adjustment methodology for 2020-2023: true if the adjustment used average ordinary time weekly earnings net of tax and the ACC earner levy; false if a different earnings measure or a gross measure was used.

veracity.statement: It actually didn’t turn out to be that; it turned out to be 4.7 and then a net average wage growth figure of 4.74 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that against the report's projection of 5.13 percent CPI for the year to April 2024, the actual outturn was 4.7 percent CPI and 4.74 percent net average wage growth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI release of 24 January 2024 (annual increase to the December 2023 quarter) and the net average wage growth figure of 7 February 2024 referenced in the supplementary analysis report: true if CPI is 4.7 percent and net average wage growth is approximately 4.74 percent; false if either figure differs materially from those stated.

specificity.statement: It makes really clear that in the forecast period, we could be looking at an estimated increase of 7,000 children under the AHC50 poverty measure, and an estimated increase of 7,000 children under the BHC50 poverty measure.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document, the paragraph numbers nearby, two distinct standard poverty measures and a numeric estimate for each. Directly checkable against the report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, building on what my colleague Carmel Sepuloni said, my understanding is that the figure that was being used with the change that our previous Government made was a figure on, net of tax and ACC earner levies, the average ordinary time weekly earnings.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statistical construct — average ordinary time weekly earnings, net of tax and ACC earner levies — rather than gesturing at 'wage growth'. Someone could go and reproduce the figure from it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The fact that we have a bill where the advice is telling us that this will increase child poverty in New Zealand is of course of concern to us on this side of the House, and I think it should be of concern to the Minister as well.
civility.explanation: Criticism sits on the bill and the official advice. The closing clause edges toward the Minister by implying she may not share the concern, but it stops short of imputing bad faith or attacking her personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I do suspect—and I’m not particularly having a go at the Minister about this particular issue because it’s actually quite complicated—what’s in the SAR might not be exactly right.
civility.explanation: Challenges the accuracy of the official analysis while expressly declining to turn it on the Minister, and concedes the difficulty of the material. Entirely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, we all signed up here to the child poverty reduction legislation, and therefore I would think that any Government has a commitment to ensure their policies across Government are constructive with respect to reducing child poverty.
rigor.explanation: Premise (Parliament collectively enacted the child poverty reduction legislation) to conclusion (a Government is committed to policies that reduce child poverty) is a fair inference, though it stretches a statutory target regime into a general obligation binding every policy across Government — a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Bear in mind that’s a goal of the Government—to bring inflation down—and so therefore wage growth significantly outstrips CPI in those later years.
rigor.explanation: The 'therefore' does real work it cannot quite carry: falling inflation on its own does not entail that wage growth outstrips CPI, which additionally requires nominal wage growth to hold up as inflation falls. A reasonable point about the projections with a genuine gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I don’t actually think that’s the calculation that we’ve been using up to now because it misses out this question of being net of tax and the ACC earner levy.
rigor.explanation: Clean inference: if the report's comparator omits the net-of-tax and ACC earner levy adjustment, then it is not the measure previously used. The conclusion follows directly from the stated difference in definitions.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I’d like to know from the Minister whether or not there are legal ramifications for this bill, given the implications for child poverty reduction targets.
focus.explanation: Names the measure before the House and a specific statutory consequence (the child poverty reduction targets). Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy against a named commitment, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So just so we’ve got everything really clear on the table, my first question is: is that CPI as calculated by Statistics New Zealand?
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the clause itself — which index series the adjustment will use — with no reference to the other party at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We know they won’t be better off in the future—in fact, they’ll be demonstrably far worse off in the future—but we can’t make those calculations accurately unless we have an understanding (a) that it is CPI, (b) what period of time that is for, and then we move to the ability to make an accurate comparison.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that beneficiaries will end up materially worse off in future years under CPI indexation than they would have been under the wage-linked adjustment it replaces. Not a promise about his own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Compare the main benefit rates set by CPI indexation from 1 April 2027 (MSD benefit rate tables) with the rates that would have resulted from indexation to net average ordinary time weekly earnings over the same period (Stats NZ QES earnings series, net of tax and ACC earner levy): true if the CPI-indexed rates are materially lower; false if they are equal to or above the wage-indexed counterfactual.

veracity.statement: Actually, the thing that will have the biggest impact is reducing the number of children growing up in benefit-dependent homes, because 60 percent of them currently grow up in benefit-dependent homes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 60 percent of children in poverty (the antecedent under discussion) currently live in benefit-dependent households.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD / Stats NZ child poverty statistics and benefit system data for 2023: the share of children below the poverty lines (or in material hardship) living in households whose main income is a main benefit. True if that share is approximately 60 percent; false if materially lower (e.g. nearer 40 percent) or higher.

veracity.statement: The time frames, as per previous Governments: CPI is taken from 31 December of the year previous, and at 7 February the date of the wage rate was 5.3 percent, and that’s publicly on record.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the wage rate used in the indexation calculation, measured at 7 February, was 5.3 percent, and that the calculation method and time frames are unchanged from previous Governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Stats NZ average wage series used for annual benefit adjustment and MSD's published indexation calculation for the April 2024 adjustment. True if the wage growth figure applied was 5.3 percent and the CPI/wage reference dates match those used in prior years' adjustments; false if the figure differs materially or the reference dates were changed.

veracity.statement: A young person under the age of 20 who comes on to welfare is expected to spend, on average, 24 years.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to the recent Taylor Fry actuarial valuation of the benefit system a projected average future duration on welfare of 24 years for entrants under 20.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taylor Fry valuation of the New Zealand benefit system referenced (the most recent report as at February 2024): the projected average future years on benefit for clients entering under age 20. True if the report gives approximately 24 years; false if it gives a materially different figure or contains no such projection.

veracity.statement: The need for them is at record levels, and one of the ways that we can mitigate the pressure on front-line staff would be by increasing baseline benefits so that people don’t fall behind that need those hardship grants.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that demand for hardship grants (special needs grants and advances) was at record levels as at February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD's quarterly benefit fact sheets / hardship assistance statistics: the number and total value of special needs grants and advances granted in the year to December 2023, compared with prior years in the series. True if at a series high; false if below earlier peaks.

rigor.statement: Actually, the thing that will have the biggest impact is reducing the number of children growing up in benefit-dependent homes, because 60 percent of them currently grow up in benefit-dependent homes.
rigor.explanation: The premise is a prevalence figure; the conclusion is about which lever has the biggest effect. That does not follow — the proportion of poor children in benefit homes says nothing about whether moving households off benefits is the largest available reduction, and it ignores in-work poverty. A gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is a direct result of welfare dependency, and I’m not willing to tolerate that.
rigor.explanation: Circular. The observation is that people remain on welfare for long periods; explaining that as 'a direct result of welfare dependency' restates the observation rather than supplying a cause. No mechanism or evidence connects the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the first issue is there is absolutely a link between benefit rates and incentives for people to move off welfare and into work, which is why when we talk about one of the intentions of the bill—about putting the welfare system on to a more sustainable footing—that is absolutely it.
rigor.explanation: Rests on an appeal to authority (unspecified MBIE advice) plus a bare assertion that a link exists. Even granting the link, nothing offered connects it to the size or direction of this bill's indexation change, which is the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I guess my question is: isn’t she contributing to the poor outcomes in that report that she’s talking about by setting lower increases to benefits?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: the cited report identifies low incomes as one of the poor outcomes, the bill lowers the rate at which incomes rise, therefore the Minister contributes to that outcome. The step is sound as far as it goes, but it treats the report's long-run dependency findings as interchangeable with an indexation-level effect without showing they are, leaving a gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If she hadn’t done that projection and assessment around the impact on hardship grants and advances, how can she be confident that the cost savings she’s projected and hoping to make will be accurate?
rigor.explanation: Valid conditional: a savings estimate that omits an identified offsetting cost cannot be relied on until that cost is quantified. The inference tracks its premise; it is short of 1.0 because it assumes the offsetting cost is large enough to matter without establishing that.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The time frames, as per previous Governments: CPI is taken from 31 December of the year previous, and at 7 February the date of the wage rate was 5.3 percent, and that’s publicly on record.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact reference dates for both inputs to the indexation calculation and gives the wage figure, and points to where it is published. Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Further to that, I was wondering whether a child impact assessment had been done in relation to this bill, and, if so, can she provide us with details of what that had produced?
specificity.explanation: Names a particular instrument (a child impact assessment) tied to a particular bill, and asks for its output. Precise enough that the Minister could either produce the document or confirm none exists. Falls short of 1.0 only for carrying no figures or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So members opposite may have a different view about our side’s motivation to support people into jobs, but I’m really clear about it.
civility.explanation: A contested exchange in which motives are being questioned, so there was a real opportunity to hit back at the questioner. She acknowledges the disagreement and restates her own position without imputing anything to anyone.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And while I recognise officials do their best in providing advice, I do draw a line around when research is being used, as opposed to just, I guess, ideological assumptions around whether that gap actually contributes to employment outcomes.
civility.explanation: Pointed and robust — it edges toward imputing that the Minister is acting on ideology rather than evidence, but it is framed around the basis of the advice rather than landing on her character, and explicitly exempts officials from the criticism.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Further to that, I was wondering whether a child impact assessment had been done in relation to this bill, and, if so, can she provide us with details of what that had produced?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — asks whether a specific, named assessment tool was applied to this bill and what it found. Scrutiny of a named process, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As the supplementary analysis report for this bill states—which we keep referring to because there’s no proper impact statement—approximately 3,200 low-income families are receiving minimum family tax credit, which is an incentive to ensure low-income working families remain better off financially in full-time work than they would be on a main benefit.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific instrument (the minimum family tax credit), cites a source document, gives a recipient count (3,200) and states the mechanism the credit is meant to create. Concrete enough for someone else to go and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Could the Minister explain the implications of this bill on the minimum family tax credit and the general summary of that particular area or concern that’s been raised in paragraph 40 of the supplementary analysis paper.
specificity.explanation: A precise question rather than a general complaint: it names the tax credit at issue and points to paragraph 40 of a named document. A precise question carries as much checkable content as a precise answer, though it stops short of naming figures or a threshold.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As the supplementary analysis report for this bill states—which we keep referring to because there’s no proper impact statement—approximately 3,200 low-income families are receiving minimum family tax credit, which is an incentive to ensure low-income working families remain better off financially in full-time work than they would be on a main benefit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 3,200 low-income families currently receive the minimum family tax credit, attributed to the bill's supplementary analysis report. The claim is about a present recipient count, not about whether the policy is desirable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report accompanying this bill, and Inland Revenue administrative data on minimum family tax credit recipients for the relevant year: true if the number of families receiving the MFTC is approximately 3,200, false if materially different (e.g. under 2,000 or over 5,000).

focus.statement: Could the Minister explain the implications of this bill on the minimum family tax credit and the general summary of that particular area or concern that’s been raised in paragraph 40 of the supplementary analysis paper.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the committee directly — a named provision of the bill and a numbered paragraph of its analysis paper. No party framing at all; this is scrutiny of the policy itself.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, if that is the case and the general adjustments are going to be based on the CPI figure of 4.7, which falls below average wage growth as I heard it, then that must mean there will be much larger fiscal savings in the forecast period.
rigor.explanation: A clean conditional inference: if benefits are indexed to CPI (4.7%) while wages grow faster (5.3%), then savings against the wage-indexed counterfactual must be larger than the modelling assumed. The conclusion tracks the premises; the small gap is that she does not establish the modelling's original wage assumption.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Which is what happens usually when the annual general adjustment (AGA) is set, because as the member will know as a previous Minister in terms of the time frames, the AGA work is prepared well in advance of 7 February when those wage figures come out.
rigor.explanation: A real reason offered for a real conclusion — the analysis predates the wage release, so it could not have used it. But it only supports 'the modelling is stale by design'; it does not reach the conclusion it is deployed for, which is that the updated savings figure need not be given. A genuine gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is the Minister, then, saying that this is simply ideology with no basis in evidence or research or evaluation from especially those groups who will be most impacted in a negative way by this bill?
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: the inference runs from 'the Minister called it an election commitment' to 'therefore it has no basis in evidence or research'. A policy can be both a manifesto commitment and evidence-based, and nothing offered rules that out. The argument is squarely about the bill, so it is a rigor failure rather than a focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because, actually, when that gap is wider, all that we’re doing is actually contributing to wage scarring, and therefore that gap contributes to people then, because of the severe poverty they enter when they lose employment—and we have to remember that people on the benefit are also people who have lost employment, who were previously in work—and if they have such a steep jump between wages and benefits, that poverty that is created as a result of that puts people in a situation where they may feel compelled to take employment that would have paid less than they previously were in, out of sheer survival.
rigor.explanation: A genuine multi-step causal chain — wider gap, deeper poverty on job loss, pressure to accept lower-paid work, wage scarring — and each link is at least plausible. But the links are asserted rather than supported: no evidence or magnitude is offered for the step from benefit adequacy to accepting lower wages, so the conclusion outruns what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, if that is the case and the general adjustments are going to be based on the CPI figure of 4.7, which falls below average wage growth as I heard it, then that must mean there will be much larger fiscal savings in the forecast period.
specificity.explanation: Names both indexation figures, the mechanism (general adjustment set on CPI rather than wage growth), and the consequence (fiscal savings over the forecast period). Someone could check it against the costings.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is exactly what’s been done for 31 of the last 35 years.
specificity.explanation: A precise, countable claim — a named indexation basis and an exact tally of years — rather than a general appeal to precedent. Whether the count is right is a separate question.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To answer the member from the Greens, Ricardo Menéndez March, no child assessment was done on this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no child impact assessment was carried out on this bill. Written before checking; the claim is against the speaker's own interest, which makes it easy to settle from the published bill papers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory/supplementary analysis documents published for the Social Security (Benefit Adjustment) Amendment Bill, and MSD's advice to the Minister: true if no Child Impact Assessment was produced for the bill, false if one exists in the published papers or the departmental record.

veracity.statement: It is exactly what’s been done for 31 of the last 35 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that CPI indexation of benefit increases has been the practice in 31 of the last 35 years. Criterion fixed before forming a view; the count turns on when wage indexation began and on the years either side of the 1990s reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statutory indexation basis for main benefits in each year from roughly 1989 to 2024 (Social Security Act annual general adjustment provisions, and the 2019 amendment moving indexation to average wage growth from April 2020): true if CPI indexation applied in 31 of those 35 years, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: Then I have a look at this—what’s this thing called, the supplementary analysis paper?—and it’s clear that there has not been any current review, evaluation, or research to inform this bill, Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, on the basis of the bill's own supplementary analysis paper, that no current review, evaluation or research informed the legislation. Settled by reading that document; criterion set before forming a view.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report published with the Social Security (Benefit Adjustment) Amendment Bill: true if it records that no current review, evaluation or research informed the policy (and no consultation with affected-sector bodies was undertaken), false if it cites contemporary evaluation or research underpinning the change.

veracity.statement: What this bill is doing is simply reducing increases to benefits.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's sole effect is to lower the size of future benefit increases, against the Minister's framing of it as being about employment outcomes. Checkable from the bill text and its fiscal costings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Social Security (Benefit Adjustment) Amendment Bill together with the Treasury/MSD costings: true if the bill's only operative effect is to switch annual benefit indexation from average wage growth to CPI and the costings show lower benefit rates over the forecast period than under the status quo, false if the bill also carries measures that raise benefit levels or if the costings show no reduction.

veracity.statement: It is important because the Minister in charge of this bill, Hon Louise Upston, has said publicly that in the first year they will be better off, and in the long term she has acknowledged that they would get less than what they would do when benefits are indexed to actual wages.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a two-part characterisation of what the Minister has said publicly about the bill's short- and long-term effects on beneficiaries. Settled from the public record; criterion fixed before forming a view.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements by Louise Upston on this bill (Hansard, press releases, media interviews around February 2024): true if she has both claimed beneficiaries are better off in the first year and acknowledged they receive less in the long run than under wage indexation, false if either half is not on the public record.

civility.statement: It’s not that difficult to understand what we’re doing.
civility.explanation: Condescension directed at the questioner rather than at her argument: the implication is that the member is failing to grasp something simple. Short of an insult, but it turns from the substance to the person, which the re-anchored scale treats as a genuine failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is the Minister, then, saying that this is simply ideology with no basis in evidence or research or evaluation from especially those groups who will be most impacted in a negative way by this bill?
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward bad faith — 'simply ideology' impugns the Minister's motive — but it is framed as a question about the bill's evidence base rather than about the Minister's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But the other thing that I wanted to unpack from her is whether she thinks that the gap which she will make worse in terms of wages and benefits could contribute to the ethnic and gender pay gap.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and a named second-order consequence of it — the wage-benefit gap and its effect on ethnic and gender pay gaps. No party framing; the mild 'she will make worse' attaches to the policy's effect, not to the other team.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s specified that there’s currently 43,700 social housing tenants receiving a main benefit who will be specifically impacted by this part of the bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific caseload figure — 43,700 people who are both social housing tenants and main benefit recipients — and attributes it to the bill's supplementary analysis report as the number affected by Part 2.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report accompanying this bill (and the underlying MSD/Kāinga Ora figures for social housing tenants receiving a main benefit): true if it states approximately 43,700 such tenants are affected by this part of the bill; false if the report gives a materially different number or does not identify this cohort as affected.

veracity.statement: I note that they’re staying the same and that hasn’t been adjusted for almost two decades.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the abatement settings for this support (the abatement rate and threshold he goes on to quote) have been left unchanged for close to twenty years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of the Working for Families abatement rate and threshold in the Income Tax Act 2007: true if the last change to the rate and threshold he refers to predates roughly 2006; false if either was amended materially since then (e.g. threshold or rate changes taking effect in the 2010s or 2020s).

veracity.statement: The first member asked about the changes to the minimum family tax credit threshold, and that increase will be from $34,216 to $35,204 after tax.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the exact before-and-after values of the minimum family tax credit annual after-tax income threshold that this bill sets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill amending the Income Tax Act 2007 (and Inland Revenue's published MFTC threshold for the relevant tax years): true if the threshold moves from $34,216 to $35,204 after tax; false if either figure differs.

veracity.statement: For those that don’t understand or have detail about what this minimum family tax credit does, it guarantees a minimum income or minimum level for sole parents who are working at least 20 hours a week and a couple or parents who are working at least 30 hours between them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the hours-worked eligibility test for the minimum family tax credit: 20 hours a week for a sole parent, 30 hours combined for a couple.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The minimum family tax credit eligibility rules in subpart MF of the Income Tax Act 2007 as administered by Inland Revenue: true if the qualifying hours are 20 per week for a sole parent and 30 combined for a couple; false if either threshold differs.

specificity.statement: It’s specified that there’s currently 43,700 social housing tenants receiving a main benefit who will be specifically impacted by this part of the bill.
specificity.explanation: A precise question: names the affected cohort, gives an exact count, and identifies the document (supplementary analysis report rather than the RIS) where the analysis should sit. Someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Indeed, if it is the intent of this Government to go back to resorting to the actuary approach—the future liability model approach that we’ve seen National use, I think, maybe in the Paula Rebstock days—it would be really great to understand at what stage the interventions are being done, and if you are tracking and monitoring some of the adjustments that are not being made, how indeed you are looking to, I guess, track those interventions at the varying stages of the transitioning of those who are on benefits.
specificity.explanation: Names one identifiable thing (the actuarial future-liability model) but the actual ask is unclear: 'at what stage the interventions are being done' and 'track those interventions at the varying stages of the transitioning' commit to no measure, figure or timeframe the Minister could answer against.
specificity.subject: speaker
