veracity.statement: In the time that I have, I want to talk a little bit about the role of Parliament here, because we’ve heard some speeches from the National members particularly, and they were all surprisingly almost exactly the same line about how a member’s bill is not the way to progress something like this change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National speakers in this first reading debate all made substantially the same argument — that a member's bill is not the appropriate vehicle for this change.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the first reading debate on the Electoral (Equal Protection of Māori Seats) Amendment Bill, 14 February 2024: true if the National speakers each argued that a member's bill is not the right vehicle for the change; false if their contributions rested on materially different grounds.

veracity.statement: We were not able to do that because the law simply did not provide for local councils to be able to make that available to elected members—prohibited by the law.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during her time as a Far North District Council member the law positively prohibited councils from offering remote participation to elected members.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Government Act 2002, Schedule 7 (in particular the remote-participation and quorum clauses, cl 25A/25B) as in force during her council term: true if the Act barred councils from permitting members to attend meetings by audio or audiovisual link; false if the Act permitted remote attendance under standing orders and only barred counting remote members toward the quorum.

civility.statement: The idea that you should not do entrenchment when the executive has not introduced the bill is bananas.
civility.explanation: Blunt to the point of derision, but the derision lands on the proposition, not on any member. Fierce dismissal of an argument is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Coming to this House with prepared speech notes from your leader’s office and reading out prepared lines about how the executive is key to Parliament’s decision-making betrays an underlying lack of respect for the role of Parliament in determining how we should operate as a democracy, and we should not tolerate it.
civility.explanation: Moves off the argument and onto the members making it — imputes that they are mouthpieces reading someone else's lines and that they lack respect for the institution. Bad faith imputed rather than a position contested, which is a genuine failure on the re-anchored scale, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a bill which simply corrects an aspect of our constitutional framework in the Electoral Act which would treat the rights of voters in general seats as different from those of voters in Māori seats.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute and identifies the asymmetry the bill addresses, but supplies no clause, no entrenchment threshold and no mechanism for how the correction operates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, for the House’s benefit, what this bill proposes to do is to amend the Local Government Act to permanently allow local authority members to participate in local authority meetings remotely and to be counted towards the quorum for those meetings.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute amended, the mechanism (remote participation), the quorum consequence and the permanence of the change. Someone could check the bill against this description.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the Far North district, there are currently four elected members who live north of the Mangamuka.
specificity.explanation: A named district, a named geographic boundary and a count. Concrete enough that a reader could check it against the council's membership.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And isn’t Te Pāti Māori a wonderful example of that in the last few weeks and months?
focus.explanation: A sarcastic aside about another party's recent conduct. No clause, figure, mechanism or outcome of the entrenchment bill is named — strip the swipe at Te Pāti Māori and nothing about the measure remains. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility is untouched; this is the tribalism case Focus exists for.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is so important—and I support my colleague Arena—because it gives our people the opportunity to be strongly Māori all the time.
focus.explanation: Directed at what the measure before the House is for, rather than at the other side. It carries little detail — Specificity would rate it low — but Focus asks what the statement is about, and this is about the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is truly striking that it was not brought when it could have fostered much further during the past three years, when Labour had that capacity to get it through.
focus.explanation: A genuine point about this measure's legislative history — it was not advanced when the sponsor's party held the numbers — so it is not content-free party-bashing. But the weight sits on Labour's conduct and timing rather than on what the bill would do, which keeps it short of the scrutiny standard where a named policy and a named outcome carry the point.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Fifty percent, an MMP record—50 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Labour's party vote at the previous election reached 50 percent and that this was a record under MMP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official results for the 2020 general election: Labour's party vote share, compared against every party vote share recorded since MMP began in 1996. True if Labour's 2020 share was approximately 50 percent and the highest any party has achieved under MMP; false if materially below 50 percent or if another party vote share since 1996 was higher.

veracity.statement: And it is a rarity—if you look at the other provisions within the 1993 Electoral Act, those that have entrenchment status are few and far between: it’s around the length of the parliamentary term, the division of general electoral districts, the allowance for adjustment of the quota of electoral districts, the voting age, the method of voting.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that only a small enumerated set of provisions in the Electoral Act 1993 carries entrenchment, and identifies which ones.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 268 of the Electoral Act 1993 (the reserved provisions). True if the entrenched provisions are confined to substantially this list — term of Parliament, division of New Zealand into general electoral districts, allowance for quota adjustment, voting age, method of voting; false if the reserved provisions materially differ from or extend well beyond that list.

veracity.statement: You don’t worry about upsetting the Atlas group who are supporting the ACT Party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Atlas Network supports the ACT Party. Atlas partners with think tanks rather than political parties, so the tie, if any, would be indirect.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Atlas Network's published list of partner organisations, plus Electoral Commission party donation and loan returns for the ACT Party. True if a documented organisational or funding tie exists between the Atlas Network and the ACT Party; false if ACT appears in neither Atlas's partner list nor in donation records traceable to Atlas or its affiliates.

veracity.statement: There are 300 clauses, and only a handful are entrenched.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a rough size for the Electoral Act 1993 and that only a very small number of its provisions carry entrenched status.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Electoral Act 1993 as currently in force: the number of sections in the Act, and the count of reserved provisions listed in section 268. True if the Act runs to roughly 300 sections and the reserved provisions number under about ten; false if the section count is materially different or if entrenchment extends to many more provisions.

rigor.statement: As my colleague, the chair of the Justice Committee, James Meager, said—and of course he is a man of the law; he was trained at one of the world’s most southern universities, Otago, and, of course, those cold, crisp winter mornings gave him the clarity that he brings to Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the weight offered for accepting the constitutional objection is the colleague's legal training, his university, and even its climate, rather than the content of the objection. The credentials do no work toward the conclusion that entrenchment is inappropriate. Scored on the inference only — the flourish is not a Civility or Veracity matter here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: She acknowledged that we’ve, basically, got it right—that New Zealand’s made our constitutional inheritance from the UK—that we’ve made it our own and we’ve, basically, got it all right. And if that’s the case, let’s not try and fix something that’s not broken.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the sponsor's general regard for New Zealand's constitutional arrangements is recast as a concession that no change is warranted, and the conclusion is drawn from that recasting. Approving of a system as a whole is consistent with wanting one part of it entrenched, so the premise as restated does not support the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And it is a rarity—if you look at the other provisions within the 1993 Electoral Act, those that have entrenchment status are few and far between: it’s around the length of the parliamentary term, the division of general electoral districts, the allowance for adjustment of the quota of electoral districts, the voting age, the method of voting.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute and enumerates the specific provisions said to carry entrenched status — parliamentary term, division of electoral districts, quota adjustment, voting age, method of voting. Anyone can go to the Act and check the list against it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the meantime, where we can spend our time in Parliament, as my learned colleague James Meager said, is improving, focusing on actually lifting Māori outcomes, lifting Māori out of dependency, reducing the cost of living for Māori, cracking down on law and order for Māori, growing the economy for Māori, lifting incomes, growing the economy, doing everything in favour of Māori.
specificity.explanation: A chain of generic goods — lifting outcomes, reducing cost of living, growing the economy — with no programme, figure, mechanism or timeframe attached to any of them. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Also, once constitutionally entrenched, provisions like these would require a 75 percent majority in the House to make a change, and if the intent is really to go through ensuring the entrenchment of the provisions that are sought, then this process is not the appropriate process.
specificity.explanation: States the actual consequence of entrenchment with a figure — a 75 percent majority to amend — which is checkable and is the mechanism the objection turns on. Marked down because the second half asserts the process is wrong without saying what the appropriate process would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is focused on delivering on all the items, all the statements that we have made. We are focused on delivering on the economy and making sure that law and order is back on track.
specificity.explanation: Slogan-level. 'Delivering on all the items', 'the economy' and 'law and order back on track' name no policy, no figure, no measure and no date; nothing here distinguishes it from any other government's statement of priorities.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So it’s all on, Mr James Meager, is it? It’s all on, Mr James Meager. The future of Māori is all on, Mr Meager. I would have backed Tama Potaka before Mr Meager.
civility.explanation: Repeating a named member's name in mock incredulity, and rating him below a colleague, targets the person rather than his constitutional argument. Short of a direct insult but squarely sneering — a real failure on the re-anchored scale, where engaging the substance is the expected standard. The insult is aimed at someone else but it is the speaker's own conduct, so subject stays with the speaker.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These standing orders make it very clear what a member can do. As long as they give two days’ written notice, they can attend by audio or audiovisual link where the member is at a place that makes their physical presence at the meeting impractical or impossible, when a member is unwell, and where a member is unable to attend due to an emergency.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete mechanism (audio/audiovisual link), the notice period (two days, written) and the three qualifying grounds. Someone could go to a council's standing orders and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s not required when it’s within the Local Government Act which was amended, I understand, Carl Bates, in 2023 to allow standing orders to give councils the discretion to allow for remote participation.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute and the year of amendment and states what it did — checkable against the legislation, though no section is cited and the point is hedged with 'I understand'.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These standing orders make it very clear what a member can do. As long as they give two days’ written notice, they can attend by audio or audiovisual link where the member is at a place that makes their physical presence at the meeting impractical or impossible, when a member is unwell, and where a member is unable to attend due to an emergency.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — what councils' existing rules already permit, which is the substantive question the bill turns on. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Listen to this busy-body, bossy Labour Government.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome — it is a characterisation of the other party as a type. Nothing survives if the party reference is removed. (No individual is insulted, so this is not a Civility item.)
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They didn’t; they just amended the local government to put it back on the councils, but now they’ve changed their mind, six months later.
focus.explanation: Points to a named legislative act (the local government amendment devolving the discretion to councils) and an identified reversal, which is legitimate scrutiny of a policy position rather than generic party-bashing — though the weight of it is still 'they changed their mind' rather than the merits of the change.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: These standing orders make it very clear what a member can do. As long as they give two days’ written notice, they can attend by audio or audiovisual link where the member is at a place that makes their physical presence at the meeting impractical or impossible, when a member is unwell, and where a member is unable to attend due to an emergency.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that existing council standing orders permit remote attendance on two days' written notice where a member is unwell, faces an emergency, or is somewhere that makes physical attendance impractical or impossible.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The standing orders of the Western Bay of Plenty District Council and Bay of Plenty Regional Council (and the LGNZ model standing orders they derive from), plus clause 25A of Schedule 7 to the Local Government Act 2002; true if those documents provide for attendance by audio/audiovisual link on two working days' notice in the grounds described, false if the notice period or grounds materially differ.

veracity.statement: It’s not required when it’s within the Local Government Act which was amended, I understand, Carl Bates, in 2023 to allow standing orders to give councils the discretion to allow for remote participation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Local Government Act 2002 was amended in 2023 to give councils discretion, through their standing orders, to allow remote participation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation record for amendments to the Local Government Act 2002 (Schedule 7, remote-attendance provisions) — true if an amendment enacted in 2023 conferred that discretion on councils via standing orders, false if the enabling provision dates from another year (e.g. the 2014 amendment inserting cl 25A) or does not exist.

veracity.statement: We don’t want a situation where the Wellington City Council was taking submissions for their long-term plan last, and an American prankster with 150,000 YouTube followers got on as a submitter and said a whole lot of rubbish, and eventually the Wellington city councillors woke up about five minutes later and realised they were being pranked.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific incident: during Wellington City Council's long-term plan submissions an American YouTuber with 150,000 followers joined remotely as a submitter and went unrecognised as a prank for about five minutes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington City Council long-term plan submission-hearing records and contemporaneous news coverage (early 2024); true if a remote submitter was an American online personality of roughly that following who was not identified as a prank for several minutes, false if no such incident occurred or the details (nationality, following, duration) are materially wrong.

veracity.statement: Forty nine action points in 100 days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's 100-day programme contains 49 action points.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The coalition Government's published 100-day plan (released December 2023); true if it enumerates 49 actions, false if the published count differs.

rigor.statement: It’s particularly important, when we’re asking as a House here, to get our public servants back into the city post-COVID. When the Chamber of Commerce and business associations here in Wellington city are telling people to get back to work to support the auxiliary businesses, the cafes, the sandwich bars, and the restaurants and the likes, then we just make ourselves and make our colleagues and local government exempt from turning up; it is totally unnecessary, given the standing orders that most territorial authorities have.
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument by loose analogy: public servants are being asked back to offices, therefore elected members should not be allowed to attend remotely. The two cases are not shown to be alike, and the conclusion also rests on characterising the bill as making members 'exempt from turning up' when it regulates remote participation and quorum rather than abolishing attendance — a strawman premise doing the work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why is that? Because there’s such a distance between elected members in the flesh and those who are teleporting themselves electronically in.
rigor.explanation: Generalises a causal claim from a single anecdote: one council being taken in by a prank submitter is offered as evidence that remote attendance creates a general disconnect. Argument from anecdote, with no mechanism or wider evidence connecting the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We don’t want a situation that Wellington City Council has got themselves into over the years, where half of them are sitting there in their pyjamas.
civility.explanation: Mockery of the councillors themselves rather than of the rule — the image of them in pyjamas ridicules the people, not the policy of remote attendance. Short of a direct insult, but no longer engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That member over there might have sat watching Parliament TV in his pyjamas for the last few months, but we need to expect more, and, frankly, the public expects more of their representatives.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at the individual member who had just interjected, imputing idleness. It lands on the person rather than on any argument they made; the insult is the speaker's own conduct regardless of who it was aimed at.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why does the Government deem those bills to warrant missing out on the public’s participation through a select committee process?
focus.explanation: Names a specific process (select committee scrutiny) and a specific set of bills being taken under urgency. Straightforward scrutiny of a government decision, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, that money will actually go into the consolidated account, where it will help pay for schools, where it will help pay for nurses, where it will help ensure we have police on our streets, where it will help ensure we lock up the offenders that they wanted running free.
focus.explanation: There is a real fiscal point — the savings go to the consolidated account rather than being hypothecated to tax cuts — but the sentence ends on a characterisation of what the other party supposedly wanted rather than on any named spending commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, the member may be concerned that she was aligned with a Government that was responsible for delivering some of these outcomes that are also reported in the Salvation Army report: the proportion of children reporting some level of food insecurity rose sharply in 2023, including 40 percent of Pacific households with children, and the number of children in benefit-dependent households increased during 2023, meaning more children are at risk of poverty.
focus.explanation: Opens on the member's political alignment rather than the question, then does supply named findings and figures from the report at issue. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has she received any reports of their requests back then, rather than the faux concern they’re showing now?
focus.explanation: Once the imputation of "faux concern" against the opposition is stripped out, what remains is a rhetorical framing rather than a policy point: no report, figure or measure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In part because the Government sought a mandate at the election to do those things quickly, and in case it has escaped the notice of the member, that mandate was delivered.
civility.explanation: "in case it has escaped the notice of the member" is condescension aimed at the questioner rather than at the argument — short of an insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In part because the Government sought a mandate at the election to do those things quickly, and in case it has escaped the notice of the member, that mandate was delivered.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to electoral mandate. Winning an election is offered as sufficient reason to remove select committee scrutiny from these particular bills; nothing connects the general mandate to the specific bills' exemption from public participation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On behalf of the Minister, as I said in answer to the primary question, the modelling that the member refers to is in the absence of any other Government policies and interventions. Our Government fully intends to take other policies and interventions, such that we can have confidence that we will be doing more to help children in poverty than that Minister ever managed to achieve.
rigor.explanation: The premise (the modelling holds other policies constant) is fair, but the conclusion — that we can be confident of a better outcome — rests on interventions that are not named or quantified. Confidence is asserted, not derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, I disagree because, actually, the single biggest thing we can do is reduce the number of children growing up in benefit-dependent households. And then the second biggest thing we can do is provide those children a decent education by ensuring they’re turning up to school and we’re teaching them how to read, write, and do maths. These are tasks that the previous Government ignored. They were prepared to see children trapped in cycles of poverty, and this Government is not.
rigor.explanation: A ranked counter-claim ("the single biggest thing") is set against the Children's Commissioner's ranking with no evidence offered for the ordering — bare assertion answering an authority with another assertion, closing on an imputation of motive that does nothing to support the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can the Government justify generating savings by reducing benefit increases for people already living below the poverty line to pay for tax cuts for the rich?
rigor.explanation: A complex question: it presupposes the very link in dispute — that the indexation savings fund tax cuts, and that those cuts go to "the rich" — so the conclusion is built into the premise rather than argued for.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Could I ask the Minister whether she is concerned, with respect to the Salvation Army’s State of the Nation report and its concerns about poverty, outlined in that report, at how it was the fact that 128,000 immigrants came to New Zealand in the year ended October last year, exacerbating all the conditions that this Government now has to deal with?
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal attribution: migration numbers are offered as "exacerbating all the conditions" reported on poverty with nothing linking the migration series to the food insecurity and benefit-dependency findings in the report.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I just wanted to ask the Leader of the House about a bill that in Opposition the National Party did ask about quite frequently to see how it was progressing through the House; just to see how the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill is progressing, because I notice it has been languishing at about 18 or 19 since this Government was elected, and of course it was a matter of some concern to that Party when they were in Opposition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill has sat at roughly position 18–19 on the Order Paper throughout this Government's term to date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Order Paper listings for Government/Members' bills from November 2023 to 15 February 2024; true if the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill appears at or around Nos. 18–19 across that period, false if it appears materially higher or lower.

veracity.statement: Given that the supplementary analysis report of the indexation bill clearly states the risk of disabled people and people with health conditions being disadvantaged by the change in indexation, does she expect more children and households with disabled parents to have increased poverty?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the supplementary analysis report accompanying the benefit indexation bill identifies a risk of disadvantage to disabled people and people with health conditions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report published with the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill; true if it identifies a disadvantage risk for disabled people or people with health conditions, false if it contains no such finding.

veracity.statement: Well, I think what the member is referring to is the fact that, unfortunately, under the last Government, we had a situation where inflation was outstripping wage growth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during the previous Labour government's term, CPI inflation exceeded wage growth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation against the Labour Cost Index / average ordinary time hourly earnings for the quarters of 2021–2023; true if annual CPI exceeded annual wage growth over that period, false if wage growth ran at or above inflation.

veracity.statement: Well, the member may be concerned that she was aligned with a Government that was responsible for delivering some of these outcomes that are also reported in the Salvation Army report: the proportion of children reporting some level of food insecurity rose sharply in 2023, including 40 percent of Pacific households with children, and the number of children in benefit-dependent households increased during 2023, meaning more children are at risk of poverty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures from the Salvation Army report: a sharp 2023 rise in children reporting food insecurity, including 40 percent of Pacific households with children, and an increase in children in benefit-dependent households during 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Salvation Army State of the Nation 2024 report's food insecurity and benefit-dependency sections, plus MSD benefit data for 2023; true if the report gives a sharp 2023 rise with a 40 percent Pacific household figure and MSD shows more children in benefit-dependent households, false if either figure is absent or materially different.

veracity.statement: We think it is shameful that under a time of declining employment, 69,000 more people went on to the jobseeker benefit under Labour, with 50,000 more children living in benefit-dependent households.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that jobseeker benefit numbers rose by 69,000 and children in benefit-dependent households by 50,000 over the previous Labour government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets for jobseeker support recipients and children in benefit-dependent households, comparing the quarters at the start and end of the 2017–2023 Labour government; true if the increases are approximately 69,000 and 50,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Could I ask the Minister whether she is concerned, with respect to the Salvation Army’s State of the Nation report and its concerns about poverty, outlined in that report, at how it was the fact that 128,000 immigrants came to New Zealand in the year ended October last year, exacerbating all the conditions that this Government now has to deal with?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 128,000 immigrants arrived in New Zealand in the year ended October 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for the year ended October 2023; true if the stated figure matches the published migrant arrivals count, false if it materially differs — note the published net migration figure for that year is close to 128,000 while gross arrivals are roughly double, so the check turns on which series the figure describes.

veracity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, the Deputy Prime Minister makes a very good point. I recently sat down with the Minister of Immigration and looked at what has happened with immigration in recent years, and what we saw was that despite the rhetoric about highly skilled migrants being targeted, what instead we saw under the last Government’s immigration settings was a significant spike in lowly skilled workers at the expense of highly skilled workers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous government's immigration settings there was a significant increase in lower-skilled migrant workers and a corresponding fall in highly skilled ones.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE work visa approvals broken down by ANZSCO skill level for 2021–2023, particularly Accredited Employer Work Visa approvals; true if lower-skilled approvals rose sharply while higher-skilled approvals fell or stagnated, false if the skill mix was stable or shifted toward higher-skilled workers.

veracity.statement: How does this change support her focus on “getting people who can work into work”, when officials have advised that “Beneficiaries that are not able to work will also be impacted by this change but will have no ability to enter work to change their situation.”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that officials advised, in the quoted words, that beneficiaries unable to work would be affected by the indexation change with no ability to enter work to change their situation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The officials' advice / supplementary analysis report on the benefit indexation change; true if the quoted sentence appears substantially as read, false if no such advice exists or the wording materially changes its sense.

specificity.statement: Well, the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary Bill is at No. 19 on the Order Paper, and when the Government is ready to make moves around it, that member will be one of the first to know.
specificity.explanation: Supplies one concrete fact (No. 19 on the Order Paper) but the substantive part — what the Government intends to do with the bill and when — is left entirely open: "when the Government is ready" carries no timeframe or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What advice has she received on how many of the forecast 7,000 extra children in poverty are likely to have a disability or live in a household with a person who has a disability?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific forecast figure (7,000 extra children), a specific policy consequence and a specific sub-population. A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, as I said in answer to the primary question, the modelling that the member refers to is in the absence of any other Government policies and interventions. Our Government fully intends to take other policies and interventions, such that we can have confidence that we will be doing more to help children in poverty than that Minister ever managed to achieve.
specificity.explanation: "Other policies and interventions" is the entire content of the answer: no policy is named, no amount given, no timeframe. She had the material to be concrete and was not.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We think it is shameful that under a time of declining employment, 69,000 more people went on to the jobseeker benefit under Labour, with 50,000 more children living in benefit-dependent households.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures attached to a named benefit and a named period — someone could go and check both against MSD's published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On behalf of the Minister, what I am pleased to see is that we have a Government that is taking action to support incomes and address the cost of living across the board. That includes policies such as the Family Boost policy to provide childcare rebates to families with children in childcare, and policies to remove the Auckland regional fuel tax, to stop petrol tax increases, and to ensure the economy is better managed so that there are more opportunities for New Zealanders in all circumstances.
specificity.explanation: Names three real policies (Family Boost childcare rebates, repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax, halting petrol tax increases) but supplies no rebate amounts, thresholds or dates, and closes on a generic claim about better economic management.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Has the Minister received any reports of requests by the previous Government of their officials as to the unheralded impact of 128,000, a record number, coming to New Zealand in just one year, and its impact on housing availability, educational facility availability, infrastructure, and health?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 128,000 people arrived in New Zealand in a single year and that this was a record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the annual period referenced (year ended late 2023); true if annual net migration was approximately 128,000 and the highest on record in the series, false if the figure or the record claim is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: It does not disguise the fact, for example, that the accounts show an increase in core Crown expenses of around 10 percent since the same statement a year ago.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that core Crown expenses in the interim financial statements rose about 10 percent year on year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Interim Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the six months ended 31 December 2023, core Crown expenses line, compared with the six months ended 31 December 2022; true if the increase is approximately 10 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: For example, GDP growth was weaker than expected in the September quarter of last year, contracting 0.3 percent, and growth in the preceding two quarters was revised down.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific GDP outturn (-0.3 percent in the September 2023 quarter) and downward revisions to the two prior quarters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series as published at February 2024; true if the September 2023 quarter shows a 0.3 percent contraction and the June and March 2023 quarters were revised down, false if the sign or magnitude differs materially or the revisions were upward.

veracity.statement: The Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update forecasts before Christmas were for three more years of operating deficits followed by a wafer-thin surplus of $100 million in the 2026-27 financial year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the December 2023 HYEFU forecast for the OBEGAL track was, including the size and year of the return to surplus.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update 2023, OBEGAL forecast track; true if it shows deficits through 2025-26 and a surplus of roughly $100 million in 2026-27, false if the surplus year or magnitude differs materially.

veracity.statement: Under that Government, I would note, rents went up considerably.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rents rose considerably over the 2017-2023 Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (and MBIE bond lodgement mean rents) from October 2017 to October 2023; true if median/mean rents rose substantially above general inflation over that period, false if rents were flat or fell.

veracity.statement: The vast majority of councils were opposed to Labour’s three waters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that most territorial authorities opposed the Water Services Entities reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Council submissions on the Water Services Entities Bill and its amendment bills, plus LGNZ and Communities 4 Local Democracy membership records; true if a clear majority of the 67 territorial authorities are on record opposing, false if opposition was a minority or the record is mixed.

civility.statement: Were there any reports requested back then by these people now today showing faux concern in the House?
civility.explanation: Imputes insincerity — 'faux concern' — to the members opposite rather than engaging their argument. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I can see that the member is getting excited because taxpayers might be getting something back from the Government! He should really wait and see when the policy is announced.
civility.explanation: Mocks the questioner's demeanour and imputes a motive to him instead of engaging the question. Condescension rather than a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Mr Speaker, let me tell you about the precedent I’m excited about. I’m excited about the precedent of tax reduction, for the first time in 14 years. The member opposite had six opportunities to do it, and he couldn’t bring himself to let New Zealanders keep more of their own money—and this Government will.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal at the edges — 'he couldn't bring himself to' characterises the member's will rather than his policy — but stops short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I find it interesting that the member opposite wishes to demonise landlords. If there were no landlords in New Zealand, there would be no tenants. No one would be able to rent a home. Under that Government, I would note, rents went up considerably. Well, we want to be a Government that delivers more housing, that actually achieves more affordable housing, unlike that Government, which colossally failed. Remember the 100,000 KiwiBuild houses?
civility.explanation: 'Wishes to demonise landlords' imputes bad faith to the questioner rather than answering the priorities point.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yesterday, the coalition Government delivered on its promise to repeal the divisive three waters programme that would’ve taken local decisions away from communities. The vast majority of councils were opposed to Labour’s three waters. This Government is delivering on our commitment to restore local council ownership and control of water assets.
civility.explanation: A contested, partisan subject where there was every opportunity to attack the members opposite; the criticism lands entirely on the policy. 'Divisive' describes the programme, not a person.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This morning, Treasury released the Government’s financial statement for the six months ending 31 December 2023. These show that most of the key fiscal indicators are slightly stronger than expected in the Treasury’s half-year forecasts before Christmas. However, saying they are slightly stronger than expected is damning with faint praise. It does not disguise the fact, for example, that the accounts show an increase in core Crown expenses of around 10 percent since the same statement a year ago.
specificity.explanation: Names the document, the period it covers, the comparison point and a percentage figure. Someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she stand by the commitment in the coalition agreement with ACT to “restore mortgage interest deductibility for rental properties with a 60 percent deduction in 2023/24, 80 percent in 2024/25, and 100 percent in 2025/26”; if so, what is the estimated cost to the Crown of this commitment?
specificity.explanation: Quotes the commitment with its exact percentages and years and asks a checkable question about the cost to the Crown.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, the Government will be implementing Local Water Done Well through two further bills. The next bill will be passed by the middle of 2024, setting out provisions relating to council service delivery plans and transitional economic regulations. A next bill to provide for the long-term replacement scheme will be introduced in December 2024.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the legislative vehicle, what each bill covers, and dates for both. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Particularly when I said that this Government will not tax Aucklanders an additional 11.5c per litre on fuel to fund more cycle lanes, red light cameras, speed bumps, and lowering speed limits across the city.
specificity.explanation: A precise figure (11.5c per litre) attached to a named tax and an enumerated list of what it would fund.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Has he already determined that the Eastern Busway and the Glenvar Road - East Coast Road adjustment projects “will be prioritised for the remaining funds” of the regional fuel tax, and will he simply continue to just tell Auckland Council which projects it will now fund?
specificity.explanation: Names the two projects, the funding source, and quotes the Minister's own wording — a precise question that could be answered precisely.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Looking ahead, while business confidence has picked up, a prolonged period of pressure on household budgets means growth is expected to remain weak, and high migration means GDP per capita is expected to continue to decline.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that headline growth stays weak and that GDP per capita keeps falling through the period ahead.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ real GDP per capita series for the quarters following February 2024; true if GDP per capita records further declines across 2024, false if it returns to sustained growth.

divination.statement: Put it this way: I think it is highly unlikely that the full set of forecasts in May will deliver any upside surprises.
divination.explanation: Predicts that the Budget 2024 economic and fiscal forecasts will contain no material improvements on the December 2023 forecasts.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget Economic and Fiscal Update, 30 May 2024, compared with HYEFU 2023; true if the growth, revenue and OBEGAL tracks are unchanged or worse, false if the May forecasts revise the fiscal or growth outlook materially upward.

focus.statement: Does she stand by the commitment in the coalition agreement with ACT to “restore mortgage interest deductibility for rental properties with a 60 percent deduction in 2023/24, 80 percent in 2024/25, and 100 percent in 2025/26”; if so, what is the estimated cost to the Crown of this commitment?
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment in the coalition agreement and asks for its fiscal cost. Textbook scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can see that the member is getting excited because taxpayers might be getting something back from the Government! He should really wait and see when the policy is announced.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely about the member opposite's reaction; the only policy content is a vague gesture at 'taxpayers getting something back'. No figure, mechanism or timeframe.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Mr Speaker, let me tell you about the precedent I’m excited about. I’m excited about the precedent of tax reduction, for the first time in 14 years. The member opposite had six opportunities to do it, and he couldn’t bring himself to let New Zealanders keep more of their own money—and this Government will.
focus.explanation: There is a real tax-policy point (tax reduction, six Budgets without one), but the weight of the answer is the member opposite's record rather than the retrospectivity question asked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is it a priority to give tax cuts to landlords, at a time when there is legislation going through the House today that will cut the incomes of the poorest New Zealanders and push thousands of children into poverty?
focus.explanation: Sets one named policy (interest deductibility for rental properties) against another before the House the same day. A priorities argument grounded in specific measures, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yesterday, the coalition Government delivered on its promise to repeal the divisive three waters programme that would’ve taken local decisions away from communities. The vast majority of councils were opposed to Labour’s three waters. This Government is delivering on our commitment to restore local council ownership and control of water assets.
focus.explanation: Names the specific programme, the repeal, and the commitment being fulfilled. Policy content throughout, with only light party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I always agree with the Prime Minister, and we will be making sure that the remaining funds go on the priority projects which Auckland Council and the mayor have identified around what are the priority projects for the remaining funds, which is the Eastern Busway, City Rail Link, and local roading projects. But if the Labour Party wants to go to Auckland and tell Aucklanders they need to pay more money for speed bumps, I wish you luck.
focus.explanation: The first half names specific projects and the process for prioritising them; the second half drops the policy for a jibe at what the Labour Party would supposedly tell Aucklanders.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I find it interesting that the member opposite wishes to demonise landlords. If there were no landlords in New Zealand, there would be no tenants. No one would be able to rent a home. Under that Government, I would note, rents went up considerably. Well, we want to be a Government that delivers more housing, that actually achieves more affordable housing, unlike that Government, which colossally failed. Remember the 100,000 KiwiBuild houses?
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus false dichotomy: the question asked why landlord tax cuts are a priority, not whether landlords should exist, so 'if there were no landlords there would be no tenants' rebuts a position nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does he agree with the Prime Minister: “Our fundamental belief is localism and devolution. We do not believe in centralisation and control through Wellington.”; and if so, why is he dictating to Auckland Council what they will and won’t build?
rigor.explanation: A real inference: a stated principle is quoted and set against a specific action said to contradict it. The gap is that 'dictating' is asserted rather than demonstrated, so the inconsistency is not fully established.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One way I intend to do this is by repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act. This section places duties on the chief executive that are at odds with the agency’s primary purpose, which is to support the wellbeing of our most vulnerable at-risk children.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism (repeal), the exact provision (section 7AA) and the statute. Someone could go and check what the section does and whether a repeal bill appears.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In one case, a caregiver had paid for counselling that was desperately needed for a child—they paid for it themselves so they didn’t have to wait months and months—only to be told that this would have to stop as it had not been approved by Oranga Tamariki.
specificity.explanation: A concrete situation with an identifiable mechanism (caregiver-funded counselling halted for want of agency approval), but no date, no place, no figure, and no named process that could be looked up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I will never apologise for adding more tools and skills to our young people so that they can cope when they come out of these facilities and have a better chance at life.
specificity.explanation: Generic virtues — 'tools and skills', 'a better chance at life'. No programme, cost, timeframe or measurable outcome. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What is the benefit of banning cellphones from classrooms at Wainuiomata High School, now that their rebuild has been cancelled by the Government and there won’t be enough classrooms for the growing number of students?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific school, a specific capital project and a specific consequence (insufficient classrooms for a growing roll). Concrete enough for the Minister to confirm or deny.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is he aware that when the panel declined the Hananui salmon farm, they found that there was a risk that even a small change in their population could have “irreversible and catastrophic effects” on the survival of critically endangered hoiho / yellow-eyed penguin in the area?
specificity.explanation: Names the project, the decision, the affected species and quotes the panel's own words. Precise enough that anyone could pull the decision and check the passage.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I haven’t read the decision of the panel in relation to that particular project, but what I would say in a more general sense is that it is possible to have environmental conditions proposed on projects that mitigate and remedy the environmental effects of a variety of projects, including, for example, renewable energy projects that will help decarbonise the economy and grow the economy at the same time, and I would have thought the member would be in favour of such projects.
specificity.explanation: Deliberately general — 'a variety of projects', 'environmental conditions' — with no named condition, threshold, or process. The one concrete element (renewable energy) is an example, not a commitment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There will be two pathways. One will be there will be a range of projects listed in the legislation, and then the second pathway will be, upon application to the Government, Ministers will be able to refer projects to an expert consenting panel.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual mechanism of the regime: two named pathways, who lists projects, who may refer them and to whom. Checkable against the bill when introduced.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One way I intend to do this is by repealing section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act. This section places duties on the chief executive that are at odds with the agency’s primary purpose, which is to support the wellbeing of our most vulnerable at-risk children.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy — repeal is justified by a claimed conflict between the section's duties and the agency's purpose — but the conflict is asserted rather than shown; no duty is quoted and no incompatibility is demonstrated. Bare assertion standing in for the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When people have heard about this Government’s plans beyond what they may get from the media or from some members on the other side of the House, people appreciate and understand that Oranga Tamariki needs to get back to its core purpose of keeping young people safe and making sure they are cared and loved for.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity: the correctness of the policy direction is supported by the claim that people agree once they hear it. Strip out the swipe at the media and the other side and an inference remains — and it is a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He was very excited about this and said he would be very excited to take part in something like this. This is just one example of the positive feedback I’ve received, not just from social workers and iwi and Māori partners but also from children and young people.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: one enthusiastic young person is offered as evidence of broad support for military academies, with the speaker herself conceding it is a single example. The conclusion about sector-wide feedback does not follow from the instance given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A Wellington student was quoted as saying that by having her phone off and in her bag, she was already paying more attention to school notices and concentrating better in lessons without her phone distracting her. This is exactly why this Government has removed the distraction of phones from schools.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote plus post hoc: one quoted student's self-report is offered as vindication of a nationwide policy ('this is exactly why'). A single reported instance cannot support the general conclusion drawn from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I haven’t read the decision of the panel in relation to that particular project, but what I would say in a more general sense is that it is possible to have environmental conditions proposed on projects that mitigate and remedy the environmental effects of a variety of projects, including, for example, renewable energy projects that will help decarbonise the economy and grow the economy at the same time, and I would have thought the member would be in favour of such projects.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur by substitution of category: asked about a project declined for catastrophic effects on an endangered species, the answer establishes only that conditions can mitigate effects on some other class of project (renewables). That conditions work somewhere does not support that they work here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is not new, by the way, because the COVID fast-track legislation also listed projects in the legislation and also set up a process for Ministers to refer projects to an expert consenting panel.
rigor.explanation: A precedent argument that tracks its premise: if the earlier Act really did both list projects and allow ministerial referral, the conclusion that this design is not novel follows. It does not address whether the two regimes differ in the panel's powers, which is a real gap but a smaller one.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When people have heard about this Government’s plans beyond what they may get from the media or from some members on the other side of the House, people appreciate and understand that Oranga Tamariki needs to get back to its core purpose of keeping young people safe and making sure they are cared and loved for.
focus.explanation: There is a policy point (the agency's core purpose), but a good share of the sentence's weight is framing about the media and members opposite rather than the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How do the Minister’s priorities meet the needs of young people for a caring and loving environment, given the six recommendations of the Auditor-General in respect of Oranga Tamariki and the lack of evidence that boot camps have any assistance in that regard, whatsoever?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific external report, a specific count of recommendations and a specific policy (boot camps), and asks how the Minister's stated priorities meet them. Holding a minister to a named finding is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: How do the Minister’s priorities meet the needs of young people for a caring and loving environment, given the six recommendations of the Auditor-General in respect of Oranga Tamariki and the lack of evidence that boot camps have any assistance in that regard, whatsoever?
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions embedded in the question: that the Auditor-General made six recommendations about Oranga Tamariki, and that there is no evidence boot camps help. Not a verdict — the recommendation count is the part most likely to be off.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Controller and Auditor-General's report on Oranga Tamariki: true if that report contains exactly six recommendations; false if the count differs. Separately, the published New Zealand evaluations of military-style activity camps / boot-camp style youth justice programmes (including the 2008–2011 MAC evaluations and reoffending statistics): true if no evaluation shows a benefit on reoffending or wellbeing, false if one does.

veracity.statement: I am hearing reports about Australian states picking up this policy, like many other countries are around the world, and I look forward to speaking more positively about it in the future as more data and evidence comes to light as to the success of the policy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australian states, and many other countries, are adopting school cellphone bans. The checkable core is whether Australian states had in fact adopted such bans by the date of the statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Announcements by Australian state governments of school mobile-phone restrictions on or before 2024-02-15: true if one or more states adopted such a ban in that period, false if none had.

veracity.statement: Can I ask the Minister as to whether she’s been told that this ban on phones in schools by school children has been so successful that the Queensland State Labour Party Government in Australia has now adopted it as well?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Queensland's Labor government has adopted a school phone ban, and implies it did so in response to the New Zealand policy's success. The adoption and the causal link resolve separately.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Queensland Government announcements on school mobile-phone policy: true if the Queensland Labor government had adopted a state-wide school phone ban on or before 2024-02-15, false if it had not. The stronger embedded claim — that Queensland adopted it because of the New Zealand policy's success — is true only if Queensland's own announcement cites New Zealand.

veracity.statement: What is the benefit of banning cellphones from classrooms at Wainuiomata High School, now that their rebuild has been cancelled by the Government and there won’t be enough classrooms for the growing number of students?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Government cancelled the Wainuiomata High School rebuild. The roll-growth claim is secondary and would be settled by Ministry roll projections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education school property records and announcements for Wainuiomata High School: true if the rebuild was cancelled or halted by the Government on or before 2024-02-15, false if it remained funded and proceeding.

veracity.statement: Is he aware that when the panel declined the Hananui salmon farm, they found that there was a risk that even a small change in their population could have “irreversible and catastrophic effects” on the survival of critically endangered hoiho / yellow-eyed penguin in the area?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quoted finding in a specific decision. A direct documentary check, either the words are in the decision or they are not.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The decision report of the panel that declined the Hananui open ocean salmon farm application: true if it contains a finding that a small change in the hoiho / yellow-eyed penguin population could have 'irreversible and catastrophic effects', false if the phrase or finding is absent or applies to something else.

veracity.statement: This is not new, by the way, because the COVID fast-track legislation also listed projects in the legislation and also set up a process for Ministers to refer projects to an expert consenting panel.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two structural features of the 2020 COVID fast-track statute. Settled by reading the Act, independently of whether the analogy to the new regime holds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Act 2020: true if that Act both listed specified projects in a schedule and provided a process for Ministers to refer projects to an expert consenting panel; false if it did only one of these or neither.

divination.statement: Speaking to the question and, also, as it relates to the primary, the cellphone ban for Wainuiomata will have similar impacts to every other school that I’m hearing from, in that students are interacting more with each other, focusing on their learning, not getting distracted, and, very soon, we are going to have evidence and data to show that this policy is working.
divination.explanation: A forecast that evidence and data demonstrating the policy's success will exist 'very soon' — a future state of the evidence base, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Publication, by the Ministry of Education or an independent evaluator, of New Zealand data or evaluation evidence on the school cellphone ban: true if such evidence is published and reports a positive effect on student engagement or achievement, false if no such evidence is published by the resolve-by date or if what is published shows no effect.

civility.statement: Will he now seek assurances that all Ministers are fully meeting their conflict of interest disclosure obligations under the Cabinet Manual, as he described yesterday in relation to decision making on potential projects; and, if so, will he also commit to ensuring that no listed projects are connected to people or companies that have made substantial donations to coalition parties?
civility.explanation: Pointed and robust — it raises the possibility that donors could benefit from ministerial referrals — but it is framed as a request for process assurances rather than an accusation against any named person. It edges toward imputing bad faith without landing on anyone.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And it is one of the first duties of this House to ensure that the executive is being accountable for their actions, and, in this case, there is extraordinary concentration of ministerial power in this bill.
focus.explanation: Engages a named feature of the bill before the House — the concentration of ministerial power over consenting decisions — rather than the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is the Minister doing to support whānau and owners of whenua Māori in Tairāwhiti and Kahungunu one year after Cyclone Gabrielle?
focus.explanation: Directed at a specific policy area (support for whenua Māori owners in named regions after a named event); no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Was he advised prior to the recent $63 million boost funding for Hawke’s Bay and Tairāwhiti announced by Minister Mitchell, and if so, did he relay any concern regarding the lack of any support for Māori and whenua Māori?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named funding decision and its coverage; no content-free party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For example, our coalition agreement with our New Zealand First friends sets out that this Government will amend the Building Act to make it easier to build granny flats—smaller structures, up to 60 square metres—and, in addition, our coalition agreement with the ACT Party also states that the Government will explore allowing builders to opt out of needing a building consent, provided they have long-term insurance for the building work.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measures themselves — what will change, under which agreement, and how.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Minister’s answer that in 80 days, the only real action he has taken as the Minister for Mental Health is to support his former member’s bill?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named Minister's actions over a stated period against a specific measure — accountability, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The report findings are clear: things have got worse, there’s no workforce plan, and, basically, they failed in mental health.
focus.explanation: Cites a real finding (the absence of a workforce plan) but wraps it in a general verdict on the other party's performance rather than the wait-time question asked.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Was he advised prior to the recent $63 million boost funding for Hawke’s Bay and Tairāwhiti announced by Minister Mitchell, and if so, did he relay any concern regarding the lack of any support for Māori and whenua Māori?
specificity.explanation: Names a figure ($63 million), the regions, the announcing Minister and the precise action asked about — a checkable question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Over the last couple of months, Ministers including myself have visited Te Tairāwhiti and throughout Te Matau-a-Māui to understand some of the challenges that those whānau are facing.
specificity.explanation: Names regions and a rough timeframe but describes only visits — no amounts, mechanisms or deadlines for the support asked about.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The latest inflation data from Stats New Zealand shows that the price of building a new house has increased by 41 percent as compared with 2019 prices.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a percentage and a baseline year — precise enough that anyone could check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, our coalition agreement with our New Zealand First friends sets out that this Government will amend the Building Act to make it easier to build granny flats—smaller structures, up to 60 square metres—and, in addition, our coalition agreement with the ACT Party also states that the Government will explore allowing builders to opt out of needing a building consent, provided they have long-term insurance for the building work.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute to be amended, the size threshold (60 square metres), the source documents and the mechanism (insurance in place of consent).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In answer to the second part: establishing the role of New Zealand’s first mental health Minister, which now includes the responsibility of the almost $2.5 billion of ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete action taken and attaches a funding figure, though it gives no timeframe or delivery detail for what the money will do.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The latest inflation data from Stats New Zealand shows that the price of building a new house has increased by 41 percent as compared with 2019 prices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Stats NZ data shows a 41 percent rise in the price of building a new house since 2019.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction cost series (CPI new dwelling construction / capital goods price index for residential buildings) as at Feb 2024 versus 2019: true if the cumulative increase is approximately 41%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In Australia, for example, the cost of building a stand-alone house is some 50—five-zero—percent higher in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that building a stand-alone house costs about 50 percent more in New Zealand than in Australia (the clause order is a live-speech inversion; the comparison intended is NZ higher than Australia).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published trans-Tasman build-cost comparisons (e.g. the 2022 NZ Infrastructure Commission / MBIE and CoreLogic cost-per-square-metre comparisons) for a standalone house: true if NZ costs are around 50% above Australian costs, false if the gap is materially smaller or larger.

veracity.statement: In answer to the second part: establishing the role of New Zealand’s first mental health Minister, which now includes the responsibility of the almost $2.5 billion of ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that this is New Zealand's first Minister for Mental Health, and that the portfolio carries almost $2.5 billion of ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial warrant records for whether a dedicated Minister for Mental Health had been appointed before December 2023, and Vote Health / Health NZ budget documents for the amount of ring-fenced mental health and addiction funding: true if this is the first such portfolio and the ring-fenced sum is close to $2.5 billion, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Well, I won’t be lectured by that member when, today, we published a report in the House from the Auditor-General that says more young people are waiting longer for specialist services when they came into Government—shame on them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a report from the Auditor-General tabled that day found more young people waiting longer for specialist mental health services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auditor-General's report tabled in the House on 15 February 2024 on mental health services for young people: true if it finds that waiting times for specialist services for young people lengthened over the previous Government's term, false if it finds no such increase.

veracity.statement: Since 2021, the Social Workers Registration Act 2003—the Act—has required all social workers to register with the Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB).
veracity.explanation: Asserts that mandatory registration of all social workers with the SWRB has been in force since 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Social Workers Registration Act 2003 as amended by the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019: true if mandatory registration for all practising social workers commenced in 2021, false if it commenced in another year or is not mandatory.

veracity.statement: This particular bill, basically, is a very small amendment to actually extend—there was an extension made where the registration could take people four years to register, but, in hindsight, with the social worker sector facing a significant workforce shortage, with an estimated 700 unfilled vacancies and growing demand for social work services due to the impact of COVID-19 and Cyclone Gabrielle, and also the number of students enrolled in social worker qualifications declining, it has been reviewed and looked at to shorten the period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an estimated 700 unfilled social worker vacancies and a decline in enrolments in social work qualifications.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: SWRB / MSD or Health NZ social work workforce data around 2023-24 on vacancies, and Tertiary Education Commission enrolment data for social work qualifications: true if unfilled social work vacancies were around 700 and enrolments were declining, false if the vacancy figure is materially different or enrolments were rising.

rigor.statement: Kiwis pay too much for building materials, for example, and ensuring more high-quality building products are approved for use in building sites across the country will increase competition, lower building material costs, and support our resilience in the event of supply chain disruption.
rigor.explanation: The chain from approving more products to more competition to lower prices is plausible but asserted rather than shown; nothing is offered on the size of the effect or on what currently blocks approval. A real inference with a real gap, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is the Minister’s answer that in 80 days, the only real action he has taken as the Minister for Mental Health is to support his former member’s bill?
civility.explanation: Pointed and dismissive of the Minister's record, but framed as a question about actions taken rather than an attack on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I won’t be lectured by that member when, today, we published a report in the House from the Auditor-General that says more young people are waiting longer for specialist services when they came into Government—shame on them.
civility.explanation: "I won't be lectured by that member" and "shame on them" turn on the questioner and her party rather than the substance; condescending rather than a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just as context for those that are new to the House—because it is important to know, when we’re considering a bill like this—previously it was not mandatory for social workers to be registered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that registration of social workers was not mandatory in New Zealand before the current mandatory-registration regime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Social Workers Registration Act 2003 and the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019, plus the Social Workers Registration Board's commencement notices: true if registration was voluntary in law until the 2019 Act's mandatory-registration provisions commenced, false if registration was already compulsory beforehand.

veracity.statement: Why I’m concerned about this—and it will be discussed, I’m sure, in more detail across the course of this committee stage—is that the social workers association themselves have written not only to me this week but also to the Minister for social development to make it clear to her that, actually, their intention is not for it to be reduced to two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Aotearoa New Zealand Association of Social Workers wrote in the week before 15 February 2024, to both her and the Minister for Social Development, stating they do not want the pathway reduced to two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The correspondence itself (later read into the Hansard record) and any ANZASW public statement or Ministerial correspondence release from February 2024: true if a letter/email of that week to both recipients opposes the two-year reduction, false if no such correspondence exists or it does not oppose the reduction.

veracity.statement: We do have a shortage of social workers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current workforce shortage of social workers in New Zealand as at February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board workforce reports and Ministry of Social Development / Oranga Tamariki vacancy data for 2023–24, and whether social worker appears on Immigration New Zealand's Green List: true if official workforce data or the shortage-occupation listing record an unmet demand for social workers, false if registered numbers meet or exceed demand.

specificity.statement: The issue that will come up over the course of this debate is the Government’s decision to put up an amendment to reduce the time frame for them to be able to access that experience pathway from four years to two years.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism at issue (the experience pathway) and the exact change proposed (four years to two years). Anyone could check the Amendment Paper against this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I’m really just asking whether that title shouldn’t be a little more descriptive of the fact that it’s a Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill in respect of the experience pathway.
specificity.explanation: Proposes a concrete, actionable change — a title qualified by reference to the experience pathway — though he stops short of offering drafted wording.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Either she didn’t receive it, it hasn’t been brought to her attention, or she is choosing to ignore the professional social work workforce associations here with regards to their recommendation.
