civility.explanation: Pointed and robust: it lays out deliberate disregard as one live possibility, which edges toward imputing indifference, but it is framed as an open set of explanations tied to the substance rather than a claim about the Minister's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d be interested if the Minister could clarify whether she has secured and appreciated the position and advice, particularly from tangata whenua, not only from the official body but from other Māori settings across the motu.
civility.explanation: A contested challenge — she is questioning whether the Minister consulted adequately — put entirely as a question about the process, with no imputation of bad faith or attack on the Minister herself.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I also just need to make the point before I sit down that the two population groups, in terms of the social workers, that would be most affected by reducing that time from four years to two years would actually be Māori and Pacific who have been working within their community and iwi organisations, haven’t yet finished their qualifications or their registration, and are going to be denied the four years to actually get up to speed and get that registration that we need them to get.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if the unregistered experience-pathway cohort is disproportionately Māori and Pacific workers in community and iwi organisations, then shortening the window falls hardest on them — the conclusion tracks the premise. Marked down because the premise about who that cohort is is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I support the idea of withdrawing, and this is why: pathways take time. Pathways of learning take time, particularly so when systemically it prejudices particularly Māori in the process of registration. And why I know this is because I was one of those that attempted the registration process some while ago.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the measure, but a weak one: the conclusion (withdraw the amendment) rests on a restatement that pathways take time plus a single personal experience of the registration process — an appeal to anecdote, with nothing offered to show the two-year window is in fact too short.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I also just need to make the point before I sit down that the two population groups, in terms of the social workers, that would be most affected by reducing that time from four years to two years would actually be Māori and Pacific who have been working within their community and iwi organisations, haven’t yet finished their qualifications or their registration, and are going to be denied the four years to actually get up to speed and get that registration that we need them to get.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: who the specific four-to-two-year change affects and why. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I support the idea of withdrawing, and this is why: pathways take time. Pathways of learning take time, particularly so when systemically it prejudices particularly Māori in the process of registration. And why I know this is because I was one of those that attempted the registration process some while ago.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the registration pathway and how it operates for Māori applicants, rather than characterising the other party. Slightly short of the top only because the case is made in general terms rather than against the specific figures.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Of course, having heard Carmel Sepuloni speak, it may well be that if the Amendment Paper isn’t withdrawn, we’ll need another amendment bill a bit later on to extend it further.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that if the Amendment Paper shortening the experience pathway to two years survives, Parliament will have to legislate again to extend the pathway before it lapses.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation register and Parliament's bills record: true if, after the two-year amendment is enacted, a further bill extending the section 13 experience pathway deadline is introduced on or before the shortened expiry date of 27 February 2026; false if no such bill is introduced by then (or if the amendment was withdrawn, leaving the antecedent unsatisfied).

veracity.statement: The Social Workers Registration Board have recently made changes to the experience pathway application process to make this more accessible for Māori and Pacific practitioners, I believe.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the SWRB has, recently and as a matter of record, altered the experience pathway application process with the aim of improving accessibility for Māori and Pacific applicants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board published policy/process documents and annual reports for 2023–24 on the experience pathway (s.13 Social Workers Registration Act) application process; true if a change to the application process aimed at Māori and Pacific applicants was made in that period, false if the process was unchanged.

veracity.statement: The ANZASW provided a submission to the Social Services and Community Committee recommending shortening the time frame to two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ANZASW's select committee submission recommended reducing the delay to the repeal of the experience pathway to two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ANZASW written submission to the Social Services and Community Committee on the Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill; true if it recommends a two-year time frame, false if it recommends any other period or makes no such recommendation.

veracity.statement: However, we understand that, as the member says, the ANZASW have softened their view on the need for a shorter time frame.
veracity.explanation: Characterises ANZASW's subsequent communication to the Minister as a softening of its position rather than a withdrawal of its submission.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 13 February 2024 letter from ANZASW (Sharyn Roberts) to the Minister for Social Development and Employment; true if the letter qualifies or moderates the two-year recommendation while leaving it standing, false if it withdraws the submission and asks for the four-year time frame.

veracity.statement: They do not want it reduced to two years—they want it at four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts ANZASW's current position: opposed to a two-year delay, in favour of retaining the four-year period in the bill as reported back.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 13 February 2024 ANZASW letter to the Minister and ANZASW's public statements on the Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill; true if ANZASW's stated position is a four-year delay, false if it supports two years or takes no position on the length.

divination.statement: We anticipate that this will support experienced Māori practitioners to register as social workers through the experience pathway over the next two years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Board's process changes will result in experienced Māori practitioners registering via the experience pathway during the two-year window created by the delay.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board registration statistics (annual reports 2024/25 and 2025/26) broken down by pathway and ethnicity; true if registrations of Māori practitioners via the experience pathway are sustained or rise over the two years to February 2026, false if they fall.

specificity.statement: If I could actually provide some context and be helpful, Ministry of Social Development officials have discussed a potential two-year time frame with sector representatives, including Social Service Providers Aotearoa, Aotearoa New Zealand Association of Social Workers (ANZASW), and the Tangata Whenua Social Workers Association.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, the exact time frame under discussion and three specific sector bodies consulted — checkable detail, though no dates or content of the discussions are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If there is to be an amendment that will change that time line from four to two years, what advice has she sought on the impacts in the intake of Māori and Pasifika social workers, any advice that she’s sought around the intake of social workers from low socio-economic backgrounds, and what conversations has she had, in between coming into the role and tabling the amendment, with those professional bodies?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact change at issue (four years to two), three distinct categories of advice sought, the affected groups, and the time window for the consultation asked about. A precise, answerable question rather than a general demand for more consultation.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All of the evidence that the Government is using to actually justify the reduction in time for the extended pathway is now null and void because the most important professional body has come forward and written to the Minister and said to her that there was a mistake in that submission.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion overreaches the premise: one professional body retracting one submission does not establish that *all* of the Government's evidence — officials' advice, other submissions, MSD's discussions with other sector bodies — is void. A hasty generalisation from a single withdrawn source to the entire evidence base.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I want to reflect on why I’m asking for the engagement of tertiary education institutions, because, being a field educator for social workers, I’ve done guest lectures for social work classes, and it’s really clear that a lot of the people who are able to get registered through the experience pathways are some of the people who are really struggling to enter the professional sector through the traditional pathways.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy — that the experience pathway serves people the degree route excludes — but the support offered is an appeal to personal experience and guest lecturing rather than data on who registers by which route. The claim is modest enough that the anecdote is relevant, so this is a gap rather than a non-sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I feel for the Minister in the chair, the Hon Melissa Lee, because she is not the Minister who is leading the actual bill, but the Minister who is leading the actual bill should be reading her correspondence and should be nimble enough to change her position.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the person — the implication that the responsible Minister has not read her own correspondence is a criticism of diligence rather than of the policy — but it is framed around a specific duty and explicitly excuses the Minister in the chair. Robust, not contemptuous.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To shorten time just to fill a shortage of workforce, this idea is an unsafe way to go—it’s unsafe. I’m talking as a clinician, and I’m talking as an experienced clinician.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the shortened pathway is unsafe rests on the speaker's own credentials and experience rather than on any stated mechanism, evidence or harm — an appeal to authority and personal anecdote. There is a real inference about the measure before the committee, so it is assessable, but the support offered is her standing rather than a reason.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is not the practice of this committee to interrupt legislation at this stage, when a submission is made, late in the piece, that is completely contradictory.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to established practice: the conclusion that the corrected submission should not change the course of the bill rests on what the committee customarily does, not on the merits of the correction or on any reason why the timing makes it less reliable. Appeal to tradition/procedure standing in for an argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: To shorten time just to fill a shortage of workforce, this idea is an unsafe way to go—it’s unsafe. I’m talking as a clinician, and I’m talking as an experienced clinician.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the amendment at issue — the length of the experience pathway and the workforce-shortage rationale for shortening it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Did she consider it and, therefore, did she ignore it and decide to proceed with this tabled amendment, which is reducing it from four years to two years?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named measure: the tabled amendment reducing the pathway from four years to two, and whether the evidence before the Minister was considered. Naming the specific amendment and the specific change is accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The extension to the pathway is a temporary measure while work is actually under way to address long-term issues. The purpose of the two-year extension is to maintain the emphasis on the sector to take steps towards addressing the pipeline of social workers into the industry.
focus.explanation: Answers on the policy itself: what the extension is for, why it is temporary, and what it is meant to achieve. No reference to opponents at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Did she consider it and, therefore, did she ignore it and decide to proceed with this tabled amendment, which is reducing it from four years to two years?
civility.explanation: Pointed — it presses on whether the Minister disregarded the correspondence — but the challenge lands on the decision and the process, not on the Minister as a person. No imputation of bad character, no mockery.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I understand that the submission and the contents of it went through the Social Services and Community Committee, and that informed the Minister’s position, but our expectation, and our question to the Minister, is about her ability to be nimble, given that this very important association, and actually not just the Aotearoa New Zealand Association of Social Workers but the Tangata Whenua Social Workers Association have both expressed fervently that they do not support the reduction from four years to two years.
civility.explanation: Mostly on the substance — the select committee process and the two bodies' stated positions — but 'her ability to be nimble' edges onto the Minister personally, framing the disagreement as a shortcoming of hers rather than of the decision. Robust and slightly pointed, well short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Did the Minister receive the correspondence on 13 February? Did her office and herself read that correspondence, give it consideration, and decide to ignore the request to set aside their submission upon which this amendment is actually basing the proposal to reduce it to two years—has that happened before we came into the House today?
specificity.explanation: Names a date (13 February), a specific document, the specific request it made (to set aside the submission), and the exact change it bears on (four years to two). Someone could check every element. It falls short of 1.0 only because the question does not identify the body or quantify anything further.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The extension to the pathway is a temporary measure while work is actually under way to address long-term issues. The purpose of the two-year extension is to maintain the emphasis on the sector to take steps towards addressing the pipeline of social workers into the industry.
specificity.explanation: Gives the duration (two years) and states the mechanism in general terms — pressure on the sector to build the workforce pipeline — but the 'work under way' is unnamed, with no programme, milestone, target number of social workers or date attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve made the decision, for a range of other reasons, that the two-year time frame is what the Government will stand with.
specificity.explanation: The decision and the timeframe are concrete, but the operative content — the 'range of other reasons' driving it — is withheld entirely. Nothing in the reasoning can be checked or engaged with.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I understand that the submission and the contents of it went through the Social Services and Community Committee, and that informed the Minister’s position, but our expectation, and our question to the Minister, is about her ability to be nimble, given that this very important association, and actually not just the Aotearoa New Zealand Association of Social Workers but the Tangata Whenua Social Workers Association have both expressed fervently that they do not support the reduction from four years to two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that two named organisations, the Aotearoa New Zealand Association of Social Workers and the Tangata Whenua Social Workers Association, have both stated they oppose reducing the experience pathway from four years to two.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The correspondence tabled in the committee on 15 February 2024 and any public statements or submissions by ANZASW and the Tangata Whenua Social Workers Association on the Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill: true if both organisations are on record opposing the reduction from four years to two, false if either did not take that position or supported the reduction.

veracity.statement: It is really important that part of the consideration was to ensure that we kept the emphasis on transitioning to a mandatory qualification regime, which has been signalled in legislation since 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the move to a mandatory qualification regime for social workers has been signalled in legislation since 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative record for social worker registration — the Social Workers Registration Legislation Bill and the resulting Act, and the Social Workers Registration Act 2003 as amended: true if a bill or Act dating from 2017 signalled mandatory qualification/registration, false if the mandatory regime was first signalled in a later or earlier instrument.

focus.statement: So I accept there is a challenge, and I accept, with the amendment that I have tabled, the two-year time frame is how we get the balance right of ensuring that we get to mandatory registration in a timely manner.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the tabled amendment and the registration timeframe it sets. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I agree with the member wholeheartedly in that lived experience is part of the reason that we have an experience pathway, so there’s no disagreement there. We’ve just made a decision that it will be two years, not four. So there are still two years for those who are interested in pursuing that path to do so.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the amendment — the experience pathway and the length of the transition window.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Minister rejecting the letter and the plea from the Tangata Whenua Social Workers Association to allow four years as opposed to two, which is in the tabled amendment?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny naming a specific document, a specific body and the specific provision of the tabled amendment. Holding a Minister to a named submission is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, 2017 has still not allowed for the systemic barriers to be removed yet, and so what that, from their perspective, will result in is that some whānau will be denied the experience and skill that only the experience pathway would have allowed for.
focus.explanation: Directly about the mechanism of the experience pathway and the effect of shortening it — the measure before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When you shorten time, particularly for Māori and social workers to gain the credentials but particularly the cultural aspects of it, and shorten it simply to fill a shortage of social workers is simply unsafe.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the amendment's effect on credentialling and cultural competence — the policy, not the party proposing it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just want to know how the Minister is able to make the adjustment known in Part 2 for the minimum family tax credit when we haven’t yet got the figures for benefit in terms of the 1 April adjustment.
focus.explanation: Puts a precise question about the mechanics of the Part before the committee — how one indexed amount can be settled while the linked one is not.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m interested to understand exactly how this bill will relate to the other debate we’ve been having and whether, in fact, it’s taking the same approach or whether it’s taking a more generous approach given that it’s a tax credit framework.
focus.explanation: Asks about the bill's indexation approach and how it compares with the parallel measure — a question about mechanism, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I accept there is a challenge, and I accept, with the amendment that I have tabled, the two-year time frame is how we get the balance right of ensuring that we get to mandatory registration in a timely manner.
specificity.explanation: Names the amendment, the two-year time frame and the goal of mandatory registration, but supplies no mechanism, evidence or milestone for how two years achieves the balance claimed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I agree with the member wholeheartedly in that lived experience is part of the reason that we have an experience pathway, so there’s no disagreement there. We’ve just made a decision that it will be two years, not four. So there are still two years for those who are interested in pursuing that path to do so.
specificity.explanation: Gives the actual figures (two years rather than four) but nothing on who can complete the pathway in that window or how.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the Minister rejecting the letter and the plea from the Tangata Whenua Social Workers Association to allow four years as opposed to two, which is in the tabled amendment?
specificity.explanation: Names the organisation, the submission, and both timeframes at issue; a reader could go and check exactly what is being asked. Falls short of 1.0 only because the letter's content is not itself detailed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At the last committee stage, we did have it clarified that net wage growth was going to be 5.3 percent versus the Consumers Price Index, which is 4.7 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two named indices with figures to one decimal place, tied to the adjustment under debate. Immediately checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I just want to know how the Minister is able to make the adjustment known in Part 2 for the minimum family tax credit when we haven’t yet got the figures for benefit in terms of the 1 April adjustment.
specificity.explanation: Names the Part, the credit, and the 1 April adjustment date, though it stops short of naming the figures or the indexation formula at issue.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m interested to understand exactly how this bill will relate to the other debate we’ve been having and whether, in fact, it’s taking the same approach or whether it’s taking a more generous approach given that it’s a tax credit framework.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the comparison to be made and the tax credit framework, but names no figure, clause or indexation basis, so it points at the question rather than pinning it down.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I agree with the member wholeheartedly in that lived experience is part of the reason that we have an experience pathway, so there’s no disagreement there. We’ve just made a decision that it will be two years, not four. So there are still two years for those who are interested in pursuing that path to do so.
rigor.explanation: The concluding 'so there are still two years' does not answer the premise it was offered against: the objection was that two years is too short for practitioners working while credentialling, and restating that two years remain assumes what is in dispute. The inference is on-policy but circular.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, 2017 has still not allowed for the systemic barriers to be removed yet, and so what that, from their perspective, will result in is that some whānau will be denied the experience and skill that only the experience pathway would have allowed for.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: unresolved systemic barriers since 2017, therefore fewer people reach registration via the experience pathway. But the warrant is the sector's stated perspective rather than anything offered here, and the step from 'barriers remain' to 'whānau will be denied' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When you shorten time, particularly for Māori and social workers to gain the credentials but particularly the cultural aspects of it, and shorten it simply to fill a shortage of social workers is simply unsafe.
rigor.explanation: Assumes the motive ('simply to fill a shortage') and then treats the conclusion of unsafety as following from it. Nothing connects a shorter window to unsafe practice; the motive attribution does the work the argument should.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know it to be so because of my experience of more than 40 years in the sector, working in social justice, working in the space with whānau who have harm just hoisted upon them, particularly by the system and by legislation that just doesn’t understand our reality.
rigor.explanation: The sole warrant offered for the harm claim is the speaker's own standing — an appeal to personal authority and anecdote. Long experience makes the claim worth hearing but does not establish it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I heard in your discussion was that you are content with your decision, which sounded to me like the Minister will go on record as rejecting the written record by the national body—two of them, in fact, the tangata whenua body—that the Minister will go on record as being satisfied that that’s the position that’ll be taken, and, in fact, rejecting tangata whenua outwardly, and therefore Māori.
rigor.explanation: A chain of escalating restatements: content with a decision, therefore rejecting a submission, therefore rejecting the tangata whenua body, therefore rejecting Māori. Each step is broader than the last with nothing bridging them — a non sequitur by accumulation.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Minister said in her earlier answers that she had other considerations outside of just what was in the select committee process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Upston stated earlier in this committee stage that her decision drew on considerations beyond the select committee process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard transcript of the committee stage of this bill on 15 February 2024; true if Upston's earlier answers state she weighed considerations outside the select committee process, false if no such statement appears in her answers.

veracity.statement: At the last committee stage, we did have it clarified that net wage growth was going to be 5.3 percent versus the Consumers Price Index, which is 4.7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the net average wage growth figure relevant to the 1 April 2024 adjustment is 5.3 percent and the corresponding CPI figure is 4.7 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual movement for the year to December 2023 and the net average wage growth figure used by MSD for the 1 April 2024 main benefit adjustment; true if the two figures are 4.7% and 5.3% respectively (± rounding), false if either is materially different.

civility.statement: So it is a set up and it will cause harm not only to our practitioners but also to our whānau, because the idea of putting in our social workers when they’re just not ready in that way, it will bring harm—more harm.
civility.explanation: Brutal about the proposal — 'a set up' that will cause harm — but the target is explicitly 'the idea', and the speaker audibly corrected herself away from addressing the Minister personally moments earlier. Harsh criticism of a policy is civil; the bad-faith flavour of 'set up' keeps it just below the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I heard in your discussion was that you are content with your decision, which sounded to me like the Minister will go on record as rejecting the written record by the national body—two of them, in fact, the tangata whenua body—that the Minister will go on record as being satisfied that that’s the position that’ll be taken, and, in fact, rejecting tangata whenua outwardly, and therefore Māori.
civility.explanation: Moves past the two-year provision to characterise the Minister as outwardly rejecting tangata whenua and Māori — an imputation about her disposition rather than her policy. Short of an insult, but no longer engaging only the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I can see that the Minister isn’t yet ready to answer that question.
civility.explanation: A pointed dig at the Minister's preparedness rather than at the substance of the tax credit question, but it stops well short of a personal insult — it comments on the state of the debate rather than on her character or competence generally.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Given the change to the indexation of main benefits to track inflation rather than wages or inflation, will this in fact have a projected fiscal saving to the Government? Because benefits are going to increase at a slower rate, I’m assuming that will also mean that the family tax credits will increase at a slower rate as well.
rigor.explanation: A clean chain of inference: main benefits are re-indexed to CPI, the minimum family tax credit is uprated in line with main benefits, therefore the credit rises more slowly and a fiscal saving should show in the forecasts. The linking premise (the credit tracks main benefits) is stated rather than assumed, and the conclusion is put as a question rather than overclaimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And when that happens, it actually creates a situation where the so-called gap that she seeks to widen between wages and the benefits actually is narrowed by the fact that people are not able to keep as much as they could from the minimum family tax credit when they enter employment, due to those abatement thresholds not being updated, effectively undermining the goals that she has talked about time and time again of relentlessly supporting people into employment.
rigor.explanation: A genuine internal-consistency argument: an un-indexed abatement threshold claws the credit back at lower real incomes over time, which erodes the very in-work gap the Minister says she is widening. The inference tracks the mechanism; the gap is that it asserts rather than quantifies how much of the work incentive is actually eaten, so the strength of the conclusion outruns what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Surely if a minimum family tax credit is being adjusted in line with the changes that are going to happen on 1 April, then we would have those changes in the bill as well.
rigor.explanation: A fair puzzle poorly closed. The conclusion does not follow from the premise: the two adjustments need not both appear in the bill, because the main benefit adjustment happens automatically under the existing section 453 machinery while the credit's prescribed amount is a figure written into statute and so has to be legislated. The inference treats 'adjusted in line with' as implying 'legislated alongside'.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Given the change to the indexation of main benefits to track inflation rather than wages or inflation, will this in fact have a projected fiscal saving to the Government? Because benefits are going to increase at a slower rate, I’m assuming that will also mean that the family tax credits will increase at a slower rate as well.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism in Part 2 of the bill — the indexation basis and its flow-through to tax credits and the fiscal forecast. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And when that happens, it actually creates a situation where the so-called gap that she seeks to widen between wages and the benefits actually is narrowed by the fact that people are not able to keep as much as they could from the minimum family tax credit when they enter employment, due to those abatement thresholds not being updated, effectively undermining the goals that she has talked about time and time again of relentlessly supporting people into employment.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the abatement threshold, its interaction with the credit, and the stated policy objective. Criticism is directed at the setting, not at the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On this side of the House, we certainly want to encourage those families to get ahead through work and through less time spent on a benefit.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy direction (work incentives, time on benefit), but it is delivered as a statement of what 'this side of the House' believes rather than engaging the abatement settings actually at issue in Part 2.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So the specific questions around the minimum family tax credit: there’s been no change in the way it is calculated, it has been calculated the same way for quite some time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that this bill changes only the threshold figure, not the formula by which the minimum family tax credit is worked out, and that the formula has been stable for some time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The minimum family tax credit provisions of the Income Tax Act 2007 (subpart MF) and their amendment history: true if the method of calculating the credit — the prescribed net income amount less the family's net income — is unamended by this bill and has been unamended for years, with only the prescribed threshold amount changing; false if the calculation method itself has been amended in the recent past or is altered by this bill.

veracity.statement: In terms of the minimum family tax credit work-hours test, “full time” is actually defined as 20 hours or more per week for a sole parent and 30 hours or more combined for a two-parent family.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the statutory full-time work test for eligibility: 20 hours for sole parents, 30 hours combined for two-parent families.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The work-hours qualification for the minimum family tax credit in the Income Tax Act 2007: true if the Act sets 20 hours or more per week for a sole parent and 30 hours or more combined for a couple, false if either figure differs.

veracity.statement: So, if there are changes from the way it is indexed, that is going to mean—although I have heard earlier contributions from $2; however, the figure is an $18 loss in their income per week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the real weekly income loss to affected families from the indexation change is $18 per week, contrasting it with a $2 figure cited earlier in the debate. The two figures likely refer to different time horizons, which the criterion has to separate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report / MSD modelling accompanying the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill: true if the projected weekly income loss to an affected beneficiary family from CPI rather than wage indexation reaches about $18 per week over the modelled forecast period, false if the modelled loss is materially smaller (e.g. of the order of the $2 per week cited by other members) at every horizon in the report.

veracity.statement: Also, in the supplementary analysis report that we received for this bill, we do have the modelling around the indexing of benefits and we do have the number of $670 million fiscal savings from this piece of legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's supplementary analysis report puts the fiscal savings from the indexation change at $670 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report published for this bill: true if it states fiscal savings of approximately $670 million arising from the benefit indexation change, false if the report gives a materially different savings figure or no such figure.

specificity.statement: In terms of the minimum family tax credit work-hours test, “full time” is actually defined as 20 hours or more per week for a sole parent and 30 hours or more combined for a two-parent family.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory hours thresholds for both household types — a listener could check it or apply it to their own circumstances directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Also, in the supplementary analysis report that we received for this bill, we do have the modelling around the indexing of benefits and we do have the number of $670 million fiscal savings from this piece of legislation.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document and the exact figure attributed to it, so the claim can be looked up and the follow-up question about what the figure covers can be answered precisely.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On this side of the House, we certainly want to encourage those families to get ahead through work and through less time spent on a benefit.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general intent with no mechanism, figure, threshold or timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we want to ensure is that there are incentives for people to work, so lifting the threshold provides that opportunity for people to be in work and not be penalised and for it not to then be a choice between working or not.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: raising the minimum family tax credit threshold removes a work-versus-benefit cliff. The mechanism is plausible and stated, but nothing is offered on the size of the threshold change or the abatement it interacts with, so the conclusion that it stops work being 'a choice between working or not' outruns what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And by not changing the abatement threshold in line with inflation, what that means is that the amount that people receive will start being eaten away a lot faster, because we haven’t changed those settings, effectively undermining the things that both the member and the Minister have just outlined.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference from a stated mechanism: if the abatement threshold is not indexed while incomes and prices rise, entitlements abate at lower real incomes and the real value of the payment erodes. The conclusion that this undermines the stated work-incentive purpose follows from that premise; no fallacy or appeal is relied on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It would be inconceivable to contemplate—and I see, I think, Mr Robertson agreeing with me—not adopting 1 April as the commencement date.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that no other commencement date could be adopted rests on an appeal to authority (a former Minister of Finance apparently nodding) and on convention, rather than on any reason why a different date would not work. Nothing is offered connecting 'it has always been 1 April' to 'it must be 1 April'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I think some of the commentary in the Chamber around it having to be 1 April—actually, when Working for Families did come in in 2005, there was some October implementation dates around that.
rigor.explanation: A counterexample used correctly: if a previous Working for Families change commenced in October, then the claim that a commencement date must be 1 April is defeated. The inference from the single counterexample to 'it does not have to be 1 April' is valid, though it establishes only possibility, not that October is preferable here.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a small measure of a suite of measures that our Government will progress in terms of making it beneficial for people to be in work.
specificity.explanation: Describing the Government's own programme with a real opportunity to name it: no figure for the threshold, no other measure in the 'suite' named, no timeframe for when any of it will 'progress'. Nobody could check or act on this.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And by not changing the abatement threshold in line with inflation, what that means is that the amount that people receive will start being eaten away a lot faster, because we haven’t changed those settings, effectively undermining the things that both the member and the Minister have just outlined.
focus.explanation: Names a specific mechanism in the bill (the Working for Families abatement threshold), its interaction with inflation, and the effect on recipients. This is scrutiny of the measure itself, not of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have a formula, right, as it is, and so not having this bill commence by that date still means that benefits will get indexed, just by the previous formula.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an existing statutory indexation formula would still adjust main benefits on the annual date even if this bill did not commence by 1 April 2024 — i.e. that the annual adjustment is not contingent on this legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The annual benefit adjustment provisions of the Social Security Act 2018 (the CPI/average-wage indexation and its adjustment date) as they stood before this Bill: true if main benefits are adjusted annually by a standing statutory formula independent of this Bill, false if the adjustment required this Bill to commence.

veracity.statement: As my good colleague on the left here, the former Minister of Finance Grant Robertson, will know, every benefit is adjusted on 1 April.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that all benefits are adjusted on 1 April, i.e. that 1 April is the universal annual adjustment date for benefit rates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The annual adjustment provisions of the Social Security Act 2018 and the annual benefit rate Orders in Council: true if every benefit rate is adjusted on 1 April each year, false if any benefit or supplementary assistance rate is adjusted on a different date.

veracity.statement: We could call it that, because that’s what it’s all about: encouraging people that—was it 67,000 people extra on a jobseeker benefit under that Government?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, in the form of a rhetorical question, that roughly 67,000 additional people were on Jobseeker Support by the end of the previous Labour-led Government's term compared with its start.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development benefit fact sheets: the number of Jobseeker Support recipients at the quarter ending September/December 2017 versus the quarter ending September/December 2023. True if the increase is approximately 67,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: So I think some of the commentary in the Chamber around it having to be 1 April—actually, when Working for Families did come in in 2005, there was some October implementation dates around that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the original Working for Families package was implemented in stages, at least one of which took effect in October rather than on 1 April.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taxation (Working for Families) Act 2004 and IRD/Treasury implementation timetables for the Working for Families package: true if any stage of the package took effect in an October, false if every stage commenced on 1 April.

divination.statement: I think we might have unanimous consent to just, all of a sudden, change the title of this bill, and I’m sure the Minister will be open to that.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the House would agree, by leave or unanimous consent, to amend the short title of the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill, and that the Minister would support that change.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The committee-stage and third-reading record for this Bill and the short title of the Act as enacted: true if the title was amended by leave during the Committee of the whole House, false if the Bill retained the title 'Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill'.

civility.statement: I think this bill should be called the “Social Security Bringing More Kids into Poverty Amendment Bill”.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested measure and a real opportunity to turn on the Minister, which she does not take. The sarcastic renaming is a hard attack on what the bill is claimed to do to children in poverty; no person's character, competence or motives is impugned. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a policy sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the reason why I stand for this amendment—to rename it the “Social Security Bringing More Kids into Poverty Amendment Bill”—is because this particular bill removes the ability and changes the way in which benefits are basically raised.
focus.explanation: Directed at the measure before the committee — the mechanism by which benefits are adjusted — though the vehicle is a rename amendment and the framing carries party weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have to call it out for what it is, which is simply an assumption that if you punish people on a benefit, that they’ll enter work, and yet, despite those assumptions, there’s nothing in this bill to adequately even change how support is provided to people who enter employment despite parts of the legislation that touch the Working for Families package, which, as the Minister in the chair previous to him being there alluded to, are not being addressed.
focus.explanation: Engages what the bill does and does not contain — the treatment of support on entering employment and the untouched Working for Families settings — rather than the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We all have a responsibility in this Chamber to those children of the lowest-paid families, families both on benefits and entitlements, those who are working, who are trying hard to get ahead.
specificity.explanation: A general appeal to shared responsibility: no figure, threshold, mechanism or timeframe that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I remind the members of the House that what this bill does is it returns the situation back to what the situation was since 2011, in which the benefits were and have been linked to the Consumers Price Index (CPI) and not to wage inflation.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (indexation basis), the two indices being contrasted, and a year — enough for someone to go and check what the bill changes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What the Government has done—and it’s been extremely explicit about this in its fiscal plans—is that this money, $670 million - odd, will be coming out of the pockets of the future recipients of main benefits.
specificity.explanation: A named dollar figure tied to a named document and a named group of people; checkable against the fiscal plan.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Based on the reports that we have, there’s actually nothing here—no report—that talks about what the previous member from the National Party said, that this bill will support people into employment.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but an argument from absence of evidence: the absence of a report on employment outcomes is offered as showing the claim untrue, when it only shows it unevidenced in the documents before the committee.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As everyone knows in this House, not even the former finance Minister sitting to my left here would be able to project with some certainty what will be higher over time and what will be lower.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to forecasting uncertainty: because no one can be certain which of CPI or wage growth will be higher, the opponents' poverty claim is treated as unsupported. He concedes in the same breath that point estimates exist in the regulatory impact statement, so uncertainty does not carry the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But ultimately, it can’t possibly be true that those on main benefits will be better off, because the Government is going to get $670 million.
rigor.explanation: The inference from a booked fiscal saving to recipients receiving less is sound in aggregate, but 'can't possibly be true' overreaches: the saving accrues across the forecast period, so it does not by itself refute the Minister's claim about the first year specifically.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He wasn’t; he was the Children’s Commissioner—he worked every day with children and advocating for children.
rigor.explanation: A bare appeal to authority: Becroft's office and his daily work with children are offered as the reason his recommendation was correct, with nothing about the evidence behind it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If the member spoke about dignity and work, there’s a gross, gross implication here about what they believe people on the benefit experience and how they should be treated.
civility.explanation: Moves from the bill to the member's beliefs, imputing that they regard beneficiaries as unworthy. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes bad faith to a person rather than testing the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Look, my reaction to this is that it’s based on a false premise.
civility.explanation: A contested exchange where he had every opportunity to turn on the two members; instead he disputes the premise of their case and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I remind the members of the House that what this bill does is it returns the situation back to what the situation was since 2011, in which the benefits were and have been linked to the Consumers Price Index (CPI) and not to wage inflation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that main benefit rates were indexed to CPI rather than to wage growth from 2011 onward, and that the bill restores that basis.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The indexation provisions of the Social Security Act and their amendment history: true if main benefits were adjusted by CPI movements from 2011 until the shift to average-wage indexation, and the bill reverts to CPI; false if the pre-2011 or intervening basis differs materially from that description.

veracity.statement: What the Government has done—and it’s been extremely explicit about this in its fiscal plans—is that this money, $670 million - odd, will be coming out of the pockets of the future recipients of main benefits.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition's published fiscal plan books roughly $670 million of savings from the change to benefit indexation, money that would otherwise have gone to main benefit recipients.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National Party/coalition fiscal plan and the Budget forecast savings line for the benefit indexation change: true if the forecast saving over the stated period is approximately $670 million; false if the figure is materially different or is not attributed to the indexation change.

veracity.statement: The other potential title for the bill would be the “Social Security (The Children’s Commissioner was Wrong) Bill”, because one of the things that we were told when we established the Welfare Expert Advisory Group was that one of the best things we could do to lift children out of poverty was to index benefits to wages.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that advice received around the Welfare Expert Advisory Group — attributed in the following sentences to then-Children's Commissioner Andrew Becroft — identified indexing main benefits to wages as one of the most effective ways to reduce child poverty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Welfare Expert Advisory Group's 2019 report and the Office of the Children's Commissioner's public submissions and statements: true if either recommends wage indexation of main benefits as a leading child poverty measure; false if no such recommendation appears.

divination.statement: And the reverse is clearly true in the material that’s on the Table and was discussed in the House today—that this bill will push 7,000 kids back into poverty.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the change in benefit indexation will result in about 7,000 additional children living in poverty, citing the official analysis tabled with the bill.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official child poverty impact analysis for the bill and subsequent Stats NZ child poverty statistics releases: true if the official estimate of ~7,000 additional children in poverty attributable to the indexation change is borne out in the published projections and the measured child poverty rate rises consistently with it; false if the official analysis carries a materially smaller number or the measured outcome shows no such increase attributable to the change.

specificity.statement: And for the sake of livable cities and a livable planet, I am prepared to work with Chris Bishop to bring back general tree protection.
specificity.explanation: Names a real, identifiable policy (general tree protection rules, removed from the RMA in 2012) and the Minister he would work with, which is more than a slogan — but there is no mechanism, no scope, no cost and no timeframe, so it stops at a direction of travel.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One thing I will support this Government in is use of structured literacy in the classroom and debunking this failed system of whole-language learning that has harmed so many through illiteracy in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that whole-language literacy instruction is a failed method that has caused widespread illiteracy in New Zealand. The pledge of support is not the checkable part; the causal claim about whole language is.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ reading-achievement data (NMSSA, PIRLS) over the period whole-language/balanced-literacy instruction predominated, plus Ministry of Education and independent NZ evidence reviews comparing whole-language with structured literacy. True if NZ literacy outcomes declined under whole-language-dominant instruction and the reviews attribute a material share of poor literacy to that method; false if outcomes show no such decline or the reviews find no link.

veracity.statement: To still suggest Māori ceded sovereignty is an audacious erasure of history in actual texts, let alone a betrayal of human relationships.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of documentary record that the texts of the Treaty do not show a cession of sovereignty, so claims to the contrary contradict the primary sources. The rhetorical wrapper ('audacious erasure', 'betrayal') is not the checkable part.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The te reo Māori text of te Tiriti o Waitangi (Article 1 'kāwanatanga' versus Article 2 'tino rangatiratanga') read against the English text, together with the Waitangi Tribunal's Te Paparahi o Te Raki stage 1 report (Wai 1040, 2014). True if the texts and the Tribunal's finding are that the rangatira who signed in February 1840 did not cede sovereignty; false if the authoritative textual/Tribunal record holds that sovereignty was ceded.

veracity.statement: When 137,000 hectares of native forest was eventually protected, we experienced firsthand that through organised political action you can change the course of history.
veracity.explanation: A specific numeric claim about how much native forest was protected following the West Coast forest campaign the speaker took part in.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Conservation and NZ Government records of the 2000-2002 end of Crown native-forest logging on the West Coast (the Timberlands West Coast beech and rimu programme) and the area of Crown native forest transferred to the conservation estate. True if the area protected is approximately 137,000 hectares; false if the official figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: I am dismayed that as the United States descends further into genocidal hegemony, we are so quickly willing to burn that hard-fought nuclear-free independence by signing away our status out of ANZUS and putting us back into AUKUS.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that New Zealand is signing out of ANZUS and into AUKUS. Extracted as a veracity item because overstatement of a country's actual treaty position is an accuracy question; the 'genocidal hegemony' characterisation is rhetoric and is not what the criterion tests.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT and NZ Government records as at 15 February 2024 on (a) whether New Zealand had signed or acceded to any AUKUS instrument, including Pillar 2, and (b) whether New Zealand had taken any formal step to leave the ANZUS Treaty. True if a signed AUKUS accession and/or an ANZUS withdrawal instrument exists as at that date; false if New Zealand had only stated a willingness to explore Pillar 2 participation and remained a treaty party to ANZUS (with US obligations suspended since 1986).

civility.statement: I cannot stand the wilful sowing of ignorance, particularly by those with political power.
civility.explanation: Genuinely contested territory (the Treaty and NZ history in schools), so there was a real opportunity to be civil or not. Saying the ignorance is 'wilful' imputes deliberate bad faith rather than error, which is a civility cost — but it lands on no named individual and stops short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: People do not cede sovereignty. Not my ancestors the Scots, not the Irish, not the West Papuans, not the Palestinians, and not tangata whenua, Māori.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real constitutional question, not a jibe — but it rests on a universal generalisation ('people do not cede sovereignty') offered without support, and the conclusion about Māori is reached by simply listing further instances rather than showing why the generalisation holds. The list also undercuts itself: the Scots parliament did formally vote itself out of existence under the 1707 Acts of Union, so at least one of the speaker's own examples is a counter-example.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I learnt of bizarre, outdated laws, such as the fact that the one native fish with explicit protection was declared extinct several decades before the law was even made.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's only explicitly legally protected native freshwater fish had already been declared extinct several decades before the protecting law was enacted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The schedule of absolutely protected wildlife under the Wildlife Act 1953 (and the Freshwater Fisheries Regulations) plus DOC/IUCN records for the New Zealand grayling (upokororo): true if the grayling is the only native freshwater fish with explicit statutory protection and its extinction was recognised decades before that statute; false if another native fish also holds explicit protection, or if the extinction was recognised at or after the date of the law.

veracity.statement: When I returned to Christchurch for the election, I got the shock of my life to discover the highest-polling candidate for Environment Canterbury was me: 55,000 people across Christchurch voted for me.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the 2016 local body elections she was the highest-polling candidate for Environment Canterbury, with about 55,000 votes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The declared 2016 Environment Canterbury constituency election results published by Christchurch City Council / ECan: true if Lan Pham's vote total was the highest of any ECan candidate and was approximately 55,000; false if another ECan candidate polled higher, or if her total differs materially from 55,000.

veracity.statement: Across all local government election results that year, only the Mayor of Auckland and Mayor of Christchurch received more votes than I did.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in that year's New Zealand local government elections, only two candidates nationwide — the successful Auckland and Christchurch mayoral candidates — received more votes than she did.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Declared results for all 2016 New Zealand local authority elections (mayoralties, council wards, regional council constituencies, DHBs): true if only the winning Auckland and Christchurch mayoral candidates recorded vote totals above hers; false if any other candidate nationwide exceeded her total.

rigor.statement: The term “radical” is defined by the Oxford Dictionary as “going to the root or origin; touching upon or affecting what is essential and fundamental.” I am so proud to be part of a bigger-picture kaupapa focused on the essential and fundamental things in life that support our earth ecosystem to function, a kaupapa focused on designing a world that prioritises the essential work of caring for each other as fellow human beings and caring for our planet as the basis of our economy and our society—not as a nice to have, not as a when we can afford it, but as an essential. It’s focused on what should be a not so radical idea: that the foundation of Government decision-making should be informed by mātauranga, evidence, and long-term mokopuna decisions over short-term quick fixes, individual reckons, and Google research. Some may call this radical, but to me it’s more accurately plain common sense.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: the dictionary sense of "radical" (going to the root) is substituted for the sense critics actually use (politically extreme), and the conclusion that the programme is "plain common sense" is drawn from the definitional switch rather than from anything about the policies themselves. A dictionary definition settles word usage, not whether a programme is moderate.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The term “radical” is defined by the Oxford Dictionary as “going to the root or origin; touching upon or affecting what is essential and fundamental.” I am so proud to be part of a bigger-picture kaupapa focused on the essential and fundamental things in life that support our earth ecosystem to function, a kaupapa focused on designing a world that prioritises the essential work of caring for each other as fellow human beings and caring for our planet as the basis of our economy and our society—not as a nice to have, not as a when we can afford it, but as an essential. It’s focused on what should be a not so radical idea: that the foundation of Government decision-making should be informed by mātauranga, evidence, and long-term mokopuna decisions over short-term quick fixes, individual reckons, and Google research. Some may call this radical, but to me it’s more accurately plain common sense.
specificity.explanation: Names no measure, figure, mechanism or timeframe; the content is a list of generic virtues (essential, fundamental, evidence-informed, long-term) that commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On review of my response, I acknowledge that there is confusion arising from my understanding of the differentiation between seeking specific advice and accepting advice being offered.
specificity.explanation: A correction that never states what the incorrect answer was or what the correct one is; it points at a conceptual 'confusion' with no dates, no wording, no fact substituted. She had a real opportunity to be precise here and was not.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This year, the Government is forecast to spend $8.8 billion just servicing New Zealand’s debt. That sum is more than the Government spent combined on secondary schools, police, and early childhood education last year.
specificity.explanation: A named figure, a named year and a named comparison basis — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The first step of this programme is an initial baseline savings exercise for Government agencies, designed to find about $1.5 billion per annum in savings to deliver on our policy commitments and to fund critical cost pressures.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (baseline savings exercise across agencies) and an annual dollar target; missing only a timeframe and which agencies bear what share.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, we want to work hard to improve Māori health outcomes. We’re going to work with local iwi, in the spirit of localism and devolution, to design solutions to improve outcomes locally. We just don’t believe that the way to go about that is building a massive health central bureaucracy here in Wellington.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel — work with iwi, devolve design — with no mechanism, funding, agency or timeframe replacing the body being disestablished. Asked what will replace the Māori Health Authority, he had a clear opportunity to name the replacement arrangements.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Was Cabinet made aware of the fact that a disabled Kiwi on the supported living payment would lose $2,300 a year by 2028 thanks to changes to benefit indexations; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable question: named benefit, named dollar figure, named year, named policy change. As specific as any answer could be.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This year, the Government is forecast to spend $8.8 billion just servicing New Zealand’s debt. That sum is more than the Government spent combined on secondary schools, police, and early childhood education last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific debt-servicing forecast for the current year and a comparison of that figure against combined actual spend on three named services last year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury HYEFU/Budget forecasts of core Crown finance costs for the 2023/24 fiscal year (true if the forecast is ~$8.8 billion), and the prior year's actual Vote appropriations/expenditure for secondary education, Police and early childhood education (true if their sum is below that figure, false if it exceeds it).

veracity.statement: What will he do to protect the takatāpui community from increased discrimination as a result of his Government’s policies, such as their policy to ban transgender athletes from competing in publicly funded sports?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as the premise of the question, that banning transgender athletes from publicly funded sport is a policy of the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–NZ First and National–ACT coalition agreements and any Cabinet paper or government policy statement on transgender participation in publicly funded sport; true if a ban is stated government policy, false if no such commitment exists in the agreements or in announced policy.

veracity.statement: We’ve been calling for a cessation of hostilities since October last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that his Government has been calling for a cessation of hostilities in Gaza continuously since October 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT and ministerial press releases and UN voting records from October 2023 onward; true if New Zealand ministers publicly called for a cessation of hostilities from October 2023, false if the earliest such call is materially later (noting the coalition Government took office on 27 November 2023).

veracity.statement: Does he stand by the statement of Christopher Luxon, “Do not be a climate denier. Do not be a climate minimalist. This is real. Give it up.”, and, if so, why did his state of the nation speech this weekend mention climate action precisely zero times?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as the premise of the question, that the Prime Minister's state of the nation speech that weekend made no mention of climate action at all.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published text of Luxon's state of the nation speech of February 2024; true if it contains no reference to climate action, false if any such reference appears.

veracity.statement: Was Cabinet made aware of the fact that a disabled Kiwi on the supported living payment would lose $2,300 a year by 2028 thanks to changes to benefit indexations; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact a specific annual dollar loss for a supported living payment recipient by a specific year arising from the indexation change.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD/Treasury modelling of the supported living payment under CPI indexation versus the previous average-wage indexation; true if the annual difference for a recipient reaches approximately $2,300 by 2028, false if the modelled gap is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Well, I’ll tell you what we’re not going to do: we’re not going to do what that Government did, which was to increase the number of people on the jobseeker benefit by 70,000 people—increased it by 58 percent, took the number of sanctions and obligations down by 57 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific figures about the previous Government's record: a 70,000 rise in jobseeker recipients, a 58 percent increase, and a 57 percent fall in sanctions and obligations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics for Jobseeker Support recipients between October 2017 and November 2023, and MSD sanctions data for the same period; true if the recipient increase is about 70,000 (~58%) and sanctions fell about 57%, false if the figures differ materially or the period used does not support them.

rigor.statement: Well, the same speech goes on to note that fiscal policy has had an impact on inflation, with the Secretary to the Treasury noting, “Our assessment is that fiscal policy has contributed to interest rates being higher than otherwise.” And, of course, that has an impact on every single family with a mortgage, every person with a credit card debt, every small business trying to repay a loan. High interest rates hurt, and what we know is that loose fiscal policy has contributed to them being higher than they might otherwise have been.
rigor.explanation: An inference from cited evidence: the Treasury Secretary's assessment supports the conclusion that fiscal policy raised interest rates, and higher rates plainly do hit mortgage-holders. Two gaps keep it off the top — it rests on an appeal to authority rather than the underlying analysis, and the conclusion upgrades the cited 'fiscal policy' to 'loose fiscal policy', which the quoted assessment does not say.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is it the Minister’s assessment that the wage subsidy, the Small Business Cashflow (Loan) Scheme, and other policies to support businesses during the COVID pandemic are redundant and that she wouldn’t have supported businesses to hold on to their employees during the pandemic?
rigor.explanation: Strawman: infers from the Minister's criticism of the trajectory of spending that she regards the named COVID business supports as redundant and would not have backed them. Criticising sustained post-crisis spending does not entail opposing the crisis-period schemes, and nothing is offered to bridge the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In particular, I stand by my statement from the weekend where I said, “I haven’t met a single young Kiwi whose ambition, creativity, and spark would be best served by a life on a benefit.” That is why I’m very proud to stand by this Government’s actions to address the legacy of welfare dependency that the previous Labour Government was all too happy to grow.
rigor.explanation: The stated basis for the welfare programme is the speaker's own personal experience of the people he has met — an appeal to anecdote. 'That is why' makes the anecdote carry the whole inference to a population-level policy conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They’re not losing anything, because we’re adjusting benefits by the amount of inflation.
rigor.explanation: Circular, and it evades the counterfactual the question depends on: the saving being claimed exists precisely because indexing to inflation pays less than the previous (wage-linked) basis would have. Restating the new basis cannot establish that no one is worse off relative to the old one.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: As I’ve just outlined in the answers to my previous questions, I concur with the view of the Secretary to the Treasury, which is that targeted and timely responses were warranted during the COVID epidemic. The real challenge that New Zealand is now facing is that the spending never got unwound and that it continued at very elevated levels without driving the kind of value and services that New Zealanders expect, and while seeing them endure a cost of living crisis in which they had far less money to spend in their take-home pay.
civility.explanation: Answering a question that accuses her of not supporting businesses through COVID — a real opportunity to hit back at the questioner. She engages the substance of the spending argument and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: On that basis, that would exclude the deputy leader of the Labour Party from running for the leader of the Labour Party one day down the road.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at a named individual (by office) rather than at any policy — using her personal circumstances as a punchline in a debate about welfare. It lands on the person, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The law was put in place with the intention of stopping gangs supplying methamphetamine; unfortunately, the law did not succeed. The evidence for that is that, since pseudoephedrine cough and cold medicine has been denied from New Zealanders through an effective ban, the price of P has actually gone down, the availability has gone up, and the volume consumed has gone up.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: three observations (price down, availability up, volume up) are offered in support of the conclusion that the ban failed in its stated aim. The conclusion tracks the evidence, but it rests on a before/after correlation with no control for other causes (domestic manufacture shifting to imported precursor, global supply), so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The law was put in place with the intention of stopping gangs supplying methamphetamine; unfortunately, the law did not succeed. The evidence for that is that, since pseudoephedrine cough and cold medicine has been denied from New Zealanders through an effective ban, the price of P has actually gone down, the availability has gone up, and the volume consumed has gone up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three empirical trends in the New Zealand methamphetamine market since pseudoephedrine-based cold medicines were restricted: the price of methamphetamine fell, availability increased, and the volume consumed increased.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police/Customs methamphetamine seizure and street-price data plus the ESR national wastewater testing programme, comparing the period since pseudoephedrine was reclassified in 2011 with the period before. True if street price per gram fell and consumption/availability indicators rose over that period; false if price rose or consumption fell.

veracity.statement: The publicly available report states that preliminary modelling shows indexing benefits to inflation in isolation as a policy, in the absence of any other Government policy interventions before 2028, may increase the number of children captured by the before-housing-cost moving line measure and after-housing-cost fixed line measures of child poverty by 7,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what a specific published report's preliminary modelling found about the child-poverty effect of CPI indexation considered in isolation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published MSD/Treasury advice on indexing main benefits to CPI rather than net average wage. True if that report's modelling gives an increase of about 7,000 children by 2028 on the before-housing-cost moving line and after-housing-cost fixed line measures; false if the figure or the measures differ materially.

veracity.statement: Absolutely, and what this Government won’t do is allow the number of children in benefit-dependent homes to grow by 45,000 like that Government did.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of children living in benefit-dependent households rose by 45,000 under the preceding Labour-led government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics on the number of children in benefit-dependent households, comparing the figure at the change of government in 2017 with the figure at the change of government in late 2023. True if the increase over that period is approximately 45,000; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Breast cancer is the most common cancer amongst New Zealand women, and that’s why the Government prioritised this crucial initiative in our 100-day plan.
