veracity.explanation: Asserts that breast cancer has the highest incidence of any cancer among New Zealand women.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Cancer Registry / Te Whatu Ora cancer registration data broken down by sex. True if breast cancer is the most frequently registered cancer among New Zealand women (excluding non-melanoma skin cancer, which is not routinely registered); false if another cancer site is more common.

veracity.statement: Is it correct that, after gaining office, talking up a crisis, he did not receive a briefing on the health workforce from Te Whatu Ora in his first two months in office?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister received no briefing on the health workforce from Te Whatu Ora during his first two months in the portfolio.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The list of briefings provided to the Minister of Health by Te Whatu Ora between the swearing-in of the government on 27 November 2023 and 27 January 2024 (obtainable via the proactively released briefing schedule or an OIA response). True if no briefing on the health workforce appears in that window; false if one does.

veracity.statement: We’re very encouraged by the increase in general practice registrars who actually start either this week or next week, which, I understand, is the largest cohort of general practice registrars, which will then feed through into the general practice network, so I’m very pleased with that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the general practice registrar cohort beginning training in the week of the statement is the largest such cohort to date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Royal New Zealand College of General Practitioners GPEP intake figures by year. True if the cohort starting in February 2024 is the largest GP registrar intake on record; false if an earlier intake was larger.

specificity.statement: It is changing pseudoephedrine from being a class B drug to a class C drug. There will still be significant restrictions around the importation, storage, and possession of pseudoephedrine within New Zealand. There will also be a change in the medicine’s regulations so that pseudoephedrine goes from being a prescription-only drug to a restricted pharmaceutical.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact legal mechanism: the schedule class before and after, the regulatory change to the medicines classification, and the resulting point of sale. Someone could check the amendment against this description.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The publicly available report states that preliminary modelling shows indexing benefits to inflation in isolation as a policy, in the absence of any other Government policy interventions before 2028, may increase the number of children captured by the before-housing-cost moving line measure and after-housing-cost fixed line measures of child poverty by 7,000.
specificity.explanation: A figure (7,000 children), a date (2028), the two named poverty measures, and the stated modelling assumption. Precise enough to check against the report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I don’t think it would be a surprise to this House that there are certain groups where there is a higher risk of children living in poverty, and our Government is focused on those, whether it is Pasifika, Māori, and disabled, that we will of course take into consideration with any policies that we are putting in place to reduce child poverty.
specificity.explanation: Names population groups but no report, no figure, no policy and no timeframe — 'take into consideration with any policies' commits to nothing checkable. The question asked whether particular reports existed; the answer supplies no identifiable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Are Ministry of Social Development figures correct that indexing benefits to wage inflation had moved over 5,000 children out of poverty, and, if yes, why is she hell-bent on making changes that increase rather than decrease the number of New Zealand children living in poverty?
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Ministry of Social Development figures), the policy (wage indexation of benefits) and a number (over 5,000 children). A precise question, and precise in the same way a precise answer would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Addressing the cost of living crisis, providing tax relief, and getting on top of ridiculous tax hikes for petrol are very practical things that will help low and middle income families as well as those who are receiving benefits.
specificity.explanation: Names three directions of policy but gives no amounts, no thresholds, no dates and no estimate of the effect on the group in question. A direction with some detail, missing the how much and the by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m advised that, once the programme is fully implemented, the extension will mean that women will become eligible for two to three extra mammograms, on average. This means around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the effect of the change two ways — extra mammograms per woman and the additional eligible population per screening cycle — and states the screening interval. Concrete enough to check against the programme's own modelling.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There is a lot of work to be done in terms of preparation. We need to grow our workforce and support them with the infrastructure required to expand our screening services.
specificity.explanation: Asked for the next steps, the answer gives generic categories — workforce, infrastructure — with no numbers of staff or machines, no funding, and no timetable. Close to a statement of intention rather than a plan.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Absolutely, and what this Government won’t do is allow the number of children in benefit-dependent homes to grow by 45,000 like that Government did.
focus.explanation: Turns to the previous government's record rather than the question asked, but names a specific measurable outcome — the number of children in benefit-dependent households and a figure for its growth — so it is closer to scrutiny of a policy outcome than content-free party-bashing. Marked down because the policy point is carried entirely by the comparison with the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Are Ministry of Social Development figures correct that indexing benefits to wage inflation had moved over 5,000 children out of poverty, and, if yes, why is she hell-bent on making changes that increase rather than decrease the number of New Zealand children living in poverty?
civility.explanation: 'Hell-bent on making changes that increase … the number of New Zealand children living in poverty' imputes to the Minister personally a determination to worsen child poverty. That is an attribution of bad faith rather than criticism of the policy, which the first half of the question had already made squarely. Short of a direct insult, but past the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it correct that, after gaining office, talking up a crisis, he did not receive a briefing on the health workforce from Te Whatu Ora in his first two months in office?
civility.explanation: 'Talking up a crisis' imputes to the Minister the motive of inflating a problem for political effect, rather than simply asking whether the briefing occurred. Pointed and edging onto the person's good faith, but well short of a personal insult, and the substantive accountability question is real.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think it’s actually more than 59, to be honest, because we are looking at a vast array of projects, and the precise list and exactly how those processes work with the process we’re setting up will be a decision for Cabinet, and it’s not too far away.
specificity.explanation: Carries one loose figure ("more than 59") but defers the list, the process and the timing to an unspecified Cabinet decision "not too far away" — a direction with no how, how many or by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, indeed, I can confirm that there were 17 listed projects in the COVID fast-track bill passed by the last Parliament: Te Ara Tupua, the Ngauranga to Petone shared path; the Wellington metro upgrade; Papakura to Pukekohe rail electrification, which I know the Hon Judith Collins is a big fan of; Britomart station eastern upgrade; Unitec Residential Development; Papakura to Drury South State Highway 1 improvements; a water storage reservoir in Kaikohe; the Queenstown Arterials Project; and a papa kāinga development in Kaitāia—more housing up Far North, which everyone supports.
specificity.explanation: A count plus nine individually named projects with locations — anyone could go and check the schedule against this list.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will he rule out including the Te Kuha coal mine in the list of projects to be approved in the primary legislation?
specificity.explanation: Names one identifiable project and one identifiable legislative mechanism; the answer would be checkable either way. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, there are a variety of hypotheses in that question, which may or may not turn out to be true. The member will have to wait for the final design of the fast-track procedure, but, as I’ve said twice now in response to previous questions, there are a variety of mechanisms through the Cabinet process and the parliamentary process and electoral law processes designed to make sure that the type of implications that the member is making are handled appropriately.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at three categories of safeguard (Cabinet process, parliamentary process, electoral law) without naming a single mechanism, test or step within any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, including my statement that Auckland light rail was an irresponsible project that would have cost taxpayers up to $29.2 billion, and which the last Government failed to deliver a single metre of track on despite spending $228 million on this project.
specificity.explanation: Two dollar figures and a concrete physical outcome (no track laid), all attached to one named project.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How does he reconcile his statement that he will not tax Aucklanders an additional 11.5c per litre on fuel to fund “more cycle lanes, redlight cameras, speed [bumps,] and lowering speed limits across the city” when Auckland Council information shows that, of the total funding available for regional fuel tax projects, safety and active transport initiatives represented just 16 percent of the regional fuel tax project spending?
specificity.explanation: A rate (11.5c/litre), a share (16 percent), a named revenue stream and a named source for the figure. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will he guarantee, right here, right now, that all stages of the Eastern Busway and the Glenvar Road - East Coast Road adjustment projects will be completed, and, if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Names two specific projects and asks about all stages of them — a commitment given or refused in response would be directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are allocating the money—the remaining $340 million—plus the money that will be collected between now and 1 July to those projects to make sure they are being delivered.
specificity.explanation: A dollar amount, a cut-off date and an allocation to previously named projects, though the split between those projects is not given.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Yes, indeed, I can confirm that there were 17 listed projects in the COVID fast-track bill passed by the last Parliament: Te Ara Tupua, the Ngauranga to Petone shared path; the Wellington metro upgrade; Papakura to Pukekohe rail electrification, which I know the Hon Judith Collins is a big fan of; Britomart station eastern upgrade; Unitec Residential Development; Papakura to Drury South State Highway 1 improvements; a water storage reservoir in Kaikohe; the Queenstown Arterials Project; and a papa kāinga development in Kaitāia—more housing up Far North, which everyone supports.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count — 17 — of projects listed in the COVID-19 fast-track consenting legislation passed by the previous Parliament, and names nine of them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Schedule 2 (listed projects) of the COVID-19 Recovery (Fast-track Consenting) Act 2020 as enacted by the 2020-2023 Parliament: true if 17 projects were listed in the legislation itself, false if the enacted schedule listed a materially different number (e.g. if most of the 17 were added later by Order in Council rather than by the bill as passed).

veracity.statement: Yes, including my statement that Auckland light rail was an irresponsible project that would have cost taxpayers up to $29.2 billion, and which the last Government failed to deliver a single metre of track on despite spending $228 million on this project.
veracity.explanation: Three separate factual assertions about the Auckland light rail project: an upper cost estimate of $29.2 billion, $228 million spent, and zero metres of track delivered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Light Rail Ltd / Ministry of Transport published cost estimates and the Government's expenditure disclosures at cancellation: true if the published upper estimate was about $29.2 billion, spend to date was about $228 million, and no track was constructed; false if any of those three figures is materially different.

veracity.statement: We’ve already scrapped this wasteful project, which is starting to address the last Government’s $200 billion funding gap in the transport budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government left a $200 billion funding gap in the transport budget.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport, NZTA or Treasury published analysis of the transport funding shortfall: true if an official estimate of approximately $200 billion attributable to the previous Government's transport programme is documented, false if no source supports a gap of that magnitude.

focus.statement: Can the Minister confirm, during that brief period of enlightenment when the earlier bill was passed, that there were actual projects in the bill that were consented by Parliament?
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point underneath — whether the earlier Act consented named projects by statute — but it is wrapped in a sarcastic characterisation of the previous Government ("that brief period of enlightenment"). The sneer is at a party, not a person, so it lands here rather than on Civility.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, given the extraordinary powers that have been granted to Ministers in this legislation, what measures is he taking to ensure that the list of projects that Ministers approve for inclusion in the legislation are not connected to people or organisations that are significant donors to coalition parties?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the ministerial approval power in the fast-track legislation and what conflict-of-interest safeguards attach to it. Names the mechanism, not the other team's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are delivering on our promises to provide cost of living relief for the motorists of Auckland, and I’m not going to be lectured from an Opposition over there which wants to spend 11.5c per litre on speed bumps.
focus.explanation: A thin policy claim (cost of living relief) with the weight of the sentence on characterising what the Opposition supposedly wants. No individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly; the tribal framing lands here.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Minister agree that it is unusual to see a Government—particularly in transport, in light of recent history—promise something and then actually deliver it?
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the whole content is a jibe at the previous Government's delivery record in general. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility is untouched; this is the tribalism Focus exists to catch. It is also not an argument, so nothing is emitted for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So, given the extraordinary powers that have been granted to Ministers in this legislation, what measures is he taking to ensure that the list of projects that Ministers approve for inclusion in the legislation are not connected to people or organisations that are significant donors to coalition parties?
civility.explanation: Framed as a safeguards question rather than an accusation, and aimed at Ministers collectively rather than at an individual, but the premise still floats the possibility that project selection could follow party donations — that insinuation sits between "pointed and robust" and imputing bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, there are a variety of hypotheses in that question, which may or may not turn out to be true. The member will have to wait for the final design of the fast-track procedure, but, as I’ve said twice now in response to previous questions, there are a variety of mechanisms through the Cabinet process and the parliamentary process and electoral law processes designed to make sure that the type of implications that the member is making are handled appropriately.
civility.explanation: Answering an insinuation about donor influence with no counter-attack on Shaw. Mildly cool — "the type of implications that the member is making" — but it engages the question rather than the questioner.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How does he reconcile his statement that he will not tax Aucklanders an additional 11.5c per litre on fuel to fund “more cycle lanes, redlight cameras, speed [bumps,] and lowering speed limits across the city” when Auckland Council information shows that, of the total funding available for regional fuel tax projects, safety and active transport initiatives represented just 16 percent of the regional fuel tax project spending?
rigor.explanation: A real inference offered with its evidence: if safety and active transport were only 16 percent of regional fuel tax spending, the Minister's characterisation of the tax as funding cycle lanes and speed bumps does not hold. The conclusion tracks the figure supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, this might sound really, really radical, but we went to the election with a campaign promise, Aucklanders overwhelmingly voted for the coalition Government, and we’re delivering it.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity: the election result is offered as the whole justification for using urgency and for the funding shortfall the question raised. Winning a vote does not answer whether the process is appropriate or the money replaced. The argument is about his own policy, so it belongs here rather than to Focus.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does the Minister accept that Aucklanders saving 11.5c per litre means very little to them if they then face significant thousands of dollars in rates increases to fund investment in vital transport and water infrastructure projects, or is he quite happy to continue to pull the rug out from under Mayor Wayne Brown?
rigor.explanation: The net-cost inference is sound in form — a fuel saving offset by a larger rates rise leaves ratepayers worse off — but the offsetting figure is left as "significant thousands of dollars" with nothing offered to support it, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why yesterday I announced that 2,500 additional people will receive greater face-to-face support through regular check-ins.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (2,500 people), a mechanism (face-to-face check-ins) and a timing anchor (announced yesterday); checkable against the announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So if we look at a recent seminar in the top of the South Island, 82 Kiwi job seekers turned up to that seminar; 64 secured interviews.
specificity.explanation: Two hard attendance and interview figures tied to an identified seminar; concrete enough to be checked against MSD records, though the seminar is only loosely located.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our coalition Government is not prepared to accept the welfare system we inherited, where work-ready job seekers were forecast to spend, on average, 13 years on a benefit, and teenagers could become trapped on welfare for 24 years of their working lives.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete forecast durations (13 years, 24 years) attached to named cohorts; a reader could go and find the underlying projection.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Unfortunately, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit has increased by 70,000 during the past six years, while sanctions applied for breaches of work obligations decreased by 35,259.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures over a stated period, one of them to the unit; directly checkable against published statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: People who have been on the jobseeker benefit for six months will be eligible for the proactive work check-ins.
specificity.explanation: States the eligibility threshold for the new policy exactly — six months on benefit — so the scope of the programme can be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What percentage of uplifts in Māori immunisation rates has the Minister seen following his $50 million announcement on 21 December last year, and what changes does he expect to see in the 12 months to follow?
specificity.explanation: A precise question: a named spend, an exact date, a defined metric and a stated horizon. A precise question carries as much checkable content as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To the first arm of the question, yes, and to the second arm, I am committed to lifting health outcomes for Māori, and this will be informed by those outcomes identified in Pae 2 in the Whakamaua action plan, including outcomes such as diabetes.
specificity.explanation: Names a plan and one condition, which gives the answer a direction, but supplies no target, figure or timeframe for the outcomes he is committing to lift.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Those discussions with the Waitangi Tribunal are sub judice, but, in a very general sense, I would say that we’ll take on board all discussions and all dialogue from all parties.
specificity.explanation: Beyond the sub judice reason, the answer commits to nothing checkable — 'take on board all discussions from all parties' names no recommendation, process or meeting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can he confirm that a fundamental difference to the COVID-19 fast-track legislation is that, under the proposed new legislation, the ultimate power to approve listed projects will lie with Ministers rather than with an expert consenting panel?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact mechanism at issue — where final approval authority sits — and contrasts it with the named comparator regime.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, final design parameters of the scheme are yet to be confirmed by Cabinet, and when the bill is ready for tabling and release, it will be done.
specificity.explanation: Conveys only that a decision is pending: no date, no design detail, nothing about where approval power will sit, which is what was asked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I am concerned about is that we spend $1.3 billion a year in this country consenting infrastructure—by most measures, some of the most expensive consenting processes in the developed world.
specificity.explanation: A concrete annual cost figure attached to a defined activity, with the source named earlier in the answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can he confirm that there are no fewer than 59 projects currently proposed for inclusion in the primary legislation?
specificity.explanation: A single exact figure put to the Minister about the content of the forthcoming bill; checkable against the project list when the bill is introduced.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can she be confident, then, that these work seminars support people into employment when MSD does not measure any outcomes after attending seminars and people risk losing their benefit if they do not engage with them?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy — the work seminars, the absence of outcome measurement, and the sanction attached to non-attendance. Legitimate scrutiny of a specific programme, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What percentage of uplifts in Māori immunisation rates has the Minister seen following his $50 million announcement on 21 December last year, and what changes does he expect to see in the 12 months to follow?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named funding commitment against a named outcome measure. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can he confirm that a fundamental difference to the COVID-19 fast-track legislation is that, under the proposed new legislation, the ultimate power to approve listed projects will lie with Ministers rather than with an expert consenting panel?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the design of the measure before the House; engages the decision-making mechanism rather than the party proposing it.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: How can she be confident, then, that these work seminars support people into employment when MSD does not measure any outcomes after attending seminars and people risk losing their benefit if they do not engage with them?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MSD collects no outcome data at all on people who attend work seminars.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD's own reporting and OIA responses on work seminars: true if MSD holds no post-seminar employment or outcome measures for attendees; false if MSD records such outcomes (even if only at site or seminar level rather than nationally aggregated).

veracity.statement: There is not one thing that will support, unfortunately, the 190,000 that are on the jobseeker benefit currently.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 190,000 people were receiving jobseeker support at the time of speaking (February 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets for the quarter to December 2023: true if jobseeker support recipients were approximately 190,000, false if materially different (e.g. below 180,000 or above 200,000).

veracity.statement: Our coalition Government is not prepared to accept the welfare system we inherited, where work-ready job seekers were forecast to spend, on average, 13 years on a benefit, and teenagers could become trapped on welfare for 24 years of their working lives.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official forecasts put average future time on benefit at 13 years for work-ready jobseekers and up to 24 years for teenagers entering welfare.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MSD benefit system actuarial valuation report: true if it projects an average of about 13 years of future benefit receipt for work-ready jobseekers and about 24 years for under-20 entrants, false if those figures are materially different or not present.

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit has increased by 70,000 during the past six years, while sanctions applied for breaches of work obligations decreased by 35,259.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 70,000 rise in jobseeker recipients and a fall of 35,259 in sanctions applied over the six years to early 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics comparing jobseeker support recipient numbers for the December 2017 and December 2023 quarters, and MSD's published count of sanctions applied for work-obligation failures over the same period; true if the changes are approximately +70,000 and −35,259, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: What I am concerned about is that we spend $1.3 billion a year in this country consenting infrastructure—by most measures, some of the most expensive consenting processes in the developed world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand spends about $1.3 billion a year on consenting infrastructure, and that this is among the most expensive consenting regimes in the developed world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Sense Partners report prepared for the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission on consenting costs: true if it estimates annual consenting expenditure at approximately $1.3 billion, false if the figure is materially different or if no such estimate appears; the international comparison checks against the same report's cross-country comparison.

rigor.statement: Had they not been there, they would not have taken that very important step of securing an interview that, for some, would have led to employment.
rigor.explanation: A bare counterfactual offered with nothing to support it: it assumes zero deadweight — that none of the 64 would have secured an interview by any other route — which is exactly the inference the attendance figure cannot establish. Post hoc reasoning about a real policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If she is unable to name direct, related outcomes to attending work seminars—people getting a job—is it that she just wants to punish people further into poverty by increasing sanctions for not engaging with workshops that have no evidence of working?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the absence of collated outcome data is presented as leaving only one explanation, a desire to punish. The inference is about a real policy, but nothing offered rules out the alternatives.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is he concerned that granting Ministers the power to fast track consents for projects, including those that have previously been declined under the existing COVID legislation because of environmental risk, is, in the words of the CEO of the Environmental Defence Society, “a return to the use of unbridled executive power [that] we thought we’d left behind.”?
rigor.explanation: The mechanism described is real and relevant, but the weight of the objection is carried by a quoted advocacy-group CEO rather than by an argument — an appeal to authority standing in for the reasoning about why ministerial approval is objectionable.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the member might want to say it’s not true, but it’s a publicly available report from Sense Partners.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: Shaw made no claim that the report was untrue, and the reply answers that invented objection instead. What is offered in support — that the report is public and was commissioned by the previous government — speaks to provenance, not to whether its finding holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If she is unable to name direct, related outcomes to attending work seminars—people getting a job—is it that she just wants to punish people further into poverty by increasing sanctions for not engaging with workshops that have no evidence of working?
civility.explanation: Imputes a punitive motive to the Minister personally — that she 'just wants to punish people' — rather than confining the attack to the sanctions policy. Bad-faith attribution, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, and I’m not going to take lectures from Gary Taylor around what we should or shouldn’t do in this country.
civility.explanation: Dismisses a named individual rather than the objection he raised — 'not going to take lectures from' is condescension toward the person, leaving the substance of the quoted criticism untouched.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill amends the Social Security Act 2018 to ensure that income support responds to the increases in the cost of living by indexing main benefits to changes in the Consumers Price Index (CPI).
specificity.explanation: Names the amending statute, the exact mechanism (indexation) and the index used. Anyone could check the bill against this description or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Some of the measures our Government is committed to taking include providing income tax relief, increasing tax credits for working households, and introducing a new childcare tax credit, as well as reducing taxes on petrol.
specificity.explanation: Four measures are named, which is real content, but there are no amounts, thresholds or dates attached to any of them — the direction is clear, the how much and by when are not.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is the method that has been used for 31 of the last 35 years, so it is not a new change; it is returning to a method that Governments of both sides of the House have utilised in more years than not.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that CPI indexation of main benefits was the method in force for 31 of the previous 35 years, and that it was used by governments of both major parties.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative and administrative history of main benefit indexation in New Zealand (Social Security Act indexation provisions and MSD indexation records) for the 35 years to 2024; true if CPI indexation was the applied method in 31 of those years and was used under both Labour and National governments, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: This change will revert the amendment, made by the previous Government in 2019, to index main benefits to net average wage growth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific fact about the previous Government's legislative record: that it changed main benefit indexation to net average wage growth in 2019.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2019 amendment to the Social Security Act 2018 (Social Security (Winter Energy Payment and Indexation) legislation and its commencement); true if the previous Government legislated in 2019 to index main benefits to net average wage growth, false if the year or the indexation basis differs.

veracity.statement: The lower than forecast CPI figure for the year ending December 2023 shows that inflation is slowing, but it still remains currently outside the Reserve Bank target range of 1 to 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Three factual assertions: the December 2023 annual CPI came in below forecast, inflation is decelerating, and the rate is still above the top of the Reserve Bank's 1-3 percent target band.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI for the December 2023 quarter (annual rate) against the RBNZ's published forecast for that quarter, and the RBNZ Policy Targets/Remit band; true if the annual CPI print came in below the forecast, was lower than the preceding print, and sat above 3 percent; false if it met or exceeded forecast, rose, or fell inside the 1-3 percent band.

rigor.statement: Employment enhances mental health, develops self-esteem, and strengthens communities. In turn, this bill will help to achieve these outcomes while also promoting the ongoing health of the income support system.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion does not follow from what was offered: nothing connects a change in the indexation basis of benefits to more people being employed, so the claimed mental-health and community outcomes rest on an unstated and unsupported premise. A non sequitur bridging a general claim about employment to a specific technical amendment.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reality is that this Government, the coalition Government, is very much focused on improving the lives of New Zealanders—those on welfare as well as those in work—and, more importantly, to reduce the number of children in benefit-dependent households.
focus.explanation: Offered in a third reading debate on a specific bill, but the sentence itself is about her side's general orientation and good intentions rather than the measure. It gestures at one policy outcome (fewer children in benefit-dependent households), which keeps it off the floor, but the weight is party framing rather than the mechanism before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Over the longer term, New Zealand will gain from savings in benefit expenditure, while benefit recipients retain a consistent level of real financial resources—a simple way to put this is that it protects their purchasing power.
divination.explanation: Forecasts two future outcomes of the indexation change: reduced Crown benefit expenditure relative to wage indexation, and preservation of the real purchasing power of main benefits.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury/MSD published benefit expenditure outturns against the pre-change baseline, plus MSD main benefit rate tables deflated by the Stats NZ CPI; true if cumulative benefit expenditure comes in below the wage-indexed counterfactual and the real (CPI-deflated) value of main benefit rates is no lower at the end of the period than in April 2024; false if there are no measurable expenditure savings, or if real benefit rates fall over the period.

specificity.statement: Back then, for our first hundred days, we had the Families Package introduced, we saw the winter energy payment and the Best Start payment introduced for the first time, we extended paid parental leave, we had the Healthy Homes Guarantee Bill setting minimum standards for rentals.
specificity.explanation: Five named policies and pieces of legislation tied to a stated window; anyone could go and check what was passed in that period.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Back then, for our first hundred days, we had the Families Package introduced, we saw the winter energy payment and the Best Start payment introduced for the first time, we extended paid parental leave, we had the Healthy Homes Guarantee Bill setting minimum standards for rentals.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that four specific welfare and housing measures were delivered in the 2017 Government's first hundred days.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative record for the first hundred days of the Sixth Labour Government (from 26 October 2017): true if the Families Package (including the winter energy payment and Best Start), the extension of paid parental leave, and the Healthy Homes Guarantee Act were all introduced or enacted within that window; false if any of these fall materially outside it or were not enacted as described.

veracity.statement: Sadly, we have a Government that is taking $670 million from the poorest New Zealanders to pay for their tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific dollar amount removed from benefit recipients by the indexation change, and that it funds the Government's tax cuts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement / supplementary analysis report and Treasury costings for the benefit indexation change before the House: true if the fiscal saving to beneficiaries is around $670 million (over the stated period) and that saving is booked toward the tax package; false if the costed figure is materially different or the fiscal linkage to the tax package is not in the documents.

veracity.statement: Any Government that can receive a supplementary analysis report on a bill where the report states very clearly that more children will be in poverty as a result of their actions should be ashamed of themselves.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the official supplementary analysis report for this bill states that more children will be in poverty as a result.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report accompanying the bill under debate: true if it states that the change will increase the number of children in poverty or in low-income households; false if it makes no such finding or finds no material increase.

focus.statement: Sadly, we have a Government that is taking $670 million from the poorest New Zealanders to pay for their tax cuts.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure, a specific figure and a specific group affected. This is scrutiny of a policy before the House, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is the playbook of Jim Bolger. It is the playbook of John Key. It is the playbook of Robert Muldoon.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other party is like across its history. No policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named; strip out the lineage of National leaders and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I said it a number of times in the House: they should be ashamed of themselves.
civility.explanation: Moral condemnation of the Government members rather than of the measure itself. No individual is insulted and no character attack is made, but 'they should be ashamed of themselves' goes past the substance to the people, so it falls short of the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We already know that excessive sanctions drive families into poverty, not lift them out, and yet those are the two measures that we have heard from.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure before the House — sanctions worsen poverty, therefore these measures will not reduce child poverty — but the key premise is carried entirely by 'we already know', an appeal to assumed common ground with no evidence offered, in a passage that had just demanded evidence from the Minister.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Ruth Richardson—she wasn’t a leader, but she made some horrible changes that were detrimental.
civility.explanation: A contested political topic where she had a genuine opportunity to keep it on the policy, and the second half does exactly that — the changes were 'horrible', which is fierce criticism of a record and costs nothing. But 'she wasn't a leader' is a judgement on the person rather than the decisions, so this lands at the failure mark rather than the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Our communities are served better than a Minister who doesn’t actually understand the welfare system she’s been put in charge of running, because she is completely ignoring the fact that this is a bill that will see lower increases to benefits over the medium term, that will see disabled people disproportionately affected.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's competence — that she does not understand the portfolio she runs. A reason is attached, but the charge is about the person's capacity rather than the merits of the bill; the same substantive point was available without it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So let’s cut the BS from the Minister and actually accept that this is a bill that will punish disabled people the hardest.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Minister's contribution as deliberate nonsense rather than engaging it — imputed bad faith with a dismissive edge, aimed at the person. Short of a direct insult, but past the point of civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yes, we acknowledge that arguments can be made both ways. This is about the indexation of benefits to the Consumers Price Index (CPI) or net wage growth, and I want to acknowledge that, yes, it was the Labour Government that indexed benefits to net wage growth because it saw that the wage growth was actually historically growing faster than inflation.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested bill after two hostile speeches, so there was every opportunity to be uncivil. She engages the substance, concedes the other side has a case, and states the previous government's rationale accurately and without derision. This is the expected standard, met.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Ten years from now, if no change occurs to fix this indexation mistake, then what we’ll have are benefits falling further and further behind. We’ll have more children living in poverty.
divination.explanation: A conditional forecast that, absent a reversal, CPI-indexed main benefits will decline relative to wages over a decade and that measured child poverty will be higher as a result. Not a promise about her own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MSD main benefit rates as a percentage of the net average wage, compared 2024 vs 2034, plus Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics (before-housing-costs 50% median and material hardship measures) for the year to June 2034. True if the benefit-to-wage ratio has fallen and the child poverty rate is higher than 2024 outside sampling error, given CPI indexation was retained. False if the ratio holds or rises, or child poverty falls, under retained CPI indexation. Void if indexation is legislatively changed back in the interim, which the speaker's own condition excludes.

divination.statement: But I’ll tell you right now: in four years’ time, what we will see is more families queuing up at Work and Income, needing hardship grants to make ends meet.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a rise in demand for MSD hardship assistance four years out, as a consequence of lower benefit indexation. A prediction about an outcome in the world, not a promise about his own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MSD hardship assistance statistics (Special Needs Grants and Advances, number of recipients and number of grants) for the year to June 2028 compared with the year to June 2024. True if both recipient numbers and grant volumes are higher in 2028; false if they are lower or flat.

focus.statement: So, focused on the cost of living for their mates that are New Zealanders but not focused on the cost of living for the most vulnerable New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath — that the cost-of-living programme excludes beneficiaries — but no measure, figure or mechanism is named, and the weight of the sentence is the party framing of 'their mates'. A policy claim wrapped in tribal framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So this bill, effectively, by widening the gap between working people and those who are out of paid employment, is punishing people who want to go into work.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the bill's mechanism (widening the earnings-to-benefit gap) and the group it is said to affect. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Every year, over the forecast period, beneficiaries fall behind because of that Government’s decision to take $670 million off the poorest New Zealanders to pay for tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific fiscal fact: that switching benefit indexation from net average wage growth to CPI reduces benefit spending by $670 million over the forecast period, and that this saving funds the tax package.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement and Treasury/Budget 2024 fiscal costings for the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) Bill: the forecast reduction in main benefit expenditure from CPI indexation over the forecast period. True if the published figure is approximately $670m; false if materially different (e.g. under $500m or over $850m).

veracity.statement: Women make up 55 percent of all beneficiaries; 80 percent of those on sole parent benefit are women.
veracity.explanation: Two demographic claims about the composition of the benefit population at the time of speaking: the female share of all main benefit recipients, and the female share of Sole Parent Support recipients.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets / national benefit statistics for the December 2023 or March 2024 quarter, gender breakdown by benefit type. True if the female share of all main benefits is approximately 55% and of Sole Parent Support approximately 80%; false if either differs by more than a few percentage points.

veracity.statement: The previous Government had a chance to accept my recommendations and amendments to index benefits to wages, or inflation, whichever was higher, to ensure that we guarantee the best and highest possible benefit increases, so that a rising tide supports everyone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that he formally proposed an amendment to index main benefits to the higher of wage growth or CPI while Labour was in government, and that it was not adopted. A factual claim about the parliamentary record, notable because it is directed at his own side's ally rather than the government of the day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and the Supplementary Order Paper / committee-of-the-whole amendment record for the benefit indexation legislation passed under the 2020–2023 Parliament. True if an amendment in Menéndez March's name proposing indexation to the higher of net wage growth or CPI was lodged and defeated; false if no such amendment appears in the record.

veracity.statement: If inflation comes down, that is a good thing, because in the last quarter, December 2023, we have seen that inflation has been 4.7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual CPI inflation for the December 2023 quarter was 4.7 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index release for the December 2023 quarter, annual percentage change. True if 4.7% (± rounding); false if materially different.

specificity.statement: Every year, over the forecast period, beneficiaries fall behind because of that Government’s decision to take $670 million off the poorest New Zealanders to pay for tax cuts.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (indexation change), a dollar figure ($670 million), a period (the forecast period) and the stated purpose. Someone could go to the RIS and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The cumulative losses will result in disabled people being over $2,000 worse off than they would have been if we kept things as they are in four years.
specificity.explanation: A named group, a dollar amount, a stated counterfactual (retaining wage indexation) and a timeframe. Precise enough to be checked against the departmental modelling.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is not true, and every decision that they have made to date is questionable, because the evidence runs contrary to the arguments, the ideology, and the policies that they are putting forward.
rigor.explanation: A hasty generalisation: the evidence offered concerns one indexation decision, and the conclusion extends to 'every decision that they have made to date'. The premise as stated is also close to a restatement of the conclusion — 'the evidence runs contrary' is the thing that needed showing, not the support for it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So this bill, effectively, by widening the gap between working people and those who are out of paid employment, is punishing people who want to go into work.
rigor.explanation: The inference has a real gap. The chain runs: wider gap → wage scarring → forced acceptance of poorly matched low-paid work → the bill 'punishes people who want to go into work'. Each link is asserted rather than evidenced, and the conclusion inverts the bill's stated mechanism without showing the intermediate step holds. An argument about the policy, but a weakly supported one — the low score here is about the inference, not about what the statement is about.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, I do acknowledge that there a lot of factors that we do need to take into consideration when we talk about inflation, but, definitely, the irresponsible spending of the previous Labour Government fuelled inflation.
rigor.explanation: Concedes multi-causality in the first clause and then asserts the single-cause conclusion in the second with the word 'definitely' and nothing else. Nothing is offered to isolate fiscal policy from the other factors she has just acknowledged — the concession is made and then abandoned rather than answered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, coming to the Green Party member, it’s really interesting to see that the Green Party member thinks that somehow if people stay on benefit rather than going to a job that is a minimum wage job, it is actually a better thing.
rigor.explanation: A strawman. Menéndez March argued that the bill harms people who cannot work and scars the wages of those who can; he did not argue that remaining on a benefit is preferable to minimum-wage work. The position rebutted for the rest of the passage is one that was not advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why do we want to imagine that somebody will be sitting on benefit for four to five years? That is not the kind of ambition we bring to New Zealanders. We have better aspirations than the Green member, because we really want people to do well.
rigor.explanation: A non sequitur answering a forecast with an aspiration. The $2,000 figure was a projection about people who are on a benefit over four years; that some of them will be is a factual question, and declaring the projection unambitious does not bear on whether it is accurate. The concluding clause is a bare appeal to good intentions.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One thing I know is that the coalition is a very caring coalition, and that is why we are going to support this bill. We are caring. We are mothers. We are fathers, sons, and daughters.
rigor.explanation: The stated reason for supporting the bill is the coalition's own character ('we are caring', 'we are mothers'), which is an appeal to emotion and self-description; nothing about what the bill does is offered to connect premise to conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, with the increase in costs and services that we are experiencing at the moment, it is clearly a good idea to index the main benefit to inflation, which is what we are doing.
rigor.explanation: There is a real inference here — costs are rising, so adjusting the benefit by the cost measure preserves its value — but it leans on assertion ('clearly a good idea') and skips the step that matters: why indexing to inflation is better than the wage indexation it replaces. A genuine gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is a tried and tested, very known fact that when young people are trying to get ahead, instead of being provided everything that they might want at that point in time or might need at that point in time, it is good for them to be able to aspire and push themselves harder and get ahead.
rigor.explanation: A bare appeal to received wisdom — 'tried and tested, very known fact' stands in place of any evidence or mechanism, and the conclusion about benefit levels rests entirely on that appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Also, the members opposite raise that the benefits will eventually have the effect of dropping by 2028, four years later, and then the picture is painted about when that happens, but we would like for others to understand, especially the ones who watch this debate, that that would mean if the main benefit is indexed on cost of living, then the cost of living would have also gone down.
rigor.explanation: Answers a claim that was not made: the opposition's point is that benefits fall relative to wages, not that the nominal rate drops, so 'the cost of living would have also gone down' does not follow. A strawman resting on a conflation of the level with its rate of growth.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Evidence, yes, evidence is great, and in many of the words spoken on the other side, I don’t hear evidence coming; I just hear accusations.
focus.explanation: A measure was before the House, but this engages none of it — it characterises how the other side is speaking. No policy, figure or outcome is named. Rigor is deliberately not scored: strip out the part about the opposition and no argument remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government continues to show they have no ngākau for our people. They are anti-Māori, anti - workers’ rights, anti-disability, and anti-beneficiaries.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of what the Government is 'really like', with no policy, clause, figure or outcome named. Civility is untouched — no individual is insulted — which is precisely the gap Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government is continuing to give tax cuts to higher-income earners but taking income away from the lowest earners.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy pairing (the tax package and the benefit indexation change) and the distributional outcome claimed to follow. This is opposition scrutiny of a named commitment, not party-bashing, and scores at the top.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Also, the members opposite raise that the benefits will eventually have the effect of dropping by 2028, four years later, and then the picture is painted about when that happens, but we would like for others to understand, especially the ones who watch this debate, that that would mean if the main benefit is indexed on cost of living, then the cost of living would have also gone down.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the measure before the House — the indexation mechanism, the opposition's 2028 projection, and what it would imply. On-policy, notwithstanding the weakness of the reasoning.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, we are not slashing benefits; we’re protecting the benefits and we’re indexing them to inflation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two present-tense facts about the bill: that it reduces no benefit, and that it sets main benefit adjustment by inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Social Security (Benefit Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill, plus MSD main benefit rate tables from 1 April 2024. True if the bill indexes main benefits to CPI and no main benefit rate falls in nominal terms; false if any rate is reduced or indexation is to something other than inflation.

veracity.statement: So we are not trying to slash the money coming in; we are protecting their purchasing power, which is why we are indexing to inflation—a policy that has been used for 31 of the previous 35 years, we note.
veracity.explanation: A specific historical claim about how long CPI indexation of main benefits has been the New Zealand practice — 31 of the 35 years preceding the statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statutory basis for main benefit adjustment year by year from 1989 to 2024 (Social Security Act annual adjustment provisions; the 2019 amendment that moved indexation to average wage growth from 1 April 2020). True if CPI indexation applied in 31 of those 35 years; false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: This very legislation and the very state of the nation speech that we just heard over the weekend from her Prime Minister is doing the opposite of improving the self-esteem of people who are struggling the most, and is why we will not only be opposing, and are opposing, this legislation, which seeks to tag income support to inflation instead of wages because that ensures that they receive less money, we are opposing this legislation and the hateful rhetoric that comes with it.
veracity.explanation: The checkable assertion is about the bill's mechanism and its effect: that it switches indexation from wages to inflation, and that this results in recipients receiving less than they otherwise would.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's text and its Regulatory Impact Statement, plus Treasury/MSD projections of main benefit rates under CPI indexation versus average-wage indexation to 2027-28. True if the bill moves indexation from wage growth to CPI and the projected rates are lower than under wage indexation; false if the mechanism is otherwise or the projections show no shortfall.

veracity.statement: We saw the Minister in charge of this legislation, the Hon Louise Upston, repeating again in the House today—we saw her talking and using the language of people “languishing” on a jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: A claim about what a named Minister said in the House on that day — specifically that she described people as 'languishing' on a jobseeker benefit. Davidson asserts this rather than relaying a claim of Upston's, so the assertion is her own.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for 20 February 2024 and Louise Upston's contemporaneous statements on the bill. True if she used the word 'languishing' of jobseeker benefit recipients; false if the word does not appear in her remarks.

veracity.statement: People like the 311 families who together mass $85 billion collectively without being fairly taxed.
veracity.explanation: Cites a specific number of families (311) and a specific aggregate wealth figure ($85 billion), drawn from the tax-fairness debate about high-wealth New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue's High-Wealth Individuals Research Project report (April 2023). True if it covers 311 families with total wealth of approximately $85 billion; false if the count or the total is materially different.

veracity.statement: This Government is continuing to give tax cuts to higher-income earners but taking income away from the lowest earners.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the tax cuts favour higher-income earners, and that the lowest earners have income taken from them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Budget 2024 distributional analysis of the personal income tax package by income decile, and MSD main benefit rates from April 2024 compared with what average-wage indexation would have produced. True if the tax gains rise with income and beneficiaries are worse off than under the previous indexation; false if the package is progressive or beneficiaries are no worse off.

specificity.statement: So we are not trying to slash the money coming in; we are protecting their purchasing power, which is why we are indexing to inflation—a policy that has been used for 31 of the previous 35 years, we note.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (indexation to inflation) and supplies a checkable historical figure (31 of the previous 35 years), though no dollar amounts or dates for the change itself.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: People like the 311 families who together mass $85 billion collectively without being fairly taxed.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, sourceable figures — a family count and a wealth total — that anyone could go and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If that previous New Zealand First member, Tanya Unkovich, would in fact have stopped reading her notes and instead read the evidence—and how about reading her own Prime Minister’s state of the nation speech right after she tried to say that we need to improve people’s self-esteem, and this very legislation that is going to deny those on the lowest incomes more income?
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at a named member — that she was 'reading her notes' rather than thinking, and needs to be told to read. Short of a direct insult, but it targets the member rather than the argument. The insult is Davidson's own conduct, so subject is speaker.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But this Government—including that speaker who just sat down from New Zealand First, the Prime Minister, and the Minister in charge of this legislation—are dehumanising and stigmatising all people who receive a benefit.
civility.explanation: Imputes to three named or identified individuals the deliberate dehumanising of beneficiaries — a charge about their character and motives rather than about the effect of the legislation. Uncivil conduct by the speaker regardless of who it is aimed at.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: There’s going to be increased whānau continuing to line up at our food banks, and increased whānau turning up at our marae requiring hardship grants.
divination.explanation: Forecasts rising demand on two supports — food banks and hardship grants — following this legislation. It is a prediction about outcomes in the community, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MSD hardship assistance statistics (Special Needs Grants for food and other hardship assistance, by recipient ethnicity where published) and food bank demand reporting such as the New Zealand Food Network's annual figures, for the 12 months following February 2024 compared with the preceding 12 months. True if both measures rise; false if both are flat or fall.

civility.statement: You should read it—go ahead and read it, Dan.
civility.explanation: A retort to Dan Bidois' interjection that implies he has not read the book; pointed and mildly condescending, but it stops short of an attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Many of them have expressed values coming from the Christian faith they profess. I would like to see that faith expressed in action, not just words.
civility.explanation: Imputes a gap between the professed faith of named-in-general government members and their conduct — a suggestion of hypocrisy directed at people rather than at the policy, though it is delivered mildly and insults no one directly.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, this is absolutely standard research that the inflation that the members of this House experience is not as bad as the inflation that people on lower incomes experience.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as settled research that low-income households face a higher effective inflation rate than high-income households (here, MPs).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Living-costs Price Indexes (HLPI) for the periods around 2023-2024, comparing the annual rate for beneficiary and lowest-expenditure household groups against the highest-expenditure group; true if low-income households show the higher rate, false if their rate is equal to or lower than that of high-income households.

veracity.statement: It gets even worse than that because, as is sitting in the impact analysis that was prepared by social welfare that was brought to the House by this Minister, the impact is going to be greater on disabled households where people are on benefit because they have disabilities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the government's own published impact analysis for this bill records a larger impact on disabled beneficiary households.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement / impact analysis published by MSD for the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill; true if that document identifies a disproportionately larger impact on households receiving disability-related benefits, false if it contains no such finding.

veracity.statement: In fact, for 31 of the last 35 years, this practice has been used to index benefits to CPI inflation changes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that CPI indexation of benefits was the practice in 31 of the last 35 years, with wage indexation (introduced by the previous government) the exception.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of main benefit indexation in New Zealand (Social Security Act adjustment provisions and the annual benefit adjustment orders) from roughly 1989 to 2024; true if CPI was the indexation basis in 31 of those 35 years, false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: The other part of this bill that I need to speak to is that it’s a relatively minor change but it increases the prescribed amount from $34,216 to $35,204.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the specific dollar values of the prescribed-amount change made by the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Social Security (Benefits Adjustment) and Income Tax (Minimum Family Tax Credit) Amendment Bill as read a third time; true if it amends the prescribed amount used in the minimum family tax credit formula from $34,216 to $35,204, false if the figures differ.

rigor.statement: Lower-income households will be experiencing a higher rate of inflation because of the basket of goods and services that they actually purchase.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is supported by the mechanism offered — that price indices weight a household's own consumption basket — which is a valid inference from the stated premise. Whether the premise holds is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have been hearing some interesting speeches from the opposite side of the House this afternoon, accusing the coalition Government of all sorts of things; ignoring the fact that past left-wing Governments have done exactly the same thing over the last 31 years. So if they are to say this is a reflection on the coalition Government, it’s a reflection on their own practice of the last 31 years.
rigor.explanation: A tu quoque: that previous Labour governments also used CPI indexation does not show the present reversal is justified. It engages the actual policy (the indexation basis), so it is an argument, but the conclusion — that the criticism rebounds on the critics — does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is a fairer mechanism, we think, for those lower-income people. I heard the speech before that said lower-income people are more affected by inflation—absolutely—based on the vast amount of goods and services that they purchase. So that’s absolutely correct. We’re at a time of higher inflation, therefore those goods and services—particularly food, electricity, etc.—that people need, this inflation affects lower-income people more. So this is indexing these benefits to the CPI—to inflation. So this is going to assist, rather than what the Opposition is claiming.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. Granting that low-income households face a higher effective inflation rate does not support the conclusion that CPI indexation assists them; the relevant comparison is CPI indexation against the wage indexation being removed, which is never made, and the conceded premise if anything tells against CPI as the measure.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, when we were in Government, we worked hard to increase the level of benefits to ensure that people living in benefit-dependant households could participate in our society, could enhance their capabilities, could be part of our society.
specificity.explanation: A claim about her own government's record with no figure, no named change and no timeframe — 'worked hard to increase the level of benefits' gives nothing checkable, and the stated aims are generic.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It gets even worse than that because, as is sitting in the impact analysis that was prepared by social welfare that was brought to the House by this Minister, the impact is going to be greater on disabled households where people are on benefit because they have disabilities.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (the bill's impact analysis) and the affected group (disabled beneficiary households), so it is locatable and checkable, but supplies no figure for the size of the impact.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, for 31 of the last 35 years, this practice has been used to index benefits to CPI inflation changes.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures and a named mechanism (CPI indexation of benefits) — directly checkable against the legislative record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The other part of this bill that I need to speak to is that it’s a relatively minor change but it increases the prescribed amount from $34,216 to $35,204.
specificity.explanation: Exact before-and-after figures for a named parameter of the minimum family tax credit formula; anyone can check it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill means that less money ends up in the pockets of the poorest New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and its distributional effect; no party framing at all. Legitimate scrutiny of the bill's consequence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Many of them have expressed values coming from the Christian faith they profess. I would like to see that faith expressed in action, not just words.
focus.explanation: Turns from the bill to what members opposite are personally like — their professed values versus their voting — with no policy, figure or mechanism named in the passage.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Let me try and rephrase that: taking from the poorest New Zealanders to pay for tax cuts is morally reprehensible.
civility.explanation: A severe moral condemnation aimed squarely at the policy — what the bill does — with no individual attacked. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a measure is civil; it edges below 1.0 only because 'morally reprehensible' carries a whiff of imputed motive toward those advancing it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I implore that Government: find another way; if not, absolutely heartless.
civility.explanation: Moves from the merits of the policy to the motives of those enacting it — 'heartless' imputes bad faith rather than error. Aimed at the Government collectively rather than a named member, so it is well short of a personal insult, but it is no longer engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The problem is that with this bill, they’re actually going to get less money in the long run.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that beneficiaries will end up worse off financially under CPI indexation than they would have been under the wage-indexation formula the bill repeals. Not a promise about her own action; a claim about a future outcome.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MSD's published main benefit rates after successive 1 April adjustments, compared with the rates the repealed wage-indexation formula (net average ordinary time weekly earnings, Stats NZ QES) would have produced over the same period. True if the CPI-indexed rates are materially lower by April 2027; false if they are equal or higher.

rigor.statement: When the Children’s Commissioner says that this is the one thing that we could do to help child poverty, it is time for our Parliament to listen to it.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to authority: the conclusion that Parliament should not proceed rests entirely on who said it, with none of the Commissioner's underlying reasoning or evidence offered. Not zero, because the authority cited is a relevant and expert one on child poverty.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because you know what? These children that are going to bed tonight—the child that I was at four who lost her mother to cancer—deserve better.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to emotion resting on a single personal anecdote. The premise (a hard childhood on a benefit) is offered as grounds for rejecting the indexation change, but nothing connects the anecdote to the effect of CPI versus wage indexation. The inference is asserted through feeling rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: For those that are watching at home, we are increasing benefits by the CPI. That actually keeps the purchasing power for those who are on a benefit—it protects that, OK?
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premise: indexing a payment to consumer price inflation does, by construction, hold its purchasing power constant. The inference is sound as far as it goes; it simply does not address relative position against wages, which is a different claim rather than a flaw in this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Find them through other mechanisms of revenue raising, but instead you want to take the money which may help our poorest New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Demands an alternative funding source without naming a single one — no tax, no rate, no figure, nothing that could be costed or acted on. The only concrete element is the object of the complaint, not the proposal.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The second thing that I’d like to say to the member is that there were 70,000 extra people on a jobseeker benefit under the last six years of that Government, and any person who is taking on the finance portfolio for Labour needs to know how much that costs the State: $1 billion extra a year.
specificity.explanation: Carries a headcount, a timeframe and a dollar cost — every element is precise enough that someone could go to the benefit statistics and check it or use it in a costing.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The second thing that I’d like to say to the member is that there were 70,000 extra people on a jobseeker benefit under the last six years of that Government, and any person who is taking on the finance portfolio for Labour needs to know how much that costs the State: $1 billion extra a year.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that jobseeker benefit recipients rose by roughly 70,000 over the six years of the previous Government, and that this increase costs the Crown about $1 billion more a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets, Jobseeker Support recipient counts for the December 2017 and December 2023 quarters — true if the difference is approximately 70,000; and MSD/Treasury main benefit expenditure figures for Jobseeker Support over the same period — true if the annual cost increase attributable to those recipients is approximately $1 billion. Materially different figures on either limb would make it false.

veracity.statement: We want to have a case of actually improving benefits modestly by the inflation rate—which, by the way, I have to remind the other side of the House that it’s 4.7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the prevailing rate of inflation at the time of speaking is 4.7 percent.
