veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index, annual percentage change for the most recently published quarter as at February 2024 (December 2023 quarter). True if that figure is 4.7%; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Now, I’m no person of history, but Ruth Richardson actually cut the benefits, and we are not cutting.
veracity.explanation: Two historical/present assertions: that the 1991 benefit changes reduced benefit rates, and that this bill does not reduce them. Note the claim is about nominal rates, not relative living standards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 1991 Budget and associated regulations on main benefit rates — true if nominal weekly rates were reduced; and the bill before the House — true if it leaves nominal benefit rates rising with CPI rather than reducing them. False if either limb is wrong on nominal rates.

focus.statement: Maybe if they had known how much inflation was, they might have done better in the last election.
focus.explanation: A jibe about the other party's election performance and a past gaffe. Strip out the part about the other side and nothing remains — no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve traversed this topic a lot in the last year, in the election campaign, which that side of the House lost overwhelmingly.
focus.explanation: The bill is nominally the subject but the weight of the sentence is the opponents' election defeat, which bears on no aspect of the indexation change before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I know that our members on the other side of the House—and I say this respectfully because I know that many of you are very lovely, beautiful people—seem to have ignored the fact that this bill also proposes another change.
civility.explanation: A contested debating point where she could have gone after opponents personally. She charges them with ignoring part of the bill rather than attacking anyone's character, though the 'very lovely, beautiful people' aside carries a faint note of mock-flattery, which keeps it just short of the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a change where we adjust the minimum family tax credit bracket in a way that we ensure more lower-income families are better off if they remain in full-time work.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the specific provision (the minimum family tax credit bracket) and who it is intended to affect. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Here, on this side of the House, the National Party, with our coalition partners, will not sit around and let the déjà true Labour legacy of dependency go unchecked.
focus.explanation: The framing is about the other party's supposed legacy rather than about a named policy, figure or outcome; the only policy content is the implicit link back to the bill. Mostly party-versus-party positioning.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s a change where we adjust the minimum family tax credit bracket in a way that we ensure more lower-income families are better off if they remain in full-time work.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism and the intended beneficiary group, but supplies no threshold figure, no dollar amount and no commencement date, so the direction is clear while the how much is not.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, there’s one part of this bill that talks about adjusting benefits to inflation, taking it back to what it was for 31 out of 35 years under successive Governments, including Helen Clark’s Government—so we’re going back to that true and tried form where we’re adjusting benefits to inflation.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise count of years, the indexation basis, and a named prior government, all of which could be checked against the statute book.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s déjà true that under Labour Governments, as we’ve seen just recently, the number of young people under the age of 25 on the jobseeker benefit has risen by 66 percent.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable claim: named benefit, named age band, a percentage change. Someone could go to the MSD series and verify it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to fight against the poverty of aspiration.
specificity.explanation: A slogan. It names no mechanism, figure, threshold or timeframe, and nothing in the surrounding sentences supplies them — nobody could check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Yes, there’s one part of this bill that talks about adjusting benefits to inflation, taking it back to what it was for 31 out of 35 years under successive Governments, including Helen Clark’s Government—so we’re going back to that true and tried form where we’re adjusting benefits to inflation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that benefits were adjusted to the Consumers Price Index for 31 of the last 35 years under governments of both stripes, Helen Clark's included, so the bill restores the long-standing default rather than introducing something new.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statutory history of main benefit indexation in New Zealand (Social Security Act adjustment provisions and the 2019 amendment moving main benefits to wage indexation from 1 April 2020). True if CPI indexation was the operative basis for 31 of the 35 years preceding the statement, including the 1999–2008 Clark Government; false if the count of CPI-indexed years is materially different or if main benefits were wage-indexed under Clark.

veracity.statement: It’s déjà true that under Labour Governments, as we’ve seen just recently, the number of young people under the age of 25 on the jobseeker benefit has risen by 66 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 66 percent increase in the number of under-25s receiving Jobseeker Support over the period of the Labour-led governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets / quarterly Jobseeker Support data for recipients aged under 25, comparing the most recent quarter before February 2024 with the September 2017 quarter. True if the increase is approximately 66 percent, false if materially different or if the percentage only holds on a different age band or start date.

veracity.statement: Déjà true: under a Labour Government since 2017, New Zealanders on the jobseeker benefit have increased by 70,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that total Jobseeker Support recipients rose by about 70,000 between 2017 and the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Jobseeker Support recipient counts, September 2017 quarter versus the latest quarter before February 2024. True if the net increase is approximately 70,000 recipients, false if materially different.

rigor.statement: The beauty of what we have here is that we acknowledge people do find themselves in difficult times, but we also acknowledge that if we allow ourselves to go too far, we’ll have a poverty of aspiration.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the welfare policy at issue, but the support offered is a single anecdote about one colleague's experience on the benefit, and the key premise ('too far') is never defined — appeal to anecdote resting on an unspecified threshold.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We know, looking back over the last 20 years or so, that in most years—around nine out of 10 years—wage increases have been higher than inflation. That is why we made this change: because the Welfare Expert Advisory Group said that this was the most significant change that could be made to benefits to ensure that people had enough to live with dignity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over roughly the last two decades, wage growth exceeded inflation in about nine years in ten — a checkable claim about the past, and the empirical basis offered for wage-indexation of benefits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ annual wage growth (Labour Cost Index / average hourly earnings from the QES) compared against annual CPI inflation for each year 2004–2024; true if nominal wage growth exceeded CPI inflation in approximately 90% of those years, false if it did so in materially fewer (e.g. only two-thirds or less).

rigor.statement: We know, looking back over the last 20 years or so, that in most years—around nine out of 10 years—wage increases have been higher than inflation. That is why we made this change: because the Welfare Expert Advisory Group said that this was the most significant change that could be made to benefits to ensure that people had enough to live with dignity.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: if wages outpace inflation in most years, indexing benefits to wages rather than prices lifts benefit levels over time. The support offered is partly an appeal to authority (the Welfare Expert Advisory Group), but the wage-versus-inflation premise does independently carry the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know, looking back over the last 20 years or so, that in most years—around nine out of 10 years—wage increases have been higher than inflation. That is why we made this change: because the Welfare Expert Advisory Group said that this was the most significant change that could be made to benefits to ensure that people had enough to live with dignity.
specificity.explanation: Carries a timeframe (the last 20 years), a rate (around nine years in ten), a named mechanism (wage indexation of benefits) and a named source (the Welfare Expert Advisory Group). Someone could go and check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: What we’re going to see now is that overall weekly benefit eroded over time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that, following the change from wage indexation, the overall weekly benefit will decline in value over the coming years. Not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MSD main benefit rates (Jobseeker Support and Sole Parent Support, net weekly) from April 2024 onward compared against Stats NZ average ordinary time weekly earnings; true if benefit rates fall as a share of the average wage over the period, false if they hold steady or rise relative to it.

divination.statement: If this Government does manage to magic up some tax cuts—I’ve got no idea how they’re going to do that, but if they do—every single one of us in this room, those of us who are parliamentarians, will get a tax cut.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a future policy outcome: that the Government will deliver income tax cuts, and that those cuts will reach every member of Parliament.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Legislated personal income tax changes announced in Budget 2024 and their effective date; true if income tax reductions took effect and applied to incomes at MPs' salary level (roughly $160,000+), false if no tax cut was delivered or if it was targeted so as to exclude that income band.

focus.statement: What we’re going to see now is that overall weekly benefit eroded over time.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the consequence of the measure before the House — what happens to benefit levels — rather than about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, we’ve heard very, very confused arguments from the other side. Some have said this is just an administrative matter; others have actually admitted it is to reduce cost.
focus.explanation: Characterises the other side's performance in the debate, but does so by naming two competing substantive rationales for the measure (administrative tidy-up versus cost saving), so it is not content-free party framing. Weight is split between the policy and the opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I ask those on the other side of the House—some of whom have been smirking and laughing and interrupting my colleagues talking about when their parents passed away from cancer—those who profess to be Christian, as I am, who go to church services each week and, I hope, would pray for the poorest of our nation, to actually think about what they’re doing to our most vulnerable people.
civility.explanation: Turns on the members opposite rather than the measure: accuses named-by-implication individuals of laughing at colleagues' accounts of a parent's death, and holds their professed religion up against their conduct. That is imputation of bad faith and hypocrisy aimed at persons, not criticism of a policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: OK, so I think it’s a thing in the Bible we call “greed”.
civility.explanation: Ascribes greed — a personal moral vice — to the members heckling opposite. Short of a direct insult, but it is an imputation of bad character rather than an argument about the tax policy.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill seeks to amend the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019 to delay the repeal of section 13 of the 2003 Act, which concerns the experience pathway for social worker registration, from 28 February 2024 to 28 February 2026.
specificity.explanation: Names the amending Act, the section, the mechanism and both commencement dates — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government believes in investing in early interventions which will be the most effective for vulnerable New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general orientation with no programme, figure, mechanism or timeframe attached; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Approximately 3 percent of the current social workers have registered through this experience pathway.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 3% of currently registered social workers obtained registration via the section 13 experience pathway rather than the qualification pathway.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board registration data / annual report for 2023-24 giving the share of registered social workers admitted under the experience pathway; true if approximately 3% (say 2-4%), false if materially outside that range.

veracity.statement: The Social Workers Registration Board currently estimates there are about 700 unfilled roles.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to the Social Workers Registration Board a current estimate of roughly 700 vacant social worker positions nationally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board workforce estimates or the MSD regulatory impact statement for this bill (2023-24); true if the Board's published vacancy estimate is about 700, false if it names a materially different figure or makes no such estimate.

veracity.statement: In February of 2021, registration became mandatory for anyone wanting to use the title “social worker” and/or practise as a social worker.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the commencement date of mandatory registration and title protection for social workers under the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provisions of the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019 on legislation.govt.nz; true if mandatory registration and title protection took effect in February 2021, false if they commenced in a different month or year.

veracity.statement: In 2017, Cabinet agreed to repeal the experience pathway and had a delayed commencement date of 28 February 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the decision to repeal the section 13 experience pathway was taken by Cabinet in 2017, with commencement deferred to 28 February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2017 Cabinet paper and minute on social worker registration (MSD proactive releases) plus the repeal date in the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019; true if the Cabinet decision is dated 2017 and the statutory repeal date is 28 February 2024, false if either the year or the date differs.

rigor.statement: Secondly, delaying the repeal of the experience pathway will also enable the sector to maximise the opportunities presented by recent pay changes for social workers. These increases provide a financial incentive for eligible practitioners to become registered.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: pay rises create an incentive to register, so keeping the pathway open lets more practitioners take it up. The mechanism is coherent, but the step from 'an incentive exists' to 'the sector will maximise the opportunity' is asserted rather than supported — no uptake figures or elasticity evidence is offered to close the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I anticipate this will support experienced Māori practitioners to register as social workers through the experience pathway over the next two years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Board's recent changes to the experience pathway application process will result in experienced Māori practitioners registering via that pathway during the two-year extension.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board registration statistics by ethnicity and pathway for the period 20 February 2024 to 28 February 2026; true if registrations of Māori practitioners via the experience pathway rise relative to the preceding comparable period, false if they are flat or fall.

focus.statement: What was disappointing with this particular bill is the Government’s decision to reduce the extension or time frame for being able to get the experience pathway from four years to two years.
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (the s13 experience pathway extension) and the specific change (four years to two). This is scrutiny of a named policy decision, not party-bashing — the top of the Focus scale.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Initially, the bill had laid out four years for people to be able to access that experience pathway, and then what happened was that this Government decided that it would reduce that to two years.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete mechanism (the s13 experience pathway), the original figure and the amended figure. Someone could act on or check this without further detail; it stops short of 1.0 only because no dates or numbers of affected social workers are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Initially, the bill had laid out four years for people to be able to access that experience pathway, and then what happened was that this Government decided that it would reduce that to two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the four-to-two-year reduction was a change made by the current Government to a bill that originally provided four years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Social Workers Registration Legislation Amendment Bill as introduced versus as amended at committee of the whole House: true if the bill as introduced set the s13 experience pathway extension at four years and a Government amendment reduced it to two, false if the bill as introduced specified two years or if the reduction came from another source.

veracity.statement: They did receive at least one submission during the select committee process from a reputable professional body stating that it could be reduced from four years to two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existence of a select committee submission from a professional body supporting a two-year extension — the submission the ANZASW letter later disowns.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published select committee submissions on the bill: true if at least one submission from a recognised social work professional body argued for a two-year rather than four-year extension, false if no such submission exists.

rigor.statement: However, because we still have that workforce shortage, it is necessary to provide this extended period of time for them to access that experience pathway, because, actually, that’s important for them but it’s important for us being able to meet the workforce shortage that we’re currently experiencing.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure before the House — shortage therefore extend the pathway — but the justifying clause largely restates the premise rather than showing that the extension relieves the shortage. Mildly circular; the underlying step is coherent but nothing is offered to connect pathway access to workforce numbers.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Secondly, I have to say, it does cause us all to question how nimble the Minister is able to be in these situations, because, actually, she should have been able to turn around, to see that the position was different from what she had first thought, and then been able to adjust accordingly.
civility.explanation: Tethered to a specific failure — not responding to the ANZASW letter — but framed as a question about the Minister's personal capacity to adapt rather than about the decision itself. Pointed and edging onto the person without landing a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I raised the point during committee stage, too, that if we find ourselves in a position 18 months from now where we still have the workforce shortages in the social work sector for qualified, registered social workers in 18 months’ time, there is a very strong chance, because of the urgent need to have social workers in these positions, that we’re going to end up back in this House, having to legislate, amend again for another extension when we could have just got it right the first time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that persistent social worker workforce shortages will force Parliament to legislate a further extension of the experience pathway, rather than a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand parliamentary legislation record for the Social Workers Registration Act s13 experience pathway: true if a further bill or amendment extending the experience pathway beyond the two-year period is introduced or passed before the pathway expires, false if the pathway lapses on the legislated two-year date with no further extension legislated.

veracity.statement: They have always been very much a supporter of the Mike King I Am Hope Foundation, which the coalition Government has now decided to support.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition Government has decided to support Mike King's I Am Hope Foundation, and that New Zealand First has long backed it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–NZ First coalition agreement and Budget/Cabinet funding records for 2024; true if the coalition Government committed funding or formal support to I Am Hope / Gumboot Friday, false if no such commitment exists.

veracity.statement: There’s simply not enough registered social workers to meet the vacancy needs in our community—believe me, I know.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a shortfall of registered social workers relative to advertised vacancies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board annual workforce reports and Ministry of Social Development / NGO sector vacancy data for 2023–24; true if registered social worker vacancies materially exceeded the available registered workforce, false if vacancy and workforce data show no shortfall.

veracity.statement: Government departments were paying $30,000 more and Māori partners could never compete with the pay equity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a pay gap of about $30,000 between social worker salaries in government departments and those paid by Māori community providers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published salary bands for social workers at Oranga Tamariki / government departments compared with NGO and Māori provider pay scales for the same roles around 2023–24; true if the gap is of the order of $30,000, false if it is materially smaller.

rigor.statement: But the person who helped me the most as a teenager was someone who had the same problem. They weren’t qualified at all; they too became qualified later in life. But it was their lived experience that enabled me to heal from inside and start speaking to someone.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single personal anecdote to the conclusion that lived experience rather than qualification is what enables healing — an appeal to anecdote; one case cannot support a claim about the workforce as a whole.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you look at 12-step programmes that have been around for decades, they are just people all coming together who want to get help, and they get help within the fellowship there. No one asks, “What is your qualification?” before they get up to speak.
rigor.explanation: Faulty analogy: peer-led mutual-aid fellowships operate without any statutory duty of care, so the fact that they ask for no qualifications does not support a conclusion about the registration requirements for professional social workers.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We feel that it is the best way to alleviate the workforce shortage that we’ve got and to encourage people to get out there and help everyone else in the community.
specificity.explanation: Claims the bill is the best way to fix the shortage but supplies no mechanism, no figure for the shortage, and no timeframe — nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we don’t support is the shortened time frame from four years to two years.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision objected to and the precise change in figures (four years to two), so the position is checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our whānau need a workforce who will believe in them, who will support whānau with their healing, but, mostly, our whānau want trusted, safe practitioners.
specificity.explanation: A string of desirable qualities — belief, support, trust, safety — with no standard, mechanism or measure attached that anyone could check or implement.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We want this Government to stop being taringa mārō, to the solutions that will improve the healing of our whānau, and Te Pāti Māori’s role is to hold this Government to account.
focus.explanation: A real call for the Government to adopt different approaches, but no specific policy, measure or outcome is named — the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the Government as deaf to solutions rather than an engagement with one.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: From the time that the first social work courses were offered in Victoria University in the 1950s through to the passage of the Social Workers Registration Act in 2003, the object of the Act was to build and retain confidence in the profession of social work.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the first social work courses in New Zealand were offered at Victoria University in the 1950s, and that the stated object of the Social Workers Registration Act 2003 was to build and retain public confidence in the social work profession.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: University of Wellington / NZ social work education histories on when the first social work courses began and where; and the purpose/object section of the Social Workers Registration Act 2003 as enacted. True if courses began at Victoria University College in the 1950s and the Act's stated object is confidence in / professionalism of social work; false if the first courses were elsewhere or in a different decade, or the Act's object section says something materially different.

veracity.statement: Now, by 2021, the Act made social workers’ registration mandatory.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that mandatory registration for social workers took legal effect by 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Commencement provisions of the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019 and the Social Workers Registration Board's own guidance on when mandatory registration began. True if mandatory registration commenced on or before the end of 2021; false if it commenced in a different year or was never made mandatory.

veracity.statement: Around a quarter of social workers registered under the experience pathway over the past 13 years have identified as Māori; however, the proportion of Māori under the section 13 applicants is increasing.
veracity.explanation: Two data claims about registrations under the section 13 experience pathway: a roughly 25% Māori share over the past 13 years, and a rising Māori proportion among recent section 13 applicants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board registration data by pathway and ethnicity, and the Social Services and Community Committee report / departmental advice on the bill. True if the Māori share of section 13 registrations since roughly 2011 is close to 25% and the recent-year share trends upward; false if the long-run share is materially different from a quarter, or the recent trend is flat or downward.

specificity.statement: Now we support this move with the amendment by the Minister to shorten that extension from four years to two.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific mechanism (the Minister's amendment to the transitional extension) and both figures, four years to two. Checkable against the amendment paper. Lacks any dates or numbers of people affected, so short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, between the years 2020 and 2022, 31 percent of social worker registrations under the experience pathway were people who identified as Māori.
specificity.explanation: A precise figure, a named time window and a named statutory pathway. Someone could take this straight to the Registration Board's data and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The opportunity has been there for quite some time, and there is really no opportunity to delay, and that’s part of the reason why a shortened extension is deemed appropriate.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: the experience pathway has been available for years, therefore a shorter extension is appropriate. But the premise (long availability) does not by itself establish the conclusion (two years is enough), and the speaker's own later point — that social workers are too overworked to take it up — cuts against it without being reconciled. A genuine gap between what is shown and what is concluded, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: She is totally ignoring that, and, in her own wisdom, insisting that we stick with the two years, and today saying it will affect a very small number of people, yet the evidence that I have in front of me is that is an increasing number of Māori social workers.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, but the rebuttal does not meet the claim: the Minister's point was about the absolute number of people affected, and the evidence offered is a rising Māori proportion of section 13 registrations. A rising share of a shrinking or small pool is consistent with a small absolute number, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise as stated.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And there are very different reasons why they could be slow in taking that up: they are steeped in work; they are working very late hours over many days—not just the normal 40-hour work week.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: why the affected group has not used the registration pathway, and what that implies for the transitional window. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I asked questions in the committee stage about whether the Minister, in her consideration of her tabled amendment, had given any or sufficient consideration to Māori impacted by her proposed changes.
focus.explanation: Names the specific amendment, the stage at which it was scrutinised, and the specific gap alleged (impact on Māori social workers). This is legitimate scrutiny of a named measure, which scores at the top, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She is totally ignoring that, and, in her own wisdom, insisting that we stick with the two years, and today saying it will affect a very small number of people, yet the evidence that I have in front of me is that is an increasing number of Māori social workers.
civility.explanation: Mostly on the decision, but 'in her own wisdom' is sarcasm directed at the Minister personally and 'totally ignoring' imputes wilful disregard rather than disagreement. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person rather than the reasoning, so below the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: As we know, social workers provide a really important service to our most vulnerable, and, as we’ve heard in debates earlier in the House this afternoon, with 7,000 more children likely to be in poverty from one single action of this Government this afternoon, we know that Māori are impacted in many of the areas that require social work services, and so I am disappointed that the Minister did not heed the request and advice of these organisations and extended it out to the four years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a single measure passed by the Government on the same day will result in approximately 7,000 additional children living in poverty. A quantified future outcome, distinct from any promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury/MSD regulatory impact and child poverty modelling for the benefit indexation change passed in February 2024, checked against Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics releases for the years the modelling covers. True if the official estimate and subsequent measured outcome show roughly 7,000 or more additional children in poverty attributable to that change; false if the attributable figure is materially smaller or the modelling shows no such effect.

specificity.statement: We too would have preferred the experience pathway to be rolled back another two years—with another extra two years—to 28 February 2028.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism (the experience pathway roll-back), the size of the change (two extra years) and a precise date (28 February 2028). Anyone could check or act on this position.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So just going with one option of qualifications may not be enough, though we know that the take-up through the experience pathway is quite small—around 3 percent. But still, when there are 700 unfilled positions, we want to make sure that there is every opportunity available to any person who is enrolled as a social worker to get registered to satisfy the Social Workers Registration Board’s requirements and to be officially called a social worker.
specificity.explanation: Carries two checkable figures (3 percent take-up, 700 unfilled positions) and names the specific mechanism and the body administering it. Precision is judged here, not whether the inference from the figures holds.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the biggest factors behind the difficulties and the barriers to receiving and being able to train and qualify and study for social work registration is poverty. We haven’t removed that as a barrier. This Government is showing only signs of making that worse, and so this is another example of why we needed to extend that pathway as part of understanding that the barriers haven’t been removed.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: if poverty is the main barrier to qualifying and it has not been addressed, more lead-in time is needed before the alternative pathway closes. The conclusion tracks the premises. Marked down because the middle step — that the Government is making poverty worse — is asserted bare, with nothing offered to support it, and it is doing load-bearing work in the chain.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, again, the rainbow community and young people were speaking to us very clearly about the need to ensure that we can maintain those experience pathways while wrapping around the qualification and safe practice support for them to continue to become the social workers that that community desperately requires.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote. The evidence offered is conversations at a single weekend festival, generalised into a conclusion about how the registration pathway should be legislated for the whole workforce. Nothing connects what those individuals said to the population-level claim about what the community requires.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So just going with one option of qualifications may not be enough, though we know that the take-up through the experience pathway is quite small—around 3 percent. But still, when there are 700 unfilled positions, we want to make sure that there is every opportunity available to any person who is enrolled as a social worker to get registered to satisfy the Social Workers Registration Board’s requirements and to be officially called a social worker.
rigor.explanation: There is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded. The speaker concedes the experience pathway accounts for only about 3 percent of registrations, then offers extending it as the response to 700 vacancies — a remedy his own figure says can only touch a small fraction of the shortfall. He does not close that gap, and 'we want to make sure there is every opportunity available' restates the intention rather than justifying it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The extension is for two years, but it’s important to note that we have to find a cut-off time, and that cut-off time needs to be reasonable, and at this stage, we support that amendment which was put through during the committee of the whole House.
rigor.explanation: Circular. The question at issue was whether two years or four years is the right cut-off; the reason offered is that a cut-off must exist and must be 'reasonable'. That is true of any cut-off and does nothing to distinguish the one chosen from the one rejected, so the conclusion is simply restated as its own justification.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, again, the rainbow community and young people were speaking to us very clearly about the need to ensure that we can maintain those experience pathways while wrapping around the qualification and safe practice support for them to continue to become the social workers that that community desperately requires.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the experience pathway, and how qualification and safe-practice support would sit alongside it. No party content at all. This is the high-focus/low-rigor pair: arguing weakly about a real policy is still arguing about the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s so much easier to tear things down and destroy decades of hard work than it is to create enduring solutions. And when you have that attitude of rushing through things to tick some boxes, these are the voices that are missed out. This is how bad laws are made.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine process point underneath — that using urgency cut short consultation with the sector organisations affected by this bill. But the weight of the passage is a characterisation of the Government's attitude ('tear things down', 'tick some boxes') rather than the consultation gap itself, and no specific submission, stakeholder or clause is named here.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We wish that the Minister had the foresight and leadership to have been able to maintain a longer lead-in. That is disappointing. I truly hope we do not end up back here in the next years to try and remedy her lack of insight.
civility.explanation: Moves off the decision and onto the person: the Minister is said to lack foresight, leadership and insight. Criticising the two-year lead-in as too short would have scored near 1.0; attributing it to a personal deficiency in the Minister is a personal attack, if a restrained one.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because there are so many positions—around 700 social worker positions—still unfilled, we realised that we need to keep the options open.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately 700 social worker positions in New Zealand were vacant at the time of the third reading (February 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board workforce survey / MSD and Oranga Tamariki vacancy reporting for 2023–24; true if reported unfilled social worker positions are in the region of 700, false if the figure is materially lower or higher (e.g. under 400 or over 1,000).

divination.statement: As I said, the experience pathway was always going to be a temporary measure, and now it is also going to be a temporary measure, but this extension of allowing people to use the experience pathway for another two years will allow some last-minute social workers, those who are out there and are considering getting registered as social workers, to really seriously consider and come on board and get their registration done.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the two-year extension will draw additional practitioners into registration via the experience pathway before it closes — an outcome about other people's behaviour, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board annual reports / registration statistics for the years to 28 February 2026; true if registrations granted under the experience (competence-without-qualification) pathway during the extension period exceed the pre-extension annual run-rate, false if they are flat or fall.

veracity.statement: We have 700 vacancies at the moment, and the reality of it is that there are many, many people who would love to enter this workforce, but the current process—what will be the process in two years’ time of between three and four years of full-time qualification—is beyond them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts: that there are currently 700 unfilled social work positions, and that the qualification pathway after the transition will require between three and four years of full-time study.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board / Ministry of Social Development social worker vacancy reporting for early 2024, and the SWRB-recognised qualification requirements taking effect at the end of the section 13 transition; true if the vacancy count is approximately 700 and recognised qualifications run three to four years full-time, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Since 2021, the Social Workers Registration Act has required all social workers to register with the board, and to be eligible for registration, applicants must have a qualification recognised by that board.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that mandatory registration of all social workers began in 2021 and that registration requires a board-recognised qualification.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provisions of the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019 and the current text of the Social Workers Registration Act 2003; true if mandatory registration took effect during 2021 and the Act conditions registration on a board-recognised qualification, false if the commencement year differs or no qualification requirement exists.

specificity.statement: We have 700 vacancies at the moment, and the reality of it is that there are many, many people who would love to enter this workforce, but the current process—what will be the process in two years’ time of between three and four years of full-time qualification—is beyond them.
specificity.explanation: Carries a figure (700), a timeframe (two years), and the length of the qualification pathway (three to four years full-time) — checkable and actionable, though the claim about who is excluded is unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, recognising that we are 700 social workers short as we speak, at least—that’s the understanding—we’re changing this to give a two-year buffer for this experience pathway to exist as it currently does, to balance that need to account for the current shortage of workers while promoting a timely transition to mandatory qualifications to enhance that public trust and confidence in the social work profession.
specificity.explanation: Names the shortfall figure (700), the exact change being made (a two-year extension of the section 13 experience pathway), and the stated purpose — enough that someone could check both the number and the mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I acknowledge and hear the concerns from the Opposition, but I am well-convinced from other people, the experts within the sector, that two minutes—sorry, two years—ironic, two minutes is not enough, but two years is.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that two years is sufficient rests entirely on an appeal to authority — unnamed 'experts within the sector' — with no mechanism, figure or reasoning offered as to why two years suffices where four would not.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I remember those young adults that were training to be social workers, a number of those institutes would send their students to those Maatua Whāngai to learn how to be a social worker and, more importantly, to learn how to work with Māori, because we all know—and we’ve all seen the statistics—that within that field of work, there are many, many shortcomings for social workers who work in mainstream who did not have the skills to be able to help Māori whānau.
rigor.explanation: The load-bearing premise is carried by 'we all know' and an unspecified 'we've all seen the statistics' — an appeal to common knowledge and to unnamed evidence, supporting the conclusion by assertion rather than by anything the House could examine.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I acknowledge and hear the concerns from the Opposition, but I am well-convinced from other people, the experts within the sector, that two minutes—sorry, two years—ironic, two minutes is not enough, but two years is.
civility.explanation: On a contested measure where the Opposition's position is being rejected, he names their concerns and engages them without imputing bad faith or turning on any member.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I suppose my big question about this is trying to understand what the country gains by only having a two-year period as opposed to a four-year period, and what we potentially lose.
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at the specific parameter of the measure before the House — the length of the transition period — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I am pleased to speak in support of this legislation, but I too want to express my disappointment that the Minister—as was mentioned by Hon Willow-Jean Prime—in her wisdom, chose to change the extension to a two-year extension only.
civility.explanation: "in her wisdom" is a sardonic aside directed at the Minister personally rather than at the decision, but it stops well short of an insult and the substance (the two-year extension) is engaged squarely. Pointed and robust, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I just feel that sometimes when we make arguments, we shouldn’t be omitting certain points.
civility.explanation: A gently-worded suggestion that opposition members left out an inconvenient fact on purpose — it edges toward imputing bad faith rather than simply correcting the record, but it is hedged ("I just feel", "sometimes") and names nobody.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We know that prior to 2021, registering as a social worker was voluntary.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that mandatory registration for social workers in New Zealand began in 2021 and that before that date registration was voluntary.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provisions of the Social Workers Registration Legislation Act 2019 and the Social Workers Registration Act 2003 as amended: true if mandatory registration commenced in 2021 (and registration was optional before that), false if mandatory registration commenced in a materially different year.

veracity.statement: And what we do know is, with the shortage of at least 700 social workers across the country, which was in 2022—which may well be more by now—that there is a large proportion that are needed that are Pasifika, that are Māori, that are disabled, etc.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a national shortage of at least 700 social workers as at 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Social Workers Registration Board / Ministry of Social Development social work workforce reporting for 2022: true if a published estimate puts the shortfall at 700 or more, false if the published shortfall figure for that year is materially below 700.

veracity.statement: In 2017, the Government of the day agreed to remove this, but we’ve since said we need to delay this removal for a number of factors, two of them being COVID and, recently, the cyclones.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the decision to remove the alternative experience pathway to social worker registration was taken by the government in 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of the Social Workers Registration Legislation Bill (introduction date and the government that introduced it) and the Cabinet/policy record for removing the section 13 experience pathway: true if the decision and the Bill's introduction date to 2017, false if the removal was agreed in a materially different year.

rigor.statement: When you study for such a long time to gain your qualification, it is important that all social workers are registered, just as it is important in the teaching profession that all teachers become registered in order to have that profession and the acknowledgment of their study recognised, but also so that the people that they work with have greater protections as well with the social workers that they are dealing with.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: mandatory registration is justified by analogy with teacher registration plus a stated consequence (client protection). The client-protection reason genuinely supports the conclusion, but the analogy to teaching is asserted rather than defended — the relevant similarity between the two professions is never established, so part of the weight rests on an unargued comparison.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My colleague Greg Fleming, he’s a gentleman that really puts himself in a lot of these fields, and he said that he, as well, has had a number of conversations with professionals in this field who also told them that, look, two years is that good kind of Goldilocks balance in terms of what we’re dealing with here today.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the policy itself — why two years is the right length — but it rests entirely on an appeal to authority (a colleague who "puts himself in a lot of these fields") layered on unquantified anecdote ("a number of conversations"). Nothing is offered about why two years in particular closes the workforce gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As my colleague Adrian Rurawhe said, what will the country be missing out on by not having a four-year extension in order for people to register as social workers?
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure at issue — the length of the extension to the experience pathway — and asks about its consequence. No party framing, no characterisation of opponents; it engages the amendment before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I would like to highlight—something that hasn’t really been highlighted in the course of our conversations today—is that all applications submitted before the repeal date of 28 February 2026 will continue to be processed by the Social Workers Registration Board.
specificity.explanation: Names an exact date, the responsible body, and the precise mechanism (applications lodged before the repeal date are still processed). Anyone affected could act on this, and it can be checked against the Bill's transitional provisions.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It changes the classification of pseudoephedrine from a class B2 drug, as it is currently listed in the Misuse of Drugs Act, to a class C3 controlled drug.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory mechanism and both classifications; anyone could check the schedule change against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: All we are doing is trying to make life easier and more comfortable for New Zealanders by removing restrictions on their freedoms.
specificity.explanation: A framing slogan offered where substance was available — no restriction, drug, threshold or effect is named, and nothing in it could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 2011, however, pseudoephedrine was reclassified as a class B2 controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific year and classification for a past regulatory change to pseudoephedrine under the Misuse of Drugs Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 schedules and the amending instrument history: true if pseudoephedrine was moved to Class B2 in 2011, false if the reclassification occurred in a different year or to a different class.

veracity.statement: The change, unfortunately, had negligible effects on the overall methamphetamine market in New Zealand, as suppliers simply adapted to the law change, notably by importing more finished product.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2011 restriction did not reduce the size of the New Zealand methamphetamine market, because supply shifted to imported finished product.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ESR national wastewater drug testing and Customs/Police methamphetamine seizure and importation data before and after 2011: true if consumption estimates show no sustained decline and the share of imported finished methamphetamine rose, false if meth availability or use fell materially after the reclassification.

veracity.statement: All we are doing is ensuring that the rules around cold and cough medicine in New Zealand will be nearly identical to Australia and nearly indistinguishable from those in other countries such as the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada, countries where people can go into their pharmacy and buy some effective cold and cough medicine if they have the winter chills and the winter ills.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that after this change New Zealand's pseudoephedrine access rules will closely match Australia's, and that pseudoephedrine cold medicines are purchasable from pharmacies without prescription in the UK, US and Canada.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The current scheduling of pseudoephedrine in each jurisdiction: Australia's Poisons Standard (Schedule 3, pharmacist-only), the UK's pharmacy-medicine classification under the MHRA, the US Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act behind-the-counter regime, and Health Canada's schedule. True if all four permit purchase from a pharmacy without a prescription and Australia's regime is pharmacist-supervised sale as described; false if any of them requires a prescription or Australia's controls differ materially from the proposed NZ rules.

rigor.statement: You’ll need a licence to import or export products containing pseudoephedrine, so customs will be able to seize unlicensed importations.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference from the stated premise: if a licence is required to import, unlicensed importation is by definition seizable. The conclusion tracks the mechanism offered, with no gap needing to be filled.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If people are going to commit crimes, the answer is to punish the people committing the crime, not every New Zealander with a cold and flu.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: punishing offenders and restricting precursor access are not mutually exclusive, and framing a supply-side control as 'punishing' cold sufferers assumes the conclusion rather than arguing for it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If people are going to commit crimes, the answer is to punish the people committing the crime, not every New Zealander with a cold and flu.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substantive objection about pharmacy robberies and the trade-off the bill makes; no party framing at all. Weak reasoning here, but the subject matter is the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think, unfortunately, it is a sad commentary on some of the worst of New Zealand that we are so focused—we are a country that appears to be afraid of the implications of cough medicine, if you listen to some in the mainstream media.
focus.explanation: A digression about journalists and commentators rather than the measure: no policy, figure, mechanism or outcome is named in it. Characterising critics is not engaging the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think, unfortunately, it is a sad commentary on some of the worst of New Zealand that we are so focused—we are a country that appears to be afraid of the implications of cough medicine, if you listen to some in the mainstream media.
civility.explanation: Sneering and condescending toward media critics and the public generally — 'the worst of New Zealand', 'afraid of cough medicine' — but no individual is named or insulted, so it stops short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So my question in addressing this bill, and I think what the Parliament and the Health Committee needs to turn its mind to, is: what’s changed? Meth hasn’t gone away, are we giving up on this issue? How do we evaluate these very valid safety concerns that communities, and pharmacies in particular, have?
civility.explanation: A contested first reading where she could readily have turned on the Minister; instead the challenge is aimed squarely at the policy rationale and the evidence base. No person is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So the point of unpacking this is to point out the ways that this law—this dog of a law—perpetuates injustices and anti-evidence outcomes for our community, much to the detriment, actually, of the public purse.
civility.explanation: Contemptuous language ('this dog of a law') aimed entirely at the statute and its effects. No person is attacked, and blunt condemnation of a law is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This included the minor ailments scheme that we brought in over winter to make sure that common conditions, even as simple as nits or skin conditions, could be treated by pharmacies conveniently without having to go for a prescription to a doctor, thereby taking work away from overburdened general practitioners and making conditions be resolved more quickly.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific scheme, the conditions covered, the delivery channel and the intended mechanism, but supplies no figures, funding or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d refer them to He Ara Oranga, the mental health and addiction inquiry, which said that we need to move to decriminalise substances so that we can enable a harm reduction approach. I point them to Turuki! Turuki!, the safe and effective justice review, which actually said that we need to go a step further and look to legalise the supply chain of certain substances, so to remove them from the hands of criminal organisations.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific reviews and the specific recommendation each is said to make, so a reader can go and check both. Falls short of 1.0 only for want of figures or a proposed timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, it will have an effect on pharmacies. For over a decade, they will have not been the targets of ram raids due to pseudoephedrine, and they could be once again. I haven’t heard compelling evidence that there are reasons why that won’t be the case.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure before the House, but the load is carried by an argument from absence of evidence — the risk is asserted to exist because she has not been shown a reason it would not. The historical analogy is offered without any link to the volumes or controls now proposed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know, if you look at the evidence—as this Government has promised us that we would—that at both ends of extremes, that being in criminal prohibition or in a complete legal free market, you have the maximisation of harms when it comes to substances. That’s because, whether you’re talking about a scenario where you have those who operate in criminal organisations who control the supply chains, or those who operate in commercial entities controlling the supply chains, you have the maximisation of harm because profit is the key motive.
rigor.explanation: A real argument about drug regulation, but it leans on an unnamed body of 'the evidence' and the causal step is close to circular: harm is maximised at both extremes because profit is the motive, with nothing offered to show profit operates identically under prohibition and under a legal market.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Unfortunately, there is a massive import of completed methamphetamine products into New Zealand, a rising crime trend that we need to combat. The pseudoephedrine is no longer the threat that it was at the time that it was re-classified.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: because finished methamphetamine is now imported at scale, domestic precursor diversion matters less. The premise supports the conclusion only partially — a large import channel does not by itself establish that pseudoephedrine diversion would not resume once the drug is back on pharmacy shelves, and no evidence is offered for that step.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Now, the Minister has said that this will be unlikely to impact the supply of methamphetamine in New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Verrall is relaying, not asserting, the Minister's forecast that returning pseudoephedrine to over-the-counter sale will not materially affect the domestic methamphetamine supply.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: ESR national wastewater methamphetamine consumption estimates and NZ Police/Customs data on domestic clandestine laboratory detections, comparing the period after pseudoephedrine returns to over-the-counter sale with the preceding baseline. True if there is no sustained rise in domestically manufactured methamphetamine or in pseudoephedrine-based clan-lab busts attributable to the reclassification; false if clan-lab detections and pseudoephedrine diversion rise materially after the change.

veracity.statement: But in order to down-classify or to declassify a substance, you need an entire amendment bill, and therefore the select committee process that comes with it, and that can take anywhere from a few months to a year-plus, and, obviously, all of the potential for fearmongering and moral panic that come with that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an asymmetry in the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975: a substance can be classified (or up-classified) by Order in Council, but removing or lowering a classification requires primary legislation and a full select committee process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The classification provisions of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 (s 4 and the Order in Council/Schedule amendment powers) and the legislative history of past reclassifications. True if adding or up-classifying a substance can be done by Order in Council while removing or down-classifying requires an amendment Act; false if an Order in Council can also effect a down-classification or declassification.

veracity.statement: We know that prescriptions are currently required to access products containing pseudoephedrine, but manufacturers have allowed their product approvals to lapse, so there’s currently no pseudoephedrine products available in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at February 2024 no pseudoephedrine-containing medicine was actually obtainable in New Zealand, because manufacturers let their Medsafe product approvals lapse rather than because of the prescription requirement itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Medsafe's register of approved and marketed medicines as at February 2024, plus Medsafe/Ministry of Health statements on lapsed pseudoephedrine product approvals. True if no pseudoephedrine-containing product held a current approval and was being supplied; false if one or more remained available on prescription.

veracity.statement: These tighter controls have not affected the overall supply of methamphetamine in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the post-2011 restrictions on pseudoephedrine produced no reduction in the total methamphetamine supply in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ESR national wastewater drug testing consumption estimates, NZ Customs methamphetamine seizure volumes and Police clandestine laboratory detections across 2009-2023. True if methamphetamine availability and consumption show no sustained decline following the 2011 restrictions; false if the series show a material and sustained fall in supply after 2011.

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, there is a massive import of completed methamphetamine products into New Zealand, a rising crime trend that we need to combat. The pseudoephedrine is no longer the threat that it was at the time that it was re-classified.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that importation of finished methamphetamine into New Zealand is now large in volume and rising, as distinct from domestic manufacture from precursors.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Customs methamphetamine seizure volumes at the border and ESR wastewater consumption estimates for roughly 2020-2023 against the 2011 baseline, together with Police reporting on the domestic-manufacture share. True if border seizures of finished methamphetamine have risen materially and dominate supply; false if seizures are flat or falling, or domestic manufacture still accounts for most supply.

focus.statement: I am proud to stand here as a member of the Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand who is the only party who have been consistent—whether it’s alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, pseudoephedrine, or otherwise—on substances.
focus.explanation: The weight of the sentence is a claim about her own party's standing relative to the others rather than about the bill; the list of substances gives it some policy anchoring, but no measure, mechanism or outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That was the language that was used around the proposed repeal of—well, the repeal of the smoke-free legislation, so there seems to be a bit of an inconsistent application of rationale here, because, on one hand, with smoke-free, the Government is saying, “We are interested in crime; we’re interested in the impacts and the way gangs will use this, and therefore we’re not going to make particular shops magnets of crime.”; and then, on the other hand, they’ve had no regard to any kind of argument around that when it comes to pseudoephedrine.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about two named policies: she states the Government's own stated rationale on smokefree retail (crime and gang exploitation of specific shops) and concludes the same reasoning is absent here. The premises are offered rather than asserted, and the conclusion tracks them. Marked down because the analogy is asserted rather than defended — tobacco retailers and opt-in pharmacies may differ materially, and she does not close that gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s hypocritical that this bill is being prioritised today as the Government’s been taking a real hard approach on addressing crime, and the purpose of this legislation was actually introduced in the first place to tackle the crime and the production of P.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure, not a bare jibe: the premises (a stated tough-on-crime stance; the original statute's anti-methamphetamine purpose) are offered and the inconsistency conclusion partly follows. The gap is that it treats repeal as automatically crime-increasing without engaging the contested premise that the ban actually reduced methamphetamine production — the very point in dispute.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It didn’t work, and so we’re going back to where we’ve come from.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the policy, but a weak one. The premise that the ban 'didn't work' is asserted with nothing offered in support, and the conclusion that reversal is therefore warranted does not follow from failure alone — a ban could have reduced harm below the counterfactual without eliminating the meth trade. The reasoning skips the comparison it needs.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I do take note of the words of Ngāi Te Rangi chief executive Paora Stanley, who has said in the New Zealand Herald that the drug was taken off the shelves to keep gangs away from it and this will only exacerbate the impact on Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Paora Stanley, chief executive of Ngāi Te Rangi, made a specific statement in the New Zealand Herald about the reason for the original ban and the effect of the change on Māori. The speaker is relaying, not asserting, the underlying claim.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Herald coverage of the pseudoephedrine bill from January–February 2024 quoting Paora Stanley of Ngāi Te Rangi; true if he is reported saying the drug was removed from shelves to keep gangs away from it and that the change will worsen the impact on Māori, false if no such reported statement exists or the reported statement differs materially.

veracity.statement: Doctors have disputed the Minister’s claims that there are no effective alternatives.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that medical practitioners have publicly contradicted the Minister's position that no effective alternative medicines to pseudoephedrine exist. The speaker asserts this in her own voice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements or media reports from New Zealand doctors or medical bodies (e.g. RNZ, NZ Herald, GP/pharmacist organisations) dated before 20 February 2024 responding to the Minister's pseudoephedrine claims; true if doctors are on record disputing that there are no effective alternatives, false if no such statements exist.

veracity.statement: It was prohibited back in 2011 to slow the meth trade.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a date and a purpose: that over-the-counter sale of pseudoephedrine was prohibited in New Zealand in 2011, and that the stated reason was to curb the methamphetamine trade.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Misuse of Drugs classification records and the relevant 2011 amending legislation; true if pseudoephedrine was reclassified to prescription-only in 2011 with methamphetamine manufacture given as the rationale, false if the year or the stated rationale differs materially.

veracity.statement: We did have the Commissioner of Police before the Justice Committee earlier—last week—and I’ll have to check the transcription, but my recollection was that he said there’d be very little impact on the crime trade.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Commissioner of Police, giving evidence to the Justice Committee in the week before 20 February 2024, said the change would have very little impact on the crime trade. The speaker is relaying that evidence, and flags that he is working from recollection.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's transcript or published evidence from the Commissioner of Police for the week of 12–16 February 2024; true if he is recorded saying the pseudoephedrine change would have very little impact on crime, false if he said the opposite, gave no such view, or did not appear that week.

focus.statement: So taking this to select committee, I think, will be a good way to explore what has caused the shift in the production and supply of methamphetamine and what the outcome will be of this law change.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and what the select committee stage should examine — the production and supply of methamphetamine and the effect of the law change. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, probably our biggest worry and concern, again, is that this bill’s offering no alternative solution to approach the meth issue that we have in Aotearoa, predominantly in Māori communities.
focus.explanation: Engages what the bill does and does not contain — the absence of any accompanying response to methamphetamine harm — and names who it affects. A substantive objection to the measure, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And sorry for me speaking while you’re interrupting, David!
civility.explanation: Sarcasm aimed at a named individual rather than at the substance. It is a mild, provoked retort about chamber conduct rather than an attack on the person's character or competence, so it sits above a genuine failure but below civil engagement.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We have the Minister here proposing that his interests are for all of Aotearoa, when, in fact, it’s for the privileged who don’t get to live, day in, day out, with the scab of this epidemic and how it is truly affecting our communities.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named individual: that the Minister's stated motive is not his real one and that he is in fact acting for the privileged. Short of a direct insult, but it targets his sincerity rather than the merits of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We’re also concerned that the introduction of this legislation will retrigger the crime rates at pharmacies, as we saw in the late 2000s.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that restoring over-the-counter pseudoephedrine sales will cause pharmacy-targeted crime to rise back toward late-2000s levels. Not a promise about the speaker's own action, and not a claim about the present.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded burglary and robbery offences at pharmacies for the 24 months after over-the-counter pseudoephedrine sales resume, compared with the 24-month baseline before resumption; true if pharmacy-targeted offences rise materially (roughly 25% or more) above that baseline, false if they are flat or fall.

specificity.statement: This bill strikes the balance between enabling New Zealanders to swiftly recover from cold and flu, and limiting public use of pseudoephedrine for the production of methamphetamine.
specificity.explanation: Names the medicine and the two competing aims, but carries no checkable content about how the balance is struck — no purchase limits, no quantity thresholds, no record-keeping requirement, no figures. A general characterisation of the bill rather than a description anyone could verify or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Today’s a great day for sniffly New Zealanders, because what this bill does is it allows for the sale of effective cold medicines across the counter at pharmacies who choose to provide it across the country.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the actual mechanism — over-the-counter sale at pharmacies on an opt-in basis — which is checkable against the bill. But it carries no quantities, no purchase limits, no commencement date and no controls, so it describes the direction without the detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Our waste-water testing around New Zealand—big towns, small towns, cities—is showing up vast amounts of methamphetamine.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that national wastewater testing is detecting very high methamphetamine consumption across large and small centres alike.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ESR's national wastewater drug testing programme quarterly reports for 2023-24; true if methamphetamine consumption is detected at high or record levels across metropolitan, provincial and small-town sampling sites, false if detections are confined to a few sites or are low/declining nationally.

veracity.statement: We know the vaccination programme saved tens of thousands of lives.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's COVID-19 vaccination programme averted deaths numbering in the tens of thousands.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published modelling of deaths averted by New Zealand's COVID-19 vaccination programme (Te Pūnaha Matatini / Ministry of Health counterfactual estimates); true if central estimates are at or above roughly 20,000 deaths averted, false if central estimates are in the thousands or lower.

veracity.statement: But, as the case stands, it is that we require an amendment bill in order to introduce a substance, or rather we require an amendment bill to down-classify or declassify a substance, whereas to increase penalties associated with any given substance, it simply requires the waving through of that Order in Council.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an asymmetry in the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975: adding a substance or raising its classification can be done by Order in Council, while removing or down-classifying one requires a full amendment bill. The mid-sentence self-correction ('or rather') makes the intended claim plain.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, ss 4 and 4A, and the procedure actually used for recent classification changes; true if adding/up-classifying is available by Order in Council while down-classifying or declassifying requires amending the Act, false if both directions are available by the same instrument.
