veracity.explanation: Asserts that Collins sought Labour's candidate selection for Manukau East in 2014 and later stood for the Auckland mayoralty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting of the 2014 Labour Manukau East selection contest and the 2022 Auckland mayoral candidate list; true if Collins is recorded as a contender in the 2014 selection and as a mayoral candidate, false if either is absent or the year is wrong.

specificity.statement: We also know that the current fragmented and outdated approach to the regulation of natural health products means that New Zealand is missing out on a significant proportion of opportunity to grow jobs and the economy.
specificity.explanation: Asserts a lost economic opportunity with no figure, no mechanism and no timeframe; "a significant proportion of opportunity" quantifies nothing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are confident we will have effective legislation that will deliver good outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Answers a question about the shape of the replacement regime with generic virtues — "effective" and "good outcomes" — no mechanism, no content, no date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Ministers take a range of advice on a range of topics.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the substantive answer to a question about a named proposal (raising the purchase age to 25) and the Ministry advice behind it; commits to nothing and conveys no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it correct that school property capital expenditure for the Botany electorate increased from $3.7 million in 2017 to $11.9 million in 2022; if so, which of those projects does he believe were of low value?
specificity.explanation: Two dollar figures, two years and a named electorate; the claim can be checked against school property expenditure records and the question can be answered directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Did his Associate Minister of Health advise Cabinet that the Ministry of Health estimated rolling back smoke-free law changes would cost the health system an estimated $5 billion and that smoking currently contributes to an average of 12 deaths per day in New Zealand; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Names the decision-maker, the advice, a costing ($5 billion) and a mortality figure (12 deaths per day); precise enough that the Minister could confirm or deny each element.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: According to Stats NZ, living costs for low-income households, as measured by the household living-costs price indexes, rose by 20 percent in just the three years between the end of 2020 and the end of 2023. That compared to growth of just 18 percent over the whole nine years that National was in Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the exact index, the population it covers, both percentages and both date ranges — every element is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, just this week, the Government is legislating to end the Auckland regional fuel tax, delivering Aucklanders relief at the pump from the start of July after years of being fleeced to pay for projects they don’t want, like cycleways and speed bumps.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure (repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax), the vehicle (legislation this week) and the effective date (start of July); no dollar figure for the household saving.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Act has a commencement date of 1 September 2026, so no changes are required from the health sector or industry.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Therapeutic Products Act 2023 has a commencement date of 1 September 2026 and therefore imposes no present obligations on the sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provisions of the Therapeutic Products Act 2023 as enacted; true if the substantive provisions are set to commence on 1 September 2026 (and no earlier duties bind the sector before then), false if the Act's operative provisions had already commenced or commence on a different date.

veracity.statement: What I have seen is the results from the last year, which has seen daily smokers go from 8.6 percent to 6.8 percent just in the last 12 months, with the legislation that we’re going to readopt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the adult daily smoking rate fell from 8.6 percent to 6.8 percent over the preceding twelve months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the two most recent survey years before February 2024; true if the series moves from 8.6% to 6.8%, false if either figure differs materially from the published rate.

veracity.statement: The smoking legislation that we’ve seen over the last decade has actually halved daily smoking in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that daily smoking prevalence in New Zealand has halved over the ten years to 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for 2013/14 compared with 2022/23; true if the later rate is at or below half the earlier one, false if the reduction is materially less than half.

veracity.statement: According to Statistics New Zealand, inflation in New Zealand was higher last year than in the US, the UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, and the European Union, which would suggest that claims made by previous Governments that this was all an international problem are not borne out by the data.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's 2023 annual inflation rate exceeded that of the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, Japan and the European Union.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Annual CPI inflation for calendar 2023 from Stats NZ and the OECD/national statistical agencies for each economy named; true if New Zealand's rate was higher than every one of them, false if any of the six matched or exceeded it.

veracity.statement: According to Stats NZ, living costs for low-income households, as measured by the household living-costs price indexes, rose by 20 percent in just the three years between the end of 2020 and the end of 2023. That compared to growth of just 18 percent over the whole nine years that National was in Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 20 percent rise in the household living-costs price index for low-income households over 2020–2023, against 18 percent across the nine years of the previous National government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Living-costs Price Indexes, lowest-expenditure-quintile series; true if cumulative growth from Q4 2020 to Q4 2023 is about 20% and cumulative growth from late 2008 to late 2017 is about 18%, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: In good news for Kiwis at the checkout, food price data released earlier this month showed food prices are increasing at their slowest annual rate since 2021, at 4 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the food price index released in February 2024 showed annual food price inflation of 4 percent, the lowest annual rate since 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Food Price Index release for January 2024; true if the annual increase is about 4% and no month since 2021 recorded a lower annual rate, false if the figure differs materially or a lower annual rate occurred within that window.

veracity.statement: That slide pack contained a paragraph which stated: “Current budget allowances are expected to be sufficient to fund critical cost pressures only, with limited room for new spending in the absence of reprioritisation and savings”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the released slide pack accompanying Treasury's November 2023 briefing to the incoming Minister of Finance contains that specific sentence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The publicly released Treasury Briefing to the Incoming Minister of Finance (November 2023) and its accompanying slide pack; true if the quoted sentence appears in it as stated, false if the wording differs materially or the text is not there.

rigor.statement: The Act has a commencement date of 1 September 2026, so no changes are required from the health sector or industry.
rigor.explanation: The inference is sound on its own premise: if the operative provisions have not commenced, repeal before commencement imposes no compliance change. Small gap in that it ignores preparatory work already under way.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have received advice that implementing the changes required to meet the commencement date would’ve been extremely challenging. This poses the real possibility of poor outcomes for New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to undisclosed authority (unnamed "advice"), plus a leap from "implementation would be challenging" to "a real possibility of poor outcomes" with nothing offered to connect the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I have seen is the results from the last year, which has seen daily smokers go from 8.6 percent to 6.8 percent just in the last 12 months, with the legislation that we’re going to readopt.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc attribution: the fall is credited to legislation that was not in force during the period measured, and the decline occurred while the smokefree law the Government is repealing was on the books. The conclusion does not follow from the figure offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: According to Statistics New Zealand, inflation in New Zealand was higher last year than in the US, the UK, Australia, Canada, Japan, and the European Union, which would suggest that claims made by previous Governments that this was all an international problem are not borne out by the data.
rigor.explanation: The comparison does not carry the conclusion: a higher rate than peers is fully consistent with a shared international shock plus domestic amplification, so ranking above six other economies does not show the pressure was not international.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it’s no surprise, then, that last week we learnt that more children were growing up in material deprivation and poverty thanks to the last Government’s disastrous economic mismanagement. That’s the price of Labour: more tax, more spending, and more families struggling with the cost of living.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: a rise in a living-costs index is treated as establishing that the previous government's management caused rising child material deprivation, with nothing offered to link the two beyond sequence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What’s clear is that future Budgets are under significant pressure because of the previous Government’s woeful fiscal and economic mismanagement.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the Treasury text quoted immediately before establishes that allowances are tight, not what caused the tightness. The causal attribution to the previous government is asserted, not derived from the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I also appreciate the member’s most recent supportive remarks correcting earlier comments from Jan Tinetti denying there was even a problem.
civility.explanation: Mock-appreciation aimed at a named individual, imputing to Jan Tinetti that she denied a problem existed. The needling is directed at the person rather than at any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Unlike the previous Government, we don’t discuss stuff that happens in Cabinet—unlike Stuart Nash.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member as a byword for leaking Cabinet material — a jab at Stuart Nash personally rather than at any argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Smoking rates are going to continue to fall under the existing legislation that we’re going to readopt.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that adult smoking prevalence will keep declining after the smokefree amendments are repealed and the earlier legislative regime restored.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for survey years after 2023/24; true if the rate is lower than the 2022/23 figure of 6.8%, false if it is flat or higher.

focus.statement: Unlike the previous Government, we don’t discuss stuff that happens in Cabinet—unlike Stuart Nash.
focus.explanation: Asked about advice the Ministry of Health gave Cabinet on the cost of repeal, the answer is entirely about the other party's past conduct. No policy, figure or measure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it correct that school property capital expenditure for the Botany electorate increased from $3.7 million in 2017 to $11.9 million in 2022; if so, which of those projects does he believe were of low value?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named programme with named figures — puts the Government's own school property spending characterisation to the test rather than attacking the party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why did his Associate Minister reject proposals to stop tobacco being sold near schools?
focus.explanation: Squarely about a specific policy proposal and a specific ministerial decision on it — accountability for a named measure, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it’s no surprise, then, that last week we learnt that more children were growing up in material deprivation and poverty thanks to the last Government’s disastrous economic mismanagement. That’s the price of Labour: more tax, more spending, and more families struggling with the cost of living.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point about child poverty and living costs, but the weight of the passage is party framing — "that's the price of Labour" — rather than the measure or the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it correct that 79 percent of the new operating allowance in Budget 2023 was for cost pressures, and does she expect Budget 2024 will require a similar percentage to meet cost pressures?
specificity.explanation: A named Budget, a named fiscal aggregate and a precise percentage; the Minister could check it or contest the figure directly. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, what I would share with her is that what we know is that even before this Government formed, the previous Government had pre-committed 68 percent of this year’s operating allowance, and we know that the sum of the fiscal cliffs they’d left behind, at $7.2 billion, would more than have evaporated the entire operating allowance before we funded another single cost pressure.
specificity.explanation: Two named figures against two named fiscal aggregates and a stated time reference. Someone could go to the fiscal update and check both.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Would the Minister’s definition of “cost pressures”, then, include discovering the books were nearly $2 billion short of funding the pharmaceuticals New Zealanders have been led to expect?
specificity.explanation: A named spending area and a figure, tied to a specific claim about the state of the accounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I can say about this Government is that we want to ensure that we are delivering the classrooms needed for roll growth and the schools needed for roll growth and that we’re ensuring that the school property programme is well funded, that it delivers good value for money, that it’s fair, and that it’s proportionate.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — well funded, good value, fair, proportionate — attached to a named programme but with no figure, no mechanism and no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Could I ask the Minister of Finance as to whether or not the Public Interest Journalism Fund, started in December 2020 and still going now—costing a colossal $55 million—is a cost pressure that could have been far more worthily spent on schools and hospitals, and not some woke programme supported by the other side?
specificity.explanation: A named fund, a start date and a dollar figure. The pejorative framing does not reduce the checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we have is a very good process to make sure we’re managing potential conflicts of interest, real or perceived. We have clear processes around that that make sure that we’re compliant with the Cabinet Manual.
specificity.explanation: Answers a question about mechanism by asserting twice that a process exists and is good, without naming a single step, threshold or safeguard. Nothing here could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Was she advised by officials that repealing the 2022 amendments to the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act would mean that the smoke-free goal would not be met until 2061?
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the year of the amendments, the action (repeal) and a precise projected date. Directly checkable against the official advice.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the last three years, we have seen 219,000 people have stopped smoking, with vaping playing a key role. Importantly, 79,000 of those who stopped smoking—36 percent of those who quit—were Māori.
specificity.explanation: Absolute counts, a proportion, a stated period and an identified population. Every element is checkable against the health survey series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We were absolutely committed to achieving the smoke-free targets, and we are going to implement systems that target addicted smokers, and not generalist, virtue-signalling approaches that are unproven.
specificity.explanation: Asked to justify a repeal, she commits to 'systems that target addicted smokers' with no mechanism, no funding, no timeframe and no named intervention. The only concrete element is the target being restated.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Say, Mr Robertson would probably define the urgent need for more back-office bureaucrats as a cost pressure.
civility.explanation: Attributes to a named individual a position he has not taken, as mockery — sneering at Grant Robertson's judgement rather than engaging the definitional point she had just raised. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why does she refuse to be interviewed on why she is repealing a law that would save $5 billion in health costs, and don’t New Zealanders deserve to know the answer to that?
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal in its framing — 'refuse to be interviewed' charges the Minister with deliberately avoiding scrutiny rather than simply noting she has not given interviews. It edges toward imputing bad faith without landing on her character or competence, and the underlying accountability point is legitimate.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: However, what I would share with her is that what we know is that even before this Government formed, the previous Government had pre-committed 68 percent of this year’s operating allowance, and we know that the sum of the fiscal cliffs they’d left behind, at $7.2 billion, would more than have evaporated the entire operating allowance before we funded another single cost pressure.
veracity.explanation: Two distinct factual assertions about the fiscal position inherited from the Sixth Labour Government: that 68 percent of the current operating allowance was already pre-committed, and that expiring time-limited funding totalled $7.2 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update (December 2023) and Budget 2024 documents: true if pre-commitments against the Budget 2024 operating allowance are recorded at approximately 68 percent, and if the identified time-limited funding expiries ('fiscal cliffs') sum to about $7.2 billion; false if either figure is materially different or if the $7.2 billion is not sourced to published fiscal documents.

veracity.statement: Would the Minister’s definition of “cost pressures”, then, include discovering the books were nearly $2 billion short of funding the pharmaceuticals New Zealanders have been led to expect?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the pharmaceutical budget inherited by the incoming Government was underfunded by nearly $2 billion relative to what had been publicly signalled.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Pharmac's published funding baseline and the Treasury/Vote Health appropriations for the pharmaceutical budget as at February 2024: true if the shortfall between committed pharmaceutical funding and the forecast requirement is close to $2 billion; false if the documented gap is materially smaller or if no such shortfall is identified in the fiscal documents.

veracity.statement: I well recall the COVID money that was used to fund consultants delivering a three waters plan, and the COVID money used to rent offices to include those three waters consultants in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that money appropriated for the COVID-19 response was spent on consultants and office rent for the Three Waters reform programme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's published allocations from the COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund: true if CRRF money was appropriated to the Three Waters reform programme and used for consultants and office accommodation; false if the reform programme was funded from other appropriations.

veracity.statement: Could I ask the Minister of Finance as to whether or not the Public Interest Journalism Fund, started in December 2020 and still going now—costing a colossal $55 million—is a cost pressure that could have been far more worthily spent on schools and hospitals, and not some woke programme supported by the other side?
veracity.explanation: Three checkable assertions bundled into the question — the fund's start date, its total value, and that it was still in existence when he spoke.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ On Air's published record of the Public Interest Journalism Fund: true if the fund was established in December 2020, was valued at $55 million, and was still operating in February 2024; false if the start date, the total value, or the claim that it was still running at that date is wrong.

veracity.statement: Has the Prime Minister and his Government considered the fact that there is a preference in using New Zealand coal rather than to be importing inferior Indonesian coal, which was the practice of the former Government?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Indonesian coal of lower quality was imported for use in New Zealand during the previous Government's term. Note the imports were made by a state-owned generator rather than by the Government as such, which is part of what a checker would have to resolve.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ coal import statistics and Genesis Energy's disclosures for 2017–2023, plus published comparisons of the calorific and sulphur content of Indonesian versus New Zealand thermal coal: true if imported Indonesian coal was burned for electricity generation during the previous Government's term and is of measurably lower quality; false if imports did not occur or the imported coal is not inferior on the standard measures.

veracity.statement: We’re not going to turn off growth opportunities in sectors across this country when we’ve had three of the last four quarters left to us in decline by the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that three of the four most recent quarters of economic growth, all falling within the previous Government's term, were contractions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP (production measure), as published at February 2024, for the four quarters ending September 2023: true if three of those four quarters recorded negative growth; false if two or fewer did.

veracity.statement: Again, we have not had fast-track consenting legislation come before the Cabinet and it has not yet been discussed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 27 February 2024 the fast-track consenting legislation had not been to Cabinet and had not been discussed there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet papers and Cabinet/Cabinet committee minutes relating to the fast-track consenting regime released proactively or under the Official Information Act: true if no fast-track consenting paper had been considered by Cabinet or a Cabinet committee before 27 February 2024; false if any such paper had been taken by that date.

veracity.statement: How does she justify repealing the 2022 amendments to the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act when she was advised that that bill would substantially close the difference in life expectancy between Māori and non-Māori?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister received official advice that the 2022 smokefree amendments would substantially narrow the Māori/non-Māori life expectancy gap.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Health's advice to the Associate Minister of Health and the regulatory impact statement for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022, as released under the Official Information Act: true if that advice states the 2022 amendments would substantially reduce the Māori/non-Māori life expectancy gap; false if it contains no such finding.

veracity.statement: Why does she refuse to be interviewed on why she is repealing a law that would save $5 billion in health costs, and don’t New Zealanders deserve to know the answer to that?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $5 billion health-cost saving attributable to the law being repealed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement and health-system cost modelling accompanying the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022: true if the projected health system saving is approximately $5 billion; false if the published estimate is materially different or if no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: We are now receiving statistics where we have a smoking rate of 6.8 percent of New Zealanders daily smoking, which is down from the 8.6 percent, which was one of the statistics that that data was based upon.
veracity.explanation: Two figures asserted: a current daily smoking rate of 6.8 percent, and a prior rate of 8.6 percent said to underlie the advice she was rejecting as out of date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence: true if the most recent published rate at February 2024 is 6.8 percent and the immediately preceding rate on which the officials' advice was based is 8.6 percent; false if either figure differs from the published series or if the 8.6 percent is not the comparator used in that advice.

focus.statement: Members opposite may have been happy that on their watch the amount spent on consultants and contractors boomed, the number of people hired in back-office roles boomed, and there were low-value programmes, but our Government makes no apologies for being on a drive to ensure that dollars spent go to front-line services, go to delivering on our commitments such as more police, and go to ensuring New Zealanders can have more income in their back pockets.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy claim here — consultant spend, back-office headcount, reprioritisation to front-line services — but the weight of the sentence is the framing of what the other side 'may have been happy' about, an attribution of motive rather than a policy point. A genuine policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, on the other side of the House, we have people who claim that everything is essential.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of what the other side is like, with no policy, figure or measure named. Strip out the part about the Opposition and nothing about cost pressures remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon, who said to the Bluegreens conference in 2023 that “National in Government will use the best scientific, financial, and environmental information available to us to chart a responsible, fair and sustainable way forward on environmental matters.”, and, if so, how is this consistent with proposals for the new fast-track consenting process for permits to be approved by Ministers rather than expert panels?
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment and a specific mechanism of a specific proposed regime — who holds the approval decision under fast-track consenting. This is scrutiny of a named policy against a named commitment, which is the job of an opposition MP.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, we have been on the record to say that we actually want to overturn the oil and gas ban, because we need gas as a transitory energy source as we make the transition to clean, green energy going forward.
focus.explanation: Squarely about an energy policy and its rationale, with no party framing. It does not answer the question that was asked, but that bears on forthrightness, not on what the statement is about.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon, who said to the Bluegreens conference in 2023 that “National in Government will use the best scientific, financial, and environmental information available to us to chart a responsible, fair and sustainable way forward on environmental matters.”, and, if so, how is this consistent with proposals for the new fast-track consenting process for permits to be approved by Ministers rather than expert panels?
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: the premise (a commitment to decide on the best scientific and environmental information) is set against the proposed mechanism (ministerial rather than expert-panel approval), and the tension between them follows. The gap is that ministerial decision-making does not strictly preclude receiving expert information, so the inconsistency is argued rather than demonstrated.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, we have been on the record to say that we actually want to overturn the oil and gas ban, because we need gas as a transitory energy source as we make the transition to clean, green energy going forward.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion offered with a reason — the exploration ban should go because gas is needed as a transition fuel. The inference is intact but thin: nothing is offered to connect reversing the ban to gas supply within the transition period, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I accept is that we will involve Māori in the monitoring and the delivery of health services to improve Māori health outcomes.
specificity.explanation: An answer that is trying to convey substance but carries no mechanism, no figure, no timeframe and no named programme — 'involve Māori in the monitoring and the delivery' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In September 2023, the Ministry of Education began a review of property projects. In January, I was informed that up to 350 projects needed to be reviewed for cost-effectiveness.
specificity.explanation: Two dates and a figure, all attached to a named process — someone could go and check when the ministry review started and how many projects were in scope.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to be clear that school property is a priority for this Government, and our inquiry will ensure that we deliver cost-effective, warm, dry classrooms to as many schools as possible.
specificity.explanation: A closing statement of intent with no number, no date and no mechanism: 'a priority', 'cost-effective, warm, dry' and 'as many schools as possible' are all unbounded. Nothing here could later be marked as met or missed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And, finally, Gisborne District Council is receiving $4.98 million to develop a remediation plan and carry out remediation works at the former Tokomaru Bay landfill.
specificity.explanation: A named recipient, an exact amount and a named site with a stated purpose — fully checkable against the fund's grant record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the Contaminated Sites Remediation Fund be spared the 6.5 to 7.5 percent funding cuts?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact fund and the exact percentage range at issue; a precise question, and precision in a question counts as much as in an answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The remedial contamination fund will be used in the way that it’s going to be best used to help the environmental and community outcomes of this country.
specificity.explanation: Circular and content-free — the fund will be used in the way it is best used. No amount, no protection stated, nothing that answers whether the fund is or is not exposed to the cuts.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does the Minister accept that given the Māori Health Authority did not exist until two years ago, the abolition of it cannot possibly be a breach of the Treaty?
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the recency of a body's creation does not bear on whether removing it breaches Treaty obligations. The premise (it is only two years old) gives no support at all to the conclusion ('cannot possibly be a breach'), which is stated at maximum strength.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Since this announcement, I have already received reports that principals are welcoming this inquiry. On RNZ this morning, Vaughan Couillault of the Secondary Principals Association of New Zealand—SPANZ—said that principals are really pleased that the Minister has listened to the sector.
rigor.explanation: The general conclusion that principals welcome the inquiry rests on an appeal to authority and anecdote — one association spokesperson on the radio, plus (immediately after) one board member's email. Nothing offered would distinguish sector-wide support from two supportive voices.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, recognising your point about the accumulation, there has to be a point at which we’re able to debate whether it’s appropriate for a ratio of 16 urgent items to one to go through the House, because the Government has the majority and is, essentially, railroading the House.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from an offered statistic — a 16:1 urgency ratio is evidence that normal process is being bypassed — but the step from that ratio to 'railroading the House' is asserted rather than argued, and nothing is offered on whether the individual bills were properly urgent. A reasonable point with a genuine gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The point is, of the 16 bills that have come through this House, a large proportion are affecting communities who are made up of tangata whenua, who are denied the right to come in and be part of an open, transparent select committee, an open, transparent consultation. This is affecting Māori more than anyone else in Aotearoa, which is why we have put this request for an urgent debate.
rigor.explanation: The premise (urgency removes select committee scrutiny, and a share of the bills affect tangata whenua) does support a claim of disproportionate effect, but 'a large proportion' is never quantified and no comparison with other affected groups is offered, so the comparative conclusion — 'more than anyone else' — outruns what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Does the Minister accept that given the Māori Health Authority did not exist until two years ago, the abolition of it cannot possibly be a breach of the Treaty?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Māori Health Authority had existed for less than about two years at the time of speaking (February 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement date of Te Aka Whai Ora / Māori Health Authority under the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022; true if the body began operating roughly two years or less before 27 February 2024, false if it had existed materially longer.

veracity.statement: In September 2023, the Ministry of Education began a review of property projects. In January, I was informed that up to 350 projects needed to be reviewed for cost-effectiveness.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ministry of Education started a property project review in September 2023 and that the Minister was advised in January 2024 that up to 350 projects required cost-effectiveness review.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education briefings/advice to the Minister for the period (obtainable via the proactive release or OIA); true if a review commenced September 2023 and advice in January 2024 cites a figure of up to ~350 projects, false if the dates or the count are materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, I think it’s brave of that member to ask a question, given that this morning on air she said that all of the properties in her portfolio, when she was the Minister, were funded and factored into the Budget. Just mere hours later, her leader had to correct her and say that he would not guarantee absolutely every single one of them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jan Tinetti said on air that morning that all school properties in her portfolio were funded and factored into the Budget, and that her leader publicly contradicted her hours later.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The recording/transcript of Tinetti's radio interview on 27 February 2024 and Chris Hipkins' public comments the same day; true if she made that unqualified funding claim and he declined to guarantee every project, false if she qualified the claim or no such correction was made.

veracity.statement: And, finally, Gisborne District Council is receiving $4.98 million to develop a remediation plan and carry out remediation works at the former Tokomaru Bay landfill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Gisborne District Council received a $4.98 million Contaminated Sites Remediation Fund grant for the former Tokomaru Bay landfill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry for the Environment's February 2024 Contaminated Sites Remediation Fund announcement and grant schedule; true if it records ~$4.98m to Gisborne District Council for Tokomaru Bay, false if the recipient, site or amount differ materially.

veracity.statement: Just in relation to that ruling, by my count, the Government has put 16 bills through urgency and one item of Government business not through urgency.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of the Government's use of urgency since taking office: 16 bills taken under urgency against a single item of Government business taken without it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of urgency motions and Government business from the start of the 54th Parliament to 27 February 2024; true if the tally of bills advanced under urgency is about 16 against roughly one non-urgent item, false if the counts are materially different.

focus.statement: Will the inquiry into school property she announced yesterday look at the cuts the previous National Government made into school property and the subsequent impact on school property assets; if not, why not?
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (the announced school property inquiry) and a specific matter of scope — whether earlier funding decisions and their asset impact fall inside it. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing, even though it is directed at a previous National government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I think it’s brave of that member to ask a question, given that this morning on air she said that all of the properties in her portfolio, when she was the Minister, were funded and factored into the Budget. Just mere hours later, her leader had to correct her and say that he would not guarantee absolutely every single one of them.
focus.explanation: A policy question about the inquiry's scope is answered almost entirely with the member's own credibility and her leader's contradiction of her. There is a faint policy thread (whether school property projects were funded in the Budget), but the weight of the statement is about the other side rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will the Contaminated Sites Remediation Fund be spared the 6.5 to 7.5 percent funding cuts?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure just announced — whether a named fund is exposed to a named savings target. Scrutiny of a specific policy commitment, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I think it’s brave of that member to ask a question, given that this morning on air she said that all of the properties in her portfolio, when she was the Minister, were funded and factored into the Budget. Just mere hours later, her leader had to correct her and say that he would not guarantee absolutely every single one of them.
civility.explanation: 'It’s brave of that member to ask a question' is condescension aimed at the questioner rather than the question — a sneer implying she lacks standing, and the follow-up that her leader 'had to correct her' compounds it. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can he justify introducing legislation to abolish Te Aka Whai Ora two days before the Waitangi Tribunal’s urgent hearing into Te Aka Whai Ora, when his Government has known since 19 January that an inquiry was set to take place?
specificity.explanation: Names the measure, the two-day gap before the hearing, and a specific date (19 January) on which the Government is said to have learned of the inquiry. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have seen tremendous halving of smoking rates amongst Māori—from memory, something like 37 percent down to 16 percent in the space of a decade—under the legislation that we’re supporting putting back into law.
specificity.explanation: Two figures and a timeframe; someone could go and check the series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are 190,000 people on jobseeker benefits. That’s a 70,000 increase under Labour.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, checkable figures attached to a named comparison period.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On Sunday, the Government announced a raft of measures aimed at addressing harm caused by gangs. Gangs’ insignia will be banned from public display, gang gatherings will be disrupted by police-issued dispersal notices, gang associates separated by court-issued non-consorting orders, and, finally, we’re giving greater weight to gang membership as an aggravating factor at sentencing.
specificity.explanation: Four named mechanisms with the instrument for each (dispersal notices, non-consorting orders, sentencing weighting). Missing only cost and commencement dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What is the purpose of his non-consorting orders when sections 112 to 123 of the Sentencing Act already have a comprehensive framework for non-association orders?
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact statutory sections said to already cover the ground. A precise question, as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve abolished the prison target reduction, we’re stopping taxpayer funding for section 27 reports, we’ll soon introduce legislation to implement our package to tackle gangs, and my colleague Minister McKee will have further announcements to make on restoring law and order very soon.
specificity.explanation: Named actions (prison reduction target, section 27 report funding), but the forward-looking half carries no dates, amounts or content — 'soon' and 'further announcements'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ll always remain open to any dialogue from any parties and from any citizens, from Māori, from anyone who wants to help us advance the cause of Māori health outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Offered in answer to a substantive question about the repeal timetable, but commits to nothing checkable: no process, no forum, no date. A statement of general openness.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: How can he justify introducing legislation to abolish Te Aka Whai Ora two days before the Waitangi Tribunal’s urgent hearing into Te Aka Whai Ora, when his Government has known since 19 January that an inquiry was set to take place?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government knew from 19 January 2024 that the Waitangi Tribunal had set an urgent inquiry into Te Aka Whai Ora, and that the repeal bill was introduced two days before that hearing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal registration/notification records for the urgent inquiry into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, and the Crown's date of notice; plus the bill's introduction date on legislation.govt.nz. True if the Crown was notified on or about 19 January 2024 and introduction fell two days before the hearing; false if notice came materially later or the gap is materially different.

veracity.statement: How can he justify dismantling the Māori Health Authority in the same week as repealing smoke-free legislation, when Māori die seven years earlier, on average, than non-Māori and smoking is our leading cause of premature death?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a life-expectancy gap of about seven years between Māori and non-Māori, and that smoking is the leading cause of premature death in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life tables for Māori and non-Māori life expectancy at birth (most recent release before Feb 2024), and Ministry of Health / IHME burden-of-disease attribution for leading cause of preventable death. True if the gap is ~7 years and smoking ranks first; false if the gap is materially smaller/larger or another cause ranks first.

veracity.statement: We have seen tremendous halving of smoking rates amongst Māori—from memory, something like 37 percent down to 16 percent in the space of a decade—under the legislation that we’re supporting putting back into law.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Māori smoking prevalence fell from about 37% to about 16% over roughly a decade, and attributes that fall to the legislative settings the Government is restoring.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for Māori across the decade to 2022/23. True if the start and end figures are within a point or two of 37% and 16%; false if materially different. Separately, the attribution is false if the decline predates the smokefree legislation being repealed.

veracity.statement: There are 190,000 people on jobseeker benefits. That’s a 70,000 increase under Labour.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current Jobseeker Support caseload of 190,000 and a 70,000 increase over the term of the previous Labour government.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets: Jobseeker Support recipients at the quarter ending December 2023 and at the quarter ending December 2017. True if the later figure is ~190,000 and the difference is ~70,000; false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: In the past five years, gangs have recruited more than 3,000 new members and there has been significant escalation in gang-related violence, public intimidation, and shootings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts net growth of more than 3,000 people on the gang population over the five years to early 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List totals for 2019 and 2024 (released via OIA / Police statistics). True if the increase exceeds 3,000; false if it is smaller.

veracity.statement: Violent crime has increased by 33 percent; gangs play a significant part in this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 33% rise in violent crime, with no base year stated; the implied comparison is the period since the previous government took office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey violent-offence victimisation counts, and Police victimisation statistics for violent offences, comparing 2017/18 with 2022/23. True if a 33% rise appears in one of those series over a defensible period; false if no standard series supports it.

rigor.statement: Because we opposed it from its very conception, we spoke about it extensively in Opposition and opposed it in Opposition, we campaigned on it in the election campaign, and we put it into our 100-day plan as part of forming a new Government.
rigor.explanation: The question asked why the legislation was introduced ahead of a scheduled Tribunal hearing; the answer offers only prior signalling and electoral mandate. Non sequitur — how long a policy has been signalled says nothing about whether the hearing was pre-empted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is the Prime Minister trying to say that New Zealand is not actually governed by the Waitangi Tribunal but instead by a Government elected by the people at democratic elections?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy and strawman: the criticism was that a scheduled inquiry was pre-empted, not that the Tribunal governs the country. The question only works by substituting a position nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, clearly, nothing was working previously and it behoves us to ensure that we try a variety of means to assist people into employment, including work seminars, including job expos, and, as I explained in my previous answer, that information about whether attending a work seminar got someone into employment is kept for that individual; it’s just not collated up across the country.
rigor.explanation: A rise in the caseload is treated as showing that 'nothing was working' — a non sequitur that ignores every other driver of benefit numbers, and which in any case does not support the specific conclusion that work seminars help.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know that the job seminars do assist people in getting into employment. We know that it helps with getting their CVs together; it helps with learning interview techniques; and we know that, for example, at a recent seminar in the top of the South Island, 82 Kiwi job seekers turned up and 64 received interviews from that.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is about employment; the evidence offered is a single anecdote about interviews. Appeal to anecdote plus a gap between what was shown (interviews at one seminar) and what was concluded (seminars get people into jobs).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, it will have an impact on gangs’ freedom to intimidate and create fear. Gang members want all the rights of being a New Zealander but none of the responsibility that comes with it. Expressing fear and intimidation is not a form of expression that this Government supports.
rigor.explanation: Begs the question: the freedom-of-expression objection is answered by redefining the expression at issue as 'intimidation', which assumes the conclusion that no protected expression is affected.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The other point of it is this very simple idea that a political party would campaign in Opposition to do something and, when elected, they do it. That’s what we’re doing in this legislation.
rigor.explanation: The question was why the change is needed when section 9 already makes gang membership an aggravating factor. Answering with electoral mandate is an appeal to authority of a kind — it addresses entitlement to legislate, not the redundancy alleged.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal will still be able to critique the legislation after enablement, so we’re very comfortable with the position that we’ve taken.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but with a gap: post-enactment critique does not answer the objection that the pre-enactment inquiry was pre-empted, since the remedy available differs once the law is in force.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he justify dismantling the Māori Health Authority in the same week as repealing smoke-free legislation, when Māori die seven years earlier, on average, than non-Māori and smoking is our leading cause of premature death?
focus.explanation: Names two specific measures and a specific health outcome. Legitimate scrutiny of named government policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How then can she be confident that the work obligations she wants to impose on people will help them get into jobs when she can’t show any evidence of these work seminars meaningfully supporting people into stable, secure employment?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of a named policy — work obligations and the evidence base for work seminars. Textbook scrutiny, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is the purpose of his non-consorting orders when sections 112 to 123 of the Sentencing Act already have a comprehensive framework for non-association orders?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure and whether it duplicates existing law. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So we’re going to continue to drive smoking rates down for Māori and for non-Māori, and we’re going to continue to get better health outcomes for Māori by using local iwi providers—localism and devolution, not centralisation and control—and I thought that member would appreciate that.
civility.explanation: The substance is on the policy, but the closing clause is a condescending aside directed at the questioner, implying she ought to agree. Short of a personal insult, past merely pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How can she be confident that work seminars support people into employment when the people in charge of running them could not be up front with select committee members about the consequences of not attending these seminars and she is refusing to present evidence on whether they support people into employment?
civility.explanation: Robust and on the substance, but 'could not be up front' and 'refusing to present evidence' edge into imputing evasiveness to officials and to the Minister rather than simply noting the evidence is absent.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Does the Minister accept that this Government’s breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi will lead to further claims before the Tribunal and further court litigation, or will he just simply do the right thing and remove his bill?
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora will generate additional Waitangi Tribunal claims and additional court proceedings.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal claim register and court filings in the year following 27 February 2024. True if one or more new claims and at least one court proceeding are filed concerning the repeal of the Māori Health Authority or related Crown action; false if no new claim or litigation is filed in that period.

civility.statement: This is a vile little bill that the Government once again is sneaking in through urgency.
civility.explanation: Harsh about the bill and the use of urgency, and 'sneaking' imputes bad faith — but to the Government collectively, not to any individual member. Pointed rather than personal.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister of Justice is basing his policies on dogma and dog whistling.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on a named individual's motives — accusing the Minister of acting from dogma and racial appeal rather than engaging his stated reasons.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He is basing it on his reckons; what his 100-day plan is; and what he hears, I imagine, down at the Epsom Bowling Club.
civility.explanation: Mockery of the Minister personally — the bowling-club jibe is ridicule of the man's judgement and social circle, not criticism of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The derisory two pages she wrote don’t address any of the real issues.
civility.explanation: Dismissive and sneering about the Attorney-General's work — 'derisory' treats her advice as contemptible rather than engaging what it said. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This Minister shouldn’t have his office.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on a named individual's fitness to hold his position, offered as a verdict on the person rather than on the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Depriving the court of useful information by defunding these reports is just one of the spiteful things he’s doing.
civility.explanation: Attributes malice to the Minister personally — 'spiteful' imputes a motive of ill-will rather than disagreement, and generalises it across his conduct.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: At this stage, section 27 reports have to do with sentencing—there is no removal of the right of anyone for evidence to be presented in their favour throughout the whole process, what is being abolished is the funding for section 27 reports, because it was created to allow family and people who knew the accused to provide evidence in support of their background.
civility.explanation: Replies to a sustained personal attack by engaging only the substance of what the bill does and does not do. Attacks no one, despite ample opportunity.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There is no lawyer, no academic, no criminologist, no psychiatrist, no judge—there is no expert at all who thinks that defunding these reports is a good idea.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a universal: that not one expert of any relevant profession supports removing legal aid funding for section 27 reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Submissions and public statements on the Legal Services Amendment Bill 2024 from legal, judicial and criminological professionals; false if any identifiable lawyer, academic, criminologist, psychiatrist or judge is on record supporting the defunding, true only if none is.

veracity.statement: It said it was the worst—the least likely to achieve the objectives. It was more expensive and less effective than many of the other options, including simply accrediting the report providers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement for this bill assessed the chosen option as the worst of five, more expensive and less effective than alternatives including accreditation of report providers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement accompanying the Legal Services Amendment Bill 2024; true if it presents five options and rates the option adopted as least likely to meet the objectives and costlier/less effective than accreditation, false if it ranks the adopted option otherwise.

veracity.statement: We know that children who have parents in jail are much more likely to end up in jail themselves.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an intergenerational incarceration effect: children of imprisoned parents are at materially elevated risk of imprisonment themselves.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed criminological literature and NZ studies on intergenerational incarceration; true if children of imprisoned parents show significantly elevated rates of later imprisonment, false if the association is absent or not statistically distinguishable.

veracity.statement: Only last week, he was in this House suggesting that home detention was some kind of not real consequence for crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Justice said in the House in the preceding sitting week that home detention is not a real consequence for crime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the House sitting days in the week preceding 27 February 2024; true if the Minister of Justice characterised home detention as not a real or genuine consequence, false if no such remark appears or the remark said something materially different.

veracity.statement: Section 27 reports are not being abolished by this amendment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill removes only the legal aid funding for section 27 reports, leaving the section 27 mechanism itself in force.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Legal Services Amendment Bill 2024 and section 27 of the Sentencing Act 2002; true if the bill amends only legal aid funding provisions and leaves section 27 in place, false if it repeals or amends section 27 itself.

specificity.statement: It said it was the worst—the least likely to achieve the objectives. It was more expensive and less effective than many of the other options, including simply accrediting the report providers.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named document's ranking, its comparative cost/effectiveness finding, and a named alternative option (accrediting providers). No figures, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All of the facts can be put in front of the judge for children of people who have salaries like we do, but it’s the kids of those people on low salaries, or the workers on the minimum wage who can’t rustle up enough to get an effective report done to put before the judge.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure: if the report is available only by private payment, access tracks income, so the outcome differs by wealth. The conclusion follows from the premise offered; the gap is that it assumes no other mechanism supplies the same information.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If they weren’t already gang-connected, they will be soon; if their connections to whānau were tenuous, well, they will be broken; and if their sense of community was fragile, it will be gone.
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope: a chain of escalating consequences — gang connection, severed whānau ties, lost community — asserted without anything offered to link defunding the reports to any step in it. The reasoning concerns the policy's effect on offenders, not the other party, so it is a genuine inference and a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At this stage, section 27 reports have to do with sentencing—there is no removal of the right of anyone for evidence to be presented in their favour throughout the whole process, what is being abolished is the funding for section 27 reports, because it was created to allow family and people who knew the accused to provide evidence in support of their background.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the reports operate at sentencing, so removing their funding does not remove any evidential right at trial. Valid as far as it goes, but there is a gap between 'the right is untouched' and the conclusion implied — that nothing is lost — since the right's practical exercise is what the funding secured.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the National Party policy is, basically, to fill up our jails—to put people away.
focus.explanation: Characterises the other party's intentions in general terms rather than engaging the bill. It gestures at a policy direction (imprisonment) but names no measure, figure or outcome — the weight is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They don’t care that home detention is useful; that supervision and alcohol and drug rehabilitation actually works; that mental health treatment can be effective; and that care in whānau, by whānau can be effective.
focus.explanation: Names four real sentencing and rehabilitation options, so there is genuine policy content — but it is framed as a claim about what the other side does not care about rather than an argument about the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Let’s be clear—and the Minister knows this—this will lead to more people in jail for longer; people who, if they had the money to pay for such a report, a judge would know all the facts and wouldn’t have imprisoned them in the same way.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that removing legal aid funding for section 27 reports will increase both the number of people imprisoned and the length of the sentences they receive.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison muster and Ministry of Justice sentencing statistics for the two years after the Act's commencement, alongside any published evaluation of the funding change; true if custodial sentencing rates and average custodial sentence lengths rise and analysis attributes part of the rise to reduced access to section 27 reports, false if custodial rates and sentence lengths do not rise or the change is attributed elsewhere.

focus.statement: The coalition parties collectively campaigned on repealing the Māori Health Authority not because we have an objection to improving Māori health outcomes—in fact, quite the converse—but we campaigned on it because we don’t think a giant new bureaucracy is the right way to go about doing that.
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (the Māori Health Authority) and gives a reason directed at its design rather than at the parties that created it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Members opposite cry crocodile tears about urgency, because I’ve sat where they sit for six years and I realise it’s grim times, and I know exactly what they are going through.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the state and motives of the other side. Strip out the characterisation of members opposite and no policy, measure or figure is left.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a Government that is mean-spirited.
focus.explanation: A bare characterisation of the other side's disposition. No policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named in it.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The coalition parties collectively campaigned on repealing the Māori Health Authority not because we have an objection to improving Māori health outcomes—in fact, quite the converse—but we campaigned on it because we don’t think a giant new bureaucracy is the right way to go about doing that.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy, but weak: the characterisation 'a giant new bureaucracy' stands in for the premise. Nothing connects the Authority's size or form to worse Māori health outcomes, so the conclusion rests on an unsupported assertion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The next point I was going to make is that all three of these bills are repeal bills—in other words, they wipe from the statute book bills that the Parliament passed. Many of them have been through select committees previously. The Government considers urgency is more than justified in this case, and we therefore move the motion.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. That a bill removes an existing Act says nothing about whether the repeal itself needs scrutiny, and the select committee stages he cites were run on the original legislation, not on these repeal bills — so neither premise supports the conclusion that urgency is justified.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The option to put it forward is still there. However, offenders that are in a situation where they do not have the financial means will not be able to have this section 27 report.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows. If the report remains permitted but is no longer publicly funded, then whether an offender obtains one turns on ability to pay — she identifies the actual mechanism by which the repeal bites, with no gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When we consider the fact that taxpayer-funded section 27 reports—the amount spent on them—has increased by at least 190-fold, when we think about $40,000 in 2017 to $7.7 million in the last financial year, I’m pretty sure that most Kiwis would agree that this money is better spent on victim services.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity. The spending figures establish that the cost rose, but the conclusion that victim services are the better use of the money rests entirely on 'most Kiwis would agree' — no comparison of what each spend achieves is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The National Party—and I think I’m right in saying that the ACT Party said the same thing—at two successive election campaigns sought a mandate from the New Zealand people to repeal the Auckland regional fuel tax, going all the way back to early 2018 when it was introduced.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National (and, he believes, ACT) campaigned on repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax at two consecutive general elections, and that the tax was introduced in early 2018.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party (and ACT) transport/tax policy documents and campaign announcements for the 2020 and 2023 general elections, plus the commencement record of the Land Transport Management (Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Act 2018. True if both parties campaigned on repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax at two successive elections and the tax dates from early 2018; false if repeal was policy at only one election, or the tax was introduced in a materially different year.

veracity.statement: These section 27 reports have cost taxpayers millions of dollars, and have done nothing for victims of crime; in fact they’ve led to further sentencing discounts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three things: that section 27 reports cost taxpayers millions annually, that they have produced no benefit for victims, and that they have caused additional sentencing discounts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice legal aid expenditure on section 27 cultural reports for recent financial years, and New Zealand sentencing case law/Court of Appeal guidance on whether section 27 reports have been used as the basis for sentencing discounts. True if annual spend is in the millions of dollars and courts have granted discounts on the strength of such reports; false if spend is well under a million or the reports are not associated with additional discounts.

veracity.statement: Especially, we understand that Māori and Pasifika offenders may not necessarily have the resources, whereas this funding is being repealed by this Government—the mean-spirited Government—to fund their tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the money saved by repealing legal aid funding for section 27 reports is being used to pay for the Government's tax cuts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and the Legal Services Amendment Bill's fiscal/regulatory material on where the savings from ending legal aid funding for section 27 reports were allocated. True if those savings were booked to the tax package; false if they were retained in justice or allocated elsewhere (e.g. victim services, police).

veracity.statement: We have heard that Māori and Pasifika offenders are overrepresented in the criminal justice system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori and Pasifika are present in the criminal justice system at rates above their share of the population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections and Ministry of Justice statistics on the ethnicity of people convicted and imprisoned, compared with Stats NZ population shares. True if Māori and Pacific peoples make up a materially larger share of convicted/imprisoned offenders than of the population; false if their shares are at or below population share.

veracity.statement: When we consider the fact that taxpayer-funded section 27 reports—the amount spent on them—has increased by at least 190-fold, when we think about $40,000 in 2017 to $7.7 million in the last financial year, I’m pretty sure that most Kiwis would agree that this money is better spent on victim services.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific expenditure figures for section 27 reports and the resulting multiple of increase between them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice legal aid expenditure on section 27 cultural reports for the 2016/17 and 2022/23 financial years. True if the figures are approximately $40,000 and $7.7 million respectively (a ratio of at least 190); false if either figure is materially different or the multiple is well below 190.

specificity.statement: The National Party—and I think I’m right in saying that the ACT Party said the same thing—at two successive election campaigns sought a mandate from the New Zealand people to repeal the Auckland regional fuel tax, going all the way back to early 2018 when it was introduced.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy, the number of election campaigns and the year it was introduced — enough for someone to go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: More importantly, the sentencing judge will have further intel or insight or extra information, providing good research, that could probably give a more purposeful report that could provide extra weight and have further information to be considered.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance but carrying almost none: a chain of near-synonyms ('intel or insight or extra information', 'further information') hedged with 'could probably', naming no figure, mechanism or threshold. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we consider the fact that taxpayer-funded section 27 reports—the amount spent on them—has increased by at least 190-fold, when we think about $40,000 in 2017 to $7.7 million in the last financial year, I’m pretty sure that most Kiwis would agree that this money is better spent on victim services.
specificity.explanation: Two dated dollar figures and the multiple between them — precisely the kind of claim someone can look up and confirm or refute.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Members opposite cry crocodile tears about urgency, because I’ve sat where they sit for six years and I realise it’s grim times, and I know exactly what they are going through.
civility.explanation: 'Crocodile tears' imputes bad faith — that the Opposition's objections are insincere performance rather than genuine concern. Short of a direct insult, but it goes at the members rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is a Government that is mean-spirited.
civility.explanation: A blunt attack on the Government as an institution, not on any individual member. Under the re-anchored scale this passes cleanly — no one is insulted.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Disestablishment was agreed to by all three governing parties in their coalition agreements and mandated by the results of the 2023 general election, where it was canvassed at length on the campaign trail.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts: that disestablishment is written into the coalition agreements of all three governing parties, and that it was a publicly campaigned position before the 2023 election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The two coalition documents published in November 2023 (National–ACT and National–NZ First) plus the National Party's 2023 health policy: true if disestablishing the Māori Health Authority is a commitment binding all three governing parties and was publicly campaigned on; false if it appears in only one agreement, or was not a stated pre-election position.

veracity.statement: There are increasingly long wait times for treatment and substantial workforce shortages.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that treatment waiting times were rising at the time of speaking and that the health workforce was substantially short-staffed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand planned-care/ESPI reporting on the number of patients waiting beyond the four-month target, comparing 2023 with prior years, and Health NZ published vacancy rates for nurses and senior doctors: true if the waiting-beyond-target count rose and vacancy rates were materially above normal turnover; false if waits shortened or the workforce was at or near establishment.

civility.statement: I want to acknowledge those who embarked on the Māori Health Authority dream and say to you that this bill is in no way a reflection of you or your good work. It is a reflection of an approach that failed to put health needs for all at its forefront, and a reflection of an implementation plan that faced significant challenges from the beginning.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested first reading abolishing an agency, where disparaging its people was available. The criticism lands squarely on the approach and the implementation plan and explicitly exempts the people who built it.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Structurally, the intent of this bill is that the Māori Health Authority staff and functions will transfer mostly to Health New Zealand, with a few to the Ministry of Health.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism and the two receiving agencies, so it is checkable in outline, but carries no numbers, proportions or dates — "mostly" and "a few" are the only quantities offered.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Across health, we are reprioritising funds from the bureaucracy and into the front line.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel with no amount, no timeframe and no named budget line; "bureaucracy" and "front line" are not defined, so nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: After 18 months in transition, under the guidance of a transition unit, before enablement in July 2022, and then given a further 18 months after that, this infant needed to be up on its feet and walking; despite the best efforts of staff, it was not.
specificity.explanation: Gives two durations and a commencement month, so the timeline is checkable, but the performance claim it supports ("it was not") has no measure, target or figure attached.
specificity.subject: speaker
