veracity.falsification_criterion: The Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 as in force from 1 July 2022, compared with the appointment provisions of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill: true if HMAC members have been ministerial appointments throughout that period and the bill leaves that unchanged; false if the Act as in force provided a different appointer or process.

specificity.statement: So the question to the Minister is: is it his intention to appoint people who will fulfil that role of local leadership, local stewardship, from iwi Māori groups, and if he could give the committee an indication of the eight people whom he intends to appoint—because their appointments are due on 30 June—that would assist the committee greatly in understanding how that local voice will be preserved.
specificity.explanation: A precise question: a named body, a stated number of appointees, and a hard date (30 June) by which the appointments fall due. What it asks for could be checked against the appointments when made. Short of full marks because the criterion it asks about ('local leadership, local stewardship') is left general.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: IMPBs are at different levels of capacity, and we’ve looked at what that will entail to bring them up to a level where they are able to analyse, to collate, to take in local information, to do local analysis of it, to then institute local actions as to how to change it, and then pass it up further for aggregation at regional and other levels, where we can get a wider view across the whole sector.
specificity.explanation: Describes a chain of activities (analyse, collate, institute local actions, aggregate) but attaches no funding figure, no timeframe, and no mechanism for how capacity is to be lifted. A direction with some detail, missing the how much and the by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve already indicated in the legislation that through Schedule 1, I think it is, locality plans will be paused and localities will be paused while I reconsider their position going forward.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (Schedule 1) and a concrete action (pausing locality plans and localities), which is checkable, but hedges on the reference ('I think it is') and gives no duration, no criteria for the reconsideration, and no date by which a position will be reached.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Under the new model, there is no legislative backstop for the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee to be able to give proactive advice that the Minister doesn’t like.
civility.explanation: A pointed structural criticism — it implies the Minister may not welcome challenging advice — but it lands on the design of the bill, not on the Minister's character or competence. Robust criticism of a proposal is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To offer advice that I need or offer advice that I may not want to hear is the privilege and the purpose of HMAC—to be in that position, to be trusted advisers to the Minister and to us so that we can do a better job.
civility.explanation: Answers a challenge that implied he would suppress unwelcome advice by engaging the substance and conceding the point, with no jab at the questioner. A genuinely contested exchange where a personal reply was available and not taken.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This may be the last call before the dinner break, and I just want to say that in the Minister’s answers, he was very light in addressing the questions and, in fact, didn’t answer a lot of the points that had been raised by my colleagues.
civility.explanation: Criticises the adequacy of the Minister's answers, not the Minister himself. Pointed but entirely about the performance of the answering; no imputation of bad faith or attack on competence as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There were a number of questions that were posed to the Minister before the dinner break which, in the opinion of members on this side of the Chamber, were a light touch in the answer from the Minister.
civility.explanation: A hedged criticism of the quality of the Minister's answers. Attacks the response, not the person; no sneering or imputation of bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, what the Minister is proposing to do is to repeal paragraphs (b), (e), (h), (i), and (j), and replace all of those things with new section 6(c).
specificity.explanation: Names the exact paragraphs being repealed and the exact provision replacing them. Anyone can open the bill and the Act and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, what the Minister is proposing to do is to repeal paragraphs (b), (e), (h), (i), and (j), and replace all of those things with new section 6(c).
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific fact about what the bill before the committee does to section 6 of the principal Act — which paragraphs it repeals and what it substitutes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 6 of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill as introduced, read against section 6 of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022: true if clause 6 repeals paragraphs (b), (e), (h), (i) and (j) of that section and inserts a new paragraph (c); false if the paragraphs repealed or the provision inserted differ.

veracity.statement: The original purpose of that particular section was about making sure that when you’ve got a Māori health authority board, what it did was it guaranteed a place for a member from that board on to Health New Zealand, and that was really important.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about the content of the existing statute — that section 12 guarantees a Māori Health Authority board member a seat on the Health New Zealand board.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 12 of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 (in particular subsection (4), which clause 8 of the amendment bill repeals): true if it requires that at least one member of the Health New Zealand board also be a member of the Māori Health Authority board; false if it contains no such guaranteed cross-membership.

focus.statement: I think that the Minister needs to answer those ones, because if all of the Government’s obligations and commitment to Te Tiriti o Waitangi is contained in the new section 6(c), then I have some serious concerns.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: a named provision of the bill and what it does to a named statutory obligation. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If the Minister can be clear with us on what “from time to time” actually means; is it what we’re hearing from members on the other side of the Chamber that it’s only every three years because “We’ve got a mandate.”—because that’s what we’re hearing from that side—or is this suggesting that there are going to be far more periodical opportunities for Māori to be able to engage with the reporting back?
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — the reporting frequency left undefined by "from time to time" in new section 16A(b) — but a substantial part of the sentence is spent characterising what "that side" says rather than the provision itself.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just gone straight out of the Act, so no Māori health strategy.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: repealing a requirement that the Hauora Māori Strategy be *jointly prepared* by the Māori Health Authority and the Ministry does not establish that no Māori health strategy will exist. The conclusion conflates the removal of a procedural requirement with the removal of the thing that requirement governs; nothing is offered to bridge the two. The statement engages the policy, so the defect is in the inference, not in what it is about.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s clear that the data and everything suggests they are all in the Māori community, so then how do we ensure that there is a Māori voice at the top of the tree?
rigor.explanation: Appeal to unspecified evidence — "the data and everything" names no source, series or measure — and there is a further gap between the premise (health need is concentrated in Māori communities) and the implied conclusion (therefore governance-level Māori representation is the remedy). The direction of the argument is reasonable; what is offered does not carry it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In doing so, I have to—because it’s my first opportunity to speak on the bill—indicate that philosophically, I find this bill repugnant.
civility.explanation: Extremely harsh language aimed entirely at the legislation, not at any member. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a bill is the expected civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know the Minister is a fan of the whiteboard in his office, and it wouldn’t be a bad idea if we could just drag the whiteboard down here and put it up behind him so that we could actually follow the logic here, because I have real concerns about how the voice of iwi and hapū will be heard in the structures that the Minister is now proposing.
civility.explanation: A light personal jibe about the Minister's whiteboard habit, implying his structure is hard to follow. Pointed and edging toward the person, but it lands on the design of the system rather than on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d like to start with a set of questions from a member before the dinner break, raising the question that, as far as could be seen, the only focus around the amendments to section 6 in clause 6 was with the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee (HMAC). This isn’t correct.
civility.explanation: A flat contradiction of another member's characterisation of the bill, directed wholly at what the clause does. No imputation of bad faith or attack on the member.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On this point, I want to note my colleague Arena Williams’ proposed amendment to section 6(2), which is to insert, after the words “to advise the Minister”, the words “including alerting the Minister proactively to any matters that impact on the health and wellbeing of Māori”.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact subsection, the exact insertion point and the verbatim wording proposed. Anyone could check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Let’s think about some of the words that have been used in it: “support and engage”, “take reasonable steps”—who’s deciding what “reasonable steps” are, Minister?
focus.explanation: Engages the operative wording of the clause before the Committee and asks who determines its threshold. No party framing at all — this is scrutiny of the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, again, I say that we’ve got the Minister and his advisory committee, we’ve got Health New Zealand, and we’ve got the iwi-Māori partnership boards. At every level, I would say to the Minister he is weakening those relationships.
rigor.explanation: An inference is offered: because the structure has these three layers, every relationship is weakened. But the enumeration of layers does not by itself establish weakening at any of them — there is a real gap between what was shown (a list of bodies) and what was concluded (uniform weakening). Not fallacious, since he gestures at the softened statutory language, but the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because this Government has deliberately introduced this legislation, knowing full well that it would restrict the jurisdiction of the Waitangi Tribunal to hear the urgent claims into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora this Thursday and Friday.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things: (a) that introducing this bill removed the Waitangi Tribunal's jurisdiction over the scheduled urgent inquiry into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, and (b) that the Government introduced it on this date knowing that effect. Extracting the checkable core, not a verdict.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 s 6(6) and the Waitangi Tribunal's Wai 3307 memoranda/directions of late February 2024: true if the Tribunal recorded that the bill's introduction on 27 February 2024 removed its jurisdiction over the scheduled urgent hearing; false if the hearing proceeded or the Tribunal held its jurisdiction unaffected. The 'knowing full well' element resolves only if official advice to the Minister on the timing/Tribunal impact was released (OIA or tabled papers) and shows the effect was foreseen.

veracity.statement: We were advised at 6 o’clock tonight from the Waitangi Tribunal that its jurisdiction to hold the urgent inquiry on Thursday and Friday, as scheduled, is now vacated.
veracity.explanation: A specific claim that the Waitangi Tribunal communicated on the evening of 27 February 2024 that the urgent hearing set down for that Thursday and Friday was vacated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal Wai 3307 memorandum-directions dated 27 February 2024: true if the Tribunal vacated the hearing scheduled for 29 February and 1 March 2024; false if no such direction issued or the hearing went ahead as scheduled.

divination.statement: Then, with the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, our whaea Tipa Mahuta will lose that position, and we are left with one.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that once Te Aka Whai Ora is disestablished, Tipa Mahuta will cease to hold her board position and only one Māori member will remain on the relevant board.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora board membership as published by the Ministry of Health after the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Act commenced: true if Tipa Mahuta no longer holds the position and only one Māori member remains; false if she retained a board position or more than one Māori member remained.

rigor.statement: I have already identified in previous responses three ways that obligations under section 6 will be met: (1) HMAC will be one representation of the Māori voice; (2) health service monitoring and decision making by IMPBs; and (3) the intent of delivering services as close to the home and the hapū as possible. So to suggest that the response to section 6 is just HMAC is clearly flawed.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure before the House: three distinct mechanisms are enumerated as premises, and the conclusion (that section 6 is not answered by HMAC alone) follows directly from them. Refuting a claim by exhibiting counter-instances is valid; no fallacy or appeal is relied on. Whether the three mechanisms actually deliver is a separate, factual question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, clearly, there’s going to need to be information passed back to IMPBs, and that would seem to be self-evident.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the policy, but the only support offered for the conclusion is that it is 'clearly' and 'self-evident' — a bare assertion. Declaring a claim self-evident is not a reason for it; nothing is offered about what information, to whom, or why the need follows.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We give self-determination in the delivery of Government services in many areas, and kaupapa Māori schools are a really good example of that, where they are designed in a te ao Māori way and delivered in a te ao Māori way. They have fantastic outcomes—we know that.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy from kura kaupapa to health delivery. The analogy is apt in structure — both are Government services delivered under Māori self-determination — but the load-bearing premise ('fantastic outcomes') is asserted with 'we know that' rather than shown, and no reason is given why the education case transfers to health. A reasonable point leaning on an unsupported appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Given that this is a massive retreat from self-determination of delivery of health services, and that you’re saying to Māori that “No, I don’t trust you to deliver”—effectively—“health services. I think this is a bloated bureaucracy.” and that having by Māori, for Māori in health is nothing more than having a bloated bureaucracy, what have you done to talk to Māori about that retreat?
rigor.explanation: A loaded question resting on a strawman: it puts a position in the Minister's mouth ('I don't trust you to deliver health services') that he has not advanced, then builds the question on that attributed position as an established premise. The contested premise — that this is a 'massive retreat' — is also asserted rather than argued. This is a defect in the reasoning about the policy, not in the speaker's conduct toward the Minister.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I would point you to one of the Māori members on the Health New Zealand board already: Dr Curtis Walker, who clearly is skills-based and brings representation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Dr Curtis Walker was, at the time of speaking, a sitting Māori member of the Health New Zealand board. The evaluative half of the sentence ('skills-based and brings representation') is the Minister's opinion; the checkable core is the board membership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora board membership record as at February 2024 (Ministry of Health board appointment announcements and Health NZ's published board list); true if Dr Curtis Walker was a serving board member and is of Māori descent, false if he was not on the board at that date or is not Māori.

veracity.statement: At the present time, metrics are currently reported quarterly, and this is a feature of the ability of Health Quality and Safety Commission and others to provide robust data.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a present fact about the reporting cadence of health system metrics — that they are reported quarterly, sourced from HQSC and comparable agencies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The publication schedule of health system performance metrics by Health New Zealand and the Health Quality & Safety Commission as at February 2024; true if the relevant performance metrics were published on a quarterly cycle, false if the cadence was monthly, annual, or irregular.

veracity.statement: I’m going to be talking on “(a), (b), (c), (d), A, E, I, O, U, (1), (2), (3), (4), (5)”, because, basically, this whole bill, in itself, knowing that we are taking a Māori Health Authority amendment bill rushing through urgency, is a complete breach of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in its full context, and even looking at this bill, with only a couple of hours to look at it, I see that “mātauranga Māori” has been axed and replaced with “cultural safety”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific drafting fact about the bill before the House: that the phrase 'mātauranga Māori' has been deleted and 'cultural safety' substituted for it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill as introduced, compared against the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 it amends; true if the Bill removes a reference to 'mātauranga Māori' and inserts 'cultural safety' in its place, false if 'mātauranga Māori' is retained or if 'cultural safety' is not substituted for it. (The accompanying 'complete breach of Te Tiriti' characterisation is a legal opinion and is not part of what is being checked.)

veracity.statement: Actually, the Wai 3307 claim was tabled in 2005, when I was only two years old, and, actually, my grandparents were the ones who tabled this health claim.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal claim numbered Wai 3307 was filed in 2005. The claim about her grandparents being the claimants and her own age are secondary; the checkable core is the filing year attached to that specific Wai number.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's register of claims (Wai number index) entry for Wai 3307; true if that claim was registered/filed in 2005, false if it was registered in a materially different year. Wai numbers are issued in registration order, so the register date settles it directly.

veracity.statement: In 1863, he actually said that Māori—he had never seen such healthy kids anywhere else in the world other than in Waikato, and such fertile land.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific observation to Governor George Grey in 1863 — that he had never seen healthier children anywhere in the world than in the Waikato, alongside remarks on the fertility of the land.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Governor George Grey's 1863 despatches, correspondence and published writings concerning the Waikato (as held in Archives NZ / the Grey collection and reproduced in the standard histories of the Waikato invasion); true if a documented 1863 statement by Grey describes Waikato children as the healthiest he had seen anywhere and the land as exceptionally fertile, false if no such statement is attributable to him in that year.

focus.statement: So, yep, that’s what I have to say, and if this Government keeps saying we’re woke, they must be asleep.
focus.explanation: A closing jibe wholly about the other side's rhetoric. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — strip out the characterisation of the Government and nothing about the bill remains. Attacks no individual, so Civility is untouched; nor is any argument advanced, so nothing is emitted for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Thank you, Madam Chair, and I thank the Minister for his brief answers that didn’t give any detail to the questions that I asked.
civility.explanation: Pointed and barbed — the thanks is sarcastic — but the complaint lands on the quality of the Minister's answers rather than on him as a person. Robust, edging toward the personal without arriving.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it accidental that this is being rammed through in urgency two days before, or is it deliberate?
civility.explanation: A loaded question whose only two options both impute improper motive — either carelessness or a deliberate manoeuvre to pre-empt the Waitangi Tribunal. It stops short of a direct insult but is an imputation of bad faith rather than a challenge to the substance of the timing.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve had decisions like the King Salmon case, for example. When legislation has words like that in it, the Government is required to follow that.
rigor.explanation: An argument from judicial precedent: courts have held mandatory statutory language binding, therefore 'require' in the Pae Ora Act binds the Crown. The inference is legitimate, but the case is invoked by name only, with no account of what it actually held or why it transfers to this statute — a real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The member that was over here raised the question of whether there was actually a reduction in autonomy; I don’t think that’s the case, because what we’ve said is that Māori will be involved in monitoring, delivery, and decision making at local levels.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (no reduction in autonomy) rests on what the Government has said it intends, not on any statutory power being retained — an appeal to the speaker's own assurance. It also equivocates: the autonomy at issue was national-level statutory co-decision rights, and involvement 'at local levels' does not address it, so the premise does not reach the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Secondly, given the coalition Government’s support for localism, at least in theory, the Minister seems to have such severe doubts about localism in this area that it’s going to take five years to introduce localities.
rigor.explanation: Infers a state of mind — 'severe doubts about localism' — from an implementation timeline. A slow rollout has many possible causes (capacity, sequencing, cost), so the conclusion does not follow from the premise; it is motive attributed from a schedule.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Māori need certainty. They went from having mana-enhancing provisions—a partnership approach to their healthcare, to their strategy, to the priorities, and to what’s going in the Government policy statement—to now having in the legislation words like the Minister will take “reasonable steps”.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: it contrasts the specific statutory language being repealed with the specific wording replacing it. Named policy, named mechanism, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Moving on to a comment, I’d like to know whether the Minister agrees with a member of his own caucus that seemed to direct the health deficit for Māori to their own fault. If that’s not victim blaming, I’m not sure what is.
focus.explanation: There is a real subject underneath — the causes of Māori health inequity — but the question is framed around an unnamed caucus colleague's remark and an invitation to disown it, rather than around any clause, mechanism or figure in the bill before the committee. The weight is on the other side's attitudes.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So the Minister is not correct when he is saying that the process has not changed at all and that it’s the same that was in there before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister's tabled amendments do change the appointment process for the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee, contrary to his statement in the committee that the process is unchanged. The claim is about the content of the amendments, not about the wisdom of them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the tabled amendments to the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill against the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 as enacted, specifically the provisions governing appointment/nomination of members to the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee and the functions of iwi-Māori partnership boards. TRUE if the amendments remove or alter the iwi-Māori partnership boards' role in nominating members; FALSE if the appointment process is carried over unchanged.

veracity.statement: From the member over here regarding timing, this has been well flagged through our 100-day commitments.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority was included in the incoming Government's published 100-day plan, so the timing of this bill was signalled in advance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National-led coalition's published 100-day action plan (released December 2023) and the coalition agreements. TRUE if disestablishing the Māori Health Authority / Te Aka Whai Ora appears as a listed 100-day action item; FALSE if it does not appear there.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister think that it’s Māori’s fault that they languish as a result of socio-economic deficit, that they tend to live far away from the centres of walkable cities and towns, that their socio-economic status means that they are not able to buy healthier food and that milk remains a lot more expensive than fizzy rubbish, despite the wonderful farmers that provide us with it?
veracity.explanation: Embedded in the question is an asserted factual premise about New Zealand retail prices: that milk costs considerably more than carbonated soft drinks. Extracting that premise only, not the surrounding rhetorical question.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare per-litre retail prices of standard supermarket milk against carbonated soft drinks in New Zealand at the time of the statement, using Stats NZ Food Price Index series and/or major supermarket shelf prices (including house brands). TRUE if milk is materially more expensive per litre than comparable soft drinks; FALSE if the per-litre prices are comparable or if soft drinks are the dearer of the two.

specificity.statement: Can the Minister please tell those in the committee and those that are listening tonight what they can expect in terms of “reasonable steps to support iwi-Māori partnership boards to achieve their purpose”?
specificity.explanation: A precise question: it quotes the exact statutory phrase from the proposed new section and asks for the operational content behind it. A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer. Short of 1.0 because it names no figure, threshold or timeframe against which 'reasonable steps' would be measured.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So health workforce will be important, targets will be important, and we have to give people the tools to do the jobs, so that talks to infrastructure. So those are three key ways that we are going to improve Māori health outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the answer to how Māori health outcomes will be improved, but it is three category headings — workforce, targets, infrastructure — with no numbers, no named programme, no timeframe and no mechanism. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Then, finally, how much worse is Māori health going to get over those five years—and I think it might be unlikely that he will still be the Minister of Health in 2029.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Shane Reti will no longer hold the Health portfolio by 2029 — a prediction about a future political outcome, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official Ministerial List as published by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet during 2029. TRUE (prediction correct) if Shane Reti does not hold the Minister of Health portfolio at any point in 2029; FALSE if he holds it.

veracity.statement: It’s very clear, I think, to anybody that looks at the stats for Māori across Aotearoa that the health system as it’s stood has not delivered—that, with health stats and life expectancy, it hasn’t worked, for whatever reason.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that health outcome statistics, including life expectancy, show the pre-reform health system has failed Māori relative to the rest of the population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life tables and Ministry of Health / Health NZ ethnicity-disaggregated outcome data for the years before 2022; true if Māori life expectancy and headline health outcomes are materially and persistently worse than non-Māori, false if the gap is absent or within statistical noise.

veracity.statement: But there was a very clear message that the country got during COVID that a delivery model that was delivered by Māori and designed by Māori was effective.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during the COVID-19 response, health services designed and delivered by Māori providers were demonstrably effective.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health COVID-19 vaccination and testing uptake data broken down by provider type, plus published evaluations of the Māori provider-led rollout (e.g. Te Whatu Ora / Waitangi Tribunal Wai 2575 COVID inquiry evidence); true if Māori-led delivery is shown to have lifted Māori uptake relative to mainstream channels, false if evaluations found no such effect.

veracity.statement: I, alongside some of my colleagues, played a pivotal role in ensuring that the requirement for a rural health strategy was included in the legislation that set up the reformed health system, and I’m incredibly proud of that, because we recognise that those that live in isolated and remote areas simply do not have the same level of access to health.
veracity.explanation: Two joined assertions: that the health reform legislation contains a statutory requirement for a rural health strategy, and that the speaker was instrumental in getting it there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 — true on the first limb if it requires a rural health strategy, false if it does not; and the Hansard record plus select committee/SOP papers for the Bill — true on the second limb if McAnulty is recorded advancing that amendment, false if the requirement originated elsewhere without his involvement.

veracity.statement: In that particular part that’s being repealed, there are separate provisions there that instruct the Minister of Health to also consult with the Minister for Māori Development.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the dispute resolution provisions being repealed (subpart 5 of Part 2) contain a statutory requirement for the Minister of Health to consult the Minister for Māori Development.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of subpart 5 of Part 2 of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 as at February 2024; true if it imposes a consultation requirement on the Minister of Health involving the Minister for Māori Development, false if no such requirement appears in that subpart.

veracity.statement: We’ve also seen that the role for Te Aka Whai Ora in drafting the Government Policy Statement is gone, and the right for Te Aka Whai Ora to directly advise the Minister is also gone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill removes two specific statutory functions of Te Aka Whai Ora: a role in drafting the Government Policy Statement on health, and a right of direct advice to the Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 provisions on the Government Policy Statement and on Te Aka Whai Ora's advisory function against the repeal/amendment clauses of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill as before the committee; true if both functions are removed without replacement, false if either survives in the amended Act.

civility.statement: You’ve gone pretty quiet now, Joseph Mooney.
civility.explanation: A taunt directed at a named individual member about his silence. Not an attack on character or competence, but it leaves the substance to needle the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I repeat, I’m not suggesting at all that this Minister—who I believe is a man of integrity; I fundamentally oppose what he is doing here.
civility.explanation: In the middle of a hostile committee debate the speaker explicitly separates the person from the policy, crediting the Minister's integrity while opposing his measure outright. Full opportunity to be uncivil, declined.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They play important roles in making sure that the Minister himself gets the support he needs to make sure that, as we work through a dispute resolution process, all voices are being heard fairly, the arbitration process is going to be heard fairly, or is the Minister suggesting to everybody, with this particular bill, that he’s going to play God on the matter, that it’s entirely up to him on how the dispute is resolved, or his decision is the final say, and he’ll play judge, jury, and executioner?
civility.explanation: Frames the Minister personally as wanting to 'play God' and act as 'judge, jury, and executioner'. Rhetorical rather than abusive, but it imputes an appetite for unaccountable personal power rather than confining the criticism to the repealed mechanism.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The fact is they wouldn’t, because rural people vote for this Government, and Māori people don’t, and the National Party is like a river: it takes the path of least resistance.
focus.explanation: Once the imputation of electoral self-interest and the characterisation of the National Party is removed, no policy, clause, figure or outcome is named. This is about the other party's motives and character rather than the measure before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What protections in clause 35 of this bill would stop a future Government imposing eight members that know nothing about Māori?
focus.explanation: Engages the measure directly: a named clause of the bill and the appointment mechanism it creates. Scrutiny of a specific drafting gap, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The question is quite clear to the Minister, who’s looking to just simply scrap any dispute resolution process here: what is the Minister going to do when there is clearly a dispute—one between, let’s say, the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee and Health New Zealand; let’s say an iwi-Māori partnership board and Health New Zealand; let’s say an iwi-Māori partnership board and its locality leadership?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism being repealed, working through the concrete institutional pairings that would be left without a dispute process. Accountability for a named provision, not party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the Minister clarify if the IMPBs will be involved in giving advice on the New Zealand Health Plan, because otherwise there is no input from the local level into what is a key instrument in the health system.
focus.explanation: Directly engages clause 6(3) and the advisory pathway into the New Zealand Health Plan — a named instrument and a named class of body. Entirely on the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What protections in clause 35 of this bill would stop a future Government imposing eight members that know nothing about Māori?
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the body, the number of members and the precise safeguard alleged to be missing. Someone could go to the bill text and check whether such a protection exists.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The question is quite clear to the Minister, who’s looking to just simply scrap any dispute resolution process here: what is the Minister going to do when there is clearly a dispute—one between, let’s say, the Hauora Māori Advisory Committee and Health New Zealand; let’s say an iwi-Māori partnership board and Health New Zealand; let’s say an iwi-Māori partnership board and its locality leadership?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific bodies whose disputes would be unresolved, which makes the gap concrete and answerable, though it stops short of naming the provision's operative sections or a remedy.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the Minister clarify if the IMPBs will be involved in giving advice on the New Zealand Health Plan, because otherwise there is no input from the local level into what is a key instrument in the health system.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact document, the exact bodies and the exact consequence claimed to follow, so the Minister could answer it and a reader could check the clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But unlike most of the other clauses, this one ditches the iwi-Māori partnership boards from their role in approving the locality plans.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clause 18(2) of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill, unlike the rest of Part 1, does more than delete Māori Health Authority references — it removes iwi-Māori partnership boards from the set of parties who must agree locality plans under s33(1)(d).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 18(2) of the bill as introduced, read against s33(1)(d) of the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022: true if the replacement paragraph omits iwi-Māori partnership boards from the agreeing parties; false if they are retained.

veracity.statement: Again, taking into context that 83 percent of Māori did not support this coalition, I therefore have some real concerns on assumptions that are made—again, through clauses 11 to 15—from a different perspective.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 83 percent of Māori did not vote for the National–ACT–NZ First coalition parties at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official 2023 general election party-vote results for the seven Māori electorates: true if the combined party vote for National, ACT and NZ First is about 17% or less, false if materially higher.

civility.statement: This is going much further—and illogically much further—because the iwi-Māori partnership boards were to be that very linkage at the local level when the locality plans are being developed.
civility.explanation: Blunt criticism of what the clause does, with a reason given. No person is impugned and no bad faith is imputed — hard on the policy, civil toward the Minister.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I remember I heard a member opposite earlier talk about her pleasure in condemning Te Aka Whai Ora to the scrap heap, and I’m shocked.
civility.explanation: Attributes relish to a named-by-reference individual member — characterising her as taking pleasure in the harm, which imputes bad faith to the person rather than engaging what she argued. Short of a direct insult, but past civil.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I find it extraordinary that a party and a Government who would tell us that they don’t like centralisation and that they want to see things done at a local level would remove the very Māori voice that has been created.
rigor.explanation: A genuine internal-consistency argument about the measure: a stated preference for localism sits awkwardly with deleting the local Māori body from locality planning. It leans on a tu quoque, though — a party's general disposition against centralisation does not by itself entail that this particular clause is wrong, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Again, taking into context that 83 percent of Māori did not support this coalition, I therefore have some real concerns on assumptions that are made—again, through clauses 11 to 15—from a different perspective.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is drawn from an appeal to electoral support: how many Māori voted for the coalition says nothing about whether the assumptions built into clauses 11 to 15 are sound. It is an argument about the policy, and a weak one — appeal to popularity/mandate standing in for the merits.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The amendments remove the requirement for Health New Zealand—I won’t go through the whole thing—to engage and removes the requirement for the relevant iwi-Māori partnership board to agree to the annual report assessing progress against outcomes in the plan.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause (28), the section it amends (55) and the precise obligations being deleted — the engagement duty and the iwi-Māori partnership board's agreement to the annual progress report. Checkable against the bill text; short of full marks only because the aside leaves the engagement obligation half-stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I have flagged in my readings, and flagged with our intent, that I absolutely support cultural competence and believe it to be important, and that I’ll seek advice from IMPBs around appointments, and that I also believe that there can be skills-based and representation with the Health New Zealand board.
specificity.explanation: Offers a direction and names who would be consulted (IMPBs) on what (board appointments), but supplies no mechanism, no statutory footing, no timeframe and no test for what 'skills-based and representation' would mean in practice — the substance is the intent rather than the how.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But I’m here to speak for many of those who’ve been denied a voice because of this outrage of urgency to force through a destructive agenda to continue to break rather than make.
focus.explanation: Attacks the other side's 'agenda' in the general — destructive, breaking rather than making — without naming a clause, a figure or an outcome. The one concrete hook is the use of urgency; everything else is party framing rather than the measure before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I am concerned that this blitzkrieg of repeals—the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora—is an abuse of urgency that denies voice to those most affected.
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora) and a specific process objection (use of urgency, denial of submissions). Criticism is directed at the legislative process before the House, not at the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to understand why the Minister is so afraid of the Waitangi Tribunal, and why is the Minister so afraid of the select committee process that would allow people to engage correctly?
civility.explanation: A loaded question that imputes a motive — fear — to the Minister personally rather than contesting the decision to use urgency. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes bad faith to the person, which is a real civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve worked with Māori and whānau in energy hardship, and what’s clear is that we need that comprehensive approach by Māori, for Māori.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote: the speaker's own experience in one sector is offered as sufficient ground for a conclusion about the national health delivery structure. The inference is about the policy (so Focus stays high) but nothing bridges the gap between the individual experience and the general claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know independent monitoring ensures accountability, it helps identify areas of improvement, and it also has the ability to safeguard against discrimination within the healthcare system, which Māori, we know, are faced with every day.
rigor.explanation: The benefits claimed for independent monitoring are asserted by appeal to shared assumption ("we know") rather than shown; no evidence, mechanism or example connects monitoring to the accountability and anti-discrimination outcomes concluded. It is a real inference about the policy, but a thinly supported one.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my specific question is: what are the hauora Māori activities of Health New Zealand? How do they relate to the funding mechanism from the Māori Health Authority directly to providers like Te Piki Oranga? What is the operational expectation that the Minister has of how that will function in practice?
specificity.explanation: Names the statutory wording being replaced, a named provider, and the specific funding mechanism at issue, and asks for an operational expectation. A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer; someone could go and verify whether it was answered.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, particularly with clause 13, which inserts new section 16A “Engaging with and reporting to Māori”, it says Health New Zealand must “(b) report back to Māori from time to time”. Now, this doesn’t, to me, sound like a robust monitoring and evaluation system, so I’d really like to hear the Minister’s comments on that.
specificity.explanation: Cites the clause number, the new section it inserts, its heading, and the exact statutory wording relied on, then states precisely what she wants the Minister to address. Fully checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What they have told me—and it’s not clear in the bill how this is going to continue, which is my question that I’m going to get to shortly with the Minister—is that with the establishment of the Māori Health Authority, they have received funding directly from the centre to their agency.
veracity.explanation: The speaker is relaying a factual claim made to her by the provider: that establishment of the Māori Health Authority replaced a DHB-to-PHO-to-provider funding chain with direct funding from the centre. The assertion is about the past commissioning arrangement, not about what the bill will do.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Aka Whai Ora / Te Whatu Ora commissioning records and Te Piki Oranga's funding agreements before and after July 2022. True if Te Piki Oranga held a direct commissioning contract with the Māori Health Authority after its establishment, having previously been funded via the DHB→PHO chain; false if its funding continued to flow through the PHO or another intermediary.

veracity.statement: Now, the reason why I want to home in on the independent monitoring is it offers a pathway to actually address the disparities that we have, and it was something that Te Aka Whai Ora was tasked with in providing independent monitoring of Te Whatu Ora.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of statutory fact that Te Aka Whai Ora held a function of independently monitoring Te Whatu Ora. This is a claim about the existing law, distinct from her opinion that the function is valuable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The functions of the Māori Health Authority as set out in the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022. True if those statutory functions include monitoring the performance of Health New Zealand in relation to hauora Māori; false if the Act confers no such monitoring function on Te Aka Whai Ora.

specificity.statement: Well, support would include cultural, professional, and financial support. Engagement is the collaborative communication and sharing of information.
specificity.explanation: Asked directly what he envisages by 'support and engagement' in clause 15, he answers with three generic categories and a dictionary-style gloss. No mechanism, no quantum of funding, no timeframe, nothing that could be checked or acted on — and he had a real opportunity to supply detail here.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s also looking at retaining section 6(h) of the Pae Ora legislation, which requires Health New Zealand and the Māori Health Authority to engage with iwi-Māori partnership boards.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statutory provision, the Act it sits in, the two bodies bound by it and the obligation it imposes. Anyone could open the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act and check what is being retained.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: At 19.41, Grant Robertson was the third speaker on clause 6.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific fact about the order and timing of contributions in this committee-stage debate: that Grant Robertson spoke at 19.41 and was the third caller on clause 6. Used to justify declining to answer further.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript for the committee stage of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill on 27 February 2024: true if Grant Robertson's contribution is timestamped 19.41 and is the third call taken on clause 6; false if the timestamp or the ordinal is materially different.

veracity.statement: There are very few groups in society where you can say that there is a higher mortality rate, a higher infant mortality rate, higher rates of smoking, higher rates of diabetes, and higher rates of the less effectiveness of some medications.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori sit at or near the worst end of the population distribution on mortality, infant mortality, smoking prevalence and diabetes prevalence — i.e. that few if any other population groups exceed them on those indicators.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Stats NZ comparative population statistics (Health Status Report, Tatau Kahukura Māori health statistics, NZ Health Survey) on age-standardised mortality, infant mortality, daily smoking and diabetes prevalence by ethnicity: true if Māori rates are among the highest of any named population group on those measures, false if several other groups routinely exceed them.

veracity.statement: My colleague Arena Williams, as she said in her contribution in this committee stage, has raised 40 amendments to Part 1, and the substantive number of those amendments relate to clause 6, which goes through—and in her particular amendment, she has deleted particular clauses in the amendment bill which we’re looking at, which then relate to the primary piece of legislation, the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a countable fact about the amendments tabled in Arena Williams' name for this committee stage: that there are 40 of them directed at Part 1, and that most concern clause 6.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The amendments / Supplementary Order Paper tabled in Arena Williams' name for the committee stage of the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill: true if 40 amendments to Part 1 appear in her name and a majority of them amend clause 6; false if the count or the clause 6 concentration is materially different.

rigor.statement: I was particularly struck when visiting the University of Auckland and actually hearing that some of the medications that are developed are less effective on some populations than on others because they’re not tested on those populations, and that does apply to Māori and Pasifika people.
rigor.explanation: Argument from anecdote and unnamed authority: the whole support for a general claim about pharmaceutical efficacy in Māori and Pasifika populations is something she was told on a single visit. No study, trial or dataset is named, and the causal step from 'not tested on those populations' to 'less effective on those populations' is asserted rather than shown. The statement is squarely on the policy question, so this is a reasoning failure, not a focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It was passed democratically by this House, where everyone had a say on who was implementing the laws, and that is why it is a part of our law, which I think is an important point to remember.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to democratic pedigree. That the Pae Ora Act passed the House gives no reason against amending it — the amendment bill before the committee is passing through the identical process, so the premise, if it worked, would equally validate the change she opposes. The inference does not carry the weight placed on it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If we look comparatively at the new piece of legislation that the Minister is introducing, it does focus in the main on ministerial appointments and those who are perhaps favoured by the Government of the day.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging past the substance: the appointment-mechanism critique is legitimate, but 'those who are perhaps favoured by the Government of the day' imputes patronage as a motive rather than arguing the design. Hedged with 'perhaps' and aimed at the Government collectively rather than at the Minister personally, so it stops short of a 0.5 bad-faith imputation.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What the experience is—in particular in Māori health—is that when Governments look towards austerity cuts, Māori kaupapa generally are the first ones out the door or on the chopping block.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: from a general historical pattern ('when Governments look towards austerity cuts') to a conclusion about these particular Te Aka Whai Ora staff. The inference form is legitimate but rests on an unevidenced generalisation — an appeal to precedent with no instance, figure or source offered to establish the pattern, and no link shown between that pattern and the 6.5–7.5% savings exercise. Not a jibe at opponents: strip the party reference and an argument about the policy remains.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But the reality is when this Government is looking towards saving 6.5 percent to 7.5 percent, guess whose heads are on the chopping block!
civility.explanation: Genuinely contested ground — a committee-stage debate on disestablishing the Māori Health Authority, where there was ample opportunity to turn on the Minister. The attack lands entirely on the Government's savings decision and its consequences for a workforce; no person's character, competence or motive is impugned. Pointed and rhetorical, but on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Our expectation from this Minister—and I would like to hear his answer to the question—is about whether or not these staff will indeed actually be, in their entirety, repatriated, and in particular when the Minister’s own finance Minister is asking for a 6.5 to 7.5 percent cut, or savings, in order to pay for tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts about the present: (a) the Minister of Finance has instructed agencies to find savings of 6.5 to 7.5 percent of baseline, and (b) those savings are being sought in order to fund tax cuts. Not a verdict on either.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Minister of Finance Budget 2024 baseline savings instructions to agencies (Budget Policy Statement and the December 2023 savings letters): true on (a) if agencies were directed to identify savings at 6.5% or 7.5% of baseline; false if the tiers were materially different. On (b), true if the Government's own Budget documents state the savings are being recycled to fund the tax package, false if the fiscal documents show the savings directed elsewhere.

veracity.statement: This Minister, in this particular bill, is looking towards tying the hands of a future Government to a bill that clearly Māori do not want.
veracity.explanation: The checkable element is the assertion about present Māori opposition to the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill — that Māori as a constituency do not want it. The 'tying the hands' characterisation is interpretation and is not what is being checked.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Submissions to the Health Committee on the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill, the positions taken by iwi-Māori partnership boards and national Māori health provider bodies, and the Waitangi Tribunal's urgent inquiry into the disestablishment: true if the large majority of Māori submitters and Māori health organisations opposed the bill; false if submissions and provider positions were mixed or supportive.

veracity.statement: I used the word “repatriation” because what we know from the independent report into the Māori Health Authority—2022, I think that report came out; could have been 2023, May 2023—was that there was some concerns that Māori with skills were taken from Health New Zealand and the Māori Health Authority and those from Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Health, leaving them somewhat eviscerated for those skills.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an independent report into the Māori Health Authority, published around 2022–May 2023, recorded concerns that skilled Māori staff were drawn out of Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Health into the Māori Health Authority, depleting those agencies of that expertise. The sentence is garbled live speech, but the intended reading is unambiguous from the surrounding sentences; what is checkable is the existence of the report and whether it records that concern.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The independent review of Te Aka Whai Ora / the Māori Health Authority published between 2022 and May 2023: true if such a report exists in that window and records concerns that skilled staff transferring from Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Health left those agencies short of that expertise; false if no such report exists in that period, or if it contains no such finding.

specificity.statement: I would like to bring the Minister’s attention to the same new Part 2, clause 34, where it says in there, at clause 34(1), “Section 54, which requires localities to be determined, takes effect on 1 July 2029.”—1 July 2029.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (new Part 2, clause 34(1)), the section it amends (section 54), the substantive requirement (localities to be determined) and the commencement date (1 July 2029). Anyone could take this to the bill and check it, and the Minister could answer it directly. A precise question, scored on the same footing as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve discussed localities at some length here tonight across Part 1, and I remain of the statements that I’ve made that localities are simply paused, pending a view as to where they sit in a new configuration. The choosing of that date was just a placeholder date. There was nothing particularly special about that.
specificity.explanation: Answering a question about a specific statutory commencement date, and there was a real opportunity to be concrete — the criteria for un-pausing, who decides, an expected timeframe, why 2029 rather than an earlier year. None is supplied: 'paused', 'pending a view', 'a new configuration' and 'placeholder' name no mechanism, no test and no date. Directionally responsive but with no checkable content attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To that effect, I have tasked the leadership, who will be transitioning also, with paying particular attention that we retain the best learnings, the best knowledge that may have come from this period of time with the Māori Health Authority so that we can take this into the new organisations.
specificity.explanation: Names an action actually taken (tasking the transitioning leadership) and the object of it, which is more than a slogan. But nothing states what retaining 'the best learnings' consists of, who is accountable, what is to be captured or documented, or by when — no mechanism, quantity or timeframe that anyone could later check against.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Where and how is the Minister proposing to hold that value?
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at the measure before the Committee — the transfer provisions in new Part 2, clauses 36 to 40, and what happens to the Māori Health Authority's staff and their accumulated expertise under them. It asks the Minister to account for a specific consequence of a specific set of clauses. No party framing, no characterisation of opponents, no tribal content at all. Low on detail, but Focus asks what the statement is about, not how precise it is.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the Minister is delaying these by years. The proposal is an arbitrary time frame that he just thought up as a placeholder, and he has given us no reason, no proper justification, as to why he has picked this time frame in the proposed legislation.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure before the House, but a weak one: it argues from absence of evidence — because no justification has been given in debate, the date is concluded to be arbitrary and invented as a placeholder. The absence of a stated reason does not establish that no reason exists.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So your delay to 2029 and 2030 means the entire community that lives within these localities are now going to have to wait to have input into the health plan, to have input into what’s going to go into the Government policy statement (GPS), to have input and what is going to receive financial support.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premise she laid out: section 55(3) makes locality plans the vehicle for community consultation, so moving the date moves the consultation. The gap is that she assumes no other consultation route exists in the interim.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So your delay to 2029 and 2030 means the entire community that lives within these localities are now going to have to wait to have input into the health plan, to have input into what’s going to go into the Government policy statement (GPS), to have input and what is going to receive financial support.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism directly — the amended commencement dates, the consultation duties they gate, and who is affected. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will their conditions be the same transferring to Te Whatu Ora, or will they become a part of the 80,000 strong workforce of Te Whatu Ora and be expected to move to Whangārei or expected to move to Auckland, Hamilton, Christchurch, or Wellington to become a part of the big 80,000-strong workforce?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the operative effect of clause 43 — employment conditions and place of work on transfer. A precise question about the mechanism, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, this has been done under urgency. There is no select committee process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two procedural facts about the bill under debate: that the House accorded urgency to it, and that it was not referred to a select committee for public submissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills record and Hansard for the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill: true if urgency was accorded and no select committee referral or submission process occurred; false if the bill was referred to a select committee or passed without urgency.

veracity.statement: However, for the past six to, now, 12 months, Te Whatu Ora, as the fund holder, have held on to the dollar. There has been no ability for iwi, hapū, marae, community, and councils to commence the work together to establish a locality.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Whatu Ora, holding the locality development funding, released none of it over roughly the preceding year, leaving groups that had lodged expressions of interest unable to begin locality establishment work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora funding records or an OIA response on locality-establishment funding distributed in Te Tai Tokerau between February 2023 and February 2024: true if no such funding was released to iwi/hapū/community groups in that period; false if allocations were made.

veracity.statement: Now, I’m mindful that there are just under 300 kaimahi within Te Aka Whai Ora and many of them are across regional spaces, the hospitals—Hokianga, Whangārei, Kerikeri, and there’s a few in the Wellington and Auckland areas too.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Aka Whai Ora employed just under 300 staff at the time of the debate, distributed across regional sites including Hokianga, Whangārei and Kerikeri as well as Wellington and Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Aka Whai Ora annual report or Public Service Commission workforce data for the period to February 2024: true if headcount was in the range ~250–300; false if materially outside it.

veracity.statement: To speak to the member before the one who has just resumed her seat—the Hon Willow-Jean Prime—the questions she raised were exactly those raised by the former Minister Peeni Henare about 16 minutes previously on clause 34(1) and section 54, and clause (2) and section 55, and I don’t envisage repeating that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the questions just put were the same ones Peeni Henare put about 16 minutes earlier in the same committee stage, on the same clauses and sections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of this committee stage debate: true if Peeni Henare's contribution roughly 16 minutes earlier raised substantially the same points on clause 34(1)/section 54 and clause 34(2)/section 55; false if his contribution covered materially different ground.

veracity.statement: I also met with whaea Moe Milne about three weeks ago, and we discussed the importance of the name.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific meeting took place with Moe Milne roughly three weeks before 27 February 2024, at which the naming of Te Aka Whai Ora was discussed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister of Health's published ministerial diary releases for late January to early February 2024: true if a meeting with Moe Milne is recorded in that window; false if no such meeting appears.

divination.statement: Well, it’s pretty late, there’s no select committee process, this will be done by tomorrow, and the very mechanisms in this legislation to make it work, to deliver pae ora for all will be gone.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the bill will complete its passage through the House by the following day. Not a promise about her own action — she is in opposition and predicting the House's outcome.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills record for the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill: true if the bill completed its third reading on or before 28 February 2024; false if it was still before the House after that date.

civility.statement: Do all New Zealanders understand that in the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, you’re actually sneaking in other fundamental changes that are impacting the way in which this legislation operates to deliver health services to our community—do they?
civility.explanation: "Sneaking in" imputes deliberate concealment — bad faith rather than a difference of policy. No individual is named or insulted, so this sits at the failure threshold rather than below it.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, I’m mindful that there are just under 300 kaimahi within Te Aka Whai Ora and many of them are across regional spaces, the hospitals—Hokianga, Whangārei, Kerikeri, and there’s a few in the Wellington and Auckland areas too.
specificity.explanation: Carries a headcount figure and names the specific locations staff are based in, which is what makes the question that follows about relocation checkable. Short of full marks because the regional/central split is given only loosely.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To the member who has just taken her seat—Hūhana Lyndon—again, that was a discussion on localities, which I have discussed in detail, and regarding the transfer of staff terms and conditions, it will, as I say, remain as the Health Sector (Transfers) Act requires.
specificity.explanation: Names the governing statute, which is a real, checkable mechanism rather than a reassurance. But it stops there — no statement of which conditions are preserved, nor of what the Act actually requires on location of work, which was the substance of the question.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I worked in this area for years, and we’ve had constant problems in terms of transfer of undertakings.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the policy before the House — transfer-of-undertaking provisions are unsafe — resting entirely on the speaker's own past experience. Appeal to personal anecdote/experience: relevant expertise, but nothing offered connecting past disputes to the drafting of this clause.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So exactly the same provisions that didn’t raise concern when they first moved there will actually be the mechanism that puts them back.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure, with a gap: that a mechanism drew no objection when staff moved into a new agency they had opted for does not establish it raises no concern when used to move them out of one being disestablished. The conclusion (no cause for worry) is broader than the premise supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is time, but, no, we’re going to pass it all under urgency by tomorrow morning, but it’s not actually going to come into effect until 30 June.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the process: because the amendment Act does not commence until 30 June, the gap between passage and commencement could have accommodated a select committee stage, so urgency is not required by the timetable. The conclusion tracks the premise; the gap is that it assumes the commencement date is fixed and independent of the passage date.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, with so much negative publicity around this, what type of guarantees can our Minister give us with regards to continual recognition of conditions, of employment, of wages?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: the transfer clause he has just read out and its effect on employment conditions and wages. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve heard about lift and shift for Te Aka Whai Ora staff. Is the Minister going to guarantee employment security for staff and their existing conditions?
focus.explanation: Engages the clause he has just quoted (clause 40, transfer of employees) and asks about a concrete consequence — employment security and existing conditions. No content about the other party as such.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There is time, but, no, we’re going to pass it all under urgency by tomorrow morning, but it’s not actually going to come into effect until 30 June.
focus.explanation: Names clause 32, the commencement date and the missing select committee stage — specific process scrutiny of the measure before the House, not general party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I was a union official for 17, 18 years.
veracity.explanation: A checkable autobiographical claim about the length of his career as a union official, offered as the basis for his standing on the clause.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Jackson's parliamentary biography and union employment records (e.g. Combined Trade Unions / Manufacturing and Construction Workers Union): true if his time as a paid union official totals roughly 17–18 years, false if materially shorter.

veracity.statement: I’ve been informed that the vast majority of people who moved from the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand to the Māori Health Authority moved under the Health Sector (Transfers) Act 1993.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the legal mechanism used to move staff into the Māori Health Authority was the Health Sector (Transfers) Act 1993, and that it covered the vast majority of them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora records of the 2022 staff transfers to Te Aka Whai Ora: true if most of those transfers were effected under the Health Sector (Transfers) Act 1993, false if they were made under other provisions (e.g. the Pae Ora (Healthy Futures) Act 2022 transitional provisions or fresh appointments).

veracity.statement: So I’d like to hear from the Minister as to his clarification on Health New Zealand’s reasonable consultation process that we’ve just heard there because of the material impacts that’s going to have, because back in December, the Government passed legislation to bring back 90-day trials for all employers and the Government has already pushed many more people and communities into precarity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in December 2023 Parliament passed legislation reinstating 90-day trial periods for all employers, offered as background to the employment-security question.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislation record for December 2023: true if an Act extending 90-day trial periods to employers of all sizes was passed that month, false if no such Act passed in December 2023 or if it applied only to a subset of employers. (The 'pushed many more people into precarity' half is not operationalised and is not part of the check.)

veracity.statement: Your own departmental disclosure statement says “no consultation”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's own departmental disclosure statement records that no consultation was carried out.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement published for the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill: true if it records that no external consultation was undertaken on the bill, false if it records consultation having taken place.

specificity.statement: I’ve been informed that the vast majority of people who moved from the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand to the Māori Health Authority moved under the Health Sector (Transfers) Act 1993.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, the two originating agencies and the mechanism, so the answer can be checked; 'vast majority' is the only imprecision, with no figure or proportion given.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know why. It’s because there’s a Waitangi Tribunal inquiry, where all of the Minister’s relations are coming to present their evidence in opposition to the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora.
civility.explanation: Imputes a bad-faith motive to the Minister personally — that the timing is chosen to get ahead of a tribunal inquiry at which his own relations will give evidence. Short of an insult, but it attributes improper purpose to the person rather than arguing the merits of the timing.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Specifically, has he met with the Public Service Association, has he met with the New Zealand Nurses Organisation, or has he met with any other health unions—or have any of his officials—to specifically talk through the transfer and the employment rights for those who will be transferring from one agency to another?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific unions (PSA, NZNO) and the specific subject of the engagement (transfer and employment rights), so the Minister could answer it or be shown not to have. No dates or figures, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Minister, I note that in terms of the new proposal, which is clause 36(1)(b), this is relating to, effectively, the transfer of assets and the transfer of information. I note that paragraph (b) talks about all of the information and documents that would be held by the Māori Health Authority are, effectively, held by Health New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: Cites the clause and paragraph by number and states the mechanism it creates (transfer of assets and of records to Health New Zealand). Concrete enough that the Minister could answer it against the text; no figures or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Specifically, has he met with the Public Service Association, has he met with the New Zealand Nurses Organisation, or has he met with any other health unions—or have any of his officials—to specifically talk through the transfer and the employment rights for those who will be transferring from one agency to another?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the employment-transfer provisions of the bill before the committee; a named, checkable accountability question rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker
