veracity.statement: I’ve said to the member there are no papers that have been received, there’s been no discussion that’s taken place, there have been no decisions that have been made in Cabinet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 27 February 2024 no Cabinet paper, discussion or decision existed on liberalising access to military-style semi-automatic firearms. A factual claim about the present state of the Cabinet process, not an opinion or a promise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet and Cabinet committee minutes and proactively-released papers for December 2023 – February 2024 on firearms law, plus Ministerial diary releases; true if no paper, agenda item or decision on MSSA access appears before 27 February 2024, false if any such paper or minuted discussion exists.

veracity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that in the year to December 2023, gang members carried out an average of 2.83 firearm offences per day, and does the Government have policies to deal to the illegal use of firearms that has mushroomed over the last few years under current laws?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific rate of firearm offending by gang members — an average of 2.83 offences per day over the year to December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded-crime statistics on firearms offences with a gang-member offender flag for the 12 months to 31 December 2023; true if the total divided by 365 is 2.83 ± rounding, false if materially different or if no such series supports the figure.

veracity.statement: The previous Government’s over-regulation on clubs and ranges have forced several to shut down.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that shooting clubs and ranges closed, and that the cause was the previous Government's regulatory regime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police club-and-range certification records and Council of Licenced Firearms Owners closure reports since the Arms Act certification regime took effect in 2022; true if several clubs or ranges closed and cited the certification requirements or their costs as the reason, false if closures did not occur or are not attributable to the regime.

veracity.statement: The coalition Government has yet to decide on this issue, but, currently, over 6,600 New Zealanders are licensed to possess semi-automatic firearms, and this occurred under Labour’s regime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 6,600 people currently hold a licence permitting possession of semi-automatic firearms in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police firearms licence statistics on E-category (and equivalent) endorsements in force as at early 2024; true if the count exceeds 6,600, false if materially below it.

veracity.statement: They were never banned under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that semi-automatic firearms of the type at issue were not prohibited by the previous Government's firearms legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the Arms (Prohibited Firearms, Magazines, and Parts) Amendment Act 2019; true if military-style semi-automatics remained lawfully available on an ordinary licence, false if the Act prohibited them (endorsement-based exemptions for specified purposes do not make the claim true).

veracity.statement: The Government is sticking with legislation and initiatives that, with bipartisan support, have seen smoking rates drop by 60 percent in the past 11 years, and we are advised those settings will continue to drive smoking rates down.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 60 percent fall in the smoking rate over the 11 years to 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for adults, 2012/13 compared with 2022/23; true if the relative fall is approximately 60 percent, false if materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with the statement made by Nicola Willis, “we have to remember that the changes to the smoke-free legislation had a significant impact on the Government books,” in response to questions on how she will pay for tax cuts in the absence of the foreign buyers ban; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Relays a direct quotation attributed to Nicola Willis and the context in which it was said — in answer to questions about funding tax cuts after the foreign buyers ban was dropped.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard, press conference transcripts and contemporaneous media reports from early 2024; true if Willis said those words in substantially that context, false if the wording or the context is misreported.

veracity.statement: Is she aware that the Ministry of Health modelling shows that an estimated $5.25 billion can be saved in health spending, and, if so, how can she justify her support for rolling back world-leading smoke-free legislation when a simple cost-benefit analysis shows the cost to the health system outweighs the benefits of the revenue gained?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ministry of Health modelling produced an estimated health-spending saving of $5.25 billion attributable to the smokefree legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health regulatory impact statements and modelling published for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Act 2022; true if a $5.25 billion health-saving estimate appears, false if the modelling shows a materially different figure or no such estimate.

specificity.statement: We’re going to balance safety, we’re going to balance compliance, and we’re going to make sure we have a good decision in Cabinet, and that’s yet to happen.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods — "balance safety", "balance compliance", "a good decision" — with no figure, mechanism, threshold or date. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that in the year to December 2023, gang members carried out an average of 2.83 firearm offences per day, and does the Government have policies to deal to the illegal use of firearms that has mushroomed over the last few years under current laws?
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise figure (2.83 per day), a named cohort (gang members) and a defined period (year to December 2023). A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the fast-track framework protect matters of national importance under the Resource Management Act by ensuring that projects will be declined if they undermine the relationship of Māori and their culture and traditions with their ancestral lands, water sites, wāhi tapu, and other taonga?
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, the category within it (matters of national importance), the decision the mechanism would have to produce (projects declined), and the interests protected. Precise enough that an answer could be checked against the resulting bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will he rule out the proposal by Trans-Tasman Resources for seabed mining off the coast of Taranaki from the list of projects in the bill, in light of the Supreme Court ruling that this application needed to be reconsidered to take account of tikanga Māori?
specificity.explanation: Names the applicant, the activity, the location, the instrument (the project list in the bill) and the court ruling relied on. Concrete enough to act on or verify directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is she aware that the Ministry of Health modelling shows that an estimated $5.25 billion can be saved in health spending, and, if so, how can she justify her support for rolling back world-leading smoke-free legislation when a simple cost-benefit analysis shows the cost to the health system outweighs the benefits of the revenue gained?
specificity.explanation: Names the source of the estimate, the figure ($5.25 billion), the category of saving and the named legislation being rolled back. Concrete enough that the Minister's answer could be checked against the modelling.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The previous Government’s over-regulation on clubs and ranges have forced several to shut down. It is imperative for New Zealanders to have access to secure venues for firearms usage. The absence of such facilities poses additional risks to the community. Therefore, we are dedicated to overturning these unnecessary regulations to ensure the safety and the availability of these important spaces.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: regulation closed ranges, fewer ranges means less safe shooting, therefore repeal the regulation. The chain is coherent but the middle step — that closures raise community risk — is asserted rather than supported, so there is a genuine gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What is the priority for this Government: tax cuts funded by more New Zealanders smoking for longer or the health and lives of everyday New Zealanders?
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: the question presumes the only two options are tax cuts funded by increased smoking or protecting health, excluding the possibility the Minister has just argued for — that excise revenue declines regardless. The argument engages the actual policy, so the defect is in the inference, not in what it is about.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Like other forecasters, the NZIER is expecting near-term weakness in the economy but recovery over the longer term.
divination.explanation: Relays a forecast of the New Zealand economy: continued weakness in the near term followed by recovery over a longer horizon. The speaker is reporting NZIER's forecast rather than making her own.
divination.subject: other
divination.subject_name: New Zealand Institute of Economic Research
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series; true if 2024 shows at least two quarters of contraction or flat growth and 2025 shows sustained positive quarterly growth, false if growth is sustained through 2024 or if no recovery appears by end-2025.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that has turned a blind eye to the fact that this bill will cost New Zealanders, the New Zealand health system, $5 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal bill carries a $5 billion cost to New Zealand and its health system, and that this figure was available to the Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Treasury regulatory impact analysis and published academic modelling of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill 2024; true if an official or peer-reviewed costing puts the health-system or fiscal cost of the repeal at approximately $5 billion, false if no costing of that order exists.

veracity.statement: Twelve people a day die from smoking-related illness in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: A rate claim: roughly twelve smoking-attributable deaths per day in New Zealand, i.e. about 4,400 a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health New Zealand smoking-attributable mortality estimates; true if the annual smoking-attributable death toll is around 4,000-4,500, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: When the Government get advice to say that these changes will push that out to 2061, it says everything that they choose to ignore that and stick to their tobacco lobby talking points.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice to the Government modelled the repeal as pushing the smokefree target out to 2061.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health advice and regulatory impact analysis on the repeal, plus the modelling it drew on; true if official advice projected the smokefree (under 5 percent prevalence) target being delayed to around 2061, false if no advice containing that projection exists.

veracity.statement: But further, Māori make up 38 percent of daily smokers.
veracity.explanation: In context, a claim about Māori as a share of all adult daily smokers in New Zealand (she has just given prevalence rates of 17.1 and 6.1 percent, so this is a different quantity).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey 2022/23 daily-smoker counts by ethnicity; true if Māori make up approximately 38 percent of all adult daily smokers, false if the share is materially lower (for example around 30 percent).

veracity.statement: You never campaigned on this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the governing parties did not put the repeal of the smokefree measures to voters at the 2023 election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published 2023 election policy platforms and campaign material of National, ACT and New Zealand First; true if none proposed repealing the smokefree generation and denicotinisation measures before the election, false if any of them did.

veracity.statement: Because under the legislation, the only people that would be profiting would be the gangs: 8.5 million illegal cigarettes were seized by Customs in 2023.
veracity.explanation: A quantified claim that New Zealand Customs seized 8.5 million illegal cigarettes during 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Customs Service seizure statistics for the 2023 calendar or financial year; true if cigarette/stick seizures were approximately 8.5 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The latest New Zealand Health Survey results show that in 2022-2023, 6.8 percent of adults were daily smokers, down from 8.6 percent the previous year and 16.4 percent the year previous to that. What is in place has been working.
veracity.explanation: Three sourced prevalence figures for consecutive New Zealand Health Survey years: 6.8 percent in 2022/23, 8.6 percent the year before, and 16.4 percent the year before that.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published New Zealand Health Survey adult daily-smoking prevalence series; true if all three figures match the years stated, false if any does not — in particular whether 16.4 percent belongs to 2020/21 or to a much earlier survey year.

veracity.statement: And then the previous Government wanted to push up to 80 percent of them out of business.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government's retailer-reduction scheme would have put up to 80 percent of small retailers out of business, as distinct from removing their tobacco licence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The retailer-reduction provisions of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 and its regulatory impact statement; true if the scheme would have ended trading for roughly 80 percent or more of those businesses, false if it only withdrew tobacco sales while the businesses continued to operate.

veracity.statement: Because no papers have been received, no discussion has been had, and no decisions have been made in Cabinet.
veracity.explanation: A factual claim about Cabinet process: that as at 27 February 2024 no papers on firearms law had reached Cabinet and no decisions had been taken.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet papers and minutes for late 2023 to February 2024, via proactive release or the Official Information Act; true if no paper on the Arms Act rewrite or semi-automatic firearms had been lodged or considered by that date, false if one had.

veracity.statement: Why won’t he rule out liberalising access to military-style semi-automatic weapons when the police have made it very clear to the Government, both present and former, that doing so would result in more of those weapons getting into the hands of gang members and others who intend to break the law?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Police have advised both the current and previous governments that liberalising access to military-style semi-automatics would put more of them into the hands of gangs and offenders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Police advice to Ministers and Police submissions on Arms Act reform; true if Police have formally advised that widening access to MSSAs would increase their availability to gangs and offenders, false if no such advice is on record.

veracity.statement: Is he intending to visit the Linwood mosque on 15 March; if so, will he tell the victims of that massacre that he is intending to change the law to make legal the purchase of those types of firearms again, given that the firearm used in that terrorist attack was legally purchased?
veracity.explanation: Contains a checkable historical claim: that the firearm used in the Christchurch attack was purchased legally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masjidain and Police records; true if the weapons were bought under a valid firearms licence, false if they were obtained unlawfully.

veracity.statement: Is it the case that the Government has no plan to bring back semi-automatic firearms because there are already approximately 6,000 New Zealanders with a licence to have one and it’s logically very difficult to bring back something that’s already there?
veracity.explanation: A quantified claim that roughly 6,000 New Zealanders currently hold a licence permitting a semi-automatic firearm of the type at issue.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Police firearms licensing data on holders of an endorsement permitting possession of prohibited or military-style semi-automatic firearms as at early 2024; true if approximately 6,000, false if materially different.

specificity.statement: Twelve people a day die from smoking-related illness in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A precise, quantified, checkable rate rather than a general claim that smoking kills.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why not raise the age to 25, as the Ministry of Health offered as a compromise?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific mechanism (a purchase age of 25) and its source, though no timing or implementation detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to ensure people who smoke have more choice and more help to quit smoking if they wish to do so. This includes effective stop-smoking services, alternative products such as vaping, and targeted campaigns aimed at quitting smoking.
specificity.explanation: Names three categories of intervention, which is more than a slogan, but supplies no funding, targets, timeframe or named programme.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As that member knows, our coalition agreement states that we will rewrite the Arms Act to provide for greater protection for public safety—greater protection for public safety—and we’re going to simplify the regulatory requirements and ensure very good, smart compliance.
specificity.explanation: Names a document and a statute, which is checkable, but the substance offered — 'greater protection', 'simplify the regulatory requirements', 'smart compliance' — carries no mechanism, threshold or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The hollow words that we just got from the Minister sponsoring the bill are nothing more than regurgitated talking points from the tobacco lobby.
civility.explanation: Does not engage the Minister's argument at all; dismisses her as a mouthpiece, imputing that she is reciting an industry script. The target is the person, not the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But it goes worse than that, because we know that the instructions she gave to the officials that prepared this bill probably came from the tobacco lobby as well.
civility.explanation: A speculative accusation of corrupt conduct against a named individual Minister — 'we know ... probably' concedes there is no evidence, yet the imputation is made anyway.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You have blood on your hands for te iwi Māori: Te Aka Whai Ora and now Smokefree.
civility.explanation: Addresses the members opposite directly and charges them personally with causing deaths. It is a moral accusation against the people rather than a criticism of the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Wow! What an animated display we are seeing over this legislation.
civility.explanation: Opens by mocking the manner of the preceding speakers rather than their argument. Condescension short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why not raise the age to 25, as the Ministry of Health offered as a compromise?
focus.explanation: Puts a concrete alternative policy option, sourced to the Ministry of Health, directly to the House. Entirely about the measure rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But there is a silver lining, of course, because we’re getting tax cuts for the rich; tax cuts for the rich and to support those of our whānau who work in the tobacco industry.
focus.explanation: Sarcasm about who the other side serves. There is a thread of policy content (tobacco revenue funding tax cuts) but it is carried by the party-characterising framing rather than any named measure or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We promised New Zealanders that we would address the rampant lawlessness driven by the previous Labour Government’s soft-on-crime approach, and our plan to reduce gangs’ ability to intimidate and to terrorise our communities is just one part of that.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent (the gang legislation), but the weight of the sentence is party characterisation — 'soft-on-crime', the previous Labour Government — rather than any mechanism or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why won’t he rule out liberalising access to military-style semi-automatic weapons when the police have made it very clear to the Government, both present and former, that doing so would result in more of those weapons getting into the hands of gang members and others who intend to break the law?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named policy question — the firearms licensing regime — citing the official advice against it. On-policy accountability, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know it will be young New Zealanders, it will be lower-income New Zealanders, and will be Māori and Pacific New Zealanders. This is overwhelmingly clear from the evidence.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the bill's distributional effect, but it rests on a bare appeal to unnamed authority — 'the evidence' is invoked as self-evident and nothing is cited to connect the bill to the groups named.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The latest New Zealand Health Survey results show that in 2022-2023, 6.8 percent of adults were daily smokers, down from 8.6 percent the previous year and 16.4 percent the year previous to that. What is in place has been working.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a falling trend to the sufficiency of current settings — a post hoc inference. The premise does support some of the conclusion, but nothing is offered to rule out the measures now being repealed having contributed to the fall.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is he intending to visit the Linwood mosque on 15 March; if so, will he tell the victims of that massacre that he is intending to change the law to make legal the purchase of those types of firearms again, given that the firearm used in that terrorist attack was legally purchased?
rigor.explanation: A loaded question: it embeds as settled the premise that the Prime Minister intends to legalise those purchases, which he had just expressly denied in the preceding answer. The conclusion is smuggled into the question rather than argued for — a strawman of the stated position.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is it the case that the Government has no plan to bring back semi-automatic firearms because there are already approximately 6,000 New Zealanders with a licence to have one and it’s logically very difficult to bring back something that’s already there?
rigor.explanation: Turns on an equivocation: the endorsement holders permitted prohibited firearms under narrow exemptions are not the same class as the general access that was removed in 2019, so 'it's already there' does not establish that nothing could be brought back.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This is a bill that will kill people; it is a bill that will increase smoking in New Zealand.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the smokefree measures will raise smoking in New Zealand — an outcome about the world, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily-smoking prevalence in the years after the repeal takes effect; true if prevalence rises above the 2022/23 level of 6.8 percent in a subsequent survey year, false if it continues to fall.

specificity.statement: Mr Speaker, I’m very happy to talk about the Government’s priorities, which are to strengthen the economy so that we can address the cost of living, which has been at a crisis for the past two years; increase the jobs and incomes available to New Zealanders; ensure they can keep more of their own money; deliver better front-line services in health and education, where attendance rates have plummeted; and increase law and order by delivering more police.
specificity.explanation: A list of policy directions — strengthen the economy, more jobs, better front-line services, more police — with no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named programmes attached to any of them. 'More police' and 'better front-line services' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the Minister of Finance aware of reports attributed to Victorian police in Melbourne that last year 27 convenience stores were attacked with firebombings as part of stand-over tactics believed to be connected with the illicit tobacco trade, and if she has considered the impacts of illicit tobacco on both health and the Government’s books, does she believe that it’s actually time to bring a bit of reality into this debate?
specificity.explanation: Names a jurisdiction, a source, a timeframe and a count (27 convenience stores firebombed in Victoria last year), and ties it to a named mechanism — stand-over tactics in the illicit tobacco trade. Someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yesterday, I laid out the Government’s work programme to fix New Zealand’s housing crisis. Five interlocking actions: firstly, going for housing growth, to smash urban limits holding our cities back, fix infrastructure funding and financing, and introduce incentives to encourage cities and regions to go for growth; secondly, improvements to the rental market to make it easier to be a landlord and easier to be a tenant; thirdly, building and construction changes to improve competition, lower building costs; better social housing to look after those who most need support; and, fifthly, reform of the Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA).
specificity.explanation: Five enumerated workstreams and one named statute (the RMA), which is real structure — but each strand is described by its intent ('improve competition', 'lower building costs') rather than by any mechanism, dollar figure or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the 1950s, our GDP per capita was 125 percent of the OECD average, and it is now below the OECD average.
specificity.explanation: A dated, quantified comparison against a named benchmark. Precise enough that a reader could pull the OECD series and check both ends of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The first element of our package will require councils to zone enough land for 30 years of housing growth.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism (a zoning requirement on councils) with a quantified standard (30 years of growth capacity). Checkable against the eventual policy; the one gap is how 'enough land' is to be measured.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Has he seen—and if he has seen it, does he accept—the Sense Partners analysis of the medium-density residential standards that showed the infrastructure costs of a house in a new greenfields area on the fringe of the city is nearly double that of an additional home within the existing urban area?
specificity.explanation: Names the analysis and its author, the policy it concerns, and the quantified finding (roughly double the infrastructure cost at the fringe versus infill). A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, if I could point to one example put forward by New Zealand First as a part of the coalition agreement, which makes its way in, which is to make it essentially legal, without a building consent or a resource consent, for granny flats of up to 60 square metres on a property, which I think will have a massive impact.
specificity.explanation: A concrete mechanism with a threshold — dwellings up to 60 square metres exempt from both building and resource consent — traced to a named source in the coalition agreement. Only the claimed 'massive impact' is unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Actually, what we need is housing choice, and, more importantly, we need urban land settings that facilitate those choices.
specificity.explanation: A statement of direction with nothing attached — 'housing choice' and 'urban land settings that facilitate those choices' name no rule, no cost, no timeframe, and offer nothing that could be checked or acted on, in answer to a question that asked for a specific affordability measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Mr Speaker, I’m very happy to talk about the Government’s priorities, which are to strengthen the economy so that we can address the cost of living, which has been at a crisis for the past two years; increase the jobs and incomes available to New Zealanders; ensure they can keep more of their own money; deliver better front-line services in health and education, where attendance rates have plummeted; and increase law and order by delivering more police.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the Government's own policy agenda across five named domains. The only party framing is the passing 'crisis for the past two years', which implies blame without turning the answer into a comment on the Opposition.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has he seen—and if he has seen it, does he accept—the Sense Partners analysis of the medium-density residential standards that showed the infrastructure costs of a house in a new greenfields area on the fringe of the city is nearly double that of an additional home within the existing urban area?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure at issue — the MDRS — and on a named piece of evidence about its cost consequences. No party framing at all; this is scrutiny of a specific policy, which is the job.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I’m not sure what the members of the Opposition are so worked up about, because it sounds like the Green councillors from Wellington are pretty happy that I’m in charge now.
focus.explanation: Answers a question about transport costs in an affordability measure by talking about the Opposition's state of mind and a newspaper headline about which councillors are pleased with him. No policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is named; the content is entirely about the other side's reaction.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Is the Minister of Finance aware of reports attributed to Victorian police in Melbourne that last year 27 convenience stores were attacked with firebombings as part of stand-over tactics believed to be connected with the illicit tobacco trade, and if she has considered the impacts of illicit tobacco on both health and the Government’s books, does she believe that it’s actually time to bring a bit of reality into this debate?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Victorian police: that 27 convenience stores in Victoria were firebombed in the previous year as part of stand-over tactics connected to the illicit tobacco trade.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Victoria Police statements and Victorian media reporting on tobacco-related arson attacks in the 2023 calendar year; true if police-attributed reporting puts the number of firebombed convenience/tobacco stores at or about 27 and links them to illicit tobacco stand-over activity, false if the police-attributed figure is materially different or no such attribution exists.

veracity.statement: In answer to the Deputy Prime Minister’s supplementary question, he makes a good point, which is that the revenue that the coalition Government is likely to receive from tobacco revenue in the forecast future years will be considerably less than was received by the previous Labour administration in 2020, where they earned $2.2 billion in tobacco excise revenue, which they happily invested in roads, hospitals, schools, and the like.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — $2.2 billion of tobacco excise revenue collected in 2020 under the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/NZ Customs tobacco excise and excise-equivalent duty revenue for the 2020 year; true if total tobacco excise revenue that year was about $2.2 billion, false if it was materially different.

veracity.statement: In the 1950s, our GDP per capita was 125 percent of the OECD average, and it is now below the OECD average.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two comparative statistics: New Zealand's GDP per capita was 125 percent of the OECD average in the 1950s, and is below the OECD average now.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD and long-run national accounts series for New Zealand GDP per capita relative to the OECD average; true if the 1950s ratio was around 125% and the current figure sits below 100%, false if either leg is materially off.

divination.statement: In answer to the Deputy Prime Minister’s supplementary question, he makes a good point, which is that the revenue that the coalition Government is likely to receive from tobacco revenue in the forecast future years will be considerably less than was received by the previous Labour administration in 2020, where they earned $2.2 billion in tobacco excise revenue, which they happily invested in roads, hospitals, schools, and the like.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that tobacco excise revenue in the coming forecast years will be considerably lower than the level collected in 2020 — a prediction about revenue outturns, not a promise about the Government's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury forecast and outturn tobacco excise revenue for the forecast years 2024/25 to 2027/28; true if annual tobacco excise revenue in those years is materially below the 2020 level she cites, false if it holds at or above it.

rigor.statement: Fixing this can be done through effective and efficient urban development, because cities are engines of productivity, and when we stop people building houses, we lock people out of cities, and that makes us all poorer.
rigor.explanation: A real chain of inference — cities raise productivity, restricting building keeps people out of cities, so restriction costs output — and each link is at least arguable. The gap is that the conclusion (urban development can fix a decades-long productivity gap) is far stronger than the premises support; no magnitude is offered to connect a housing constraint to the whole GDP shortfall.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So does he acknowledge, in light of that answer, that making medium-density residential standards optional, all else being equal, will lead to less potential housing in the existing urban area, precisely where it is most needed and where infrastructure costs are lower?
rigor.explanation: A clean inference built on the answer just given: if infill infrastructure is cheaper and the rule that forces infill capacity becomes optional, then holding everything else constant, infill capacity falls. The ceteris paribus condition is stated explicitly rather than smuggled in, which is what keeps it valid.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That would be true if all else was being equal. The point is: it’s not. We’re making the MDRS optional at the same time as requiring councils to zone it for enough development capacity.
rigor.explanation: Attacks the inference at exactly the right joint — concedes the conditional and denies the antecedent by naming the offsetting change bundled with the opt-out. Valid as far as it goes; it stops short of showing the offset is large enough to cover the loss, which is the remaining gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Was she being truthful when she said, “I haven’t looked at a freeze on excise at all.” in an interview with Guyon Espiner?
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific quotation attributed to Casey Costello in a named RNZ interview with Guyon Espiner — the checkable element is whether Costello said those words.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RNZ recording/transcript of Guyon Espiner's interview with Casey Costello; true if she said she had not looked at a freeze on excise at all, false if no such statement appears.

veracity.statement: Yes, I have received a range of reports, specifically at the current level of smokers being at 6.8 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current smoking prevalence figure in the reports she has received is 6.8 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for the most recent year before February 2024; true if 6.8% ± rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Importantly, that data also noted that the smoke-free legislation that the previous Government based their positioning on was 2019-2020 data, and since that data on which they based their legislation, 305,000 people have quit smoking, and youth smoking fell from 10.3 percent to 3 percent, proving the existing legislation was highly effective.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two quantities — 305,000 people quitting since the 2019-20 data, and a fall in youth smoking from 10.3 percent to 3 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health New Zealand Health Survey (and ASH Year 10 survey) smoking prevalence series: the change in total smokers since 2019/20 and the youth smoking rate for 2019/20 versus 2022/23; true if the quit count is ~305,000 and the youth rate moved 10.3% to 3% on a like-for-like measure, false if the figures come from incompatible measures or differ materially.

veracity.statement: Vaping as a cessation tool has worked successfully, and I would like to recognise that the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Vaping) Amendment Bill 2020, introduced by New Zealand First, which regulated vaping, has been a monumental factor in the smoking reduction rates we are seeing today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the named 2020 vaping bill was introduced by New Zealand First.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Vaping) Amendment Bill — the member in charge at introduction; true if that member was a New Zealand First MP, false if the bill was introduced by a member of another party.

veracity.statement: The first thing I did as a Minister was raise the excise tax in a Cabinet paper that I submitted in November 2023 and came into effect on 1 January 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that she submitted a Cabinet paper in November 2023 raising tobacco excise, which took effect on 1 January 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The proactively released Cabinet paper record for November 2023 and the excise order/indexation notice effective 1 January 2024; true if a Costello Cabinet paper raised excise with that commencement, false if the 1 January increase was the standing CPI indexation requiring no such paper.

veracity.statement: Well, look, the evidence that I’m most interested in is the 50 percent increase in gang membership in the last five years under the previous Government, which has led to a sense of disorder on our streets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that gang membership rose 50 percent over the five years to early 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Police National Gang List membership totals for 2018/19 compared with 2023; true if the increase is approximately 50%, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: How can he justify targeting gang members when the tribunal has found that 80 to 90 percent of Mongrel Mob and Black Power members have come from State wards, and, therefore, both gangs are largely a creation of the State?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a tribunal finding that 80 to 90 percent of Mongrel Mob and Black Power members were formerly State wards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal report on the Oranga Tamariki/State care claims; true if it records a finding in the 80-90% range for Mongrel Mob and Black Power membership having been in State care, false if no such finding appears or the figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: But also we are a party that believes in personal responsibility, and I should note that the Long-term Insights Briefing on imprisonment states that “Most people serving sentences in prison [in New Zealand] have been convicted of serious sexual or violent offending.”, and no society can function if people are not held personally responsible for their actions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Long-term Insights Briefing on imprisonment contains the quoted finding that most people serving prison sentences were convicted of serious sexual or violent offending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Department of Corrections/Ministry of Justice Long-term Insights Briefing on imprisonment; true if that sentence (or its substance) appears, false if the briefing says no such thing or the prison population breakdown contradicts it.

veracity.statement: Disestablishment was agreed to by all three governing parties in their coalition agreements and mandated by the results of the 2023 general election, where it was canvassed at length.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that disestablishing the Māori Health Authority was agreed to by all three governing parties in their coalition agreements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The texts of the National–ACT and National–New Zealand First coalition agreements (November 2023); true if disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority appears as a commitment binding all three parties, false if it appears in only one or neither.

specificity.statement: In the context of the interview that was conducted, the answer I gave to the question that was put within the 25-minute interview was accurate in the response and framework that question was put.
specificity.explanation: A circular restatement ("the answer I gave ... was accurate in the ... framework that question was put") with no content anyone could check — no quotation, no date, no substance about excise policy. The only concrete detail is the interview's length.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Importantly, that data also noted that the smoke-free legislation that the previous Government based their positioning on was 2019-2020 data, and since that data on which they based their legislation, 305,000 people have quit smoking, and youth smoking fell from 10.3 percent to 3 percent, proving the existing legislation was highly effective.
specificity.explanation: Carries a data vintage, a count of quitters and a before/after youth smoking rate — all figures someone could go and check against the survey series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The first thing I did as a Minister was raise the excise tax in a Cabinet paper that I submitted in November 2023 and came into effect on 1 January 2024.
specificity.explanation: A named instrument (a Cabinet paper), a submission month and a commencement date — concrete enough to be verified against the record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, look, the evidence that I’m most interested in is the 50 percent increase in gang membership in the last five years under the previous Government, which has led to a sense of disorder on our streets.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a figure and a period — a 50 percent rise over five years — which someone could check, though the "sense of disorder" half carries no measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: People will be perfectly entitled to attend a tangi if they’re not wearing a gang patch and they are not subject to a dispersal order.
specificity.explanation: States the operative conditions precisely — no patch, no dispersal order — so an affected person could work out where they stand.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This afternoon, the Government passed the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill. This transfers Māori Health Authority staff and functions to Health New Zealand and the Ministry of Health.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, the timing, and the receiving agencies, and identifies what moves (staff and functions) — concrete, though no numbers or transition dates are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The steps towards better health outcomes include some of the outcomes that are present in Pae Tū, some of the outcomes that are present in Whakamaua, and some of the health outcomes that we’ll identify in our Government policy statement.
specificity.explanation: Names two strategy documents but identifies no step, target or timeframe — "steps ... include some of the outcomes" is circular, and the third limb defers entirely to a document not yet written.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government will ensure the health system is performing, after six long years of deteriorating health metrics.
specificity.explanation: Commits to nothing checkable: no metric is named, no target level, no date by which "performing" would be demonstrated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she stand by her statements reported in Radio New Zealand that sports shooters may be permitted to own semi-automatic weapons, or does she agree with the Police, who have said such a change would introduce an unacceptable risk of high-capacity semi-automatic centre-fire firearms again becoming readily available in the black market through theft or provided by non-compliant licence holders?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the firearm class, the affected group, the source of the reported statement and the specific risk mechanism (theft and non-compliant licence holders) — detailed enough to be answered or checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Importantly, that data also noted that the smoke-free legislation that the previous Government based their positioning on was 2019-2020 data, and since that data on which they based their legislation, 305,000 people have quit smoking, and youth smoking fell from 10.3 percent to 3 percent, proving the existing legislation was highly effective.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc: the falls occurred after 2019-20 but the conclusion that they prove the pre-existing regime was "highly effective" is not supported — no counterfactual or attribution is offered, and declines that predate a law cannot be evidence of that law's effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, look, the evidence that I’m most interested in is the 50 percent increase in gang membership in the last five years under the previous Government, which has led to a sense of disorder on our streets.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the question was what evidence shows patch bans reduce crime, and growth in gang membership bears on the size of the problem, not on whether the proposed remedy works. The offered premise cannot support the conclusion drawn from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, the evidence I see and that we’ve received is the intimidation that people have seen right across the country, and we’ve also seen the progress that similar gang patch bans have had in Western Australia and in other countries.
rigor.explanation: Offers public perception of intimidation as evidence that a ban reduces crime — an appeal to anecdote — plus an unspecified appeal to overseas "progress" with no result attached. There is a real inference here about the policy, and it is weakly supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can he justify targeting gang members when the tribunal has found that 80 to 90 percent of Mongrel Mob and Black Power members have come from State wards, and, therefore, both gangs are largely a creation of the State?
rigor.explanation: The evidence cited is real and relevant, but the conclusion overreaches: that most current members were once State wards supports State causation of individual harm, not that the gangs as institutions are "largely a creation of the State" — a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But also we are a party that believes in personal responsibility, and I should note that the Long-term Insights Briefing on imprisonment states that “Most people serving sentences in prison [in New Zealand] have been convicted of serious sexual or violent offending.”, and no society can function if people are not held personally responsible for their actions.
rigor.explanation: Red herring: the question was about the State-care origins of gang members, and what offences prisoners were convicted of does not bear on whether State care produced them. The conclusion rests on a stated principle rather than on the evidence cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Again, I would emphasise that there’s all sorts of excuses that can be offered for crime, but people need to be personally responsible for their actions.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: recasts an evidence-based causal argument about State care as an "excuse", then rebuts the caricature rather than the claim. Causal explanation and individual responsibility are not mutually exclusive, so the implied dichotomy is false.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Disestablishment was agreed to by all three governing parties in their coalition agreements and mandated by the results of the 2023 general election, where it was canvassed at length.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to mandate: a general election result does not confer authorisation for any particular measure, and "canvassed at length" is not evidence that voters endorsed this one. The coalition-agreement half is a fact, not support for the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This distraction is evident from the report today by the independent ministerial advisory committee, which uncovered a significant number of problems which can be associated with a lack of ministerial oversight and political failure.
rigor.explanation: The inference runs from problems found to a specific cause via "can be associated with" — a possible association is offered as though it established that the previous Government was distracted. The evidence cited is consistent with the conclusion but does not demonstrate it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why has she refused requests to release the document under the Official Information Act if it is merely, as she has said in this House, a range of historical policy positions and notes?
focus.explanation: Names a specific document, a specific statutory process (the OIA) and the Minister's own prior characterisation of it. This is scrutiny of a named decision, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: With respect to the mystery of who wrote the document that appeared on her desk, has she considered calling in a former detective to investigate?
focus.explanation: Once the joke about her background is removed there is no policy content: no measure, figure or outcome is named, only the Minister herself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is she still actively considering freezes to tobacco excise tax, and, if so, has she been honest in all her statements to the Prime Minister?
focus.explanation: A genuine policy question (an excise freeze) carrying a second question about the Minister's personal honesty; roughly half the weight is on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What evidence and research does the Minister have that shows banning gang patches will reduce crime in our communities?
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure (a gang patch ban) and asks for the evidence base behind it — squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Do the steps taken by the Minister to improve health outcomes include opting out of the international health regulation amendment days after taking office, repealing world-leading smoke-free legislation, and repealing the Māori Health Authority?
focus.explanation: Names three specific decisions and tests them against the Minister's own stated goal. Legitimate scrutiny of named actions, not general party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she stand by her statements reported in Radio New Zealand that sports shooters may be permitted to own semi-automatic weapons, or does she agree with the Police, who have said such a change would introduce an unacceptable risk of high-capacity semi-automatic centre-fire firearms again becoming readily available in the black market through theft or provided by non-compliant licence holders?
focus.explanation: Puts a named potential policy change against the police advice on its consequences — entirely about the measure and its risks.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: With respect to the mystery of who wrote the document that appeared on her desk, has she considered calling in a former detective to investigate?
civility.explanation: A jibe at the Minister's own former police career rather than at the withholding decision — mockery aimed at the person, short of direct abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is she still actively considering freezes to tobacco excise tax, and, if so, has she been honest in all her statements to the Prime Minister?
civility.explanation: The second limb imputes dishonesty to the Minister personally rather than contesting the excise policy — an allegation of bad faith, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does he deem it appropriate for a Minister of Justice to say he does not care about the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act?
civility.explanation: Puts into the Minister's mouth a contemptuous attitude to a statute — an imputation about the person's disposition rather than a challenge to a policy, and one he immediately denies making.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You’re not the Speaker, and you never will be at your age.
civility.explanation: A direct personal jibe at another member's age and future prospects, with nothing about the substance under discussion. The insult is the speaker's own conduct regardless of who it was aimed at.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Does she agree with Nicole McKee when she said of gun reforms at the Justice Committee on 24 June 2021 “And finally, just on the firearms changes in itself, I think it’s really important to remember not only the loss of lives in Christchurch and Aramoana but the quarter of a million people who’ve been affected by rushed legislation changes.”?
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific prior statement attributed to McKee at a named select committee on a named date, including the claim that a quarter of a million people were affected by the 2019-20 firearms law changes.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Justice Committee transcript/Hansard record for 24 June 2021: true if McKee spoke those words on that date, false if the words or the date do not match; and Police firearms licence-holder statistics for 2021 for the ~250,000 figure — true if licence holders numbered roughly 250,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Does she accept that even stringent licensing, like that for handgun licences, will not stop all misuse of weapons such as that of Ian Dallison, who used his licensed pistol to attempt to murder his landlord on 4 August 2022?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a named individual, Ian Dallison, used a pistol held on his own licence in an attempted murder of his landlord on a stated date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Court records and contemporaneous reporting of the Dallison prosecution: true if he held a pistol licence, used that licensed pistol, and the offending against his landlord occurred on 4 August 2022; false if the weapon was unlicensed, the target was someone else, or the date is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: Does she believe that Christopher Luxon was telling the truth in September last year, when challenged that under his Government people would have more access to semi-automatic firearms, when he said “It’s not going to happen.”?
veracity.explanation: Relays a quoted assurance attributed to Luxon in September 2023 that access to semi-automatic firearms would not widen under his government; the claim being checked is Luxon's, not Webb's.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media/debate record of Christopher Luxon's September 2023 statements: true if he said "It's not going to happen" when challenged on wider access to semi-automatic firearms, false if no such statement exists or the words are materially different.

veracity.statement: How would permitting semi-automatic weapons address situations like that of Quinn Patterson, who in July 2017 murdered his property manager and her daughter with a semi-automatic rifle illegally supplied by a licensed firearms holder Michael Hayes?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Quinn Patterson murdered two named-by-relationship victims in July 2017 with a semi-automatic rifle that a named licensed holder, Michael Hayes, supplied to him illegally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Court records and reporting of the July 2017 Whangārei shootings and the subsequent prosecution of the supplying licence holder: true if two victims were killed with a semi-automatic rifle unlawfully supplied by licensed holder Michael Hayes; false if the weapon, the supplier, or the manner of supply differs.

veracity.statement: I’m not going to speak for the Prime Minister, but what I will say is that legitimate use, legitimate ownership—and our coalition agreement agrees to rewrite the Arms Act to make sure that we have a good, safe system for New Zealanders, those legitimate owners and those that have been deemed to be fit and proper by the New Zealand Police.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the governing coalition agreement contains a commitment to rewrite the Arms Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements (November 2023): true if either contains an undertaking to rewrite or replace the Arms Act 1983, false if no such commitment appears.

veracity.statement: The Secondary Principals Association welcomed the review and the president said that longstanding issues with school property had become “horribly acute”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Secondary Principals' Association welcomed the ministerial inquiry and that its president used the words "horribly acute" about school property issues.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements and media comment from the Secondary Principals' Association of New Zealand and its president around February 2024: true if the association's response was supportive and the president used that phrase, false if the association's response was critical or no such phrase was used.

veracity.statement: And in the last three years, 219,000 people have stopped smoking, with 36 percent of those being Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of people who stopped smoking over a three-year window and a specific Māori share of that count.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence applied to population estimates for 2020/21 to 2023/24: true if the implied decline is about 219,000 people with roughly 36 percent Māori, false if either figure is materially different or cannot be derived from the survey series.

specificity.statement: Does she accept that even stringent licensing, like that for handgun licences, will not stop all misuse of weapons such as that of Ian Dallison, who used his licensed pistol to attempt to murder his landlord on 4 August 2022?
specificity.explanation: Names the person, the weapon type, the licence category, the victim and an exact date — anyone could go and check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How would permitting semi-automatic weapons address situations like that of Quinn Patterson, who in July 2017 murdered his property manager and her daughter with a semi-automatic rifle illegally supplied by a licensed firearms holder Michael Hayes?
specificity.explanation: Names the offender, the month and year, the weapon class, the victims' relationship to him and the named supplier — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Absolutely. I agree with what Nicole McKee said back then—that we need to make sure that everybody is considered when it comes to legislation, including not only those of the mosque shooting but those that have been affected by gun crime that has been allowed to take place under the previous Government’s regime.
specificity.explanation: "Make sure that everybody is considered" commits to no mechanism, threshold or timeframe; the only concrete anchor is a gesture at past events.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I agree that it’s time that we had legislation that actually looks after the security and the safety of New Zealanders, and that’s precisely what this Government will deliver in this term.
specificity.explanation: "Legislation that actually looks after the security and the safety of New Zealanders" names no provision, standard or measurable outcome; the only detail is the term-length horizon.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What an excellent question, because I’m so glad to be able to speak to the regime that the Arms Act, that is going to be rewritten by the end of this term, is going to present for New Zealanders, which includes ensuring stricter compliance, security, and fit and proper assertations from those that are in possession and use.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute and an end-of-term horizon, but the content of the promised regime is a string of generic virtues — "stricter compliance, security, and fit and proper" — with no threshold, test or provision attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And in the last three years, 219,000 people have stopped smoking, with 36 percent of those being Māori.
specificity.explanation: A precise count, a stated period and a stated demographic breakdown — checkable against the published survey series.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Absolutely. I agree with what Nicole McKee said back then—that we need to make sure that everybody is considered when it comes to legislation, including not only those of the mosque shooting but those that have been affected by gun crime that has been allowed to take place under the previous Government’s regime.
focus.explanation: A real point about who firearms legislation should consider, but the weight of the sentence lands on blaming the previous Government's "regime" in general terms rather than on any named measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How much longer will kura kaupapa, wharekura, and kura ā iwi—all Māori immersion schools who have already been waiting for decades for their classroom rebuilds—have to wait for their school rebuild projects to be delivered in order to provide for our tamariki the best possible learning environments; and how long will this Government’s inquiry take, and what is the time line for our kura receiving the school rebuilds that have already been promised to them?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: names the specific school types affected, the specific programme (classroom rebuilds already promised) and asks for the inquiry's timeline. Scrutiny of a named commitment, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Look, smoking rates have been falling consistently for some time, and that trend will continue under our Government.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the decline in smoking prevalence continues through this parliamentary term — an outcome in the population, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence, annual releases from 2024/25 onward: true if the rate falls in each release through the term, false if it flattens or rises.

divination.statement: If those trends continue, New Zealand will hit the deadline smokefree goal of less than 5 percent of the population daily by 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that daily smoking prevalence falls below the 5 percent Smokefree 2025 threshold by 2025 — a population outcome with a stated numeric target and deadline.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for the 2025 measurement year: true if below 5 percent of adults, false if 5 percent or above.

rigor.statement: Labour’s changes would have created a black market with more smuggling, more ram raids, but it doesn’t have to be that way.
rigor.explanation: Engages the repealed measure itself, so this is a policy argument rather than a party jibe — but the inference is bare assertion sliding into slippery slope: nothing whatever is offered to connect denicotinisation and retailer limits to smuggling, still less to ram raids.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is well known that Māori have the highest smoking rates and we have the highest rate of death and tobacco-related illnesses, so to sit here and say that these decisions aren’t being made against us is an absolute myth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori have both the highest smoking prevalence and the highest rate of tobacco-related death/illness of any group in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey (Ministry of Health) daily smoking prevalence by ethnicity, and Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora tobacco-attributable mortality rates by ethnicity, for the years around 2023-24. True if Māori rates are the highest of the reported ethnic groups on both measures; false if another group ranks higher on either.

veracity.statement: We know what this Government’s agenda is, and we will continue to call it out for what it is so that our people can see, because we’ve got to keep reminding ourselves, Aotearoa: 83 percent of Māori did not support this Government—83 percent of Māori did not support this Government—which is why there is such a comfort in how and what it is that they are rolling out in this hundred days of absolute colonising chaos.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure: 83 percent of Māori voters did not support the parties now in government (National, ACT, NZ First) at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 general election party-vote results for the seven Māori electorates (and/or Māori-roll turnout breakdowns). True if the combined party vote for National, ACT and NZ First is approximately 17 percent or less; false if materially higher.

veracity.statement: So, again, when the Prime Minister was asked “How many lives might be lost by making this change; have you focused on that?”, the answer was no.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on 4 December the Prime Minister, asked whether he had considered how many lives might be lost through the repeal, answered no. The claim is about what was actually said in that exchange.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The transcript or recording of the Prime Minister's 4 December 2023 media interview on the Smokefree repeal. True if he answers 'no' to a question in substantially those terms; false if he gave a different answer or was not asked.

veracity.statement: We’re on track to hit the smokefree target of 2025 and continue to drive down our smoking rates.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at early 2024 New Zealand was on trajectory to meet the Smokefree 2025 goal (daily smoking prevalence under 5 percent) without the repealed legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for 2022/23 and 2023/24, overall and for Māori, against the under-5-percent Smokefree 2025 definition. True if the trend line reaches under 5 percent by 2025 for the population and for Māori; false if prevalence in either remains materially above that on the observed trajectory.

veracity.statement: It matters because tobacco is the most harmful product in New Zealand. It kills 50 percent of the people who use it. It is the leading preventable cause of death in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Three linked factual assertions: tobacco is the most harmful consumer product in NZ, it kills half of its users, and it is the leading preventable cause of death here.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: WHO tobacco fact sheets and Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora burden-of-disease statistics. True if published sources state that tobacco kills up to half of long-term users and rank it the leading preventable cause of death in NZ; false if the mortality fraction is materially lower or another cause is ranked first.

veracity.statement: It would have got us to our Smokefree 2025 goal, which previously was a bipartisan-held goal, and without that legislation, it’s predicted that this Government will take until 2061 to achieve that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existence and content of a published projection: that without the 2022 amendment the Smokefree goal is not reached until 2061. The checkable claim is what the modelling actually says, not what will happen in 2061.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published NZ smokefree modelling (e.g. University of Otago BODE3 / Ministry of Health projections) cited around 2023-24. True if a peer-reviewed or official projection gives 2061 (or close) as the achievement date absent the legislation; false if no such projection exists or gives a materially different date.

veracity.statement: We know that that legislation is incredibly popular, and 60 percent of New Zealand don’t think this repeal should go ahead.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific level of public opposition to the repeal: 60 percent of New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published NZ opinion polling from 2023-24 asking about repeal of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act. True if a reputable poll puts opposition at approximately 60 percent; false if published polling shows materially lower opposition or no such poll exists.

rigor.statement: It is well known that Māori have the highest smoking rates and we have the highest rate of death and tobacco-related illnesses, so to sit here and say that these decisions aren’t being made against us is an absolute myth.
rigor.explanation: The premise (disproportionate Māori smoking harm) is offered to support the conclusion that the repeal is being made 'against us' — i.e. deliberately. Disparate impact does not establish intent; there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded. The reasoning is about the policy, so this is a Rigor failure rather than a Focus one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we take Auckland for an example, a 90 percent reduction in retail outlets will cause chaos. That would make for probably about 30 outlets for approximately 90,000 smokers. If you do the rough maths, they would need to serve two customers every minute, which kind of does point out that this legislation—there’s no way to make this happen; it does not make sense.
rigor.explanation: A genuine quantitative argument about the measure: outlet reduction, smoker population, implied throughput. But the arithmetic is asserted rather than shown, and it silently assumes every smoker buys daily; the jump from 'busy counters' to 'there's no way to make this happen' is a bigger step than the numbers support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The 2022 amendment to the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act was evidence-based. The denicotinisation of cigarettes has been studied in multiple clinical trials. Retail outlets are known to be associated with undermining people’s efforts to quit.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion ('evidence-based') is supported by the two things offered — trial evidence for denicotinisation and an association between outlet density and quit failure, matching the Act's two main levers. The support is asserted rather than cited, but the inference itself tracks the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we have here is an ability for a Government to actually do the right thing by its indigenous peoples and by tangata w’enua, but they are so hell bent and so bitter and twisted by what has happened in the past to them, and so vengeful against Māori not supporting them in the last election, that we continue to see this absolute kick in the face of advocates such as our whaea Tariana Turia, Hone Harawira, who are champions of Smokefree Aotearoa; many of our advocates who are upstairs in the gallery.
focus.explanation: A bill is before the House, but this passage engages none of it — no mechanism, cost, timeframe or named provision. Its whole content is a characterisation of the other side's motives ('bitter and twisted', 'vengeful'). Strip the party-motive claim out and nothing about the policy remains.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We are being told and guaranteed that he will act in the best interests of us as Māori, and I guess that helps us in some way, to put to rest that this isn’t about a billion-dollar tax revenue opportunity for this Government’s rich mates—absolutely not!
civility.explanation: Sarcastic imputation of a corrupt motive — that the Minister's assurances are cover for enriching 'this Government's rich mates'. This goes past hard criticism of the decision to attributing bad faith and self-dealing to those making it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That’s why that side of the House was silent on this issue at the last election, and in the coalition agreement the voters learnt that a dirty deal was done behind closed doors, and we found out that these proposals that are a wish list from the tobacco industry were making their way into our households.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith rather than arguing the merits: concealment at the election, a 'dirty deal' struck secretly, and policy taken from a tobacco-industry 'wish list'. Criticising the coalition agreement's substance would be fully civil; alleging a corrupt bargain is the failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The cartoonists have had their turn too, calling out “Dr Cigareti” and “Nicotine Willis” and making the Government a laughing stock.
civility.explanation: Repeats mocking nicknames aimed at two named individual ministers into the record. The target is the people, not the policy, and the point of the sentence is ridicule.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And speaking of a laughing stock, we have the mystery of the document that miraculously appeared in the Minister’s office, but she can’t say how it got there, and she can’t really give satisfactory answers to the House about whether or not she spoke the truth to a journalist on this matter.
civility.explanation: A personal attack on a named minister's honesty, delivered with mockery ('laughing stock', 'miraculously'). Questioning the provenance of the document is legitimate; the framing here goes to the person's truthfulness rather than the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are calling for bold and systemic action—we are not going to see it from this Government, whānau mā.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the speech's positive alternative, so it is trying to convey substance, but 'bold and systemic action' names no measure, mechanism, figure or timeframe. Nobody could act on or check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we take Auckland for an example, a 90 percent reduction in retail outlets will cause chaos. That would make for probably about 30 outlets for approximately 90,000 smokers. If you do the rough maths, they would need to serve two customers every minute, which kind of does point out that this legislation—there’s no way to make this happen; it does not make sense.
specificity.explanation: Carries a percentage, an outlet count, a population figure and a derived service rate, all tied to a named city. Someone could check every number and redo the calculation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want an approach that is practical and helps smokers to quit. We are supporting a package of initiative—an initiative that’s focused on those who need them the most—to ensure we reach the Smokefree 2025 goal.
specificity.explanation: Presented as the Government's alternative to the repealed regime, so it is meant to convey substance, but nothing in it is checkable: no measure named, no funding figure, no mechanism, no timeframe beyond the goal itself, and no definition of 'those who need them the most'.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They are going to take the money that’s going to be provided through taxes and they’re going to give it to their rich mates. It’s as simple as that.
civility.explanation: Imputes a corrupt motive — that members opposite are legislating to enrich their associates. Short of a named personal insult, but well past robust criticism of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker
