civility.statement: It’s quite clear to me that on this side of the House—and to many of my colleagues on this side of the House—when that side talks about a black market, actually what they mean is targeting Māori.
civility.explanation: Imputes a concealed and malicious motive to members opposite — that their stated argument is a cover for deliberately targeting Māori. That is an attack on their good faith rather than on the black-market argument itself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Firstly, I want to comment that, unfortunately, even today it is clear that there is a lack of understanding on what is being done and the approach that is being taken.
civility.explanation: Mildly condescending — attributes the opposition's position to a failure to comprehend rather than to disagreement — but it is directed at the debate as a whole rather than at any member, and stops short of sneering.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They are going to take the money that’s going to be provided through taxes and they’re going to give it to their rich mates. It’s as simple as that.
focus.explanation: No policy content survives: no measure, figure or outcome is named, only an assertion about who the other side really serves.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The lines they read come straight from the lobby industry for tobacco.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speeches given by government members in this debate were supplied by the tobacco industry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Documentary evidence — OIA releases, ministerial diaries, lobbying disclosures or published investigations (e.g. RNZ/Stuff reporting on tobacco industry contact with Ministers in 2023-24) — showing speaking notes or lines used by government members in this debate originated with tobacco companies or their lobbyists; true if such material is identified, false if the record shows the material originated with the Ministry of Health, Parliamentary Service or party research.

veracity.statement: In the period since the data was used, 305,000 people have quit smoking.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 305,000 New Zealanders stopped smoking between the 2019-20 data used in the repealed legislation's modelling and the present.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health NZ Health Survey smoking prevalence estimates for 2019/20 and 2022/23 applied to the adult population: true if the implied fall in the number of smokers is approximately 305,000, false if the fall is materially different (e.g. nearer 200,000) or if the figure counts a different measure than the one implied.

veracity.statement: Youth smoking in that time fell from 10.3 to 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fall in youth smoking prevalence from 10.3% to 3% between roughly 2019/20 and the present.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey youth smoking prevalence (and/or the ASH Year 10 Snapshot) for 2019/20 and 2022/23: true if the rate for the age band the Minister is using fell from 10.3% to about 3%, false if the endpoints differ materially or the figures come from two non-comparable measures or age bands.

veracity.statement: Currently, we have 284,000 daily smokers that need our help.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current number of daily smokers in New Zealand is 284,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey 2022/23 daily smoking prevalence applied to the adult population: true if the estimate is approximately 284,000, false if materially different.

divination.statement: It’s going to be Māori people, Pacific people, low socio-economic people who will be hugely impacted by this.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the harm from the repeal will fall disproportionately on Māori, Pacific and low-income communities.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / NZ Health Survey daily smoking prevalence broken down by ethnicity and deprivation quintile for the years following the repeal: true if Māori, Pacific and high-deprivation prevalence stalls or rises relative to the pre-repeal trend while other groups continue to fall, false if those groups' prevalence continues declining at or above the pre-repeal trend.

rigor.statement: I just don’t believe that this, the actions that we’re repealing, would have actually substantially reduced smoking rates even further, so I commend this bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a bare statement of personal belief about a counterfactual. The preceding premise — that tax rises and attitude change drove past declines — does not entail that the repealed measures would add nothing; that past drivers worked does not show future ones cannot.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the period since the data was used, 305,000 people have quit smoking.
specificity.explanation: A single figure tied to a defined period and a defined baseline — a reader can go to the survey series and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I will bring a paper to Cabinet next week, and that will provide for immediate actions and longer-term strategies to achieve our collective objective.
specificity.explanation: A firm timeframe for the process step, but the content is described only as "immediate actions and longer-term strategies" — no measure, mechanism or amount is named, so nobody could check what was actually promised.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Tobacco, despite being the most harmful consumer product there is, that kills half the people who use it, is not regulated with respect to who can sell it, and that means that we do not even know where tobacco outlets are.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable things: that tobacco kills half of its users, and that as at February 2024 New Zealand had no regulation of who may sell tobacco and therefore no register of outlets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: WHO/Ministry of Health published estimate of tobacco-attributable mortality among long-term users (true if 'up to half' is the standard figure); and the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act 1990 as in force in Feb 2024 plus Ministry of Health advice on whether any retailer licensing scheme or national outlet register was in operation. False if a retailer registration/licensing requirement existed.

veracity.statement: This proposal, the denicotinisation proposal, was incredibly popular with the National Party when we debated this in 2022.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National Party members supported the denicotinisation measure during the 2022 passage of the Smoked Tobacco Amendment Bill. Not scored here; the resolver checks the record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the 2022 debates on the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill, and National Party statements of the period: true if National members, including Shane Reti, expressed support for the denicotinisation measure; false if National members opposed denicotinisation itself rather than the wider bill.

veracity.statement: In fact, the modelling also showed that the Act would have eliminated one-third of the life expectancy gap for Māori women—one-third.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantitative finding of the modelling presented to the Health Committee: elimination of roughly one-third of the Māori female life-expectancy gap.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The modelling submitted to the Health Committee on the Smoked Tobacco Amendment Bill (University of Otago BODE³ / Ouakrim et al. published estimates): true if it projects a reduction of approximately one-third in the Māori female life-expectancy gap; false if the projected reduction is materially different.

veracity.statement: Now, the advice we had was that we would miss that goal and we would not achieve it until 2061 without doing something differently, and that is why the 2022 amendments are so important.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice projected the 5 percent Smokefree goal would not be met until 2061 on the pre-2022 trajectory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health advice and the modelling underpinning the Smokefree Aotearoa 2025 Action Plan: true if a projection of reaching 5 percent prevalence around 2061 (for Māori or overall) appears in that advice; false if the advice projects a materially different date.

veracity.statement: We had over $20 million allocated in the recent Budget for supporting those initiatives.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Budget appropriation of more than $20 million for smoking cessation and smokefree support initiatives.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Health Budget appropriations for smoking cessation / smokefree services in the Budget referred to: true if the allocated amount exceeds $20 million; false if it is materially lower or no such line exists.

rigor.statement: It’s not prohibition, as some have suggested; there is still nicotine available in the form of vapes.
rigor.explanation: A genuine rebuttal with a reason offered, but the reason shifts the term: the objection is that smoked tobacco is prohibited for a birth cohort, and pointing to nicotine availability in another product does not meet that. A real inference about the measure, with a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That kind of leaves us with the outlying question of whether it’s the case that this Government sees that simply because there’s an election every three years, we can revert to authoritarian rule outside of that.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the Government's argument was that an election result mandates the policy, and this recasts it as a claim to unconstrained rule between elections. Nothing is offered to bridge the use of urgency on one bill to the abandonment of democratic limits generally.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have it on record, as tabled today, that half a billion dollars in extra revenue will be added to the Government coffers as a result of this change. Once again, that gives us irrefutable evidence that there will be an increase in consumption of tobacco, and, as a result, more New Zealanders will die.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur dressed as proof. A higher excise revenue forecast is consistent with several states of the world — unchanged consumption over a longer period, different price and volume assumptions, or a slower decline rather than an increase — so it cannot be 'irrefutable evidence' of an increase in consumption. The conclusion is asserted to be beyond dispute where the premise supports it only weakly.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason for that is that whether you have commercial entities or criminal organisations who are responsible for the supply chain of these substances, you have the maximisation of harm. That is because profit is the core motive.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument with a stated premise and conclusion about substance regulation, but the step from 'profit is the core motive' to 'maximisation of harm' is asserted rather than shown, and no evidence is offered for why both extremes converge on the same outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Act says that this will be enforced by fines against retailers who sell to those people; it does not regulate social supply.
specificity.explanation: Names the enforcement mechanism (fines), who it falls on (retailers), and the explicit limit of the scheme (social supply is untouched). Someone could check this against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, the modelling also showed that the Act would have eliminated one-third of the life expectancy gap for Māori women—one-third.
specificity.explanation: A named quantity (one-third), a named population (Māori women) and a named source (modelling presented to the select committee). Checkable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have it on record, as tabled today, that half a billion dollars in extra revenue will be added to the Government coffers as a result of this change. Once again, that gives us irrefutable evidence that there will be an increase in consumption of tobacco, and, as a result, more New Zealanders will die.
specificity.explanation: A named figure (half a billion dollars), a named mechanism (revenue forecasts) and a named, tabled source (Treasury OIA correspondence). Whether the inference drawn from it holds is a separate question.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think it really behoves the members on the other side to listen to the perspectives of hundreds of organisations that have called out how awful this bill is, how shameful it is that such violence and harm is being done to the health of our people.
civility.explanation: Extremely hard language — 'awful', 'shameful', 'violence and harm' — but every word of it lands on the bill and its consequences, not on any member. Under the re-anchored scale this is near the standard; a small deduction because 'shameful' edges toward the members being addressed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Guys, I hope you’re waking up and realising that you’re the bad guys.
civility.explanation: Addressed directly at Government members and lands on them as people — telling them they are 'the bad guys' is a judgement of character, not of the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because, freely and frankly, looking through the select committee submissions and the public outcry that we’ve seen in response to this track of agenda from this Government, and the support that we saw when this world-leading legislation came in, is that the only entities that we can identify who are asking for this legislation to go through the House today are New Zealand First and the tobacco industry.
focus.explanation: There is a real accountability point underneath — the repeal originates in a coalition commitment rather than public submissions — but the statement's weight is on characterising who the other parties serve rather than on the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Guys, I hope you’re waking up and realising that you’re the bad guys.
focus.explanation: Strip out the part about the other side and nothing remains: no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. Entirely about what the members opposite are.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: But the really simple question for them, which they have not been able to front up to and be honest with the New Zealand public about, is that this legislation will—must, by virtue of the evidence and the advice that they themselves have commissioned—result in a slower decline in rates of smoking in this country.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that smoking prevalence in New Zealand will fall more slowly after the repeal than it would have under the 2022 amendments. Not a promise about the speaker's own action, and not a claim about the present.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily-smoking prevalence series: true if the average annual percentage-point decline in the years following the March 2024 repeal is smaller than the average annual decline over the 2019–2023 period; false if the decline holds steady or accelerates.

rigor.statement: There’s evidence accumulating over the Tasman, over our own borders, and in container ships coming in in my home city with black market tobacco on board. A small and illegal market versus, as we currently have, a large legal market will invert.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy: scattered evidence of black-market tobacco (Australia, the border, container ships in Tauranga) is offered as grounds for the conclusion that the legal and illegal markets will swap places. The evidence is anecdotal and unquantified, and nothing is offered to connect isolated seizures to a wholesale inversion of the market — a hasty generalisation, though it does reason about the measure rather than about opponents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The third “but” is that this is done through urgency. So those experts, and those that know a heck of a lot better than you and I in this House—I beg your pardon, e te Speaker—are not given the opportunity to share what it is that, in their expertise, they know we’re going to have to contend with as a country beyond the three years of Governments—the three-year terms, six; whatever.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference from a stated premise: passing the bill under urgency removes the select committee stage, and the conclusion that expert and affected-community submitters therefore get no chance to be heard follows directly from how urgency works. The reasoning is sound; the added claim about consequences 'beyond the three-year terms' is asserted rather than shown, which is the only real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You cannot debate with 47,000 signatures. If we are going to use these positions of influence to ignore that, then what else are we going to ignore going down the track?
rigor.explanation: Two flawed steps in one breath. 'You cannot debate with 47,000 signatures' is an appeal to popularity — the number of signatories bears on how strongly a view is held, not on whether it is correct, and petitions are precisely the sort of thing a legislature does debate. The second sentence is a slippery slope: nothing is offered to link declining to follow this petition to a general habit of ignoring the public.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Look, Action on Smoking and Health (ASH) says New Zealand’s progress is unprecedented and we are on track to hit the smoke-free target.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ASH (Action on Smoking and Health New Zealand) has characterised New Zealand's smoking-rate progress as unprecedented and has said the country is on track to reach the Smokefree 2025 target.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ASH New Zealand's published statements, media releases and Year 10 Snapshot Survey commentary from roughly 2023–early 2024. True if ASH described New Zealand's progress as unprecedented AND said New Zealand is on track for the Smokefree 2025 target; false if ASH's published position was that New Zealand is not on track (for example that the target will be missed for Māori, or that repealing the smokefree generation measures puts it out of reach).

veracity.statement: I remember when we were having this discussion last year and—he was the Opposition health spokesperson at the time—Dr Shane Reti put through a few Supplementary Order Papers around vaping, which would have made a tangible difference to the significant uptake in youth vaping we’re seeing in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in 2023, while Opposition health spokesperson, Shane Reti lodged several Supplementary Order Papers dealing with vaping to the smokefree/vaping legislation then before the House. (The embedded claim that they 'would have made a tangible difference' is counterfactual and is not part of what is being checked.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parliament Supplementary Order Paper register and the Hansard committee-of-the-whole record for the smokefree/vaping legislation of 2023. True if SOPs on vaping were lodged in Reti's name while he held the Opposition health portfolio; false if no such SOPs appear in the record or if they were lodged by someone else.

veracity.statement: And yet there were 47,000 signatures on the petition that we received that asked us to be extremely loud and extremely vocal and make sure the views of those who had opposing views were heard and seen.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a petition opposing the repeal of the smokefree measures, carrying about 47,000 signatures, was presented to and received by members of Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parliament petitions register and the associated Hansard record of petitions presented in late 2023 / early 2024 on the smokefree repeal. True if a petition on this subject was presented with a signature count of approximately 47,000; false if the recorded count differs materially or no such petition was presented.

veracity.statement: And this continuously is the theme because we are a Government, and have a Government, that did not get supported by 83 percent of Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 83 percent of Māori voters did not vote for the parties that formed the government after the 2023 general election. Read as a claim about Māori party-vote support for National, ACT and New Zealand First, not about the general population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 general election results — party vote in the seven Māori electorates and/or party vote among voters on the Māori roll. True if the combined party vote for National, ACT and New Zealand First among those voters was approximately 17 percent (i.e. about 83 percent did not support them); false if their combined share was materially higher.

veracity.statement: So they urged—they urged—that we don’t support this bill and that we stay focused on the Smokefree 2025 vision that’s been in place since 2006.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's Smokefree 2025 goal has been in place since 2006.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The official adoption date of the Smokefree Aotearoa 2025 goal — the Government's response to the Māori Affairs Select Committee inquiry into the tobacco industry and its consequences for Māori, and Ministry of Health documentation of the goal. True if the goal dates from 2006; false if it was adopted in a later year, such as 2011.

specificity.statement: We will provide people with the practical tools to stop smoking and vaping, and better protection for young people to stop them accessing vaping products.
specificity.explanation: A statement of intent with no checkable content: 'practical tools' and 'better protection' name no mechanism, no funding, no product restriction and no timeframe. Nobody could act on this or verify later whether it was delivered.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But, you know, this is a much better approach to the prohibition-style approach that the Opposition has put forward and planned by the previous Government. We’re going to be a lot less punitive than they were.
civility.explanation: A contested second reading where an uncivil turn was readily available. The criticism lands entirely on the previous Government's regulatory approach — 'prohibition-style', 'punitive' — and imputes nothing to any individual's character, competence or motives.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It doesn’t matter that you may have relationships. It doesn’t matter that you may have had a side conversation. The reality is that the stats are the stats; the facts are the facts. And while you have a mandate, you do not have a Māori mandate.
focus.explanation: The bill before the House is not engaged at all here — no measure, provision, figure or outcome is named. The passage is about the governing parties' electoral standing and legitimacy with Māori. It is not content-free party-bashing (the mandate point is a real argument about whose voice the House should carry), which keeps it off the floor, but the weight sits on who the other side is rather than on what the bill does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I think it’s really rich—it’s really rich—that we continue to see a Government that promotes and says, “Māori, get up off your backside and go and look after yourselves.”—that’s my summary of what “personal responsibility” is.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's general attitude toward Māori through a paraphrase the speaker herself labels 'my summary'. No measure, figure or named policy is engaged — it is about the other side's disposition rather than the bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But every time we go to do it, we have a Government to my left, who has absolutely no reach in that community, saying that you should repeal, that they will disestablish, and they will counsel every move we make.
focus.explanation: Gestures at repeal and disestablishment, so there is a thread of policy, but the weight of the sentence is a claim about another party's standing and general posture ('absolutely no reach in that community') rather than any named measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is just the tobacco lobbies and this is just for tax cuts, and you know it.
focus.explanation: Gestures at tax cuts and lobbying but names no clause, cost or outcome of the repeal; the content is an accusation about the other side's motives rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As we’ve heard today—and, in particular, around smoke-free and the cuts that are going to come—it’s pūtea; it’s a dollar, because the tax cuts that are to come need to be funded from somewhere, and it’s this Government’s proposal that it’s going to come from the pockets of those addicted to nicotine.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy — repeal is explained by a need for excise revenue — but the only support offered is that tax cuts must be funded from somewhere. That the funds must come from this source does not follow; the motive is imputed rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We would suggest that people stop smoking, but we don’t think the previous amendment legislation will do it. That’s why we support this bill.
rigor.explanation: An inference about the measure before the House, but the load-bearing premise — that the previous legislation would not reduce smoking — is asserted with nothing offered in support, and no reason is given why repeal follows even if it were true. Bare assertion standing in for a reason.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They didn’t campaign on it because it wasn’t a priority for them at the time. It wasn’t a priority for them at the time because it wasn’t until afterwards, when New Zealand First and ACT got in on the act, that they realised that they now had to fund those tax cuts somehow.
rigor.explanation: Near-circular: the second sentence restates the first as its own explanation, then substitutes an imputed motive for evidence. Nothing is offered connecting the coalition negotiations to a revenue need, so the causal conclusion does not follow from what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Five-thousand people die annually from smoking-related illnesses, and I’ve been on the front line in my history, working as a quit coach.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an annual New Zealand death toll of 5,000 attributable to smoking-related illness.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health New Zealand published estimates of annual deaths attributable to smoking in New Zealand; true if the accepted estimate is approximately 5,000 per year, false if materially lower or higher (e.g. under 3,000 or over 8,000).

veracity.statement: And the Health Coalition Aotearoa, they released an analysis around, actually, if we maintained the trajectory of Smokefree 2025 and implemented it as planned, we could save $1.3 billion in health spend.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to Health Coalition Aotearoa an analysis finding $1.3 billion in health-spend savings from implementing the Smokefree 2025 measures as legislated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health Coalition Aotearoa's published analysis or media release on the smokefree legislation; true if it states health-system savings of about $1.3 billion, false if no such analysis exists or it gives a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: Yet I can’t find anywhere in the National Party’s campaign where they said they were going to repeal smoke-free legislation—something that’s world-leading, that the entire sector looks to us for leadership—can’t find it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National Party's 2023 election campaign contained no commitment to repeal the smokefree legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party 2023 election health policy documents, manifesto and campaign statements; true if no commitment to repeal the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act appears, false if a repeal commitment is documented in the campaign material.

veracity.statement: But I am glad that over the last number of years we’ve seen a steady decrease in the number of smokers, down from 16.4 percent in 2012 to 6.8 percent last year, and those rates have been continuing to fall before even this last amendment comes into effect.
veracity.explanation: Asserts adult smoking prevalence fell from 16.4 percent in 2012 to 6.8 percent in the most recent year, and that the decline predates the 2022 amendment taking effect.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence series; true if the 2011/12 figure is about 16.4% and the 2022/23 figure about 6.8%, false if either figure is materially different from the published series.

veracity.statement: In the last three years, 219,000 people have stopped smoking with vaping playing a key role.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of 219,000 people quitting smoking over three years, and attributes a key causal role to vaping.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey smoking prevalence change over the three years to 2023 applied to the adult population, plus published evidence on vaping's contribution to cessation; true if the implied fall in smokers is about 219,000 and cessation research supports vaping as a major route, false if the population change is materially smaller or the attribution to vaping is not supported.

specificity.statement: And the Health Coalition Aotearoa, they released an analysis around, actually, if we maintained the trajectory of Smokefree 2025 and implemented it as planned, we could save $1.3 billion in health spend.
specificity.explanation: Names the source organisation, the counterfactual (maintaining the Smokefree 2025 trajectory) and a dollar figure. Someone could go and find the analysis and check the number.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And yet we have a Government now and this legislation wants to remove the approvals of the Director-General of Health to sell tobacco products, remove the limits on the number of retailers so that there can be more than nine in Kawakawa, remove the Director-General of Health’s approval of products to be manufactured and produced and sold in New Zealand, and remove the requirement of tobacco products to meet the low nicotine limit of 0.8.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates four concrete mechanisms the bill removes — retailer approvals, the outlet cap, product approvals and the 0.8 mg nicotine limit — each checkable against the bill itself.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I am glad that over the last number of years we’ve seen a steady decrease in the number of smokers, down from 16.4 percent in 2012 to 6.8 percent last year, and those rates have been continuing to fall before even this last amendment comes into effect.
specificity.explanation: Two dated prevalence figures against a named trend; directly checkable against the health survey series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There were compromises offered to the Minister to introduce a purchase age of 25, which was not ideal, but it still would have saved some lives and it still would have saved some money; there were compromises being offered to the Minister to introduce a nicotine limit of 1.3 milligrams per gram, which was a little bit more than the 0.8 that we were aiming for, but an awful lot less than the 15 that exists at the moment; and there were compromises offered to the Minister to consider maybe even a higher cap of 600 outlets, maybe a few more, maybe a sinking-lid policy.
specificity.explanation: Three named alternatives with exact parameters — a purchase age of 25, a 1.3 mg/g nicotine limit against the 0.8 sought and the 15 current, and a 600-outlet cap or sinking lid. Concrete enough to legislate from.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: If these trends continue, New Zealand will hit the smoke-free goal of less than 5 percent of the population smoking daily by 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that daily smoking prevalence in New Zealand will fall below 5 percent by 2025, conditional on existing trends continuing.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the 2024/25 or 2025/26 year; true if the published daily smoking rate is below 5.0%, false if it is 5.0% or above.

civility.statement: Why I’m not so sure where to start is because I just listened to the previous contribution and I expected something a little bit more passionate from a cancer researcher.
civility.explanation: Aimed at the individual member rather than his argument: it implies a personal failure of conviction given his professional background. Short of a direct insult, but it is sneering at the person, not engaging what he said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is just the tobacco lobbies and this is just for tax cuts, and you know it.
civility.explanation: 'And you know it' imputes bad faith to the members opposite — that they are knowingly acting for the tobacco lobby. No individual is named or abused, so this is a failure of civility rather than a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look, I do feel for some members opposite because I think they’re being forced to get up and take a call and talk about something that, in their heart of hearts, they know is absolutely the wrong thing to do.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's internal state and supposed private beliefs; no policy mechanism, figure or named outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Look, I do feel for some members opposite because I think they’re being forced to get up and take a call and talk about something that, in their heart of hearts, they know is absolutely the wrong thing to do.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to named opponents — that they are speaking against their own conscience under duress. Short of a direct insult, but it goes to the members rather than the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is, effectively, a report card on a Minister who is deficient in her ability to actually deliver change that is meaningful for our community up and down Aotearoa New Zealand.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's personal competence — she is 'deficient in her ability' — rather than on the decision or the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I say to members opposite that this is not going to be an easy run through the House—this piece of legislation—because members of our community all around Aotearoa New Zealand who submitted to the select committee and who didn’t expect us to hold members opposite to account—and we intend to do that because this is a crap piece of law.
civility.explanation: Blunt to the point of crude — but the contempt is aimed squarely at the bill ('a crap piece of law'), not at any member. Under the re-anchored scale, harsh criticism of a measure is civil.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I know that, for example, the Health Committee that looked at these particular amendments at the time did consider things like a sinking lid, but in the end decided not to head down that particular path, instead limiting the number of licensed premises.
specificity.explanation: Names the select committee, a specific alternative mechanism (a sinking lid) and the mechanism actually adopted (limiting outlet numbers). Checkable, though no figures are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A member across just asked “Why haven’t they done the policy work?”, and can I just remind the House and those viewing today of a couple of key pieces of legislation: the 2011 Smoke-free Environments (Controls and Enforcement) Amendment Act and the 2016 Smoke-free Environments (Tobacco Standardised Packaging) Amendment Act, all under a previous National Government.
specificity.explanation: Two Acts named in full with their years and the government that passed them. Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I know that, for example, the Health Committee that looked at these particular amendments at the time did consider things like a sinking lid, but in the end decided not to head down that particular path, instead limiting the number of licensed premises.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the select committee examined a sinking lid for tobacco retail, declined it, and settled on limiting the number of premises able to sell smoked tobacco.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill (2022) and its associated departmental advice: true if the committee considered and rejected a sinking-lid approach and instead adopted a cap on the number of approved retailers; false if no sinking lid was considered or if the retailer cap did not originate there.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that is very eager and keen to remind everyone that they won a general election. Well, I tell members of this House that they did not win a general election going to the polls based on this particular policy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal of the 2022 smokefree amendments was not a policy the governing parties put to voters at the 2023 election, so no electoral mandate covers it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's, ACT's and New Zealand First's 2023 general election manifestos and published campaign policy releases: true if repealing the smokefree generation / denicotinisation / retailer-cap amendments does not appear as a campaign policy in them, false if any of those parties campaigned on the repeal before the 2023 election.

veracity.statement: I recall going to South Auckland, and not a single member of the National Party members of that committee bothered to turn up to that select committee hearing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no National member of the Health Committee attended the committee's South Auckland hearing of oral evidence on the smokefree bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's attendance records / minutes for its South Auckland hearing of evidence on the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill: true if no National member of the committee was present at that hearing, false if one or more attended.

veracity.statement: A member across just asked “Why haven’t they done the policy work?”, and can I just remind the House and those viewing today of a couple of key pieces of legislation: the 2011 Smoke-free Environments (Controls and Enforcement) Amendment Act and the 2016 Smoke-free Environments (Tobacco Standardised Packaging) Amendment Act, all under a previous National Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existence and dates of two named smokefree Acts and attributes both to a previous National government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand statute book and parliamentary record: true if both the Smoke-free Environments (Controls and Enforcement) Amendment Act 2011 and the Smoke-free Environments (Tobacco Standardised Packaging) Amendment Act 2016 exist under those titles and years and were enacted under a National-led government; false if either title, year, or the government of the day is wrong.

rigor.statement: I can attest to the fact that those young folk who are there—who are largely from members of our Māori cohort—were absolutely dumbfounded that this was something that this Government wishes to progress, that this is a Government that, effectively, is prepared to sign the death warrant for future generations by this particular piece of legislation.
rigor.explanation: The reaction of one group of students at one school is offered as grounds for the conclusion about the legislation's effect — an appeal to anecdote, with an appeal to emotion ('sign the death warrant') doing the rest of the work. It is about the measure, so Focus is unaffected.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: As Dr Campbell said, we are on track to reach Smokefree 2025, where 5 percent or less smoke.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand will meet the Smokefree 2025 goal of daily smoking prevalence at or below 5 percent.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the survey year covering 2025: true if it is 5 percent or less, false if it is above 5 percent.

focus.statement: Why is it that the purpose statement that read “to prevent the harmful effect of other people’s smoking on the health of others, and especially on young people and children;” is now removed from the purpose of the Act?
focus.explanation: Names the exact provision of the purpose clause that has been deleted and asks about that change. Entirely about the measure before the House, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The language in the previous Act said “preventing”. That is much stronger language, and so when we hear about the Minister’s other plans, which we’re told will be the subject of a future Cabinet paper—and we recognise that we do have to wait to hear what these initiatives will be, uncomfortable though that is—it does seem that there are rather large policy changes afoot here.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the drafting of the bill's purpose clause and the government's stated policy programme; no party characterisation at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why is it that the purpose statement that read “to prevent the harmful effect of other people’s smoking on the health of others, and especially on young people and children;” is now removed from the purpose of the Act?
specificity.explanation: Quotes the specific statutory paragraph being removed; anyone could check the bill text against the principal Act. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Tragically, babies die from second-hand smoking through sudden, unexpected death in infancy (SUDI).
veracity.explanation: Asserts that second-hand smoke exposure contributes to infant deaths from SUDI.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / peer-reviewed SUDI epidemiology on risk factors: true if exposure to second-hand smoke is established as a causal or strongly associated risk factor for sudden unexpected death in infancy; false if the literature does not support such an association.

veracity.statement: In 2022 the amendment Act said, “to restrict” marketing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2022 amendment's purpose section used the verb “restrict” in relation to marketing, in contrast to the bill's “regulate and control”.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 3A of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act as amended by the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022: true if the marketing paragraph of the purpose section uses the word “restrict”, false if it uses different wording.

veracity.statement: We also have plain packaging—a change proudly brought in by a National Government, as we heard during the second reading.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that New Zealand has plain packaging of tobacco and that it was introduced by a National government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enactment record of the Smoke-free Environments (Tobacco Plain Packaging) Amendment Act 2016: true if standardised/plain packaging was legislated for while a National-led government held office, false if it was enacted under a different government.

rigor.statement: The language in the previous Act said “preventing”. That is much stronger language, and so when we hear about the Minister’s other plans, which we’re told will be the subject of a future Cabinet paper—and we recognise that we do have to wait to hear what these initiatives will be, uncomfortable though that is—it does seem that there are rather large policy changes afoot here.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: a weakening of the purpose verbs from “preventing” to “discouraging”, combined with an unseen Cabinet paper, is offered as evidence of larger policy change. The textual premise is genuine, but there is a gap between a change in purpose wording and a conclusion about substantive policy intent, and the unseen paper is an argument from what has not been shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I do hope that we’ll be able to get answers for those because, of course, as we’ve heard, we have not been able to have a select committee on this bill.
civility.explanation: A contested point in an urgency debate — the absence of select committee scrutiny — put entirely as a criticism of process. No imputation of bad faith and nothing aimed at the Minister personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I find it appalling that members of the Government stand and read off notes, that they have not acquainted themselves with the arguments of this incredibly serious matter before us today.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith and wilful ignorance to named opponents (Government members) rather than engaging what they argued — sneering at how they are behaving, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So it is disingenuous for the previous speaker, Cameron Brewer, to say that it was their Government.
civility.explanation: Calls a named member disingenuous, i.e. imputes deliberate deception to the person rather than simply disputing the historical claim.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why does the Minister seem to have lines that echo very clearly with those of the tobacco lobby?
civility.explanation: Insinuates that a named individual is acting for the tobacco industry — an imputation of corrupt motive aimed at the person, framed as a question.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m not going to be lectured to by those who drove our health system into the ground, to hear the Leader of the Opposition, who clearly cares so much about this that we haven’t seen him in the House ever since he spoke.
civility.explanation: A sarcastic attack on a named individual's sincerity and attendance rather than on any argument he made — a personal jibe, not a policy criticism.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’ll tell you why, because they seem to hate Māori—they seem to hate Māori.
focus.explanation: An assertion about the other side's motives with no policy mechanism, figure or outcome named; strip out the claim about what the Government is 'really like' and nothing about the bill remains. No individual is insulted, so this is a Focus failure, not a Civility one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There have been Official Information Act requests on vaping from leading New Zealand media. The Minister has failed to answer any one of them.
focus.explanation: Named process (OIA requests on vaping) and a named specific failure to respond. This is scrutiny of a policy record, which is the opposition's job, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Madam Speaker, I’m not going to stand here and listen to members opposite parading around on their moral high horses as if they’re the Midas of anti-smoking.
focus.explanation: Entirely about how the other side is posturing; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. Remove the characterisation of opponents and nothing about the bill is left.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They haven’t banned smoking; the ban was going to trickle in slowly over the next 80 to 90 years. Well, frankly, I say a ban in 90 years is not a ban at all.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the design and phase-in of the smokefree generation ban — with a timeframe named. On-policy even though the inference drawn from it is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We heard from Dr Tracey McLellan that perhaps there could be changes around the nicotine levels that were a compromise, or the age of sale, or perhaps, at least—at least—get the outlets away from our schools.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete amendable mechanisms — nicotine levels, age of sale, retailer proximity to schools — but supplies no figures, thresholds or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is a product that kills half the people that use it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that tobacco kills approximately 50% of long-term users. A quantified epidemiological claim, not an opinion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: WHO tobacco fact sheets and the long-running British Doctors Study / equivalent cohort mortality literature; true if roughly half of lifelong smokers are found to die of a smoking-caused disease, false if the established figure is materially below that (e.g. nearer a quarter).

veracity.statement: It happened in 1984 when Marilyn Waring was nearly stopped from speaking on a nuclear bill. She threatened to cross the floor and it resulted in a snap election.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two historical facts: that Waring was nearly prevented from speaking on nuclear-free legislation, and that her threat to cross the floor caused the 1984 snap election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary reporting and parliamentary/historical accounts of June 1984; true if Waring publicly said she would cross the floor to support the Nuclear Free New Zealand Bill and Muldoon cited that in calling the snap election, false if the crossing-the-floor threat is not linked to the election call or the 'nearly stopped from speaking' element is unsupported.

veracity.statement: She was told that the health gains for Māori would be five times that of the general population.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice to the Associate Minister quantified Māori health gains from the smokefree measures at five times those for the general population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Health advice and regulatory impact material released to Guyon Espiner / RNZ in February 2024; true if that advice states a roughly fivefold differential in health gain for Māori, false if no such figure appears or the stated multiple is materially different.

veracity.statement: They haven’t banned smoking; the ban was going to trickle in slowly over the next 80 to 90 years. Well, frankly, I say a ban in 90 years is not a ban at all.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2022 smokefree generation measure was not in force and would have taken 80 to 90 years to take effect.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 commencement dates and the design of the birth-cohort sale ban; true if the sale ban had not commenced as at February 2024 and full cohort coverage would take roughly 80-90 years, false if the ban was already in force or reaches full effect materially sooner.

veracity.statement: They have halved smoking in New Zealand in the last 10 years, and they will get us through the next 10 as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that smoking prevalence in New Zealand fell by at least half over the decade to 2024 under the existing measures the bill retains.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for adults, 2013/14 compared with 2022/23; true if the 2022/23 rate is at or below half the 2013/14 rate, false if the decline is materially less than half.

rigor.statement: They haven’t banned smoking; the ban was going to trickle in slowly over the next 80 to 90 years. Well, frankly, I say a ban in 90 years is not a ban at all.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: from the premise that the generation ban phases in over decades it concludes it is 'not a ban at all', which does not follow — a delayed or gradual prohibition is still a prohibition. Nothing is offered to bridge slow onset to non-existence.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They have halved smoking in New Zealand in the last 10 years, and they will get us through the next 10 as well.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the retained tobacco control measures alone will continue to drive smoking prevalence down over the following decade.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence in 2033/34 compared with 2023/24; true if the rate has continued to fall substantially (reaching or approaching the 5% Smokefree goal), false if it plateaus or rises.

veracity.statement: A regulatory impact statement was not prepared for the bill, as this was part of the Government’s 100-day plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no regulatory impact statement was prepared for the Smokefree repeal bill, and that the stated reason was its inclusion in the Government's 100-day plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) (Repeal) Amendment Bill (2024), section on regulatory impact analysis; true if it records that no RIS was prepared and cites the 100-day plan, false if a RIS is recorded as prepared.

veracity.statement: Well, I would ask the Minister: what is her definition of “external consultation”, given that we have 9,000 doctors who were begging for this repeal not to happen and who wrote to the Prime Minister?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 9,000 doctors wrote to the Prime Minister opposing the repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The open letter from health professionals to the Prime Minister on the smokefree repeal (early 2024) and contemporaneous reporting of its signatory count; true if roughly 9,000 doctors signed a letter addressed to the PM, false if the signatory count or the addressee is materially different.

veracity.statement: The purpose of the original Act, the one that is being repealed, the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022, is to stop people taking up smoking in the first place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the purpose provision of the named 2022 Act is.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The purpose section of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022; true if it states an aim of preventing/reducing uptake of smoking, false if its stated purpose is materially different.

veracity.statement: But, as I said in my second reading speech, the only entities or organisations that we can meaningfully identify in the public realm who were opposed to the Government in the last term passing the legislation were the likes of New Zealand First—the only party, I might add, of Government to propose that the legislation should be repealed—and the tobacco industry.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the only publicly identifiable opponents of the 2022 smokefree legislation were New Zealand First and the tobacco industry, and that NZ First was the only current governing party to propose repealing it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record for the readings of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill 2022, the submissions received by the Health Committee, and the three 2023 coalition/confidence-and-supply agreements; false if other parties now in government (e.g. National or ACT) voted against the 2022 Bill or proposed its repeal, or if identifiable non-tobacco organisations submitted against it; true if only NZ First and tobacco-linked entities are on record opposing.

veracity.statement: Notably, the tobacco industry was backing a campaign that was fronted by those dairy owners.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the public campaign run by dairy owners against the smokefree measures was backed by the tobacco industry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reporting, company statements and any disclosed funding records for the retailer campaign against the smokefree law (e.g. the dairy/retailer 'save our stores'-type campaign); true if a tobacco company is documented as funding, organising or supplying material for it, false if the campaign is shown to be independently funded by retailers.

veracity.statement: As previous speakers have alluded to, in the departmental disclosure statement, we have here at paragraph 2.5 a point from departmental officials saying that there has not been any analysis on potential costs and benefit, yet we have it—to be read contemporaneously with Official Information Act requests from Treasury and officials advising the Government—that there is going to be an approximate $500 million increase in revenue.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that paragraph 2.5 of the disclosure statement records no cost-benefit analysis, and that Treasury/officials' advice released under the OIA projects roughly $500 million of additional revenue from the repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Paragraph 2.5 of the Bill's departmental disclosure statement, and the Treasury/Ministry of Health advice released under the OIA in early 2024; true if the disclosure statement records no cost-benefit analysis and the released advice estimates additional excise revenue of about $500 million, false if either the paragraph or the revenue figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Actually, I’d point the Minister to one of the clauses that we got in the legislation, which is presently being repealed, which required the Ministry of Health to review the efficacy of the legislation, which is something that I managed to get in through the Health Committee process, because these were novel, world-first measures.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2022 Act contains a clause requiring the Ministry of Health to review the legislation's efficacy, and that this clause was inserted at her instigation during the Health Committee stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The review provision of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 and the Health Committee's report on the Bill (including the committee's recommended amendments and their attribution); true if such a review clause exists and the committee record shows it was added at select committee, false if no review clause exists or it was in the Bill as introduced.

rigor.statement: And that’s a really interesting point that I would like to understand, because all the evidence would show that those who are affected by smoking-related illness, many of them will suffer a huge loss of income or wealth that would be avoidable should they not have taken up smoking.
rigor.explanation: Advances an inference about the disclosure statement's 'no substantial unavoidable loss of income or wealth' answer, but rests it on a bare appeal to unnamed evidence ('all the evidence would show'); it also conflates 'unavoidable' in the disclosure sense with 'avoidable by not smoking', so the conclusion slides past the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m really struggling with the idea that going to Government agencies is considered external consultation.
rigor.explanation: The inference is short but sound: 'external' consultation is contrasted with internal government process, and the listed consultees are all government agencies, so the conclusion tracks the premise. Weakness is only that the definitional premise is left implicit.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I would ask the Minister: what is her definition of “external consultation”, given that we have 9,000 doctors who were begging for this repeal not to happen and who wrote to the Prime Minister?
specificity.explanation: Carries a named figure (9,000), a named group (doctors) and a named action (a letter to the Prime Minister) — checkable rather than a general appeal to public opinion.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As previous speakers have alluded to, in the departmental disclosure statement, we have here at paragraph 2.5 a point from departmental officials saying that there has not been any analysis on potential costs and benefit, yet we have it—to be read contemporaneously with Official Information Act requests from Treasury and officials advising the Government—that there is going to be an approximate $500 million increase in revenue.
specificity.explanation: Names the document, the paragraph number, the source of the counter-evidence (Treasury OIA material) and a figure ($500 million) — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m really struggling with the idea that going to Government agencies is considered external consultation.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific line in the bill's disclosure statement — which bodies were consulted and whether they count as external — rather than the other party's character or record in general.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: More so than that, why is it that every stage of this is going through under urgency—what is she afraid of?
civility.explanation: The procedural question is legitimate, but the closing rhetorical jab imputes fear and concealment to the Minister personally rather than criticising the use of urgency itself — bad faith imputed to a person, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is clause 7, which repeals section 3AB(a) to (c) of the principal Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause of the bill and the exact section of the principal Act it repeals — precisely checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The clauses have been drafted to remove the purposes that reflected the previous Government policies regarding retail reduction, low nicotine, and smoke-free. That is the reason why that language has changed.
specificity.explanation: Names the three policy strands being removed from the purpose section, but gives no drafting detail, figures or replacement mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Under my time as the Minister, we established 11 of them, and there were a couple more still in the pipeline.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 11 iwi-Māori partnership boards were established during his own time as Minister, with more in progress — offered to rebut the claim that the boards do not yet exist.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Ministry of Health records of iwi-Māori partnership boards formally established before the November 2023 change of government; true if 11 were established during Henare's tenure with further boards in progress, false if the number established under him was materially different.

veracity.statement: I will note that the matter for urgency arises from both New Zealand First and ACT’s coalition agreement with National, which placed this into the 100-day plan, which is why the urgency is required.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that both coalition agreements (NZ First–National and ACT–National) contain this repeal and that it was placed in the Government's 100-day plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–NZ First and National–ACT coalition agreements (November 2023) and the Government's 100-day plan; true if the repeal of the smokefree retail measures appears in both coalition agreements and in the 100-day plan, false if it appears in only one agreement or is absent from the 100-day plan.

veracity.statement: So we have retained the requirement to consult, and we will continue to do so.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a consultation requirement survives the repeal of section 3AB, i.e. that the bill as drafted still obliges the Minister to consult on these matters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill 2024 as passed, compared with section 3AB of the principal Act; true if a provision requiring consultation with Māori or Māori interests remains in force after the repeal, false if only a weaker duty to "consider" risks and benefits, or no duty at all, remains.

veracity.statement: But, you know, when we had this going through the House supported by experts as world-leading and incredibly important as far as evidence-based policy goes, the only opposition that we heard was from the tobacco industry—granted, with the astroturf sometimes of those involved in the dairy sector—but also from the likes of New Zealand First.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that opposition to the original smokefree legislation came only from the tobacco industry, dairy-sector-aligned groups, and New Zealand First.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Submissions to the Health Committee on the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill 2022 and the recorded readings; true if every opposing submitter and party falls into those three categories, false if other independent opposing submitters or parties (e.g. ACT, retail bodies unconnected to the dairy sector, individual public health or civil-liberties submitters) are on the record.

civility.statement: Now, Mr Simeon Brown might chirp away on that side of the Chamber in arrogant bliss of what’s taking place here, but the fact of the matter is that in his electorate, Ngāi Tai, or the iwi there, I’m pretty sure they haven’t spoken to Minister Costello about this particular bill, and that’s the point that I want to make.
civility.explanation: "Chirp away ... in arrogant bliss" is a personal jibe at a named member's character and attentiveness, not at his argument. The consultation point that follows does not undo the opening insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to thank the Minister for making an attempt to engage in some of those questions, but with complete and full respect—because I genuinely would like to meaningfully dig into this—I don’t quite feel as though we got a very clear answer.
civility.explanation: Criticism aimed entirely at the adequacy of the answer, with explicit acknowledgement of the Minister's attempt. "Making an attempt" carries a faint edge, short of anything personal.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, Mr Simeon Brown might chirp away on that side of the Chamber in arrogant bliss of what’s taking place here, but the fact of the matter is that in his electorate, Ngāi Tai, or the iwi there, I’m pretty sure they haven’t spoken to Minister Costello about this particular bill, and that’s the point that I want to make.
focus.explanation: A real policy point — that a named iwi in a named electorate has not been consulted on this bill — but it is carried on the back of a swipe at the member opposite.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The clauses have been drafted to remove the purposes that reflected the previous Government policies regarding retail reduction, low nicotine, and smoke-free. That is the reason why that language has changed.
focus.explanation: Answers squarely on the mechanics of the clause before the Committee; no party framing beyond identifying whose policy is being removed.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What it does is it actually continues, despite the words of the Prime Minister, saying that they won’t support a Treaty principles bill by the ACT Party past the second reading, but the National Party are going to do it by subterfuge anyway.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the repeal of one Treaty clause in a tobacco Act is offered as sufficient to conclude the Government is enacting a Treaty principles bill covertly. Nothing is offered to bridge the single repeal to that far broader conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I will note that the matter for urgency arises from both New Zealand First and ACT’s coalition agreement with National, which placed this into the 100-day plan, which is why the urgency is required.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that urgency "is required" rests only on the measure appearing in a self-imposed 100-day plan — an appeal to the Government's own timetable rather than a reason why the House must forgo normal process.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we had there was an outlining of the reason that this is being introduced to the House—it’s because it’s in the coalition agreement between New Zealand First and the National Party—and this is, in philosophy, known as a tautology, where we are hearing that something is occurring because it’s in the plan, because it’s in the plan, because it’s in the plan, because it’s in the plan.
rigor.explanation: Correctly identifies that citing the coalition agreement answers "why is it happening" only by restating that it was decided — circular as a justification. Slightly mislabelled (it is circularity, not strictly a tautology), but the inference itself holds.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Where has this come from, if not from the tobacco industry? Because that’s where logic takes us.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy resting on absence of evidence: because no other supporting organisation has been identified, the tobacco industry is treated as the only remaining source. Unenumerated alternatives are excluded without argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So we are ending up with, instead of being on the track for a reduced number of people as a result of the plan that this Government is now repealing, more people going to be smoking than otherwise would.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the retail-reduction, denicotinisation and smokefree-generation measures will leave smoking prevalence higher than it would have been had those measures remained.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence together with published Ministry of Health or peer-reviewed modelling of the repeal; true if observed prevalence exceeds the projected path under the retained measures, false if prevalence matches or beats that projected path.

civility.statement: We understand that sometimes urgency is needed, but certainly not in the passage of this bill where it is only seeking to deprive us of the opportunity to hear from those who might have a contrary view to the Government.
civility.explanation: Pointed and robust: it imputes a suppressive motive, but to the Government's handling of the bill rather than to any individual member, and no person's character or competence is touched. Sits just below the civil standard because of the motive imputation, not because the criticism is hard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I asked the Minister earlier a series of questions about the purpose, and I don’t believe she has adequately answered them because what her amendment bill is changing is effectively repealing the 2022 amendment. And yet there are changes to the purpose statement that alter the interpretation of other parts of the original Act from 1990.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the bill's purpose clause, the 2022 amendment it repeals, and the 1990 Act whose interpretation is affected. Named provisions, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I call on the Government, I call on coalition parties in the Government, to honour the statements that they are making in this House to reduce rates of smoking and to take my amendment and to just add on “to support personal choice”.
focus.explanation: Addressed to the coalition parties, but the ask is a named, specific amendment to the measure before the committee rather than a characterisation of the other side. Slightly below full marks because the appeal is framed around the parties' consistency rather than the amendment's effect.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I asked the Minister earlier a series of questions about the purpose, and I don’t believe she has adequately answered them because what her amendment bill is changing is effectively repealing the 2022 amendment. And yet there are changes to the purpose statement that alter the interpretation of other parts of the original Act from 1990.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from stated premises: if the bill is only a narrow repeal, the purpose statement should not be altered in ways that reach other parts of the parent Act; since it is, the stated scope and the drafted scope diverge. The conclusion tracks the premises; the gap is that she does not spell out which interpretive consequences follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If this Government does have a conscience, if the Government does indeed want to reduce rates of smoking, then it will accept my amendment, which adds on to or builds on the 2003 conventions from the World Health Organisation, which says we want to reduce harm from tobacco smoking.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: wanting to reduce smoking does not entail accepting this particular amendment, since a government could pursue the same goal by other means or object to this drafting. The conditional also converts rejection into evidence of bad conscience, an appeal to motive that does nothing to support the amendment's merits.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The excise tax increases in New Zealand that have been successful at bringing down smoking rates means that we have some of the highest priced cigarettes in the world, and therefore you’d think we would have the biggest illicit market in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that New Zealand cigarette prices are among the highest in the world and (b) that excise increases have reduced smoking rates. The closing clause is a rhetorical set-up for her question about the illicit market, not itself a factual assertion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cross-country retail price comparison for a 20-cigarette pack (WHO Report on the Global Tobacco Epidemic price/tax appendix, or an equivalent PPP-adjusted price table) for the year of the statement: true if New Zealand sits in the top handful of countries by pack price, false if it is materially outside that top group. The subsidiary premise — that excise increases coincided with falling smoking rates — is checkable against Stats NZ / Ministry of Health adult smoking prevalence over the excise-increase period.

veracity.statement: I was there. I was the Associate Minister of Health and I was advised by one Ashley Bloomfield.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker attended the Geneva adoption of the WHO FCTC in May 2003 in the capacity of Associate Minister of Health, advised by Ashley Bloomfield.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand ministerial warrants / ministerial lists for May 2003 and the record of the New Zealand delegation to the World Health Assembly that adopted the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control in Geneva on 21 May 2003: true if O'Connor held the Associate Minister of Health portfolio at that date and was part of the delegation, false if he held neither.

veracity.statement: Indeed, it’s said that nicotine is more addictive than heroin. That is, people who use it find it harder to break away from that than they do from heroin.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a comparative empirical claim — that nicotine dependence is harder to break than heroin dependence. He introduces it as reported speech but immediately endorses it ("That's a fact"), so it is his own assertion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparative dependence-liability evidence: expert drug-harm and dependence rankings (e.g. Nutt et al.), DSM-based dependence prevalence among users of each substance, and cessation/relapse rates for smoking versus opioid dependence. True if those standard measures place nicotine's dependence liability, or the difficulty of quitting, above heroin's; false if heroin ranks at or above nicotine on them.

specificity.statement: What I want to know from the Minister is: what advice did she receive about the size of the illicit market in New Zealand?
specificity.explanation: Names a definite thing to be produced — official advice on the size of the illicit tobacco market — so it is actionable and checkable. But it carries no figure, date or document title, so it is short of a fully precise ask.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And I would create clarity around the fact that this was in both ACT and New Zealand First’s coalition—so it has come from two parties in the three coalition Government and that’s why we are moving it through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal of the smokefree measures appeared in the coalition agreements of both ACT and New Zealand First, i.e. in two of the three governing parties' agreements with National, rather than only one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published texts of the National–ACT and National–New Zealand First coalition agreements (24 November 2023); true if a commitment to repeal/amend the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act amendments appears in both documents, false if it appears in only one.

veracity.statement: And finally, just in terms of the final comment from the member, “We know more outlets create greater uptake”, I would suggest that that is contrary to our evidence we’re sitting with at the moment given that we have seen a massive reduction with the same amount of outlets that we’ve got currently.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of fact that New Zealand has seen a large fall in smoking while the number of tobacco retail outlets has stayed at its current level.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey daily smoking prevalence series over the decade to 2023 alongside estimates of tobacco retailer numbers (Ministry of Health / Smokefree Environments retailer estimates); true if prevalence fell substantially while retailer numbers were broadly unchanged, false if prevalence was flat or retailer numbers fell materially over the same period.
