veracity.statement: So when we have 6,000 outlets which are unregulated, selling these products, they are very likely having an effect on our psychology at the very least—and the psychology of our children who are walking past those outlets all the time, because we had normalised that behaviour.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual premise: that there are around 6,000 tobacco retail outlets in New Zealand and that who may sell these products is not regulated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act documentation on tobacco retailer numbers as at February 2024, and whether a retailer registration or approval scheme was then in force; true if the estimate is near 6,000 and no retailer licensing regime was operative, false if the count is materially different or retailers were already registered/licensed.

veracity.statement: What we are having here is a bill that we only saw yesterday and that we are now debating in all-stages urgency.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts about the passage of this bill: that members first saw it the day before this debate, and that it is being taken through all stages under urgency in a single sitting.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's introduction date and Order Paper/urgency motion record on legislation.govt.nz and the Hansard for 26–27 February 2024; true if the bill was introduced/made available the day before this debate and all stages were taken under urgency, false if it had been available longer or was not being progressed through all stages.

rigor.statement: But I’d note that this illicit market existed at a time when none of these measures that we’re talking about were in place, and, therefore, it would be hard to quantify what the illicit market would look like if these measures, which we were now repealing, had been implemented.
rigor.explanation: A valid counterfactual point: if the illicit market predates the measures, then the measures' effect on it cannot be read off the current level. The conclusion drawn ('hard to quantify') is appropriately modest and follows from the premise offered; it does not overclaim that the measures would have had no effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And finally, just in terms of the final comment from the member, “We know more outlets create greater uptake”, I would suggest that that is contrary to our evidence we’re sitting with at the moment given that we have seen a massive reduction with the same amount of outlets that we’ve got currently.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur against the claim being rebutted. The member's claim is about the marginal effect of *more* outlets; a fall in smoking while outlet numbers held constant is consistent with that claim, since other interventions (price, packaging, cessation) are uncontrolled confounders. Falling prevalence at fixed outlet density is not evidence about varying outlet density.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The health impacts of tobacco mean that people who already have the least may struggle to access the health services that they need to address some of that harm, and so that’s why I’m focusing on those agencies.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with a stated premise and conclusion: if tobacco harm compounds for low-income people who face access barriers, then the social-sector agencies' consultation feedback is relevant to the bill. The step holds, but it is hedged ('may struggle') and the link from the general premise to the specific agencies named is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So when we have 6,000 outlets which are unregulated, selling these products, they are very likely having an effect on our psychology at the very least—and the psychology of our children who are walking past those outlets all the time, because we had normalised that behaviour.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to analogy and anecdote. The conclusion that outlet density is 'very likely' shaping public psychology rests on the earlier analogy with the indoor smoking ban and on the speaker's own change of attitude; no evidence is offered connecting outlet numbers to the psychological effect claimed, and the analogy is to a different intervention (where people smoke, not where it is sold).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Obviously, there are a lot of sitting days in that 100 days and there would have been ample opportunity for the Government to be true to all their policy decisions—which, of course, I think are terrible but I’m commenting here on the process.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premise offered: if the 100-day window contained many sitting days, the deadline does not by itself require all-stages urgency, so the stated justification is insufficient. The speaker also explicitly quarantines her view of the policy from the process argument, so the conclusion does not rest on it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I’m interested to know whether a child impact assessment report was done as part of the process of this bill, and, if not, I’m really interested to understand why that wasn’t the case, because that is a tool that exists to further assess the impacts of policy on children.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and the process that produced it — a named analytical instrument applied to this bill. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I wanted to know whether the Minister had sought advice, or would seek advice, over the impact of the number and availability of those outlets and would consider, while she waits for that advice, not changing the law here, because this itself could be an experiment.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at the provision before the committee — whether advice exists on outlet number and availability, and whether the repeal should wait on it. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I’m interested to know whether a child impact assessment report was done as part of the process of this bill, and, if not, I’m really interested to understand why that wasn’t the case, because that is a tool that exists to further assess the impacts of policy on children.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific, existing instrument (a child impact assessment report) and asks a question with a determinate answer — it was either done or it was not. Short of full marks because no timeframe, threshold or figure is attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I wanted to know whether the Minister had sought advice, or would seek advice, over the impact of the number and availability of those outlets and would consider, while she waits for that advice, not changing the law here, because this itself could be an experiment.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific advice sought (impact of the number and availability of outlets) and a specific alternative course (leave the law unchanged while the advice is obtained), but carries no figures, no timeframe and no named report.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If there were concerns from those agencies, actually we would invite a more robust debate, because that doesn’t even have anything to do with the use of urgency, which we oppose.
civility.explanation: A contested point — the speaker's party opposes the urgency and the bill — argued entirely on the substance of process and evidence. No person is characterised, no bad faith imputed. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I’ve heard from her today is she simply doesn’t consider that is an issue because this hasn’t happened yet, so how would we tell?
civility.explanation: Pointed and slightly dismissive in characterising the Minister as 'simply' not considering it an issue, which edges toward the person's attentiveness, but it lands on her stated position rather than on her character or competence. Robust rather than uncivil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Obviously, there are a lot of sitting days in that 100 days and there would have been ample opportunity for the Government to be true to all their policy decisions—which, of course, I think are terrible but I’m commenting here on the process.
civility.explanation: 'Terrible' is aimed at the Government's policy decisions, not at any person, and the speaker expressly sets that judgement aside to argue the process point. Harsh about the policy, civil toward the people.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Previously, it was to regulate the safety of vaping products and smokeless tobacco products.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the pre-amendment wording of the purpose provision (now clause 5's new paragraph (g)) referred specifically to vaping products and smokeless tobacco products, rather than the generic "regulated products".
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 3A of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act as it stood immediately before the bill, compared with clause 5 of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill; true if the earlier paragraph names vaping products and smokeless tobacco products and the new one says "regulated products", false if the wording is unchanged.

veracity.statement: So we are looking to change the legislation, but none of these measures are actually implemented as of yet, so I think we need to work forward from that position.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the measures the bill repeals had not yet come into force at the time of the debate (27 February 2024) — that is, the retailer-reduction, denicotinisation and smokefree-generation provisions of the 2022 amendments were enacted but not operative.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provisions of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 and the dates on which each measure was to take effect; true if none of the repealed measures were in force on 27 February 2024, false if any of them had already commenced.

veracity.statement: I think that that’s why we keep going back to the statistics: we have driven down demand significantly with what’s in place and our young smokers have been a significant reduction—down to just 19,000 young smokers now—so we will continue to work on those aspects that are working.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific current figure — 19,000 young smokers in New Zealand — as evidence that demand has fallen significantly.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Health Survey (or ASH Year 10 Snapshot) estimate of young smokers current at February 2024, on the age band the Minister is using; true if the figure is approximately 19,000 on a defensible reading of the published series, false if the published estimate is materially different or if no published series supports it.

veracity.statement: I have some focus questions and I’m wanting to examine, with the Associate Minister of Health the Hon Casey Costello, clause 5, amending the purpose of the Act, noting that there’s a removal of the purpose to reduce disparities in smoking rates and illness between the New Zealand population and the Māori population.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clause 5 removes from the Act's purpose section the objective of reducing the disparity in smoking rates and smoking-related illness between the New Zealand population and the Māori population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The purpose provision (section 3A) of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act as amended in 2022, compared with the replacement purpose section in clause 5 of the bill; true if a Māori-disparity purpose appears in the former and not the latter, false if it is retained or was never there.

veracity.statement: In closing, thinking about, you know, iwi Māori engagement, as members of te Iwi o Ngātiwai, Minister, I noted on Facebook today that te Poari o Ngātiwai, our Iwi Trust Board, made a post to remind the Minister of Health, Dr Shane Reti, that on 14 December a letter was furnished to the Minister outlining concerns around the smoke-free environments repeal to come.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim made publicly by te Poari o Ngātiwai: that a letter dated 14 December 2023 raising concerns about the smokefree repeal was sent to the Minister of Health, Shane Reti. The speaker is reporting the trust board's post, not asserting it from her own records.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The te Poari o Ngātiwai / Ngātiwai Trust Board public Facebook page on or about 27 February 2024, plus any Ministerial correspondence record released under the OIA; true if such a post exists describing a 14 December 2023 letter to Minister Reti, false if no such post or letter is evidenced.

civility.statement: There may be a great policy reason for this change, but I don’t know it and this is the only time we get to scrutinise this bill.
civility.explanation: A pointed criticism of the Government's use of all-stages urgency, aimed entirely at the process and the drafting change. It imputes no bad faith and attacks no person, while conceding there may be a good reason for the change.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Further, wanting to dig into Te Tiriti compliance, were there any Te Tiriti audits conducted on this repeal, or have you had any advice, whether it’s from Crown officials or legal advisers, in terms of whether this repeal is Te Tiriti compliant?
civility.explanation: A challenge on genuinely contested ground — whether the repeal breaches Te Tiriti — put entirely as a question about process and advice. It would have been easy to allege bad faith or indifference here; she does not, and attacks no person.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what this is is to add in section 20OA, “Proximity of tobacco retailers to schools”, and that is that the director-general must ensure, when granting a person approval to be an approved smoked tobacco retailer, that any premises is not within 1 kilometre of a school.
specificity.explanation: Names the new section, the decision-maker (the director-general), the trigger (granting approved smoked tobacco retailer status) and an exact distance (1 kilometre). Fully checkable and directly actionable as drafted.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I want to unpack that a little bit, and query with the Minister: did she consider the 2011 Māori Affairs Committee inquiry into the tobacco industry and the impacts of tobacco on Māori?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific, identifiable document — the 2011 Māori Affairs Committee inquiry into the tobacco industry and the consequences of tobacco use for Māori — so the question is precisely answerable and the answer checkable. Short of full marks only because it asks whether the report was "considered" without specifying what use of it would count.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Obviously, if you cannot have premises near a school, that is a good way of achieving that purpose.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy — the proximity restriction is offered as a means to the stated statutory purpose of reducing appeal and harm to children — but the connection is asserted as self-evident ("Obviously") with no evidence or mechanism supplied linking retailer distance to youth uptake. A gap between what was shown and what was concluded, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that that’s why we keep going back to the statistics: we have driven down demand significantly with what’s in place and our young smokers have been a significant reduction—down to just 19,000 young smokers now—so we will continue to work on those aspects that are working.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: a fall in youth smoking numbers is attributed to "what's in place" and used to conclude that those measures are "working" and should continue. Nothing is offered to separate the effect of existing policy from the long-running secular decline in youth smoking, and no counterfactual is addressed. The conclusion outruns the evidence given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because these policies have been removed from the Act, the purpose statement was revised to reflect the substance of what remains in the Act.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference on its own terms: if the substantive provisions a purpose clause described are repealed, revising the purpose clause to match what remains follows directly. The premise (that the underlying policies were removed) is a Veracity question, not a defect in the reasoning.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And it really perplexes me, as a Māori who is heavily impacted by smoking, why we remove a piece of the legislation that actually provides focus—it provides focus for our policy makers and then for those who will procure services to meet these new legislative guidelines.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy: a statutory purpose directs officials and service procurement, so deleting it weakens that direction. The mechanism is named, but the claim rests on assertion plus the speaker's own experience rather than any evidence that the purpose clause has in fact shaped procurement decisions — a partial appeal to personal standing.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I have some focus questions and I’m wanting to examine, with the Associate Minister of Health the Hon Casey Costello, clause 5, amending the purpose of the Act, noting that there’s a removal of the purpose to reduce disparities in smoking rates and illness between the New Zealand population and the Māori population.
focus.explanation: Names the specific clause (clause 5), the specific provision being amended (the purpose section) and the specific element removed (the disparities purpose). Squarely on the measure before the committee, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In Tāmaki-makau-rau, there are 250,000 Māori, 80 percent of them do not belong to the iwi in Tāmaki-makau-rau.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two population facts: that Auckland has 250,000 Māori, and that 80 percent of them are not affiliated to Auckland iwi (i.e. are mataawaka).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census figures for Māori ethnicity/Māori descent usually resident in the Auckland region, and the census iwi affiliation tables for Ngāti Whātua and other Tāmaki-makaurau iwi; true if the Auckland Māori count is approximately 250,000 and roughly 80% report no Tāmaki iwi affiliation, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Hashtags were the core group that had a petition and lobbied Government to ban smoking in cars, and they were successful in that legislation being passed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Wainuiōmata youth group, the Hashtags, were the core petitioners/lobbyists behind the ban on smoking in cars carrying children, and that the ban was enacted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary petition records and Health Committee reports on smoking in vehicles, plus the enactment record of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Prohibiting Smoking in Motor Vehicles Carrying Children) Amendment Act 2020; true if a Hashtags petition/submission is on the record and the Act passed, false if no such petition exists or the group had no identifiable role.

veracity.statement: I would remind and reiterate that we are retaining the requirement to consider the impact on Māori in regulating a constituent, including to both users and non-users of smoked tobacco products, so we are continuing to ensure that that is addressed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the requirement to consider the impact on Māori when regulating a constituent of smoked tobacco products survives this bill rather than being repealed with the retail-reduction provisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill (No 2) as against the principal Act's constituent-regulation provisions; true if the duty to consider impacts on Māori, including users and non-users, remains in the Act after the amendments, false if the bill repeals or narrows it.

veracity.statement: I think that we are needing to kind of consider that when you talk about single cigarette sales etc., those are the unfortunate flags of the black market, which are imported as single cigarette quantities, and that’s what we’re hoping to ensure that we can control moving forward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that single cigarettes sold at retail in New Zealand are an indicator of the illicit market and are imported already in single-cigarette form, rather than being loose sticks broken out of legally purchased packets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Customs illicit tobacco seizure data and NZ tobacco-control research (e.g. ASH/University of Otago retail studies) on the source and packaging of single cigarettes sold in New Zealand; true if the evidence shows single cigarettes are predominantly imported as singles via the black market, false if they are predominantly split from legally sold packets.

specificity.statement: In Tāmaki-makau-rau, there are 250,000 Māori, 80 percent of them do not belong to the iwi in Tāmaki-makau-rau.
specificity.explanation: Carries a population count and a percentage, both checkable against census data, in support of a named representation gap.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have an amendment to be inserted after clause 9, and that is new clause 9C which inserts new section 20OC and that is that “The Director-General must ensure, when granting a person approval to be an approved smoked tobacco retailer, that any premises is not within one km of a marae”, a kaupapa that follows on quite nicely from the previous speaker, Takutai Tarsh Kemp.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the inserted section, the duty holder (the Director-General), the trigger (granting retailer approval) and an exact distance. Fully actionable and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are going to be focusing on building on the great work that has been highlighted, and we will continue to do so as we move forward, as I’ve previously noted in the recommendations of the next steps.
specificity.explanation: Offered as an answer on what the Government will do, but names no measure, figure, mechanism or timeframe — 'building on the great work' and 'as we move forward' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question is: how will the Minister ensure that the urban Māori voice will be heard and will be at the decision-making table alongside iwi Māori?
focus.explanation: Directed at the mechanism in the bill — how representation on iwi Māori partnership boards will cover urban Māori. No party framing; a precise question about the measure before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Marae are a physical depiction of the tinana—of the person, of the body—te mana, te tapu o te tangata, an argument which, sadly, I have not heard coming from that side of the House.
focus.explanation: A genuine substantive point about why marae warrant protection under the amendment, but half its weight is a characterisation of what 'that side of the House' has failed to say rather than of the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I also love that when you ask someone, “Got a light?”, the answer is usually “No.” these days, and that can be largely attributed to the fact that marae, of their own volition, made their premises smoke-free to protect their whakapapa and our mokopuna.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy (voluntary smokefree marae reduced smoking), but it rests on a single conversational anecdote and attributes a broad decline in smoking to one cause without offering anything to rule out others — appeal to anecdote plus post hoc attribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill stops them from growing up in a smoke-free New Zealand, and this House stops them from having their voice heard when it directly impacts upon their wellbeing and their livelihoods, and I find that despicable.
civility.explanation: Extremely strong condemnation — 'despicable' — but aimed at the bill and at the House's decision to skip select committee, not at any member's character, competence or motives.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As the member over here mentioned, we know—the evidence is clear—that nicotine is more addictive than heroin.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as settled evidence that nicotine's addictive potential exceeds that of heroin.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed comparative dependence rankings (e.g. Nutt et al. drug dependence ratings) and WHO/NIDA statements on relative addictiveness; true if nicotine is rated more dependence-producing than heroin, false if heroin is rated at or above nicotine.

veracity.statement: Clause 12 repeals section 57I of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act. That section limited the content of nicotine in tobacco products to 0.8 milligrams.
veracity.explanation: Two factual claims: that clause 12 of the bill repeals s 57I, and that s 57I caps nicotine content at 0.8 mg.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 12 of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill and of section 57I as inserted by the 2022 Amendment Act, plus the prescribed limit; true if clause 12 repeals s 57I and the prescribed cap is 0.8 mg (per gram of tobacco), false if the section or figure differs.

veracity.statement: Denicotinisation takes that most addictive product known to man—nicotine—out of cigarettes, so that people can take control of the effect that this product has on them, and many, many people successfully quit when cigarettes are denicotinised.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that denicotinised cigarettes produce successful quitting in large numbers of smokers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Randomised controlled trials of very-low-nicotine cigarettes (e.g. Donny et al., NEJM 2015; University of Auckland trials); true if denicotinised cigarettes yield significantly higher cessation than normal-nicotine controls, false if cessation rates are not significantly improved.

veracity.statement: In fact, he moved amendments that the bill should remove the retail components but focus on denicotinisation because it was so impactful.
veracity.explanation: Claims Shane Reti moved amendments to the 2022 bill that would have stripped the retailer-reduction provisions while retaining denicotinisation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Supplementary Order Papers and committee-stage amendments lodged by Shane Reti on the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill 2022, per Hansard and the Order Paper; true if such an amendment exists, false if no amendment of that effect was moved by him.

specificity.statement: Clause 12 repeals section 57I of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act. That section limited the content of nicotine in tobacco products to 0.8 milligrams.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the section it repeals, the parent Act and the numeric limit at stake — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I just think, to quickly, again, reiterate—and I’m sorry to harp on—but the whole purpose of this legislation is to repeal the reduced retailers and the denicotinisation and the removal of the ban on persons born after 1 January 2009, so we’re revisiting these components.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the three provisions the bill repeals and gives the dated birth-cohort threshold; concrete enough to check against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would like to comment on and reinforce that we fully understand the issues of harm and, therefore, we are going to continue to work on those initiatives, as I’ve repeatedly said.
specificity.explanation: Responds to a direct question about advice and modelling with an assurance of understanding and unnamed 'initiatives' — no measure, mechanism, figure or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So what we’re seeing in this change is a reduction of the limits on nicotine in cigarettes, which is just beyond belief that anyone could consider doing such a thing.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on an appeal to incredulity — 'beyond belief that anyone could consider' does no work in showing the repeal is wrong. The preceding addictiveness premise is asserted rather than connected to the effect of removing the cap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But I’ve got a couple of questions here for the Minister that I would really like an authentic and deep response to, rather than a once over, just fly past.
civility.explanation: Pointed about the Minister's manner of answering and implies her replies are perfunctory, edging toward the person without landing on her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It would be very strange indeed if a party that supported that approach immediately before the election was now voting that approach down. That would be quite shameful and show a lack of respect for their health Minister, Dr Reti.
civility.explanation: 'Quite shameful' and 'a lack of respect' impute bad faith to opponents over a voting choice rather than engaging their reasons, though no individual is insulted.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What impact is the removal of nicotine limits expected to have on rates of quitting smoking?
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure before the committee and the specific outcome it is meant to affect; entirely on the policy, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It would be very strange indeed if a party that supported that approach immediately before the election was now voting that approach down. That would be quite shameful and show a lack of respect for their health Minister, Dr Reti.
focus.explanation: A named proposal (the denicotinisation amendment on the Table) and a specific vote are at issue, but the weight of the sentence is party-consistency framing rather than the merits of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There’s one question I have here: who wrote this bill?
civility.explanation: A rhetorical question that insinuates the bill was drafted by an outside interest rather than the Minister — pointed and edging toward an imputation, but oblique and aimed at no named person's character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I’m asking the Minister that if she’s not going to engage in substance when put those questions by the media, I would hope that at least she would honour the feedback that she’s been given by enriching us in this debate about what her response is to those papers that raise concern around reputation damage.
civility.explanation: Implies the Minister is dodging substantive questions, which edges toward the person rather than the policy, but it is framed conditionally and as a request for engagement rather than as an attack on her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I was Associate Minister of Health, and, indeed, I was the Minister at the time we took smoking out of bars.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker personally held the Associate Health portfolio and was the responsible Minister when smoking was removed from bars.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ ministerial lists (Beehive/Parliament records) and the bill record for the Smoke-free Environments Amendment Act 2003, which banned smoking in bars from December 2004; true if O'Connor held the Associate Minister of Health portfolio with responsibility for that legislation at the time, false if he did not.

veracity.statement: As was said, nicotine is more addictive than heroin, so it is critical that we reinsert a maximum level of nicotine.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a comparative factual claim about the addictiveness of nicotine relative to heroin, used as the premise for reinstating a nicotine cap.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published comparative dependence rankings (e.g. Henningfield–Benowitz expert ratings, WHO/NIDA addiction literature) for nicotine versus heroin; true if the weight of that literature ranks nicotine above heroin on dependence potential, false if heroin ranks at or above nicotine on the standard dependence measures.

veracity.statement: In fact, the provisions under clause 12—which my amendment refers to—remove any measurement, assessment, or limitation on the level of nicotine in tobacco.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the named clause strips out all nicotine measurement, assessment and limits for smoked tobacco.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 12 of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill as introduced; true if it repeals the provisions requiring nicotine limits and the associated testing/assessment requirements, false if any nicotine measurement or limit provision survives it.

veracity.statement: I wanted to pick up on a journalistic piece by Guyon Espiner from RNZ, who talked about Ministry of Health documents that were sent to the Associate Minister of Health, in which those papers talked about the risk to reputational damage that we could potentially face, particularly because of legislation that the UK and the US are pursuing.
veracity.explanation: Relays a media report of the contents of official advice — that Health officials warned the Associate Minister of reputational risk, with UK and US legislation as the comparison.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RNZ article by Guyon Espiner and the Ministry of Health advice to the Associate Minister of Health it is based on; true if that advice raises reputational risk to New Zealand and cites tobacco legislation being pursued in the UK and US, false if the documents contain no such advice.

rigor.statement: This is at the heart: in every area of alcohol, we have limits and we have different steps. In gambling, we have limits on the time that poker machines can return to zero. That is, that the cycle time affects the addiction of all of these things. The higher the nicotine level, the more addiction.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy: other addictive products are regulated by limiting the dose or cycle time, and a dose-response premise is supplied to link that to nicotine. The inference is real and stated, but the analogy is asserted rather than established and the dose-response premise carries the whole weight of the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Our ability to sell and our reputation at the international markets will be degraded by passing this legislation that will increase the number of people smoking and taking up tobacco and will have unlimited levels of nicotine and products that will drive addiction.
rigor.explanation: The support offered is a single trade-magazine item about NZ being perceived as 'collectivist and progressive'. Moving from that perception claim to a concrete degradation of export sales is a large unbridged gap, and the intermediate step — that overseas buyers will price in tobacco policy — is never argued. An appeal to a single authority carrying a conclusion it cannot bear.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But in the coalition agreement, there’s also stuff in relationship to using the best available data and evidence. The best available data and evidence that we have actually suggest that there will be harm that will come as a result of this bill, and so I’m keen to understand whether there has been any work done around making sure that this bill is actually compliant with the coalition agreement, because if this Government is taking this coalition agreement seriously, and it’s using it as an excuse to pass bills under legislation, I would hope that the bit about data and evidence isn’t just lip service and that actually robust work is being done with this piece of legislation, to ensure that it actually matches this.
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument: the Government justifies the bill by the coalition agreement; the same agreement commits it to best available evidence; the evidence points to harm; therefore the justification is in tension with itself. The inference is valid given its premises — the weakness is that the key premise ('the evidence suggests harm') is asserted rather than cited here, which is a matter for Veracity, not for the validity of the argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, the provisions under clause 12—which my amendment refers to—remove any measurement, assessment, or limitation on the level of nicotine in tobacco.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific clause and states exactly what it does — removes measurement, assessment and limitation of nicotine levels. Checkable against the bill text without further detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I would invite the Minister to table those papers from Health New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, actionable request naming the source of the documents and the action sought. Falls short of full precision only because the particular papers are not individually identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The coalition Government makes a lot of noise about trying to double exports, they say—that’s the old hat approach—and grow the wealth of this country.
focus.explanation: Names a real policy goal (doubling exports) and links it to his soft-power argument, but the framing — 'makes a lot of noise', 'old hat' — is directed at the coalition rather than at the mechanism. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But in the coalition agreement, there’s also stuff in relationship to using the best available data and evidence. The best available data and evidence that we have actually suggest that there will be harm that will come as a result of this bill, and so I’m keen to understand whether there has been any work done around making sure that this bill is actually compliant with the coalition agreement, because if this Government is taking this coalition agreement seriously, and it’s using it as an excuse to pass bills under legislation, I would hope that the bit about data and evidence isn’t just lip service and that actually robust work is being done with this piece of legislation, to ensure that it actually matches this.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny anchored to a named commitment — the evidence provision of the coalition agreement — and to the bill before the committee, asking whether a specific compliance check was done. Accountability for a named undertaking, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Our ability to sell and our reputation at the international markets will be degraded by passing this legislation that will increase the number of people smoking and taking up tobacco and will have unlimited levels of nicotine and products that will drive addiction.
divination.explanation: Forecasts two future outcomes: that repeal will increase tobacco uptake, and that it will degrade New Zealand's standing in export markets.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for the years following the repeal, plus any documented market-access or trade barrier arising from it; true if smoking prevalence rises above its pre-repeal level or a trade/market consequence is documented, false if prevalence continues its downward trend and no trade consequence is recorded.

specificity.statement: I’m wanting to find out from the Minister what advice she did receive around risks, in terms of repealing the number of retail outlets—in particular, whether any evidence was presented to her that a higher density of retail outlets would, in fact, lead to increased smoking rates; then, within that question, whether there was any advice to her about any distinctions between youth and adult smoking rates when there is a higher density of outlets.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable question: it names the provision at issue (repeal of the retail-outlet cap), the causal mechanism to be evidenced (outlet density → smoking rates), and the specific breakdown sought (youth versus adult). A precise question is as specific as a precise answer; what it lacks is any figure or threshold, which he asks for separately.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what we have in this legislation, is clause 5, which repeals section 3A(1)(a)(i), which states that the purpose is to reduce disparities in smoking rates and illnesses between the New Zealand population and the Māori population.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the exact statutory provision it repeals, and what that provision says. Anyone can go to the bill and the principal Act and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And why there are no limits, I would reiterate that what we’re talking about here is repealing the denicotinisation—which, I’ve said before, we’re repealing the denicotinisation, we’re repealing the number of retailers, and we’re repealing the prohibition of those born after January 2009 to buy cigarettes.
specificity.explanation: Names the three concrete measures being repealed, including the birth-date cut-off for the smokefree generation. Checkable against the bill; short of full marks only because no dates or quantities attach to the repeals themselves.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We said repeatedly before about how we’re focused on achieving the outcomes and we will continue to visit the actions that will work, and we will consult extensively with smokers and what tools they need in order to quit smoking.
specificity.explanation: A direction with one identifiable action — consulting smokers — but no mechanism, no timeframe, no amounts, and no named tools. 'Focused on achieving the outcomes' and 'the actions that will work' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think most members will know that it is a fairly logical connection between the availability of a product and how much product will be used. It is quite a simple kind of connection to make.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House — availability drives consumption — but the only support offered is an appeal to what 'most members will know' and to the connection being 'simple'. That is an appeal to obviousness, not evidence. It is not a bare fallacy, because the premise is a plausible general economic claim and he immediately asks the Minister for the actual evidence rather than resting on the intuition.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why is it in the coalition agreement? Well, because it’s in the coalition agreement. But why is it in the coalition agreement? Because it’s in the coalition agreement. That is, as I alluded to before, known as, logically, a tautology.
rigor.explanation: A sound structural criticism of the justification actually offered: the Minister's stated reason for the bill and its urgency is that it is in the coalition agreement, which is self-referential rather than substantive, and Swarbrick names the defect correctly. Marked down slightly because the Minister also cited the 100-day plan and the election result, so the reconstruction is a shade more circular than the answers given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At one end of the extreme, you have complete criminal prohibition. At the other end of the extreme, you have a complete legal free market, which is largely unregulated. At both ends of those extremes, you get the maximisation of harm, because whether it is players like criminal organisations or commercial organisations that are those in control of the supply chain, with that profit motive, you have the maximisation of harm.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument with a stated mechanism — that the profit motive sits with whoever controls supply at either extreme, so both extremes maximise harm — and the conclusion tracks that mechanism. Held below the top because the harm claim at both poles is asserted rather than evidenced, and the symmetry is stipulated rather than shown; nothing is offered to establish that the two extremes produce comparable harm.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can only acknowledge that I can accept that this answer isn’t being accepted, but it is a fact that it is part of our coalition agreement. It is in our 100-day plan, and that’s where the urgency has come from to drive this piece of legislation.
rigor.explanation: The question was why the repeal is being done under urgency; the reason offered is that the Government itself put it in the coalition agreement and the 100-day plan. That is an appeal to the Government's own prior decision — the premise and the conclusion are the same commitment restated, so nothing independent supports the need for urgency. Not zero, because a self-imposed 100-day deadline is at least a genuine, stated cause of the timetable rather than a non sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is a really important point, because we know, based on the facts, the data, and evidence that this Government has told us that they ostensibly care about, the daily smoking rates for non-Māori are approximately 6 percent. It is around triple that for Māori at around 17 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two current prevalence figures — daily smoking of about 6 percent for non-Māori and about 17 percent for Māori — and that the Māori rate is roughly triple the non-Māori rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey (most recent release before February 2024, i.e. 2022/23) adult daily-smoking prevalence broken down by ethnicity. True if the non-Māori daily rate is approximately 6% and the Māori daily rate approximately 17%, giving a ratio near 3:1; false if either figure or the ratio is materially different.

veracity.statement: The number of outlets—I just wanted to clarify that I wasn’t saying that there is no impact on the number of outlets; I’m saying that we have achieved significant reductions in smoking with the current number of outlets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand has achieved significant reductions in smoking prevalence under the existing, uncapped number of tobacco retailers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily-smoking prevalence across the years preceding February 2024, together with whether the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act retailer cap was in force during that period. True if daily smoking fell materially over a period in which no retailer limit operated; false if smoking did not materially fall, or if the retailer cap was already in force over that period.

veracity.statement: Again, we’d go back to the position about reputation by national markets, and I can only observe that even from Action on Smoking and Health, in December 2023, they reported that New Zealand had one of the lowest smoking populations in the world and we had achieved unprecedented success.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Action on Smoking and Health published a statement in December 2023 saying New Zealand had one of the lowest smoking populations in the world and had achieved unprecedented success.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Action on Smoking and Health New Zealand media releases and public statements dated December 2023. True if a December 2023 ASH release describes New Zealand as having one of the world's lowest smoking rates and characterises the result as unprecedented success; false if no such release exists, or if the release's characterisation is materially different from the one attributed to it.

civility.statement: So some specific questions that I have again for the Minister, given that she has outlined that she’s not particularly interested in answering where that came from in the coalition agreement, are particularly about consultation.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the person: it characterises the Minister as uninterested in answering rather than merely noting that no answer was given. It stops short of an attack on her competence or character, and the underlying complaint is about her conduct in the debate, not about who she is.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: With respect to the Minister, she didn’t answer the question that I asked, so I will repeat it.
civility.explanation: Contested committee exchange with a real opportunity to be uncivil. The complaint lands on the answer, not on the Minister — no bad faith imputed, no sneer, no attack on competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m reminded of a book by George Orwell that said, “Ignorance is strength.” Well, boy, you guys are looking pretty strong at the moment.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic mockery calling the members opposite ignorant. Aimed at the government benches collectively rather than a named individual, so short of a direct personal insult, but it is a sneer at their capacity rather than engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The only reason I can see for doing it is to sell a highly addictive substance and to hook people on to something that is highly addictive.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith: the Minister's only conceivable motive is to hook people on an addictive drug. Framed as 'the only reason I can see' rather than a direct insult, but it attributes a corrupt purpose to the person she is questioning rather than contesting the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to know whether the Minister has been informed by advice, including by experts, on whether or not the thing that is being repealed under clause 9 of this bill actually is evidentially based to mean that it would help to lower smoking rates.
focus.explanation: Names the specific clause before the House and asks about the evidence base for that clause. Entirely on the measure; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I would like to know if the coalition Government has a commitment to investigate using regulatory powers to reduce the risk of additives in nicotine levels, what other policy options were explored on nicotine limits rather than removing them altogether?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism: what regulatory options were considered on nicotine limits instead of repeal. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I want to ask the Minister: does she think it’s right that tobacco retailers don’t need to be licensed to sell tobacco or approved to sell tobacco, and yet for the much less harmful product of alcohol, retailers of alcohol do have to be licensed?
focus.explanation: Engages the regulatory design directly — approved-retailer/licensing requirements for tobacco, compared with the existing alcohol licensing regime. Named regimes, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We were denied that without a select committee process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill was progressed without being referred to a select committee, so no expert or public evidence was taken on it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bill record for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill 2024: true if the bill was progressed without referral to a select committee and without public submissions; false if a select committee process with submissions was held.

veracity.statement: The threshold for entry into the market—there were no minimum requirements previously, before this legislation was put in place, to reduce the retailers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that minimum requirements for tobacco retailers did not exist in law before the amendments now being repealed, so repeal restores the prior position rather than removing a long-standing safeguard.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act 1990 as it stood immediately before the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022: true if it contained no approved-retailer scheme or minimum entry requirements for tobacco retailers; false if such requirements pre-dated the 2022 amendments.

veracity.statement: This bill is repealing a process; it does not change the target.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Amendment Bill removes implementation mechanisms only, leaving the statutory smokefree target/goal provision untouched.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill 2024 against the principal Act: true if no clause amends or repeals the provision stating the smokefree prevalence goal (including the purpose section); false if any clause alters or removes it.

veracity.statement: In terms of why we are taking the action to remove the denicotinisation aspect, that is what we have positioned in our coalition agreement, and that is what we’re delivering.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that repealing the denicotinisation (very low nicotine) requirement is a commitment contained in the governing coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the National–NZ First coalition agreement of 24 November 2023: true if it commits to repealing the SERPA amendments/regulations that impose the denicotinisation requirement; false if the agreement contains no such commitment.

veracity.statement: We’re talking about the approved retailer scheme in the Act, and what I want to understand is not that it’s being repealed, because it’s being repealed; what I want to understand is: why is it appropriate, in the Associate Minister of Health’s view—why is it risk proportionate that tobacco, that kills half the people that use it, does not need a retail premise to be licensed, but for a less harmful product like alcohol, it is appropriate that it be licensed?
veracity.explanation: Embedded factual premise: that tobacco kills roughly half of the people who use it. The claim is about long-term users, not about all users in any given year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: WHO tobacco fact sheet and the underlying cohort literature (e.g. Doll & Peto's British Doctors Study) on the proportion of long-term smokers killed by tobacco: true if the accepted figure is around half (up to one in two users); false if the established figure is materially lower.

rigor.statement: And I have to look at this bill and wonder what parts meet the criteria of racism and I see quite a few, actually, because this will impact the people who are already the most disadvantaged.
rigor.explanation: The premise offered is disparate impact on the most disadvantaged; the conclusion drawn is that parts of the bill 'meet the criteria of racism'. The cited paper establishes inequitable outcomes, not that this measure is racially structured, so the conclusion outruns what was shown — a hasty generalisation from disparate impact, with the criteria never stated.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of why we are taking the action to remove the denicotinisation aspect, that is what we have positioned in our coalition agreement, and that is what we’re delivering.
rigor.explanation: Asked why the nicotine limit is being removed, the reason offered is that the coalition agreement says so. That is an appeal to authority (mandate): it accounts for the decision's provenance but supplies no premise bearing on whether removal is warranted on the merits, so the conclusion does not follow from anything about the policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But given the Minister’s words around “revisit, review, make sure the settings are right”, good policy development tells me that a review must take place.
rigor.explanation: Premise: the Minister has stated that the settings should be revisited and reviewed. Conclusion: repealing the statutory review in clause 23 is inconsistent with that stated intention. The inference holds — it applies the Minister's own standard to the clause before the House — but it assumes a statutory review requirement is the only route to the review she described, which is a small gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is not an end position, as I’ve said repeatedly; we’re looking at a range of tools moving forward, to ensure that we are targeting the demographics that we know are most adversely affected and we will continue to work on those targets.
specificity.explanation: An answer intended to convey substance that carries none: 'a range of tools', 'moving forward', 'targeting the demographics'. No tool is named, no demographic is named, no timeframe or measure is given, and nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would remind the House that despite having no idea where these retailers are or whether they’re compliant, we have achieved outstanding success in reducing smoking rates.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of a counterfactual: the repealed measures were never in force, so past falls in smoking achieved without them say nothing about what they would have added. The conclusion (the measures are dispensable) does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, therefore, we need to understand who of the retailers are actually reckless, or who are those who are skirting around the laws here. And the only way to do that, I put to the Minister, is through a review.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy in the second clause: 'the only way' to identify non-compliant retailers is asserted rather than shown, with no consideration of enforcement data, controlled purchase operations or prosecutions. The underlying premise — that non-compliance needs to be identified — is fine; the leap to a single exclusive mechanism is not.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I heard from contributions from some members on the other side that this bill is being passed out of concerns for small business. Well, in that case, those concerns could be met, and no one would go out of business if the approved retailer scheme was kept in place.
rigor.explanation: A valid conditional: given her stated premise that the scheme can operate at any number of outlets, retaining it while leaving outlet numbers alone would not close any business, so the small-business rationale does not require repeal. The conclusion tracks the premise; whether the premise is true is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In an earlier response, the Minister said that the goal was to reduce smoking rates, which is why we are repealing this, and I can’t quite understand that, because, actually, the evidence that I’ve seen is that repealing this won’t lead to reducing smoking rates to the extent that we need to in order to achieve the goals.
rigor.explanation: The counter-claim rests entirely on 'the evidence that I’ve seen', which is never named or characterised — an appeal to unstated authority. The identification of the Minister's apparent contradiction is fair, but nothing is offered to support the conclusion that the repeal will fall short.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I would remind the House that despite having no idea where these retailers are or whether they’re compliant, we have achieved outstanding success in reducing smoking rates.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand has achieved a large reduction in smoking rates without the retailer approval/compliance regime being in place.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence series to 2023/24: true if the rate has fallen substantially over recent years (e.g. roughly halved since the early 2010s), false if it has been flat or risen.

veracity.statement: Has anyone told her that the approved retailer scheme could operate at any level of retail outlets? She could make it 8,000, which is the upper estimate of what it is now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 8,000 is the upper estimate of the current number of tobacco retail outlets in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health New Zealand estimates of the number of tobacco retail outlets in New Zealand as at early 2024: true if the upper estimate is around 8,000, false if the accepted upper estimate is materially different.

veracity.statement: So I’m specifically interested in any advice that the Minister has seen to specifically look at reaching the goals that we need to reach under the legislation, that were put in place, may I remind members, by members of the National Party in the past.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the smokefree goals now in legislation were originally established by National Party members in government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government response to the Māori Affairs Committee inquiry into the tobacco industry (March 2011) and the associated Cabinet decisions: true if the Smokefree 2025 goal was adopted by the then National-led Government, false if it originated under a different government.

specificity.statement: So we are committed to achieving the less than 5 percent smoke-free targets across all populations, and we will continue to drive those initiatives.
specificity.explanation: Carries one checkable figure (the under-5 percent target) and a scope (all populations), but no date, no mechanism, and 'continue to drive those initiatives' names nothing that could be acted on or checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Has anyone told her that the approved retailer scheme could operate at any level of retail outlets? She could make it 8,000, which is the upper estimate of what it is now.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (the approved retailer scheme decoupled from outlet numbers) and attaches a concrete figure — 8,000 outlets — that the Minister could act on or that anyone could check.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, therefore, we need to understand who of the retailers are actually reckless, or who are those who are skirting around the laws here. And the only way to do that, I put to the Minister, is through a review.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — retailer compliance and the review provision being repealed. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I heard from contributions from some members on the other side that this bill is being passed out of concerns for small business. Well, in that case, those concerns could be met, and no one would go out of business if the approved retailer scheme was kept in place.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism and the stated rationale for the repeal directly. The reference to 'members on the other side' is quoting their argument, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We currently have significant fire restrictions, and I’d be interested to know if the Associate Minister of Health would consider making such an amendment, because we are at serious risk of a fire if there were to be somebody using a cigarette in close proximity to a national park.
focus.explanation: Directed at a specific amendment before the committee (the proposed smoking ban in national parks) and gives a concrete reason tied to conditions in her electorate. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think, notwithstanding the rather circular logic, where it feels like we’ve fallen down the rabbit hole and we’re being told that the changes are made because the changes are being made, I think it’s important that it’s clear for the record what the approved retailer scheme is, because it may be that not everyone in this committee, including those in positions of responsibility for this bill, understand it.
civility.explanation: Lands on the person rather than the policy: the closing clause implies the Minister in charge of the bill does not understand her own scheme, and 'fallen down the rabbit hole' adds mockery. Condescension aimed at an individual, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In an earlier response, the Minister said that the goal was to reduce smoking rates, which is why we are repealing this, and I can’t quite understand that, because, actually, the evidence that I’ve seen is that repealing this won’t lead to reducing smoking rates to the extent that we need to in order to achieve the goals.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the denicotinisation, reduced-retailer and generational-ban provisions will leave smoking rates short of the statutory smokefree goals.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey daily smoking prevalence by population group: true if prevalence fails to reach under 5 percent across all populations (notably Māori and Pacific) by the Smokefree 2025 target date, false if the under-5-percent goal is met across all groups.

focus.statement: This is the unfortunate situation that we are in, where we are being asked to slow down on saving lives, with no information about what’s to come next and a Government that likes to pretend, at least in the text of its own coalition documents, so farcically and so ridiculously, and not worth the paper that it’s written on, that their decisions are based on data and evidence.
focus.explanation: There is a real accountability point inside this — no information has been supplied about what replaces the repealed measures, and the coalition documents claim evidence-based decision-making — but most of the sentence's weight is a characterisation of the Government as a whole ('likes to pretend', 'not worth the paper that it's written on') rather than engagement with the measure. A policy point wrapped in party framing. Civility is untouched: no individual is attacked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The questions that I have are: when she says that they will be, who will be consulted, how will those people be selected, when will that consultation take place, and how can she reassure this House that the consultation will be appropriate to have the interests of Māori heard adequately given that there is now, in the repealed bill, as it stands, no other obligation on her to consult with Māori?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: what Part 2 leaves in place, what consultation obligation survives the repeal, and how it would be discharged. No party characterisation at all — this is scrutiny of a named provision, which is the job.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think my point has been made, including by the fact that Government members are completely unwilling to stand up and defend this.
rigor.explanation: Argument from silence (argumentum ex silentio): the conclusion that her point is established rests entirely on opponents not having risen to rebut it. Silence in a time-limited committee stage supports no such inference. Scored here rather than under Focus because an actual inference is offered, not merely a characterisation of the other side.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You’ve talked about not hearing it from across the House, but it was in both the ACT and New Zealand First coalitions with National, so clearly it was important enough to be in both our coalition agreements, and to suggest we’re left with no progress—I think I’ve reiterated a few times here that we have made enormous progress.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the premise ('it was in both coalition agreements') and the conclusion ('it was important enough to be in both our coalition agreements') are the same proposition restated. It also does not engage the objection actually raised, which was about the election campaign rather than the post-election agreements — the presence of a policy in a negotiated agreement is no evidence it was put to voters.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So here’s the opportunity for the Minister to tell us, in repealing section 2(1)—and, I believe, it’s actually most of that section; section 2(1) to (3) of the 2022 Act—what is the Minister going to replace it with and when is the Minister going to do that, because otherwise we’re left with this void that shows the Government doesn’t actually have a plan at all and is simply doing this for political reasons, which I think is particularly dangerous when we’re dealing with tobacco.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: the inference runs from 'no replacement has been described in this debate' to 'there is no plan at all', and then to a motive ('simply doing this for political reasons'), neither of which the absence of an answer establishes. The inference is at least about the measure itself and the demand for a timeline is a fair one, so it is a weak argument rather than no argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We think there’s a great opportunity to build on the success that vaping has achieved in cessation of smoking, and we will continue to engage with Māori as we progress those things that we believe will allow us to achieve our smoke-free targets.
specificity.explanation: An answer that could have carried detail and carries none: no mechanism for the engagement, no participants, no timeframe, no target figure, and 'those things' is left undefined. A string of directional phrases ('great opportunity', 'continue to engage', 'smoke-free targets') that nobody could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The specific commencement clause—clause 2(1)—brings a number of those sections into force on 1 January 2027.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision and the exact date. Anyone can open the Act and check it or act on it. High specificity is warranted whether or not the reading of the clause turns out to be right — accuracy is Veracity's question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The questions that I have are: when she says that they will be, who will be consulted, how will those people be selected, when will that consultation take place, and how can she reassure this House that the consultation will be appropriate to have the interests of Māori heard adequately given that there is now, in the repealed bill, as it stands, no other obligation on her to consult with Māori?
specificity.explanation: A precise question is as specific as a precise answer. It itemises exactly what is being asked — who, by what selection, by when, and under what legislative safeguard — and identifies the concrete gap (no residual statutory duty to consult once the provision is repealed). Short of 1.0 only because no figure, named body or date is attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You’ve talked about not hearing it from across the House, but it was in both the ACT and New Zealand First coalitions with National, so clearly it was important enough to be in both our coalition agreements, and to suggest we’re left with no progress—I think I’ve reiterated a few times here that we have made enormous progress.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that repeal of the smokefree measures appeared in both the ACT–National and the New Zealand First–National coalition agreements of November 2023. Not a verdict on whether it was campaigned on — only on whether the commitment sits in both documents.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published texts of the National–ACT and National–New Zealand First coalition agreements (28 November 2023); true if both contain a commitment to repeal the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 or its measures, false if the commitment appears in only one or neither.

veracity.statement: The specific commencement clause—clause 2(1)—brings a number of those sections into force on 1 January 2027.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that section 2(1) of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 brings a number of its sections into force on 1 January 2027.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement provision (section 2) of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 as enacted; true if subsection (1) commences one or more sections on 1 January 2027, false if that date does not appear there or applies to no sections.

veracity.statement: Because right now there’s a lot of confusion about what those targets actually are and whether there are protections for adequate consultation so that Māori, who represent the higher statistics—17 percent still smoking versus significantly lower for the rest of the population—they deserve to know what will happen about that consultation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 17 percent of Māori still smoke, and that this is markedly higher than the rate for the rest of the population. The checkable content is the Māori smoking prevalence figure and the size of the gap, not the surrounding argument about consultation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health New Zealand Health Survey (2022/23 release, the most recent at the date of the statement), Māori adult daily smoking prevalence; true if that figure is approximately 17 percent and materially exceeds the non-Māori rate, false if it differs materially from 17 percent or does not exceed the non-Māori rate.

veracity.statement: I would also point out that there has been a careful debate earlier today in the repeal of Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori Health Authority, where there was a question around the appropriateness or not of referring to the Waitangi Tribunal hearings and there was a decision made that it was appropriate, that sub judice laws did not apply.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that earlier the same sitting day, during the committee stage on the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, a ruling was given that references to the Waitangi Tribunal proceedings were permissible because the sub judice rule did not apply.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for 27 February 2024, committee of the whole House on the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill; true if the Chair ruled that the sub judice rule did not bar reference to the Waitangi Tribunal proceedings, false if no such ruling was made or the ruling went the other way.

civility.statement: Now, it’s completely ludicrous to repeal the legislation here and not have any idea what you’re going to do.
civility.explanation: Blunt to the point of scorn, but the scorn lands on the legislative act, not on the Minister. 'Ludicrous' describes repealing without a replacement plan; no character, competence or motive of any individual is impugned. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a decision sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We are, as many members have indicated, left with going backwards in terms of the number of people who will now suffer smoking-related illnesses or will take up smoking.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the 2022 measures will reverse New Zealand's progress on smoking — that smoking uptake and smoking-related illness will increase relative to the path that was in place. Not a promise about his own action, and not a claim about the present.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the years following the February 2024 repeal, together with Ministry of Health smoking-attributable mortality/hospitalisation reporting; true if daily smoking prevalence rises, or its year-on-year decline halts, in any two consecutive survey years after the repeal, false if prevalence continues to fall year on year through to the resolve-by date.

specificity.statement: I'd like to ask about clause 35, which amends the regulations that were passed in 2021 and revokes subparts 2A, 2B, and 2C of those regulations.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the year of the regulations and the exact subparts being revoked — anyone could go and check what is at issue. Precise legislative reference rather than a general complaint about the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The specific format of that will be developed further as we move forward with the recommendations we want to put in place.
specificity.explanation: Answering how consultation with Māori will actually work, this commits to no mechanism, no participants, no timeframe and no recommendations by name. 'Developed further as we move forward' carries no content anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Anyone who's spent any time in a pathology lab, as I did during my medical training, knows intimately what tar causes, because we've all had that experience where you attend a post-mortem with someone who smokes.
rigor.explanation: The support offered for the harm of unregulated cigarette constituents is the speaker's own professional experience and a shared anecdote at post-mortem, not evidence — an appeal to personal authority plus anecdote. The claim it supports may well be true, but as offered the conclusion rests on 'I saw it' rather than on anything shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It seems to me that there are a lot of products on the shelves that are far less harmful than cigarettes that the Government does choose to regulate. So, of course, mussels would be an example.
rigor.explanation: An argument from regulatory inconsistency: less harmful products are tested, so removing testing for a more harmful one needs justification. The inference is reasonable as far as it goes, but it assumes harm ranking is the only relevant basis for a testing regime and so leaves a gap between the premise and the conclusion that this revocation is unjustified.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, prior to the election, I have no doubt that she talked to retailers and their association, and I suspect—and I would invite the Minister to stand up and say it's not the case that she spoke to the tobacco industry either through lobbyists or directly; and, if she didn't do that, stand up and say so.
