rigor.explanation: Reverses the burden of proof: the suspicion of tobacco-industry lobbying is advanced on no evidence, with the Minister's failure to deny it treated as the thing that would settle it. Arguing from a demand for rebuttal is an appeal to ignorance, not support for the claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Those clauses relate to the repeal of the denicotinisation, and all of that relates to the actions that we're doing to repeal the denicotinisation.
rigor.explanation: Offered as the reason for clause 35, but the conclusion restates the premise: the clauses repeal denicotinisation because the Government is repealing denicotinisation. Circular reasoning — nothing independent of the conclusion is offered in support of it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There are more regulations on a sandwich than there are on the safety of a cigarette, and you really have to wonder why.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, once these revocations take effect, food regulation constrains the contents of a sandwich more than tobacco regulation constrains the contents of a cigarette. Comparative but operationalisable against the two regulatory regimes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the composition, testing and labelling requirements applying to a ready-to-eat sandwich under the Food Act 2014 and the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code against the tobacco product composition and testing requirements that would remain after clauses 35 and 36 of this bill revoke subparts 2A-2C of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Regulations 2021. True if the food regime imposes materially more requirements on what the product may contain; false if tobacco composition remains equally or more regulated.

veracity.statement: We saw that happen with vapes in the United States, and people went to the ICU because of this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that vaping products in the United States were adulterated and that this sent users to intensive care, offered as evidence that unregulated product contents can cause acute harm.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: US CDC reporting on the 2019-20 EVALI outbreak (e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury), including hospitalisation and intensive-care figures and the attribution to adulterants such as vitamin E acetate. True if adulterated vaping products in the US are documented to have put people in intensive care; false if no such documented cases exist.

veracity.statement: I'm more than happy to respond to the member regarding my engagement with the retail sector, which I did have none in reference to that; I have not met with any lobbyists, tobacco lobbyists, or any tobacco organisations—and I provide that assurance repeatedly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as Minister she has had no engagement with the retail sector on this matter and has met no tobacco lobbyists or tobacco organisations. The claim is about meetings actually held, which the diary record would settle.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister's proactively released ministerial diary and OIA responses covering the period from her appointment to 27 February 2024, plus any lobbying-register or company disclosure. True if no meetings with tobacco companies, tobacco retail associations or their lobbyists appear; false if any such meeting is recorded.

veracity.statement: I have met with Action on Smoking and Health on two occasions, and I have met just this last week with the Cancer Society, and I will continue to do so.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific meeting record with two named public-health organisations — two meetings with ASH, one with the Cancer Society in the preceding week — offered in answer to whether she has heard the other side.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister's released ministerial diary for the period to 27 February 2024, and confirmation from Action on Smoking and Health and the Cancer Society. True if two ASH meetings are recorded and a Cancer Society meeting falls in the week before 27 February 2024; false if the counts or timing are materially different.

veracity.statement: I can just provide assurance that clause 36 testing relates specifically to the testing for the low nicotine rates only.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the testing provisions affected by clause 36 exist only to verify denicotinisation, and so that nothing broader in product testing is lost — directly contradicting Verrall's account that they enable testing of harmful constituents generally. Settled by reading the regulations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the product-testing provisions of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Regulations 2021 that clause 36 amends or revokes. True if those testing requirements apply solely to verifying the very low nicotine product standard; false if they also cover other constituents or general product composition.

civility.statement: We don't want to spend the entire evening in this circle going round and round, hearing more and more that the reason why something is being done is because it's being done. This is absolutely pointless.
civility.explanation: Moves past the substance to characterise the Minister's answers as circular and the exchange as worthless. Imputes evasion rather than engaging what she said — short of a personal insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Some members opposite may have had a career as a crash test dummy in the past—product testing for seatbelts.
civility.explanation: A jibe implying members opposite are dummies. Dressed as a joke about seatbelt testing, but it lands on the members rather than on any argument they made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We have heard her go around in smoke rings in terms of "We're repealing it because we're repealing it."
civility.explanation: Mockery of the Minister via a pun on the subject matter. Aimed at how she has answered rather than at her character, so it stops short of a personal attack, but it is a sneer rather than engagement.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, prior to the election, I have no doubt that she talked to retailers and their association, and I suspect—and I would invite the Minister to stand up and say it's not the case that she spoke to the tobacco industry either through lobbyists or directly; and, if she didn't do that, stand up and say so.
civility.explanation: Imputes to the Minister personally that she may have been covertly lobbied by the tobacco industry, framed as a challenge to deny it. It is bad faith attributed by insinuation rather than shown.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Some members opposite may have had a career as a crash test dummy in the past—product testing for seatbelts.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy analogy underneath — seatbelts as an example of product testing — but the weight of the sentence is a swipe at the other side rather than the consenting content of the analogy.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because this is my first contribution to this bill, I would like it on the record, alongside my colleagues on this side of the Chamber, that I find this bill abhorrent.
civility.explanation: About as harsh as a judgement of a measure can be, but the target is the bill itself — no member, minister or person is impugned. Under the re-anchored scale fierce criticism of a policy is the civil standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When more people smoke, more people die. That’s the reality, it’s the evidence, and it would be helpful if all of us in this House cared passionately about that and tried to prevent the harm rather than enable it.
civility.explanation: Imputes indifference to preventable death and a willingness to 'enable' harm to the members opposite. Short of a direct insult and aimed at a bloc rather than a named person, but it attributes a motive rather than engaging the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Further, my last question for the Minister—and I hope we can get some authentic responses—in repealing clause 29 and considering the revenue that will be gained, the revenue from this tobacco excise as a consequence of the repeal, have you given any consideration to the casualties of this legislation and the repeal, that there might be some equity shown to our low socio-economic communities who will take the impact on the front line from the repeal of the smoke-free legislation, rather than just tax cuts for a particular ilk of friends and taxpayers of the Government?
civility.explanation: Two imputations of bad faith against the Minister personally: that her earlier answers were not 'authentic', and that the repeal serves 'a particular ilk of friends' — an allegation of favouritism rather than an argument about the clause.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If we have a surge of people dying and an upsurge in smoking, is the Minister prepared to resign?
civility.explanation: Pointed and personally directed, but it asks for accountability against a stated outcome rather than attacking the Minister's character or competence. Robust, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So in clause 35, whether it relates to my current question, which is about product information, or my earlier question about product testing, it seems like there is an unawareness of the actual implications of revoking these subparts, and it really leaves consumers in New Zealand incredibly exposed to unsafe products.
civility.explanation: 'An unawareness of the actual implications' edges toward the Minister's grasp of her own bill rather than the bill's contents, but it is framed around the unanswered clause-35 questions rather than as a claim about her competence generally.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But here we are, this Government’s 100-day plan, and this is what it’s delivering for Kiwis: greater access to tobacco companies to harm our people, greater access to delivering nicotine addiction to what was intended to be our smokefree generation, and higher nicotine levels to ensure that that addiction sticks.
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme (the 100-day plan) and three specific effects of the repeal — retail access, the smokefree generation cohort, nicotine levels. The 'this is what it's delivering' framing is party-directed, but the substance is squarely the measure before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You could heckle us with it, because, really, that’s what you’re all about, isn’t it?
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of what the governing parties 'are all about'. No clause, figure, mechanism or outcome is named — once the jibe about the other side is removed nothing remains. This is the content-free party-directed case Focus exists to catch; no individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched, and there is no inference to assess for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I would love to hear the Minister share with us the advice she’s received on current modelling of how many more deaths per year to the end of the year 2030 will be caused by smoking if the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Act is repealed.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, the quantity sought (additional deaths per year), the horizon (end of 2030) and the counterfactual (repeal). A precise question is as specific as a precise answer — the Minister could answer it or be shown not to have the advice.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My first point is actually one where I may just not be reading the papers right, but I cannot, for the life of me, find Part 6A, so I would like the Minister to look at clause 37.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause and the exact Part said to be revoked by it, so the point can be checked against the bill immediately. Falls short of 1.0 only because the drafting defect alleged is left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, I want to pick up on this because there’s a number of very serious environmental issues that come from the proliferation of cigarettes in the environment, and just one of those is that, actually, cigarettes make up one of the most common forms of litter worldwide, and, obviously, in New Zealand, it’s no different here.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that cigarettes (butts/filters) are among the most common litter items both globally and in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: International litter-audit counts (e.g. Ocean Conservancy International Coastal Cleanup item rankings) and the Keep New Zealand Beautiful National Litter Audit; true if cigarette butts rank among the most frequently collected litter items in both, false if they rank outside the leading items in either.

veracity.statement: In terms of the environmental impact that was questioned before, there were no restrictions on filters in the 2022 Act, so there has been no change in that area.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 contained no provisions regulating cigarette filters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacted text of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 and the regulations made under it; true if no provision regulates filters, false if any filter restriction or filter-related product standard appears.

veracity.statement: In terms of the smoke-free generation, I think we’ve reiterated previously that we are down to 19,000 young smokers, and that’s continuing to track down.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current count of roughly 19,000 young smokers in New Zealand and that the number is still falling. The age band is unstated, so the check must identify which published series yields that figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Health Survey daily-smoking prevalence and population estimates for the youth age band the figure is drawn from (and the ASH Year 10 Snapshot); true if an official series puts young smokers at approximately 19,000 as at early 2024 with a continuing downward trend, false if the number is materially different or the trend is flat or rising.

rigor.statement: I think we are achieving our smoke-free generation without the virtue of this legislation even being in place.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur from a trend to a counterfactual: that youth smoking fell before the 2022 measures commenced does not establish that the target will be reached without them. The declining figure is offered as though it were evidence about a policy that has not yet operated, so nothing connects the premise to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I’d love to know what happens if you have created a regime that’s actually more liberal in the smoking area than it is in the vaping, and you get a sudden movement over into smoking, because it’s less regulated, and you get more people going into the smoking space, which would be absolutely terrible.
rigor.explanation: A coherent substitution argument: differential regulation of two substitute products creates a relative price/access advantage, which shifts consumption. The mechanism is stated and the conclusion tracks it, but nothing is offered on the size of the effect, so the step from 'more liberal' to 'a sudden movement' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it seems to me that this lack of provision around product information is bizarre, because with cigarettes, you breathe the smoke into your internal organs, and yet if you are selling a pottle of yoghurt, you need to have product recall information in there because it could give you an upset tummy.
rigor.explanation: A clean a fortiori argument from the stated principle that regulation should be risk-proportionate: a lower-harm product carries recall obligations, so a higher-harm one should carry at least as much. The premise and the conclusion are connected and no fallacy is doing the work.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the question I have for the Minister is: can she please explain the purpose of clause 23, which repeals section 105, which requires the ministry to conduct a review of smoke-free legislation and policy and prepare a report for the Minister no later than 2029?
specificity.explanation: Names the clause (23), the section it repeals (105), the obligation it removes (a ministry review and report) and the statutory deadline (2029). Precise enough that anyone could look it up and check it — a precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my question to Minister is whether she believes that it is appropriate to simply wipe that regulation in its entirety, and, if so, what does she say to the provision of some sort of process to ensure that there is product safety for those that want to raise some concerns?
specificity.explanation: Identifies a specific regulation being repealed and the concrete mechanism at stake (a registered complaints process for product safety), but the ask — 'some sort of process' — carries no detail of what should replace it, and no figures or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It states that the test for nicotine levels “must be independent from the manufacturer or importer of the smoke tobacco product”.
specificity.explanation: Quotes the operative words of the regulation he is defending, so the requirement being repealed is exactly identifiable and anyone could go to the regulation and verify what the bill removes. Concrete mechanism, no vagueness.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But the question I have for the Minister is: can she please explain the purpose of clause 23, which repeals section 105, which requires the ministry to conduct a review of smoke-free legislation and policy and prepare a report for the Minister no later than 2029?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: a named clause and the specific oversight mechanism it removes. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Perhaps our colleagues opposite might want to, in addition to adopting “back on baccy”, adopt the other slogan they could throw at us, that “ignorance is strength”, because this is where they’re going. They really do not want to understand the implications of what they’re trying to do.
focus.explanation: There is a thin policy referent ('the implications of what they're trying to do'), but the weight of the passage is a characterisation of the other side's motives and slogans rather than the clause under debate. Nothing scored for Rigor: strip out the part about the other side and no argument remains — a jibe is not an inference.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Perhaps our colleagues opposite might want to, in addition to adopting “back on baccy”, adopt the other slogan they could throw at us, that “ignorance is strength”, because this is where they’re going. They really do not want to understand the implications of what they’re trying to do.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that the members opposite actively do not want to understand their own policy — and wraps it in an Orwell jibe. Short of a direct insult to any individual, but sneering and no longer civil. Note it is aimed at a bloc rather than a named person, which is why it is not lower.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So my question to Minister is whether she believes that it is appropriate to simply wipe that regulation in its entirety, and, if so, what does she say to the provision of some sort of process to ensure that there is product safety for those that want to raise some concerns?
civility.explanation: A contested urgency debate where he had every opportunity to attack the Minister personally; instead the challenge lands entirely on the regulation being repealed and the consequence for the complaints process. Pointed about the policy, civil toward the person — the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So if the Minister is sincere—as she has said in numerous media interviews and in this House—that she wants to see the use of cigarettes to continue to reduce, surely a big part of that would be to have integrity in the testing methods that outline the level of nicotine.
civility.explanation: 'If the Minister is sincere' floats a doubt about her good faith, which edges toward the person, but he immediately grounds it in her own public statements and turns straight back to the testing regulation. Pointed and robust without landing on her character.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is really, really important because if we don’t understand what we’re doing, we can’t review, we can’t change, we can’t change course, we can’t correct course—we’re running blind.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: removing the statutory review removes the information needed to detect and correct policy failure. The chain from 'no review' to 'cannot correct course' is sound in outline, but leans on repetition and asserts rather than shows that no other monitoring exists. A gap between what is offered and what is concluded, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, naturally, when a piece of legislation is progressing through the House under urgency, with no select committee scrutiny opportunity, that opportunity to the community is gone.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference from an accurate premise about process: select committee submissions are the mechanism by which the public is heard, so passing a bill under urgency without that stage does remove the opportunity. The conclusion follows directly from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So as we’ve seen a significant turn-round from smoking, I can’t see that there would be any logic to raise alarm about smoking increasing.
rigor.explanation: Argument from personal incredulity, resting on a non sequitur: a past decline in smoking rates says nothing about whether tightening vaping regulation causes substitution back to smoking, which is the mechanism the concern rests on. The premise offered does not bear on the conclusion drawn, and 'I can't see any logic' substitutes for engaging the substitution argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So if the Minister is sincere—as she has said in numerous media interviews and in this House—that she wants to see the use of cigarettes to continue to reduce, surely a big part of that would be to have integrity in the testing methods that outline the level of nicotine.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure: if the goal is reducing smoking, then consumer information about nicotine content should be trustworthy, so removing the independence requirement for testing works against the stated goal. Reasonable, but 'surely' does the connecting work — nothing is offered to show that independent nicotine testing materially affects consumption, so there is a real gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I think that’s particularly important, given that this is something that the coalition Government, in the lead-up to the election, didn’t campaign on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no party in the coalition Government put the repeal of the smoke-free generation provisions to voters during the 2023 general election campaign — i.e. that the policy emerged only in coalition negotiations. Not a verdict on whether that is so.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published 2023 general election manifestos and campaign policy releases of National, ACT and NZ First. True if none of the three campaigned on repealing the smoked-tobacco/smokefree-generation provisions; false if any of them carried such a commitment in its manifesto or announced policy before election day.

veracity.statement: We’re not changing any other components of the smoking regulations that currently exist—we’re only making amendments to things that are not yet in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill touches only provisions that had not yet come into force, and leaves every currently operative smoking regulation untouched. Directly contested in the same debate by McAnulty, who points to an in-force nicotine-testing regulation the bill repeals.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill as before the committee in February 2024, checked against the commencement dates of each provision it amends or repeals. True if every amended or repealed provision was not yet in force on 27 February 2024; false if it amends or repeals any provision of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Regulations 2021 or the principal Act that was already operative.

veracity.statement: The point being that I have handled a lot of cigarette packets, and in doing so, I know that there are cigarette brands that clearly label on the sides the level of nicotine on the packets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that some cigarette brands sold in New Zealand print nicotine levels on the sides of their packs. This is the factual premise his whole argument about testing integrity rests on.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Products and Packaging) Regulations governing permitted pack markings as at February 2024, plus inspection of tobacco packaging lawfully sold in New Zealand. True if nicotine yields or levels appear on the packs of some brands on sale; false if such emission-yield labelling is absent or prohibited on New Zealand packaging.

specificity.statement: That fee, which we find in Schedule 8 of the regulations, is $1,475.
specificity.explanation: A named schedule, a named regulation instrument and an exact dollar figure — fully checkable and directly usable by anyone following the clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That fee, which we find in Schedule 8 of the regulations, is $1,475.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fee payable under Schedule 8 of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Regulations 2021 by an applicant to be an approved smoked tobacco retailer is $1,475.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Schedule 8 of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Regulations 2021 as in force on 2024-02-27; true if the listed fee for an applicant to be an approved smoked tobacco retailer is $1,475, false if it is a materially different amount or no such item exists.

veracity.statement: It doesn’t change any other testing that currently exists.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clause 36 of the bill affects only the denicotinisation testing levels and leaves every other existing testing requirement for smoked tobacco products untouched.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Clause 36 of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Repeal Amendments) Bill read against the testing requirements in the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Regulations 2021; true if the only testing obligations amended or revoked relate to denicotinisation levels, false if it also removes or alters other product testing obligations.

veracity.statement: I’m not sure of the exact numbers—in the proximity of about 400.
veracity.explanation: Estimates that roughly 400 retailers had paid the approved smoked tobacco retailer application fee before the repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Director-General records of applications to be an approved smoked tobacco retailer with fees paid before the commencement date; true if the count is in the range of roughly 300–500, false if it is materially outside that (e.g. under 100 or over 1,000).

veracity.statement: Certain brands of cigarettes have different levels of nicotine—presumably to allow people, if they so choose, to reduce the nicotine in them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that nicotine content or yield varies measurably between brands of cigarettes sold in New Zealand. (The 'presumably' clause about manufacturer intent is speculation and is not part of the checkable claim.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Manufacturer product returns filed under the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Regulations, or published nicotine-yield testing for cigarette brands on sale in New Zealand; true if reported nicotine levels differ materially across brands, false if brands are uniform within testing variance.

focus.statement: I want to know if there has been any analysis or advice on how many of those fees have been paid, how many might have to be paid back, and, most importantly, how this all fits with the Minister’s point that nothing is really in play yet.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the refund provision in Schedule 1, the advice behind it, and whether it is consistent with the Minister's stated rationale. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There was no mechanism by which that money could be repaid. Therefore, this amendment related to the ability to be able to refund those fees that had been paid in the event this legislation goes through.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: retailers paid fees under a regime being repealed, and the existing instrument contained no refund power, so a refund provision is required. The conclusion follows directly from the stated premises; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Her answer was that this was supposed to be about denicotinisation. That doesn’t stand when this entire subpart doesn’t mention that once. This could stay in there and not undermine the intent of this bill.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: if the justification offered is denicotinisation but the subpart under discussion never refers to it, the justification does not cover this repeal. Valid given its premise; the small gap is the unsupported step from 'not mentioned' to 'would not undermine the intent'.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My next question is directly related to that response from the Minister, which, frankly, was totally inadequate because it is not appropriate—or at least adequate—for a Minister to stand up, ignore the question, and say that these regulations are for this reason, when the question was why not keep them to enable integrity in the system.
civility.explanation: Robust and pointed about the Minister's answer, and it edges toward imputing that she deliberately ignored the question, but it stays on what was said rather than attacking her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it’s a shame, actually, that this wasn’t subject to select committee, because I doubt very much, outside of the people in this Chamber, where people are very interested in this, specifically Part 2, whether anyone actually understands exactly what this bill does.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the bill and its process — the absence of select committee scrutiny for a named Part of a named bill. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it’s a shame, actually, that this wasn’t subject to select committee, because I doubt very much, outside of the people in this Chamber, where people are very interested in this, specifically Part 2, whether anyone actually understands exactly what this bill does.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real process: the bill is hard to understand, therefore it warranted select committee scrutiny. The link is reasonable, but the sole premise offered is the speaker's own doubt about what others understand — an appeal to personal impression rather than anything shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I’ve previously stated, there was no filters restriction on the current legislation. That’s not relevant to this amendment that we’re seeking. There’s nothing in there currently, and we’re not undoing anything that’s in there.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premises offered: if no filter provision currently exists, a repeal cannot remove one, so a question about the effect of this bill on filter waste is out of scope. Valid given its assumptions, though it answers a narrower question than the one asked.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: However, when I looked up the regulations, I saw that the forms that are in the existing regulations actually only go up to form 4.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the schedule of forms in the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Regulations contains only forms 1 to 4, i.e. there is no existing form 5 to be replaced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The schedule of prescribed forms in the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Regulations 2021 as in force on 27 February 2024; true if the highest-numbered form is form 4, false if a form 5 (or higher) already exists.

veracity.statement: So form 5—and I’d be interested if the Minister has any more information on this—is actually a brand new form that inserts, very surprisingly, additional regulatory requirements on tobacco retailers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the form 5 inserted by clause 41(2) is newly created and imposes additional annual reporting obligations on retailers of tobacco products.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 41(2) and the new form 5 as printed in the bill; true if form 5 imposes reporting duties on tobacco retailers that no existing form imposes, false if it replaces or corrects an existing requirement or applies to a different product class (e.g. vaping products).

veracity.statement: Clarifying the last member’s question about Schedule 2, the new form actually has nothing to do with the tobacco products. It was a correction of a misconsequence of the original legislation, and it was about vaping reporting.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the new form in Schedule 2 concerns vaping-product reporting rather than tobacco products, and exists to correct a drafting consequence of the original Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the new form in Schedule 2 of the bill and the departmental disclosure statement / bill commentary; true if the form's reporting obligations attach to vaping products and it is described as correcting the earlier Act, false if it attaches to smoked tobacco products.

veracity.statement: As I’ve previously stated, there was no filters restriction on the current legislation. That’s not relevant to this amendment that we’re seeking. There’s nothing in there currently, and we’re not undoing anything that’s in there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act as currently in force contains no restriction or requirement relating to cigarette filters, and that the bill removes nothing on that subject.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act 1990 (as amended) and its regulations as at 27 February 2024, searched for provisions governing cigarette filters; true if no filter provision exists, false if the Act or regulations contain one.

veracity.statement: Most of them end up getting washed down drains when people stub out their cigarettes on the ground, and a lot of them end up in our marine environment and end up being consumed by marine life and fish, and so forth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a quantified disposal pathway: that a majority of discarded cigarette filters enter stormwater drains and that a substantial share reach the marine environment and are ingested by marine life.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published litter-composition and cigarette-butt fate studies (e.g. Keep New Zealand Beautiful national litter audits, peer-reviewed reviews of cigarette butt pollution pathways); true if a majority of discarded butts are documented as entering stormwater systems, false if the documented majority are collected as street/receptacle litter or the pathway share is materially lower.

veracity.statement: As I do this, I just remind this committee and the Minister that we’re speaking here about a product that kills half the people who use it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that tobacco kills half of the people who use it — a mortality rate claim about long-term smokers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: WHO tobacco fact sheets and the long-running cohort mortality studies they rest on (e.g. Doll & Peto British Doctors Study); true if roughly half of long-term/lifelong smokers are found to die of a smoking-caused disease, false if the established figure is materially below half.

focus.statement: I’m wondering if the Minister shares my concern that that is, I would say, a misleading word in the context of this bill because the effect of the bill is not really to regulate; the effect of the bill is to broaden the scope of the way the sector is able to work—certainly what was going to come into effect when the principal Act came into effect.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: it names the specific wording in the bill's title and argues about the bill's operative effect on the sector, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It does raise the question of whether this bill and the Minister’s statements around it about wanting to reduce smoking at a fast pace are actually sincere because the only evidence that we’ve heard for her to say that she’s intending to reach smoke-free targets is the fact that the track record has already been good.
civility.explanation: Moves from the bill to the Minister's sincerity, questioning whether her stated intentions are genuine. Short of a direct insult, but imputing bad faith to a named person is a real civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister has told us it’s not going to have any impact on the number of smokers, but we know—and, in fact, the finance Minister was in the media confirming—that it’s going to have massive financial impacts so important that they’ll be able to save her reckless tax cuts.
civility.explanation: Imputes a motive to the Minister — that the repeal exists to fund her tax cuts — and characterises those cuts as 'reckless'. The attack on the tax policy itself would be fine; ascribing the bill to that ulterior purpose is an imputation of bad faith against a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We dispute that, obviously, because what the bill is doing is removing restrictions that would have achieved that.
civility.explanation: Direct disagreement with the Minister's stated position, framed entirely around what the bill does. Contests the substance without touching the person.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just to reassure the member: it’s the title of the existing Act, and the bill will not change the title of the existing Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts about the legislative text: that the phrase 'Regulated Products' is inherited from the existing Act's title, and that the bill before the committee contains no provision altering that title.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The title of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 (and the principal Act it amends) compared with the clauses of the repeal bill as introduced; true if the wording is carried over from the existing statute and no clause of the bill amends the title, false if the bill changes the title or the wording is new to this bill.

veracity.statement: We know very well from the detailed research that was done when the 2022 Act was brought in that the underlying bill, the bill that’s being repealed, would have saved $5.25 billion in health expenditure over the period studied.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific figure — $5.25 billion of health-expenditure savings over the modelled period — to the official analysis produced when the 2022 Act was passed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Health / Treasury modelling and regulatory impact statement accompanying the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022; true if the published estimate of health-system savings is approximately $5.25 billion over the period modelled, false if the published figure is materially different or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: The Minister has told us it’s not going to have any impact on the number of smokers, but we know—and, in fact, the finance Minister was in the media confirming—that it’s going to have massive financial impacts so important that they’ll be able to save her reckless tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Finance Minister publicly confirmed the repeal carries large fiscal impacts that bear on the Government's tax package.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media statements by Finance Minister Nicola Willis in the period before 27 February 2024; true if she publicly confirmed that the repeal's revenue effects were significant and counted toward funding the Government's tax package, false if she made no such statement or explicitly denied the link.

veracity.statement: It is very clear—it’s an indisputable fact; it’s not even a political point—that this bill removes restrictions that are currently in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of legislative fact that the bill's effect is to remove restrictions that currently exist in the Act being amended.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the repeal bill compared with the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022; true if the bill repeals restrictive provisions such as the nicotine-level limit and the smokefree-generation purchase-age restriction, false if those restrictions survive the bill.

specificity.statement: We know very well from the detailed research that was done when the 2022 Act was brought in that the underlying bill, the bill that’s being repealed, would have saved $5.25 billion in health expenditure over the period studied.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise dollar figure, a named piece of legislation and a stated evidence source, so a listener could go and check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are many examples where this bill removes a restriction that is currently in place in the Act, and simply including “(Removing Restrictions)” after “Products” is an appropriate proposal for the title.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises he actually laid out: he cites the nicotine-level limit and the purchase-age restriction as provisions the bill removes, then concludes the title should describe that effect. The inference is sound given its assumptions; a small gap remains in that 'many examples' rests on the two he named.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Government has told us—in the form of the finance Minister, Nicola Willis—that this legislation will raise revenue for the Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Finance publicly stated this legislation would raise revenue for the Government, in the context of replacing revenue lost from the foreign-buyer ban.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transcript/recording of Nicola Willis's Newshub Nation interview of November 2023 (and her other public statements before 27 Feb 2024); true if she stated that revenue forgone under the smokefree legislation was being counted on / that repealing it raises revenue, false if no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: That is an estimate of around about $500 million a year, or $1.5 billion because it rises up over the forecast period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury advice released under the OIA and tabled by Barbara Edmonds estimates additional tobacco tax revenue of roughly $500 million a year, totalling about $1.5 billion across the forecast period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury OIA material tabled in the House on 2024-02-27; true if it estimates additional tobacco excise revenue of about $500m per annum and about $1.5b over the forecast period, false if the figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: However, half of the bill is focused on amendments to other enactments and regulations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately half of the bill consists of amendments to enactments and regulations other than the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act 1990.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill as introduced; compare the clauses/schedules in Part 2 amending other enactments and regulations against those in Part 1 amending the principal Act. True if roughly half the substantive provisions sit outside the principal Act, false if Part 2 is a small fraction.

veracity.statement: That is because we haven’t had a select committee process, and a number of the things that are being repealed in the Act are not yet enforced.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of record that this bill did not go through a select committee process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Repeal Amendments) Amendment Bill; true if it shows no select committee referral (passage under urgency), false if a select committee stage occurred.

specificity.statement: That is an estimate of around about $500 million a year, or $1.5 billion because it rises up over the forecast period.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete figures with a stated basis (per year and across the forecast period), sourced to a tabled Treasury document — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And I wondered if we could perhaps consider the “Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Extending Smokefree Targets to 2061)”.
specificity.explanation: A concrete alternative wording with a named date rather than a general call for a better title, but she supplies no source or mechanism for the 2061 figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s halting initiatives. It’s not going forward; it’s going backwards.
specificity.explanation: A directional characterisation of the bill with no named provision, initiative, figure or timeframe — nothing here that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, it has become clearer to members in this House exactly how much tax revenue that is, which is another justification for why we should change the title—and that is in the form of an Official Information Act request that my colleague Barbara Edmonds tabled in the House today.
rigor.explanation: Engages the measure, but the inference does not track: the size of the revenue is offered as a reason to change the title, when the argument he has actually made turns on whether revenue is the bill's purpose. Magnitude does not bear on nomenclature — a non sequitur between the quantum and the naming point.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is because we haven’t had a select committee process, and a number of the things that are being repealed in the Act are not yet enforced.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: no select committee scrutiny plus provisions not yet in force therefore commencement should be deferred to allow their effect to be observed. The conclusion follows from what she offers, though the link between deferral and 'better consultation' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The day of Royal assent is very difficult to ascertain when you’re reading back on a piece of legislation, because it’s sometimes difficult to know, without reading the exact movements and passage of legislation through the office of the Governor-General, exactly when Royal assent took place.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the claim that the assent date is difficult to ascertain is supported by the assertion that it is difficult to know when assent took place. The premise restates the conclusion, and no obstacle to finding the date is actually identified.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So that’s why I think a more appropriate title for this bill is my amendment to insert the words “Raising Tax Revenue”.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — a named clause, a tabled amendment, and a fiscal claim about the bill itself. No party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wondered if the Minister was interested in looking at outcomes, because I’ve often heard that the Government is all about outcome—measuring outcomes, striving for outcomes; all sorts of things to do with outcomes.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine proposal underneath (frame the title around the bill's outcome), but most of the weight is a swipe at the Government's general rhetorical habits rather than at any provision of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Ah, well, it doesn’t sound it like from the member’s contribution.
civility.explanation: Not a direct insult, but a condescending jab at another member's grasp of the legislation rather than at anything she argued — it engages no substance and imputes incompetence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I do want to make some remarks relating to the commencement of this bill because I studied, with some interest, the coalition agreement, and I note that from the outset there was a plan to have this repeal done by March.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition agreement set out, from the start, a plan to complete this repeal by March.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–NZ First coalition agreement and the Government's 100-day plan (released late November 2023); true if either document commits to repealing the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 with a deadline on or before March 2024, false if no such repeal commitment or no such timeframe appears.

veracity.statement: But the reason I thought that would be a good idea was that perhaps, at that point, the influence, I guess, of New Zealand First in putting forward a policy here that wasn’t campaigned on by the National Party, I don’t believe—in fact, the National Party thought two of the parts of this bill that are being repealed were good things, things they supported—the undue influence, where we’ve got a very small representation in the House having a very large influence over a piece of legislation that is going to have an enormous impact on the population of New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things about National's record: that the repeal was not part of its election campaign, and that it had previously regarded two of the repealed provisions as good.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's published 2023 election health policy and campaign statements, plus National MPs' recorded positions on the provisions of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 (Hansard speeches and division records). True if National did not campaign on repealing these measures and its members are on record supporting at least two of the repealed provisions; false if the repeal appeared in National's campaign policy or if National opposed the provisions throughout.

rigor.statement: That relates to the point that the policy objectives of the Minister could have been met while retaining the approved retailer section. That would mean that tobacco would be no more—in fact, still less—regulated than products like alcohol, that is licensed. And those retailers would have standards to meet in terms of whether the person was a responsible person or not. It would be easier to enforce all of those policies.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: retaining the approved retailer provision would leave tobacco no more regulated than licensed alcohol while preserving the Minister's stated objectives. The premises support the conclusion, though the enforcement claim is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I just want to go to Part 1 of this very bill, where of course the bill itself amends the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products—bracket—Smoked Tobacco—bracket—Amendment Act 2022. There’s another one just like that about vaping, which I don’t happen to have in front of me. But that is a perfectly normal drafting technique: to use brackets to explain the type of amendment that you are doing.
rigor.explanation: A valid counterexample: the Minister's claim was that the title must track the principal Act, and the bill's own Part 1 cites an amendment Act carrying bracketed words. The instance directly refutes the general claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason why I’ve put that specific amendment on the Table tonight is that there are so many cost pressures on our health system, and we know from the evidence and we’ve seen from the evidence that repealing this bill will put more pressure on our health system. We already have struggling wait-lists. We already have struggling GP practices. We have nurses that need to be paid more. We have health practitioners that need to be paid more.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to unnamed evidence — 'we know from the evidence' is repeated without any of it being produced — and the supporting list (wait-lists, GP practices, pay) describes existing pressures rather than establishing that this repeal adds to them.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That relates to the point that the policy objectives of the Minister could have been met while retaining the approved retailer section. That would mean that tobacco would be no more—in fact, still less—regulated than products like alcohol, that is licensed. And those retailers would have standards to meet in terms of whether the person was a responsible person or not. It would be easier to enforce all of those policies.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the bill — a specific provision, what it would do, and how it interacts with the Minister's objectives. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reason why I’ve put that specific amendment on the Table tonight is that there are so many cost pressures on our health system, and we know from the evidence and we’ve seen from the evidence that repealing this bill will put more pressure on our health system. We already have struggling wait-lists. We already have struggling GP practices. We have nurses that need to be paid more. We have health practitioners that need to be paid more.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House and its fiscal consequences for the health system; the argument is weak but it is about the policy, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister herself could have been better prepared for the questions—quite reasonable questions about the operation of this bill—that she has been unable to answer.
civility.explanation: Moves off the policy and onto the Minister's personal preparedness and competence in the Chamber. Short of a direct insult, but it is condescension aimed at the person rather than the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I just want to go to Part 1 of this very bill, where of course the bill itself amends the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products—bracket—Smoked Tobacco—bracket—Amendment Act 2022. There’s another one just like that about vaping, which I don’t happen to have in front of me. But that is a perfectly normal drafting technique: to use brackets to explain the type of amendment that you are doing.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named Act with its exact bracketed form and points to the clause of the bill where it appears — checkable against the text. Loses some ground on the vaping example she could not produce.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m proposing that we replace the words “the day after Royal assent.” in clause 2 with the words “1 June 2025”.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the exact words to be struck out and the exact replacement date. Fully actionable and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m suggesting this because we’ve heard through the policy debates that we’ve had in the House today—and, of course, that we had in the House in 2022—that the point of the legislation that has been repealed was to make us achieve those targets and that the impact of this repeal will be that those targets will not be met.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the 2022 Act means the Smokefree 2025 targets will not be reached.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for 2025; the Smokefree 2025 goal is under 5% daily smoking for the total population and for each population group. False if the published figures show the goal met by 2025, true if prevalence (overall or for Māori and Pacific populations) remains at or above 5%.

divination.statement: Now, I’ve picked this date for a very specific reason, and the reason is that on 31 May 2025, Winston Peters will stop being the Deputy Prime Minister.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a specific handover date for the Deputy Prime Ministership under the coalition arrangement.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official record of Deputy Prime Minister appointments (Governor-General's warrants / DPMC ministerial list); true if Winston Peters ceased to hold the office of Deputy Prime Minister on or about 31 May 2025, false if he remained in the role past that date.

veracity.statement: The most obvious instance of that was when we forbid there to be smoking in bars and clubs and pubs and so forth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand legislated a ban on smoking in bars, clubs and pubs as part of the tobacco-control regime he is describing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand statute record: true if a smoking ban covering licensed premises (bars, pubs, clubs) was enacted — e.g. the Smoke-free Environments Amendment Act 2003 taking effect December 2004; false if no such indoor hospitality ban exists.

veracity.statement: Because we have a situation here that the finance Minister herself has conceded, that the National Party’s support for this—keeping in mind that they did not campaign on this and, in fact, as a proportion of the current Government the vote share in favour of this is actually quite small, but the finance Minister has said, herself, that the reason they support it is because it will assist her in paying for tax cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Finance publicly stated that the reason for supporting the smokefree repeal is that the retained tobacco excise revenue helps fund the Government's tax cuts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of the Minister of Finance's statements (Hansard, press conferences, media interviews) up to 27 February 2024: true if she is on record linking revenue from not proceeding with the smokefree measures to funding the tax package; false if no such statement exists and she has only denied the link.

veracity.statement: I’m saddened to be here on a day where two times in one day we are discussing items which have not been heard by the Waitangi Tribunal though there are claims before them—in particular, a claim by a group such Te Rōpū Tupeka Kore o Aotearoa, which holds so much authority in this kaupapa in Aotearoa, is not being given the chance to be heard.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a claim concerning this legislation, lodged with the Waitangi Tribunal by Te Rōpū Tupeka Kore o Aotearoa, was before the Tribunal and had not been heard as at 27 February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal register of claims and its urgency decisions: true if a claim by Te Rōpū Tupeka Kore o Aotearoa relating to the smokefree repeal was registered and unheard on 27 February 2024; false if no such claim was lodged or it had already been heard by that date.

rigor.statement: This is a reduction in the regulatory framework that protects the wider community from the impacts of tobacco and nicotine, and this will mean smokier environments.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: he has established that adding restrictions coincided with less smoking, and concludes that removing them reverses it. The premises support the direction but not the magnitude — the restrictions being repealed had not yet taken effect, which is a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This is a reduction in the regulatory framework that protects the wider community from the impacts of tobacco and nicotine, and this will mean smokier environments.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the smokefree restrictions will increase smoking in New Zealand ('smokier environments').
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the years following the repeal: true if prevalence rises, or the pre-repeal downward trend halts, relative to the 2023/24 baseline; false if daily smoking prevalence continues to fall.

civility.statement: It’s a back-to-the-past piece of legislation, and that is what I seriously propose to the Minister that this should be correctly called, if there is going to be honesty as to what this amendment bill does.
civility.explanation: Pointed — the conditional 'if there is going to be honesty' edges toward suggesting the Minister is being dishonest — but the charge stays attached to the bill's title rather than landing on her character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know that they haven’t been here that long, but this is how it works, particularly when it comes to urgency.
civility.explanation: Condescension toward members opposite — dismissing their interjection by reference to their inexperience rather than to anything they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the amendment that I’m speaking in favour of is the Hon Grant Robertson’s proposal that after “Products” in clause 1, “(Raising Tax Revenue)” be included.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, the exact insertion point and the exact words proposed; anyone could act on it or check it against the amendment paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I have several questions, but number one: why, once again, is this process being rushed and Te Rōpū Tupeka’s claim before the Waitangi Tribunal not given the opportunity to be heard before this bill is passed?
specificity.explanation: Names the claimant group and the specific decision point (hearing before passage), so the question is answerable and checkable, but it carries no dates, figures or clause references.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is true, when you consider the make-up of this Government—three parties, one of which is considerably larger than the other two, and the National Party did not campaign on this; they only support it because New Zealand First want it.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine point bearing on the amendment before the committee — whose policy this is and why the title should say so — but most of the weight is on the composition and motives of the governing parties rather than on the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New Zealand First, as my colleague Rachel Boyack said, is “the tail wagging the dog”.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the internal power dynamics of the other side. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named; strip out the characterisation of the coalition and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I have several questions, but number one: why, once again, is this process being rushed and Te Rōpū Tupeka’s claim before the Waitangi Tribunal not given the opportunity to be heard before this bill is passed?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure and its handling: names the specific outstanding Tribunal claim and ties it to the commencement of this bill. Legitimate scrutiny of a named process, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Members over there might wish to be arrogant and ignorant of the process, but over here, we are standing up for the rights of individuals, for the rights of communities for whom this piece of legislation will have a significant impact.
civility.explanation: Characterises the members opposite themselves as 'arrogant and ignorant' — the target is the people, not their argument or the policy. Short of sustained abuse, but a clear attack on the opposing members' character rather than on what they are doing.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’re actually learning something over there, for once.
civility.explanation: Condescension and mockery aimed at the members opposite — 'for once' implies they habitually learn nothing. It stops short of a direct insult to any named individual, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine failure rather than contempt.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, while members opposite and the Minister may want to just sit there and not take this seriously, that is an absolute abomination—a disgrace.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that the Minister and government members are deliberately not taking the bill seriously — rather than criticising the decision not to speak on its merits. The vehemence ('abomination', 'disgrace') attaches to their motives, not to a policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Members over there might wish to be arrogant and ignorant of the process, but over here, we are standing up for the rights of individuals, for the rights of communities for whom this piece of legislation will have a significant impact.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point buried here — that the bill will significantly affect communities — but the sentence's weight is a virtuous us-versus-them contrast with the other side. No measure, figure or provision is named, so it sits between substance and party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’re actually learning something over there, for once.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side and their general capacity to learn. Strip out the jibe at the opposing benches and nothing about the bill, its clauses or its effects remains. This is the content-free party-directed remark Focus exists to catch; no Rigor score is emitted because a jibe is not an argument.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What that means, and the third point I want to make, is that smoking rates are falling because what we are doing is something that works.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what the regulatory regime does and whether it is producing the observed fall. No party framing, no characterisation of opponents — the argument is about the policy even though the inference itself is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, let’s give a lesson on 101, and that is this is the House of Representatives, where we are here to represent the numerous number of people that are not having an opportunity on this very bill because it is not subject to the scrutiny of a select committee process.
rigor.explanation: A real inference against the interjection 'let's just vote': because the bill bypassed select committee, the public had no other route to be heard, so the committee stage is where representation happens. The premise supports the conclusion. It is docked for leaning partly on an appeal to the House's constitutional dignity rather than showing what scrutiny the extra debate would actually add.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What that means, and the third point I want to make, is that smoking rates are falling because what we are doing is something that works.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc ergo propter hoc. The premise is that smoking rates fell over a period; the conclusion is that the retained regulatory regime caused the fall. Nothing is offered to rule out the alternative causes she herself has just cited — vaping uptake, prior excise and marketing measures — or to separate the regime's effect from the trend. The inference from 'rates fell under X' to 'X works' is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To remind the House what those are, we used the evidence from multiple scientific studies, multiple clinical trials to denicotinise cigarettes, because this is one of the most effective tools for helping people quit, and yet we are told that these interventions are not effective enough and that there are other effective alternatives.
rigor.explanation: Grounds the denicotinisation policy in cited trial evidence and then points to the tension in the government's position — that the measure is simultaneously dismissed as ineffective while alternatives are called effective. The inference tracks what is offered. It is docked because the studies are gestured at rather than characterised, so the strength of the support is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: But, I tell you what, she probably won’t take a call because she has failed to do so since many of these issues have been raised.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Minister, Casey Costello, will not speak again during the committee of the whole House stage on this bill. Hedged with 'probably' but tied to a specific person, a specific action and a bounded window.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Hansard record for the committee of the whole House stage of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill, 27 February 2024: false if Casey Costello takes a call on the part under debate before the committee stage closes; true if she does not speak again before the closure motion.

veracity.statement: I would emphasise the fact that this coalition agreement was not only between National and New Zealand First but it was also between National and ACT, and that was consistent across both parties around this amendment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal of the smokefree amendments appears in both post-2023 coalition agreements — National–New Zealand First and National–ACT — and in consistent terms, not solely as a New Zealand First concession.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published texts of the National–New Zealand First and National–ACT coalition agreements (December 2023): true if both contain a commitment to repeal the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act amendments/regulations; false if the commitment appears in only one of the two.

veracity.statement: Firstly, this bill does not change a single regulation around smoking, around the sale and use of smoked tobacco products, that is in place today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every provision the bill repeals was scheduled to commence in future, so nothing operating on the day of the third reading is altered by it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the repealing provisions of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill (2024) against the commencement dates in the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 and regulations in force at 27 February 2024: true if every repealed measure had a commencement date after 27 February 2024; false if any repealed provision was already operative.

veracity.statement: In the last three years, 229,000 people have stopped smoking, and more than a third of those who quit were Māori.
veracity.explanation: Two linked quantitative claims: a headcount of 229,000 people who stopped smoking over roughly 2020/21–2022/23, and that over one third of that reduction was among Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily-smoking prevalence, total and Māori, for 2019/20 through 2022/23, applied to Stats NZ adult population estimates: true if the implied fall in smoker numbers is approximately 229,000 and the Māori share of that fall exceeds one third; false if either figure is materially off (say, more than ~20% adrift on the headcount, or a Māori share below one third).

veracity.statement: The latest New Zealand Health Survey figures show an overall smoking rate of 6.8 and a youth smoking rate of 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Attributes two specific prevalence figures to a named official source — 6.8% overall smoking and 3% youth smoking — as the most recent available at February 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey 2022/23 annual data explorer: true if the adult daily-smoking rate is 6.8% (± rounding) and the youth (15–17) rate is 3% (± rounding); false if either figure differs materially or comes from a different survey.

veracity.statement: It was our colleague Dr Reti who told us during the debate on the 2022 bill that this was so outstandingly effective that it should be brought in on its own.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Shane Reti, during the 2022 legislative debate, described denicotinisation as so effective it warranted implementation as a standalone measure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of Shane Reti's speeches on the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill 2022: true if he described denicotinisation in substantially those terms and argued it should be advanced on its own; false if no such remarks appear or his position was materially different.

specificity.statement: In the last three years, 229,000 people have stopped smoking, and more than a third of those who quit were Māori.
specificity.explanation: A headcount, a time window and a breakdown by ethnicity — anyone can take this to the Health Survey series and check it. Whether the numbers survive that check is Veracity's problem, not this one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will ensure the continued provision of effective stop-smoking services and supporting marketing campaigns, and we will ensure initiatives are targeted at those who need it the most.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no mechanism, no funding figure, no timeframe and no named service or programme. 'Effective', 'supporting' and 'those who need it the most' are all left undefined, and nothing nearby in the speech supplies the missing detail. Nobody could check whether this was delivered.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It told us not only that the smoke-free goal wouldn’t be reached until 2061 without our Act; it also told us that it would take away a third of the life expectancy gap for wāhine Māori.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named source (the modelling), a dated projection (2061) and a quantified effect (a third of the life expectancy gap for wāhine Māori) — someone could go and check both figures against the published model.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Instead, because there are no financial consequences of this bill, because there’s been no regulatory impact statement, we don’t know if the Government has been properly advised on the impacts of this bill on the health system, but I know from the advice that I got that it’s likely to cost the health system $5 billion.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific missing document (the regulatory impact statement) and gives a dollar figure ($5 billion) for the health system cost, both of which are checkable rather than directional.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s now just getting to 11 p.m., and in the blink of an eye, in nine to 10 hours of debating time in this Chamber, the Government has pushed through, under urgency, world-leading, evidence-based, harm-minimisation legislation for one of the most deadly substances that we know of—a substance that will kill 50 percent of its consumers.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the process complaint (nine to ten hours of debate, same day introduction to third reading) and the harm claim (50 percent of consumers killed), rather than asserting generally that the process was rushed.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It told us not only that the smoke-free goal wouldn’t be reached until 2061 without our Act; it also told us that it would take away a third of the life expectancy gap for wāhine Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two outputs of the peer-reviewed modelling commissioned for the Smokefree Aotearoa 2025 action plan: that the smoke-free goal would not be reached until 2061 absent the 2022 Act, and that the Act would close a third of the life expectancy gap for Māori women.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published modelling underpinning the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 (Ouakrim et al., University of Otago / Lancet Public Health tobacco endgame modelling): true if that modelling projects the smokefree prevalence target being met only around 2061 under business-as-usual AND reports a reduction of approximately one third in the life expectancy gap for Māori women; false if the modelled year or the gap-reduction fraction is materially different.

veracity.statement: Instead, because there are no financial consequences of this bill, because there’s been no regulatory impact statement, we don’t know if the Government has been properly advised on the impacts of this bill on the health system, but I know from the advice that I got that it’s likely to cost the health system $5 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that no regulatory impact statement accompanied the repeal bill, and (b) that advice she received as Minister put the health system cost of repeal at around $5 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament/Treasury regulatory impact statement register and the bill's explanatory note for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Amendment Bill (introduced 27 February 2024): true if no RIS was produced or published for it, false if one exists.
