For the second limb: Ministry of Health advice to the Minister of Health on the 2022 Act, released under OIA or in the Budget/health cost-saving modelling: true if it estimates health system savings/costs of the order of $5 billion, false if the advice contains no such estimate.

veracity.statement: The more than 60 percent of New Zealanders who support the bill in its original form; they don’t support your repeal—we’re not thinking about them tonight at all.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 60 percent of New Zealanders supported the smokefree legislation as originally enacted and oppose its repeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published public opinion polling on the smokefree generation legislation and its repeal (e.g. ASH/Hāpai te Hauora, Horizon Research or Health Coalition Aotearoa polls, 2023–early 2024): true if a reputable poll puts support for the original measures above 60 percent, false if the available polling puts it materially below that.

veracity.statement: We’ve been transacting with the Minister at question time, for multiple weeks, the issue of how a mystery document seeking tax breaks for the tobacco industry turned up in her office, and there’s been no good enough answer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a document of unknown authorship advocating tax breaks for the tobacco industry appeared in the Associate Minister of Health's office, and that repeated questioning at question time over several weeks produced no explanation of its origin.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard oral question records for late 2023–February 2024, plus OIA releases and contemporaneous reporting on the unattributed briefing on tobacco excise/heated tobacco tax found in Associate Minister Casey Costello's office: true if such a document existed and its authorship was not disclosed in answers over that period, false if no such document existed or its origin was disclosed.

veracity.statement: It’s now just getting to 11 p.m., and in the blink of an eye, in nine to 10 hours of debating time in this Chamber, the Government has pushed through, under urgency, world-leading, evidence-based, harm-minimisation legislation for one of the most deadly substances that we know of—a substance that will kill 50 percent of its consumers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal bill was introduced and passed through all stages under urgency within roughly nine to ten hours on a single day, and that tobacco kills half of the people who use it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and the bill's stages record for 27 February 2024: true if introduction and third reading both fall on that day within about nine to ten hours of debate, false if the stages were spread more widely. For the harm claim: WHO tobacco fact sheet and the underlying cohort mortality literature: true if the standard finding is that up to half of long-term tobacco users die from its use, false if the accepted figure is materially lower.

civility.statement: I wonder what Dr Reti thinks. He hasn’t taken a call on this bill. Well, I just wonder if it’s shame.
civility.explanation: Turns from the bill to a named member's personal state, publicly speculating that his silence and seating position are motivated by shame. That is mockery aimed at the person rather than the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So if the Minister wants to describe that frustration as emotional, then perhaps she could take some responsibility for it by being able to give some proper answers.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal in address — it puts the blame for the mood of the debate on the Minister — but it stays on her conduct in answering questions rather than attacking her character or competence as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The action that the Government is taking is deeply unpopular. It is unpopular because everyone in the country knows it’s wrong.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity, and circular with it: unpopularity is offered as evidence of wrongness and universal knowledge of wrongness is offered as the explanation of the unpopularity. Nothing independent of the public mood is advanced to show the repeal is wrong.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve been transacting with the Minister at question time, for multiple weeks, the issue of how a mystery document seeking tax breaks for the tobacco industry turned up in her office, and there’s been no good enough answer.
focus.explanation: Names a specific, identifiable matter — an unattributed document proposing tobacco tax concessions in the Minister's office — and the specific failure to account for it. This is scrutiny of a named episode, not general party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I guess I just wanted to say to members of the Government and the governing parties who are heckling me at the minute that I get that this is a game for you guys, at this point.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the governing parties' supposed motives and conduct in the Chamber. No provision, figure or consequence of the bill is engaged; strip out the characterisation of the other side and nothing about the measure remains.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because it was recognised that smoking and cigarettes were harmful, we moved towards an environment which was less and less smoky and, actually, fun fact, it wasn’t until 2016—2016—that the entire premises of Parliament finally became entirely smoke-free, including our lawn.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific date — that Parliament's entire precinct, including the grounds, only became fully smoke-free in 2016.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Service / Speaker's office records and contemporary news reports on when the Parliamentary precinct (buildings and grounds) became entirely smoke-free; true if that took effect in 2016, false if it was earlier or later.

veracity.statement: So not only are we left in this kind of haze as to why the Government’s progressing this through, because the only entities that we saw advocating for the repeal of this smoke-free generation legislation throughout the past year or so were New Zealand First and the tobacco industry, but who benefits?
veracity.explanation: Asserts an exclusivity claim: that in roughly the year to February 2024 the only public advocates of repealing the smokefree generation law were New Zealand First and the tobacco industry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of advocacy for repeal between early 2023 and February 2024 — party policy documents, submissions and media statements. True only if no other identifiable advocate (e.g. ACT, retailer/dairy owner associations, other lobby groups) publicly called for repeal in that period; false if any did.

veracity.statement: Well, it’s not the more New Zealanders who are going to be addicted for longer only filling up this Government’s coffers by an approximate $500 million per annum as a result of increased excise in tobacco tax; it’s going to be the tobacco industry.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a figure: approximately $500 million per year in additional tobacco excise revenue to the Crown as a consequence of not proceeding with the smokefree measures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Ministry of Health costings and Budget forecasts of the additional tobacco excise revenue attributable to the repeal; true if the annual figure is around $500 million, false if it is materially different (e.g. an order of magnitude lower, or a total across several years rather than per annum).

veracity.statement: There’s actually no cost-benefit analysis that sits alongside this legislation, I might add, which again leaves us with the question of why this is occurring under the urgency.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no cost-benefit analysis was published alongside the repeal bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's page on legislation.govt.nz and the Ministry of Health/Treasury disclosure documents for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill; true if no regulatory impact statement or cost-benefit analysis accompanied its introduction, false if one was published.

veracity.statement: We’ve seen it drop significantly over the past 12 years, from around 16 percent down to 8.6 percent last year, to 6.8 percent this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific series of adult smoking prevalence figures: about 16 percent twelve years ago, 8.6 percent in the prior year and 6.8 percent in the current year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for 2011/12, 2021/22 and 2022/23; true if those releases give approximately 16%, 8.6% and 6.8% respectively, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I’d like to note that Action for Smokefree 2025 has said that the progress we’re making is unprecedented.
veracity.explanation: Relays a characterisation attributed to ASH New Zealand — that the progress being made on smoking rates is unprecedented.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: ASH New Zealand public statements, media releases and survey commentary from 2023–24; true if ASH described the decline in smoking rates as unprecedented, false if no such statement exists or if ASH's published commentary contradicts the sense in which it is being cited here.

veracity.statement: Look, no regulations or programmes that were in place before the election have been stopped.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that nothing operative — no regulation in force, no funded programme — was discontinued by the incoming Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health and Cabinet records for October 2023 to February 2024; true if no smokefree regulation then in force and no funded cessation programme was revoked or defunded, false if any was.

rigor.statement: So that kind of begs the question of whether they believe that authoritarian rule is “all g” simply because every three years we have a general election.
rigor.explanation: Strawman and slippery slope: the Government's stated justification (an electoral mandate lets it use urgency for this bill) is escalated to a belief in authoritarian rule, with nothing offered to bridge the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we’ve kind of heard all of these weird arguments, which, on the one side, have said that this thing isn’t in effect yet, so therefore it’s not important, but yet we have a piece of repealing legislation that is being pushed through under urgency in order to repeal that thing which apparently is also not going to be effective but is also going to be far too effective.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: identifies an internal inconsistency between 'the law isn't in force so it doesn't matter' and 'it must be repealed urgently'. The conclusion tracks the premises, though both opposing positions are stated in the speaker's own paraphrase rather than quoted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are not going to take the punitive regulatory approach that the Opposition would like us to do; we’re going to build on what has worked—what has continued to drive down smoking rates.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the policy approach, but with a real gap: the falling trend is offered as grounds for keeping the current settings, when that trend occurred under a regime that included the measures now being repealed. The Opposition's position is also restated as 'punitive' rather than engaged.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They are ripping off the band-aid really, really quickly in the hopes that this is swept under the rug amongst all of the other heinous things that they are doing under urgency and super-quickly with hopes that, into the future, New Zealanders forget it.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — deliberate concealment and a hope that the public forgets — rather than engaging the case made. Aimed at the Government collectively, so no individual is insulted, but attributing dishonest motive is a civility failure.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They are ripping off the band-aid really, really quickly in the hopes that this is swept under the rug amongst all of the other heinous things that they are doing under urgency and super-quickly with hopes that, into the future, New Zealanders forget it.
focus.explanation: Anchored loosely to the use of urgency, which is a genuine process complaint, but the weight of the sentence is on the Government's supposed motives rather than any named measure or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We haven’t heard the Opposition give an intelligent reckoning with a second and third order of facts of prohibition of cigarettes on an emerging black market.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point inside it — the black-market consequences of restricting tobacco supply — but it is delivered as a characterisation of what the other side has failed to do, with no mechanism, figure or evidence attached.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve seen it drop significantly over the past 12 years, from around 16 percent down to 8.6 percent last year, to 6.8 percent this year.
specificity.explanation: Three dated figures and a defined trend period — someone can look each of them up against the published survey.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re supporting a package of initiatives to make sure we ensure a smoke-free goal of 2025.
specificity.explanation: 'A package of initiatives' names nothing — no measure, no funding, no timeframe — and the surrounding text does not supply any.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: On the way we’re going, we will reach our goal of having the average under 5 percent by 2025.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an outcome in the world — that national smoking prevalence falls below the 5 percent Smokefree 2025 threshold — rather than promising a government action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence covering 2025; true if the published rate is below 5 percent, false if it is 5 percent or higher.

veracity.statement: So I would like to share some of those voices that were part of the 45,000 submissions that came through to us, and make sure that those who are a part of this petition—those who are out there hoping that the politicians would hear and see them—that we indeed use this platform to use our sphere of influence to bring their voices to the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 45,000 submissions/signatures were received in connection with the petition against the repeal of the smokefree legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary Petitions Committee record and the petition's own published signature/submission count for the 2024 petition opposing the repeal of the smokefree amendment; true if the figure is approximately 45,000, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: The Māori stats are 6.2 percent of year 10s across the country; for non-Māori, it is 2 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the ASH Year 10 Smokefree Snapshot, 6.2% of Māori year 10 students smoke against 2% of non-Māori year 10 students.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Action on Smoking and Health (ASH) Year 10 Smokefree Snapshot survey, most recent release before February 2024: true if the Māori and non-Māori smoking prevalence figures are 6.2% and 2% (± rounding) on the measure cited, false if materially different or if the survey reports no such breakdown.

veracity.statement: But tobacco impacts te iwi Māori more than any other population in New Zealand; 5,000 people die of smoking-related illnesses, te nuinga ko te iwi Māori [the majority of whom are Māori people].
veracity.explanation: Two joined assertions: that around 5,000 people die annually in New Zealand of smoking-related illness, and that the majority of those deaths are Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health New Zealand smoking-attributable mortality estimates: true if annual smoking-attributable deaths are approximately 5,000 AND Māori account for more than half of them; false if either the total is materially different or Māori are a minority of smoking-attributable deaths (higher per-capita rates alone would not satisfy 'the majority of whom').

veracity.statement: We have traversed the area multiple times today that, before this previous amendment came into power, we had already reduced smoking rates to a point where we have reached or nearly reached our smoke-free targets, which is less than 5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's smoking rate had reached or nearly reached the Smokefree 2025 target of under 5 percent before the 2022 smokefree amendment took effect.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the years preceding December 2022: true if the rate was at or close to 5%, false if materially above it (e.g. at or above roughly 7%). The Smokefree 2025 goal definition of 'less than 5 percent' should be taken from the Ministry of Health's published target.

civility.statement: We stand in opposition to this disgusting bill.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation aimed entirely at the legislation. No person is attacked, no bad faith imputed to an individual; under the re-anchored scale harsh criticism of a measure is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, and now the repeal of our smoke-free legislation, within hours of each other, shows we have a Government that doesn’t care for the existing health disparities between Māori and non-Māori, and those impacted most in low socio-economic communities.
focus.explanation: Names two specific measures — the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora and the smokefree repeal — and ties them to a named policy outcome (Māori/non-Māori health disparities). This is scrutiny of identifiable government decisions, not content-free party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora, and now the repeal of our smoke-free legislation, within hours of each other, shows we have a Government that doesn’t care for the existing health disparities between Māori and non-Māori, and those impacted most in low socio-economic communities.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the temporal coincidence of two repeals is offered as evidence of an internal state ('doesn't care'). Timing establishes sequence, not motive, and no mechanism linking either repeal to the disparities is supplied at this point in the argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, there’s been none, because there was never a campaign on it. There’s been none, because there’s been no hui. There will be none, because we’re in urgency, and New Zealanders and te iwi Māori are shut out of the process.
rigor.explanation: Three reasons are offered for the conclusion that no engagement has occurred. The third is sound — passing under urgency does foreclose select committee consultation. The first is a non sequitur: the absence of an election campaign on a policy does not establish that no consultation took place afterwards, and the second is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You can choose to smoke; you don’t choose to be a victim of crime.
rigor.explanation: False analogy offered as a justification for deprioritising tobacco control. The choice/no-choice contrast with crime victimisation supports no conclusion about whether the smokefree measures should be repealed, and the 'choose' premise is asserted about a product whose defining feature is addiction — but even granting the premise, nothing connects it to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Prohibition approaches do not have the greatest track record. Therefore, I recommend this bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a bare unsupported generalisation about 'prohibition', with no evidence offered, and on a strawman: the repealed measures (a smokefree generation, denicotinisation, retailer reduction) are characterised as prohibition. The recommendation does not follow from what was supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Māori stats are 6.2 percent of year 10s across the country; for non-Māori, it is 2 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures for a named cohort, sourced in the preceding sentence to the ASH Year 10 Smokefree Snapshot survey. Directly checkable against a published dataset.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill changes the process, not the goal, and there are better ways to reduce harm.
specificity.explanation: The central claim of the case for the bill, carrying no checkable content: no alternative harm-reduction measure is named, no figure, mechanism or timeframe is given, and 'changes the process, not the goal' identifies neither the process nor the change.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 would have reduced tobacco outlets from 6,000—6,000—to 600, denicotinised tobacco, and created a smoke-free generation—a smoke-free generation.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, gives the before-and-after retailer figures, and lists the three specific mechanisms it contained. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The smoking rates for Māori remain alarmingly high at 17.1 percent, compared to our non-Māori counterparts at 6.1 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two named population rates to one decimal place; a reader can go to the health survey and check them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our policy is to help people quit smoking and to stop young people from starting smoking and vaping.
specificity.explanation: States an aim rather than a policy: no mechanism, no funding, no target and no timeframe, and nothing in the surrounding speech supplies them. Someone could not check or act on this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can tell you that the latest data from the Health Coalition Aotearoa is 53,000 signatures, not 45,000.
specificity.explanation: A named source and an exact figure, offered as a correction to another figure. Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 would have reduced tobacco outlets from 6,000—6,000—to 600, denicotinised tobacco, and created a smoke-free generation—a smoke-free generation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2022 Act provided for a reduction of tobacco retailers from about 6,000 to about 600, for denicotinisation of smoked tobacco, and for a smokefree generation (birth-cohort) restriction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022 and Ministry of Health implementation material; true if the Act provided for an approved-retailer cap of roughly 600 (down from roughly 6,000), for a maximum nicotine level in smoked tobacco, and for a birth-cohort ban; false if any of those three was not in the Act or the retailer figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: The smoking rates for Māori remain alarmingly high at 17.1 percent, compared to our non-Māori counterparts at 6.1 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Māori adult smoking rate of 17.1% against a non-Māori rate of 6.1% at the time of speaking (February 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence for the most recent year published before February 2024; true if the Māori rate is 17.1% (± rounding) and the non-Māori rate 6.1% (± rounding), false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Low-income communities have four times more tobacco retailers situated in their communities, hooking more whānau into addiction.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that tobacco retailer density in low-income New Zealand communities is roughly four times that of higher-income communities.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published New Zealand tobacco retailer density research by NZDep deprivation decile (e.g. University of Otago / ASPIRE retail outlet mapping); true if the most deprived areas have approximately four times the retailer density of the least deprived, false if the ratio is materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: I can tell you that the latest data from the Health Coalition Aotearoa is 53,000 signatures, not 45,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Health Coalition Aotearoa's petition against the repeal had reached about 53,000 signatures as at 27 February 2024, rather than the 45,000 figure previously cited.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health Coalition Aotearoa's petition records and contemporaneous reporting of the signature count on 27 February 2024; true if the count was approximately 53,000 that day, false if it was materially lower (e.g. still around 45,000).

veracity.statement: There was no campaign on this. There was no select committee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two procedural facts: that no party campaigned on repealing the smokefree legislation at the 2023 election, and that the repeal bill was not referred to a select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 election policy documents of National, ACT and New Zealand First, and the Parliamentary record for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Repeal Bill; true if no party's published 2023 campaign policy included the repeal and the bill passed under urgency without select committee referral, false if either a campaign commitment or a select committee stage can be identified.

divination.statement: If you read Hāpai te Hauora’s comments on this particular kaupapa, Māori will not reach the 5 percent target for a smoke-free 2025.
divination.explanation: Relays Hāpai te Hauora's forecast that Māori smoking prevalence will still be above the 5 percent smokefree threshold in 2025. The speaker is reporting someone else's forecast rather than making his own.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / New Zealand Health Survey reporting of Māori adult daily smoking prevalence for 2025; the forecast is true if that prevalence is still above 5% when the 2025 figures are published, false if it is at or below 5%.

civility.statement: It is an embarrassment that you have chosen to ram through such legislation through this House in urgency, not allowing those voices to have a say.
civility.explanation: Harsh, but the target is the Government's procedural decision to use urgency, not any individual member's character. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a decision sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I am disgusted that that previous speaker, Carlos Cheung, on this important kaupapa, gave 12 seconds of his care, his life, and his attention to this incredibly important matter.
civility.explanation: A named member is attacked personally — not his argument, but the amount of care and attention he is said to have for the subject. That is a direct attack on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister was not prepared to budge on it, and there were no reasons given as to why she was so firmly positioned supporting the tobacco lobbies with this bill.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named individual — that the Minister's position is explained by support for the tobacco lobby rather than by any stated reason. Short of a direct insult, but it attacks her motives rather than her case.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They will have blood on their hands.
civility.explanation: Accuses members personally of causing deaths. This is an attack on the moral character of the people opposite rather than on the bill, and it drew a point of order as unparliamentary.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The arrogance that I have seen from that side of the House, in such a sensitive kaupapa this evening, is disgraceful.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the demeanour of the other side of the House. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so nothing survives once the characterisation of opponents is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to say that the sniggering and sneering and treating with contempt and the joking kind of approach that we have seen from members opposite says so much about the fact of what they think about this kaupapa and how they feel about the fact that 8,000 lives are at stake—8,000 lives that could’ve been saved.
focus.explanation: The weight of the statement is on how members opposite are behaving and what that reveals about them, with the 8,000-lives figure attached at the end. There is a real policy number in it, but the statement is directed at the other side rather than at the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just because we use a different approach doesn’t mean that we can’t achieve the same outcome.
rigor.explanation: Engages the policy but the inference is empty: it establishes only that a different approach is not logically incompatible with the same outcome, and offers that bare possibility as grounds for concluding the goal will still be met. Nothing is supplied connecting the replacement approach to the target.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Aucklanders voted for change at the last election, last year; 57.8 percent of Aucklanders voted for the coalition Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 57.8% of Auckland voters supported the three coalition parties (National, ACT, NZ First) at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official 2023 general election party-vote results aggregated across Auckland general electorates; true if the combined National + ACT + NZ First party vote is approximately 57.8%, false if materially different (e.g. nearer the ~52-53% national figure).

veracity.statement: The most expensive speed bumps in the world, in fact: close to $500,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland Transport speed bumps cost close to $500,000 each and that these are the most expensive anywhere in the world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport cost records / OIA releases for raised crossings and speed tables; true if documented per-unit costs approach $500,000 and no higher documented per-unit cost exists internationally, false if AT's typical per-unit cost is materially lower or comparable costs are documented elsewhere.

veracity.statement: There is over $300 million—over $300 million—sitting in a bank account, unspent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than $300 million of Auckland regional fuel tax revenue was unspent as at the date of the speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Transport regional fuel tax financial reporting as at early 2024; true if the unallocated or unspent RFT balance exceeded $300 million, false if materially less.

veracity.statement: It will be delivered under the coalition Government in 2026—unlike light rail, or “light fail”, as I call it: $228 million and not one metre of track laid after six years, spinning the wheels on the ghost train in Auckland and not getting anywhere.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $228 million was spent on Auckland light rail over six years with no track laid.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / Auckland Light Rail Ltd expenditure disclosures and construction records; true if cumulative spend was approximately $228 million and no track was laid, false if the spend figure is materially different or any track was constructed.

focus.statement: So when members opposite will get up shortly, maybe in another part of this debate, and try and claim that they have some sort of moral mandate on what Aucklanders think—well, Aucklanders voted for change, they voted for the parties in this Government, and we were elected on the promise of axing the Auckland regional fuel tax.
focus.explanation: A named policy commitment (axing the Auckland regional fuel tax) is present, but the weight of the statement is an electoral-mandate contest with the other parties rather than the merits of the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So you’ve got 11.5c per litre additional fuel tax being charged on Aucklanders, and what do they get? A speed bump to slow them down.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: names the tax, its rate, and what the revenue is said to have funded. On-policy scrutiny, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, for those who drive a Toyota Corolla, around $5.75 per tank; for those who drive a Toyota Hilux, around $9.20 per tank—this will make a significant difference.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the effect of the repeal per vehicle with named examples and dollar figures; someone could check the arithmetic against tank size and the 11.5c rate.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So you’ve got 11.5c per litre additional fuel tax being charged on Aucklanders, and what do they get? A speed bump to slow them down.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation / cherry-picking: one category of spend is offered as if it were the whole of what the tax bought, and the conclusion that Aucklanders 'get' only a speed bump does not follow from a single example of expenditure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That date is intentional: it aligns with the Auckland Council’s annual budget plan, in terms of the fact that we don’t want to end the tax partway through their budget year.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered that genuinely supports the conclusion: if disrupting the council's budget year is undesirable, aligning the end date with that year follows. No fallacy or gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It will be delivered under the coalition Government in 2026—unlike light rail, or “light fail”, as I call it: $228 million and not one metre of track laid after six years, spinning the wheels on the ghost train in Auckland and not getting anywhere.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the City Rail Link will be delivered during 2026.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: City Rail Link Ltd / Auckland Transport opening records; true if CRL is delivered and opens for passenger service during calendar year 2026, false if delivery slips into 2027 or later.

civility.statement: We think that is the right approach, rather than this rinky-dink approach that has been employed by the last Government and has failed to deliver whilst increasing taxes for Aucklanders.
civility.explanation: Dismissive language ('rinky-dink') but aimed at the previous government's policy approach and delivery record, not at any person's character or competence. Robust criticism of a policy is civil under this scale.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I want to pay tribute to Dame Tariana and the work that she did and to tell her that we will reinforce that work, we will reinvigorate that work, we will recharge that work, and we will relaunch that work.
specificity.explanation: Four near-synonymous verbs offered as a commitment — reinforce, reinvigorate, recharge, relaunch — with no mechanism, funding, measure or timeframe attached. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Polling commissioned by Health Coalition Aotearoa showed that 67 percent of New Zealanders supported our smoke-free legislation.
specificity.explanation: A named commissioning body, a numeric result and an identified subject of the poll. Someone could go and find the poll and check the number.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s about killing the demand. It’s about giving people the tools to actually tackle this.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the alternative approach to the repealed measures, but names no tool, no programme, no funding and no target. 'Giving people the tools' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, on 18 October in the New Zealand Herald: “Dame Tariana Turia believes more can be accomplished for Māori health under National”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand Herald published, on 18 October, a headline in those words reporting Dame Tariana Turia's view that National could accomplish more for Māori health.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Herald archive for 18 October (2023): true if an article carries that headline or wording materially identical to it; false if no such article or headline exists on that date.

veracity.statement: We are committed to Smokefree 2025, and we’re on track.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand is currently on track to meet the Smokefree 2025 goal — daily smoking prevalence below 5%.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence, latest release before the statement and the 2025 release: true if the overall rate is at or below 5% by 2025 and the Māori and Pacific rates are trending to meet it; false if prevalence for the overall or Māori population remains materially above 5% in 2025.

veracity.statement: And the evidence—actual evidence—shows us that the smoke-free legislation that we introduced in 2022 that’s been hiffed out tonight would have saved about 8,000, and that is nothing to sniff at, is it?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the published modelling of the 2022 Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act put the lives saved at approximately 8,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The peer-reviewed modelling underpinning the 2022 Act (Ait Ouakrim et al., Lancet Public Health / BMJ tobacco endgame modelling) and the Ministry of Health regulatory impact statement: true if a published estimate of deaths averted is about 8,000; false if the published estimates are materially different (e.g. around 5,000, or an order of magnitude apart).

veracity.statement: It would have extended Māori life expectancy and it would have saved about $5 billion in healthcare costs, and that’s a real shame.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two modelled outcomes of the repealed 2022 legislation: a gain in Māori life expectancy, and roughly $5 billion in avoided healthcare costs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The health-system cost savings figure in the modelling and regulatory impact statement for the 2022 Act: true if a published estimate is about NZ$5 billion; false if the published savings estimate is materially lower (e.g. the ~$1.3 billion figure cited elsewhere in the debate).

veracity.statement: Polling commissioned by Health Coalition Aotearoa showed that 67 percent of New Zealanders supported our smoke-free legislation.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific polling result — 67 percent public support for the 2022 smokefree legislation — to a poll commissioned by Health Coalition Aotearoa.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Coalition Aotearoa commissioned poll released before 27 February 2024: true if it reports support at 67 percent (± rounding) for the smokefree measures; false if no such poll exists or its support figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Now, many people have said, and let me reiterate, the National Party did not campaign on this repeal at the election.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that repealing the smokefree legislation formed no part of the National Party's 2023 general election campaign.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 manifesto, health policy documents and published fiscal/tax plan: false if any pre-election National campaign document names repeal of the smokefree measures (including as a revenue line in the tax plan); true if the repeal appears only after the election, in the coalition agreements.

veracity.statement: They said things like there would be only one store in Northland retailing tobacco, when there would actually be 35.
veracity.explanation: Two claims: that the repeal's proponents publicly said Northland would be left with a single tobacco retailer, and that the actual number allocated under the retailer-reduction regulations was 35.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Health / Health NZ regional allocation of approved tobacco retailers under the 2022 Act: true if the Northland allocation is 35; false if it is materially different. The first half is settled by the public statements of National and NZ First MPs before the repeal.

civility.statement: I think that Cameron Brewer’s contribution that he just made possibly sounded a little bit different in his head, because I’m not entirely sure that anybody he referenced in that contribution would be thinking the same things as he just regaled us with.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at a named member rather than at his argument — the jibe is that his speech only worked inside his own head. Sneering and condescending, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yet throughout this process, she hasn’t been able to give anyone any confidence whatsoever that she has a single idea, let alone a good idea, that will actually work.
civility.explanation: Lands on the Minister personally — that she has not a single idea — rather than on the content of the repeal. A clear attack on her capability, not on the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Just because the first thing he did was to callously delegate this to a brand new Minister, who is clearly out of her depth, who clearly does not understand the legislation, does not take away from the part that he’s played in turning this legislation backwards.
civility.explanation: Direct attack on the personal competence of two members — one 'callous', the other 'clearly out of her depth' and not understanding her own legislation. Aimed at the people, not the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I feel embarrassed for all of the people on that side of the House.
civility.explanation: Condescension toward members collectively — pity rather than argument. No individual is insulted, but it is a sneer, not engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s an indictment on this Government’s priorities that we’re literally here repealing smoke-free laws to fund tax cuts that are disproportionately favourable to our most wealthy.
rigor.explanation: An argument about the measure itself, not a jibe: if the repeal's revenue funds tax cuts skewed to the wealthy, the conclusion about the Government's ordering of priorities does follow. The gap is that the funding link is asserted rather than shown, so the inference rests on an unestablished causal premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I feel embarrassed for all of the people on that side of the House.
focus.explanation: A verdict on the other side of the House as people. No policy, figure, mechanism or named commitment survives once the party framing is removed — this is the content-free case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’re asking for consistency and they want to have a smoke-free generation, but the Green Party also want to introduce new drugs to smoke.
focus.explanation: Entirely about another party's positions and their alleged inconsistency, not about the bill before the House. No clause, cost, mechanism or outcome is named. (Deliberately not scored for Rigor: strip out the part about the other side and no argument about the policy remains.)
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Could the Leader of the House please tell us when we can expect a piece of legislation to go through a full and proper process, with no urgency, no instruction to the select committee, and, hopefully, with a regulatory impact statement being published?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named practice — use of urgency, select committee instructions, and publication of regulatory impact statements. It engages how the Government is legislating rather than characterising Labour's opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Some of the legislation I’ve just read out is exactly that; the fast-track consenting bill will go to a committee, the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill will go to a committee, the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill will go to a committee, and the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill will go to a committee.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the legislative programme before the House; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Reserve Bank was trying to fight inflation with higher interest rates while the Government was busy fuelling it with its high spending and ever-growing debt.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point about the interaction of fiscal and monetary settings, naming spending and debt, though delivered with partisan framing about the previous Government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This sovereign risk is a result of the economic vandalism threatened by some, and their woke fellow travellers, who have no comprehension at all of international business and investment.
focus.explanation: Once the characterisation of opponents is removed, almost nothing about the decommissioning or bonds policy remains — the content is what the other side is like.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Other countries have done that already, which is the reason why those countries have investment and we have lost all of it.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the measure under question — compensation bonds and their effect on investment — even though the inference drawn is weak.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government is committed to deliver net zero by 2050, including by doubling New Zealand’s renewable electricity and removing consenting barriers.
focus.explanation: Wholly about energy and emissions policy; no party framing or characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What was the cost to the New Zealand taxpayer of having to clean up the mess of Tamarind when the company left New Zealand because we had lax decommissioning laws that that Minister is now looking to bring back?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: a named case (Tamarind), a named policy area (decommissioning liability) and a specific outcome (cost to the taxpayer). Holding a Minister to account for a named policy direction is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has he sought advice on whether compensation bonds to multinational oil and gas companies would contravene New Zealand’s free-trade agreement with the EU?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the policy under consideration and its legal constraints; nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Could the Leader of the House please tell us when we can expect a piece of legislation to go through a full and proper process, with no urgency, no instruction to the select committee, and, hopefully, with a regulatory impact statement being published?
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete, checkable process elements (urgency, committee instruction, regulatory impact statement), but asks for no figure or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Some of the legislation I’ve just read out is exactly that; the fast-track consenting bill will go to a committee, the Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill will go to a committee, the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill will go to a committee, and the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Bill will go to a committee.
specificity.explanation: Four bills named individually with the process step each will take. Someone could check it against the order paper. Falls short of 1.0 only because no timeframe is attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Inflation has declined from a peak of 7.3 percent in mid-2022 to 4.7 percent in the December quarter, and the bank’s forecasts show it falling towards the 2 percent mid-point of the target band.
specificity.explanation: Two dated figures, a named source and a named target band. Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is committed to deliver net zero by 2050, including by doubling New Zealand’s renewable electricity and removing consenting barriers.
specificity.explanation: A named target with a date (net zero by 2050) and a quantified sub-goal (doubling renewable electricity), but "removing consenting barriers" carries no mechanism, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What was the cost to the New Zealand taxpayer of having to clean up the mess of Tamarind when the company left New Zealand because we had lax decommissioning laws that that Minister is now looking to bring back?
specificity.explanation: Names the company and the specific cost being asked about, though it supplies no figure or date of its own.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Has he sought advice on whether compensation bonds to multinational oil and gas companies would contravene New Zealand’s free-trade agreement with the EU?
specificity.explanation: A precisely bounded question: a named instrument (compensation bonds), a named counterparty class, and a named agreement (the NZ–EU FTA). Answerable yes or no and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Inflation has declined from a peak of 7.3 percent in mid-2022 to 4.7 percent in the December quarter, and the bank’s forecasts show it falling towards the 2 percent mid-point of the target band.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific historical CPI readings (a 7.3% peak in mid-2022, 4.7% in the December quarter) and characterises the RBNZ's published forecast track.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ consumers price index annual inflation series: true if the peak annual CPI rate was 7.3% in a mid-2022 quarter and the December 2023 quarter rate was 4.7%; false if either figure is materially different. The forecast claim is settled by the RBNZ February 2024 Monetary Policy Statement CPI projection track — true if it projects inflation returning toward the 2% mid-point.

veracity.statement: The Reserve Bank was trying to fight inflation with higher interest rates while the Government was busy fuelling it with its high spending and ever-growing debt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that fiscal policy under the previous Government was expansionary (rising spending and debt) at the same time as the Reserve Bank was tightening monetary policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury fiscal impulse estimates (Budget/HYEFU) and core Crown expenditure and net core Crown debt for 2021–2023, set against the RBNZ's OCR track: true if the fiscal impulse was expansionary and net core Crown debt rose over the period in which the OCR was being raised; false if fiscal policy was contractionary or debt fell over that period.

civility.statement: This sovereign risk is a result of the economic vandalism threatened by some, and their woke fellow travellers, who have no comprehension at all of international business and investment.
civility.explanation: "Economic vandalism", "woke fellow travellers" and "no comprehension at all" attack the character and competence of the people opposite rather than their argument. No individual is named, which keeps it above the floor.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And if I was responsible for the closure of Marsden Point, thereby imperilling our very critical supply in a time of a supply emergency, I’d be keeping my mouth shut.
civility.explanation: Tells the questioner she should stay silent and pins a specific failure on her personally. It lands on the member, not on the argument she made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And it’s unbelievable that we have Standing Orders and Speakers’ rulings, and some people have been here for all those years and seemingly have learnt nothing.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the questioner's competence — that after years in the House she has "learnt nothing". A personal attack, not a point about the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, please, catch up. I know it’s early 2024, but this is serious, and there could be many decades waiting around to be a good Opposition.
civility.explanation: Sneering and condescension directed at the questioner — an instruction to "catch up" and a jibe about her fitness for the job, in place of engagement with what she asked.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Other countries have done that already, which is the reason why those countries have investment and we have lost all of it.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc / single-cause fallacy: that other countries use such bonds and also attract investment is offered as proof the bonds caused the investment, and the absence of bonds caused New Zealand's loss of it. No mechanism or evidence connects the two, and competing explanations are not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How is it fair to New Zealand taxpayers to ask them to underwrite multibillion multinational oil and gas companies’ return to New Zealand and then shoulder the clean-up and decommissioning costs when they leave without paying their bills?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question — who carries decommissioning and clean-up liability under the oil and gas settings. Names a specific cost mechanism rather than characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I tell you what the taxpayer’s going to be paying for: they’ll be paying for a shutdown economy brought about by people who came to Parliament with no idea how business works.
focus.explanation: Beyond the bare assertion of a "shutdown economy", the content is a characterisation of who the other side are, not of any policy, figure or measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think it was probably legislation that Stuart Nash brought in, because, actually, he was a very good police Minister, unlike the three that followed him.
focus.explanation: Asked which statute authorised the confiscations and the convoy policing, the reply names no legislation and instead ranks the other party's Ministers against each other.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On Sunday, Minister Goldsmith, Minister McKee, and I announced part of the coalition Government’s proposed crackdown on gangs, including banning gang patches and insignia in public, dispersal notices, non-consorting orders, and making gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the substance of the proposed gang policy; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If 12 front-line police officers have gone public to say that this gang patch ban is unworkable and that they are not resourced to enforce it, how does he justify to the New Zealand public introducing this legislation?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named measure on a named ground — whether the patch ban can actually be enforced with the resourcing available. This is the job of an opposition MP.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can justify it because, unlike the Labour Party who are gang apologists, we have a deeply capable New Zealand police force that is motivated and wants to go out there and protect the communities that they serve and clamp down on gangs.
focus.explanation: Asked about resourcing and enforceability, the answer offers no policy content — the weight is on what the Labour Party are supposedly like, plus a general tribute to police morale.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he agree with National MP Tama Potaka, who said on 9 September 2023 that “National will increase the number of social housing places funded by Government”?
focus.explanation: Holds the Government to a specific, dated, quoted commitment on social housing places — named policy, named commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Last week, I announced that the Government will repeal the Business Payment Practices Act 2023. This piece of legislation was an ineffective, costly solution to the problem of large market players paying invoices late, and evidence from abroad supports the repeal of the Act.
focus.explanation: Names the statute, the action being taken and the problem it was meant to address — entirely on the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What does the Minister say to my constituent who worked as a sole trader for one of our biggest companies and had his payments consistently and mindfully delayed by three months; is that fair and reasonable practice?
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance of the late-payment problem the repealed Act addressed, testing the policy against a concrete case rather than attacking the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think the Opposition is going to have a real problem here in that they have confused spending money with delivering results, because if spending $100 billion of borrowed money on every problem actually worked, this country wouldn’t have any problems after the last Government.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point about inputs versus outcomes in school property, but it is carried almost entirely by framing about the Opposition and the last Government rather than by anything about the property programme.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she stand by her guarantee of 27 February that there will be no cuts to school property capital expenditure; if not, why not?
focus.explanation: Holds the Minister to a dated, specific undertaking on a named budget line. Scrutiny of a named commitment, not party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The answer to that is that this country’s supply of gas is imperilled for the next five years now, and no planning forward has been admitted—worse still, it’s been stopped.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand's gas supply will be in jeopardy over the five years following February 2024. Not a promise about his own action; a claim about how the gas market will behave.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE gas production and supply statistics plus Gas Industry Company reporting to 2029: true if New Zealand experiences material gas supply shortfalls or curtailment of industrial gas users during the period; false if supply meets demand without curtailment or shortfall notices.

veracity.statement: And we have, at the same time, Marsden Point, which right now has been allowed to close down in supply when, in a critical phrase of non-supply to this country by tankers, we could’ve supplied 50 percent of the country’s critical needs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Marsden Point refinery, before it was closed, could have met about 50 percent of New Zealand's critical fuel needs in a tanker supply disruption. ("critical phrase" is an obvious spoken slip for "critical phase" and is not the claim being checked.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE oil statistics and Refining NZ / Channel Infrastructure records on the share of New Zealand refined fuel demand the Marsden Point refinery met before its 2022 conversion to an import terminal: true if the refinery's share was around 50 percent or higher, false if materially below 50 percent.

veracity.statement: Recently, as reported, I was present as six gold-plated Harley-Davidson motorcycles, formerly the prized possessions of the Comancheros, were shredded into scrap metal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that six gold-plated Harley-Davidson motorcycles forfeited from the Comancheros were destroyed, with the Minister present.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Police media releases and contemporaneous news reporting from February 2024: true if six gold-plated Harley-Davidsons forfeited from the Comancheros were destroyed with the Minister of Police present, false if the number, the gang of origin or the Minister's attendance is materially different.

veracity.statement: If 12 front-line police officers have gone public to say that this gang patch ban is unworkable and that they are not resourced to enforce it, how does he justify to the New Zealand public introducing this legislation?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as the premise of the question that twelve front-line police officers have publicly said the gang patch ban is unworkable and under-resourced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: News reporting from January–February 2024 on serving front-line police officers speaking publicly about the gang patch ban: true if reporting records around twelve front-line officers making that criticism, false if no such reporting exists or the number of officers is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: I think the member who’s yelling out, who’s a former Minister of Housing, will recall that the funding for social housing places ceases after June 2025, so that is indeed a fiscal cliff.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that appropriated funding for social housing places stops after June 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 appropriations and the Vote Housing and Urban Development forecast tables: true if funding for the public/social housing places programme is not appropriated past June 2025, false if appropriations continue into 2025/26.

veracity.statement: Back in 2020, Australia implemented a very similar scheme named the Payment Times Reporting Act. A recent independent review of the scheme’s effectiveness found that despite imposing significant IT compliance costs on businesses, overall payment times had not reduced.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australia enacted the Payment Times Reporting Act in 2020 and that an independent review found significant IT compliance costs with no reduction in overall payment times.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Australian Payment Times Reporting Act 2020 and the statutory independent review of it (the Emerson review, reported 2023): true if the review found compliance costs significant and no material reduction in payment times, false if it found payment times improved or did not make that compliance-cost finding.

veracity.statement: I read recently in media that Macleans College in Auckland had funded and built five new classrooms in nine months after being advised by the Ministry of Education that it would take three years to deliver the same learning spaces. They did it for $2.5 million, and the ministry then commented they were surprised it could be done so cost-effectively, thinking it should have cost over twice that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Macleans College built five classrooms in nine months for $2.5 million after the Ministry of Education advised the same work would take three years, and that the ministry expected it to cost more than twice as much.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous news reporting and Macleans College / Ministry of Education records on the school's classroom build: true if five classrooms were delivered in about nine months for about $2.5 million against ministry advice of three years, false if the number of rooms, the timeframe or the cost is materially different.

veracity.statement: Will she guarantee that the requested 7.5 percent cuts to the education budget will have no impact on kids and their learning, and, if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as the premise of the question that the education budget has been asked to find cuts of 7.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's Budget 2024 baseline savings instructions to departments: true if the Ministry of Education was asked for savings of 7.5 percent of baseline, false if it was asked for a materially different percentage (for example the 6.5 percent applied to most departments) or no such request was made.

civility.statement: I tell you what the taxpayer’s going to be paying for: they’ll be paying for a shutdown economy brought about by people who came to Parliament with no idea how business works.
civility.explanation: Turns from the gas policy to the members opposite themselves, attacking their competence and experience ("no idea how business works") rather than anything they have argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think it was probably legislation that Stuart Nash brought in, because, actually, he was a very good police Minister, unlike the three that followed him.
civility.explanation: A pointed comparative slight on the competence of three identifiable individuals (Nash's successors as Minister of Police), delivered in place of an answer.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The reality is the last Government didn’t fund places beyond 2025, into 2026 or 2027, because they wanted to create the illusion of a surplus later on.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — deliberately manufacturing an "illusion" — to the previous Government, addressed at a former Minister of Housing present in the House. Short of a direct insult but no longer just criticism of the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: However, this Government takes a much more benign view of the role of public servants, and we will be ensuring that those people who are productive and useful for delivering outcomes for the teachers, the kids, and the parents are well employed and properly guided to do the job properly, which may initially be a surprise to them after the last six years of Chris Hipkins and Jan Tinetti, but I think they’re up for it.
civility.explanation: Names two individuals and implies, by way of a sneer rather than an argument, that under them public servants were neither properly employed nor properly guided. Condescending toward the named members and toward the officials.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On Sunday, Minister Goldsmith, Minister McKee, and I announced part of the coalition Government’s proposed crackdown on gangs, including banning gang patches and insignia in public, dispersal notices, non-consorting orders, and making gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing.
specificity.explanation: Four named measures, the Ministers responsible and the timing of the announcement — concrete enough for anyone to look up and act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If 12 front-line police officers have gone public to say that this gang patch ban is unworkable and that they are not resourced to enforce it, how does he justify to the New Zealand public introducing this legislation?
specificity.explanation: Gives a count of officers, names the policy and states the precise objection (workability and resourcing); a precise question, not a slogan.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he agree with National MP Tama Potaka, who said on 9 September 2023 that “National will increase the number of social housing places funded by Government”?
specificity.explanation: Names the MP, the date and the exact wording of the undertaking, so the question can be checked directly against the record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Last week, I announced that the Government will repeal the Business Payment Practices Act 2023. This piece of legislation was an ineffective, costly solution to the problem of large market players paying invoices late, and evidence from abroad supports the repeal of the Act.
specificity.explanation: A named Act, a named action (repeal) and a stated timeframe for the announcement; the supporting evidence is gestured at rather than cited, which holds it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Furthermore, we will incentivise SMEs to adopt e-invoicing by reducing Government entity payment times to an expected target of five working days, thereby significantly improving their cash flow.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism (e-invoicing uptake driven by faster Crown payment) with a numeric target attached; checkable against published payment-time data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I read recently in media that Macleans College in Auckland had funded and built five new classrooms in nine months after being advised by the Ministry of Education that it would take three years to deliver the same learning spaces. They did it for $2.5 million, and the ministry then commented they were surprised it could be done so cost-effectively, thinking it should have cost over twice that.
specificity.explanation: A named school, a count of classrooms, two timeframes and a dollar figure — every element is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she stand by her guarantee of 27 February that there will be no cuts to school property capital expenditure; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Names the date of the guarantee and the exact expenditure category it covered; precise enough to be checked, though no figures are attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will she guarantee that the requested 7.5 percent cuts to the education budget will have no impact on kids and their learning, and, if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Attaches a precise figure to a named budget and asks for a guarantee against a stated consequence; the consequence itself ("impact on kids and their learning") is the loose part.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can justify it because, unlike the Labour Party who are gang apologists, we have a deeply capable New Zealand police force that is motivated and wants to go out there and protect the communities that they serve and clamp down on gangs.
rigor.explanation: Setting the party jibe aside, the residual inference is a non sequitur: the objection was that officers lack the resources to enforce the ban, and willingness and capability of the police does not answer whether the resources exist.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think the member who’s yelling out, who’s a former Minister of Housing, will recall that the funding for social housing places ceases after June 2025, so that is indeed a fiscal cliff.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premise offered: if funding for a programme stops at a date certain, calling that a fiscal cliff follows. The support is a stated fact about the appropriation, not an appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reality is the last Government didn’t fund places beyond 2025, into 2026 or 2027, because they wanted to create the illusion of a surplus later on.
rigor.explanation: The motive is asserted, not derived. Nothing is offered to connect the absence of out-year appropriations to a deliberate intent to flatter the surplus; the alternative explanations (fixed-term programme funding, standard Budget practice) are not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Back in 2020, Australia implemented a very similar scheme named the Payment Times Reporting Act. A recent independent review of the scheme’s effectiveness found that despite imposing significant IT compliance costs on businesses, overall payment times had not reduced.
rigor.explanation: A reasonable argument from a close analogue: a comparable scheme, independently reviewed, produced cost without effect, therefore the local equivalent should go. The gap is that no evidence is offered that the two schemes are alike enough for the finding to carry across.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think the Opposition is going to have a real problem here in that they have confused spending money with delivering results, because if spending $100 billion of borrowed money on every problem actually worked, this country wouldn’t have any problems after the last Government.
rigor.explanation: A strawman wrapped in a false dilemma: nobody claimed that spending alone solves every problem, and the reductio only works against that invented position. The residual point — spending is not the same as delivery — is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On behalf of the Minister, I’m in possession of correspondence from well-respected Auckland property engineering firms who say that you could easily get rid of 75 percent of the Auckland Ministry of Education staff and be better off.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to unnamed authority. The conclusion about the ministry's staffing rests entirely on the standing of correspondents who are neither identified nor shown to have any basis for the 75 percent figure; no reasoning is offered for the number itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason that’s possible is that there has been so much waste in the past six years that you can reduce expenditure by 6.5 percent very easily—hell, some of our coalition partners in this Government would go a lot further.
rigor.explanation: Concludes a 6.5 percent cut is painless from a bare assertion that 'so much waste' exists; nothing is offered to size the waste against the cut, and the closing clause is an appeal to what coalition partners want rather than evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You see, there’s a thing called the sunk cost fallacy, and just because money has been spent on something in the past does not mean that continuing to waste money is a good idea.
rigor.explanation: The sunk-cost point is correctly stated and does support the conclusion, but the phrasing assumes what is in dispute — that the continued spending is 'waste' — so the inference is partly question-begging.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In taking this course of action, in which the Government works to drive more value from every dollar it invests in the education system so as to improve achievement, has he considered an alternative approach in which the Government simply appropriates money from the magic money tree at the end of the garden?
rigor.explanation: Strawman: it engages the education spending question but sets against it a position nobody advanced — costless money — so the contrast does no argumentative work.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, but I hope that the example she gave, with Western Australia, shows that the gang patch ban was working because they wanted to leave.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: treats gang members relocating as proof the ban 'was working', which is precisely the displacement objection put to him rather than an answer to it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I hope that the students at Andersons Bay primary go on to learn economics better than that member has.
civility.explanation: A direct jibe at another member's competence — the target is the person's understanding, not the argument they made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Opposition and Harry Tam may not like it, but that is what is happening.
civility.explanation: Pairs the Opposition with a named gang advocate, imputing shared motive rather than answering the objection — sneering by association, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: However, we are pressing on to ensure that on Budget day that member will know, and so that then the only uncertainty at that point in time will be whether or not he is rightfully the leader of the Labour Party.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the questioner's personal standing in his own party rather than at anything he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Andersons Bay primary will have its property needs catered to by this Government, and it will be done in a much more responsible and prudent way than they might have expected over the last six years.
specificity.explanation: An assurance with no figure, no scope of work and no timeframe; 'property needs catered to' and 'responsible and prudent' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Given that Ōpōtiki has only two full-time front-line officers and also covers Te Kaha, how will they remove the jackets of the approximate 1,400 gang members who live in the area?
specificity.explanation: Names the locality, the staffing number and the gang-member count, so the enforcement question it poses is concrete and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On Friday, I announced a $5 million boost to the upper North Island community’s fight against the invasive seaweed Caulerpa.
specificity.explanation: Dollar figure, named pest, named region and a date — the commitment can be checked against the appropriation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: With the assistance of this budgetary money, it is our intention to get a result in India as fast as we possibly can.
specificity.explanation: 'A result in India' is never defined, no amount is attached to 'this budgetary money', and 'as fast as we possibly can' supplies no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Given that Ōpōtiki has only two full-time front-line officers and also covers Te Kaha, how will they remove the jackets of the approximate 1,400 gang members who live in the area?
veracity.explanation: Asserts two factual premises: Ōpōtiki has two full-time front-line officers covering Te Kaha as well, and approximately 1,400 gang members live in that area.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police staffing figures for the Ōpōtiki station and its Te Kaha coverage area as at February 2024, plus the National Gang List count for that area; true if there were two full-time front-line constabulary staff and roughly 1,400 listed gang members, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Given the concerns that have been publicly outlined by front-line officers on enforcing the gang patch ban, how does he explain to the New Zealand public a 6.5 percent cut to the Police budget?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Police budget is subject to a 6.5 percent cut, and that front-line officers have publicly raised enforcement concerns about the patch ban.
veracity.subject: speaker
