veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's 2024 baseline savings targets as applied to Vote Police (Treasury/Budget documents and the Minister of Finance's savings instructions); true if Police was required to find savings of 6.5 percent of its baseline, false if a different target applied or front-line policing was carved out.

veracity.statement: Given the Western Australian gang patch ban simply displaced gangs over the state border, does he consider that this law change will simply displace gang members to parts of New Zealand where police are not resourced to enforce the law?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as established fact that the Western Australian patch ban displaced gangs across the state border rather than reducing gang activity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Evaluations of Western Australia's gang insignia and anti-consorting laws (WA Police reporting, Australian criminological studies); true if documented gang relocation across WA's state borders followed the ban, false if no such displacement effect is recorded.

veracity.statement: This exotic pest arrived in 2021 and has now been found in five locations across Northland and Greater Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable claims: the year exotic Caulerpa was first detected in New Zealand, and the number of confirmed infestation sites in the upper North Island at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Biosecurity NZ / MPI records for exotic Caulerpa; true if first detected in New Zealand in 2021 and confirmed at five separate locations across Northland and Greater Auckland as at February 2024, false if the arrival year or the number of confirmed sites differs.

veracity.statement: It is targeted to go to 0.23.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's ODA-to-GNI ratio is on track to fall to 0.23 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT and OECD DAC figures for New Zealand's official development assistance as a share of gross national income; true if the forecast/target ratio for the period referenced is 0.23 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: But what I am concerned about is resolving the growing court backlog that was allowed to persist under his party’s watch since 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the court backlog grew and persisted throughout the 2017-2023 Labour-led Governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court caseload and disposal statistics for the District and High Courts; true if active case backlogs grew over the 2017-2023 period, false if they were flat or declining across that period.

focus.statement: Well, the Government’s going through a cost-saving exercise because of the vandalism, the economic vandalism, of the previous Government, and I’ve got full confidence in our New Zealand police and their capability.
focus.explanation: Asked about a specific budget cut and its effect on enforcement; answers with a characterisation of the previous Government's record plus a general expression of confidence, naming no figure, mechanism or staffing outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: However, we are pressing on to ensure that on Budget day that member will know, and so that then the only uncertainty at that point in time will be whether or not he is rightfully the leader of the Labour Party.
focus.explanation: Asked about savings within MFAT; the reply carries no policy content at all, only a jibe about the other party's internal leadership situation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But what I am concerned about is resolving the growing court backlog that was allowed to persist under his party’s watch since 2017.
focus.explanation: Identifies a real and specific policy problem — the court backlog — but frames it as the other party's watch rather than engaging the funding question actually put to her.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How does the Minister intend to reduce the backlog of court cases while also delivering 6.5 percent cuts in funding?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure at issue: names the specific outcome sought (backlog reduction) and the specific fiscal constraint (6.5 percent cuts), with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And what we have not heard in these 100 days is a positive agenda from the new Government.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of the other side's first 100 days in the round — no measure, figure, target or named policy is engaged, so there is nothing on-policy to hold the Government to. This is party framing rather than scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’re all in the building, and they are the ones setting the agenda of this Government.
focus.explanation: A claim about who the Government 'really' serves, listing industry lobbies without naming a single policy, decision or document that a lobby is said to have shaped. It is about the character of the other side rather than about any measure, so the deciding test — does it name a specific policy or outcome — fails.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have seen, this week, the repeal of a policy that was going to do real and meaningful work around saving the lives of New Zealanders—the work around the smoke-free legislation that was world leading.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure — the smokefree legislation and its repeal — and the outcome she says is at stake. This is scrutiny of a particular Government decision, which is the opposition's job and scores at the top of the scale regardless of whether one agrees with the claim.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This afternoon, we saw a line-up of potential new leaders—a line-up of them.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal state — who might challenge for its leadership — with no policy, measure or outcome anywhere in view. This is the pure-tribalism case the attribute exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But I do understand the negative impacts of putting in place a policy that would punish those who aren’t able to, for a variety of reasons, use EVs.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages a named policy — the vehicle charge he calls the ute tax — and who it falls on. It carries little detail about the mechanism or the numbers, but Focus asks what the statement is about, and this is about the measure rather than about Labour.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I did note in question time today, though, that David Seymour must have got so excited when he heard about 7.5 percent cost cuts, he read that as 75 percent at the Ministry of Education.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at a named individual: Seymour is cast as gleeful over cuts and as having misread a figure by a factor of ten. The target is the person's conduct and judgement rather than the savings policy itself, which puts it below the 0.5 'sneering/mockery' failure line, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: An inquiry to cover up the fact that they simply do not have the money to pay for what has already been promised to schools around this country.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Minister of Education — that the inquiry was launched as concealment rather than as an inquiry. That is an accusation about motive, not about the merits of the school property programme, which places it at the 'imputing bad faith' failure level rather than the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’re seeing Air Marshal Short saying that the 6.5 percent cuts from Defence would mean they had to divest themselves of capability.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Chief of Defence Force publicly stated that a 6.5 percent baseline savings requirement would force NZDF to give up military capability. The claim is about what a named official said, not about whether the cuts are wise.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZDF/Chief of Defence Force statements or select committee evidence around February 2024 on the Government's baseline savings exercise; true if Air Marshal Kevin Short is on record saying a 6.5 percent savings target would require divesting capability, false if the figure or the attributed warning differs materially.

veracity.statement: We saw a Government that repealed it under urgency at a point where lives will be lost.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the smokefree legislation was repealed under urgency in the week to 29 February 2024. The 'lives will be lost' clause is a projection and is not what is being checked here; the checkable assertion is the repeal and the use of urgency.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record and bill progress for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Repeal Bill; true if the House passed the repeal under urgency in the sitting week ending 29 February 2024, false if it was not passed under urgency or not passed in that week.

veracity.statement: Then, of course, this Government has already stopped that mind-bogglingly wasteful experience called the Auckland light rail.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition Government had, by late February 2024, cancelled the Auckland light rail project. The 'mind-bogglingly wasteful' characterisation is rhetoric; the checkable assertion is that the project was stopped.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/Cabinet announcements on Auckland Light Rail; true if the project was formally cancelled or wound up before 29 February 2024, false if it was still live, merely paused, or under review at that date.

rigor.statement: That’s what this coalition Government has had to do during its first hundred days: stop the bleeding, the wasteful profligate spending, the arrogant assumption that they know best on every issue, and the arrogant assumption that New Zealand voters, using the democratic ballot box available to them, have made a decision about the future direction of this country, and it wasn’t the direction that was being taken by that Government over the last six years.
rigor.explanation: The whole weight of the argument rests on an analogy drawn from a childhood anecdote — first aid for a stubbed knee stands in for fiscal management — and an appeal to the election result. Neither establishes that the spending was in fact wasteful, and the analogy is asserted rather than shown to hold, so the conclusion outruns what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But as we approach the completion of this coalition Government’s first hundred days, I want to remind the House about the 49 points of action that we will have completed by this time next week or next Friday.
specificity.explanation: Carries a count and a date — 49 actions, complete by 8 March — which is checkable. It stops short of the top of the scale because not one of the 49 actions is named or costed here, so the listener knows how many and by when but not what.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the year since January 2023 alone, there’s been a 3 percent increase in the District Court criminal backlog, rising to a total backlog of 37 percent of active cases.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific court-statistics figures: a 3 percent increase in the District Court criminal backlog over the year from January 2023, and a resulting backlog equal to 37 percent of active cases.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice District Court criminal case backlog statistics for January 2023 and January 2024; true if the criminal backlog rose by about 3 percent over that year and stood at about 37 percent of active cases, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: What commitment, if any, can the media industry expect from the Government, given that there were no commitments to media in the National Party manifesto or the 100-day plan?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as the premise of the question, that neither the National Party's election manifesto nor the coalition Government's 100-day plan contained any commitment relating to media.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the National Party's 2023 election manifesto and the coalition Government's published 100-day plan; true if neither document contains a media or broadcasting commitment, false if either does.

veracity.statement: Considering the fact that when the Warner Bros. Discovery came for help to the previous Government’s Minister of broadcasting and they said no, I can say that that is a very rich question coming from the member.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Warner Bros. Discovery sought assistance from the previous Labour Government's Broadcasting Minister and was refused.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public reporting, ministerial statements or official records of any approach by Warner Bros. Discovery (or Three) to the Labour Government's Minister of Broadcasting seeking support, and the response given; true if such an approach was made and declined, false if no approach was made or if assistance was provided.

veracity.statement: We repealed the hopeless Clean Car Discount, repealed fair pay agreements, and expanded 90-day trials to apply to all businesses so that more workers can get a job.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three completed legislative actions as at the date of the statement: the Clean Car Discount repealed, fair pay agreements repealed, and 90-day trial periods extended to employers of all sizes. The "so that more workers can get a job" clause is a stated purpose, not the checkable part.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand statute and Gazette record as at 29 February 2024; true if by that date the Clean Car Discount had been ended, the Fair Pay Agreements Act 2022 repealed, and 90-day trial periods extended to businesses of all sizes, false if any of the three had not yet occurred.

veracity.statement: So my message to submitters is to visit the website and make a submission. And they have until 24 March before submissions close.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific closing date — 24 March — for public submissions on the expanded terms of reference for the royal commission of inquiry into COVID-19.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published closing date for public submissions on the terms of reference for the Royal Commission of Inquiry into COVID-19 Lessons Learned (Department of Internal Affairs / inquiry website); true if submissions closed on 24 March 2024, false if the deadline was a different date.

specificity.statement: I’m so happy to let that member on that side know that this Government is going to be releasing—as part of our 100-day plan—early next week, our initiatives to address the mess that was left behind for us to fix.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a rough timeframe ("early next week") and a named vehicle (the 100-day plan), but names none of the initiatives themselves, no mechanism and no measure of the problem being fixed. The question asked what initiatives; the answer carries almost no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can I thank that member for saving me a supplementary question—what is the projected increase in the number of court cases as a result of the Government’s proposed legislation banning gang patches?
specificity.explanation: Identifies a named measure and the exact quantity sought (projected increase in case numbers), but the question itself carries no figures, timeframe or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is committed to working with the sector on ways to ensure sector sustainability while still preserving the independence of our fourth estate and avoiding market interference.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic commitments — "working with the sector", "sustainability", "independence", "avoiding market interference" — with no named mechanism, funding, instrument or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We repealed the hopeless Clean Car Discount, repealed fair pay agreements, and expanded 90-day trials to apply to all businesses so that more workers can get a job.
specificity.explanation: Names three distinct measures by title and states what was done to each; a reader could go and check every one. No dates or amounts, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my message to submitters is to visit the website and make a submission. And they have until 24 March before submissions close.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete action and a hard deadline a listener could act on, but leaves "the website" unnamed.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I thank that member for saving me a supplementary question—what is the projected increase in the number of court cases as a result of the Government’s proposed legislation banning gang patches?
focus.explanation: Names a specific piece of proposed legislation and asks for a specific projected consequence of it. Squarely on the policy and its second-order effects, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she stand by her statement that New Zealanders can just watch Sky News, and is she aware of who produces Sky News’ New Zealand content?
focus.explanation: Targets a specific ministerial statement and a concrete factual question about who produces a named outlet's New Zealand content. Scrutiny of a named position, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What commitment, if any, can the media industry expect from the Government, given that there were no commitments to media in the National Party manifesto or the 100-day plan?
focus.explanation: Names two specific policy documents and asks for a policy commitment on a named sector. Legitimate scrutiny of a stated programme, entirely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What reports, if any, has the Minister seen into how much money the previous Government spent on the failed RNZ-TVNZ merger?
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme and a specific outcome (money spent on the abandoned RNZ-TVNZ merger). Accountability for a named policy rather than general party characterisation, though the "failed" framing carries some party weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is the kind of stuff that Peter Fraser and the great Labour Party that understood workers would understand, but they have utterly forgotten.
focus.explanation: A claim about what the other party has become — that it has forgotten its own tradition. No policy, figure or outcome is named within it; the content is entirely the character of the opposing party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Considering the fact that when the Warner Bros. Discovery came for help to the previous Government’s Minister of broadcasting and they said no, I can say that that is a very rich question coming from the member.
civility.explanation: "A very rich question coming from the member" imputes hypocrisy and bad faith to the questioner personally rather than answering the point. Short of a direct insult, but it turns on the member rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There’s no use trying to get you to catch up now.
civility.explanation: A condescending jibe at the Speaker's ability to follow proceedings. It engages no substance at all and lands on the person in the chair.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She doesn’t even get the great theme; all around Western society where they spoke English, it was three Rs, but genius over here knows better.
civility.explanation: "Genius over here knows better" is sarcastic mockery of another member's intelligence, and "doesn't even get" attacks her comprehension. A clear personal attack on competence rather than on anything she argued.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we know is that the existing terms of reference are currently inadequate and that this Government is seeking public submissions to expand those terms on the basis that we need, at the end of this inquiry, to have public confidence in the process and in the outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: expand the terms of reference because public confidence in the inquiry's process and outcome is needed. The step from "confidence is needed" to "these terms must be expanded" is coherent, but the load-bearing premise — that the existing terms are inadequate — is simply asserted as "what we know", with nothing offered to support it. A genuine gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Lloyd Burr followed Christopher Luxon for two whole weeks asking him to explain the tax cuts, and he couldn’t.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Newshub reporter Lloyd Burr pursued Christopher Luxon for a fortnight during the 2023 campaign seeking an explanation of the tax package, and that Luxon failed to provide one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Newshub broadcast and online records from the 2023 general election campaign; true if Burr can be shown pursuing Luxon on the tax plan over roughly a two-week stretch without obtaining a costed explanation, false if no such sustained pursuit occurred or if Luxon gave the explanation sought.

veracity.statement: They are dedicated, and yet just this question time, we had David Seymour call them bureaucrats.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that David Seymour referred to public servants as 'bureaucrats' during question time on the same sitting day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript of oral questions for 29 February 2024; true if Seymour used the word 'bureaucrats' of public servants in that question time, false if he did not.

veracity.statement: Public services working across education have led to the building of 2,000 new classrooms during the last Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately 2,000 new classrooms were built during the 2017–2023 Labour-led government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education school property delivery figures for the 2017–2023 period; true if the count of new teaching spaces delivered is around 2,000, false if materially lower or if the figure counts planned rather than completed classrooms.

veracity.statement: He literally said to me that he doesn’t want to come along and stand in front and lecture the providers about what he’s doing, like maybe they would have had under a previous administration—of course, they couldn’t have had that because there wasn’t a Minister for Mental Health under any previous Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no Labour-led government has ever had a minister holding a dedicated Mental Health portfolio.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DPMC ministerial lists and Cabinet portfolio records for every Labour-led government; true if no minister has held a portfolio designated Mental Health (as distinct from an associate health delegation covering mental health), false if any Labour-led government appointed one.

veracity.statement: As the Prime Minister indicated in the state of the nation address last week, we face an immense challenge left by the previous Government, and it’s great to see the progress that’s already been achieved in the last hundred days as we count down to 8 March next week and getting those 49 actions done.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's 100-day plan comprises 49 actions and that the 100 days conclude on 8 March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National-led coalition 100-day plan and its commencement date; true if the plan lists 49 actions and the hundredth day falls on 8 March 2024, false if the action count or the end date differs.

civility.statement: Pre-election, we were told not to worry about this, because Nicola Willis said Ministers would be going through line by line to find savings and instances of wasteful spending, as if the Ministers in that Government were financial whiz-kids.
civility.explanation: The substantive point about line-by-line savings is legitimate, but the closing 'as if the Ministers in that Government were financial whiz-kids' is a sneer at the personal competence of named individuals rather than at the policy. Short of a direct insult, so a real but not severe civility failure.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The hard-working people in Customs have been asked to take voluntary redundancy. Now, that is the definition of an untargeted cut.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a named policy: voluntary redundancy lets the holder of any role self-select, so it does not discriminate between necessary and unnecessary functions. The conclusion largely tracks the premise, though 'the definition of' overstates it — a definitional assertion offered in place of an argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is no example of waste that I have heard put forward in Customs by the Government; it’s just cuts.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: the speaker's not having heard an example of waste is offered as grounds for concluding none was identified. Her personal awareness is weak support for the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And that contracting out has happened multiple times whenever there have been Governments formed by the National Party. They’re manufacturing the conditions to allow public services to be hocked off so that the legions of lobbyists that are circling the Beehive have more opportunities to make money.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: a historical pattern of contracting out under National-led governments is offered as grounds for a conclusion about present intent — that the cuts are deliberately engineered to enrich lobbyists. Nothing connects the pattern to the imputed motive.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The feedback from rural and provincial New Zealand was overwhelmingly in favour of the progress that this Government is making.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: conversations at a single A & P show are generalised into the settled view of rural and provincial New Zealand. Nothing is offered to show the sample is representative.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Public services working across education have led to the building of 2,000 new classrooms during the last Government.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure attached to a named sector and a defined period, so someone could go and check it against Ministry of Education delivery records.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I must say, over my short time in this House and in this place, I’m starting to get a bit sick of the Opposition and their view that you can just spend more money to achieve an outcome, and that every dollar that they seem to have spent, committed to, and over-committed to magically delivers an outcome.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is supposedly like. No spending programme, figure or measure is named — strip out the characterisation of the Opposition and no policy content remains.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: More than 700 doctors have asked this Government to justify the decision to scrap the Māori Health Authority.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a specific number of doctors (more than 700) have publicly asked the Government to justify the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Open letters, joint statements or petitions from medical professionals published in early 2024 on the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora; true if a documented letter or statement carries 700 or more doctor signatories, false if the documented count is materially lower or no such letter exists.

veracity.statement: In fact, Al Jazeera yesterday even reported on the loss of indigenous rights and indigenous health outcomes by the deeds and actions of this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Al Jazeera published a report on 28 February 2024 covering loss of indigenous rights and indigenous health outcomes attributed to the New Zealand Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Al Jazeera's published output dated on or about 28 February 2024; true if an Al Jazeera item of that date covers New Zealand indigenous rights or Māori health outcomes under the current Government, false if no such item exists around that date.

veracity.statement: Of course, we’ve heard all week how disappointed we are that, through urgency, no public consultation has taken place for such important pieces of legislation: the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority and the smoke-free repeal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that neither the Māori Health Authority disestablishment nor the smokefree repeal received any public consultation, because both were passed under urgency.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill and the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Repeal) Amendment Bill; true if neither was referred to a select committee for public submissions before passing, false if either had a public submission process.

veracity.statement: I’d also like to—possibly not to converge the two—mention the situation yesterday with the Newshub staff, those 300 employees, and particularly the press gallery here who coexist in this strange ecosystem.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Newshub closure announcement of 28 February 2024 affected approximately 300 employees.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Warner Bros. Discovery's announcement of 28 February 2024 and contemporaneous reporting on the number of Newshub roles proposed for disestablishment; true if the figure is about 300, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: New Zealand First, in our coalition agreement with National, are proud to have secured that and reversed that travesty.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the requirement to use wool in government buildings was secured as a provision of the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published text of the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (November 2023); true if it contains a commitment to require or prefer wool fibre in government buildings, false if no such provision appears.

veracity.statement: There will be no repeat of the shameful situation where rural schools had been forced to put in synthetic carpets—in a kick in the guts to the farmers that send their children to school there, and to those rural communities that rely on that wonderful fibre.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as past fact that rural schools were compelled to install synthetic rather than wool carpet. The forward-looking half is a commitment about his own Government, so only the past claim is at issue here.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education flooring and procurement design standards in force before the 2023 election; true if they directed or required synthetic carpet in school builds and refurbishments, false if wool remained a freely permitted option for schools.

rigor.statement: We hear from the other side of the House that outcomes in health are really important. I want to highlight to the Government that the outcomes they speak of are things like surgery waiting lists, emergency room waiting lists. Yes, that’s true. That’s the job of Health New Zealand; that’s not the job of Te Aka Whai Ora.
rigor.explanation: A genuine distinction rather than a fallacy: he grants the Government's premise (waiting lists matter) and argues it does not bear on the case for the Māori Health Authority, because those outcomes sit with a different agency. The inference holds, though it stops short of showing Te Aka Whai Ora was delivering its own distinct remit.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We hear from the other side of the House that outcomes in health are really important. I want to highlight to the Government that the outcomes they speak of are things like surgery waiting lists, emergency room waiting lists. Yes, that’s true. That’s the job of Health New Zealand; that’s not the job of Te Aka Whai Ora.
focus.explanation: Engages the remit and division of functions between two named agencies — squarely on the policy being repealed, not on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I have been absolutely overwhelmed by—and I know that members on this side of the House up and down the country are feeling it—is the wave of sentiment behind us out there in rural and regional New Zealand. They are pleased to have a Government that understands what they’re about, what their key drivers are, how to deal with them, and how to engage with them.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, measure, figure or outcome — it is entirely about how his own side is regarded versus the other. Team sentiment, not policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it’s great to have the adults in the room. It’s great for us in New Zealand First to be in this coalition—back in Parliament, back contributing, and we look forward to getting New Zealand back on track.
focus.explanation: Pure party framing: an implied contrast with the previous Government's maturity plus a slogan about being back on track. No individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly, and no policy is named at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They were there with a clear focus on public health outcomes, good messaging to bring better health outcomes to Māori, encouraging rangatahi Māori to pursue a career in health and to make sure that we continue to support communities to look after communities so that there wasn’t a need to have an ambulance at the bottom of the cliff.
specificity.explanation: Names several concrete functions (public health messaging, workforce pipeline for rangatahi, community support) but supplies no figures, programmes, budgets or timeframes — a direction with some detail rather than checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Myself and the Hon Todd McClay have announced that during April we will be going round the country to wool sheds up and down New Zealand to engage with farmers to seek their feedback as we look to rally this rather disparate industry where farming leadership has got a little bit fragmented.
specificity.explanation: Names the ministers involved, a month (April) and a concrete mechanism (a wool shed roadshow to gather farmer feedback). No numbers, no funding and no stated output, so it falls short of fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s really disappointing when we hear from the other side that they have a mandate from the election—and, of course, that’s how this works and that’s why they’re on the Treasury benches and we aren’t; I understand that. But also, with that power comes huge responsibility: the responsibility to allow the public to have their voice on all matters that actually relate to them and are important to them.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested repeal debate where he had every opportunity to attack. He concedes the Government's electoral mandate outright and confines his criticism to the use of urgency — no person is targeted, no bad faith imputed.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But this year, 2024, was the first year it came back, and what an event it was.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2024 Art Deco Festival in Napier was the first festival held after successive years of cancellation or disruption from COVID-19 restrictions and weather events.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Art Deco Trust event records for the Art Deco Festival 2020-2024. True if festivals in the intervening years (notably 2021-2023) were cancelled, postponed or substantially curtailed and 2024 was the first full festival held; false if a full festival ran in 2022 or 2023.

veracity.statement: They’re not going to follow through in the set-up of the Māori Health Authority.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of record that the coalition Government has abandoned the establishment of the Māori Health Authority (Te Aka Whai Ora) rather than continuing it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand legislative record as at February 2024 for the Pae Ora (Disestablishment of Māori Health Authority) Amendment Bill. True if the Government legislated to disestablish or wind up Te Aka Whai Ora; false if the Authority was retained and continued to be stood up under government policy.

veracity.statement: The hundred nights of darkness, which we’ve almost got to, have shone no light on what this Government intends to do, to the point that the removal of the three waters legislation says that Standard & Poor’s now is downgrading many councils and they will pay higher rates of interest.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Standard & Poor's is currently downgrading multiple New Zealand councils, and that the repeal of the three waters legislation is the cause.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: S&P Global Ratings' published rating actions on New Zealand territorial authorities during 2023-2024 and the rationale given in those releases. True if S&P downgraded or lowered outlooks on multiple councils and cited the repeal of the water reforms or the resulting balance-sheet pressure; false if no such actions occurred or the actions were attributed to unrelated causes.

veracity.statement: And then the ultimate insult to the life and objectives of Efeso Collins is to take away and destroy and remove the Māori Health Authority—set up to address the real issue in our country, and it’s been there for a long time: the disparities in longevity for Māori and for Pasifika versus people like me, who live on average now about eight years longer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that non-Māori/non-Pasifika New Zealanders live on average about eight years longer than Māori and Pacific peoples.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ period life tables (life expectancy at birth, Māori and Pacific compared with non-Māori/European), most recent release before February 2024. True if the gap is approximately eight years; false if materially different - for instance below six or above ten years.

specificity.statement: In his last message, he asked for some practical, pragmatic consideration of an unworkable law that means that these buildings rely on kindness and generosity.
specificity.explanation: A genuine policy ask about earthquake-strengthening requirements for heritage buildings, but it names no statute, no threshold, no timeframe and no proposed change - 'practical, pragmatic consideration' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But this week, in this House, this coalition Government, through this Parliament, have doubled down on so many dumb and stupid things that go completely against everything that he stood for.
civility.explanation: Harsh language ('dumb and stupid') but aimed at the Government's legislative decisions, not at any individual member. No person's character, competence or motive is impugned, so this passes near the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s to help your mates. The coalition Government wants to help its mates—the people who funded it into Government.
civility.explanation: Imputes a corrupt motive - that government policy is being set to repay donors. Short of a direct personal insult and directed at the coalition collectively, but it attributes bad faith rather than engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But this week, in this House, this coalition Government, through this Parliament, have doubled down on so many dumb and stupid things that go completely against everything that he stood for.
focus.explanation: A blanket characterisation of the coalition Government's week in the House. No measure, figure, mechanism or outcome is named - strip out the reference to the other side and no policy content remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Not back on track; it’s a back-track Government, nothing more than backtrack.
focus.explanation: Pure slogan-inversion of the Government's own branding. Entirely about the other side's identity, with no policy, measure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s to help your mates. The coalition Government wants to help its mates—the people who funded it into Government.
focus.explanation: About who funds the governing parties and whose interests they serve, not about any policy's design or effect. No measure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ll give tax cuts to rich people, because they are always the beneficiaries of a tax regime designed to be cut for people at the top and shift the impost to people at the bottom.
focus.explanation: A real policy point - the incidence of the Government's tax changes - but carried mostly by class-and-party framing rather than by the design of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And then the ultimate insult to the life and objectives of Efeso Collins is to take away and destroy and remove the Māori Health Authority—set up to address the real issue in our country, and it’s been there for a long time: the disparities in longevity for Māori and for Pasifika versus people like me, who live on average now about eight years longer.
focus.explanation: Names the specific policy being removed, the problem it was created to address, and the outcome measure - a life-expectancy gap. Squarely on the substance of the measure rather than on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ll give tax cuts to rich people, because they are always the beneficiaries of a tax regime designed to be cut for people at the top and shift the impost to people at the bottom.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion about this particular tax package rests on a sweeping universal premise ('they are always the beneficiaries') that is asserted rather than shown, and which already assumes what is to be proved about the regime's design - a circular generalisation with no distributional evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, I know that, technically, it doesn’t come into effect until the start of term 2, but the smart principals—which is most of them—and the school boards are already bringing it in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two present/near-past facts: that the school cellphone ban's legal commencement is the start of term 2 (2024), and that a majority of principals and boards had already implemented phone bans before that date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Government announcement of the cellphone ban's commencement date — true if the ban took legal effect at the start of term 2 2024 (late April 2024), false if a different date; and Ministry/ERO or media survey data on the share of schools with a phone ban in place before that date — true if most schools already had one, false if only a minority did.

veracity.statement: During this time, there has also been an increase in violent crime of over 33 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that violent crime rose by more than 33 percent over the six years of the previous Government referred to in the preceding sentences.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded victimisations data (Victimisations Time Series) or Ministry of Justice NZ Crime and Victims Survey for violent offence categories, comparing the 2017 baseline with 2023 — true if the increase in the violent crime measure exceeds 33%, false if materially lower. Note which series is used, as recorded-crime and survey measures diverge.

veracity.statement: Last year, New Zealand experienced half its yearly average gun deaths in just 17 days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of firearm deaths in New Zealand in the first 17 days of 2023 equalled roughly half the average annual firearm death total.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police firearm-homicide records and Coronial/Ministry of Health firearm death statistics — establish the annual average firearm death count for the preceding years, then count firearm deaths occurring within a 17-day span of 2023. True if that span's count reaches about half the annual average, false if materially below. The claim is ambiguous between all firearm deaths and firearm homicides; check both.

rigor.statement: My mother-in-law, who’s a resource teacher: learning and behaviour, has espoused the value of phonics for such a long time, and she’s absolutely right.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that phonics teaching is correct rests entirely on the advocacy of a single named relative described by her job title. That is a bare appeal to authority (and to anecdote) — no evidence about phonics outcomes is offered, though such evidence exists and could have been cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: You might find someone that doesn’t like losing their phone at school, but I’d challenge you to find many parents that don’t think it’s a great thing to get their kids off the phones and focused on learning the basics, like in primary schools, where they’ll be spending an hour every day learning maths, an hour every day on reading, and an hour every day on writing.
specificity.explanation: Carries genuinely checkable content in its second half — an hour a day each on maths, reading and writing in primary schools, a named and quantified curriculum requirement. The opening clause is unquantified sentiment, which keeps it short of the top of the scale.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That package will allow police to issue dispersal notices requiring gang members to immediately leave the area and to not associate with one another for seven days.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (police-issued dispersal notices), who it applies to, what it compels, and for exactly how long. Someone could look up the provision and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, well, well, what a run it has been for criminals over the last six years under the Labour Government—a soft on crime, former Government so self-obsessed that it wrapped criminals in cotton wool and blamed the rest of New Zealand for their offending.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other party's disposition — 'soft on crime', 'self-obsessed', 'wrapped criminals in cotton wool'. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing here to hold anyone to account for. This is the content-free party framing the attribute exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That package will allow police to issue dispersal notices requiring gang members to immediately leave the area and to not associate with one another for seven days.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the measure being announced — the power created, its target and its duration. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, well, well, what a run it has been for criminals over the last six years under the Labour Government—a soft on crime, former Government so self-obsessed that it wrapped criminals in cotton wool and blamed the rest of New Zealand for their offending.
civility.explanation: Aimed at a party and a former Government, not at any individual member. No person's character, competence or worth is attacked, so despite the heat it passes Civility cleanly; the tribalism is Focus's problem, not this one's.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Somewhere deep inside Christopher Luxon, I’m sure there’s also a little dream that’s slowly dying, you know, a little inspiration that’s slowly wizening.
civility.explanation: Sneering, condescending speculation about a named individual's inner life rather than about any policy. Short of a direct insult, but it mocks the person, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine civility failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’ve literally repealed world-leading legislation so they can fund tax cuts, and that is shameful.
civility.explanation: Brutal about the decision and the legislation — 'shameful' is aimed at the Government's action, not at any member's character, competence or worth. Harsh policy criticism scores high under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: National promised there would be no cuts to front-line services.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National Party made a specific pre-election commitment: that its tax plan would involve no cuts to front-line services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 campaign tax plan document and Nicola Willis's on-record 2023 campaign statements (including the AM Show interview cited); true if a clear public commitment to no front-line service cuts is documented, false if no such commitment was made or if it was materially qualified.

veracity.statement: At the height of the fire, it got to nearly 700 hectares.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the peak burn area of the February 2024 Port Hills fire was close to 700 hectares.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Fire and Emergency New Zealand / Christchurch City Council situation reports for the February 2024 Port Hills fire; true if the reported peak area is approximately 650–700 ha, false if materially smaller or larger.

rigor.statement: They can give all the excuses in the world, but that’s what it comes down to. There is a clear choice about what their priority is, and this Government has said that schools and health is not theirs.
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus false dichotomy: the Government did not say schools and health are not a priority, and the conclusion is asserted rather than derived — deferred building projects are treated as equivalent to a stated repudiation of the sector, with the alternative explanations pre-emptively dismissed as 'excuses' rather than addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So this was an example where under an emergency response, having one organisation in the centralised command and control actually makes a huge difference and everybody understands who has the rights and roles and everything worked very well.
rigor.explanation: Generalises a structural conclusion about emergency-management design from a single case (argument from anecdote), and attributes the good outcome to centralised command without excluding the other causes she herself named moments earlier — the 2017 lessons-learnt document, the pre-existing relationships, and the early declaration by the two mayors. The inference does not isolate the variable it credits.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think we have to really acknowledge the fact that the “back” part was doing a lot of heavy lifting in that campaign slogan, wasn’t it. Everything is about going backwards.
focus.explanation: Wordplay on the other party's campaign slogan and a general characterisation of them as regressive. No measure, figure, mechanism or named commitment is engaged — strip out the party framing and nothing about policy remains.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Helping to fight the fire at any one time, we had up to about 130 firefighters from all around the country. They were supported by 27 trucks, up to 15 helicopters, and two fixed-wing planes.
specificity.explanation: Concrete, checkable counts of personnel and each class of appliance deployed. Someone could verify every figure against the Fire and Emergency response record.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, when I was Minister, I tried to get a permanent change included by way of leave of the House, and the National Party opposed that leave.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that while he held the local government portfolio he sought leave of the House to make remote participation in council quorums permanent, and that the National Party denied that leave.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record for the sitting day on which McAnulty, as Minister of Local Government, sought leave to make remote participation permanent: true if leave was sought and an objection was raised from the National benches, false if no such leave was sought or if the objection came from elsewhere.

veracity.statement: This was something that Local Government New Zealand said that their members wanted.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Local Government New Zealand publicly stated its member councils wanted permanent remote participation counted toward quorum.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: LGNZ public submissions, remits or media statements on remote participation in council meetings, 2021-2023: true if LGNZ stated that its members sought a permanent change, false if LGNZ took no position or opposed it.

veracity.statement: The council I’m involved in has 15, and that includes the mayor.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Marlborough District Council's membership, counting the mayor, totals 15.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Marlborough District Council's official membership for the 2022-2025 triennium (council website / Local Government Commission representation determination): true if mayor plus councillors totals 15, false if it totals any other number.

veracity.statement: In those meetings, you only need a quorum of one, under standing orders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that standing orders permit a subcommittee meeting to be quorate with a single member present.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Local Government Act 2002, Schedule 7, clause 23 and the standard LGNZ standing orders on quorum for committees and subcommittees: true if a quorum of one member is permitted, false if the minimum quorum is two or more members.

rigor.statement: But, nevertheless, what that demonstrates is that the rules that are currently in place around remote participation in local government aren’t actually fit for purpose.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from stated premises — standing orders requiring good reason and two days' notice, set against a cyclone response — but with a gap the speaker created himself: he had just said many areas were cut off entirely, in which case remote participation would not have been possible either, so the cited case does not fully carry the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This Parliament has adapted to the return of the normal situation and so has local government, therefore we won’t be supporting this bill and we do not believe it should proceed.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur relative to the speaker's own concession. He had just accepted that there may be future occasions — severe weather events — needing remote participation by exception; that a return to normality has occurred does not bear on whether provision for those exceptions should exist. The premise addresses routine conditions and the conclusion rejects an exceptional-case power.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you can’t trust the rest of your councillors to make the right decision, then you actually aren’t making a very good debate in the first place.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy built on a strawman: it recasts a councillor's wish to have their own vote counted as distrust of colleagues, and treats trusting others to decide as the only alternative. Wanting to exercise a vote you were elected to cast implies nothing about trust, so the conclusion does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, we’ve never seen any instance, so far, from this Government that they like select committees, but, for those that are new and haven’t experienced a bill going through select committees, it’s actually a fruitful exercise.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine procedural proposal here — send the bill to select committee to hear from the local government sector — but it is carried on a general characterisation of the Government's attitude rather than on the bill's provisions.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’ll tell you what: the member asks whether we were part of a team of 5 million; in Auckland, we felt like we were a million in a prison, of the former Labour Government’s making.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the previous Government's pandemic record and how it felt, with no engagement with the remote participation provisions before the House. No policy, figure or mechanism in the bill is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Parliament has adapted to the return of the normal situation and so has local government, therefore we won’t be supporting this bill and we do not believe it should proceed.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: states the ground on which ACT opposes the bill in terms of the bill's own subject matter, the need for remote participation.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In most meetings, under standing orders, you will need four out of seven or four out of eight to make the quorum, so that shouldn’t be too hard to actually achieve.
specificity.explanation: Names the governing instrument (standing orders) and gives the actual thresholds as ratios — four of seven, four of eight — so the claim is concrete enough for someone else to check against the rules.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m surprised at that member, Jamie Arbuckle, actually, because, as I understand it, he’s double-dipping with the Marlborough District Council.
civility.explanation: "Double-dipping" imputes self-interested impropriety to a named member rather than engaging his argument about the bill. Short of a direct insult, but it lands on the person, not the position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, there’s the safeguards, but what is incredible is the bizarre interjections from Simon Court over there talking about democracy, saying it’s anti-democratic, when all we’ve seen in this House over the last hundred days is legislation getting ran through with no due process, under urgency, no select committee hearings.
civility.explanation: Calling a named member's contributions "bizarre" and "incredible" is dismissive of him rather than of what he argued — it treats his position as not worth answering. It stops short of an attack on his character, so it sits just below the pointed-but-not-personal line.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m surprised at that member, Jamie Arbuckle, actually, because, as I understand it, he’s double-dipping with the Marlborough District Council.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Arbuckle was drawing remuneration from both Parliament and the Marlborough District Council at the time of the debate. Hedged with "as I understand it", but it is a claim of fact about a present arrangement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Marlborough District Council's register of elected members and remuneration records for the 2024 calendar year, cross-checked against the Register of Pecuniary Interests of Members of Parliament: true if Jamie Arbuckle simultaneously held a paid Marlborough District Council elected position while serving as an MP in February 2024; false if he had vacated or was unpaid for that seat.

veracity.statement: In fact, Kenepuru Road, which, as you can imagine, goes up to Kenepuru Sound and out to the outer Sounds, is still impassable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at the date of the debate Kenepuru Road remained impassable as a consequence of the 2022 heavy weather events. The distinction that settles it is closure versus restricted access.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Marlborough District Council / Waka Kotahi road status notices for Kenepuru Road as at 29 February 2024: true if the road was closed to general traffic along its length; false if it was open, including on a restricted, escorted or limited-hours basis.

veracity.statement: I can tell you that out of the 78 councils, four of the 10 biggest regional councils by land are based in the South Island, and for territorial authorities nine out of 10 of them.
veracity.explanation: Three separate arithmetic claims: the total number of councils, the South Island share of the ten largest regional councils by area, and its share of the ten largest territorial authorities by area.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / LINZ land area figures for New Zealand's regional councils and territorial authorities, ranked by area: true if four of the ten largest regional councils and nine of the ten largest territorial authorities by land area are in the South Island, and there are 78 councils in total; false if the counts differ.

veracity.statement: Now, there’s the safeguards, but what is incredible is the bizarre interjections from Simon Court over there talking about democracy, saying it’s anti-democratic, when all we’ve seen in this House over the last hundred days is legislation getting ran through with no due process, under urgency, no select committee hearings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the first hundred days of the Government, every piece of legislation passed under urgency without due process or select committee hearings. The word "all" is what makes it checkable — a single bill that took public submissions in that window falsifies it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliamentary record of bills passed between the Government's swearing-in (27 November 2023) and 29 February 2024: true if no bill passed in that window was referred to a select committee for public hearings; false if any bill in that period went through the normal select committee process.

rigor.statement: So the other side of the House are doing what they always do. They say, “Well, let’s have the same rules for everyone, because everyone should be a bit like me.” But, no, they haven’t thought about this.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opposing case for uniform attendance rules is restated as "everyone should be a bit like me", a motive no one advanced, and the conclusion that they "haven’t thought about this" is drawn from that substituted version rather than from anything they said.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is just a common-sense bill. It makes no sense to say, “You can participate, you just can’t vote.” The reason we get elected to democratic positions is to vote.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: if the purpose of election is to exercise a vote, a rule permitting remote attendance but not remote voting is internally incoherent. The premise about the purpose of election is asserted rather than established, which is the gap, but the conclusion does track it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The other thing I found very bizarre from one of the speakers opposite was them saying that “It’s OK to participate; just don’t vote and trust the other people on the regional authority to vote for you.” Well, I wish the people in the territorial authorities in my area got on that collegially, but they are hammer and tongs against each other, and I think that’s a sign of a good, robust democracy.
rigor.explanation: Engages the opposing argument on its own terms and attacks its load-bearing premise — that absent members can rely on colleagues to vote in their stead — by pointing out that councils are adversarial by design. The counter rests on her own electorate as the evidence base, so it is anecdotal, but the inference itself is sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And I’m surprised that the so-called champions of farmers over in the corner there haven’t thought about that as well, because we know that farmers actually have a lot to say in local and regional governance, and yet they also have significant demands on their time.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point underneath — that time demands on farmers limit their participation in local and regional governance, which is exactly what the bill addresses — but it is delivered as a charge about which party really champions farmers, so a good part of the weight is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Once again, this Government—interested in Auckland, interested in building roads up north, interested in everything that happens in the North Island—is not thinking about the consequences for the people of the South Island.
focus.explanation: A gesture at roading investment is the only policy content; the rest is a characterisation of what the Government as a whole is "interested in". No measure, figure or outcome is named, so this reads as regional framing rather than scrutiny of a specific commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They are so backward, and what they are missing out on is a chance to impress their rural communities, the ones that they say they champion, the ones that are wanting them to go into bat for them.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's character and its supposed hypocrisy toward rural voters. No policy, figure or outcome is named — strip out the claim about what the other parties are really like and nothing about the bill remains.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I’m disappointed that the parties on the other side of the House have chosen to once again take a narrow view of democracy—an exclusive view of democracy—and not try to use the very tools we’ve got at our disposal to have a more inclusive, more effective, and more robust democratic framework.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — "more inclusive, more effective, and more robust" — with "the very tools we’ve got at our disposal" standing in for the actual mechanism. Nothing here names what would change or by how much, even though the bill immediately at hand supplies both.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can tell you that out of the 78 councils, four of the 10 biggest regional councils by land are based in the South Island, and for territorial authorities nine out of 10 of them.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete, countable figures with a stated unit of comparison (land area) and a stated population of councils. Someone could pull the rankings and check it, which is what specificity asks.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, if I look at the bill, if we go to clause 4 inserting new clause 25A(6) in Schedule 7 of the principal Act—it’s just a short bill, but subclause 6 says that when a local authority is including things in its standing orders, it can also add any other requirements that it considers are “appropriate to maintain public confidence in the transparency and integrity of decision-making processes and the conduct of members”.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the subclause, the schedule and the parent Act, and quotes the operative wording. Anyone could open the bill and verify the safeguard she says it contains.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I point you to Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023. It’s already given them the ability to do this. All they have to do is change their standing orders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023 already empowers councils to permit remote participation, and that the only step required is a council amending its own standing orders — i.e. that the bill before the House is redundant.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023 and the resulting provisions of the Local Government Act 2002 (Schedule 7, remote attendance/quorum clauses). True if councils may already authorise remote attendance, including for quorum purposes, by amending their standing orders without further legislation; false if the existing law still bars remote attendance or bars remote attendees from counting toward a quorum absent this bill.

veracity.statement: Environment Canterbury is our largest regional council. It’s over 44,000 kilometres squared. That’s bigger than Denmark. It’s four times the size of Jamaica.
veracity.explanation: Four factual assertions: that Environment Canterbury is New Zealand's largest regional council, that its area exceeds 44,000 km², that this exceeds the area of Denmark, and that it is roughly four times the area of Jamaica.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / LINZ regional boundary areas for the Canterbury region compared against the other regional council areas, and published national land areas for Denmark and Jamaica. True if Canterbury is the largest regional council area, exceeds 44,000 km², exceeds Denmark's land area, and is between 3.5 and 4.5 times Jamaica's; false if any of those fails materially.

specificity.statement: I point you to Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023. It’s already given them the ability to do this. All they have to do is change their standing orders.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific statute, the specific power it confers and the exact mechanism a council must use (amending standing orders). Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Environment Canterbury is our largest regional council. It’s over 44,000 kilometres squared. That’s bigger than Denmark. It’s four times the size of Jamaica.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure for the area and two checkable comparisons; someone could verify each without further information.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think the aim of local democracy is to remove barriers to participation. This bill does that. I think the aim of local democracy is to make it easier for people to be part of the very decisions that directly affect them. This bill does that.
specificity.explanation: General aims paired with a bare assertion that the bill meets them. No clause, mechanism, figure or timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If the community want it so they don’t have to take their friend’s helicopter, to ride their bike, or whatever that analogy was meant to be—and I tell you what: if Ingrid Leary’s worried about bizarre comments, she should take hers, wrap them in cellophane, and put them on a plinth; I haven’t heard anything so bizarre in a long time.
civility.explanation: Turns from the bill to ridiculing a named member — her contribution is mocked as a museum exhibit and dismissed as the most bizarre thing he has heard in a long time. Sneering directed at the person rather than criticism of the policy, though short of a direct insult to her character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t like the thought of Grant Robertson inspecting me in the shower, quite frankly!
civility.explanation: A personal jibe naming an individual member and casting him in a demeaning, faintly prurient image. It engages no policy content; the target is the man, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We heard it from them not just with this; we heard it from three waters: “Give us all your ratepayer assets, we’ll take control of them, and we’ll decide what you’re going to do with them.” We heard it with Te Pūkenga: “We’ll centralise everything. Wellington knows best. We’ve got the answers.” We saw it with health. Nothing gets better.
focus.explanation: Names three policies, but only as props for a characterisation of what the other party is 'really like'. No mechanism, cost, figure or outcome of the bill before the House is engaged; the weight of the passage is party framing with invented quotes.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I actually think this bill is about digital democracy, because it removes barriers to participation and it will make it easier for people to be involved in the decisions that are directly affecting them.
focus.explanation: Squarely about what the measure before the House does and who it affects. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I think that there’s a real risk here in not doing this, and that is that representation becomes a luxury for those who can afford it. People won’t seek office. People won’t be able to represent their communities, because they can’t take the time off work, off family, off study, off their other life commitments to stand up and represent their communities.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain is offered (time pressure discourages candidacy) but the conclusion overshoots it: nothing connects the failure of this particular bill to representation becoming 'a luxury for those who can afford it', and it presents the bill as the only alternative when councils can already amend standing orders. Slippery slope resting on a false dichotomy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve got two standing orders from two local Bay of Plenty councils, saying they’ve got this provision already. Simply said—and as my colleague Tim Costley said previously—this bill is a solution in search of a problem. Councils already have the ability to meet remotely.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: two councils already carry a remote-attendance provision, therefore the bill is unnecessary. The reasoning tracks, but it generalises from two Bay of Plenty councils to 'councils' as a class — a hasty generalisation, since nothing in the two examples shows every council has adopted such a standing order. Not fact-checked here; the premise that these standing orders exist is Veracity's question.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023 made permanent the ability for elected members to meet remotely if the council’s standing orders allow this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a named statute, the Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023, permanently authorised remote attendance by elected members where the council's standing orders permit it — i.e. that the earlier temporary COVID-era provision was made permanent by that Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023 and the resulting amendments to Schedule 7 of the Local Government Act 2002 on the legislation.govt.nz reprint: true if the remote-attendance provision is permanent and conditioned on the local authority's standing orders; false if it is time-limited, was not enacted by that Act, or does not depend on standing orders.

specificity.statement: The Local Government Electoral Legislation Act 2023 made permanent the ability for elected members to meet remotely if the council’s standing orders allow this.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact statute, the year, the mechanism (permanence of remote attendance) and the condition attached to it (standing orders allowing it). Anyone could go and check or act on this. Whether it is accurate is Veracity's question, not this one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we are intending to do is provide hope for those incarcerated to rehabilitate themselves and actually reintegrate back into society.
specificity.explanation: Introducing his own bill at first reading, with a full opportunity to state what it requires — the bill's title turns on mandatory completion of rehabilitative programmes — he gives only its aspiration: 'provide hope', 'rehabilitate themselves', 'reintegrate'. No mechanism, threshold, cost or timeframe. Close to a statement of good intentions rather than content.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Legislation like this is just another example of Labour’s Wellington-knows-best approach to local government, which imposes rules on councils instead of allowing them to do what works best for them.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point inside this — that the bill prescribes to councils rather than leaving the rule to them — but it is carried on party framing ('Labour's Wellington-knows-best approach', 'just another example'), and no specific measure, figure or outcome is named. A real policy claim wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill demonstrates how out of touch the other side of the House are, and the National Party does not support it.
focus.explanation: Strip out the characterisation of the other side and nothing about the bill remains — no mechanism, cost, timeframe or named outcome, just an assertion about what the opposing parties are like, plus a voting intention. This is the party-versus-policy case Focus exists to catch. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched, and there is no argument left to assess for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As of 2023, around 56.5 percent of people with serious convictions are reconvicted within two years following release, and again another 35.8 percent are reimprisoned after two years following prison.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific NZ recidivism rates for 2023: 56.5% reconviction and 35.8% reimprisonment within/after two years of release for people with serious convictions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections recidivism statistics (reconviction and reimprisonment within 24 months of release) for the 2023 reporting year; true if the published figures are 56.5% and 35.8% (± rounding) for the serious-conviction cohort, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Our own Corrections department estimates that around 60 percent of prisoners have literacy and numeracy skills below that of NCEA level 1—so that’s like school certificate for 15-year-olds.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to the Department of Corrections an estimate that roughly 60% of prisoners have literacy and numeracy below NCEA level 1.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections published literacy/numeracy assessment data or its Annual Report; true if Corrections estimates approximately 60% of prisoners below NCEA level 1 in literacy and numeracy, false if the department's figure is materially different or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: Despite the clear benefits I’ve outlined, this time last year less than 20 percent of sentenced prisoners in Corrections-run facilities were attending rehabilitation programmes.
veracity.explanation: Claims that in early 2023 fewer than 20% of sentenced prisoners in Corrections-run (i.e. non-privately-run) facilities were attending rehabilitation programmes.
veracity.subject: speaker
