Also, did he consider option five: amend the Sentencing Act 2002 to introduce a threshold for provision of section 27 reports based on the seriousness of the offence?
specificity.explanation: Names three numbered alternatives from the regulatory impact statement, each with its own mechanism, and names the Act to be amended. Precisely checkable against the RIS.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That sort of touting for business for these reports was something that has led over the last six years to a very steady and substantial increase in the outlays for these reports: starting off about 40,000 in 2017 and stepping up to a million and then to 2 million and then to 3 million, and by the time we got to 7.5 million last year and the graph was going up like that [gestures a steep incline].
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific spending series for legal aid funding of section 27 cultural reports: roughly $40,000 in 2017 rising to $7.5 million in the most recent full year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services Agency figures for legal aid expenditure on section 27 cultural reports by financial year; true if the series runs from roughly $40,000 in 2016/17 to roughly $7.5 million in 2022/23, false if the start or end figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: So the broad issue, if I could cast people’s minds to a website that is a company led by Harry Tam, a former gang-member, which is touting for business in these cultural reports and saying, “Come to us, get a cultural report.”, and, “We’ve managed to get discounts off sentences of up to 35 percent.”—I think was the figure that they referred to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a company led by Harry Tam advertises cultural report services online and claims on that site to have obtained sentence discounts of up to 35 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The live or Wayback-archived website of the company named; true if it advertises section 27 / cultural report services and states a figure of up to 35 percent off sentences, false if no such site or no such claim exists.

civility.statement: And it’s just your reckon, and it’s the kind of laziness with the facts, especially around these important reports that the National Party uses to attack other good practitioners who do prepare these reports, and you slew them by calling them a cottage industry on the back of someone who you don’t know has provided a single report; all you know is that he’s touting for business.
civility.explanation: "Just your reckon" and "laziness with the facts" move from the evidentiary point onto the Minister himself — imputing carelessness as a personal trait rather than identifying the gap in the evidence. Short of an insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But this is a significant clause of the bill because it is so swift to make a change which will have a deep impact on people’s access to justice, particularly access to justice for Māori, who are most impacted by the section 27 changes that the Minister is proposing.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: it names the commencement clause, the section 27 changes and who they affect. No party framing at all, in a debate where attacking the Government would have been the easy alternative.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is going to be a bomb of work that lands on these practitioners because there’s no phasing out.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the operation of the commencement clause and its effect on practitioners. No reference to the other party's record or character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think that, on this side of the Chamber, you know, there is a real concern that there has not been adequate consideration given to the reduction of available legal services that this bill inevitably will create.
focus.explanation: Addressed to what the bill does to legal services, not to the Government's record or character. This is the pair to notice: high focus with low specificity — genuinely about the policy, but a vague statement about it.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Also, has the Minister considered extending the commencement date specifically for those situations which are already in train now, where reports are being written, given that those are something which a judge has overseen, has had an involvement in asking for, that counsel have also been involved in asking for, that Parliament should respect the convention of not interfering in?
rigor.explanation: A real inference: reports already ordered are part of proceedings a judge has directed, Parliament observes comity toward matters before the courts, therefore a transitional saving is warranted. The premise is an institutional principle rather than a bare appeal to tradition, and the conclusion tracks it; the gap is that she does not establish that removing funding actually interferes with a court order rather than with its cost.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know the Minister came to the Justice Committee and said you want to work on the backlog. This is going to exacerbate it because we don’t have a transitional phasing in; it doesn’t commence in a period of time for practitioners and judges, prosecutors, and defence lawyers to have time to adjust their frameworks to it.
rigor.explanation: A coherent chain: the work transfers to counsel, no transition period is provided, participants cannot adjust in time, so the stated goal of reducing the backlog is undercut. The step from 'no adjustment period' to 'the backlog worsens' is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the gap; the inference itself is sound and does not rest on any characterisation of the Minister.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Do you want the lawyers to do this work? Do you want them to spend hours at the highest rate doing this work, or do you want these reports not to be put before the judge for poor people at all?
rigor.explanation: Presses a dilemma that follows from the amendment being debated, but frames it as exhaustive — a false dichotomy, since the Minister could also intend the reports to continue at private expense, at reduced volume, or in shorter form. A real inference about the policy, weakened by the closed choice.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But what will happen is the two-week time frame is to allow for legal aid providers to be advised of the change. Requests up until commencement could still be approved by the commissioner.
specificity.explanation: Gives the purpose of the two-week window and the operative rule — the commissioner may still approve requests up to commencement — which is a checkable mechanism. Short of 1.0 because no numbers, volumes or notification method are supplied for what the fourteen days are meant to accomplish.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, these practitioners with 150 criminal files on their desk will have to do that themselves. That’s not something they’re geared up to do within 14 days.
specificity.explanation: Carries a caseload figure, a named group and the statutory timeframe, so the claimed burden is concrete enough to be argued with. Not higher because the 150 figure is offered as illustration with no source and no estimate of how many files are actually affected.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What a professional person was doing for $1,200, probably at $80 an hour, lawyers will now start doing for—you know, legal aid rates are pretty abysmal, but for $120 an hour, because it’s part of the work of a lawyer to advocate at sentencing, to gather the evidence, and to present it in as compelling way as they can.
specificity.explanation: Two hourly rates, a per-report cost and the substitution being alleged — a listener could go and check every number. Hedged with 'probably', which is the only thing keeping it off the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think that, on this side of the Chamber, you know, there is a real concern that there has not been adequate consideration given to the reduction of available legal services that this bill inevitably will create.
specificity.explanation: Nothing here is checkable: 'adequate consideration' is undefined, and no figure, mechanism or service is named for the claimed reduction. The direction of the concern is clear, the content is not.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what we really need to be clear on—and the Minister is able to speak to this—is that this bill, effectively, removes legal aid funding for a report or a statement, whether it be oral or written, for a person, and that section stops that information from being heard from not just someone who’s an expert but also potentially from family, whānau, or community, that might help that further offending.

veracity.statement: What a professional person was doing for $1,200, probably at $80 an hour, lawyers will now start doing for—you know, legal aid rates are pretty abysmal, but for $120 an hour, because it’s part of the work of a lawyer to advocate at sentencing, to gather the evidence, and to present it in as compelling way as they can.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice published criminal legal aid hourly rates in force in March 2024, and Ministry of Justice / Legal Services reported average cost per section 27 cultural report. True if the report figure is around $1,200 and the criminal legal aid hourly rate is around $120 and exceeds the implied report-writer rate; false if either figure is materially different or the legal aid rate is at or below the report-writer rate.

veracity.statement: So what we really need to be clear on—and the Minister is able to speak to this—is that this bill, effectively, removes legal aid funding for a report or a statement, whether it be oral or written, for a person, and that section stops that information from being heard from not just someone who’s an expert but also potentially from family, whānau, or community, that might help that further offending.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Legal Services Amendment Bill as reported back in March 2024 and section 27 of the Sentencing Act 2002. civility.statement: This is going to be a bomb of work that lands on these practitioners because there’s no phasing out.

veracity.statement: We’ve all read the regulatory impact statement and the disclosure, and we know that you’ve received advice which is contrary to the course of action that you’ve adopted: that the status quo was, in fact, as good as what you’re doing now, and other options were presented to you.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Announcements and policy documents of the 2017–2023 Labour-led Government (Prime Ministerial statements, Corrections/Justice sector strategy documents); true if a 30 percent prison population reduction target was formally adopted, false if no such numeric target exists.

veracity.statement: So 2019-20, it was $1.5 million; 2021-22, it had gone up to $5.6 million; and it kept on accelerating.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services Commissioner reported legal aid expenditure on section 27 cultural reports by financial year; true if the 2019/20 and 2021/22 figures are approximately $1.5m and $5.6m, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: That’s 8,000 in our country—8,000 people out of 5 million people.

specificity.statement: We’ve all read the regulatory impact statement and the disclosure, and we know that you’ve received advice which is contrary to the course of action that you’ve adopted: that the status quo was, in fact, as good as what you’re doing now, and other options were presented to you.

rigor.explanation: Non sequitur in reply to the question asked: that Māori are also disproportionately victims, and that everyone benefits from safety, does not bear on whether removing funding for section 27 reports falls disproportionately on particular communities. rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because you can’t make rules about people and expect them to follow those rules without actually talking to them in the first place.

rigor.statement: But I hope for an extended debate, because this bill, which is an important bill, has not been to select committee, and so the committee hasn’t had the opportunity to fully hear and consider the views of the many interest groups that would submit on it.

rigor.statement: Now, the difficulty is, of course, that we had a period of 15 or so—maybe 13 or 14—years when the legislation was passed and people didn’t have access to legal aid for writing these reports. rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: nobody is said to have complained during the earlier period, therefore no access-to-justice or Bill of Rights problem arises now. rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think most New Zealanders would appreciate this focus on making sure that money in the legal aid system, which is under pressure generally—as every element of Government spending is under pressure given the deficits that we’ve faced for a long period of time and the very big increase in debt that this country has taken on in the last six years.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity — supposed public approval is offered as the support for the measure. The fiscal premise is general to all spending and does nothing to single out this particular cut, so the conclusion outruns what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Isn’t tailored sentencing to prevent reoffending good for victims of crime because of the reduced likelihood of reoffending?
rigor.explanation: The inference is valid given its assumption — if tailored sentencing reduces reoffending, fewer future victims follows. But the causal premise is asserted inside the question rather than supported, so there is a real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.

veracity.statement: But I hope for an extended debate, because this bill, which is an important bill, has not been to select committee, and so the committee hasn’t had the opportunity to fully hear and consider the views of the many interest groups that would submit on it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that this bill was not referred to select committee and therefore received no public submissions process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Parliament bill record for the legal aid / section 27 reports amendment bill before the House on 2024-03-05: true if the bill had no select committee stage (passed under urgency), false if it was referred to and reported back by a select committee.

veracity.statement: So, Minister, I say to you that the submission of the Law Society is that this results in unequal treatment before the law, it’s a breach of human rights, and it impedes access to justice for those who cannot afford these section 27 reports.

veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Law Society's submission and public statement on this bill: true if it argues the change produces unequal treatment before the law, breaches human rights and impedes access to justice for those unable to fund section 27 reports; false if the submission makes materially different claims.

veracity.statement: I have read the regulatory impact statement and the disclosure statement, and in there it says they cannot see how this bill is actually meeting our international obligations.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement and the disclosure statement published for this bill: true if either document states officials could not establish that the change is consistent with New Zealand's international obligations, false if neither contains such a caveat.

veracity.statement: Now, the difficulty is, of course, that we had a period of 15 or so—maybe 13 or 14—years when the legislation was passed and people didn’t have access to legal aid for writing these reports. I don’t think people said there was no access to justice or that we were failing the Bill of Rights.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual gap of some 13–15 years during which legal aid did not fund the writing of these reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Legal Services legal aid policy records: true if legal aid funding was unavailable for section 27-type reports for roughly 13–15 years between the Sentencing Act 2002 and funding beginning around 2017, false if such funding was available materially earlier or the gap is materially shorter.

veracity.statement: I think most New Zealanders would appreciate this focus on making sure that money in the legal aid system, which is under pressure generally—as every element of Government spending is under pressure given the deficits that we’ve faced for a long period of time and the very big increase in debt that this country has taken on in the last six years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that New Zealand's debt increased very substantially over the preceding six years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury fiscal data on net core Crown debt (dollar and %GDP) from 2018 to 2024: true if debt rose substantially over that six-year period, false if it was flat or fell.

veracity.statement: What is being dealt with by this legislation is an additional cottage industry that had developed since 2017 and was gathering great momentum and speed with each passing year and costing more and more.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual pattern: the funded provision of these reports began in 2017 and grew in volume and cost every year thereafter.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice legal aid expenditure on section 27 cultural reports, by financial year from 2017 to 2023: true if the number of reports funded and the annual spend rose year on year, false if spend was flat or fell in any material part of that period.

veracity.statement: For example, that is one of the reasons why my colleague the Hon Mark Mitchell this week announced the fact that this Government will be ensuring that prisoners on remand will have access to rehabilitation programmes, so there are many ways in which society and Government encourages people to rehabilitate.

civility.statement: Now, it’s quite right and appropriate for the Law Society to make some observations on that. veracity.statement: The original intention of this piece of legislation was for people to give brief oral accounts in the court—generally, family members—and for that to be considered, and there is nothing stopping that from happening.

civility.statement: If the Minister just replies with “It’s in our 100-day plan.”, I’m sorry, but that’s actually not good enough.

focus.statement: So what my Amendment Paper does is it suggests that reports about the victim in the context of the offending should be put before the court and should be funded by legal aid—so a report about the victim context.

specificity.statement: So what my Amendment Paper does is it suggests that reports about the victim in the context of the offending should be put before the court and should be funded by legal aid—so a report about the victim context.

rigor.statement: Of course, we know that if someone doesn’t go into prison and they go into a good residence for home detention, they’re much more likely not to reoffend and more able to effectively engage in rehabilitation as part of that sentence because they don’t have to use the prison system; they can use, essentially, the civilian system of psychologists, alcohol and drug treatment, all of those kinds of things.

civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government’s proposal to simply defund this, as we have heard in the debate tonight, is creating access-to-justice issues, serious ones—serious ones that disproportionately affect Māori in the criminal justice system.
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure before the House (defunding section 27 reports) and a specific claimed outcome (access-to-justice effects falling disproportionately on Māori). This is opposition scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing, and belongs at the top of the scale.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So this is one probation officer emailing you, versus the Law Society, Māori Law Society, Bar Association, Defence Lawyers Association?
rigor.explanation: A sound point about evidential weight: the Minister had just rested on correspondence from a single retired probation officer, and this identifies that as an unrepresentative anecdote set against the submissions of four professional bodies. The inference is left implicit but it tracks — it engages the evidence base for the policy rather than the people opposite. Marked down slightly because counting bodies is itself close to an appeal to authority.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Putting justice aside, which I think should be the primary consideration, this is a cost-saving exercise by this Government within the justice system, but what the evidence suggests to us is that there will be more costs to the justice system from this section 27 defunding proposal that we are debating tonight—and they are significant costs.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: that a saving in one part of the justice system is offset by costs elsewhere. There is support nearby — the Defence Lawyers Association warning she quoted about sentencing times and judge time blowing out — but the sentence leans on an unspecified 'the evidence', and the leap to 'significant costs' outruns what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because surely, if it is true that we want a society that is authentically trying to reduce the number of victims, we would want to break that cycle and we would want to understand that cycle. And surely understanding the cycle is the means to breaking it.
rigor.explanation: The load-bearing step — that understanding the cycle of victimisation is the means of breaking it — is asserted rather than argued; 'surely' does the work that evidence should. Understanding a causal process does not establish that a report describing it changes sentencing outcomes or reoffending. Bare assertion presented as self-evident, with the conclusion resting on an unsupported premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As we’ve outlined a number of times, Māori are more likely to be the victims of crime than other members of society, and so they benefit also from the wise use of limited legal aid resources and, you know, some discipline around the extent of discounts in sentencing, which is a broader issue that the Government is concerned about in order to have real consequences for crime.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. Even granting the premise, higher victimisation of Māori does not establish that Māori benefit from removing funding for the reports — the people bearing the loss (Māori defendants at sentencing) are not shown to be the people gaining from the redirected spending, and no link is offered between defunding the reports and any reduction in offending. The premise and the conclusion are about different groups and the connecting step is missing.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the issue that many of people have raised is the implication that the passing of this law will mean that, somehow, judges can no longer have any information around the background of offenders, which is complete nonsense.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. No member argued judges would be left with no background information at all; the argument put was that defunding removes expert, funded reports and shifts the burden elsewhere. Refuting the extreme version leaves the actual objection untouched.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Putting justice aside, which I think should be the primary consideration, this is a cost-saving exercise by this Government within the justice system, but what the evidence suggests to us is that there will be more costs to the justice system from this section 27 defunding proposal that we are debating tonight—and they are significant costs.
specificity.explanation: She invokes a cost-benefit analysis and names the specific proposal, but supplies no figure for either the saving or the offsetting cost. 'Significant costs' commits to nothing checkable, in a passage that is explicitly about the numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My answer is that it fits very comfortably with our international agreements and our focus on ensuring that all New Zealanders get to live in a peaceful and safe society.
specificity.explanation: Answering a question about what steps were taken to test the proposal against ICERD, he names no step, no advice, no analysis and no test — only an assurance of comfortable fit plus a generic statement of purpose. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Those sentencing judges say those cultural reports are helpful for them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that sentencing judges have stated section 27 cultural reports assist them in sentencing. The claim is about what members of the judiciary have said, not about whether the reports are in fact useful.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published judicial sources on the utility of section 27 reports — sentencing remarks/decisions citing s27 reports as assisting the sentencing exercise, judicial or Law Commission commentary, and any judiciary submissions on the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes)/section 27 funding changes. True if identifiable sentencing judges are on record saying the reports are helpful to them; false if no such judicial statement can be found, or if the judicial record shows the opposite view.

veracity.statement: As we’ve outlined a number of times, Māori are more likely to be the victims of crime than other members of society, and so they benefit also from the wise use of limited legal aid resources and, you know, some discipline around the extent of discounts in sentencing, which is a broader issue that the Government is concerned about in order to have real consequences for crime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Māori are more likely than other New Zealanders to be victims of crime. A present-tense claim about victimisation rates by ethnicity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey (NZCVS), adult victimisation rate by ethnicity for the most recent cycle before March 2024. True if the Māori victimisation rate is higher than the rate for non-Māori/the national average by more than the survey's margin of error; false if it is equal or lower.

civility.statement: Now, the issue that many of people have raised is the implication that the passing of this law will mean that, somehow, judges can no longer have any information around the background of offenders, which is complete nonsense.
civility.explanation: 'Complete nonsense' is blunt and dismissive, but it lands on the claim rather than on any member — no bad faith imputed, no person disparaged. Under the re-anchored scale, hard dismissal of an argument is civil; the misrepresentation of that argument is scored under Rigor, not here.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve read section 99, had a read, and it’s got some quite wide, sweeping powers. From my initial assessment, I question whether or not this particular amendment was actually required, in that there is quite a lot of discretion for the commissioner to be able to make denials for those who claim for reimbursement.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the committee: the existing s99 discretion is wide, therefore the new subsection is unnecessary. The premise is stated and the conclusion tracks it, but it leans on an unstated assumption that a general discretion and a statutory exclusion are interchangeable — a gap the Minister's answer then fills. Sound but incomplete rather than fallacious.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of why legislate for this change, it is that the commissioner, who’s responsible for the legal aid decisions, is statutorily independent. So for the Government to just send a message to him or her that we no longer want them to fund those reports would be to impinge upon that independence. So it’s appropriate for legislation to state that as the will of the Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Valid: if the decision-maker is statutorily independent, then an executive instruction would compromise that independence, and legislation is the constitutionally proper instrument. The conclusion follows from the premise offered, and it answers the objection that was actually put.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Given the urgency with which we’ve moved on this, there has not been formal consultation with different groups—with the legal community or with iwi—but it is something that we’ve flagged very carefully and clearly in our election campaign. We said we’re going to do it, and, lo and behold, we are going to do it.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy process — an election mandate is offered as the ground for proceeding without consultation — but the conclusion outruns the premise: campaigning on a measure establishes a mandate to legislate, not that a consultation obligation has been discharged. The two are treated as equivalent without argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’ve read section 99, had a read, and it’s got some quite wide, sweeping powers. From my initial assessment, I question whether or not this particular amendment was actually required, in that there is quite a lot of discretion for the commissioner to be able to make denials for those who claim for reimbursement.
focus.explanation: Engages the clause itself — the named section, the scope of the commissioner's power, and whether the amendment adds anything. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In terms of why legislate for this change, it is that the commissioner, who’s responsible for the legal aid decisions, is statutorily independent. So for the Government to just send a message to him or her that we no longer want them to fund those reports would be to impinge upon that independence. So it’s appropriate for legislation to state that as the will of the Parliament.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the amendment — statutory independence, the list of exclusions, why a legislative route is used. No reference to the opposing party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And I do note that that member, of course, is famous for his comment that “democracy has changed” in this country. Nobody was quite sure when they voted for the referendum where the democracy had changed, but, nevertheless, he stated that it had.
focus.explanation: Asked which iwi he had consulted, the Minister answers by characterising the opponent's past remarks. No policy, measure or figure is named in this passage; it is about the member opposite.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So given the fact that we’re here, that TPK did not support the policy due to the constraints within the 100-day plan, I ask the Minister sincerely: which iwi did you consult, which organisations in the pan-tribal area did you consult?
focus.explanation: Names a specific departmental position (Te Puni Kōkiri's advice), a specific cause (the 100-day plan timeframe), and puts a concrete question about the consultation this bill received. Scrutiny of a named process, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can’t—you know, we know on this side, I wouldn’t imagine anyone on that side knows, because they don’t know many Māoris and they don’t consult Māoris, but they do consult Winston Peters.
focus.explanation: Characterises the governing parties in general — what they are like, who they know — rather than naming a consultation requirement or a step in this bill. It brushes the consultation issue, but the weight is entirely on the other side's nature, so it sits near the tribalism end.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So that one’s a pretty straightforward question, and I’m pretty confident the Minister will be able to come and stand to his feet and be able to answer that.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Minister will stand and answer the question about which Māori Cabinet colleagues and community representatives he consulted. Not a promise about the speaker's own action, and settleable from the same committee-stage record.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of this committee stage on the Sentencing Amendment / legal aid clause; true if Goldsmith rises and names the consultation he undertook, false if he does not respond or declines to address the consultation question.

civility.statement: And I do note that that member, of course, is famous for his comment that “democracy has changed” in this country. Nobody was quite sure when they voted for the referendum where the democracy had changed, but, nevertheless, he stated that it had.
civility.explanation: Sardonic needling of the member himself rather than of any argument he made — the target is Jackson's standing and credibility, not the consultation point he raised. Short of an insult, but past pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because it’s really important—we always thought he was from Ngati Porou, and I think the National Party thought he was from Ngati Porou too, also, for a while.
civility.explanation: Leaves the consultation argument to needle the Minister about his own whakapapa, with the implication that he once let a claim of Ngāti Porou descent stand. It imputes something about the person rather than engaging what he said — a real failure, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And I do note that that member, of course, is famous for his comment that “democracy has changed” in this country. Nobody was quite sure when they voted for the referendum where the democracy had changed, but, nevertheless, he stated that it had.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Willie Jackson publicly said 'democracy has changed'. The check is whether the attributed words were said, not whether they were sound.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Broadcast transcripts and news reports of Jackson's interviews on co-governance and the Māori Health Authority; true if he is recorded saying 'democracy has changed' (or 'democracy as we know it has changed') in that context, false if no such statement is on record.

veracity.statement: Given the urgency with which we’ve moved on this, there has not been formal consultation with different groups—with the legal community or with iwi—but it is something that we’ve flagged very carefully and clearly in our election campaign. We said we’re going to do it, and, lo and behold, we are going to do it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that no formal consultation occurred with iwi or the legal profession before this bill, and (b) that the change was signalled in the National Party's election campaign.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's departmental disclosure statement and regulatory impact statement, plus National's 2023 law-and-order policy documents; true if the disclosure records no formal consultation with iwi or the legal profession AND the campaign material names ending legal aid funding for the reports at issue, false if consultation is documented or the commitment does not appear in the campaign policy.

veracity.statement: So given the fact that we’re here, that TPK did not support the policy due to the constraints within the 100-day plan, I ask the Minister sincerely: which iwi did you consult, which organisations in the pan-tribal area did you consult?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Puni Kōkiri advised against the policy, and that its objection was to the compressed timeframe imposed by the Government's 100-day plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Puni Kōkiri's departmental advice and the regulatory impact statement / disclosure statement for the bill; true if TPK is recorded as not supporting the proposal on timeframe or consultation grounds, false if TPK supported it or provided no such advice.

specificity.statement: So was there consultation with Nga Whare Waatea Marae? Has there been consultation with the Waipareira Trust, which is the biggest, as the Minister will know, Māori provider in the country?
specificity.explanation: Names particular organisations that either were or were not consulted, so the Minister's answer can be checked against a fact rather than a sentiment. A precise question, and precise in the same way a precise answer would be; short of 1.0 only because no date or process is attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So we appreciate that the Minister has made election promises to get rid of section 27 reports, but in those same election promises there was a real commitment made—and it is on record—that there needs to be a greater focus on victims.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the same election policy platform that promised to abolish legal-aid funding for section 27 reports also contained an explicit commitment to a greater focus on victims of crime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party / coalition 2023 election law-and-order policy documents and the coalition agreements; true if those published documents contain both a commitment to remove or defund section 27 reports and an explicit commitment to greater focus on victims, false if the victims commitment is absent from that same platform.

veracity.statement: You know we’ve supported legislation that you have introduced into this House, and we would hope that there would be a little bit of reciprocity there, that you would look at these Amendment Papers—we only saw this bill goodness knows when.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Labour Opposition has voted in support of Government-introduced legislation during this parliamentary term, contrary to the suggestion that it votes reflexively against.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard division records for the 54th Parliament from October 2023 to March 2024; true if Labour is recorded voting Aye on at least one Government bill at any reading, false if Labour opposed every Government bill put to a division.

veracity.statement: When we know, as the Minister has articulated, that Māori are more likely to be the victims of crime, and when we know that there are shameful statistics about the disproportionate and the unjust treatment of Māori in our justice system, such that we have prisons that have disproportionate representation of Māori, it would be very concerning that decisions that impacted the rightful justice applied to citizens that were not in the majority would be made simply by the dictate of the majority.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Māori are more likely than others to be victims of crime and that Māori are disproportionately represented in the prison population relative to their share of the population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics and the NZ Crime and Victims Survey, compared against Stats NZ census population shares; true if the Māori share of the prison population and of victimisation materially exceeds the Māori share of the general population, false if either is at or below population share.

veracity.statement: So you have not consulted with iwi; you have not consulted with justice experts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no consultation with iwi and no consultation with justice-sector experts was undertaken in the development of this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's disclosure statement and the Ministry of Justice regulatory impact statement / departmental advice for the Legal Services Amendment Bill; true if these record no iwi and no external justice-sector consultation, false if either records consultation having taken place.

specificity.statement: It would provide it to be at the discretion of the judge, so if there are certain aspects of the case that is being heard before the courts; if the judge felt that a section 27 report would provide additional information that is necessary; and if that presiding officer can see that there is real financial obstacles to the person accused before the court, then the judge would be able to make an order for there to be legal aid funding for that.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual mechanism of her amendment — who decides (the presiding judge), on what tests (necessity of the additional information, the defendant's financial means), and what follows (an order for legal aid funding). No figures or threshold amounts, so short of fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this one here is a good one, Amendment Paper I: cost of the report is less than $2,000, excluding GST, or such other sum as may be set by the commissioner from time to time; and the report is provided by a person or entity who was approved by the commissioner for that purpose.
specificity.explanation: Names the amendment paper, states a dollar threshold ($2,000 excluding GST), the discretion to vary it, and the approval mechanism and who exercises it. Fully checkable against the Amendment Paper as drafted.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It would provide it to be at the discretion of the judge, so if there are certain aspects of the case that is being heard before the courts; if the judge felt that a section 27 report would provide additional information that is necessary; and if that presiding officer can see that there is real financial obstacles to the person accused before the court, then the judge would be able to make an order for there to be legal aid funding for that.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the committee: the drafting of her own new clause and how it would operate. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m sure the Minister would welcome the opportunity to correct the misperception that may have been created by the suggestion that the majority can dictate how our justice system works, and particularly in a context of a Government that is so willing to articulate the overriding of Te Tiriti o Waitangi; so willing to say that it is prepared to take, potentially to a referendum, the question of whether we should uphold a constitutional commitment made in the founding of our country in 1840.
focus.explanation: Names a specific and identifiable measure — the proposed Treaty principles referendum — so it is not content-free party-bashing. But the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of what the Government as a whole is 'willing' to do, imported from outside the bill under discussion, rather than engagement with the section 27 provisions before the committee.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it’s really difficult to try and really comprehend, if you’re focused on increasing victim voice—if you’re focused on reducing the numbers of victims in New Zealand—why would you not agree to an amendment that enables the voice of the victim to be taken into consideration from all of those aspects and put before the court when the sentencing of that offender is being considered.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: the Government's stated aim (victim focus) is offered as a premise from which support for the amendment should follow. The gap is that it assumes without argument that legal-aid-funded section 27 reports containing a victim's voice are the way to serve that aim, and that reducing reoffending follows from them — the connecting steps are asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that would be a very, very easy way to address much of the ill that the Minister has identified in these reports—that they’re too expensive and that they’re not value for money.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion largely tracks the premises: a hard cost cap does directly address 'too expensive', and provider approval on the basis of past report quality plausibly addresses value for money. The looseness is in 'very, very easy' and in treating a price ceiling plus an approval list as sufficient for a quality problem the Minister framed more broadly.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When we know, as the Minister has articulated, that Māori are more likely to be the victims of crime, and when we know that there are shameful statistics about the disproportionate and the unjust treatment of Māori in our justice system, such that we have prisons that have disproportionate representation of Māori, it would be very concerning that decisions that impacted the rightful justice applied to citizens that were not in the majority would be made simply by the dictate of the majority.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: from disproportionate Māori exposure to the justice system, he concludes that majoritarian mandate is an unsound basis for settling this question. The premises support concern about minority-affecting justice decisions, but the step from 'a group is over-represented' to 'an electoral mandate cannot legitimate this particular change' is asserted rather than argued — the connecting principle is only supplied later, by appeal to the bill of rights.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So it’s really difficult to try and really comprehend, if you’re focused on increasing victim voice—if you’re focused on reducing the numbers of victims in New Zealand—why would you not agree to an amendment that enables the voice of the victim to be taken into consideration from all of those aspects and put before the court when the sentencing of that offender is being considered.
civility.explanation: Presses hard on an apparent inconsistency in the Government's position while attacking no one. The challenge is aimed entirely at the policy stance, not at the Minister's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That’ll be the most consultation the Minister’s done so far on this bill, would be a good tweet.
civility.explanation: Mockery directed at the Minister personally — the running joke that he is texting or tweeting during the debate is used to sneer at him. It is aimed at his conduct rather than his character or intelligence, so it falls short of a direct insult, but it is no longer civil engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my suggestion is that we make it clear that whilst this Government is going to defund these reports by and large, there’s a carve-out, and there’s a carve-out for kids, because anyone under the age of 18 years at law is a child.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: it names his own Amendment Paper's mechanism (a carve-out from the defunding) and the class it applies to. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But ultimately, it is the majority of the Parliament that passes the legislation, and that member is part of a party that was part of the Government in the previous term with a clear majority that passed a whole lot of things against the wishes of a whole lot of people.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine constitutional point in here about how majorities pass legislation, but half the sentence's weight is on the opposing party's record in the previous term rather than on this bill's process. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If New Zealanders don’t get the opportunity to comment on this, if they don’t have the right to submit at select committee or have their voices heard, how is it fair that they have to pay for something that looks flash in a sound bite, that gets a great tweet, that ticks a box on your 100-day plan?
focus.explanation: The core is on-policy and is legitimate scrutiny — no select committee stage, and a cost falling on taxpayers. But a third of the sentence is about how the Government wants to look rather than about the measure, which pulls it below a clean 1.0.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my suggestion is that we make it clear that whilst this Government is going to defund these reports by and large, there’s a carve-out, and there’s a carve-out for kids, because anyone under the age of 18 years at law is a child.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (a carve-out) and a precise threshold (under 18), so someone could draft it — but gives no cost, no numbers affected, and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When you look at the forecast—and that’s what’s done in this article very well; they’ve broken it right down—for those currently serving a sentence of over two years, an additional 136 prison beds will be required; for those currently serving a sentence of two years in prison or less, an additional 120 beds will be required; and for those currently serving a sentence of home detention, 124 beds will be required.
specificity.explanation: Three named cohorts with a bed figure attached to each, and a stated source. Fully checkable and actionable — whether the figures are right is Veracity's problem.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s nowhere where it’s more important, because we know that the earlier the intervention and the highest quality intervention, the highest likelihood of there being a change of direction.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion offered with a reason: if early, high-quality intervention raises the chance of desistance, then youth is where intervention matters most. The inference tracks the premise; the deduction is that the premise arrives as 'we know that' — asserted rather than evidenced. Whether it is actually true is Veracity's question, not this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But ultimately, it is the majority of the Parliament that passes the legislation, and that member is part of a party that was part of the Government in the previous term with a clear majority that passed a whole lot of things against the wishes of a whole lot of people.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque. The objection was that this bill is being passed under urgency without select committee scrutiny; the reply is that the questioner's own party used its majority the same way. That the other side did it does not establish that doing it here is warranted — the premise, even if wholly true, leaves the conclusion unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not rocket science that you can’t reduce the budget of the justice cluster, increase the costs that are required to the justice sector, and then champion yourselves as heroes of the cost of living crisis.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from stated premises — a 6.5 percent baseline cut plus new bed and court costs is genuinely hard to reconcile with the claimed savings. The gap is the final step: relief of household cost of living and the Crown's own operating spend are different things, so the inconsistency is asserted rather than shown, and 'it's not rocket science' stands in for the working.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Call it what you like, but those 16- and 17-year-olds are in concrete cells, and they’re in concrete cells with other young people who are serious offenders.
civility.explanation: Blunt, deliberately unsoftened criticism of a custodial arrangement — 'call it what you like' pushes back on the euphemism, not on any person. Attacks no one; this is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If New Zealanders don’t get the opportunity to comment on this, if they don’t have the right to submit at select committee or have their voices heard, how is it fair that they have to pay for something that looks flash in a sound bite, that gets a great tweet, that ticks a box on your 100-day plan?
civility.explanation: Imputes motive rather than engaging the reasons given: the bill is characterised as pursued for publicity and box-ticking. It stops short of a personal insult and is aimed at the Government rather than the Minister's character, but sneering at another's motives is no longer civil under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Call it what you like, but those 16- and 17-year-olds are in concrete cells, and they’re in concrete cells with other young people who are serious offenders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 16- and 17-year-olds are held in cells within an adult prison's youth wing, together with other young serious offenders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections records and Ombudsman/Inspectorate inspection reports for the youth unit at Christchurch Men's Prison: true if sentenced 16- and 17-year-olds are held there in cells alongside other young people convicted of serious offending; false if that cohort is not held in adult-prison youth units or is not co-located with other young serious offenders.

veracity.statement: You’ve got a Minister for Children who’s talking about military academies, as well as, at the same time, today I see on the Beehive website, seeking further advice on serious youth offending.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable assertions about what the Minister for Children has said publicly and what was published on the Beehive site that day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: beehive.govt.nz releases on or about 5 March 2024 from the Minister for Children: true if there is a release that day about seeking further advice on serious youth offending, and if the Minister has publicly promoted military-style academies; false if no such release exists or the academies claim is not attributable to that Minister.

veracity.statement: So in terms of getting this legislation through, it’s worth noting that the change whereby legal aid was used to fund these reports was not the subject of consultation or legislation or any democratic process—it just happened through a change of process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that legal aid funding for section 27 reports was introduced administratively rather than by legislation or consultation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice and Legal Services Commissioner records on how section 27 cultural reports came to be funded from legal aid: true if that funding was effected by an administrative change to legal aid grants policy without amending legislation and without public consultation; false if it was introduced by statute or regulation, or followed a public consultation process.

veracity.statement: When you look at the forecast—and that’s what’s done in this article very well; they’ve broken it right down—for those currently serving a sentence of over two years, an additional 136 prison beds will be required; for those currently serving a sentence of two years in prison or less, an additional 120 beds will be required; and for those currently serving a sentence of home detention, 124 beds will be required.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official forecasting attributes three specific additional prison-bed requirements to the bill, broken down by current sentence type.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement and the December 2023 official advice on the Sentencing (Cultural Reports) Amendment Bill, and Emma Hatton's Newsroom article: true if those documents forecast approximately 136, 120 and 124 additional prison beds for the over-two-years, under-two-years and home-detention cohorts respectively; false if the forecast beds differ materially or are not broken down that way.

rigor.statement: Because this is not the centrepiece of legal aid—this is off to one side. Despite the Minister’s protestations, this isn’t kind of the main grist to the mill for a legal aid lawyer. civility.statement: Yeah, it’s quite interesting Mr van de Molen seems to have quite a lot to say on this bill but hasn’t managed to take a call.

specificity.statement: So if that happens, then after the 14 days, when the bill comes in, the commissioner can approve, defer, or decline the payment. So the payments could continue past the 14 days if, in this period, the grant for disbursement is approved, and that is the transitional period.

civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the same way, those cultural reports are about whakapapa; they’re about understanding what kind of an upbringing somebody had, what kinds of challenges they face in their everyday lives, whether they have health disabilities, whether they struggle with addiction, whether they have experienced abuse in their upbringings or in their lives, whether they have experienced abuse at the hands of the State.

specificity.statement: Let me be clear—I’ve heard a lot of discussion tonight; let me be clear one more time: this makes no changes to section 27 of the Sentencing Act.

focus.statement: Because we know, based on evidence and the lack of evidence underpinning this particular bill that this is not going to make our communities any safer.

rigor.statement: Actually, I would say that it is much more valuable for the judge to get a report from people—the whānau, the friends; the people who know the offender rather than somebody who needs to be paid for it.

rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Of course they’ll exist—it is simply who is going to present the reports.

veracity.statement: But the Minister did say one thing I want to latch on to and he said that the savings to be made here—we know it’s about $7 million a year—now, in the National Party’s Real Consequences for Crime election document, it said that every penny of that money would go to victims.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National Party's 'Real Consequences for Crime' policy document from the 2023 campaign; true if it states that the savings from ending section 27 report funding go to victims (in terms equivalent to 'every penny'), false if it makes no such commitment or ring-fences the savings differently.

civility.statement: The implication from members opposite is that if they were approached by an offender who asked them for help, they’d say, “Yes, but only for a fee.” That is shameful. Reports remain; use them well; do it for free.

veracity.statement: There’s been some excellent work—Newsroom, one of them that’s picked up on this; there’s been some other really good reporting on this space: that back in December, the Minister received very clear advice that the long-term outcome of passing this legislation would, in fact, have a heavier burden on the taxpayer.
