rigor.statement: There is no certainty that the code will attach the reputational risk to big business that is available to them in the current Act, and when we speak about big business, we are speaking here about big tobacco, big pharmacy, big fast-food business, and those who want to pay their employees just the minimum wage.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that a voluntary code will not carry the current Act's reputational risk — is supported not by anything about how the code operates, but by naming industries the audience already dislikes (tobacco, fast food, minimum-wage payers). That is guilt by association and an appeal to emotion standing in for the missing comparison between the code and the Act.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One way to think about it is that you’ve got some of the largest, most powerful corporations in the land routinely late paying small businesses because they know they can get away with it, and they’re either doing it deliberately to look after their own cash flow, using small businesses, effectively, as a bank, taking advantage of no-interest loans from struggling small-business owners.
rigor.explanation: The load-bearing step is a motive — 'because they know they can get away with it' — and nothing is offered to establish it; the observed behaviour (late payment) is simply redescribed as intent. The 'either' framing then narrows the explanation to two deliberate motives without excluding the ordinary alternatives, so the conclusion outruns the evidence supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve heard that the Government is wanting to finish its block of work under its 100-day plan—its coalition agreement—but that is no justification to be using urgency to move bills that do not speak to what was campaigned on in the election.
focus.explanation: Names the urgency motion, the 100-day plan and the coalition agreement, and elsewhere the specific bills at issue. This is process scrutiny of a named commitment, not a characterisation of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That means also that today, over the next few hours, we will see this repeal bill go through; normally, that would take a minimum of four days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, absent urgency, this bill's passage would require a minimum of four sitting days. The claim is about the ordinary requirements of the legislative process, not about this bill's merits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Standing Orders of the House of Representatives (2023 edition) governing the stages a Government bill must pass and the prohibition on taking successive stages on the same sitting day; true if the stages required outside urgency cannot be completed in fewer than four sitting days, false if the ordinary process permits fewer.

veracity.statement: They account for 97 percent of all of our enterprises, they employ vast numbers of New Zealanders, there’s half a million or more small businesses, and I would say everybody in this House recognises that the people who start and run small businesses work incredibly hard.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable quantitative assertions about the New Zealand small-business sector: that small businesses are 97 percent of all enterprises, and that there are half a million or more of them. The trailing clause about hard work is an opinion and is not part of the checkable claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Small Business Factsheet and Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics for the year to February 2023; true if firms meeting the standard small-business threshold (fewer than 20 employees) are approximately 97 percent of enterprises and number at least 500,000, false if either figure is materially different.

civility.statement: It’s a shame he’s not giving them the opportunity to do that, and I cannot support this bill.
civility.explanation: Opposes the Minister's decision and the bill squarely, with no imputation of bad faith and nothing aimed at the Minister personally. A contested vote is a real opportunity to be uncivil and she takes none of it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: One way to think about it is that you’ve got some of the largest, most powerful corporations in the land routinely late paying small businesses because they know they can get away with it, and they’re either doing it deliberately to look after their own cash flow, using small businesses, effectively, as a bank, taking advantage of no-interest loans from struggling small-business owners.
civility.explanation: Harsh about the conduct of large corporations, but it lands on a commercial practice rather than on any member. Twyford is disagreeing with the Minister's approach throughout and attacks nobody in doing so.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I came to this House to support faster innovations and to support creative innovations that small, medium, and large businesses can actually go out, grow their business, and bring more for everyday New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A speech commending a bill, so it is trying to convey substance, but it supplies no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision — 'faster innovations' and 'bring more for everyday New Zealanders' commit to nothing checkable. The surrounding sentences add no detail to credit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They account for 97 percent of all of our enterprises, they employ vast numbers of New Zealanders, there’s half a million or more small businesses, and I would say everybody in this House recognises that the people who start and run small businesses work incredibly hard.
specificity.explanation: Carries two hard figures — a percentage share and an absolute count — that a listener could look up or act on. Marked down slightly because 'vast numbers of New Zealanders' for employment is left unquantified alongside them.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There’s a word for where you profess sincere concern for a problem, but, actually, your actions don’t reflect that. There’s a word for it, and it’s gaslighting. I can’t help but conclude that that is what is going on here.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate manipulation and insincerity to those advancing the bill rather than engaging the argument. Short of a direct personal insult — no individual is named — but 'gaslighting' is an accusation of bad faith, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine civility failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I just want to put on the record that this is a smart Minister who knows that, in 100 days, we haven’t seen many plans from this Government, if any.
civility.explanation: A backhanded compliment aimed at the Minister personally: the framing 'a smart Minister who knows' imputes that he is knowingly claiming a plan he does not have. Sneering and an imputation of bad faith, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It takes away a public disclosure regime that would name and shame the large corporations that are ripping off small businesses. It takes that away and replaces it with a voluntary code of conduct.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the mechanism being removed (a public disclosure regime) and what replaces it (a voluntary code). No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m afraid to say it, but this is an example that we see so often with the National Party, and that is a deference to powerful, vested interests. The National Party loves to say it’s the party of small business, but, time and time again, they actually line up and defend the interests of large private corporations, of big business, and that is transparently what is happening here.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely a characterisation of what the other party is 'really like' — its habitual deference and the gap between its branding and its conduct. The only policy anchor is the passing 'what is happening here'; no measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Late payments by big companies are anti-competitive. They are taking money out of the till of small businesses: the garages, the barbers, the suburban accountants, the shop owners, and the small entrepreneurs. It is anti-competitive. It makes it harder for small businesses to become medium-sized enterprises.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the substance of the problem the repealed Act addressed — who bears the cost and what effect it has. No reference to the other party at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My colleagues are also right that this is yet another example of this Government using urgency and using the time of this House to repeal legislation without any clear or credible plan to replace it. It is the theatre of the politics of revenge—that’s all it is—and I’m afraid to say that it actually doesn’t do justice to a party that claims to be a Government for all of New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Contains a real procedural-policy point — repeal under urgency with no replacement — which is legitimate scrutiny, but the weight of the passage is party framing ('politics of revenge', what the party claims to be) rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So this here seems to be an admission by the Minister in this repeal bill that there isn’t a fair and competitive landscape that small business can compete in. Now, that seems to me to go against the purposes of the bill and to show that, actually, what the Act does is it does have that mechanism to try and level the playing field.
focus.explanation: Engages the text of the general policy statement and the mechanism of the Act being repealed. Pure policy scrutiny with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It takes away a public disclosure regime that would name and shame the large corporations that are ripping off small businesses. It takes that away and replaces it with a voluntary code of conduct.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism on both sides of the repeal, which is checkable against the bill, but carries no figures, thresholds or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we do want, though, is legislation that is efficient and is effective in delivering on the purpose that it serves, and we’ve already got evidence being presented by the Minister that across the Tasman Sea, that is not the case. So we need to be outcomes-focused.
specificity.explanation: Points at a real comparator (the Australian regime) but supplies no finding, figure or source from it, and 'efficient', 'effective' and 'outcomes-focused' carry no checkable content on their own.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister has also presented what he plans to do with the seven initiatives, the seven focus areas, subsequent to the repealing of the particular piece of legislation.
specificity.explanation: Gives a count and a sequence relative to the repeal, which is more than a platitude, but none of the seven initiatives is named and no timeframe or mechanism is supplied, so nothing here could be acted on or checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve heard a lot from members on the other side about compliance costs and red tape, and how terrible compliance costs and red tape are. Yes, it’s true that the legislation that’s being repealed will remove compliance costs for our large private corporations—it will—because they will no longer have to comply with a public disclosure regime. But if there wasn’t a problem to be solved in the first place, we wouldn’t need to ask them to comply with a disclosure regime.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: concedes the opposing premise (repeal does cut compliance cost) and answers it by noting the cost is the price of addressing a problem the regime exists to fix. The conclusion follows, though it leans on the unargued premise that the problem is real — that is Veracity's question, not this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Late payments by big companies are anti-competitive. They are taking money out of the till of small businesses: the garages, the barbers, the suburban accountants, the shop owners, and the small entrepreneurs. It is anti-competitive. It makes it harder for small businesses to become medium-sized enterprises.
rigor.explanation: Offers a mechanism (late payment withdraws working capital from small firms, impeding growth) that supports the anti-competitive conclusion, but the key term is asserted three times rather than shown, and no link is made to any competition standard or evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What we do want, though, is legislation that is efficient and is effective in delivering on the purpose that it serves, and we’ve already got evidence being presented by the Minister that across the Tasman Sea, that is not the case. So we need to be outcomes-focused.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on an appeal to authority: evidence 'presented by the Minister' about the Australian scheme is gestured at but never stated, so the step from 'it did not work there' to 'repeal here' is left unsupported. The inference form is sound; the connecting evidence is absent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There’s an assertion that small businesses don’t have time to do their due diligence. In fact, small businesses, in my experience, are more likely to do due diligence on anything to do with their business because it is such a vulnerable place for them to be in a market awash with big players.
rigor.explanation: Rebuts a claim about the behaviour of small businesses generally by appeal to personal experience — an argument from anecdote. There is a plausible supporting reason (vulnerability creates an incentive to check counterparties), which lifts it above a bare appeal, but no evidence is offered for the generalisation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So this here seems to be an admission by the Minister in this repeal bill that there isn’t a fair and competitive landscape that small business can compete in. Now, that seems to me to go against the purposes of the bill and to show that, actually, what the Act does is it does have that mechanism to try and level the playing field.
rigor.explanation: Turns the bill's own general policy statement against it, which is a real inference, but it treats a claim about the limited effect of disclosure as an admission about market fairness — a gap between what the statement says and what is concluded from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I just want to put on the record that this is a smart Minister who knows that, in 100 days, we haven’t seen many plans from this Government, if any.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government produced few or no plans in its first 100 days. The claim is about the recent past and turns on what the Government actually published in that window, not on whether those plans were good.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Documents published by the National-led coalition Government between its swearing-in (27 November 2023) and the end of its first 100 days (early March 2024): the published 100-day plan and any accompanying policy or action plans. True if no or very few plans were released in that period; false if the Government published a 100-day plan and further named policy plans within it.

veracity.statement: It was referred to the select committee on 8 November 2022. It was reported back on 26 April 2023, so it spent 169 days at select committee, and reading the select committee report, we can see a number of amendments and changes that were made in order to make the particular model work better, because, obviously, that’s what select committees do.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific referral and report-back dates for the original Business Payment Practices Bill and derives a 169-day select committee period, and asserts the committee made amendments to the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bills database and select committee report for the Business Payment Practices Bill: true if the bill was referred to select committee on 8 November 2022 and reported back on 26 April 2023 (an interval of 169 days) and the report records amendments to the bill; false if either date or the interval is materially different, or the committee recommended no amendments.

veracity.statement: Then there’s the committee membership, so you can see the people who participated in the discussion, including Andrew Bayly, who is now the Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Andrew Bayly, the current Minister for Small Business and Manufacturing, was a member of the select committee that considered the original Business Payment Practices Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The committee membership list printed in the select committee report on the Business Payment Practices Bill: true if Andrew Bayly is listed as a member (or participating member) of that committee, false if he is not.

specificity.statement: It was referred to the select committee on 8 November 2022. It was reported back on 26 April 2023, so it spent 169 days at select committee, and reading the select committee report, we can see a number of amendments and changes that were made in order to make the particular model work better, because, obviously, that’s what select committees do.
specificity.explanation: Two exact dates, a derived day count, and a named documentary source (the select committee report) — anyone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Often, these payments aren’t being paid even in a contractual time frame; they are often a breach of contracts which say, “invoice will be paid within seven days” or “invoice will be paid within a month”, and they are being breached.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (contractual payment terms) with illustrative periods of seven days and a month, but gives no figures on how often, or which sectors, so it stops short of fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m really interested in, in particular: what were the stakeholder consultations that were conducted to proposing the repeal of the Business Payment Practices Act to Cabinet?
specificity.explanation: A precise, answerable question: a named statute, a named decision point (the Cabinet paper), and a defined thing being asked for (the stakeholder consultations). A precise question counts as much as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Here we are in urgency, and this particular bill is being rushed through—a first reading, a second reading, the committee of the whole House stage, and a third reading—bang, bang, bang—following after each other.
focus.explanation: Names the specific legislative stages the bill is passing through under urgency — scrutiny of how this measure is being handled, not a characterisation of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m really interested in, in particular: what were the stakeholder consultations that were conducted to proposing the repeal of the Business Payment Practices Act to Cabinet?
focus.explanation: Names the specific Act being repealed and asks about a specific step in the policy process — legitimate scrutiny of the measure before the House, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Without that, we can’t have faith that this Government cares about our community. Without that, we can’t have faith that this Government wants to see thriving communities with innovative, risk-taking businesses and individuals who are willing to engage and make this place a better country.
focus.explanation: Strip out the characterisation of the Government's motives and nothing about the repeal remains — no measure, figure or outcome is named, only what the other side is 'really like'.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This nudge effect has clearly had a place here, because I told a story earlier in one of my speeches about somebody at Fonterra, and my understanding is Fonterra no longer don’t pay people months in.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the reporting regime demonstrably changed behaviour rests on a single second-hand anecdote about one firm, with no counterfactual — argument from anecdote, and the word 'clearly' overstates what a single case can support. This is a genuine inference about the measure before the House, so it is scored here rather than treated as a jibe.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I’m assuming that the Minister has done due diligence and the Minister, not wanting to take 160-plus days to get some legislation done, has gone out and has consulted widely with businesses, the small and medium enterprises, before doing such a ludicrous act as repealing something without having consulted anyone.
civility.explanation: Sustained sarcasm at the Minister's expense — a mock assumption of due diligence that presupposes the opposite, plus 'ludicrous'. Short of a direct insult, but it imputes bad faith rather than engaging the reasons given for the repeal.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I have already acknowledged and said that there is an issue with businesses, particularly smaller businesses, paying late, so there is no disagreement across the House.
civility.explanation: In a contested repeal debate he concedes the opposition's underlying concern and frames the disagreement as one of method, attacking no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But I’d really like you to address why we are not prohibiting behaviour that we all agree, in this House, as far as I understand it, is actually really despicable behaviour.
civility.explanation: 'Despicable' is aimed at the practice of not paying suppliers, not at any member; the Minister is addressed with a direct request to answer. Harsh about the conduct at issue, civil toward the person.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And I back up that statement by saying that in the review in Australia, where they’ve had this arrangement in place since 2020, the Minister, in his summary of the scheme, noted only 1 percent of Australian entities knew where to find this information.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Australian minister's summary of the statutory review of the Payment Times Reporting scheme recorded that only 1 percent of Australian entities knew where to find the reported payment-times information.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Australian statutory review of the Payment Times Reporting Act 2020 and the responsible minister's summary of it; true if a figure of about 1 percent awareness of where to find the payment-times data appears there, false if the review reports a materially different awareness figure or no such finding.

veracity.statement: I note that when this Act that you are repealing was going through last time, you actually suggested a trial.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Andrew Bayly, then in opposition, proposed a trial of the payment-practices reporting regime by Supplementary Order Paper during the passage of the Business Payment Practices Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supplementary Order Papers lodged against the Business Payment Practices Bill in the 53rd Parliament; true if one in Andrew Bayly's name proposes a trial or pilot of the scheme, false if no such SOP exists or it was lodged by someone else.

veracity.statement: If we’re relying on the Australian report, it’s right at number one of the bullet points: prohibit unfair payment practices; do that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Australian review the Minister is relying on lists prohibiting unfair payment practices as the first of its recommendations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The recommendation list of the Australian statutory review of the Payment Times Reporting Act 2020; true if a recommendation to prohibit unfair payment practices appears and is listed first, false if no such recommendation is made or it is not the first item.

specificity.statement: And I back up that statement by saying that in the review in Australia, where they’ve had this arrangement in place since 2020, the Minister, in his summary of the scheme, noted only 1 percent of Australian entities knew where to find this information.
specificity.explanation: Names the jurisdiction, the year the scheme started, the source (the minister's summary of the review) and a precise figure — someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I’ve said on countless occasions, and as I kept saying during the select committee process, why doesn’t the Government recognise that they can go to four credit agencies—and I gave the cost—for a mere sum of $35, get up-to-date information on payment systems and times, and actually get a lot more information that’s absolutely relevant to due diligence considerations, rather than spend at least many millions for the Government, but multiple millions across industry coming up with an out-of-date system?
specificity.explanation: A named alternative mechanism (four credit agencies), a unit cost ($35) and a cost comparison against the scheme; concrete enough to act on, though the 'many millions' side is unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I would point him to the amendment on this point that talks about a prohibition, and it says that there’s a prohibition, so we wouldn’t just repeal; we would replace and we would do a prohibition on the late payments of over three months.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (a statutory prohibition in a tabled Amendment Paper) and the threshold it would bite at (payments over three months late); no figures on scope, penalty or who it covers.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Even if you ran a very expensive process to try and make them aware of the data, many would not know it, because simply they do not understand Government entities, unlike members of the House.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy — awareness campaigns would fail — but the premise rests on his own impressions from talking to small businesses in three towns, i.e. an appeal to anecdote, with a gap between 'don't know MBIE's full name' and 'couldn't be made aware'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Initially, I considered mandating payment times might be an effective approach, but following deeper analysis, including considering those in comparable jurisdictions overseas, I found mandating would create problems that would overwhelm its usefulness and do more harm than good for small business.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is supported by named causal mechanisms he sets out immediately after (perverse incentives, procurement substitution), which is genuine reasoning; but the weight-bearing step — that the harms 'overwhelm' the benefit — leans on an appeal to his own unshown 'deeper analysis' rather than on evidence presented.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I, for one, have used that builder, I know lots of small businesses that have, and I wonder if you’ve got any data about something that’s an established product used by small businesses and whether it’s used in this country, because it’s not really the same when we’re talking about Australia with a different threshold of amount, etc., and a different entity involved.
rigor.explanation: Argues from anecdote: her own use of MBIE's employment agreement builder and that of people she knows is offered against a general claim about small-business awareness of MBIE. The disanalogy with Australia is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As I’ve said on countless occasions, and as I kept saying during the select committee process, why doesn’t the Government recognise that they can go to four credit agencies—and I gave the cost—for a mere sum of $35, get up-to-date information on payment systems and times, and actually get a lot more information that’s absolutely relevant to due diligence considerations, rather than spend at least many millions for the Government, but multiple millions across industry coming up with an out-of-date system?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the reporting mechanism, its cost and a substitute for it. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m wanting to know why the Minister wouldn’t consider just including that requirement of the public sector in the existing framework that has been set up by the primary bill.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: whether a prompt-payment requirement for the public sector could be added to the existing statutory framework rather than dealt with outside it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to know if the Minister has considered whether there could be a judicial review of that ministerial directive, what advice has he received about the use of the ministerial directive, and can he assure us that there wouldn’t be some kind of “Henry VIII” element to it, given that he is planning to put in some fundamental changes without going through the normal parliamentary process.
civility.explanation: A hard challenge — it raises judicial review and a 'Henry VIII' bypass of Parliament — but every word is aimed at the process and the instrument, not at the Minister as a person. Under the re-anchored scale this pointed, substance-only challenge sits at the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To be asked, “Who are the four credit agencies?”, well, I think there’s Centrix, Equifax, and illion, and I can’t remember the fourth, but I’m sure if the member pulls out her phone, she might be able to find the fourth.
civility.explanation: The substance (naming the agencies) is fine, but the closing turns on the member rather than the question — a mild sneer suggesting she look it up on her phone. Condescension toward the questioner rather than a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The late payment practices that are currently being endured by small business have been around for ever and so we we’re deeply cynical about the offer of big business to suddenly say that it wants to set in place a voluntary code.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: a long-standing problem is offered as the reason to doubt a voluntary remedy. The premise is relevant but does not carry the conclusion — persistence of late payment does not establish that a code offered now is insincere, so it leans on an argument from past record plus imputed motive.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we know what large entities are. This is not going to affect smaller business. So all the talk from the other side of the House about compliance costs, simply, for most business in New Zealand does not apply.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference engaging the substantive objection: if the obligation attaches only to entities above the stated thresholds, then compliance-cost concerns about the bulk of New Zealand businesses are off-point. The conclusion follows from the coverage premise; the small gap is that it does not address compliance costs for the large entities that are captured.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of the amendments to the bill—and I note there’s quite a few Amendment Papers being put up by members of the Opposition—one thing I’d say to them is that if we repeal the bill, which is the Government’s intent, then obviously you cannot attach the amendments to a bill that no longer exists.
rigor.explanation: Begs the question. The amendments are proposals about whether the repeal should proceed in that form; dismissing them because the repeal will have happened assumes the very outcome that is still before the committee. The conclusion is only available once the premise it is meant to defend is granted.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, “large entities”, we know that that is the entities that have the cap of $33 million of revenue or $10 million owing to third parties, which I had thought the Minister was comfortable with when we had amended that in the primary legislation at select committee.
specificity.explanation: Two named monetary thresholds tied to a defined statutory term, and the point in the legislative process at which they were set. Anyone could look up the definition and check the amendment's coverage against it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are three options, actually, for how we might bring about the changes in terms of payment times. In respect of Government agencies and after consultation with Government entities, that could either be by way of a directive, it could be by way of a Cabinet decision, or it could actually be through the procurement rules, but probably most likely by way of directive, and the Minister can do that pretty easily.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete mechanisms and indicates which is most likely, which is real actionable content. Falls short of the top because there is no timeframe, no payment-time figure and no detail of what the directive would actually require.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, “large entities”, we know that that is the entities that have the cap of $33 million of revenue or $10 million owing to third parties, which I had thought the Minister was comfortable with when we had amended that in the primary legislation at select committee.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the statutory definition of 'large entity' in the payment-practices legislation is set by thresholds of $33 million of revenue or $10 million owed to third parties, and that those thresholds were amended in at select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The definition of 'large entity' in the Business Payment Practices Act 2023 and its regulations, plus the select committee report on the bill; true if the revenue threshold is $33 million and the third-party-liability threshold $10 million, false if the Act sets materially different figures or uses different criteria.

divination.statement: And I would suggest that some of the suggestions from the last member, who was obviously trying to be helpful, those are the type of things I would expect to be taken up in the industry code which will be developed and, hopefully, in place by the end of this year, which I would expect, because that will pick up some of those elements.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that an industry code on business payment practices will be developed and in place by the end of 2024. The code is to be developed by industry rather than legislated by the Minister, so this is a forecast about an outcome rather than a promise about his own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Whether a voluntary business payment / prompt payment industry code was published and operative in New Zealand on or before 31 December 2024 (MBIE announcements, the Minister's press releases, or the code's own launch materials); true if the code was in place by that date, false if it was still unlaunched or launched only in 2025 or later.

veracity.statement: Obviously, the previous Government chose to use its majority to push through the changes; I acknowledge that there were amendments made, but it was driven through even though National was very clear, and, I think, ACT were very clear, to put a dissenting report in the select committee’s report back to the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that both National and ACT recorded dissenting views in the select committee report on the payment practices legislation passed by the previous Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report on the Business Payment Practices Bill as reported back to the House: true if it contains differing/dissenting views recorded by both National and ACT members; false if either party recorded none.

veracity.statement: Also, many, many businesses are also asking—the 3,000-plus businesses that this will affect—me the same thing: please provide clarity around whether we need to incur significant amounts of money to upgrade our IT systems to be able to reflect these changes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure for the number of businesses that would fall within the reporting scheme being repealed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's regulatory impact statement / departmental advice on the Business Payment Practices Act and the revenue threshold for reporting entities: true if the estimated population of affected entities is approximately 3,000 or more; false if materially fewer (e.g. in the hundreds).

veracity.statement: As the Australian Government’s review of their own system has shown, on the recent report on it, it is not a practical way of getting a better outcome, and that’s why I have proposed a whole range of additional measures, because I do want to make sure that both businesses and the Government make sure they are paying on time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Australian statutory review of its Payment Times Reporting scheme found the scheme is not a practical means of improving payment outcomes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statutory review of Australia's Payment Times Reporting Act (the 2023 Emerson review) and its recommendations: true if the review concluded the reporting scheme is not a workable way to improve payment times; false if it recommended retaining the scheme with strengthening/streamlining amendments.

veracity.statement: The simple fact: if the Government starts paying on time in 10 working days—and we hit a target of five working days for payment times if people use e-invoicing—that will be the greatest nudge, because, as members across the way will know, the Government accounts for about a third of the economy, and that’s where the Government in the last term should’ve first of all directed its own focus.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that government accounts for roughly one third of the New Zealand economy — offered as the premise for the size of the payment-timing lever.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Stats NZ figures for total Crown expenditure as a share of GDP in the 2023/24 year: true if the share is approximately one third (roughly 30–37%); false if materially outside that band.

veracity.statement: I’ve already said countless times in the House that one of the greatest drivers of productivity—and if you just pick up or google Xero’s report, they talk about an $8.5 billion uplift for the New Zealand economy if small businesses, in particular, pick up and do one more app.
veracity.explanation: Relays a third-party estimate: that Xero's published research puts an $8.5 billion economy-wide uplift on New Zealand small businesses each adopting one additional software application. The claim under test is what that report says, not whether the uplift will occur.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Xero's published New Zealand small business / app-adoption report: true if it estimates an economy-wide gain of approximately $8.5 billion from small businesses adopting one further app; false if it states a materially different figure or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: Why not take the Australian approach, which is not to throw the baby out with the bathwater, but to see how the approach, the legislation, can be strengthened or improved or streamlined?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australia's response to reviewing its equivalent scheme was to retain and improve the legislation rather than repeal it — the direct contrary of the Minister's characterisation of the same review.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative status of Australia's Payment Times Reporting Act following its statutory review: true if Australia retained the Act and passed amending legislation to strengthen or streamline it; false if Australia repealed the scheme or allowed it to lapse.

veracity.statement: And that is the fact that small businesses can go to some credit ratings entities and get a report on a business for the sum of $35.
veracity.explanation: Relays the Minister's own claim, restated back to him for confirmation: that a small business can obtain a credit report on another business from a credit rating agency for $35.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published pricing from New Zealand credit bureaux (Centrix, Equifax, illion) for a single business credit report as at March 2024: true if a report is available at approximately $35; false if the cheapest comparable report is materially more expensive or only sold by subscription.

rigor.statement: Now, the issue around the urgency and why we’re doing this today, and why this particular piece of legislation is going through today, is the issue of: if we do not do this quickly, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment is required under legislation set down by the previous Parliament to actually start incurring costs, and that is why we need to do this as soon as practicable.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House: a statutory commencement obligation would force MBIE to spend on a scheme about to be repealed, therefore acting before that trigger avoids the spend. The conclusion (urgency) follows from the stated premise; no fallacy or appeal. Not fact-checking whether the commencement date is as described — that is Veracity's question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No one could answer that question. That question cannot be answered. The only place where it has taken place is in Australia, and it’s been in place for two years, and so they’re the best people to look at what the impact is.
rigor.explanation: Engages the policy question squarely — it is an answer to a demand for analysis — but the inference is weak in two ways. 'The question cannot be answered' is a non sequitur: the request was for ex ante cost-benefit modelling of compliance costs, which does not require the scheme to have run. And the conclusion then rests on an appeal to authority ('they're the best people to look at'), substituting the Australian reviewers' standing for the New Zealand-specific evidence being asked for.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Thirdly, what makes him think that a voluntary code of conduct will change behaviour, when we’re talking about an entrenched pattern of behaviour that confers substantial financial benefit on the late-paying corporations, at the expense of small businesses?
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the replacement mechanism, not a jibe: if late payment confers a financial benefit on the payer, a voluntary code asks the beneficiary to give it up unprompted, so the incentive runs against compliance. The conclusion tracks the premise. It is short of 1.0 because it treats the financial benefit as settled rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The simple fact: if the Government starts paying on time in 10 working days—and we hit a target of five working days for payment times if people use e-invoicing—that will be the greatest nudge, because, as members across the way will know, the Government accounts for about a third of the economy, and that’s where the Government in the last term should’ve first of all directed its own focus.
specificity.explanation: Carries two concrete, checkable targets (payment within 10 working days, five working days where e-invoicing is used) and a named mechanism. Short of 1.0 because no commencement date or coverage figure is attached to the targets.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We don’t need to do legislation; we can do it by the Minister issuing a directive. We do need to consult with the Crown entities; it will take approximately two to three months to do that, and we can bring about that change very, very quickly.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (a ministerial directive rather than legislation), the step required (consultation with Crown entities) and a rough duration (two to three months). Missing a start date, a coverage list, or any cost figure, so it stops short of fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what we’ve said is we’re going to require Government agencies and entities, in time, to be capable of e-invoicing, both to be able to receive and to send, and to incentivise businesses to do it, because they’re going to have even quicker payment times.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism with a defined technical scope (agencies capable of both receiving and sending e-invoices), but 'in time' supplies no deadline, no list of which entities, and no figures. A direction with some detail, missing the by-when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Has the Minister been able to have the benefit of some kind of quantifying of the compliance costs to big business? Surely that modelling shouldn’t be too difficult to obtain. What’s the likely cost, what’s the incidence of it, the number of corporations that would be affected, the frequency, and so on?
specificity.explanation: A precise question is as specific as a precise answer: it itemises exactly what is sought — the quantum of compliance cost, its incidence, the number of affected corporations, the reporting frequency. It carries no figures of its own, which is what keeps it below the top of the scale.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Could he please name those agencies? It would be useful to know who they are.
specificity.explanation: Pins the Minister to a checkable particular — the identity of the four or five credit rating entities he relied on — rather than asking a general question about the measure. It carries no figures or mechanism itself, so it sits in the middle of the scale.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re not talking reckons here; we’re talking about a Minister who has actually reviewed the scheme that’s been in place, which the Labour Government just obviously picked up and carried over here without much further thought.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point — the evidence relied on is a completed review of an operating scheme — but the sentence's weight lands on a characterisation of the other party's diligence rather than on the review's content. A real policy point wrapped in party framing. No individual is attacked, so this is Focus's business, not Civility's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would suggest that Helen White’s Amendment Paper that would, essentially, retain the current law but give it a trial period would be a much more thoughtful and responsible approach.
focus.explanation: Names a specific amendment paper before the committee and a specific alternative mechanism (retain the law with a trial period). Entirely about the measure, with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That is the biggest nudge you will see, because that will drive CEOs of our large Government agencies, and, in time, the Crown entities—nearly 100 entities spending over $50 billion a year—to promptly pay.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an outcome in the behaviour of others: that publishing agency payment times will cause chief executives of government agencies, and later Crown entities, to pay suppliers promptly. The publication itself is the speaker's own action; the resulting behaviour change is the prediction.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE's published payment-times data for government agencies: true if, once published, average or median agency payment times improve materially against the first published baseline; false if they are unchanged or worse, or if agency payment times are never published.

civility.statement: But I want to give the Minister an opportunity to convince the committee that that characterisation wasn’t fair. And I think that the way that he can do that is by providing us with the data, the analysis, the modelling, the projections that informed his decision. I want to be assured that it’s not just reckons and ideology and political shortcutting.
civility.explanation: Pointed and robust: 'reckons and ideology and political shortcutting' edges toward impugning the Minister's motives rather than his case. It is pulled back by explicitly inviting him to rebut and by tying the whole thing to a producible artefact — the modelling. It does not land on the person, but it is not clean substance either.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There are 21,000 Māori-run businesses here in Aotearoa, and I’d just like to know if you’ve consulted one around this particular issue.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of Māori-run businesses in New Zealand at the time of speaking (March 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE/Stats NZ counts of Māori-owned businesses or Māori authorities (e.g. Te Matapaea/Māori business statistics); true if the published count is of the order of 21,000, false if materially different (e.g. under 10,000 or over 40,000).

veracity.statement: You said the Government contributes to 33 percent of this country’s economy; 29 percent—over a quarter of New Zealand’s GDP—is contributed by small businesses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that small businesses contribute 29 percent of New Zealand's GDP (the 33 percent figure is attributed to the Minister).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Small Business Factsheet / Stats NZ measure of the share of GDP contributed by small businesses (firms under 20 employees); true if the published share is approximately 29%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Unfortunately, 35 percent of companies, year on year, are filing for liquidation. Why? It’s because they’re not paid on time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 35 percent of companies file for liquidation each year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Companies Office / Insolvency and Trustee Service liquidation appointments for 2023 divided by the number of registered NZ companies; true if the annual rate is near 35%, false if it is an order of magnitude lower.

veracity.statement: Just on the issue of failure of companies, there are many reasons why nine out of 10 businesses fail over 10 years, and a lot of it is due to undercapitalised businesses simply not having enough capital. A lot of it is to do with the fact of poor management and the way they market their companies. The reasons are varied. So to attribute it always to late payment is not actually correct.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that nine out of ten businesses fail within ten years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics survival rates; true if roughly 10% or fewer of new enterprises survive to ten years, false if the ten-year survival rate is materially higher.

veracity.statement: I do understand that there is no regulatory impact statement provided with this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal legislation before the committee was introduced without a regulatory impact statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's supporting documents on legislation.govt.nz and the MBIE/Treasury regulatory impact statement register for the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill; true if no RIS was published with the bill, false if one exists.

veracity.statement: New Zealand is right up there in the world as being one of the poorest countries to provide small-business owners with some way of accessing finance.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand ranks among the worst countries internationally for small-business access to finance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD 'Financing SMEs and Entrepreneurs' Scoreboard and World Bank Enterprise Survey indicators on SME credit access and rejection rates; true if New Zealand sits in the bottom quartile of comparable OECD economies, false if it sits mid-range or above.

rigor.statement: Unfortunately, 35 percent of companies, year on year, are filing for liquidation. Why? It’s because they’re not paid on time.
rigor.explanation: A single cause is asserted for the liquidation figure with nothing offered to connect them — the 'why' is answered by assertion, not by evidence, and no alternative causes are addressed. The claim is squarely about the policy at issue, so it is a real (and weak) inference rather than a jibe.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Just on the issue of failure of companies, there are many reasons why nine out of 10 businesses fail over 10 years, and a lot of it is due to undercapitalised businesses simply not having enough capital. A lot of it is to do with the fact of poor management and the way they market their companies. The reasons are varied. So to attribute it always to late payment is not actually correct.
rigor.explanation: Premises (multiple documented causes of failure) genuinely support the conclusion (late payment cannot be the sole cause). The inference tracks what is offered and he concedes the part that stands.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I took myself to have a quick look at those websites to have a look at the sort of information that is available from those credit ratings agencies, and there are, in fact, a variety of credit reports available. But—to the Minister, respectfully—the information that is available from those credit agencies does not seem to be the same sort of information that is available in this Business Payment Practices Bill that would have been made available by that.
rigor.explanation: Offers her own check of the named sources and draws the conclusion that follows from it — the substitute the Minister points to supplies a different kind of information. Small gap in that a quick look at websites is a limited sample, and she flags it as such.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I put to the Minister—and I’d be really interested to hear his feedback—is that while this Government has come in claiming to get a lid on inflation, to bring inflation down, which we all want to see, what we are actually seeing is some unintended causes in the economy, as a result of cost cutting, of reducing spending. There’s been some really interesting reports—Bernard Hickey, one of these—that are saying that inflation is actually being pushed out and up into the economy.
rigor.explanation: A real argument about a real policy — fiscal restraint displacing costs into rates, fees and user charges — but the causal link is carried by an appeal to a named commentator rather than by anything shown, and 'unintended causes' is asserted rather than traced.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think that it’s insulting to say that small businesses wouldn’t know how to navigate through a particular process. I think that’s insulting, when, you know, these are intelligent professionals who are able to start a business and contribute.
civility.explanation: Contested exchange with the Minister, so there was a real opportunity to be uncivil. He calls a position insulting rather than the person who holds it; the target stays the argument, with only a slight edge in characterising the Minister's attitude to small business owners.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the other question I have for the Minister is: how can he give assurance or security to those vulnerable communities, and especially those firms that employ Māori, Pasifika, and vulnerable Pākehā people, that they’ll be able to pay their bills on time?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — what the repeal does to on-time payment and who bears the consequence. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I took myself to have a quick look at those websites to have a look at the sort of information that is available from those credit ratings agencies, and there are, in fact, a variety of credit reports available. But—to the Minister, respectfully—the information that is available from those credit agencies does not seem to be the same sort of information that is available in this Business Payment Practices Bill that would have been made available by that.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the bill being repealed and whether the proposed alternative delivers the same information. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve had 40 people to a meeting three weeks ago and I’ve got another meeting with them, I think, the week after next, where I’m actually seeking the view of many people from across the small-business sector, whether they’re in tourism, whatever sector they are, they are being represented, and I’m asking these sorts of questions of them because I want to make sure that when we’re responding, as the Government, to the issues, we’re responding to the needs that small businesses have identified, not some Minister sitting in the chair opining on it and coming up with a view and imposing $3 billion worth of additional regulatory cost, which we saw over the last six years.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (the reinstated ministerial small-business advisory group), a headcount and rough timings, but the consultation itself is described loosely — no terms of reference, output or date by which anything follows.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So there are a couple of things there that I guess you could address. One is the extent to which businesses can get that information, or that length of payment time, but also whether—you know, perhaps they could get it one way or another, but is that available at what you have suggested is the low cost of $35, or would they, in fact, have to pay a higher fee to those various credit ratings agencies in order to get that kind of information?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a named figure ($35) and a precisely identified piece of information (payment time rather than creditworthiness), though the ask itself is loosely framed. A precise question, not an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would just like to ask the Minister if he’s considered still doing some sort of analysis, because, while he is repealing the bill, it still requires some level of analysis to understand what the impacts are on small business by not implementing this regime.
specificity.explanation: Directed at a named instrument (impact analysis of the repeal) but the ask is hedged throughout — 'some sort of analysis', 'some level of analysis' — with no scope, method or timeframe attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Someone can have a great credit rating but can be a lousy payer of their bills, but do it on the last day or, like, the day after—that’s still not fair on small businesses.
rigor.explanation: A counterexample offered against the explanatory note's premise that credit-agency data already covers late payment: creditworthiness and payment timeliness are shown to come apart, which is exactly what would be needed to defeat the substitution claim. No fallacy; the conclusion tracks the example.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason why we are doing this so quickly—as I’ve said in our opening speech in the debate—is that we are very conscious that unless we repeal the Act, the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment have a statutory requirement to go ahead and spend the $2 million to $3 million, to maybe $5 million, but also we want to be clear with industry, who are probably going to be spending tens of millions of dollars to actually do that.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference: if the Act imposes a live statutory duty to implement, then repealing before implementation begins is what avoids the spend, so urgency follows from the premise. Marked down only because the cost figures are offered as a widening range and a 'probably', so the magnitude of the harm — which is what justifies bypassing normal process — is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what reassurances can he provide the business community that there is a plan in place where all of those who are affected by this legislation being repealed are informed in enough time to be able to make those quite potentially technical IT changes to their systems to make sure that they’re not incurring costs unnecessarily?
specificity.explanation: Names the affected group, the concrete kind of work at risk (IT/payment-system changes) and the harm (unnecessary cost), but asks for a 'plan' without specifying any channel, deadline or threshold that would count as sufficient notification.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It was, in fact, the Taxation Principles Reporting Act Repeal Bill which had a self-repeal clause on it of one year, and so the Minister has said that 28 days is the standard.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific Act and the exact period (one year), set directly against the 28 days in the bill before the Committee. Anyone could go to the statute and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, examples of where this has taken place recently are the Taxation Principles Reporting Act Repeal Bill, fair pay agreements, the New Zealand Productivity Commission—a whole raft of them, right?
specificity.explanation: Three named precedents a listener could look up, which is what makes the claim checkable — but they are named loosely (two by subject rather than by Act) and the list trails off into 'a whole raft of them' rather than a count or a date range.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s a new practice, as I understand it—we didn’t used to do that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that including a self-repeal clause in a repeal bill is a novel drafting practice not used by previous Parliaments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ legislation database and Parliamentary Counsel Office drafting guidance: search repeal Acts enacted before October 2023 for self-repeal/expiry clauses. True if such clauses are effectively absent before the current Government; false if repeal Acts from earlier Parliaments routinely carry them.

veracity.statement: It was, in fact, the Taxation Principles Reporting Act Repeal Bill which had a self-repeal clause on it of one year, and so the Minister has said that 28 days is the standard.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Taxation Principles Reporting Act Repeal Bill — one of the precedents the Minister had just cited — carried a self-repeal period of one year rather than the 28 days he described as standard.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taxation Principles Reporting Act Repeal Act 2023 as enacted: read its self-repeal/expiry provision. True if it provides for repeal approximately one year after commencement; false if it provides 28 days or another materially different period.

veracity.statement: Well, some members won’t be aware of it, but this has been a practice for 10 years now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that self-repeal clauses in repeal bills are a drafting practice roughly a decade old, in direct contradiction of Helen White's claim that it is new.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ legislation database plus PCO drafting guidance: repeal Acts enacted 2014–2023 containing a self-repeal clause. True if such clauses recur across that decade and PCO guidance so provides; false if the practice effectively begins with the 2023 Parliament.

civility.statement: I am somewhat sorry to ask this of this Minister, because I know he is diligent, but this Government, famously, has come into Government saying it had a 100-day plan.
civility.explanation: A contested urgency debate where she is about to criticise the timing of the bill, and she explicitly separates the Minister's own diligence from the Government's programme. The criticism lands on the record, not the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I see the member; she’s probably the only one in the House that probably understands it.
civility.explanation: A compliment to Russell that lands as condescension toward the rest of the House — an implication that other members cannot follow the tax point. Short of a personal insult, and he retracts it moments later ('I apologise to you—there are some very diligent people'), but it is a slight on colleagues' competence rather than an engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the fact that most of the 100-day plan seems to have consisted of “stop, repeal, replace, remove” is neither here nor there—let’s see the positive stuff.
focus.explanation: There is a named commitment here (the 100-day plan), which keeps it above pure tribalism, but the point is a general characterisation of the Government's agenda rather than anything about this repeal — and she concedes as much herself with 'neither here nor there'.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, one of the amendments, which wasn’t spoken about, is adding a clause which is about allowing interest for a default so that when payments are not made by a big entity, there is an automatic interest rate that would apply.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete legislative mechanism — an automatic default interest rate on unpaid invoices — so the proposal could be drafted or costed. Stops short of the top because no rate, threshold or trigger period is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, we’ve certainly heard about the cost to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment for doing this, but we know that there’s a $425 million cost to small businesses in the status quo.
specificity.explanation: Puts a precise dollar figure on the harm the repealed regime addresses and sets it against the administrative cost, which is exactly the comparison a decision-maker would need. Loses a little for not naming the source or the period the $425 million covers.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s also exactly in line with what the Australians did in terms of reviewing their own legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australia subjected its equivalent payment-times legislation to a review after a trial period, and that her proposed two-year trial matches that approach.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Australian Payment Times Reporting Act 2020 and its review provisions: true if the Act provided for a statutory review roughly two years after commencement and such a review was conducted; false if no review period was built in or the review occurred on a materially different basis than a two-year trial.

veracity.statement: Yes, we’ve certainly heard about the cost to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment for doing this, but we know that there’s a $425 million cost to small businesses in the status quo.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that late payment to small businesses imposes a cost of $425 million on the New Zealand small business sector under current arrangements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published New Zealand research on the cost of late payments to SMEs (e.g. NZIER/Xero Small Business Insights, or MBIE's regulatory impact statement for the Business Payment Practices Act): true if a credible published estimate of around $425 million for New Zealand small businesses exists, false if the figure is materially different, refers to another jurisdiction, or has no traceable source.

veracity.statement: Well, it’s to get paid on time, and part of what the Business Payment Practices Act did was it required big business to disclose how long it was taking them to pay bills.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Business Payment Practices Act imposed a disclosure obligation on large entities to report their actual payment times.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Business Payment Practices Act 2023: true if it requires large entities to disclose/report their payment terms and times (e.g. to a public register), false if it contained no such disclosure duty.

veracity.statement: So research from the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research shows that it costs small businesses when they get paid late.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to NZIER a research finding that late payment imposes a cost on New Zealand small businesses. Note the speaker first attributed the research to Xero and then corrected the attribution to NZIER.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZIER's published output around 2023 on business payment times: true if an NZIER report exists finding a cost to New Zealand small businesses from late payment, false if no such NZIER work exists or the finding belongs to a different organisation.

rigor.statement: We could give it a go, and if the Minister was not satisfied with the results at the end of that two years, he could pull the trigger, because it would already be happening.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: because repeal remains available at any point, delaying it forecloses nothing, so the option value of a trial is positive. The conclusion tracks the premise; the gap is that it treats the set-up costs of running the register for two years as nil, which is the very cost the Minister has raised.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He says that he is concerned for small business, he does care about what happens to them, and he does care about them. But the solution he’s proposed isn’t going to work, because it’s one that requires people to play nicely.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy: a voluntary code fails where the incentive runs the other way, which she supports nearby with the working-capital argument. As phrased here, though, the reason offered ('it requires people to play nicely') largely restates the conclusion that voluntariness will not work, leaving a gap between the incentive analysis and the flat claim of failure.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Despite it being railroaded through urgency, I think there has been some very, very constructive and productive discussion at the moment.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the process — 'railroaded through urgency' — aimed at how the bill is being handled, not at anyone's character, and paired with credit to the other side for engaging. Attacking a procedure is not attacking a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He says that he is concerned for small business, he does care about what happens to them, and he does care about them. But the solution he’s proposed isn’t going to work, because it’s one that requires people to play nicely.
civility.explanation: Explicitly accepts the Minister's good faith and concern for small business, then attacks only the instrument he has chosen. The disagreement is total and the treatment of the person is generous — this is the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On commencement, my question concerns clause 2, and I’m interested very much—as Helen White mentioned—to know from the Minister whether he considered a commencement date after the register had been allowed to be established.
focus.explanation: Engages a named clause of the bill before the committee and a specific alternative mechanism (deferred commencement until the register is operating). Entirely about the measure; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You guys know all about what doesn’t work.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the other party's record in general. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, and there is nothing left once the jibe at the other side is removed. Deliberately not scored for Rigor: it is not an argument, and no fallacy label applies to it.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s important to make clear that the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has not made any determination of genocide in this case and, indeed, has not released any final ruling on the matter.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 5 March 2024 the ICJ had made no determination of genocide and issued no final ruling in the South Africa v. Israel proceedings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ICJ case record for South Africa v. Israel as at 5 March 2024; true if the Court had issued only the 26 January 2024 provisional-measures order with no merits judgment and no finding of genocide, false if any determination of genocide or final ruling had been made.

veracity.statement: Since the ICJ provisional ruling, I have engaged with representatives of around 50 countries, and developments in Gaza have been a regular topic of discussion and none of those 50 countries are left in any doubt as to what New Zealand’s position is.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of diplomatic engagements — representatives of roughly 50 countries — between the 26 January 2024 ICJ order and 5 March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister of Foreign Affairs' public diary and MFAT records of bilateral meetings and calls between 26 January and 5 March 2024; true if engagements with representatives of approximately 50 countries are recorded, false if the number is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Will he unequivocally condemn Israel’s use of starvation as a weapon of war, which has resulted in the deaths of at least 10 children, so far, by starvation?
veracity.explanation: Embedded factual claim that at least ten children had by this date died of starvation in Gaza.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reports from the Gaza Ministry of Health, WHO and UN OCHA on deaths from malnutrition or dehydration in Gaza up to 5 March 2024; true if at least ten child deaths from starvation were documented by that date, false if fewer were reported.

veracity.statement: Will the Government intervene as a third party in the case against Israel under the genocide convention, now that Israel has failed to comply with the court orders including by obstructing basic aid into Gaza and deliberately opening fire on civilians who are seeking aid?
veracity.explanation: Embedded factual claims that Israel obstructed aid entry contrary to the ICJ's interim measures and deliberately fired on civilians seeking aid.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: UN OCHA aid-access records for Gaza and investigations into the 29 February 2024 aid-convoy deaths in Gaza City; true if credible investigation establishes that Israeli forces fired on civilians seeking aid and that aid entry was restricted contrary to the 26 January order, false if those findings are not established.

veracity.statement: How much more will Kiwis be paying per litre at the pump as a consequence of his Government’s policy of relying almost solely on the emissions trading scheme (ETS) pricing scheme to achieve transport emissions reductions to align with the Climate Commission’s projections that economic modelling has shown needs a carbon price of $235 per tonne by 2030?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that economic modelling behind the Climate Commission's projections requires a carbon price of $235 per tonne by 2030 to meet the transport emissions reductions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Climate Change Commission advice and the emissions-price modelling underlying it; true if a published projection puts the required emissions price at approximately $235 per tonne by 2030, false if no such published figure exists or the published figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Has the Minister received advice on the $30 billion Lake Onslow scheme and how much money was spent by the previous Government developing the scheme?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $30 billion cost for the Lake Onslow pumped-hydro scheme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE NZ Battery Project business-case cost estimates for the Lake Onslow pumped-hydro storage scheme; true if the published capital cost estimate is approximately $30 billion, false if it is materially lower.

civility.statement: This is what happens when one goes to academia for an expert opinion, and academia has never been in a court of law. That is not what the ICJ ruled, and that’s still in abeyance in terms of the final decision, as we speak.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the question by sneering at the source the questioner is presumed to have relied on, implying naivety rather than engaging the point. Condescension short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I appreciate that the former Minister may not have been particularly listening to my answer to the question, but, as I have stated—and I will state again for the purposes of repetition—that aspect of that process will form part of the ERP 2 process.
civility.explanation: Opens by suggesting the questioner was not paying attention and offers repetition as if for a slow listener. Condescension aimed at the person rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is what happens when one goes to academia for an expert opinion, and academia has never been in a court of law. That is not what the ICJ ruled, and that’s still in abeyance in terms of the final decision, as we speak.
focus.explanation: Half of the answer is a swipe at 'academia' rather than the measure at issue, but the second sentence does return to what the ICJ actually ruled and the status of the case.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will the Government intervene as a third party in the case against Israel under the genocide convention, now that Israel has failed to comply with the court orders including by obstructing basic aid into Gaza and deliberately opening fire on civilians who are seeking aid?
focus.explanation: Names a specific, actionable step — third-party intervention under the genocide convention — and the specific conduct said to justify it. Squarely on the policy question, not on the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will he guarantee the continuation of New Zealand’s annual funding for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) as the main provider of humanitarian aid in Gaza?
focus.explanation: Asks about a named funding commitment to a named agency. Concrete policy scrutiny with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will he consider introducing an Israel sanctions bill to Parliament to send a clear message that Aotearoa will not tolerate war crimes and genocide, just as we did in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine?
focus.explanation: Proposes a specific legislative mechanism and cites the existing Russia sanctions precedent as the model. Entirely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker
