focus.statement: What I can say is unfair to New Zealanders is the fact that this coalition Government has inherited a situation where there isn’t a clear pathway in order to meet some of our reductions, because of the inaction by the prior Government and that former Minister.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point (no clear pathway to the emissions reductions), but the weight of the answer is a general charge of inaction against the previous Government and the questioner personally, with no named measure or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will the cutting of funding for measures in his Government’s draft GPS that were recommended by the climate commission as being required to meet the first emissions reduction target, such as substantially increasing the share of central government funding dedicated to active and public transport infrastructure and reducing public transport fares to encourage greater use of public transport, put meeting emissions budget 1 in jeopardy?
focus.explanation: Names the specific document (draft GPS), the specific recommended measures and the specific target (emissions budget 1). Textbook scrutiny of a named government decision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has the Minister received any advice on the doomed light rail project and how much was wasted on that before it was cancelled?
focus.explanation: Names a specific project and a specific question (money spent), which is real accountability content, but it is put to a Minister on an unrelated portfolio question and framed to score against the previous Government rather than to advance the emissions matter before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Look, I have advice that the estimated impact of removing some of the initiatives which this coalition Government have signalled will have an inconsequential impact in regards to the impacts around those budgets.
specificity.explanation: 'Inconsequential impact' carries no figure, no named initiative and no identification of the advice. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I’ve advised to the Minister, there is a range of advice that I have received, but I have not received specific advice in regards to the emissions reduction impacts in that draft GPS. That will be part of the emissions reduction 2 process, of which I will welcome the Minister’s input into that process, and we start consultation in May.
specificity.explanation: Names the process that will handle the question and gives a timing marker (consultation starting in May), but no content, no figures and no description of what the advice covers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How much more will Kiwis be paying per litre at the pump as a consequence of his Government’s policy of relying almost solely on the emissions trading scheme (ETS) pricing scheme to achieve transport emissions reductions to align with the Climate Commission’s projections that economic modelling has shown needs a carbon price of $235 per tonne by 2030?
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (ETS pricing), the source (Climate Commission modelling), a precise price ($235 per tonne) and a date (2030). Fully checkable, as a question rather than an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, I have advice that the estimated impact of removing some of the initiatives which this coalition Government have signalled will have an inconsequential impact in regards to the impacts around those budgets.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests entirely on an appeal to unproduced and unattributed advice; no evidence or mechanism is offered to connect removing the initiatives to a negligible emissions effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does he think it is fair that Kiwis will be hit with a petrol price hike of between 40c and 50c a litre, based on that carbon price of $235 a tonne, because of his Government’s plan of cutting transport projects and programmes that will reduce emissions?
rigor.explanation: The inference is laid out in steps — cutting transport programmes leaves the ETS as the sole lever, the Commission's modelling puts the required price at $235 a tonne, and that price converts to a per-litre figure. The chain is traceable; the weak link is the unstated assumption that the price actually reaches that level.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Does he think it is fair that Kiwis will be hit with a petrol price hike of between 40c and 50c a litre, based on that carbon price of $235 a tonne, because of his Government’s plan of cutting transport projects and programmes that will reduce emissions?
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the pump price of petrol will rise by 40c to 50c a litre as a consequence of the emissions price reaching $235 per tonne.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE retail petrol price data and the NZ ETS carbon price series; true if the ETS-attributable component of the pump price is 40-50c per litre higher than in March 2024 by 2030, false if the increase is materially smaller.

specificity.statement: In the current financial year, Treasury is forecasting that the cost of financing Government debt—which is almost entirely interest payments—will be $8.8 billion, and according to forecasts in the half-year update, which assume the previous Government policies are continued, this is expected to rise to $9.7 billion in the next financial year, and $10.4 billion in the year after that.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Treasury half-year update), the stated policy assumption, three separate figures and the years they attach to. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Finance costs are expected to be $8.8 billion this year. By comparison, finance costs in 2017-18 were $3.5 billion, so they have more than doubled, or grown more than 150 percent, since that time.
specificity.explanation: Two dated figures plus the derived percentage; anyone could check the baseline and redo the arithmetic.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can she confirm what she is saying is that pretty soon, on the fiscal track we’ve inherited, the Government will be paying $10 billion a year, $200-plus per citizen, or $1,000 a year for a family of five just on the interest on the debt these guys left?
specificity.explanation: A total, a per-citizen figure and a per-household figure. Precise and checkable — whether the arithmetic holds is Veracity's question, not this one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At $8.8 billion, finance costs are forecast to be higher this year than spending on primary and secondary schools combined, or, putting it another way, finance costs are forecast to be higher this year than Government spending on the Defence Force, the Police, Corrections, and Customs combined.
specificity.explanation: A figure anchored to two explicitly named spending comparators, with the margin quantified. Someone could pull the Votes and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, as a proportion of GDP, those finance costs are high.
specificity.explanation: Offered as an answer to a request for a specific ratio, and carries no number, no comparison and no period. 'High' commits to nothing checkable, in a context where the figure was plainly available.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, I stand by all my statements and actions, particularly when I said that investments in the draft Government policy statement (GPS) 2024 will ensure key connections are provided so that Kiwis can get to where they need to go quickly and safely. These investments will also reduce congestion on our roads, provide low-emission transport options in our main cities, and create a more productive and resilient transport network, driving economic growth and unlocking land for thousands of new houses.
specificity.explanation: Names one real document (draft GPS 2024), but everything claimed for it is a string of generic benefits — connections, congestion, resilience, growth — with no funding figure, mechanism, corridor or date. 'Thousands of new houses' is the only quantity and it is unbounded.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Because the reality is—the reality is—that the GPS outlines exactly how we’re going to fund—I think it’s on page 27, for the member’s benefit, or 29; I can’t quite remember right now—the projects and the outcomes in our draft GPS document.
specificity.explanation: Points at a document and hedges between two page numbers rather than stating any funding parameter. The claim that funding is set out 'exactly' carries no figure, source or instrument of its own.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, Simeon Brown is correct, because this GPS is not increasing fuel excise duty and road-user charges in the three years of this Government’s term.
specificity.explanation: Names the two revenue instruments and the exact period over which the commitment is said to hold.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But what I’d point out is there are a number of key projects in the South Island that we’ll be prioritising: the Woodend Bypass—advocated by the member Matt Doocey—the Ashburton bridge, the Hope Bypass, and better road maintenance.
specificity.explanation: Four named projects, which is real checkable content, but offered in answer to a question about cost with no dollar figure, funding source or timeframe attached to any of them. 'Better road maintenance' carries nothing at all.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, the good news for the good people of Nelson and Tasman is that they will be getting the Hope Bypass under this GPS. I encourage the regional land transport plan to put forward its proposals, and the national land transport programme will be developed by the NZTA over the coming six months.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific project, the region it serves, the funding document it sits under, the process step required, the responsible agency and a timeframe. No cost or construction date, which is what holds it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many schools and tamariki would be impacted by a 30 percent to 50 percent cut to the free school lunches?
specificity.explanation: Names the programme, quantifies the cut as a range, and asks for two specific counts. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the current financial year, Treasury is forecasting that the cost of financing Government debt—which is almost entirely interest payments—will be $8.8 billion, and according to forecasts in the half-year update, which assume the previous Government policies are continued, this is expected to rise to $9.7 billion in the next financial year, and $10.4 billion in the year after that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the December 2023 HYEFU forecasts for core Crown finance costs across three years, on the stated assumption that previous-Government policy continues. The claim is about the content of a published forecast, not about what will actually happen.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update 2023, core Crown finance costs track: true if the forecast finance costs are approximately $8.8bn for 2023/24, $9.7bn for 2024/25 and $10.4bn for 2025/26; false if any figure differs materially from the published forecast.

veracity.statement: Finance costs are expected to be $8.8 billion this year. By comparison, finance costs in 2017-18 were $3.5 billion, so they have more than doubled, or grown more than 150 percent, since that time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific 2017/18 baseline for core Crown finance costs and derives a growth rate from it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Crown financial statements core Crown finance costs for the 2017/18 financial year: true if approximately $3.5 billion, false if materially different. The derived growth claim resolves arithmetically against that figure and the $8.8bn 2023/24 forecast.

veracity.statement: Can she confirm what she is saying is that pretty soon, on the fiscal track we’ve inherited, the Government will be paying $10 billion a year, $200-plus per citizen, or $1,000 a year for a family of five just on the interest on the debt these guys left?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a per-head and per-household breakdown of a $10 billion annual interest bill. The two derived figures are internally consistent with each other, so this is not a single-word slip; what is tested is whether the division is right.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: $10 billion of annual finance costs divided by New Zealand's resident population (Stats NZ, approximately 5.2 million at March 2024): true if that quotient is about $200 per person and about $1,000 for a household of five; false if it is materially different — for example about $1,900 per person and $9,600 for five.

veracity.statement: The Minister makes real an issue that the last Government left to us, and to further his analysis, I would put it this way: the finance costs alone of meeting our debt this year will equate to $1,666 for every person in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a per-capita figure derived from the $8.8 billion finance cost forecast; resolves against the population estimate used.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Forecast 2023/24 core Crown finance costs ($8.8bn) divided by Stats NZ estimated resident population at the date of the statement: true if the result is approximately $1,666 per person, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: At $8.8 billion, finance costs are forecast to be higher this year than spending on primary and secondary schools combined, or, putting it another way, finance costs are forecast to be higher this year than Government spending on the Defence Force, the Police, Corrections, and Customs combined.
veracity.explanation: Two comparative claims sizing forecast finance costs against named clusters of Vote appropriations for the same year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023/24 appropriations: sum of Vote Education primary and secondary schooling appropriations, and separately the sum of Vote Defence Force, Vote Police, Vote Corrections and Vote Customs. True if $8.8bn exceeds each sum (and exceeds the second by roughly $1bn), false if either sum equals or exceeds $8.8bn.

veracity.statement: The cost of borrowing at the moment relates to the official cash rate as it sits very high, at 5.5 percent, and the cost of servicing our debt as a proportion of GDP has risen to 43 percent by the old measure we used to measure debt before that member changed the measure to make it look lower.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an OCR level, a debt-servicing-cost-to-GDP figure, and that the debt measure was changed by the previous Minister. What is being tested is chiefly whether 43 percent describes the cost of servicing debt at all, as against the debt stock itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Three checks: (a) the RBNZ official cash rate on 5 March 2024 — true if 5.5%; (b) whether any published series shows debt-servicing cost at 43% of GDP, versus net core Crown debt under the pre-2022 measure at about that level — the claim as worded is false if 43% is the debt stock rather than the servicing cost; (c) Treasury records on whether the headline debt indicator was changed while Grant Robertson was Minister of Finance and whether the new measure yields a lower figure.

veracity.statement: Well, Simeon Brown is correct, because this GPS is not increasing fuel excise duty and road-user charges in the three years of this Government’s term.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the draft GPS 2024 does and does not do to fuel excise duty and road-user charges over a stated three-year window. Resolves against the document itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the draft Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024: true if it schedules no increase in fuel excise duty or road-user charges within the 2024, 2025 and 2026 calendar years; false if it signals or schedules any FED or RUC increase inside that window.

veracity.statement: How can the Government deliver reliable, effective, and efficient public transport as a priority for Kiwi households when it intends to scrap free and half-price fares for under-25s, and when its draft GPS takes over $1.5 billion from public transport, which also cuts the ability of local councils to provide additional transport fare subsidies?
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the under-25 concessionary fare scheme is being scrapped, and that the draft GPS removes over $1.5 billion from public transport. The second depends on which baseline and which activity classes are compared, and is contested.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The draft GPS 2024 public transport activity class funding ranges compared with the GPS 2021 ranges for the equivalent period: true if the reduction is $1.5 billion or more, false if materially less. Separately, whether the Government had announced the end of free and half-price fares for under-25s by 5 March 2024.

veracity.statement: Well, if the member read the draft GPS document, it outlines the fact that under the last Government, farebox recovery fell from 40 percent of running public transport services to 13 percent, and so the reality is that we need to ensure that people who use public transport are helping support it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific fall in the farebox recovery ratio and attributes the period to the previous Government. Resolves against NZTA's published recovery ratios.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The draft GPS 2024 and NZTA farebox recovery statistics: true if the national farebox recovery ratio fell from about 40 percent to about 13 percent over the 2017–2023 period, false if the figures or the direction differ materially.

veracity.statement: But I’d also point out to the members opposite, they had six years in Government, they spent $228 million on “Auckland Light Fail” and failed to deliver it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a total figure spent on the Auckland light rail project by the previous Government and that nothing was delivered for it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Light Rail Ltd and Ministry of Transport financial reporting on total spend on the Auckland light rail project to the end of 2023: true if approximately $228 million, false if materially different. Delivery resolves on whether any track was constructed.

veracity.statement: How is it appropriate for this Government to put a Minister in charge of the Ka Ora, Ka Ako free school lunch programme who described it as “wasteful”, “unaffordable”, and a “marketing stunt” while in Opposition, without any evidence?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the responsible Minister used three specific characterisations of the school lunch programme while in Opposition. Resolves against his statement record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements and Hansard record of the Minister responsible for Ka Ora, Ka Ako prior to October 2023: true if he described the programme using the words 'wasteful', 'unaffordable' and 'marketing stunt' or close equivalents; false if no such statements exist.

civility.statement: The member opposite is concerned that interest rates are very high after six years of his economic mismanagement.
civility.explanation: Attributes 'economic mismanagement' personally to the member rather than to a named decision or policy. It is criticism of a record, which the rubric protects, but the possessive framing lands on the individual's competence rather than on what was done — pointed and edging toward the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The cost of borrowing at the moment relates to the official cash rate as it sits very high, at 5.5 percent, and the cost of servicing our debt as a proportion of GDP has risen to 43 percent by the old measure we used to measure debt before that member changed the measure to make it look lower.
civility.explanation: 'changed the measure to make it look lower' imputes a deliberate intent to mislead to a named member. Short of an outright insult, but it is an accusation of bad faith rather than a criticism of the measurement change on its merits.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Minister think that the confusion behind that penultimate question relates to the fact that Waka Kotahi is actually a boat on the road, and while the potholes were building up in their tens of thousands of kilometres, they went ahead with that sort of behaviour?
civility.explanation: Frames the questioner's contribution as 'confusion' and builds a joke on it. It stops short of a direct insult, but the mockery is aimed at the member's grasp rather than at anything they said.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The member opposite is concerned that interest rates are very high after six years of his economic mismanagement.
focus.explanation: Characterises six years of an opponent's tenure in the aggregate. No policy, measure or figure is named in the sentence — the content is who is to blame rather than what was done.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Finance costs of $8.8 billion this year equate to $1,666 for every person in New Zealand. Government debt in New Zealand is too high, thanks to the financial mismanagement of the previous Government.
focus.explanation: The first sentence is squarely on the fiscal substance with a figure attached; the second drops the policy content and attributes the position to the previous Government's 'financial mismanagement' in general terms. A real policy point closing with party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When he said yesterday, “but the reality is—the reality is—that we need to ensure that we set out the funding parameters to be able to deliver the infrastructure New Zealanders need”, how can New Zealanders have any confidence that he won’t be introducing other taxes, fees, or levies to cover the fiscal holes that his transport plan clearly has?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the transport funding plan — quotes the Minister's own words about funding parameters and asks about the revenue instruments that follow from them. A named policy and a named mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can the Government deliver reliable, effective, and efficient public transport as a priority for Kiwi households when it intends to scrap free and half-price fares for under-25s, and when its draft GPS takes over $1.5 billion from public transport, which also cuts the ability of local councils to provide additional transport fare subsidies?
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme (free and half-price fares for under-25s), a specific document and a specific figure, and asks how the stated objective survives them. Textbook scrutiny of a named commitment against a named outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Minister think that the confusion behind that penultimate question relates to the fact that Waka Kotahi is actually a boat on the road, and while the potholes were building up in their tens of thousands of kilometres, they went ahead with that sort of behaviour?
focus.explanation: Turns on a pun about an agency's Māori name and a general gibe at what 'they' did. Potholes are gestured at, but no policy, figure or decision is named — strip out the material about the other side and nothing is left.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How is it appropriate for this Government to put a Minister in charge of the Ka Ora, Ka Ako free school lunch programme who described it as “wasteful”, “unaffordable”, and a “marketing stunt” while in Opposition, without any evidence?
focus.explanation: Names the programme and quotes specific prior statements about it — legitimate scrutiny rather than tribalism. Held below the top because the question is directed at the appropriateness of an appointment rather than at the programme's design or funding.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he believe that hunger impacts a child’s ability to learn, and, if so, will he commit to preserving the school lunch programme, given that poverty is not a choice for tamariki?
focus.explanation: Directed at a named programme and at whether it will be preserved. The moral framing about poverty is attached to the policy question rather than substituting for it, and no party is characterised.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, finance costs were relatively moderate even two years ago, but have skyrocketed since then because of higher interest rates and greater debt issuance.
rigor.explanation: A causal claim with the two mechanisms actually named — interest rates and debt issuance are the two terms that determine finance costs, so the conclusion tracks the premises. Marked down only because the causal attribution is asserted rather than quantified; no fallacy is present.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When he said yesterday, “but the reality is—the reality is—that we need to ensure that we set out the funding parameters to be able to deliver the infrastructure New Zealanders need”, how can New Zealanders have any confidence that he won’t be introducing other taxes, fees, or levies to cover the fiscal holes that his transport plan clearly has?
rigor.explanation: Begs the question: the existence of 'fiscal holes' is asserted as established ('clearly has') and then used as the premise for the inference that new taxes must follow. Nothing is offered to show the shortfall, and a statement about needing to set funding parameters does not by itself support the conclusion drawn from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if the member read the draft GPS document, it outlines the fact that under the last Government, farebox recovery fell from 40 percent of running public transport services to 13 percent, and so the reality is that we need to ensure that people who use public transport are helping support it.
rigor.explanation: Evidence is offered and the conclusion tracks it in direction — a falling user-funded share does support the claim that users should contribute more. The gap is that nothing is said about why the ratio fell (fare-free periods and patronage collapse are not the same cause as policy choice), so the inference from the number to the remedy is left unbridged.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, as my colleague the Hon Chris Bishop says, it is the National Land Transport Fund. Last time I saw, our ships run on water, and cars and trucks run on the land. This is about the land, not the sea. We’re not continuing the coastal fund under the last Government.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that coastal shipping should not be funded — rests entirely on what the fund is called. An argument from nomenclature: the word 'land' in a fund's title says nothing about whether coastal shipping belongs in the transport network it finances. Squarely on the policy, and badly reasoned.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Well, the good news for the good people of Nelson and Tasman is that they will be getting the Hope Bypass under this GPS. I encourage the regional land transport plan to put forward its proposals, and the national land transport programme will be developed by the NZTA over the coming six months.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that NZTA — a body other than the speaker — will develop the national land transport programme within a stated six-month window. Extracted as a forecast, not as the Minister's own promise.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZTA publication record: true if the 2024–27 National Land Transport Programme is developed and adopted by NZTA within roughly six months of 5 March 2024; false if the NLTP is not produced within that window.

veracity.statement: How can he be confident that these boot camps will work when the last time a National Government introduced them in 2008, 85 to 87 percent of those in the programme went on to reoffend within two years?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that of those who went through the military-style activity camps introduced by the National-led government from 2008, 85–87 percent reoffended within two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development / Child Youth and Family evaluations of the 2008–2011 Military-style Activity Camps (MAC) and the Chief Science Advisor / Justice Ministry reviews citing them; true if the published two-year reoffending rate for MAC participants falls in the 85–87% band, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Advice and modelling show that the supply of gas is uncertain and may not match future demand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice and modelling available to the Minister project uncertain gas supply that may fall short of future demand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE gas supply and demand projections and the Gas Industry Co / MBIE advice to the Minister for Resources current in early 2024; true if those documents project supply shortfalls or material supply uncertainty against demand, false if they project supply adequate to forecast demand.

veracity.statement: I would also note for the member that the vast majority of the funding that Fire and Emergency New Zealand receives is received by way of levy, not by Crown funding.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that most of FENZ's revenue comes from the insurance-based levy rather than Crown appropriation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FENZ annual report revenue breakdown for the most recent completed financial year; true if levy revenue exceeds 50% of total revenue (and materially exceeds Crown funding), false if Crown funding is the larger share.

veracity.statement: Perhaps if members opposite had had a thought about efficiency over the past six years, we wouldn’t have 80 percent increases in spending without better public services delivered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that government spending rose by 80 percent over the six years of the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses in the Financial Statements of the Government, 2017/18 compared with 2023/24; true if the increase is approximately 80% on a like-for-like measure, false if materially lower (e.g. nearer 70%) or if the figure only holds on a cherry-picked sub-appropriation.

veracity.statement: Does she stand by the Government’s commitment to 6.5 percent savings in Police, when they have advised their Minister that the cuts they would need to make would undermine their ability to recruit an additional 500 front-line police officers?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand Police advised their Minister that meeting the 6.5 percent savings requirement would undermine the recruitment of an additional 500 front-line officers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police briefings/advice to the Minister of Police on Budget 2024 savings options (released under the OIA or to the Estimates committee); true if that advice states savings would compromise the 500-officer recruitment commitment, false if no such advice exists or it says the opposite.

veracity.statement: Why did she conduct her line-by-line analysis of wasteful spending in a way that puts public servants out of work but didn’t manage to uncover that the Prime Minister was claiming an accommodation allowance for a mortgage-free home he owns while being able to stay at Premier House?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Prime Minister claimed a parliamentary accommodation allowance for a Wellington property he owns mortgage-free, while entitled to stay at Premier House.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Service accommodation-allowance records for the Prime Minister and his register of pecuniary interests / public statements on the mortgage status of the Wellington apartment; true if he claimed the allowance for a mortgage-free property while Premier House was available to him, false if the property was mortgaged or no allowance was claimed.

veracity.statement: Well, as the member should know, the outgoing Government left an enormous fiscal cliff for the school lunch programme. What that meant was there wasn’t funding provided for that programme into the future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government left no baseline funding for the school lunch programme (Ka Ora, Ka Ako) beyond a near-term expiry date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2023 Estimates and forecast appropriations for the Ka Ora, Ka Ako Healthy School Lunches programme; true if appropriations end at a fixed date with no out-year funding, false if ongoing baseline funding was appropriated.

specificity.statement: How can he be confident that these boot camps will work when the last time a National Government introduced them in 2008, 85 to 87 percent of those in the programme went on to reoffend within two years?
specificity.explanation: Names the programme, the year it was introduced, a numeric reoffending rate and the follow-up window — a precise, checkable question. Scored high even though it is a question rather than an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, obviously, the present Government has learnt from the past experience, learnt from the mistakes, has got the record of the Limited Service Volunteers success story, and, more importantly, in the Māori world, where so many people are so disconnected, this is one utility that will connect them to the rest of the country and make their lives real.
specificity.explanation: Answers a question containing a hard reoffending statistic with no figure, mechanism, design change or timeframe of its own — 'learnt from the mistakes' and 'make their lives real' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Today, I’ve announced one petroleum exploration permit has been granted to Greymouth Gas Turangi Ltd. I have also announced that I’ll be introducing a bill later this year that will overturn the previous regime’s ban on new permits for petroleum exploration beyond the onshore Taranaki region.
specificity.explanation: Names the permit holder, the legislative vehicle, the rough timing ('later this year') and the precise geographic scope of the ban to be overturned. Concrete enough to check against the permit register and the order paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, how wrong she is—let me count the ways. Fire and Emergency New Zealand has not been set a savings target. As a Crown entity, it has been asked by its monitoring agency, the Department of Internal Affairs, to look for savings and to operate efficiently.
specificity.explanation: Names the entity, its legal status, the monitoring agency giving the instruction, and draws a precise distinction between a savings target and a request to look for savings. All of it is checkable against DIA correspondence.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she stand by the Government’s commitment to 6.5 percent savings in Police, when they have advised their Minister that the cuts they would need to make would undermine their ability to recruit an additional 500 front-line police officers?
specificity.explanation: Carries the savings percentage, the agency, the named recruitment commitment and its size — precise enough that the underlying advice could be requested and checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I have said on a number of occasions, our Government will ensure that front-line services are protected in the Budget 2024 savings exercise. We have asked agencies to put forward their proposals for delivering more efficiency; for eliminating back-room waste; for ensuring that they’re not spending too much on consultants and contractors, low-value programmes, and ineffective programmes. Agencies have been asked to put forward proposals. We will then, as Ministers, evaluate those proposals before making any decisions.
specificity.explanation: Names the Budget exercise and describes a real process (agencies propose, Ministers evaluate) and the categories targeted, but supplies no figures, no dates and no test for what counts as 'front-line' — a direction with some detail but no how-much or by-when.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The evidence is to be found in a very insightful piece of work that began in 2017 with the Limited Service Volunteers, which was so successful under Ron Mark, an enlightened Minister of Defence at the time, that they decided to enlarge it. The evidence is all there. Ask people like punanga, ask people who actually were the head of the military of this country of their understanding.
rigor.explanation: Asked what evidence supports boot camps, the answer produces no evidence: it asserts that a different programme was 'so successful', that 'the evidence is all there', and then directs the questioner to ask named individuals and military leaders. Bare appeal to authority plus assertion of the conclusion; the inference about the policy is left unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The former ban, soon to disappear, created inordinate sovereign risk for investment in New Zealand. Advice and modelling show that the supply of gas is uncertain and may not match future demand. We need gas to keep the lights on in the electricity system, and, as the responsible Minister, on a cold and chilly night, I don’t want to see the men and women of New Zealand reduced to jiggling to keep warm.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: advice and modelling show a supply shortfall, therefore gas is needed for security of supply. But the step from 'supply may not match demand' to 'we must reverse the exploration ban' is not made, and the weight of the conclusion is carried by an emotive image of people shivering rather than by the modelling cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, it may be the view of that member that every single extra public servant her Government employed was the best use of a Government dollar.
rigor.explanation: Straw man: attributes to the questioner the absurd position that every single additional public servant was optimally spent, then argues against that instead of the question asked about the Prime Minister's accommodation allowance.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And in doing so, in line with our values, we will ensure that we’re delivering it in a cost-effective, high-value manner, because unlike that member, we don’t think it’s a good use of taxpayers’ funds to have uneaten lunches stacked a tower high.
rigor.explanation: Straw man: the contrast rests on attributing to the questioner the position that wasting uneaten lunches is a good use of public money, which nothing in the question supports. The conclusion about the redesign is carried by that invented contrast rather than by the waste evidence itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Weren’t New Zealanders entitled to know before the election that cuts to the 111 emergency call centre and vital supports for firefighters were part of her plan, and that her promise of no front-line cuts was worthless?
civility.explanation: Goes past criticising the savings programme to imputing bad faith: that the Minister knew before the election her promise was 'worthless' and withheld that from voters. Robust scrutiny, but it lands on the Minister's honesty rather than on the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, it may be the view of that member that every single extra public servant her Government employed was the best use of a Government dollar.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy subject here — public service headcount and the value of spending — but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of what the other side supposedly believes rather than engagement with the specific claim put to her.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It will be fair to say this is one of the biggest public policy failures in New Zealand history.
civility.explanation: A brutal verdict on a policy and a record, aimed at no person. Under the re-anchored scale that is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Under the last Government’s watch, thousands of children were just consigned to growing up in motels.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of children housed in emergency housing motels during the 2017-2023 Government ran into the thousands.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD emergency housing special needs grant data on children in emergency housing motels, 2017-2023; true if the count of children in motels at any point exceeded roughly two thousand, false if it remained in the hundreds.

veracity.statement: Is he aware that no previous Government policy statement, including under the last National Government, ever treated transport funding and delivery in this way—there was no comparable statement in previous GPSs that excluded multimodal funding from State highway projects?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, in the form of a question, that no earlier Government Policy Statement on land transport barred multimodal improvements from the State highway improvements activity class.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The State highway improvements activity class text in the GPS on land transport for 2009, 2012, 2015, 2018 and 2021; true if none of them excludes cycleways/busways from that class, false if any earlier GPS contains a comparable exclusion.

veracity.statement: The last Government, in their last draft GPS, wanted to use the road maintenance budget to build cycleways.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government's most recent draft Government Policy Statement proposed funding cycleway construction from the road maintenance activity class.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The maintenance/pothole prevention activity class text in the previous Government's final draft GPS on land transport; true if it permits walking and cycling construction from maintenance funding, false if cycleways sit only in a separate walking and cycling improvements class.

veracity.statement: Under the last Government, there was no consideration for people’s time.
veracity.explanation: An absolute claim that travel time was absent from the previous Government's transport policy, not merely ranked lower. Extracted as hyperbole, which is a veracity matter.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The strategic priorities and objectives sections of the GPS on land transport 2018 and 2021; false if either names travel time, journey reliability or congestion reduction as an objective, true if neither mentions them at all.

veracity.statement: There were over 62,000 potholes needing repair on the State highway network last year—a new record made by that last Government—causing damage to vehicles and travel disruptions for Kiwis around the country.
veracity.explanation: Two joined assertions: that over 62,000 potholes on the State highway network needed repair in 2023, and that this was an all-time high.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA State highway pothole repair records; true if the 2023 count exceeds 62,000 and no earlier year in the published series is higher, false if the count is materially lower or an earlier year exceeds it.

veracity.statement: Reports show that this project is expected to contribute up to $500 million a year to New Zealand’s GDP, benefiting all New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that published analysis projects the SH1 Cambridge to Piarere project as contributing up to $500 million a year to GDP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZTA business case or economic assessment for SH1 Cambridge to Piarere; true if a published report gives an annual GDP contribution of up to $500 million, false if no such report exists or its figure is materially different or is a whole-of-life rather than annual number.

veracity.statement: Road maintenance levels are down by 27 percent in the last five years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 27 percent fall in road maintenance over five years; the measure being counted (spend, resurfacing kilometres, or renewals) is not stated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA/National Land Transport Fund maintenance and renewals data for 2019-2024; true if any standard maintenance measure fell about 27 percent over that period, false if the measures are flat or rising.

specificity.statement: Between now and August, we’ll be working to strengthen emergency housing verification processes, review eligibility settings, limit discretion, and clarify an applicant’s responsibilities while in emergency housing.
specificity.explanation: Four named workstreams and an end-date, but no thresholds, no target numbers and no statement of what the eligibility settings would become.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Prime Minister has agreed that between Ministers Upston, Potaka, and myself, the housing-related functions of MSD, including emergency housing, will sit within the housing portfolio, and that will be delegated to Minister Potaka as Associate Minister of Housing.
specificity.explanation: Names the functions moved, the portfolio they move to, the three Ministers involved and who holds the delegation. Checkable against the ministerial delegation record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will take those bold and radical steps to end the scourge and blight on our landscape of thousands of kids growing up in motels.
specificity.explanation: Asked what the next steps are, the answer is 'bold and radical steps' — an adjective in place of a mechanism, with no measure, cost or date, and the surrounding sentences add only 'exploring a range of options'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There were over 62,000 potholes needing repair on the State highway network last year—a new record made by that last Government—causing damage to vehicles and travel disruptions for Kiwis around the country.
specificity.explanation: A named network, a named year and a hard figure that someone could go and check against NZTA records.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is the purpose of the code, which is to make sure that there are good measures in place to make sure the large companies in New Zealand—and the proposed code is going to cover the top 180 businesses—do adhere to good policy around payments.
specificity.explanation: One concrete detail — coverage of the top 180 businesses — surrounded by 'good measures' and 'good policy', with no enforcement mechanism or payment term named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m working towards a payment of five working days.
specificity.explanation: A hard figure with the surrounding sentences supplying who it applies to (Government agencies) and why (to incentivise e-invoicing), but no date and no agency list.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, there is also another activity class called public transport improvements and if the New Zealand Transport Agency or a council would like to make an investment which includes improvements to the roads, they would apply for funding under the State highway improvements.
focus.explanation: Answers the funding question with the mechanism actually at issue — which activity class pays for what — and says nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Reports show that this project is expected to contribute up to $500 million a year to New Zealand’s GDP, benefiting all New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to unnamed authority — 'reports show', with no report identified — and the conclusion 'benefiting all New Zealanders' does not follow from an aggregate GDP figure, which says nothing about distribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is the purpose of the code, which is to make sure that there are good measures in place to make sure the large companies in New Zealand—and the proposed code is going to cover the top 180 businesses—do adhere to good policy around payments.
rigor.explanation: Circular: asked what in a voluntary code would stop a large business withholding payment, the answer is that stopping it is the code's purpose. The aim is offered as the mechanism, so nothing connects the code to the outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just this morning, the Legal Services Amendment Bill passed its third reading; it will stop taxpayer funding for section 27 cultural reports that proliferated out of control under the former regime, consuming more than $7 million out of the legal aid budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts: that the named bill passed its third reading on the morning of 5 March 2024, and that section 27 cultural reports consumed more than $7 million of the legal aid budget.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and legislation.govt.nz records for the Legal Services Amendment Bill (third reading, 5 March 2024), plus Ministry of Justice legal aid expenditure figures for section 27 cultural reports. True if the bill passed its third reading that morning AND reported expenditure exceeds $7 million; false if either the reading did not occur then or the spend is materially below $7 million.

veracity.statement: Gang membership has increased by 51 percent in the previous six years, violent crime up by 33 percent, ram raids went up by 290 percent, and victims of retail crime by 110 percent.
veracity.explanation: Four separate quantified claims about changes in gang membership, violent crime, ram raids and retail crime victimisation over the six years to 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police National Gang List membership counts for the six years to 2023, and the NZ Crime and Victims Survey / police victimisation statistics for violent offences, ram raids and retail crime victims over the same period. True if each stated percentage change matches the official series within a few percentage points; false if any figure is materially overstated or the baseline period does not support it.

veracity.statement: Well, I do note one commentator, who said, in response to the Government plans to address harm caused by gangs, “If police have probable cause and know someone’s a gang member they should be able to go after them with the full force of the law knowing that Parliament, politicians and the community has their back.” That commentator was one Stuart Nash.
veracity.explanation: Goldsmith is relaying a quotation and attributing it to a named person; the checkable assertion is that Stuart Nash said these words in response to the Government's gang plans.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published reporting or a broadcast transcript of Stuart Nash's remarks on gang policing around early 2024. True if Nash is on record with substantially this wording in that context; false if the quote is not his, or is materially altered or stripped of a qualifying context.

veracity.statement: Only 1 percent of small businesses were even aware of the scheme, and, in many cases, they weren’t making use of the information.
veracity.explanation: Quantified claim about awareness of the Australian payment times reporting scheme among small businesses, sourced from the independent review he has just referred to.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Australian independent review of the Payment Times Reporting Act 2020 (Emerson review, reported 2023). True if it records small business awareness of the scheme at approximately 1 percent; false if the reported awareness figure is materially higher, or if no such finding appears in the review.

veracity.statement: And it should be worthwhile just bearing in mind that the Government accounts for about a third of the economy and spends about $50 billion to $55 billion a year on procurement of goods and services.
veracity.explanation: Two quantified claims about the size of government: its share of the economy, and annual procurement spend.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Stats NZ figures for core Crown expenditure as a share of GDP, and NZ Government Procurement's published estimate of annual government spend on goods and services. True if government spending is around one-third of GDP and procurement falls within $50–55 billion a year; false if either is materially outside that range.

veracity.statement: Xero are quoted every year saying that if small businesses were to adopt one new application, such as e-invoicing, then they estimate a benefit to the economy of $8.5 billion.
veracity.explanation: He is relaying a third party's estimate; the checkable assertion is that Xero has published an $8.5 billion economy-wide benefit estimate for small business adoption of an additional application.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Xero's published research (Small Business Insights or equivalent) on app/e-invoicing adoption in New Zealand. True if Xero has estimated an economy-wide benefit of about $8.5 billion on those terms; false if no such estimate exists, or the figure or its basis differs materially.

specificity.statement: Just this morning, the Legal Services Amendment Bill passed its third reading; it will stop taxpayer funding for section 27 cultural reports that proliferated out of control under the former regime, consuming more than $7 million out of the legal aid budget.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, the statutory provision, a dollar figure and the budget it came from — a listener could go and check every element.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Gang membership has increased by 51 percent in the previous six years, violent crime up by 33 percent, ram raids went up by 290 percent, and victims of retail crime by 110 percent.
specificity.explanation: Four named measures, each with a percentage change and a stated time window. Maximally checkable, whatever the figures turn out to be.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: After the hundred-day plan commitments are delivered, we will progress work including the reinstatement of the three-strikes legislation and limiting excessive sentencing discounts.
specificity.explanation: Two named policies, but no timeframe, no mechanism and no detail on what 'limiting excessive sentencing discounts' would actually do. The contrast with its high Focus is the point — on-policy but thin on detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The issue of this is that even if we were to put this process in place in New Zealand, the information is only up to date if made up to date every six months, and companies have four months to then work out what the response is. So, at any point in time, the information is 10 months old.
specificity.explanation: Names the reporting interval, the response window and the resulting age of the data — concrete enough that someone could dispute each number.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: First of all, I’m working with the Minister of Finance to ensure that Government agencies meet their payment time of 10 working days, and we will be proactively publishing the results on the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment website.
specificity.explanation: A named target (10 working days), a named actor, and a named publication channel — checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Xero are quoted every year saying that if small businesses were to adopt one new application, such as e-invoicing, then they estimate a benefit to the economy of $8.5 billion.
specificity.explanation: Named source, named mechanism and a dollar estimate — precise enough to be looked up and disputed.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: After the hundred-day plan commitments are delivered, we will progress work including the reinstatement of the three-strikes legislation and limiting excessive sentencing discounts.
focus.explanation: Squarely on policy: names two identifiable legislative measures rather than characterising opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It wouldn’t quite pay off the interest rate that we’re having to pay everywhere because of the huge amount of debt we’ve assumed over the last six years, but it would go some way towards growing the economy.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine economic point about debt servicing against productivity gains, but it is carried on a swipe at the previous government's six years, and no debt figure, policy or programme is actually named. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason why we’re putting through the repeal bill is that, simply, the proposals that were put forward by the previous Government will not work, will not derive any tangible benefit. This was borne out by the Australian example where this similar arrangement was put in place in 2020, and the independent review of it late last year concluded that, basically, it wasn’t working.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument from analogy: a comparable Australian scheme was independently reviewed and found not to work, therefore the NZ version should be repealed. The inference is real and evidence-backed, but rests on a single foreign case whose comparability to the NZ regime is asserted ('this similar arrangement') rather than established.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The issue of this is that even if we were to put this process in place in New Zealand, the information is only up to date if made up to date every six months, and companies have four months to then work out what the response is. So, at any point in time, the information is 10 months old.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the mechanism: a six-monthly reporting cadence plus a four-month response window is chained to a conclusion about data staleness. The arithmetic follows, though the 10-month figure is the worst case presented as if it held at every point in time — a modest gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There is no issue or argument across the House—it is important that small businesses get access to payments on a timely basis because cash is the lifeblood of small businesses.
civility.explanation: Repealing the previous government's Act is genuinely contested and there was ample opportunity to attack; instead he concedes shared ground on the objective and confines his disagreement to whether the mechanism works. Attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It said that in the UK, small businesses face a $1.6 billion deficit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Xero's UK research quantifies the cost of late payment to UK small businesses at $1.6 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Xero UK late-payment research reported in The Times in early March 2024; true if it puts the shortfall to UK small businesses from late payment at 1.6 billion in the currency stated (or sterling reported as such), false if the figure or the population it describes differs materially.

veracity.statement: Independent research by Kordia, today, gives us some reasons as to why: more than two-thirds of people using e-invoicing experienced an impact from a cyber incident, with nearly half, 46 percent, finding it took more than a month to resolve the incident, including 9 percent saying it took more than five months. E-invoicing is not a solution.
veracity.explanation: Attributes three specific figures to a Kordia report released that day, and attributes them specifically to users of e-invoicing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Kordia New Zealand Business Cyber Security Report released March 2024; true if it reports that more than two-thirds of e-invoicing users were affected by a cyber incident, 46% took over a month to resolve one and 9% over five months; false if those figures describe a different population (e.g. surveyed NZ businesses generally) or differ materially.

veracity.statement: Moreover, 70 percent of business leaders say they would consider paying a ransom to a cyber-criminal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a survey finding that 70% of business leaders would consider paying a ransomware demand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Kordia New Zealand Business Cyber Security Report released March 2024; true if it reports approximately 70% of surveyed business leaders would consider paying a ransom, false if the figure differs materially or no such question was asked.

civility.statement: And so it is hurting our small businesses, and those big businesses are absolutely doing something reprehensible when they withhold payment in this way.
civility.explanation: Harsh condemnation, but of a commercial practice rather than any person; on the re-anchored scale fierce criticism of conduct or policy sits at the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is of concern to me that we are having a law go through where these kinds of real crises, paid by small businesses, are not at the forefront of the priority of our Minister for small business, or his colleagues in the Government, because there is an underlying ideology and there is an ideological difference.
civility.explanation: Pointed — it questions the Minister's priorities and motives — but stops at ideology rather than character or competence, and never lands an insult on him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve heard that there’s seven or maybe nine points coming, but, as usual, the Government is ignoring those who are doing it hard now—and those who take risks, those who are the innovators, those who are really trying hard—and it is rewarding the slackers, the big businesses who simply want to screw their customers.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — deliberate indifference and the rewarding of "slackers" — rather than arguing the policy point, though no individual member is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Our productivity is a problem in New Zealand because those small businesses are undercapitalised.
rigor.explanation: A single-cause explanation asserted without support: undercapitalisation is offered as the reason for national productivity performance with no evidence connecting the two, and no other factors considered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We have not seen it trickle down. If we look at our productivity stats, we will see that there is a real problem in this country.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: poor aggregate productivity is offered as proof that a specific distributional mechanism has failed, but nothing links the statistic to the mechanism being rejected.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Independent research by Kordia, today, gives us some reasons as to why: more than two-thirds of people using e-invoicing experienced an impact from a cyber incident, with nearly half, 46 percent, finding it took more than a month to resolve the incident, including 9 percent saying it took more than five months. E-invoicing is not a solution.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the evidence offered is about cyber-incident exposure, which bears on the security of e-invoicing, not on whether e-invoicing addresses late payment — the question the conclusion answers.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, this is exactly a difference between the Labour Party and the current Government. The Labour Party actually believes in small business.
focus.explanation: Sits inside a real policy debate but names no measure, figure or outcome — the content here is a claim about which party has the right beliefs.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Isn’t the Government tired of simply rejecting things? Isn’t it time to invest in some solutions? Don’t you get tired of saying no? Don’t you get tired of breaking stuff?
focus.explanation: A run of rhetorical questions about the other side's general disposition; strip out the characterisation of the Government and no policy, measure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are talking about businesses where they are contracting for services for over $10 million a year. They are businesses worth $33 million per annum.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete thresholds defining the class of firms the reporting duty would bite on; someone could check the scope against the repealed regime.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I do think that we have heard a lot in a short time, but we haven’t heard a lot of common sense from the opposite side and that is really disappointing.
focus.explanation: A general complaint about the quality of the other side rather than about the repeal itself; no policy, mechanism or figure is named. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility is untouched — this is the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We can work together, and we can hear from small business who would love to contribute to something better than this dog’s breakfast of a repeal.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure and proposes a concrete alternative route (select committee, hearing from small business), though the substantive content is thin.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As the financial year comes to a close, businesses need some certainty, and these businesses who are now feeling a little bit concerned about the additional compliance costs will now have certainty that that will not happen.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the effect of the measure — compliance costs and timing for affected businesses. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These are the issues that I put to the Minister during the committee of the whole House stage to answer: who are the Māori organisations, the small-business owners, you have consulted?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names the stage of the bill, the Minister's obligation, and a precise question about who was consulted. Holding a Minister to account on a named process is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I simply would like the Government to consider what the Government and the party opposite has heard from this side of the House: the willingness to engage, the desire to find a solution for our small to medium sized enterprises, for those people who are doing it hard, those people who are the backbone of business in New Zealand, those people we care about, but clearly you don’t.
civility.explanation: "clearly you don't [care]" imputes indifference to small businesses to the members opposite — an imputation of bad faith rather than engagement with their argument. Short of a direct insult, but past the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We can work together, and we can hear from small business who would love to contribute to something better than this dog’s breakfast of a repeal.
civility.explanation: "dog's breakfast" is brutal, but it is aimed squarely at the repeal, not at any member. Fierce criticism of a measure is the civil standard, not a failure of it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I heard the Minister say that he had a dinner with them—I doubt very much that he actually talked to them about this specific bill—and say that he’s got another dinner with them this weekend.
civility.explanation: Imputes to the Minister that his consultation was hollow — not an argument that the consultation was inadequate, but a suggestion he is not being straight about what he discussed. Bad faith imputed to a named person, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m absolutely honoured to stand here in support of this, and, actually, as a small-business owner, I think we might have a bit of consultation, actually, on this side of the House.
rigor.explanation: Answers the charge that the bill was not consulted on by offering members' own business ownership as a substitute for consultation — an appeal to personal anecdote. Having run a business is not evidence that affected parties were consulted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We only have to look to Australia to see the results of their inquiry after the 2020 bill that went in there to see that it’s actually not the right way about this.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy — Australia's experience is offered as evidence against the New Zealand regime — but it rests on a bare appeal to an unnamed inquiry whose findings are never stated, and no reason is given why the Australian scheme is comparable.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are a party of common sense, and we see that supporting this bill is common sense.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the bill is supported because it is common sense, and common sense is defined by what the party supports. No premise is offered that is independent of the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And then to insult small-business owners to say that they cannot navigate their way through the current system I think is an insult to those small-business owners.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the case for a payment-times regime is that large firms can dictate terms, not that small-business owners are incapable of navigating the system. The sentence is also circular — the characterisation is called an insult because it is an insult, with nothing offered in between.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can’t see how this House and this Government can support this type of bill, because it makes absolutely no sense to me.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal incredulity: the speaker's inability to see the case is offered as the reason the bill should not be supported. No premise about the bill's effects is supplied to carry the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, the reason that this is under urgency—there are a couple of reasons, but the main one is that 3,000-plus businesses would have to upgrade their technology, and then the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment would have to spend an enormous amount of money to get the system up and ready to go.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure (3,000-plus businesses) and names the responsible agency and the mechanism (technology upgrade, system build), but the cost — the load-bearing part of the urgency argument — is left as "an enormous amount of money".
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are already, actually, protections under the Fair Trading Act, the Construction Contracts Act, and the Contract and Commercial Law Act to protect small businesses.
specificity.explanation: Three statutes named exactly; a reader can go and check whether each contains protections bearing on small-business payment and contracting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As the financial year comes to a close, businesses need some certainty, and these businesses who are now feeling a little bit concerned about the additional compliance costs will now have certainty that that will not happen.
specificity.explanation: Names the general mechanism (removal of compliance costs) and a rough timeframe (end of the financial year), but no figure, no estimate of the costs avoided, and no identification of which businesses.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There are already, actually, protections under the Fair Trading Act, the Construction Contracts Act, and the Contract and Commercial Law Act to protect small businesses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that existing law already provides the small-business protections the repealed regime was aimed at. The check is whether the three named Acts contain such provisions at all, not whether they are adequate substitutes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Fair Trading Act 1986, the Construction Contracts Act 2002 and the Contract and Commercial Law Act 2017; true if each contains provisions that in fact protect small businesses in their dealings with larger counterparties (e.g. unfair contract terms, retention/payment regimes, contract remedies), false if one or more contains nothing bearing on small-business protection.

veracity.statement: Like I said in the other readings, this Government continues to prioritise corporations, who actually have a different tax rate to many others.
veracity.explanation: The checkable assertion is the narrow one: that corporations are taxed at a different rate from many other taxpayers. The surrounding claim about the Government's priorities is opinion and is not what is being checked.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue's company tax rate and individual income tax rates in force in March 2024; true if the company rate (28%) differs from the marginal rates paid by many individuals and unincorporated small businesses (up to 39%), false if the rates are the same.

veracity.statement: They make up a quarter of the country’s GDP.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that small businesses (the referent of "they" in the preceding sentence) contribute about 25% of New Zealand's GDP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Small Business Factsheet / Stats NZ business demography data on the share of GDP contributed by small businesses; true if the published share is approximately 25%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We’ve got 21,000 Māori business owners out there.
veracity.explanation: A specific headcount of Māori business owners in New Zealand. Published estimates vary with definition (Māori authorities vs Māori-owned SMEs vs Māori self-employed), so the check must state which series is used.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / Te Puni Kōkiri estimates of the number of Māori-owned businesses or Māori self-employed as at 2023–24; true if the published figure is approximately 21,000, false if materially different (e.g. an order of magnitude out).

veracity.statement: If I can’t ensure that the goods and services I provide to those big companies, those companies that have a hold on the duopoly here in Aotearoa, especially the supermarkets who made over $400 million in one year, there’s an issue there—there’s an issue there.
veracity.explanation: The checkable assertion is that the supermarket duopoly made over $400 million in profit in a year. The rest of the sentence is a conditional about the speaker's own trading position and is not a factual claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Commerce Commission grocery market study reporting, and the published annual results of Foodstuffs and Woolworths New Zealand; true if grocery retail profit in New Zealand exceeded $400 million in a single year, false if annual profits were materially below that.

divination.statement: By then, it will be too late; it would have passed in the next hour.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the bill will complete its passage within roughly the next hour, before the Minister's stated further consultation dinner takes place. A forecast about the House's action, not a promise about the speaker's own conduct.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record and division for the third reading of the bill before the House on 5 March 2024; true if the bill completed its third reading that sitting, within about an hour of the statement, false if it did not pass that day.

focus.statement: They go out and position themselves as the champions of small business, but when they get into power, we see whose interests they really represent.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the governing parties are 'really like' — no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named in the statement. This is the content-free party characterisation Focus exists to catch; it insults no individual, so Civility is untouched.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the Government and the people providing the advice are out of touch, and while they say they’re reducing cost and red tape, what they’re really doing is shifting the burden of it on to small businesses who don’t have the power to go chase up their late payments from the big corporates.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — what the repeal does to who bears the compliance cost. On-policy even though the framing is adversarial.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, very, very transparent, through their actions, who National, ACT, New Zealand First represent: it is the 1 percent, who keep getting richer through making the economy fundamentally imbalanced and not functioning.
focus.explanation: A claim about whose interests three parties serve in general. It gestures at 'their actions' but names no policy, figure or outcome — the weight is party framing rather than the repeal itself.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The fact that this is being repealed under urgency shows that the Government is more interested in protecting the power of big corporates.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy action, and a weak one: the conclusion about whose interests the Government serves is drawn solely from the procedural fact that urgency was used. Non sequitur — urgency is used for many reasons and nothing is offered to connect the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the Government and the people providing the advice are out of touch, and while they say they’re reducing cost and red tape, what they’re really doing is shifting the burden of it on to small businesses who don’t have the power to go chase up their late payments from the big corporates.
rigor.explanation: The burden-shifting conclusion is genuinely supported by the premise that small firms must now buy the information themselves. But 'the Government and the people providing the advice are out of touch' rests on a single anecdotal price check by colleagues — a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If you actually study the economics, people on the other side of the House, and not just, like, Econ 101 in the 1990s or, you know, as part of their commerce degree or their MBA, they might understand what actually makes an economy work, and it’s not letting huge amounts of money get hoarded by small groups of people or organisations.
civility.explanation: Condescension directed at members opposite — a sneer at their education and their capacity to understand economics, rather than at their argument.
