Short of a direct insult but no longer civil. Nothing emitted for Rigor: strip out the part about the people opposite and there is no inference left to assess.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, can I bring us back to reality. We heard from the excellent Minister—clearly the others weren’t listening—that he is going to address all of these issues through regulation.
civility.explanation: Mostly on the substance, but 'clearly the others weren't listening' is a dig at members opposite rather than at their argument — pointed and mildly dismissive, edging onto the people.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, it so happens that one of my colleagues has been—in fact, several of them have been small-business owners, and they’re able to let us know that if you go get a Centrix report, it doesn’t actually cost $35; it costs $49 plus GST per company.
specificity.explanation: Names the provider, the unit (per company) and an exact price, set against the $35 figure attributed to the Cabinet paper. Directly checkable by anyone who cares to look.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: He is actually doing this to save businesses who had ahead of them, if this Act wasn’t repealed, quite a significant cost to upgrade their own systems to meet the requirements of that Act, and also $2 million to $3 million at least of cost to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to develop and put in place a computer system to actually deal with it.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named agency, a named mechanism and a dollar range for the Crown cost. Held below the top because the cost to businesses themselves is left as 'quite a significant cost' with no figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, it so happens that one of my colleagues has been—in fact, several of them have been small-business owners, and they’re able to let us know that if you go get a Centrix report, it doesn’t actually cost $35; it costs $49 plus GST per company.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific market price for a Centrix company credit report, and asserts that the advice underlying the Cabinet paper understated it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Centrix's published price for a single company credit report as at March 2024: true if a per-company report cost $49 plus GST, false if it cost $35 (the figure attributed to the Cabinet paper) or was materially different.

veracity.statement: He is actually doing this to save businesses who had ahead of them, if this Act wasn’t repealed, quite a significant cost to upgrade their own systems to meet the requirements of that Act, and also $2 million to $3 million at least of cost to the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to develop and put in place a computer system to actually deal with it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that implementing the Act would have cost MBIE at least $2–3 million to build a computer system, plus unquantified system-upgrade costs for businesses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Cabinet paper / regulatory impact statement for the repeal of the Business Payment Practices Act and MBIE's implementation costings: true if MBIE's estimated cost to build and operate the reporting system is at least $2–3 million, false if the documented estimate is materially lower.

civility.statement: They are gaslighting the New Zealand public and the small-business sector: half a million small and medium sized enterprises around this country, who employ vast numbers of New Zealanders and generate a very large share of this country’s wealth.
civility.explanation: Accuses the Minister and Government of deliberately deceiving the public — an imputation of bad faith directed at people rather than a criticism of the repeal's design or effect. Short of abuse, but past the line into questioning sincerity.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why would he think that large companies with a significant financial benefit from not paying their bills on time would voluntarily change their practice when there’s no transparency?
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the policy: the premise (large firms gain financially from late payment) supports the conclusion that a voluntary code without disclosure will not change behaviour. The incentive argument tracks, though no evidence on voluntary-code performance is offered and the rhetorical-question form leaves the step implicit.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve had to listen to hours of infantile rhetoric from the Government benches about red tape as if all regulation was somehow bad, when the law that is being repealed here would have imposed an obligation for public disclosure on New Zealand’s largest companies, and, no doubt, there would have been some cost associated with that.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: it attributes to the Government the position that 'all regulation was somehow bad', which is not the case they argued, and then rebuts that instead. There is a real argument underneath (a disclosure duty carries cost but delivers a benefit), so it is not content-free, but the inference rests on the misattributed premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think, in this debate today, we’ve all noted that we all want businesses to pay on time, but we don’t achieve it through more regulation and more red tape. There’s no point creating rules for the sake of creating rules.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that regulation will not achieve on-time payment — is asserted with nothing offered to support it, and the follow-on rests on a strawman: nobody argued for rules for their own sake, the disclosure duty was proposed for a stated purpose. Bare assertion plus misattributed premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: National’s lack of interest in actually doing anything that would create a more competitive market gives the lie to their claim to be the party of small business.
focus.explanation: There is a policy thread (competition policy) but the weight of the sentence is a hypocrisy charge about what the other party claims to be, rather than a named measure or outcome. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’ve seen that in the building supplies industry, we’ve seen it in the fuel industry, and we’ve seen it in relation to the supermarket duopoly, and those reports, indeed, laid out a pro-competition reform agenda that our Government went some way towards implementing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Commerce Commission conducted market studies in building supplies, retail fuel and groceries, that those reports set out pro-competition reforms, and that the previous Labour Government partially implemented them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Commerce Commission market study final reports; true if final reports exist for retail fuel, residential building supplies and retail grocery, each containing pro-competition recommendations, and if legislation or regulation implementing at least some of those recommendations was enacted under the 2017–2023 Labour Government; false if any of those three studies was not completed or no recommendations were acted on.

specificity.statement: We need good competition policy. We need competitive markets that make our firms more successful, tougher, more innovative, and more fleet of foot, but we also need competitive markets that allow small firms to grow into medium-sized firms and into large firms.
specificity.explanation: A string of desirable qualities — successful, tougher, more innovative, more fleet of foot — with no mechanism, no figure, no named policy and no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I’d just like to support the third reading of this bill, and I’d like to just pick up on a word that a member on the other side of the House used—optimism—because optimism is what we are going to be pumping back into our economy and into small business, because we believe in less regulation, less red tape, and less compliance.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the substantive case for the bill, but carries only slogans: optimism, less regulation, less red tape, less compliance. No figure, mechanism, timeframe or named replacement measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Small business can’t make claims for all sorts of strange, unusual, unexplainable, unreasonable demands and have them included into the business arrangement or a business relationship. That is a power dynamic that I would suggest is exclusive to recent politics.
focus.explanation: Pivots from the repeal to a swipe at the coalition's negotiating 'bottom lines'. No policy, figure or outcome is named; once the jibe at the other side is removed there is nothing about the bill left. Insults no individual, so this is a Focus failure rather than a Civility one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So if I can bring everyone in this House back to the intention of this bill, which is to improve payment times, ramping up the use of e-invoicing; incentivising small and medium enterprises to adopt e-invoicing; expanding payment targets to Crown entities—all of these will contribute to business efficiency.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: what the bill is intended to do and by which mechanisms. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And I’m expecting a breeze to drift across the House from all the nodding heads from the other side, because those words come from the Minister’s own document and paper with the rationale and the reasons for what this bill, now being repealed, addresses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the wording he has just read out (large organisations paying late harming small businesses with limited working capital; large players unfairly using market power) is taken from the Minister's own explanatory material for the repeal bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The general policy statement, disclosure statement and regulatory impact material for the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill (2024). True if that wording, or wording materially identical to it, appears in the Minister's own accompanying documents; false if it appears only in the 2023 Act's original material or in no ministerial document for the repeal.

veracity.statement: I’d like to start my contribution by just acknowledging the small businesses that are out there, the 97 percent of businesses in New Zealand operated mainly by families, by small groups of people who are doing the hard yards for our economy—and many of them come from migrant families—I really want to acknowledge them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 97 percent of New Zealand businesses are small businesses, operated mainly by families or small groups.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Demography Statistics / MBIE small business factsheet for the period: the share of NZ enterprises with fewer than 20 employees. True if that share is approximately 97%; false if materially different (e.g. below 95% or above 99%).

veracity.statement: But the very report that he quoted from, he cherry-picked out the things that he wanted to say and left out the most important point, which is that the report recommended that Australia maintain its payment practice system and hinge it more firmly around reputational risk.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Australian review of the payment times reporting regime actually recommended: retaining the system and anchoring it more firmly in reputational risk, rather than scrapping it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 statutory review of Australia's Payment Times Reporting Act 2020 (the Innes review) and the Australian Government's response. True if the review recommended retaining the payment times reporting regime and strengthening its reputational-risk mechanisms; false if it recommended abolishing the regime.

veracity.statement: There was no regard to that and certainly it hasn’t come from any select committee process, because I would remind this House that, once again, we are doing this under urgency.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal bill is being progressed under urgency and has had no select committee stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Order Paper and Hansard for the sitting day: whether urgency was accorded for the Business Payment Practices Act Repeal Bill and whether the bill was referred to a select committee. True if it passed under urgency without select committee referral; false if it was referred to a select committee or taken without urgency.

civility.statement: This repeal does what I’m doing to you to small business—it condescends. This is a condescending repeal.
civility.explanation: He states outright that he is condescending to members opposite, having just mimicked the Minister's verbal habits ('aerate the issues', 'zoom out') to mock him. Mockery and condescension aimed at people rather than at the merits of the repeal — short of a direct insult, but a real Civility failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But, having listened to the debate, I cannot help but think that the Act, the current system is being repealed as a vanity project by the new Minister.
civility.explanation: Imputes a personal motive — vanity — to the Minister as the explanation for the repeal, rather than contesting the repeal on its merits. A judgement about the person's character, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So although the Minister was generous in the committee of the whole House stage with his contributions, my sense is that he is a Minister who’s very hands on, he thinks he knows better than the officials, he thinks he knows better than the public consultation.
civility.explanation: Opens with a genuine concession but lands on the Minister's character — arrogance, thinking he knows better than officials and the public. Sneering at the person rather than the process, though hedged as 'my sense'.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I hear the Minister’s priorities—seven of them—to support small business. My challenge is: do eight.
specificity.explanation: References a defined set of ministerial priorities, but the ask itself — 'do eight' — names no mechanism, cost, timeframe or measure. A direction with a count attached and nothing checkable behind it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So if I can bring everyone in this House back to the intention of this bill, which is to improve payment times, ramping up the use of e-invoicing; incentivising small and medium enterprises to adopt e-invoicing; expanding payment targets to Crown entities—all of these will contribute to business efficiency.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete mechanisms (e-invoicing uptake, SME incentives, extending payment targets to Crown entities) but attaches no figures, targets or dates to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So faster payment between and across businesses in New Zealand is the intention that we have for this bill, and with great intention, it comes with great delivery, and the speed of delivery for this National-led Government.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the conclusion that delivery will follow rests on nothing but the strength of the intention. Nothing is offered — no mechanism, no track record, no evidence — to connect intending an outcome to achieving it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, he can’t have it both ways; either we know how to use data, or we don’t.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy. The two ministerial positions she contrasts — that a register is hard for small businesses to access, and that the policy statement assumes they cannot interpret data — are not actually contradictory, and data capability is not the binary the sentence requires it to be.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We are the easiest country in the world in which to do business, and that is something we should be proud of.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand currently holds the top place in the World Bank's ease-of-doing-business ranking, offered as a present-tense fact about the country's standing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The most recently published World Bank ease-of-doing-business ranking (Doing Business series, or its B-READY successor): true if New Zealand is ranked first in the latest published edition, false if another economy is ranked first. Also check whether the World Bank published any such ranking in 2023, as the claim is framed as a current standing.

veracity.statement: What’s really interesting is that this is a bill, a proposal, that had no regulatory impact statement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no regulatory impact statement was produced for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's disclosure documents and the Treasury/Ministry of Transport regulatory impact analysis register: true if no RIS was prepared or published for this bill, false if a regulatory impact statement exists for it.

veracity.statement: When we have a look at this particular disclosure statement, what it identifies there is that removing the RFT will result in modest savings for households and businesses in Auckland, and that that figure comes out to around $1.85 for each motorist that’s going to use it—$1.85.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the departmental disclosure statement for this bill quantifies the saving from removing the regional fuel tax at approximately $1.85 per motorist.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement prepared by the Ministry of Transport for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill: true if it states a per-motorist saving of about $1.85 (on the timeframe implied), false if the stated figure is materially different or absent.

civility.statement: But over that side of the House, you’ve got some naive people—very, very naive.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the judgement and intelligence of the members opposite rather than on their argument. Not sustained abuse, but it lands on the people, not the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Indeed, he is correct that that organisation did bring in what I consider were some very challenging times for suppliers to that entity.
civility.explanation: A contested urgency debate in which he had been named personally by the previous speaker; he concedes the point on the substance and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So all the rhetoric, all the ranting we hear over there about the Labour Government imposing costs and difficulties on small businesses, it’s simply not true.
rigor.explanation: Infers from a single aggregate international ranking that the previous government imposed no costs or difficulties on small business. Fallacy of composition: a top-line ease-of-doing-business score is compatible with specific compliance costs being added, so the conclusion outruns the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A small business at a time of global inflation, when the economy’s being squeezed by the Reserve Bank, doesn’t have the spare cash to get the data and to go to court.
rigor.explanation: A direct and valid-shaped rebuttal of the Minister's alternative-remedy argument: if the substitute protection requires litigation, and the affected firms cannot fund litigation, the substitute is not equivalent. The premise about cash constraints is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But it’s actually more than those 3,500 entities as well, there are other businesses that actually cause a huge amount of stress on other companies as well. So this wasn’t the silver bullet to solve the whole problem.
rigor.explanation: Nirvana (perfect-solution) fallacy: the premise that the Act covered only part of the problem is offered as grounds for concluding it was not worth keeping. Partial coverage does not entail no benefit, and no comparison of partial to zero coverage is made.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If this is a Government that is serious about addressing cost of living pressures, this is not the way to go for Auckland.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks what he has just laid out: an official estimate of a very small per-motorist saving plus the department's own view that the change is unlikely to have a substantive impact. The inference from 'small measured effect' to 'not an effective cost-of-living measure' follows; it stops short of 1.0 because no alternative baseline for what would count as effective is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So we brought in legislation to ensure that small businesses had a fair go, and this coalition Government—ACT, National, and New Zealand First—is removing the protection for half a million small businesses across this country.
focus.explanation: Names the measure before the House and the specific effect he attributes to it, with an affected population. Legitimate scrutiny of a named repeal, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is an example of a Government that has no new ideas, and the only aspect of new funding that is coming Auckland’s way is a 22c increase to the fuel excise duty and a 50 buck increase in the form of a drivers tax that will be placed on registrations when folks go to register their licence for their vehicle.
focus.explanation: Opens on a general characterisation of the Government, but the weight of the sentence is two named, quantified transport funding measures. A real policy point carried inside party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a stupid piece of legislation, which is becoming, actually, in the vein of this coalition Government—they like to do things that are stupid in nature.
focus.explanation: Gestures at the bill but names nothing about it — no clause, cost, mechanism or outcome. The substance of the sentence is a general characterisation of the coalition's habits. No individual is insulted, so Civility is untouched; this is the tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Dare I say it, we’ve just got a different method of actually delivering a solution for this, on this side of the House.
specificity.explanation: He is defending a repeal by pointing to an alternative approach and names nothing about it — no mechanism, no instrument, no timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we have a look at this particular disclosure statement, what it identifies there is that removing the RFT will result in modest savings for households and businesses in Auckland, and that that figure comes out to around $1.85 for each motorist that’s going to use it—$1.85.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document, the affected group and a precise dollar figure. Anyone could pull the disclosure statement and check the number.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This will result in cuts to critical transport projects that will make a huge difference.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax will force cancellation or reduction of transport projects that the tax was funding.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council and Auckland Transport programme decisions and the Regional Land Transport Plan following the repeal: true if projects on the RFT-funded list are cancelled, deferred or reduced in scope as a consequence of the lost revenue; false if the RFT-funded programme proceeds substantially unchanged.

specificity.statement: So let’s compare $200 million to the cost of the next additional Waitematā Harbour crossing, which is going to be somewhere between $20 billion and $50 billion.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific project and gives a costed comparison with figures ($200m vs $20–50bn); a listener could go and check both numbers. Marked down slightly because the harbour crossing figure is a wide range rather than a costing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are better ways of funding roads, and we as a coalition Government are looking at tolling and electronic road-use charging along with city and regional infrastructure deals and time-of-use charging.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete funding mechanisms rather than gesturing at 'better funding', but attaches no rates, revenue figures or timeframes, and 'looking at' leaves the how and the by-when open.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Let’s also look at some numbers here: $780 million has been raised to date, $341 million of that is still left in the kitty at the moment.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable figures for revenue raised and revenue unspent, offered as the basis for the argument that follows. Someone could look both up.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And by using it for a busway, they spent a mere $200 million—incredibly effective investment—and now, $200 million, they were able to build the Northern Busway, which now carries as many people as all the lanes of traffic on the Auckland Harbour Bridge.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts about the past/present: that the Northern Busway was built for about $200 million, and that it now moves as many people as all the general traffic lanes of the Auckland Harbour Bridge combined.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transit NZ/NZTA project cost records for the Northern Busway, and Auckland Transport / NZTA person-throughput counts for the Northern Busway versus the general traffic lanes of the Auckland Harbour Bridge. True if the capital cost is ~$200m and busway person-throughput is at least equal to the traffic lanes on the comparison basis used; false if the throughput figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: We know this because back in early 2000s, the National Party in Opposition opposed, with many other doubters, the Northern Busway.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the National Party, then in Opposition, opposed the Northern Busway project in the early 2000s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard and contemporaneous news reporting from roughly 2001–2005 on the Northern Busway. True if National MPs are on record opposing the project; false if no such record exists or National is recorded supporting it.

veracity.statement: As I say, this was a regressive tax and it ended up with an unspent $341 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $341 million of regional fuel tax revenue remained unspent at the time of the debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Transport regional fuel tax financial reporting as at early 2024, and Ministry of Transport figures on collected-but-unspent RFT revenue. True if the unspent balance is ~$341m; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This legislation should come as absolutely no surprise to anybody because our National Party colleagues and partners campaigned explicitly on it, and we have joined in a coalition agreement with them to deliver this, and that is exactly what we are doing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National campaigned explicitly on repealing the regional fuel tax and that repeal is a commitment in the coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 election transport policy documents and the National–NZ First and National–ACT coalition agreements. True if repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax appears as an explicit campaign policy and as a coalition commitment; false if it appears in neither.

veracity.statement: I’ve also noted that Mayor Brown has said that removing the scheme would cost something like $1.2 billion in possible revenue.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown that repealing the regional fuel tax would forgo about $1.2 billion in revenue. The checkable content is both that Brown said it and that $1.2bn is the figure he used.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, submissions or media releases by Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown in late 2023 / early 2024 on the revenue impact of repealing the regional fuel tax. True if he cited a figure of about $1.2 billion; false if he cited a materially different figure or made no such claim.

civility.statement: OK, I know numbers aren’t their strong suit, but let’s picture this.
civility.explanation: Sneering condescension toward the members opposite — implies they cannot do arithmetic, then walks them through it. No direct insult, but it is mockery of the people rather than the policy, which is a genuine civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, unfortunately, we have a Government that is mostly innumerate, incapable of accurately forecasting the costs of the projects they campaigned on, extremely, extremely irresponsible in Opposition, and just opposed things for the sake of it, like the regional fuel tax.
focus.explanation: There is a policy hook — cost forecasting of campaigned projects and the regional fuel tax — but the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of the other side ('innumerate', 'irresponsible in Opposition', 'opposed things for the sake of it') rather than engagement with the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the more people who use bikes for short urban trips, the better off the people who are driving the cars, the better the quality of the roads, the less the congestion, the lower the transport costs.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises actually offered in the preceding sentences — bikes take less road and parking space and do not cause potholes, so shifting short trips to bikes leaves drivers better off. The final clause ('lower the transport costs') outruns what was shown, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There was no accounting for time shifting or trying to make your workday fit around the use of the road, so it wasn’t improving congestion, which is one of the bigger problems that the Auckland City motorists face.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the instrument: a flat fuel tax carries no time-varying price signal, therefore it cannot shift trips out of the peak and cannot reduce congestion. The conclusion follows from the premise; it slightly overstates by treating congestion relief as the tax's purpose.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So even if you didn’t raise a cent from now until the 10 years of this scheme coming to its conclusion, in the last six years $73 million a year has been spent. But in the next four years, you would have to spend at $85 million a year to spend all that money—in other words, $12 million more than the Auckland authorities have managed to spend in the last six years.
rigor.explanation: An arithmetic argument that does the work it claims: dividing the spent and unspent balances over the elapsed and remaining years supports the conclusion that the remaining fund would need a higher annual spend rate than has been achieved. The gap is that a modest increase in spend rate is not shown to be infeasible.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, I’m sure that our friends in the Opposition would say that the tax should be kept going, but the reality is: if you look at what’s in here, and the purposes for which the tax was intended, you could just about put anything into it—just about put anything into it—and it makes it, effectively, almost just an extra slush fund, if you like—it’s a bit of a pejorative word, but a “slush fund”—for the Auckland authorities.
rigor.explanation: The inference runs from breadth of the statutory purposes to the conclusion that the fund is 'effectively a slush fund'. Breadth of permitted use does not establish misuse — no instance of improper spending is offered — so the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: What we also know, on that side of the House and on this side of the House, is that road-user charges are coming and that is going to be the way of the future in terms of charging, rather than petrol taxes.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that road user charges will replace fuel excise as the primary means of charging for road use in New Zealand.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand transport revenue legislation and Ministry of Transport revenue statistics. True if legislation extending road user charges to light petrol vehicles is enacted and RUC becomes the principal road-charging mechanism in place of fuel excise; false if fuel excise duty remains the primary charging mechanism with no enacted transition.

focus.statement: The message that this Government sends to our mokopuna and to our tamariki is that their future in this country does not matter, and that a short-term profit or the short-term pacification of a small demographic will be prioritised over mokopuna.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy consequence at issue (what the repeal does to future generations), but the weight of the sentence is an imputation of motive to 'this Government' rather than engagement with the measure. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whether the other side of the House actually knows that and can comprehend what this actually means, in either language—I’m happy to share, when I’ve got patience for it.
focus.explanation: Once the characterisation of the other side is removed there is no policy content at all — it is entirely about what the other team can and cannot understand.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These projects moved towards transitioning Tāmaki—that’s Auckland—from an unsustainable reliance on fossil fuels and instead towards sustainable transport options, which in turn decongest roads, support the longevity of our already existing transport infrastructure, and relieve the pressure we as consumers place on our environment.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance: what the funded projects were for and what effects they were expected to have. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Introducing legislation to remove this regional fuel tax was part of our 100-day action plan, and, unlike Governments previous, this is actually a Government of delivery.
focus.explanation: Half of the sentence names a real commitment and the measure delivering it; the other half is a general contrast with previous Governments carrying no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Government speaker after Government speaker has stood up from Wellington and from the regions and told Aucklanders on this side of the House that we should be grateful for cuts to our public transport and our roading budget; that Aucklanders should be so grateful that Wellington is telling them that they are having cuts to the long-term kind of investment that we need to be the city of the future that we can be.
focus.explanation: There is a policy subject underneath — cuts to Auckland's transport and roading investment — but it is delivered as a characterisation of how Government speakers have behaved rather than engagement with what the bill does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He was the closest they could get to standing a speaker near to Auckland.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's choice of speaker. Strip that out and no policy, figure or outcome remains.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has failed to carefully plan and to consider the applications of the promises that they have set to the public.
specificity.explanation: A substantive charge with no checkable content: no promise is named, no planning failure identified, no figure or timeframe given. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Safety upgrades, including the installation of speed bumps, red-light cameras, and lower speed limits in Tāmaki—that’s Auckland—all funded by the regional fuel tax, were done in an effort, in fact, surely, done as response to the 50 lives that Auckland roads take each year.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific interventions, the funding source and a fatality figure. Falls short of 1.0 because no spend, timeframe or programme name is attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Not only that, but a few years down the track, they’re going to whack the fuel tax back up again by another 22c a litre, and, on top of this, something that just simply cannot be justified by reference to the cost of living, the other side is increasing vehicle registration fees, so another $50 a year—whack!—out of people’s back pockets.
specificity.explanation: Two figures, both named measures, with a rough timeframe. Short of 1.0 because 'a few years down the track' is not dated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill legislates that the remaining unspent revenue from the Auckland regional fuel tax is ring-fenced to fund the Eastern Busway, electric trains, stabilising for the City Rail Link, and road-corridor improvements.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (ring-fencing of unspent revenue) and four specific projects the money goes to. No dollar amounts or dates, which is what holds it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Whether the other side of the House actually knows that and can comprehend what this actually means, in either language—I’m happy to share, when I’ve got patience for it.
civility.explanation: Condescension directed at other members' capacity to comprehend, with an added suggestion they exhaust her patience. Short of a direct insult and aimed at a group rather than a named person, but it has left the substance behind.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So whatever the other side thinks might be saved by repealing the regional fuel tax, whatever they think it might save households, well, they’re giving it with one hand but taking it away with the other, and taking away not just the short-term monetary savings but the savings that would have been made by having better transport infrastructure in our biggest city.
civility.explanation: A hard, adversarial attack on the policy in a contested first reading, with no attribution of bad character to any member. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He was the closest they could get to standing a speaker near to Auckland.
civility.explanation: Mockery of a named member, belittling him as a geographic stand-in rather than a contributor. Not an attack on his character or competence, so short of a direct insult, but it is no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Safety upgrades, including the installation of speed bumps, red-light cameras, and lower speed limits in Tāmaki—that’s Auckland—all funded by the regional fuel tax, were done in an effort, in fact, surely, done as response to the 50 lives that Auckland roads take each year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 50 people die on Auckland roads annually, and that speed bumps, red-light cameras and lower speed limits were funded from the regional fuel tax.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA/Ministry of Transport annual road-death statistics for the Auckland region (Crash Analysis System) for the years preceding March 2024: true if annual deaths are approximately 50, false if materially different (e.g. under 30 or over 80). Secondary check: Auckland Transport's Regional Fuel Tax programme schedule, for whether road-safety works of the kinds named were RFT-funded.

veracity.statement: This Government has labelled these safety projects as wasteful spending.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ministers of the coalition Government have publicly characterised Auckland's road-safety works (speed bumps, red-light cameras, lower speed limits) as wasteful spending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, press releases or Hansard contributions by coalition Ministers before 5 March 2024 describing speed bumps, raised crossings, red-light cameras or speed-limit reductions as wasteful or a waste of money: true if such statements exist, false if no Minister so characterised them.

veracity.statement: But it’s going to save—at the most, it will save a household $2.70 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an upper bound of $2.70 per week as the household saving from repealing the 11.5c/litre Auckland regional fuel tax.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / Treasury regulatory impact statement or departmental advice on the bill, giving the estimated per-household weekly saving: true if the stated maximum is approximately $2.70 a week, false if the official estimate is materially higher or lower.

rigor.statement: Speaking to the oranga of our people, how can the Government claim that this bill will aid our people during living cost crisis when the funding for infrastructure that is currently sourced from the regional fuel tax will only be sourced elsewhere? It is now the responsibility of ratepayers and all of those who pay road-user charges to cover the revenue lost to this bill.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure: if the infrastructure still has to be paid for, a saving at the pump is offset by rates and road-user charges, so the cost-of-living justification is weakened. The gap is that the premise — that the same revenue will simply be raised elsewhere from the same people — is asserted rather than shown, and the incidence may differ.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At the last election, we campaigned on reducing the cost of living for Aucklanders, and one of the ways to do it was to remove this regional fuel tax. Guess what! They listened to us, they voted for us, and a number of the people on the other side of the House lost their seats.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to popularity standing in for an argument: that voters elected the party is offered as the reason the repeal is right. Election results establish a mandate but say nothing about whether removing the tax reduces the cost of living, which was the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, the problem with removing it is not just that it removes the funding that Auckland Transport could have used but it removes the capacity to borrow more money, because it changes the council’s debt ceilings.
rigor.explanation: A mechanism-based argument: a revenue stream supports a borrowing headroom, so removing it costs more than the revenue itself. The conclusion follows from the stated premise; the link to debt ceilings is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the only gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: See, what the other side fails to do is to recognise that every cyclist on the road is one less car on the road. That is a person who has chosen transport which imposes less costs on other people.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy, but it rests on an unstated assumption — that each cyclist would otherwise have driven that trip — which does not hold for riders who would have walked, taken public transport or not travelled. The conclusion overshoots the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Not only that, but a few years down the track, they’re going to whack the fuel tax back up again by another 22c a litre, and, on top of this, something that just simply cannot be justified by reference to the cost of living, the other side is increasing vehicle registration fees, so another $50 a year—whack!—out of people’s back pockets.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government will raise fuel excise by a further 22 cents a litre within a few years, and increase annual vehicle registration fees by $50.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Legislated/gazetted fuel excise duty rates and the Government Policy Statement on land transport: true if cumulative fuel excise increases announced or implemented by the end of 2029 total approximately 22c per litre, false if materially less (e.g. the 12c signalled in GPS 2024) or if no increase occurs. Registration fee element checked against NZTA motor vehicle licensing fee schedules.

veracity.statement: And for what? For $1.80 a week in savings for most Auckland households.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the repeal of the Auckland regional fuel tax will save a typical Auckland household about $1.80 per week, and attributes that figure to the departmental disclosure statement prepared for the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental disclosure statement / Ministry of Transport regulatory advice for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill (March 2024); true if it estimates an average Auckland household saving of about $1.80 per week, false if the stated saving is materially different or if no such estimate appears there.

veracity.statement: Well, the reality is that it has helped pay for $500,000 speed bumps—slowing people down.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that regional fuel tax revenue paid for individual speed bumps costing $500,000 each.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport's published regional fuel tax expenditure and project cost records; true if a speed bump (or comparable single traffic-calming device) funded from the regional fuel tax cost about $500,000, false if the $500,000 figure covers a wider project scope — a full raised crossing, intersection or corridor safety upgrade including drainage, lighting and kerbing — rather than a speed bump.

veracity.statement: So, for six years, Aucklanders have been taxed over $340 million—that is, over two years’ worth of the revenues collected from Aucklanders has not even been spent; it’s sitting in a bank account, collecting interest.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than $340 million of regional fuel tax revenue collected since 2018 remains unspent, equivalent to more than two years of collections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Transport regional fuel tax financial reporting as at early 2024 (annual RFT reports and the Council's disclosed unspent balance); true if the unspent balance exceeded $340 million and exceeded two years of average annual RFT collections, false if materially lower or if the balance was committed to contracted projects rather than unspent.

rigor.statement: You’d see the regional fuel tax saving Aucklanders perhaps $600 million in revenue that would otherwise go to these specific transport projects, but the $50 increase would then net the Government another $660 million—almost conveniently, the same amount of money—that will then be going into a general pot for general transport projects.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: money is being taken back through registration fees rather than returned. But the two figures are not like-for-like — the $600m is an Auckland-only foregone revenue and the $660m is a nationwide take from a registration increase — so the 'same amount of money' equivalence that carries the conclusion is a false parallel. The point partly stands; the arithmetic argument for it does not.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And the number one issue that came up time and time again—and I suspect she might be the Labour candidate for Northcote at the next election—was the cost of living, and I’m really happy to support this because this bill addresses the cost of living of those in Northcote, it addresses the cost of living of those in Pakuranga, those in Takanini, those in Mount Roskill, those in Upper Harbour, and I really support this bill.
rigor.explanation: Argues from door-knocking anecdote to policy conclusion: cost of living was the top doorstep issue, therefore this bill addresses it. Appeal to anecdote, plus a gap in the middle — nothing is offered to connect repealing the fuel tax to any material change in a household's cost of living, and listing further electorates repeats the assertion rather than supporting it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It means slowing everyone down, and the last Government’s plans, of course, were to make us crawl around in our cars with people walking in front with red flags to tell us how fast we could go.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: speed management plans are recast as a Red Flag Act requiring a person to walk ahead of every car. The characterisation is not derived from anything in the plans, and the conclusion about what they 'mean' rests entirely on the caricature. This engages a real policy and reasons badly about it, so it is scored here rather than under Focus.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So when the members on this side of the House say that Aucklanders voted for this, it’s true: Aucklanders voted in overwhelming numbers to repeal the Auckland regional fuel tax.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity/mandate, and near-circular: the claim that Aucklanders voted for the repeal is offered as proof of itself, with no vote share, polling or electorate result put forward. A general election result is also not evidence of a verdict on one specific tax.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: You’d see the regional fuel tax saving Aucklanders perhaps $600 million in revenue that would otherwise go to these specific transport projects, but the $50 increase would then net the Government another $660 million—almost conveniently, the same amount of money—that will then be going into a general pot for general transport projects.
specificity.explanation: Two named revenue figures, the named instrument ($50 registration increase), and a stated destination for the money (a general pot rather than ring-fenced projects). Checkable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This cannot be treated as something of a political football. We need to grow up and resource our biggest city to be a city that is somewhere where everyone wants to live.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance (what Auckland needs) but supplies no figure, mechanism, project or timeframe — 'long-term investment' and 'resource our biggest city' commit to nothing checkable, and the surrounding sentences add no detail here.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, for six years, Aucklanders have been taxed over $340 million—that is, over two years’ worth of the revenues collected from Aucklanders has not even been spent; it’s sitting in a bank account, collecting interest.
specificity.explanation: A named figure, a stated period, and a stated comparison to annual revenue — precise enough that someone could go to the Council's accounts and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Here’s where we get back to my point about Wellington telling Auckland that we should be grateful for this, because those are projects which have been ring-fenced not by Aucklanders, but they have been saved because of the choices of this Government.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — who decides which projects the residual fund is ring-fenced for — but carried inside a centre-versus-Auckland framing about being told to be grateful. On the measure, with framing taking some of the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The big red zero is coming out—the big red zero which featured with the last Government; a big fat zero.
focus.explanation: Entirely party-directed: a prop and a slogan about the previous Government delivering nothing. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named at this point. (Nothing scored for Rigor — strip out the part about the other side and no argument remains.)
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It will require the remaining funding to go towards our priority project, which is the City Rail Link, trains and stabling for the City Rail Link—and, by the way, the last Government talked big about public transport, but we started the City Rail Link and we will complete it—the Eastern Busway, which will ensure more transport choices for those in East Auckland, including the Reeves Road flyover; and there are some local roading improvement projects, which are important to Auckland.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: what the bill does with the residual fund, and the specific projects it is directed to (City Rail Link and stabling, Eastern Busway, Reeves Road flyover). The jab at the last Government is a passing aside within an otherwise substantive account.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: During the election campaign, I door-knocked 80 percent of the streets in my community of Northcote—I actually door-knocked Camilla Belich’s home.
civility.explanation: Names an individual opponent and needles her, but attacks nothing about her character, competence or worth — pointed and personal in direction without landing on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It means slowing everyone down, and the last Government’s plans, of course, were to make us crawl around in our cars with people walking in front with red flags to tell us how fast we could go.
civility.explanation: Mockery, but aimed at a policy and the previous Government's programme rather than at any individual. Under the re-anchored scale, ridiculing a policy is not an incivility.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: And the number one issue that came up time and time again—and I suspect she might be the Labour candidate for Northcote at the next election—was the cost of living, and I’m really happy to support this because this bill addresses the cost of living of those in Northcote, it addresses the cost of living of those in Pakuranga, those in Takanini, those in Mount Roskill, those in Upper Harbour, and I really support this bill.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Camilla Belich will be the Labour candidate for the Northcote electorate at the next general election. Not a promise about his own action; a prediction about another party's selection.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Labour Party's confirmed electorate candidate for Northcote at the next general election, per the Electoral Commission candidate nominations and Labour's own announcements; true if Camilla Belich is selected as Labour's Northcote candidate, false if any other person is.

veracity.statement: But the New Zealand Herald had to retract that number. Radio New Zealand, who had repeated it, had to retract that number.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two named news organisations formally retracted the $500,000 speed bump figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Corrections/retraction notices published by the New Zealand Herald and RNZ on their 2023-24 reporting of a $500,000 Auckland speed bump or raised crossing; true if both published a retraction or correction of that figure, false if the figure was never retracted by either.

veracity.statement: So the estimated cost of crossings is between $19,000 and $31,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a unit cost range for raised crossings/speed bumps of the kind installed on Meola Road.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport's published or OIA-released unit cost estimates for raised pedestrian crossings and speed tables in 2023-24; true if the typical estimate falls in the $19,000-$31,000 band, false if the published estimates are materially higher.

veracity.statement: There has been no select committee process here, yet again—yet again, no select committee process.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill before the House was not referred to a select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Land Transport Management (Repeal of Regional Fuel Tax) Amendment Bill; true if the bill passed without referral to a select committee, false if it was referred and took submissions.

veracity.statement: Now, I know that people in Devonport, quite overwhelmingly, voted for that Government; I’m beginning to wonder if they regret their choices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Devonport voters supported the governing parties by an overwhelming margin at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission 2023 general election booth-level results for Devonport (North Shore electorate); true if National/ACT/NZ First party votes there substantially exceeded the opposition parties', false if the margin was narrow or reversed.

veracity.statement: He has had to call for a stop on all sorts of transport projects because the regional fuel tax is no longer in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Auckland Mayor halted transport projects, and that the cause was the removal of the regional fuel tax.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Transport decisions and Wayne Brown's public statements from December 2023 to March 2024; true if projects were paused or cancelled and the loss of regional fuel tax revenue was given as the reason, false if no such pauses were announced or they were attributed to other causes.

specificity.statement: So the estimated cost of crossings is between $19,000 and $31,000.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable cost range attached to a named class of works; someone could go and verify it against Auckland Transport's figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve already traversed a little bit of the information that was there about the actual impact on people’s back pockets, which we know is going to be about $2.70 a week per household—big deal!
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure sourced to the bill's disclosure statement — $2.70 a week per household — which someone could check. Short of full marks because the household basis and time period are left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, they’re going to whack up the cost of registration by $50.
specificity.explanation: A named charge and an exact amount; checkable and actionable, though no date or phasing is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I’m going to ask the Minister to treat this with a bit of integrity, to treat this with a bit of being straightforward, and to treat this going with what the real numbers are.
civility.explanation: Framed as a request, but the implication is that the Minister personally lacks integrity and is not being straightforward — an imputation of bad faith against an individual rather than criticism of the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Gone, and the March madness will persist.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that removing the regional fuel tax will leave Auckland's annual March congestion peak unrelieved.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / NZTA congestion data and reporting for March 2025 on the choke points named in the speech; true if severe March congestion recurs at those points, false if congestion at them measurably eased.

divination.statement: Well, they’re going to whack up the cost of registration by $50.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government will increase the annual motor vehicle licensing fee by $50.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZTA's published motor vehicle licensing fee schedule; true if the annual licensing fee rises by a cumulative $50 relative to its early-2024 level, false if it rises by materially less or not at all.

rigor.statement: So taking out the regional fuel tax has left people in Devonport stuck with their deeply congested road.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with a stated premise — the Lake Road improvements were funded by the tax and have been stopped — so the conclusion largely tracks the evidence offered. Marked down because 'left stuck' assumes the improvements would have fixed the congestion, which was not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But one of the things about the way those prices fluctuate means it is going to be very hard to be sure that that 10c a litre is actually going to be passed on to consumers.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premise she supplied immediately before — that pump prices already vary by more than 10c across Auckland on a single day, so a 10c change cannot be isolated by observing prices. No fallacy; the inference is proportionate to what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, I know that people in Devonport, quite overwhelmingly, voted for that Government; I’m beginning to wonder if they regret their choices.
focus.explanation: Shifts from the transport project to how a suburb voted and whether they regret it. There is a faint policy tether to the preceding argument, but the statement itself is about electoral allegiance rather than any measure, cost or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I haven’t heard a word yet from the other side of the House as to how they are going to ensure that the actual benefit of that cut is going to be passed on to the consumers, instead of just quietly absorbed by the fuel companies.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the measure before the House — whether the 10c cut reaches consumers or is captured by fuel retailers. Phrased as 'the other side of the House' but the content is a specific policy gap, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As I said in my first contribution on this bill, I think that it’s really a shame that the current coalition Government took such an antagonistic approach to being in Opposition and developed such knee-jerk policies and didn’t really do the work to figure out how they would raise enough revenue to pay for the projects they’re promising.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — the repeal leaves no identified replacement revenue for committed projects — but it is carried inside a characterisation of the coalition parties as antagonistic and knee-jerk. Real substance wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And, now, New Zealand has actually just surpassed the US for highest car-ownership rate in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's per-capita car ownership has overtaken the United States and is now the highest in the world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vehicles (or light passenger vehicles) per 1,000 population for New Zealand and the United States as at 2023–24, from the Ministry of Transport fleet statistics alongside a comparable international series (OECD/ITF or US FHWA). True if the NZ rate exceeds the US rate and no other country is higher; false if the US or another country ranks above New Zealand on the same measure.

veracity.statement: So all of our dairy exports do not cover the cost of the private vehicles that we import and the fuel that we need to use to run them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's dairy export earnings are smaller than the combined import bill for private vehicles and the fuel to run them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade for a full year: total dairy export earnings compared with the combined import value of motor vehicles plus petroleum and petroleum products. True if the combined import value exceeds dairy export earnings; false if dairy export earnings are the larger figure.

veracity.statement: The average private vehicle is sitting parked 96 percent of the day, taking up valuable urban land in our cities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific utilisation figure for the average private car — in motion about 4% of the day, parked the rest.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport New Zealand Household Travel Survey average daily driving time per light passenger vehicle. True if the average vehicle is in use for about one hour a day or less (i.e. parked ~96% of a 24-hour day); false if average daily use is materially above roughly 1.5 hours.

veracity.statement: Now, there’s three toll roads in New Zealand, two of which are paid for in Tauranga, and we are enjoying these very much.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of New Zealand's tolled roads and the share of them located in Tauranga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi's register of tolled roads as at March 2024. True if exactly three roads were tolled nationally and two of them serve Tauranga; false if the national count or the Tauranga count differs.

civility.statement: I think that must be projection, and on the part of the Minister, he actually does hate people who walk and ride bikes, because why else would he have such a policy that is trying to stop every safe, evidence-based pedestrian crossing in front of every school that might have been proposed?
civility.explanation: Moves off the policy and onto the named Minister's inner motives — asserting he 'hates' a class of people. A direct attack on the person's character rather than on his transport decisions, and one the Chair was asked to rule on as an imputation of improper motive.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But the point is that they benefit more from the busway or from the pedestrian connection than they do from a few kilometres of extra lane of motorway, because that is very quickly filled up with more cars when people have no choice but to drive.
rigor.explanation: A real inference with a stated mechanism: the induced-demand premise (added lanes refill with traffic where driving is the only option) does support the conclusion that drivers gain more from the alternative mode. The mechanism is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A regressive thing such as a regional fuel tax sets a precedent for the rest of the country that we do not want.
rigor.explanation: Two claims stacked without support: regressivity is labelled rather than shown, and the step from one region's tax to a nationwide spread is a bare slippery slope — no mechanism is offered for why an Auckland tax would propagate to the Bay of Plenty.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In order to give people effective choices, we need to significantly invest much, much more in public transport, walking, and cycling.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel with no amount, no funding source, no timeframe and no named project. 'Significantly ... much, much more' quantifies nothing; nobody could check or act on it. (Squarely on-policy — that is Focus's question, not this one.)
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: But what people are going to notice is that projects they were expecting to be built—like the Lake Road upgrade in Devonport and a whole lot of other ones—are no longer going to happen.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that projects Aucklanders were expecting from regional fuel tax revenue, the Lake Road upgrade specifically, will not be delivered once the tax is repealed.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / NZTA project records for the Lake Road (Devonport–Takapuna) upgrade. False if the upgrade as scoped proceeds to construction under an alternative funding source; true if it is cancelled, indefinitely deferred, or cut back to a materially smaller scheme following the regional fuel tax repeal.

divination.statement: Cutting the regional fuel tax at this time means either a rates rise or a cut in projects.
divination.explanation: Relays the Auckland mayor's forecast that repealing the regional fuel tax forces Auckland Council into one of two outcomes — higher rates or fewer transport projects.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's adopted 2024–34 Long-term Plan and transport programme. True if, relative to the pre-repeal plan, the council adopts a higher rates increase or removes/defers transport projects previously funded by the regional fuel tax; false if the programme and rates path are both maintained without either.

civility.statement: I would agree with her, because I would say that the more things that we can get long-term consensus on in the community and across the political divide, the better, especially on things like transport, which, often, you’re putting in transport infrastructure and it will be there for 100, 200, 300 years, and will have an effect across that long period of time.
civility.explanation: A contested repeal debate in which he is rebutting the Opposition, so there was a real opportunity to be dismissive; instead he engages an opponent's point on its merits and concedes it. Attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: However, my recollection was that Jacinda Ardern, as Prime Minister, actually ruled out any more regional fuel taxes, and she did, indeed, do that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Ardern, while Prime Minister, publicly ruled out any further regional fuel taxes. The claim is about a past public statement, not about whether the policy was wise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of Jacinda Ardern's statements while Prime Minister (Hansard, post-Cabinet press conferences, contemporaneous news reports). True if she publicly ruled out any further regional fuel taxes beyond Auckland's during her premiership; false if no such ruling-out exists or if she left the option open.

veracity.statement: But we’re talking here about $130 million - odd a year. The National Land Transport Fund from fuel taxes, etc., $4.5 billion a year. Auckland would usually get roughly a third of that—$1.5 billion a year. So we’re talking about 8 percent or so of the money which would be, effectively, going to Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three quantities: Auckland regional fuel tax revenue of roughly $130m a year, National Land Transport Fund revenue of roughly $4.5b a year, and an Auckland share of roughly one third of that.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA National Land Transport Fund annual revenue and National Land Transport Programme regional allocations for 2023/24, plus Auckland Council/Auckland Transport reporting of regional fuel tax receipts. True if RFT revenue is about $130m a year, NLTF revenue about $4.5b a year, and Auckland's NLTP share about a third; false if any of the three is materially different (e.g. RFT revenue well above $150m, or Auckland's share far from a third).

veracity.statement: We also haven’t heard the recognition that—in fact, I think it was both under a National- and a Labour-led Government that 4c a litre regularly went on the petrol tax.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that regular petrol excise increases of about 4c a litre occurred under governments of both stripes, not just under Labour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA/Treasury record of petrol excise duty rate changes since 2008. True if scheduled increases of about 4c per litre were applied repeatedly under both National-led (2008-2017) and Labour-led (2017-2023) governments; false if the increases were materially smaller than 4c, or occurred under only one of the two.

specificity.statement: But we’re talking here about $130 million - odd a year. The National Land Transport Fund from fuel taxes, etc., $4.5 billion a year. Auckland would usually get roughly a third of that—$1.5 billion a year. So we’re talking about 8 percent or so of the money which would be, effectively, going to Auckland.
specificity.explanation: Three named figures and a derived proportion, all attached to identified funding streams. Anyone could go to the NLTF accounts and check the arithmetic and the share.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, in fact, if you said 4c a litre over six years, you’d be 24c a litre anyway, so there’s probably not a lot between the two sides there.
rigor.explanation: The arithmetic is fine, but the conclusion outruns it: a hypothetical six-year accumulation of past-rate increases is compared with the current proposal without establishing that the two schedules match. False equivalence built on an unstated assumption that both sides would have raised the tax at the same rate for the same period.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They won’t be cancelled; Auckland can still put them up into the National Land Transport Programme, and if they are good projects, they will get through that process.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real funding mechanism, but with a gap between premise and conclusion: eligibility to bid into the NLTP does not establish that funding will follow, since the fund is contested and finite. The 'if they are good projects' step assumes the outcome it needs.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Auckland’s issue is not just about the transport system; it’s about its form. It’s such a big city that to get around it, for many people, the car is the only option.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of who the fuel tax falls on and why — urban form, car dependence, the regressive-impact argument raised against the repeal. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let’s start, firstly, by saying that this is not about the cost of living. We’ve already heard from this Government about their anti-beneficiary, anti - wage earner policies, where they want to sanction beneficiaries and cut the yearly increase for minimum wage.
rigor.explanation: Concludes that this bill is not a cost-of-living measure from unrelated welfare and wage policies. Non sequitur: other policies of the same government do not settle what this measure does to household costs.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: By disincentivising electric vehicles while at the same time cutting public transport, this Government is fuelling climate change.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about two identified policy changes, but the step from them to "fuelling climate change" is asserted rather than shown — no magnitude, no emissions pathway connecting the premises to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Here’s the thing: this Government wants to cancel projects. However, these projects are already under way. They’ve still got to go ahead. We’ve still got to find the money for them. They can’t just stop.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — the money must still be found — rests on the premise that projects under way cannot be stopped, which is simply restated rather than argued. Begs the question; no contract, cost or legal obligation is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What is worse is that by cutting revenue streams—that would have enabled greater investment in public transport—and locking in polluting infrastructure, carbon-intensive infrastructure, and locking people into cars, what we are also doing is leaving our communities more prone to severe weather events, like the ones that Auckland experienced last year, effectively putting more of our communities at risk of climate change.
rigor.explanation: A long causal chain — repeal a regional fuel tax, therefore car dependence, therefore emissions, therefore more severe weather in Auckland — with nothing offered at any link. The conclusion far outruns the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the other important aspects of this bill is the removal of the opportunity for other regional fuel taxes. The people of Northland certainly do not want one.
rigor.explanation: The measure is supported solely by an asserted constituent preference, with no polling, consultation or reasoning offered — a bare appeal to popularity standing in for an argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I want to start by talking about some of the things that my colleagues have talked about today, about the fear they have of the war that’s being waged in this situation: I would have thought that the issue of transport and proper funding of transport was almost apolitical because it affects our entire community.
rigor.explanation: Infers that transport funding should be apolitical from the fact that it affects everyone. Non sequitur — universal impact is a reason a question matters politically, not a reason it stops being contested.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Let’s start, firstly, by saying that this is not about the cost of living. We’ve already heard from this Government about their anti-beneficiary, anti - wage earner policies, where they want to sanction beneficiaries and cut the yearly increase for minimum wage.
focus.explanation: Names real policies (benefit sanctions, the minimum wage increase) but the weight of the passage is a characterisation of the Government's general posture rather than the bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By disincentivising electric vehicles while at the same time cutting public transport, this Government is fuelling climate change.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the policy content — EV charges and public transport funding — and their consequence, not about the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is worse is that by cutting revenue streams—that would have enabled greater investment in public transport—and locking in polluting infrastructure, carbon-intensive infrastructure, and locking people into cars, what we are also doing is leaving our communities more prone to severe weather events, like the ones that Auckland experienced last year, effectively putting more of our communities at risk of climate change.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure's consequences for transport funding and infrastructure rather than the other party's record or character.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our policy is for free public transport that is accessible and efficient. This could be implemented immediately with tamariki, students, and community services card holders, and be made free for everyone within five years.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (free fares), the groups it starts with, and a five-year horizon for universality. Missing the cost and how it would be funded.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government campaigned to build 15 new roads and has pledged $500 million to fix potholes.
specificity.explanation: Two checkable figures attached to named commitments — anyone could look both up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On top of road-user charges, they are putting up regos by $50. That money will go towards funding 50,000 roadside drug-tests, which they will be making back by increasing fines.
