rigor.statement: And to suggest that those people have less interest or should have less rights than other residents is clearly the wrong approach.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the bill ties the franchise to residency, which is not a claim that non-resident owners have "less interest" or fewer rights generally. The conclusion is drawn against a position the other side did not advance.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if we go to the most recent by-election, as the member said, that was 45 votes. That was 0.5 percent. It wasn’t even 1 percent of the votes, so it could make a huge difference.
rigor.explanation: The margin figure supports the claim that a small bloc could be decisive, but the step to "could make a huge difference" needs the number of ratepayer-roll voters in that contest, which is never supplied. A real inference with a missing link.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Excuse me, but we expect, generally, that the rents would cover the costs of the house, including the rates. So I say the citizenship, the residency is what matters.
rigor.explanation: The premise (rates are passed through in rent) is offered as settling the franchise question, but who bears a cost economically does not by itself establish who should hold the vote. A real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m sure the member opposite wouldn’t want to see a situation where a New Zealand citizen, who also has voting rights in another country, forfeits their voting rights in New Zealand, because that is the level of analysis being done on the other side tonight.
rigor.explanation: False analogy: holding a vote in a foreign country is not the case at issue, which is holding votes in two local authorities within the same national system. The reductio does not follow from the position it is aimed at.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Sometimes, when your property has been left in a state of disrepair and you must go through the process of renovations, because of a leaky-home crisis or some such, you’re still paying rates. So it’s not always on the renter.
rigor.explanation: A valid counterexample to the claim that renters bear rates, and the conclusion drawn is appropriately narrow ("not always"). The speaker also concedes its limited weight rather than overclaiming from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member opposite discussed turnout in local elections and how it was so low, and his answer for low turnout was to reduce the number of eligible voters, which doesn’t make any sense at all.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the member's argument ("doesn't make any sense at all") but lands entirely on the reasoning, not on the person. Robust criticism of a position is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Don’t let those margins be caught up by a narrow pressure group that cares more about the value of their property and low rates than for libraries, community services, swimming pools, roads, cycle lanes.
civility.explanation: Imputes motive — that the people on the other side of this argument care about their own property values over community services — rather than engaging their stated case. Aimed at a class rather than a named member, so short of a personal attack, but it is bad-faith attribution.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is much the same as New Zealanders who live in overseas jurisdictions, such as Australia or the UK, who are still eligible to vote in our general elections here in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealanders resident overseas remain eligible to vote in New Zealand general elections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Act 1993 and Electoral Commission rules on overseas voters: true if NZ citizens living abroad remain enrolled and eligible to vote in general elections (subject to the requirement to have visited New Zealand within the past three years); false if residence abroad by itself ends eligibility.

veracity.statement: The UK, the USA states that I’ve been able to look at, France, Switzerland, Denmark—there’s a fairly random set of countries we call democratic; none of them—none of them—have got a ratepayer roll.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that none of the named comparator democracies extends a local-government vote to non-resident property owners.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Municipal franchise law in the UK, France, Switzerland, Denmark and the US states referenced: true if none of them grants a local vote on the basis of property ownership rather than residence; false if any of them operates a property- or business-based local franchise.

veracity.statement: Now, Tauranga residents have had a long time of being rated without representation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Tauranga ratepayers have gone an extended period paying rates with no elected council.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tauranga City Council governance records: true if the council was run by Crown-appointed commissioners with no elected mayor or councillors from February 2021 while rates continued to be levied; false if elected representatives were in place over that period.

specificity.statement: We would be far better as a country to get more engagement in local and regional government processes or elections than trying to penalise those who demonstrate an active interest in their community.
specificity.explanation: States a direction — more engagement — with no mechanism, target, funding or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on, and the speaker had ample room to name how engagement would be lifted.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, if we go to the most recent by-election, as the member said, that was 45 votes. That was 0.5 percent. It wasn’t even 1 percent of the votes, so it could make a huge difference.
specificity.explanation: Carries a vote count and two percentage figures tied to a named contest — concrete enough that someone could go and check the margin.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, I think, another benefit on that train of thought is that people who have worked hard, started businesses, provided goods to the community, have used their skills and whatever natural endowments they have, talent wise, to produce wealth and have been able to invest it in more property—what we want to see is those people investing in areas perhaps outside of their immediate neighbourhood, spreading the wealth and the knowledge around the community.
specificity.explanation: A long claim about benefits with no figures, mechanisms or named effects — "spreading the wealth and the knowledge" carries nothing anyone could measure or check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want more democracy, not less.
specificity.explanation: A slogan offered as the conclusion of the turnout argument; it names no measure, figure or action.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I do not think that the level of analysis has been properly applied by the members opposite tonight.
focus.explanation: Once the characterisation of the members opposite is removed there is no policy content left — no mechanism, figure or named consequence of the bill. This is about the other side rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: And thank you to the Minister of Local Government for declaring that we will be having an election in July.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a Tauranga City Council election will be held in July, an event outside the speaker's own control.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission and Tauranga City Council records: true if polling for the Tauranga City Council election closed during July 2024; false if the election was held outside July 2024 or deferred again.

civility.statement: Be quiet; you might learn something.
civility.explanation: Directed at an interjecting member rather than at any argument: a condescending instruction implying the other member is ignorant. Short of a direct insult, but it turns on the person, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine failure rather than mere robustness.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why was that abolished? Because that was multiple votes for one electorate, and that electorate was this electorate: Parliament.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: he distinguishes the 1890s abolition of plural voting (several votes in one electorate) from voting once in each of several separate local jurisdictions, which is what undermines the bill's stated premise. The distinction is drawn cleanly and the conclusion tracks it; the gap is that he asserts rather than evidences what the 1890s reform targeted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And what you want to do, on that side of the House, is you want to give people who contribute, essentially, virtually nothing to the cost of running a city—you want to give them the vote, but you want to take it away from people who contribute an enormous amount to the running of a city.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The bill removes a second vote from non-resident ratepayers; it does not enfranchise anyone new, so the 'give them the vote' half of the contrast describes a measure that is not before the House. The conclusion also rests on an unstated premise that residents who are not property owners contribute 'virtually nothing' to a city's costs, which is asserted, not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He shouldn’t be working with himself if it’s one man, one vote, because you get the opportunity to vote in two spaces.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque. The inference is that because Luxon may personally benefit from a second local vote, his invocation of one-person-one-vote is self-defeating — but a person's own circumstances bear on their consistency, not on whether the principle is right. The conclusion ('he shouldn't be working with himself') is a rhetorical flourish that does not follow, and it also assumes without support that Luxon is enrolled as a non-resident ratepayer elector anywhere.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In Wellington City, close to 50 percent of the rates are paid by about 18 percent of the value of the city.
specificity.explanation: Two figures, a named city and a named revenue base — someone could go to Wellington City Council's rating data and check it. Marks down slightly because the second quantity ('18 percent of the value of the city') is loosely expressed, leaving it ambiguous whether he means capital value or rateable value.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In Wellington City, close to 50 percent of the rates are paid by about 18 percent of the value of the city.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that commercial ratepayers in Wellington City, holding roughly 18 percent of the city's rateable value, contribute close to half of total rates revenue — i.e. that the commercial differential produces a roughly 3:1 cross-subsidy of the residential sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington City Council's Long-term Plan / annual rating information for the 2023-24 rating year: the commercial-sector share of total general rates revenue and the commercial share of total rateable capital value. True if the shares are approximately 50 percent and 18 percent respectively; false if either departs materially (say by more than 10 percentage points).

veracity.statement: They didn’t get the right to vote until 1965 through the civil rights legislation.
veracity.explanation: In context 'they' is Black Americans: the assertion is that African Americans had no right to vote until the US civil rights legislation of 1965 (the Voting Rights Act).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text and dates of the Fifteenth Amendment (1870) and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. True if the franchise was first conferred in 1965; false if the right was conferred earlier and 1965 legislation instead enforced an existing right against disenfranchisement.

veracity.statement: If you own one house in one city, and you own another house in another city, you get two votes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under current New Zealand local electoral law a person owning property in two different territorial authority districts is entitled to cast a vote in each — one as a resident elector and one via the non-resident ratepayer roll.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Local Electoral Act 2001 provisions on the ratepayer electoral roll and the Electoral Commission / DIA guidance on non-resident ratepayer enrolment. True if a non-resident ratepayer may enrol and vote in a second district in addition to voting where they reside; false if no such second entitlement exists.

veracity.statement: Christopher Luxon said he would not work with Te Pāti Māori because he believed in one man, one vote.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Christopher Luxon publicly ruled out working with Te Pāti Māori and gave a commitment to 'one person, one vote' as his reason.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Luxon's public statements and interviews in the 2023 general election period (transcripts, news reports). True if he both ruled out working with Te Pāti Māori and cited one-person-one-vote or equivalent opposition to differentiated voting rights as the reason; false if he did not rule them out, or ruled them out on some other stated ground.

veracity.statement: They are paying for a holiday house; they are not paying for anything else.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that non-resident holiday-home owners contribute nothing to a district beyond the cost of the house itself — i.e. that they do not fund the district's wider services.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Rating records and the funding impact statement of a district with high holiday-home ownership (e.g. Ōpōtiki District Council): whether non-resident ratepayers pay general rates and district-wide targeted rates that fund roads, water, waste and community services. True if their rates fund only property-specific charges; false if they pay general rates funding district-wide services.

focus.statement: And you’re going to tell me that those people that own those holiday homes get a right to determine what happens with the people who were born and bred there, who live there, who contribute to the economy, who have lived there for many, many years, post- and pre-colonisation, that we’re going to allow people to determine what happens in our particular area.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: it names who the ratepayer franchise affects (non-resident holiday-home owners versus permanent residents) and in a named place, and argues about the consequence of the entitlement rather than about the other party. On-policy even though it is delivered as a rhetorical question.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The problem is that you do not believe in true democracy, you do not believe in universal—they do not, Madam Speaker.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of the other side's beliefs. No policy, figure, mechanism or outcome is named — strip out the claim about what the Government 'believes' and nothing about the bill remains. Nothing is emitted for Rigor: there is no argument here to assess, only the attribution of bad motives.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But it’s important to understand that the only reason Christopher Luxon said that is because he was under the pump on his position on co-governance, in terms of the Treaty.
civility.explanation: Imputes a bad-faith motive to a named individual — that his stated position was cover for political trouble rather than belief. Short of a direct insult, but it attacks the person's sincerity rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is actually an affront to the basic principle of one person, one vote—the very principle that they used to oppose the opportunity for tangata whenua to have a say in their customary rights. There is a word for that, I will not say it; people can draw their own conclusions.
civility.explanation: The refusal to say 'the word' while inviting the House to draw its own conclusions is an unstated imputation about members' motives — sneering insinuation aimed at people rather than argument, and unanswerable precisely because it is left unsaid.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Referring to the last speaker, Cameron Brewer, most of those people could still vote if their primary place of residence was still where they’re not currently living. If they’re currently displaced from their house and their primary place of residence remains their old home, they can still vote there. So that’s a nonsense argument.
civility.explanation: 'Nonsense argument' is blunt, but it lands on the argument and not on Brewer; the speaker names him only to identify what he is answering.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would’ve thought even Mr Foster would be able to count and work that out.
civility.explanation: A condescending jab at a named member's basic competence — 'even Mr Foster' — rather than at anything he argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’ve watched particularly the speakers on the other side stand up, and you always know, and as you’ll know yourself, Madam Speaker, when someone’s standing up, they actually don’t believe what they’re saying.
civility.explanation: Imputes insincerity to the members who spoke against the bill — a claim about their honesty rather than about anything they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But it’s important to understand that the only reason Christopher Luxon said that is because he was under the pump on his position on co-governance, in terms of the Treaty.
focus.explanation: A measure (the ratepayer roll) is at issue, but this sentence engages none of it — it is entirely about why an opponent leader supposedly said what he said.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They stood there tonight and justified that someone who owns a property in this district should get a vote and also get a vote by owning a property in that district. What about renters? What if someone owned a property in one district, but, for their work purposes, rented a property in another? They wouldn’t support that, so what’s the difference? The difference is property ownership, and that is the guts of this issue.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism of the bill — who qualifies for a vote and on what basis — rather than the other party's general character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They are sticking up for their mates. They are sticking up for people that own property.
focus.explanation: Characterises whose side the other parties are on rather than naming a policy, figure or outcome; the only policy trace is the generic reference to property owners.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are representing, Mr McAnulty, people like those that were victims of the Christchurch earthquakes, for example, that might have moved out to other suburbs beyond Christchurch and are in a fight with the Earthquake Commission (EQC) and insurance and the Christchurch City Council and they’ve been forced out of their homes. Why can’t they have a say? Why can’t they have a say on who governs and how their property taxes are spent?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: identifies a specific class of people the bill would disenfranchise and the specific interest (rates paid on a property they cannot occupy) at stake.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’ve watched particularly the speakers on the other side stand up, and you always know, and as you’ll know yourself, Madam Speaker, when someone’s standing up, they actually don’t believe what they’re saying.
focus.explanation: Contains no policy content at all; it is entirely about what the speaker believes the other side privately thinks.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As my colleague Greg O’Connor pointed out, the leader of the National Party expressed support on behalf of his party for the idea of removing the ratepayer roll.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, relaying Greg O'Connor's earlier point, that the National Party leader publicly backed abolishing the ratepayer roll for local elections.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements and interviews by Christopher Luxon, and National Party statements, on the non-resident ratepayer electoral roll prior to 20 March 2024; true if he expressed support for removing the ratepayer roll on behalf of National, false if no such statement exists or he stated the opposite.

veracity.statement: I really think that if the National Party and ACT and the New Zealand First Party let this go to select committee, they’d hear that most people in New Zealand don’t think that there should be a right that is accorded to an owner of property who doesn’t live in an area to vote.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a majority of New Zealanders oppose the non-resident ratepayer franchise — a claim about present public opinion, not about what a select committee would do.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A representative New Zealand public opinion poll on whether non-resident property owners should be able to vote in local elections; true if a majority oppose that right, false if a majority support it or are not opposed.

rigor.statement: They stood there tonight and justified that someone who owns a property in this district should get a vote and also get a vote by owning a property in that district. What about renters? What if someone owned a property in one district, but, for their work purposes, rented a property in another? They wouldn’t support that, so what’s the difference? The difference is property ownership, and that is the guts of this issue.
rigor.explanation: A consistency test: if a stake in two districts justifies two votes, a renter with the same dual connection should qualify too; the asymmetry is offered as evidence that ownership, not stake, is the operative criterion. The inference tracks the premises, though it assumes rather than shows that opponents would refuse the renter case.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I would put to them: what about teenage workers that pay tax? Are they going to advocate for them to have a vote on local councils? What about immigrants who pay, through a work visa, work hard for our economy, contribute to their community? They pay tax. Is the Government going to advocate for them to have a vote in this community? No, they’re not.
rigor.explanation: A reductio of the 'no taxation without representation' principle: if paying tax confers a vote, taxpaying teenagers and visa holders should get one too. Valid as far as it goes, but it slides between national tax and local rates, which weakens the parallel the conclusion rests on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are representing, Mr McAnulty, people like those that were victims of the Christchurch earthquakes, for example, that might have moved out to other suburbs beyond Christchurch and are in a fight with the Earthquake Commission (EQC) and insurance and the Christchurch City Council and they’ve been forced out of their homes. Why can’t they have a say? Why can’t they have a say on who governs and how their property taxes are spent?
rigor.explanation: A real inference — displaced owners still pay rates and remain in dispute with the council, therefore should retain a vote there. The conclusion follows from the premise, but the premise that they would otherwise be voteless is assumed rather than established.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Referring to the last speaker, Cameron Brewer, most of those people could still vote if their primary place of residence was still where they’re not currently living. If they’re currently displaced from their house and their primary place of residence remains their old home, they can still vote there. So that’s a nonsense argument.
rigor.explanation: Directly rebuts the premise of the opposing argument by pointing to how residence is defined for enrolment; if displacement does not change primary residence, the disenfranchisement case dissolves. The conclusion follows from the stated mechanism.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What is wrong with limiting the right of people to vote in a local election to the people who live there? What’s wrong with that? It’s a pretty simple proposition. It’s what happens overseas. In most jurisdictions, they seem to operate fairly enough.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to common practice: the arrangement is defended because other jurisdictions use it and 'seem to operate fairly enough', with no account of why residence-based franchise is the right criterion here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I did think that the Rotorua bill was wrong. I do think it is important that suffrage be on the basis of one person, one vote, and I did think that having wards that had different numbers of voters in them were wrong. I extend that same principle to here, where if you have a ward that, effectively, doesn’t have voting that is in proportion to the number of residents that live in an area, that, to me, is a distortion of the voting system as well.
rigor.explanation: States a principle, notes he applied it against his own side's earlier measure, and derives the present position from it. The conclusion follows from the premise and the premise is held consistently across cases.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I did think that the Rotorua bill was wrong. I do think it is important that suffrage be on the basis of one person, one vote, and I did think that having wards that had different numbers of voters in them were wrong. I extend that same principle to here, where if you have a ward that, effectively, doesn’t have voting that is in proportion to the number of residents that live in an area, that, to me, is a distortion of the voting system as well.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific prior measure and the concrete mechanism at issue (wards with unequal numbers of voters relative to residents), but supplies no figures or thresholds.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We escaped that when we left that terrible class system of Europe, the class system that meant you were what you were born. The whole system entrenched privilege. We don’t want to entrench privilege.
focus.explanation: Engages the principle actually at issue in the bill — whether a property-based vote entrenches privilege — rather than the record or character of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We escaped that when we left that terrible class system of Europe, the class system that meant you were what you were born. The whole system entrenched privilege. We don’t want to entrench privilege.
rigor.explanation: Weak analogy plus appeal to national self-image: the European hereditary class system is asserted to be the same kind of thing as the landowner vote in the bill, and the conclusion rests on that identification rather than on anything shown about the measure's effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Jock McKenzie—we’ve got the statue out the front of Richard John Seddon, but it could well have been the statue of Jock McKenzie, because he was responsible for the land reform that meant the estates were broken up.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the statue standing outside Parliament is of Richard John Seddon, and that John ('Jock') McKenzie was the minister responsible for the land reform that broke up the great estates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ historical record (Te Ara / NZ History / Parliament's own record of statuary): true if the statue in front of Parliament House is of Richard John Seddon AND John McKenzie, as Minister of Lands in the Liberal Government, drove the land-settlement legislation (Land for Settlements Act 1894 and amendments) under which the large estates were subdivided; false if the statue is of someone else, or if the estate break-up legislation is attributed to a different minister.

specificity.statement: Jock McKenzie—we’ve got the statue out the front of Richard John Seddon, but it could well have been the statue of Jock McKenzie, because he was responsible for the land reform that meant the estates were broken up.
specificity.explanation: Names a person, an identifiable programme of reform and a concrete outcome (estates broken up); no dates or figures, but enough for someone to check or look up.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But I do leave this: I know you’ve been told what to do by your whips. I also know that each one of you knows inherently that this is a right bill; this is the right thing to do.
civility.explanation: Imputes to members opposite that they are voting on instruction against their own convictions — an imputation of bad faith, though aimed at a group and framed as an appeal to conscience rather than as mockery of any individual.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wonder if the member can tell us when we can see some legislation around the Local Water Done Well proposals, given the parlous state of water in Wellington and elsewhere.
focus.explanation: Names a specific government policy programme (Local Water Done Well) and asks about its legislative timetable. Straightforward scrutiny of a named measure, no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, the member will have to wait, and that legislation will come through in due course and it’ll be a much better solution to water issues than the widely condemned three waters proposal of the previous Government.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent (the forthcoming water legislation), but most of the weight of the answer is a comparison to the previous Government's programme rather than any content of the new one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The previous Labour Government was aware of this increase but did nothing to address the sustainability of the disability support service budget, but I assure the community that no disabled person will lose access to funding for essential services, equipment, or support.
focus.explanation: The disability support budget and its sustainability are named, so there is genuine policy content, but the framing carries a general 'did nothing' charge against the other party rather than a specific outcome or target.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On what dates did she first advise the finance Minister of a forecast overspend in disability support services that would require a change to the purchasing rules and equipment and modification services?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named decision — the purchasing-rule change in disability support services — and of when the Minister escalated it. Squarely on the policy and its handling.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Minister saying that she first learnt about the cost blowout here on 15 December and that, prior to that, no prior warning had come to any Minister in charge of that portfolio?
focus.explanation: Tests a specific factual claim about the timeline of ministerial advice on the disability support overspend. On the substance of the matter before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I wonder if the member can tell us when we can see some legislation around the Local Water Done Well proposals, given the parlous state of water in Wellington and elsewhere.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy and the problem area, but the ask is an open 'when' with no figures, mechanism or milestone attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, the member will have to wait, and that legislation will come through in due course and it’ll be a much better solution to water issues than the widely condemned three waters proposal of the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: 'In due course' commits to no date, no mechanism and no content; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The context of this is that since 2018, the number of people accessing disability supports has increased by around 50 percent compared to population growth of 8.5 percent over that same period.
specificity.explanation: Two figures with a stated baseline year and a like-for-like comparison; anyone could go and check both numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On what dates did she first advise the finance Minister of a forecast overspend in disability support services that would require a change to the purchasing rules and equipment and modification services?
specificity.explanation: Asks for a specific, checkable thing: dates of advice to a named Minister about a named change. A precise question, not a general grievance.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, the member will have to wait, and that legislation will come through in due course and it’ll be a much better solution to water issues than the widely condemned three waters proposal of the previous Government.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of the question and scathing about the previous Government's policy, but attacks no person. Hard criticism of a policy is the standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The access to that funding, under the settings that were there previously—absolutely nothing wrong was done by the person who accessed that.
civility.explanation: Answering a pointedly personal constituent story, she declines to impugn the carer or the questioner and expressly clears the person named. Fully on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also stand by my statement yesterday that there has been no reduction in funding for disabled people and no disabled people will lose access to funding for essential services, equipment, or support.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the overall funding envelope was not cut and that the 18 March purchasing-rule change costs no disabled person access to essential services, equipment or support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Health / Whaikaha appropriations for disability support services before and after March 2024, plus the purchasing-rule changes that took effect 18 March 2024: true if total funding was not reduced AND no category of disabled people lost access to funding for essential services, equipment or support; false if either the appropriation fell or the rule change removed access that people previously had.

veracity.statement: The context of this is that since 2018, the number of people accessing disability supports has increased by around 50 percent compared to population growth of 8.5 percent over that same period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a ~50% growth in people accessing disability supports since 2018 against ~8.5% population growth over the same window.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whaikaha / Ministry of Health client counts for disability support services in 2018 versus 2024, against Stats NZ national population estimates for the same period: true if client numbers rose by roughly 50% while population rose roughly 8.5%, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The previous Labour Government was aware of this increase but did nothing to address the sustainability of the disability support service budget, but I assure the community that no disabled person will lose access to funding for essential services, equipment, or support.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government knew of the growth in demand and took no step to address the sustainability of the disability support budget.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget documents and Cabinet papers 2018–2023 for disability support services, and the establishment of Whaikaha in 2022: true if no appropriation increase, policy-setting change or sustainability work was undertaken in response to the growth in uptake; false if funding was increased or settings work commenced.

veracity.statement: It is regrettable that there were no settings put in place by the previous Government to assist Whaikaha with the management of this fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no funding settings or regulations governing the fund were established by the previous Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The purchasing rules, guidelines and funding criteria in force for Whaikaha's flexible/individualised funding before 18 March 2024: true if no such settings or regulations existed, false if published purchasing guidelines or criteria were in place.

veracity.statement: This morning, Statistics New Zealand released the latest GDP figures. These showed that real GDP fell 0.1 percent in the December quarter of last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Stats NZ release of 21 March 2024 showed real GDP falling 0.1 percent in the December 2023 quarter.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Gross Domestic Product release for the December 2023 quarter (published 21 March 2024); true if real production-measure GDP fell approximately 0.1%, false if the figure differs materially or moved the other way.

veracity.statement: Looking a little further back, the release also shows that GDP fell in the December quarter of 2022, the March quarter of 2023, and the September quarter of 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that quarterly real GDP was negative in three named earlier quarters, as shown in the same Stats NZ release.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP series as revised in the 21 March 2024 release; true if all three of Dec-2022, Mar-2023 and Sep-2023 show negative quarterly growth, false if any one of them is flat or positive.

veracity.statement: These include delivering tax reductions to provide cost of living relief to New Zealanders who have seen no change in personal income tax rates and thresholds for 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that neither personal income tax rates nor thresholds have changed in the 14 years to March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue / Income Tax Act records of personal income tax rate and threshold changes since 2010; true if neither rates nor thresholds were altered in that window, false if any rate or threshold changed (e.g. the introduction of a new top personal rate in 2021).

veracity.statement: Given that data today confirms our economy has experienced a double-dip recession, I know those hard-working New Zealanders will be appreciative of soon being able to keep more of their money.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the GDP data released that morning confirms a double-dip recession — two separate recessionary episodes within the recent series.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP series as at the 21 March 2024 release; true if it contains two distinct runs of two or more consecutive quarters of negative growth, false if only one such run (or none) is present.

veracity.statement: Would the Minister consider addressing that structural deficit in the economy, which she just cited, through recommendations from the Treasury, or even the likes of the IMF, whose recent reports stated—and I quote—that we could achieve a more efficient, equitable tax system with a comprehensive capital gains tax?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about the content of recent IMF reporting on New Zealand — specifically that the IMF recommended a comprehensive capital gains tax as the route to a more efficient and equitable tax system.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IMF's recent Article IV consultation staff report for New Zealand; true if it recommends a comprehensive capital gains tax in those terms, false if it makes no such recommendation or recommends against it.

veracity.statement: Why did she decide to increase the level of cuts required of Whaikaha to 7.5 percent rather than the 6.5 percent she campaigned on, and is requiring of other agencies, given she received a briefing from the Minister of disabilities in late 2023?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Whaikaha was required to find 7.5 percent savings while the campaign commitment, applied to other agencies, was 6.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 fiscal plan / public service savings target and the Budget 2024 savings targets issued to Whaikaha and other agencies; true if Whaikaha's required saving was 7.5% against a 6.5% campaign and general-agency figure, false if both figures were the same or differ from those stated.

specificity.statement: This morning, Statistics New Zealand released the latest GDP figures. These showed that real GDP fell 0.1 percent in the December quarter of last year.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the exact quarter and the exact figure; a listener could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can I reinforce to members that those tax reductions will be funded by reprioritisations, savings, and new revenue measures. This package of measures will not add to debt.
specificity.explanation: Names three funding mechanisms and a debt-neutrality test, but supplies no amounts, no timeframe and no identified savings.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I disagree with quite a lot of the Treasury advice and I also agree with quite a lot of the Treasury advice, and what I think the member opposite should be very careful about is cherry-picking Treasury advice, because I can tell her that Treasury don’t agree with her anti-growth, pro-regulation perspective. They know that that’s a recipe for disaster in our economy.
specificity.explanation: Asked about a named piece of Treasury advice on capital gains tax, the answer carries no advice, no document, no figure and no mechanism — only that she agrees with some of it and disagrees with some of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Ministry of Disabled People had been invited to submit for cost pressures as part of Budget 2024 as we view the services they provide as critical front-line services and intended to provide them more funding in the Budget, and they did so with the Minister. Subsequent to that request, I was advised in early March that there was a risk of the disability services—Whaikaha—exceeding its appropriation.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named agency, a named Budget process, a sequence of steps and an approximate date for the advice; short of exact dates or dollar figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would just assure the member that the ministry for disability services is expected to get vast orders of magnitude more in additional funding for front-line services—vast orders of magnitude more than any small changes they make to ensure their back office is more efficient.
specificity.explanation: Answers a question containing exact percentages with "vast orders of magnitude" repeated twice — no amount, no baseline, no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she agree with Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters, who said that the Sunday Star-Times is “right, of course” when they reported that the Government is facing a fiscal hole of $5.6 billion?
specificity.explanation: A precise question: names the person, the publication, the quoted words and the exact figure, so the answer can be checked against all of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why did she decide to increase the level of cuts required of Whaikaha to 7.5 percent rather than the 6.5 percent she campaigned on, and is requiring of other agencies, given she received a briefing from the Minister of disabilities in late 2023?
specificity.explanation: Two exact percentages, a named agency, a named briefing and a timeframe — precisely checkable, and a precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: GDP is expected to pick up this year, although strong population growth will limit per capita growth.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that GDP growth recovers during calendar 2024 while per capita growth lags behind headline growth because of population growth.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP and GDP per capita series covering calendar 2024; true if real GDP growth turns positive over 2024 (headline growth exceeding per capita growth), false if quarterly real GDP contracts over that period rather than picking up.

focus.statement: The truth is that members opposite believe the Government can spend money better than New Zealanders can on their own families; well, I disagree.
focus.explanation: Entirely a characterisation of what the other side supposedly believes; no policy, figure or measure is named once that characterisation is removed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I ask the Minister of Finance: alongside the 100,000 ways that she has received by way of advice to spend the taxpayers’ money, has she received one idea on how the taxpayers may make some money from those parties over there?
focus.explanation: A question whose whole content is a characterisation of the opposition parties as having no revenue-generating ideas; no policy, measure or figure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I disagree with quite a lot of the Treasury advice and I also agree with quite a lot of the Treasury advice, and what I think the member opposite should be very careful about is cherry-picking Treasury advice, because I can tell her that Treasury don’t agree with her anti-growth, pro-regulation perspective. They know that that’s a recipe for disaster in our economy.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to authority: the conclusion rests on an assertion about what Treasury thinks, offered without citing any Treasury document, in reply to a question that did cite one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We haven’t exempted them from the process we are asking all Government agencies to do, because we are conscious every dollar that is saved by not spending it on another policy adviser or administrative person, consultant, or contractor is a dollar that can actually go to support people with disabilities.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the savings policy, but it leans on an unshown premise that back-office savings are in fact redirected to front-line disability support rather than to the fiscal bottom line; the conclusion is reasonable but the fungibility step is asserted, not demonstrated.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she stand by her statement that she was “surprised” by this decision, and, if so, is that because the Minister for Disability Issues never alerted her to the situation, or does she just not read the paper setting out the rationale for an early decision?
civility.explanation: "Or does she just not read the paper" imputes personal negligence to the Minister rather than pressing the decision itself; pointed scrutiny that lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At this time, the evidence is that a special humanitarian visa is not a solution to the current crisis. For example, I’m told that Canada, the only country that have created a special visa, has received 986 applications—on 1 January, they opened that—and only 14 of those people have managed to complete secondary screening.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy before her: the comparator case (Canada's special visa producing almost no completed screenings) is offered as evidence that a special visa would not solve the problem. The step is reasonable but rests on a single country and slides from 'the Canadian scheme has been slow' to 'a special visa is not a solution' — an argument from one instance, with the intermediate premise (that the binding constraint is the border, not visa category) left implicit here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I do agree with that member in Opposition, and the reason I do is because those people in Ukraine were able to leave—they were able to get on a plane and get to New Zealand. The situation in Gaza is that they cannot leave, and I’m not going to be issuing visas, which is issuing false hope, for people on a great scale who cannot leave.
rigor.explanation: Confronted with her own earlier position, she draws a disanalogy rather than dodging: the Ukraine case worked because departure was possible, so the comparison does not carry to Gaza where it is not. The conclusion follows from the stated premise. It stops short of addressing whether a visa could still have value once a border opens, which is the gap left.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know that people in Palestine who have temporary visas to get out have not been able to get out. We granted visas in December and people still are unable to get out. It is, unfortunately, not a visa issue; it is a border issue, and as I’ve said a number of times, if that changes, we will reconsider our position.
rigor.explanation: A clean modus tollens on the policy question: if visas were the binding constraint, the December grantees would have left; they have not, so the constraint lies at the border. The evidence offered does support the conclusion. It is short of complete because it addresses only whether visas are sufficient, not whether granting more of them earlier would have helped at the margin — the claim actually put to her.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, I take a range of advice, and if that member had read her own regulatory impact statement from the legislation she passed in 2021, she would have seen that advice.
rigor.explanation: There is a genuine argument here once the jibe is stripped out: advice on an illicit market exists in the questioner's own 2021 regulatory impact statement, so the claim was not unsupported. But it is a tu quoque in structure — pointing to advice she received does not answer what advice he was given, which is what was actually asked. Real evidence, offered against the wrong proposition.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: For example, I’m told that Canada, the only country that have created a special visa, has received 986 applications—on 1 January, they opened that—and only 14 of those people have managed to complete secondary screening.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable things: that Canada is the only country to have created a special Gaza visa, that its pathway opened on 1 January (Canada's own announcements put the opening in early-to-mid January), and that of 986 applications only 14 had completed secondary screening.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada published statistics on its temporary resident pathway for extended family in Gaza: the opening date of the pathway, the number of applications received, and the number that had completed secondary screening as at 21 March 2024. True if Canada is the only state to have created such a visa and the figures are ~986 applications with ~14 completing secondary screening; false if the counts or the opening date are materially different, or if other states had created comparable special visas.

veracity.statement: Is she aware that, since October last year, only 10 visitor visa applications by Palestinians have been granted, whilst 13 have been rejected, and that seven times more visas are still being granted to Israeli nationals than Palestinian nationals when both of them are supposedly prioritised?
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific INZ decision counts for Palestinian applicants since October 2023 and a seven-to-one disparity in grants to Israeli over Palestinian nationals. The Minister disputes the visa counts in her reply, so the two sets of figures may be counting different things (applications lodged worldwide versus decisions made).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Immigration New Zealand visa decision data by nationality for October 2023 to March 2024: counts of visitor visa applications by Palestinian nationals approved and declined, and the ratio of visas granted to Israeli nationals versus Palestinian nationals over the same period. True if approvals are ~10, declines ~13, and the Israeli:Palestinian ratio is about 7:1; false if the counts or ratio are materially different.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with MP Erica Stanford, who said, 14 days after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, that “Desperate Ukrainians in New Zealand have been unable to rescue wider family members because immigration Minister Kris Faafoi has not created a [special] pathway to let them come to New Zealand”, and, if so, will she afford the same urgency to Palestinian New Zealanders who are urgently waiting to be reunited with their families?
veracity.explanation: The speaker is relaying a quotation attributed to Erica Stanford in opposition in March 2022; the checkable element is whether she said it, and roughly when, not whether the sentiment was right.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party press releases and media statements attributed to Erica Stanford in the fortnight after 24 February 2022 (i.e. around 10 March 2022). True if a statement in substantially these words, criticising Kris Faafoi for not creating a special pathway for Ukrainian families, was made by her at about that time; false if no such statement exists or the wording materially misrepresents what she said.

veracity.statement: Since 7 October, we’ve received 71 applications from Palestinian nationals around the world. Of these, we believe 15 applications are from people who, to the best of our knowledge, may have been in Gaza at the time of their application or shortly before lodging. We’ve issued seven visas to people who are immediate family members of New Zealand citizens or permanent residents, and I would encourage any Palestinian New Zealander who has immediate family members in Gaza that they would like to travel to New Zealand to go to the Immigration New Zealand website to apply for a visa, which will be promptly assessed by the specialist team.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three official operational figures — 71 applications received since 7 October, 15 of them from people believed to have been in Gaza, and seven visas issued to immediate family of New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Immigration New Zealand data for 7 October 2023 to 21 March 2024: applications received from Palestinian nationals worldwide, the subset assessed as being in Gaza at or near lodgement, and visas issued to immediate family members of NZ citizens or residents. True if the figures are ~71, ~15 and ~7 respectively; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand Government has also provided a total of $15 million in humanitarian assistance, including through the World Food Programme, UNICEF, and the International Committee of the Red Cross to address the urgent humanitarian situation in Gaza.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a cumulative dollar figure for New Zealand's Gaza humanitarian contribution to date and names the three multilateral channels it flowed through.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MFAT humanitarian funding announcements for Gaza from October 2023 to 21 March 2024, summed. True if the cumulative total is $15 million and the named channels include WFP, UNICEF and the ICRC; false if the total is materially higher or lower, or the funding went through different channels.

veracity.statement: A wide range of sectors will see these immediate benefits: 99.5 percent of fish and seafood trade will enter tariff-free from day one, as will 97 percent of New Zealand’s wine and mānuka honey exports.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific day-one tariff-elimination coverage percentages for named export sectors under the agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ–EU FTA tariff schedules and MFAT's published national interest analysis / sector factsheets. True if the share of NZ fish and seafood trade entering the EU duty-free on day one is ~99.5% and the share for wine and mānuka honey is ~97%; false if the schedules give materially different day-one coverage for those sectors.

veracity.statement: Why did he issue a statement on 29 November that said Labour’s smoke-free changes would have resulted in an illicit market for tobacco when he had been advised that the evidence did not support that statement?
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable things: that a statement making the illicit-market claim was issued on 29 November, and that advice contradicting it had already been received by the Minister at that point.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister of Health's public statements dated 29 November 2023, and the Ministry of Health / officials' advice provided to him before that date on whether the smokefree amendments would drive an illicit tobacco market. True if a 29 November statement makes that claim and advice held before it said the evidence did not support it; false if no such statement exists on that date or no such contrary advice had been given to him beforehand.

specificity.statement: For example, I’m told that Canada, the only country that have created a special visa, has received 986 applications—on 1 January, they opened that—and only 14 of those people have managed to complete secondary screening.
specificity.explanation: Names the comparator country, the opening date, an application count and a completion count — anyone can go to the Canadian statistics and check it. Precision here is independent of whether the numbers turn out to be right.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is she aware that, since October last year, only 10 visitor visa applications by Palestinians have been granted, whilst 13 have been rejected, and that seven times more visas are still being granted to Israeli nationals than Palestinian nationals when both of them are supposedly prioritised?
specificity.explanation: Carries hard numbers and a defined period — grants, declines and a stated ratio — so the question can be answered or refuted directly. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Since 7 October, we’ve received 71 applications from Palestinian nationals around the world. Of these, we believe 15 applications are from people who, to the best of our knowledge, may have been in Gaza at the time of their application or shortly before lodging. We’ve issued seven visas to people who are immediate family members of New Zealand citizens or permanent residents, and I would encourage any Palestinian New Zealander who has immediate family members in Gaza that they would like to travel to New Zealand to go to the Immigration New Zealand website to apply for a visa, which will be promptly assessed by the specialist team.
specificity.explanation: Gives a start date, three counts, the eligibility category the visas were issued under, and the concrete route for applying. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In particular, this early entry into force date means our kiwifruit industry will see $43 million worth of tariff savings this year. We also estimate that 35,000 tonnes of onions will be exported to the EU after 1 May, saving our onion exporters $3 million per season.
specificity.explanation: Two named sectors, a tonnage, two dollar figures and the date they attach to. Someone could take these numbers to the export data and check them, which is what specificity asks.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is she aware that, since October last year, only 10 visitor visa applications by Palestinians have been granted, whilst 13 have been rejected, and that seven times more visas are still being granted to Israeli nationals than Palestinian nationals when both of them are supposedly prioritised?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the operation of a named policy: visitor visa processing for Palestinian nationals and the priority category both nationalities are said to sit in. This is scrutiny of a specific administrative outcome, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Sorry, I got it—if this legislation is so important, why did the Government prioritise the removal of smoking protection, over the passage of this legislation?
focus.explanation: Names two specific measures — the smokefree repeal and the EU FTA legislation — and asks about the ordering between them. That is a question about the Government's legislative programme, not about what the other party is like, so it sits on the policy side. Marked down slightly because the point rests on the priority framing rather than on anything about the FTA legislation itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s no wonder that member is no longer the Minister responsible. But what I would like to do is thank him for his hard work on an agreement that will help deliver for all New Zealanders, and recognise how hard it must be to be a Minister for Trade in a Labour Government.
focus.explanation: A specific question about legislative priorities was asked; the answer contains no policy content at all. It is entirely about the member's demotion and about what it is like to serve in a Labour Government. Nothing here names a measure, a figure or an outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why did he issue a statement on 29 November that said Labour’s smoke-free changes would have resulted in an illicit market for tobacco when he had been advised that the evidence did not support that statement?
focus.explanation: Names a dated ministerial statement, a specific policy (the smokefree changes) and a specific claim about illicit tobacco, and asks how it squares with the advice held. Holding a Minister to a named statement is exactly the accountability role, and scores at the top.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Today, the House will complete the final legislative process required to bring the New Zealand - European Union free-trade agreement (FTA) into force on 1 May, many months earlier than expected.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a dated outcome that depends on more than the House's own vote — the agreement actually taking effect on 1 May, months ahead of the previously expected timetable.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official entry-into-force date of the New Zealand–European Union Free Trade Agreement, per MFAT and the EU's Official Journal. True if the agreement entered into force on 1 May 2024; false if it entered into force on any later date or not at all.

civility.statement: It’s no wonder that member is no longer the Minister responsible. But what I would like to do is thank him for his hard work on an agreement that will help deliver for all New Zealanders, and recognise how hard it must be to be a Minister for Trade in a Labour Government.
civility.explanation: Opens by tying the member's loss of his portfolio to the question he asked — a jibe at his competence rather than at anything he said — and closes with mock sympathy ('how hard it must be'). The thanks in the middle is the vehicle for the sneer, not a mitigation of it. A clear personal put-down, though not sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, I take a range of advice, and if that member had read her own regulatory impact statement from the legislation she passed in 2021, she would have seen that advice.
civility.explanation: 'If that member had read her own regulatory impact statement' imputes that she did not read her own document — condescension aimed at the member rather than at the argument. Short of a direct insult, but it is a dig at her diligence rather than a point about the advice.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is the Government’s position that education and every other utility should be used to combat racism in our society, and we’re going to go to the ends of the earth to ensure that that happens.
specificity.explanation: States a direction with no mechanism, no named programme, no measure and no timeframe; "every other utility" and "the ends of the earth" are rhetorical rather than checkable. There was a real chance to name what education actually does here, and none was taken.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Changes to the brightline test will come into force from 1 July 2024 alongside the gambling duty changes. Interest deductibility will be restored in stages, with 80 percent of a deduction allowed from 1 April 2024 and 100 percent from 1 April 2025.
specificity.explanation: Named measures, exact commencement dates and staged percentages. Anyone could act on this or check it against the Amendment Paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why is his Government prioritising a $2.9 billion tax cut for landlords over other election promises that would have helped middle-income families and cost less from Crown accounts, like raising the Working for Families abatement threshold?
specificity.explanation: Carries a costing figure, a named alternative policy (the Working for Families abatement threshold) and an explicit comparison of fiscal cost. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What is a priority for this Government is actually delivering on our coalition agreement and putting downward pressure on rent, and this is what these changes will do.
specificity.explanation: Given the question named a figure and a named alternative, this answer supplies no amount, no mechanism and no timeframe — "delivering on our coalition agreement" and "downward pressure on rent" commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the Government’s own analysis of the Auckland regional fuel tax repeal correct that “Removing the RFT is unlikely to have a substantive impact on households”; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific measure, quotes the departmental analysis verbatim and puts a checkable proposition to the Minister. Someone could retrieve the document and test the quote.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I’ll be saying to them that they’ll be very pleased—well, they’ll be very concerned that they’re driving around in Auckland, whether they’re in cars or on buses, crawling around at 30 kilometres an hour and going over speed bumps everywhere because of the strange priorities of the previous Government, and my message to them is: help is on its way.
specificity.explanation: Beyond the "30 kilometres an hour" reference there is no named action, no cost and no timing; "help is on its way" commits to nothing that could be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why we’re trying to reduce the inflationary pressures in this city by bringing some discipline back to Government spending and by reducing the regulatory burden that many businesses, including the providers of water services in this country, have to deal with.
specificity.explanation: Two mechanisms are named in general terms — spending restraint and regulatory relief, with water services identified — but there are no figures, no named programme and no timeframe attached to either.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: From 1 May, 99.5 percent of our fish and seafood exports to the EU, including hoki, mussels, and squid, will enter duty free, saving the industry $20 million in tariffs each year.
specificity.explanation: A commencement date, a coverage percentage, named product categories and an annual dollar saving. Fully checkable against the agreement's schedules.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Currently, the only tax that applies to offshore online casinos is GST, where casinos in New Zealand are facing much higher taxes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at March 2024 offshore online casino operators were liable for GST alone, while domestic operators bore materially heavier gambling-specific taxes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ tax legislation and IRD guidance in force at 21 March 2024: true if offshore remote-gambling operators were liable only for GST on remote services with no gaming duty/problem gambling levy, and domestic operators were liable for gaming duty and levies in addition; false if any further tax already applied offshore or if domestic operators faced no additional gambling taxes.

veracity.statement: This means that around 87 percent of all trusts in New Zealand are unlikely to be impacted by the change to the top tax rate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific share — about 87% — of New Zealand trusts fall below the $10,000 trustee income de minimis and so escape the 39% trustee rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue's officials' report / regulatory impact analysis to the Finance and Expenditure Committee on the $10,000 trustee income de minimis: true if the estimated proportion of trusts with trustee income at or below $10,000 is approximately 87%, false if the departmental estimate is materially different.

veracity.statement: Why is his Government prioritising a $2.9 billion tax cut for landlords over other election promises that would have helped middle-income families and cost less from Crown accounts, like raising the Working for Families abatement threshold?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that restoring interest deductibility for residential rental property carries a fiscal cost of $2.9 billion, and that raising the Working for Families abatement threshold would cost less.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/IRD costings for the restoration of interest deductibility published with the 2023 coalition agreements and the 2024 Budget forecast period: true if the forecast revenue foregone is approximately $2.9 billion, false if the official costing is materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, for example, New Zealand kiwifruit exporters currently pay a tariff of 8.8 percent on their exports to the EU, while their competitors in Chile pay nothing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things: that the EU applied an 8.8% tariff to New Zealand kiwifruit as at March 2024, and that Chilean kiwifruit entered the EU duty free.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The EU TARIC tariff schedule for kiwifruit (HS 0810.50) as applied to New Zealand in March 2024, and the tariff schedule of the EU–Chile Association Agreement: true if the NZ rate is 8.8% and the Chilean rate is zero, false if either rate materially differs.

rigor.statement: Well, I think the member will be pretty aware that when he goes to the petrol station and people pay less money for the petrol because they’re not paying a regional fuel tax, they will have more money in their pockets. And that’s what we’re setting out to achieve.
rigor.explanation: The question was whether the Government's own analysis — that removal is unlikely to have a substantive impact on households — is correct. The answer restates the conclusion as self-evident rather than deriving it: it assumes the full duty is passed through at the pump, and treats "more money in their pockets" as establishing a substantive impact, which is the very quantum in dispute. Essentially begging the question.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I think the member will be pretty aware that when he goes to the petrol station and people pay less money for the petrol because they’re not paying a regional fuel tax, they will have more money in their pockets. And that’s what we’re setting out to achieve.
civility.explanation: "the member will be pretty aware" carries a note of condescension — implying the questioner should already know the obvious — but it stops short of landing on him. Pointed rather than a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I’ll be saying to them that they’ll be very pleased—well, they’ll be very concerned that they’re driving around in Auckland, whether they’re in cars or on buses, crawling around at 30 kilometres an hour and going over speed bumps everywhere because of the strange priorities of the previous Government, and my message to them is: help is on its way.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent — speed limits and traffic calming — but the weight of the answer is a characterisation of the previous Government's "strange priorities", and the question about public transport costs, registration fees and tolls goes untouched. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Can the Minister recall that the regulatory impact statement said that the illicit market in tobacco was decreasing, at a time when New Zealanders had one of the highest prices of cigarettes in the world, and, if so, how can he justify his decision to make a statement that the smoke-free laws that Labour put in place would increase the illicit market?
veracity.explanation: Asserts two factual premises: that the 2021 regulatory impact statement recorded the illicit tobacco market as decreasing, and that New Zealand cigarette prices were among the highest in the world at that time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the 2021 Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) regulatory impact statement, plus WHO/OECD comparative cigarette price data for that period; true if the RIS describes the illicit market as decreasing and NZ prices rank near the top internationally, false if the RIS records the illicit market as growing or stable.

veracity.statement: How is it truthful to repeatedly claim that the legislation will grow the black market when, subsequent to the regulatory impact statement and before the Minister made his statement on 29 November, he had been advised that there was no evidence to support that claim?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that between the 2021 regulatory impact statement and 29 November, the Minister received official advice stating there was no evidence the smoke-free legislation would grow the illicit market.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Health New Zealand advice to the Minister released under the OIA or to the Health Committee, dated between the 2021 RIS and 29 November; true if any such briefing states there is no evidence the legislation would increase the illicit market, false if no advice to that effect exists in that window.

veracity.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, I receive a range of advice, including another statement from that regulatory impact statement in 2021 that said organised syndicates were involved in illicit tobacco trade.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2021 regulatory impact statement states organised syndicates were involved in the illicit tobacco trade.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published text of the 2021 Smokefree Environments regulatory impact statement; true if it records organised syndicate involvement in illicit tobacco, false if it contains no such statement.

veracity.statement: On behalf of the Minister of Health, what is correct is that I’ve received a range of advice from many different stakeholder groups, including submissions from stakeholders during the process when that bill went to select committee, such as the Food and Grocery Council, who submitted to the Health Committee that limiting retail could create significant additional opportunities for organised crime, including gangs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Food and Grocery Council made a submission to the Health Committee to that effect during the bill's select committee stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Food and Grocery Council's written submission to the Health Committee on the smoked tobacco bill, in the published committee record; true if the submission contains that claim, false if no such submission or claim is on the record.

veracity.statement: I’ve been advised that between 13,000 and 14,000 people present annually to EDs with mental health issues.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific annual national figure for emergency department presentations involving mental health issues.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health ED presentation data coded to mental health and addiction for the most recent full year; true if the annual national total falls in the 13,000–14,000 range, false if it is materially outside it (noting the count depends on the coding definition used).

veracity.statement: As the situation currently stands, as we inherited, it takes, for example, 361 days, on average, for a disablement pension claim to be processed and provided.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the average processing time for a disablement pension claim at Veterans' Affairs currently stands at 361 days.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Veterans' Affairs New Zealand claim processing statistics for the period referenced, as published in its annual report or released under the OIA; true if the mean time to process and provide a disablement pension claim is approximately 361 days, false if materially different.

focus.statement: How is it truthful to repeatedly claim that the legislation will grow the black market when, subsequent to the regulatory impact statement and before the Minister made his statement on 29 November, he had been advised that there was no evidence to support that claim?
focus.explanation: Names the specific legislation, a specific ministerial statement with a date, and the specific advice said to contradict it. This is scrutiny of a named policy position, not party-bashing, and scores at the top of the scale.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I can commit to is this Government will get more money out of the Beehive to the grassroots NGOs that are ready to respond to the needs in mental health. That’s exactly what we’ve done today with uncommitted funding that they left sitting in the Beehive.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point — redirecting uncommitted funding to community providers — but half the weight of the answer is the jab at the previous government for leaving money 'sitting in the Beehive'. A policy claim wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he believe suspending entitlements to the Veterans’ Independence Programme is acceptable when his Government campaigned on ensuring veterans receive the care, recognition, and support they deserve?
