veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Amendment Paper (Supplementary Order Paper) to the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill on legislation.govt.nz/Parliament's website; true if its page count is 39, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We have heard about that in relation to high - net-worth individuals paying 8.9 percent versus an average annual tax rate of around 22 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures: an effective tax rate of 8.9 percent for high-net-worth individuals, against an average annual tax rate of about 22 percent for other New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Inland Revenue High-Wealth Individuals Research Project (2023) effective-tax-rate figure and the companion Treasury analysis of average effective tax rates for middle-wealth New Zealanders; true if the reported HWI rate is ~8.9% and the comparator ~22%, false if either figure is materially different (e.g. HWI rate reported as 9.4–9.5%, comparator as 20.2%).

rigor.statement: I’m just here trying to tease out the lack of logical consistency from the Minister, because we’re hearing, on one account, that the changes to tax deductibility were campaigned upon and, therefore, they deserved to be in this Amendment Paper and bypass the opportunity for a select committee process and public participation in legislative processes, but changes to income tax rates, which the National Party, the ACT Party, and New Zealand First also campaigned on, somehow are not due the same level of bypassing that legislative process and, therefore, the public scrutiny as due.
rigor.explanation: A genuine consistency argument: it takes the Minister's own stated criterion (the measure was campaigned on) and shows it would equally license a different treatment of income tax changes. The inference tracks the stated premise. Short of 1.0 only because it does not address the obvious disanalogy the Minister could offer — that the rate changes are tied to the Budget.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But you’ve got a whole lot of other people who are way, way wealthier, and they are actually earning money. In the same time period, the money’s going up exponentially more, and yet they’re not paying any money on it, because they’re sinking that money straight into businesses or property, where, in fact, it’s recognised as a loss, not a profit.
rigor.explanation: A real causal mechanism is offered — gains reinvested into businesses or property are recognised as loss rather than profit — and the conclusion that little tax is paid follows from it. The gap is the absolute 'not paying any money on it', which the premise supports only for the unrealised portion, not for all income.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m just here trying to tease out the lack of logical consistency from the Minister, because we’re hearing, on one account, that the changes to tax deductibility were campaigned upon and, therefore, they deserved to be in this Amendment Paper and bypass the opportunity for a select committee process and public participation in legislative processes, but changes to income tax rates, which the National Party, the ACT Party, and New Zealand First also campaigned on, somehow are not due the same level of bypassing that legislative process and, therefore, the public scrutiny as due.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: the Amendment Paper, tax deductibility, and whether the select committee process is bypassed. Parties are named only to identify who campaigned on what, not as a target.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Or, if the Minister is really honest, is it just that the average tax rates kind of end up like that and no further thought has been given, because that’s how they’ve always been done?
civility.explanation: The conditional 'if the Minister is really honest' implies his previous answers may not have been, and the question suggests he has given the matter no thought. That edges past robust into imputing candour problems and idleness to the person, though it stops well short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How much is the Minister expecting tax transfers such as Working for Families—how much is he expecting Inland Revenue to be paying out to those individuals in the sum of a Working for Families entitlement, such as an in-work tax credit, the family tax credit?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: the individual tax take and the transfers paid back out. Names Working for Families, the in-work tax credit and the family tax credit. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So we’ve heard from the Minister, previously, that this is because these changes around tax deductibility were signalled at the election, yet the same could be said of those promises when it comes to income tax rate changes so, again, that logical inconsistency is abundantly apparent.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure: the Amendment Paper, tax deductibility, and the income tax rate changes. Named policy, named process, no party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How much is the Minister expecting tax transfers such as Working for Families—how much is he expecting Inland Revenue to be paying out to those individuals in the sum of a Working for Families entitlement, such as an in-work tax credit, the family tax credit?
specificity.explanation: Names three specific entitlements and asks for a quantum, so the answer would be checkable. Falls short of 1.0 because the question itself carries no figure or timeframe — it asks for one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, of course, that remains the case—if the argument is to be consistent—for these tax deductibility changes, where the Government has to find $2.9 billion to pay for their tax deductibility changes for landlords.
specificity.explanation: Carries a figure ($2.9 billion), a named policy (interest deductibility for landlords) and a named process (Budget). Someone could go and check the costing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We don’t think it makes logical sense. There is a good, rational basis for regarding as different income versus net income. Obviously, in the usual way that is understood deducting expenses.
specificity.explanation: Asserts that a 'good, rational basis' exists without stating it, then gestures at one mechanism — deducting expenses. Some substance is supplied, but no figures, no test, and no account of what the distinction between wealth and income would turn on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If that is correct, I want to ask the Minister how much of those individuals—because almost half of the total tax collected is actually just via the collection of individual taxes; so wages and salaries.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that individual income tax (PAYE on wages and salaries) makes up almost half of all tax collected in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Inland Revenue tax outturn data for the 2023/24 year: individuals' income tax as a share of total core Crown tax revenue. True if that share is in the mid-40s to around 50 percent; false if it is materially below (say under 40 percent) or above.

veracity.statement: But, of course, that remains the case—if the argument is to be consistent—for these tax deductibility changes, where the Government has to find $2.9 billion to pay for their tax deductibility changes for landlords.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fiscal cost to the Government of the tax deductibility changes for residential landlords is $2.9 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury/Inland Revenue fiscal costing published for the restoration of interest deductibility on residential rental property (Budget 2024 documents, regulatory impact statement, or the bill's disclosure statement), over the forecast period. True if the costing is approximately $2.9 billion; false if it is materially different.

civility.statement: I didn’t get a response to my previous line of questioning and noting that the Minister has now manifested in another form, I will try once again but perhaps articulate these as coherently as I possibly can, to lay it out for the Minister in the chair.
civility.explanation: Pointed and sardonic — 'manifested in another form' and the offer to articulate things 'as coherently as I possibly can' imply the Minister failed to follow. It edges toward the person without landing on them: no attack on character or competence is actually made.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we’ve heard from the Minister, previously, that this is because these changes around tax deductibility were signalled at the election, yet the same could be said of those promises when it comes to income tax rate changes so, again, that logical inconsistency is abundantly apparent.
rigor.explanation: A genuine consistency argument: the stated justification (signalled at the election) applies equally to the income tax changes, so it cannot on its own explain treating the two differently. The premise is stated, the conclusion tracks it. Not 1.0 because she does not rule out an independent reason for the difference, which is exactly what the Minister then supplies.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, as to logical consistency, the fact that we could, on the basis of our argument, do both those things, but, nevertheless, we’ll do one but not both, just reflects a little bit of the constraints of time.
rigor.explanation: A real reason is offered — capacity and time — and it does answer 'why not both'. But there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded: the question was why the election-mandate argument licenses bypassing select committee scrutiny here and not there, and time constraints do not bear on that. A reasonable point that leaves the inference incomplete.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Finally, in terms of the comments by Ingrid Leary regarding tax rates, and, obviously, describing the progressive nature of the tax system, you know, she’s articulated actually, I think, quite a good argument, if one were inclined to make it, for a flatter tax system, noting, quite rightly, that going from one bracket to another by earning more income arguably has that disincentive.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: bracket progression creates a marginal disincentive, therefore a flatter system has something to be said for it. The premise is offered and the direction follows, but the step is under-supported — only income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate, so the disincentive claim needs a magnitude it never gets. A reasonable point with a genuine gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m personally confident, based on, you know, the history of these things, in terms of how long it takes to thrash out these arguments as fully as I think we’re doing now, that we will be done in time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the House will complete the remaining stages of the bill before the 1 April deadline the debate is working to, rather than running into Easter weekend.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard and Order Paper record for the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill. True if the bill completed its committee of the whole House and remaining stages before 1 April 2024; false if the House was still on the bill on or after that date.

veracity.statement: I did my sums as he was giving out the numbers on the amount of personal income, corporate tax, and goods and services tax as levied, and, according to my calculations, over 90 percent of the total tax take would be generated by those three areas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that personal income tax, company tax and GST together account for more than 90 percent of New Zealand's total tax revenue.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Inland Revenue core Crown tax revenue tables for the fiscal year referenced: sum individual income tax, company tax and GST and divide by total core Crown tax revenue; true if that share exceeds 90 percent, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: Now, the Schedule 1, as it sits at the moment, changes nothing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Part 1 of the bill, as it stands before the Amendment Paper is applied, leaves the income tax rates and thresholds in Schedule 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007 unaltered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of Part 1 of the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill as reported, compared with Schedule 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007; true if the rates and thresholds are set at the existing levels, false if Part 1 itself alters any rate or threshold.

focus.statement: What advice has the Minister considered about whether the level of horizontal equity in New Zealand’s tax system is appropriate, given the IMF’s recent findings on that and the comparison to other OECD countries where New Zealand stands out as having a reliance on taxation on personal income?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee: names a tax principle (horizontal equity), a named source (the IMF report) and an international comparison. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think that the bill that’s before us represents a willingness to be flexible, a willingness to adapt—specifically, to respond to the mood of the electorate, as expressed through the general election, but also to provide maximum certainty that, obviously, we need, in time for the tax year that is upcoming: a known set of circumstances, a known set of tax rates, a known set of mechanisms, such as this bill does achieve.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the bill before the committee and the design principles put to him; no characterisation of the Opposition.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What advice has the Minister considered about whether the level of horizontal equity in New Zealand’s tax system is appropriate, given the IMF’s recent findings on that and the comparison to other OECD countries where New Zealand stands out as having a reliance on taxation on personal income?
specificity.explanation: Names the principle being tested, the evidence source and the comparator set, so the Minister could answer it concretely; stops short of a figure or a threshold that would make it fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I want to know what work the Minister has been doing with respect to ensuring the long-term sustainability of our income tax system.
specificity.explanation: Names the concern (long-term sustainability of the income tax base) and elsewhere cites the IMF report and the Treasury BIM, but the request itself carries no figure, mechanism or timeframe the Minister could be held to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As for Ms Williams’ points around compliance costs, we do think that the degree of breadth is appropriate.
specificity.explanation: Answering a detailed question about compliance costs and base breadth with a bare assertion of appropriateness — no figures, no advice cited, no mechanism. He had the material to be concrete and was not.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It just raises the interesting point: does the Minister know what the tax rates and tax thresholds are, and could he perhaps tell everyone in the House so that people here and people at home know what we’re talking about?
civility.explanation: The rhetorical framing insinuates the Minister may not know the rates in his own bill — mild condescension aimed at the person rather than at the drafting, though well short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m sure that that will be given just as much consideration as Opposition Amendment Papers always have had in the committee of the whole House stage.
civility.explanation: Sardonic dismissal of the amendment's prospects. Pointed and mocking of the Opposition's position, but the target is the class of amendment papers, not any individual member's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that the bill that’s before us represents a willingness to be flexible, a willingness to adapt—specifically, to respond to the mood of the electorate, as expressed through the general election, but also to provide maximum certainty that, obviously, we need, in time for the tax year that is upcoming: a known set of circumstances, a known set of tax rates, a known set of mechanisms, such as this bill does achieve.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: the question was about flexibility and adaptability as tax-design principles — the system's capacity to adjust to changing fiscal circumstances — and the answer substitutes a different sense, responsiveness to an election result, then treats that as having satisfied the principle. The electoral mandate premise does not support the conclusion drawn about the tax system's adaptability.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Or, actually, it could be the Associate Minister of Finance, because David Seymour has taken claim for that particular interest deductibility rule change, which is in this Amendment Paper.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that David Seymour has publicly claimed credit for the interest deductibility rule change contained in this Amendment Paper.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ACT Party press releases, Seymour's public statements and media coverage between the 2023 election and 26 March 2024; true if Seymour or ACT publicly claimed credit for the restoration of interest deductibility, false if no such claim is on record.

veracity.statement: I’m not sure that the Minister necessarily addressed that, but it made me think about this concept of tax revenue forecasts and the fact that New Zealand, obviously, is in a technical recession and we need to think about encouraging growth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that New Zealand was in a technical recession as at 26 March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series as published before 26 March 2024; true if the two most recently released consecutive quarters both recorded negative real GDP growth, false if they did not.

veracity.statement: In relation to Working for Families, in the March year 2022, some 265,000 families received a Working for Families tax credit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific recipient count for the Working for Families tax credit in the year ended March 2022.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue / Treasury Working for Families recipient statistics for the March 2022 tax year; true if the number of recipient families is approximately 265,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: And in the spirit of helpfulness, as best that I can understand it—this may be helpful too—in the 2023 fiscal year, core Crown tax revenue was $112 billion or 28.4 percent of GDP and comprising various proportions on a consolidated basis, of which 52 percent was from individuals.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three linked figures for the 2023 fiscal year: core Crown tax revenue of $112 billion, equal to 28.4 percent of GDP, of which 52 percent came from individuals.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2023; true if core Crown tax revenue is approximately $112 billion and 28.4 percent of GDP with roughly 52 percent sourced from individuals, false if any of the three figures is materially different.

veracity.statement: But, look, the point is that the tax rates we are debating so enthusiastically, on the income tax scale, the first $0 to $14,000, the tax rate is 10.5 percent; from $14,001 to $48,000, the tax rate is 17.5 percent; from $48,000 to $70,000, the tax rate is 30 percent; from $70,000 to $180,000, the tax rate is 33 percent; and for income over $180,000, the tax rate is 39 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the full set of personal income tax thresholds and marginal rates in force at the date of the debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Schedule 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007 as in force on 26 March 2024; true if every threshold and rate stated matches, false if any one differs.

focus.statement: Then my next question is: under what criteria did they believe that that Amendment Paper should be brought forward before the Budget?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — the criteria used to decide the Amendment Paper's timing. Names the specific instrument and asks about a specific decision; this is scrutiny of a process, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On this side of the House, we believe there are actually some other pressing types of policies that could have been brought forward before May, which we will probably discuss quite in depth as part of Part 2.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance — an alternative set of priorities — but names no policy, no figure and no mechanism. "Some other pressing types of policies" commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In relation to Working for Families, in the March year 2022, some 265,000 families received a Working for Families tax credit.
specificity.explanation: A named scheme, a named period and a precise recipient count. Directly answers the question with a checkable figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the criteria, quite simply again, from the Government’s point of view in terms of what it was both willing and able to bring forward ahead of what would otherwise be a normal Budget process, it was that which was possible and desirable within the available time frame.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the answer to a direct question about criteria, but the content restates the question: the criterion was that it was "possible and desirable". No threshold, test, document or timeframe that anyone could check or apply.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, look, the point is that the tax rates we are debating so enthusiastically, on the income tax scale, the first $0 to $14,000, the tax rate is 10.5 percent; from $14,001 to $48,000, the tax rate is 17.5 percent; from $48,000 to $70,000, the tax rate is 30 percent; from $70,000 to $180,000, the tax rate is 33 percent; and for income over $180,000, the tax rate is 39 percent.
specificity.explanation: Every threshold and every rate on the income tax scale, stated exactly. Maximally concrete and immediately checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Certainly, from my perspective, I would have thought, therefore, that we have to be really mindful of not engaging in austerity measures as a means by which to deal with the potential of those drops in tax revenue, given that we’ve got this $10 billion discrepancy sitting there.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the fiscal response to a revenue shortfall, but the load-bearing premise — that spending restraint in a downturn worsens growth — is left unstated and unsupported. The conclusion is a reasonable one that does not actually follow from the $10 billion figure alone; there is a genuine gap between what was offered and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Overall, however, I think we can agree—or certainly the colleagues on my right-hand side would agree, no doubt—that by growing a strong economy and increasing the opportunity for revenue, for the Government as well as well as for those businesses, community organisations, and individual households, is the way to guard against those external fluctuations as best we can.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on an appeal to agreement ("I think we can agree", "colleagues on my right-hand side would agree, no doubt") rather than on any offered reason. Appeal to popularity/consensus: no mechanism is given connecting growth to insulation from revenue fluctuations.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, of course, having that variety of tax rates—the more tax rates, probably the less efficient the system. So that does invite the Government to think about whether or not that particular tax scale that I’ve just quoted is actually appropriate in terms of efficiency.
rigor.explanation: The premise linking number of rates to collection cost is asserted rather than evidenced, and hedged ("probably"). But the conclusion drawn is correspondingly modest — that the scale is worth examining on efficiency grounds — so it does broadly track what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I could look them up myself—and the member herself could look them up too, for what that’s worth.
civility.explanation: Pointed and a little barbed — "for what that's worth" is a dig returned to the member — but it stops short of landing on her character or competence. Robust rather than a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I’ve just given the Minister, for his benefit—and perhaps a quiz later, Minister, on those numbers.
civility.explanation: Light mockery aimed at the Minister for declining to recite the rates from memory. Jocular rather than abusive, but it is directed at the person's grasp of his portfolio rather than at any policy, which puts it below the robust-but-civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it to avoid the scrutiny that comes with such a debate around the Budget time?
civility.explanation: Imputes an improper motive (dodging scrutiny) to the Government, but aims it at the Government's process rather than at the Minister personally, and frames it as a question he immediately invites a rebuttal to. Pointed and edging toward bad faith without landing on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: With all due respect, I don’t accept the argument of the member Ingrid Leary that a passing reference to the phrase “wasteful spending” opens us up, on this bill, to every matter of Government expenditure. We’ve talked about the impending public holiday, which doesn’t, likewise, invite a discussion about the existence of the Easter Bunny.
civility.explanation: The Easter Bunny comparison ridicules the argument rather than the member, and is cushioned with 'with all due respect'. Robust and faintly mocking, but it does not land on Leary herself.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I cannot, for the life of me, understand why Government members would think that spending money on school lunches, for example, would be wasteful.
civility.explanation: Expresses incomprehension at a position, not contempt for the people holding it. The disagreement is sharp and about the spending decision; no member's character, competence or motive is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In fact, if it wasn’t here, then we could have had more opportunities to debate the substantive parts of this bill; the parts of the bill that do need to be passed by a certain date.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: committee-stage time is finite, the Amendment Paper is consuming some of it, therefore removing it would leave more time for the parts with a statutory deadline. The conclusion follows, though it rests on an unstated premise that the total time allocated would have stayed the same.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Following the Budget, famously, debates are rushed through under urgency. It would be usual, in that process, for debates to take place with one stage after another, where this is a relatively sedated, pedestrian process, so, with all due respect, I don’t think I can allow that accusation to stand without at least some refuting thereof.
rigor.explanation: Answers the accusation with a comparison that actually bears on it: if post-Budget tax debates run under urgency and this one does not, then the chosen timing gives more scrutiny, not less. The conclusion tracks the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: With all due respect, I don’t accept the argument of the member Ingrid Leary that a passing reference to the phrase “wasteful spending” opens us up, on this bill, to every matter of Government expenditure. We’ve talked about the impending public holiday, which doesn’t, likewise, invite a discussion about the existence of the Easter Bunny.
rigor.explanation: A reductio by analogy, and a weak one — the analogy is false. Easter and the Easter Bunny are incidental to each other, whereas Leary's point was that expenditure and taxation are directly linked as the two sides of the fiscal balance, which is precisely the link the analogy assumes away rather than answers.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is relevant, Madam Chair, because, if I am reading this correctly, this is an indication from Government members that they believe that kind of expenditure is wasteful.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: a general commitment to 'reducing wasteful spending' is inferred to mean that the specific programmes she has listed are the spending regarded as wasteful. Nothing was offered connecting the general phrase to those particular items — the hedge 'if I am reading this correctly' acknowledges the gap without closing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just briefly, in relation to the question posed by the Hon Barbara Edmonds, the trustee tax rate being increased to 39 percent for the year 2024-25 exists in subsequent parts to this bill because Part 1 deals with the annual rates for the year 2023-24.
specificity.explanation: Names the rate, both income years and the structural reason for the placement — a reader could check the drafting against the bill directly. No figures are hedged or left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re confirming in Part 1 the current tax rates, which are in Subpart BB of the Act, but then in Part 2 of this bill, we’re saying that this is what the rates should be.
specificity.explanation: Locates the alleged drafting inconsistency precisely — named parts of the bill and the named subpart of the Income Tax Act — so the Minister (or anyone else) can go to the text and check it. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I’m really keen to understand what this Minister in the chair, if he can speak on behalf of the Minister of Revenue, means by wasteful spending.
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance — the definition of 'wasteful spending' that is driving expenditure decisions — rather than at the character or record of the other party. It carries little detail, but Focus asks what the statement is about, not how precise it is.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I know we’ve heard an allegation that some of the food does not get eaten, but we’ve also seen evidence that that food often goes out into the community and goes home and that, actually, only around 6 percent of the food doesn’t get used.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 6 percent of food supplied under the school lunch programme goes unused, and that uneaten food is commonly redistributed to the community or sent home with students.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education reporting and the published evaluations of the Ka Ora, Ka Ako Healthy School Lunches programme on food waste. True if a departmental or evaluation source puts unused/wasted food at approximately 6 percent; false if the reported waste rate is materially higher, or if no such measurement exists in the programme's reporting.

veracity.statement: We now know that there’s a whole lot of people who have money to burn in comparison, who are not facing the cost of living crisis, and they are actually paying rates which are so much—dramatically—lower, and they’re doing that in a way.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that high-wealth New Zealanders pay materially lower effective tax rates than people on ordinary incomes. A factual claim about the present, resting on the research she refers to earlier in the contribution.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue's High-Wealth Individuals Research Project (2023) and Treasury's companion effective-tax-rate paper: true if the measured median effective tax rate for high-wealth families is substantially below that of middle-income earners; false if the published rates are comparable.

veracity.statement: Part 1 sets out the annual rates of the current year, 2023-24. And Part 2 introduces a 39 percent trustee tax rate, which would apply from 2024-25.
veracity.explanation: A factual assertion about what each part of the bill before the committee does, and from which tax year the new trustee rate applies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill as reported back: true if Part 1 confirms the 2023–24 annual rates and Part 2 enacts a 39% trustee rate commencing in the 2024–25 income year; false if either part does otherwise.

veracity.statement: In some calculations, it’s going to cost the Government $2.9 billion to do that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fiscal cost for restoring interest deductibility for landlords. Hedged with 'in some calculations', but a specific number is claimed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue/Treasury costings for the restoration of interest deductibility on residential rental property (regulatory impact statement and Budget 2024 forecasts): true if a published costing puts the revenue cost at roughly $2.9 billion over the forecast period; false if the published costings are materially different.

veracity.statement: That brightline test was originally introduced by the then National Government and set at two years, even though Treasury advised that it should be set at five years.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions about the past: that National introduced the bright-line test at two years, and that it did so against Treasury advice recommending five.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Taxation (Bright-line Test for Residential Land) Act 2015 for the original two-year period, and the released Treasury/IRD advice and regulatory impact statement of that year for the recommended duration: true if the advice recommended five years and the enacted period was two; false if the advice recommended two years or the enacted period differed.

specificity.statement: We now know that there’s a whole lot of people who have money to burn in comparison, who are not facing the cost of living crisis, and they are actually paying rates which are so much—dramatically—lower, and they’re doing that in a way.
specificity.explanation: The claim is offered without any of the figures that exist for it — no effective rate, no threshold for 'high wealth', no source named. 'A whole lot of people', 'money to burn' and 'dramatically lower' carry a direction but nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But given that we are actually changing a rate of tax, regardless of whether it’s the same or different income tax year, given our Standing Orders Committee and the way that review was done in 2011, given that particular outcome that had come from that Standing Orders Committee review, why then isn’t just that part—the increase from 33 percent to 39 percent—not in Part 1 of the particular bill?
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the exact rate movement (33 to 39 percent), the parts of the bill, the Standing Orders Committee and the year of its review. Anyone could go and check the point.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Part 1 sets out the annual rates of the current year, 2023-24. And Part 2 introduces a 39 percent trustee tax rate, which would apply from 2024-25.
specificity.explanation: Answers with the rate, the two income years and the part of the bill each sits in — precise enough to act on, though it gives no reason beyond 'standard process'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In some calculations, it’s going to cost the Government $2.9 billion to do that.
specificity.explanation: A single named figure attached to a named change, checkable against the published costings.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And what I understood the Minister did when he answered my question was talk about it as a kind of highfalutin philosophical approach.
civility.explanation: A contested exchange where she could have gone at the Minister personally. She characterises his answer as detached rather than attacking him — pointed and faintly mocking of the reply, but it lands on the answer, not the man.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So what we have here is base rates that we’re setting to compel New Zealanders who are on limited incomes, and we are setting them today without, what it seems to be, thought or even a plan about what we’re going to do to make that system fair, when we know—we can’t unpack this genie; it’s come out of the bottle.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the clause before the committee — the base rates being set and the absence of an accompanying fairness plan. No party framing at all, despite ample opportunity in a tax debate.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So, in an Amendment Paper to a bill, which has a constraint on it that this bill must go through by 31 March or the Government will have failed in its duty, the Government has, nevertheless, introduced an entirely new tax.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named measure by a named route — a new offshore gambling duty inserted by Amendment Paper into a bill under a hard commencement deadline. It names the mechanism, the vehicle and the date rather than characterising the Government.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But given that we are actually changing a rate of tax, regardless of whether it’s the same or different income tax year, given our Standing Orders Committee and the way that review was done in 2011, given that particular outcome that had come from that Standing Orders Committee review, why then isn’t just that part—the increase from 33 percent to 39 percent—not in Part 1 of the particular bill?
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the premise is the Standing Orders Committee's rule that annual taxing provisions get separate consideration, the conclusion is that a rate change belongs in Part 1. The step from 'annual taxing provision' to 'any rate change' is asserted rather than established, and she concedes the different-tax-year point without answering it, so there is a genuine gap — but the reasoning tracks the authority she cites.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what I have done is propose to delete clause 8, which would, essentially, mean that no amendment proposed by the Minister to clause 8 would be possible, and the effect of that would be that there would be no clause 8 to amend, and so the new Amendment Paper proposed by the Minister could be dealt with in a new piece of legislation.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, the exact procedural mechanism (deleting the clause so there is nothing left to amend) and the consequence. Someone could check the Amendment Paper and act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So that’s a complicated little set of rules, used in this new part—the global anti-base erosion model rules, defined elsewhere in the Act, so, in the definition section, then bumped back to HP 3 (3)(b)(i) and (ii).
specificity.explanation: Traces the definitional chain by exact statutory reference — new subpart HP, the clause 59 definition section, and the specific subparagraphs HP 3(3)(b)(i) and (ii). Any reader can follow the same path through the bill and verify it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So what I am proposing in my amendments tonight is that—you know, it is the Government’s prerogative to make the sorts of changes in policy which are set out by the Minister in the amendment, but what members on this side would object to is it being done in this way, when we cannot use the select committee process and use the House’s time to consider the policy implications of those changes.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: she concedes the premise that the policy is the Government's to set, and rests the objection solely on the stated consequence — that a substantive change introduced by Amendment Paper skips select committee scrutiny. The conclusion follows from that premise; no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that if you boil it down to quite a simple aspect, levelling the playing field around that is something that we believe is pretty sensible, and, actually, the broader industry’s feedback as well is to say that they are comfortable with that.
rigor.explanation: The competitive-neutrality premise does support taxing offshore and domestic operators alike, so there is a real inference here. But the only evidence offered for the measure being right is that the affected industry is comfortable with it — an appeal to authority (and to an interested party) rather than to the policy's effects.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Nevertheless, we are resigning some of our legislative powers to a foreign body and I would like to hear the Minister’s justification for making that move, preferably—well, you know, tax can be quite complicated, so I would like to understand why it is a viable process to go to the OECD for defining our tax law instead of defining it ourselves.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is earned: she walked the definitional chain from clause 44 to HP 3(3)(b)(i)–(ii) and showed that the operative content sits in OECD commentary and 'most recent guidance' outside New Zealand law, which does support the claim that legislative content is being determined offshore. Marked down because 'resigning legislative powers to a foreign body' overstates what incorporation by reference does — Parliament can amend or repeal the referring provision — so the conclusion runs slightly ahead of the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Both parties have taken very political stances on the effect of that, but what hasn’t happened is a reasoned debate in this House or at a select committee level about the impact on individual homeowners of the difference between two and 10 years for the brightline test to apply.
focus.explanation: The brightline test is one of the most partisan issues available here, and she names the specific measure and the specific outcome at stake (the effect on individual homeowners of a two- versus ten-year test) rather than the other party's record. She even books her own side into the criticism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also want to ask the Minister a fourth question, which is: under the Labour Government in the last three years the number of first-home buyers in the market, as a proportion of the market share, doubled.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the first-home-buyer share of the New Zealand residential market doubled over 2020–2023 under the Labour government. FHB share is a published series, so the size of the rise is checkable independently of the causal attribution.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: CoreLogic NZ (or REINZ) first-home-buyer share of residential property purchases, comparing 2020 with 2023. True if the FHB share of market transactions roughly doubled over the last three years of the Labour government (the c.17%→30% she cites in the following sentence); false if the rise is materially smaller than a doubling, or if the share was already near 30% at the start of the period.

veracity.statement: The gambling tax: well, quite simply, this is closing a loophole around overseas casinos that are able to operate without paying what domestic casinos pay in terms of their tax.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, as the law stood, overseas online casino operators serving New Zealand customers escaped the tax borne by domestic casinos — i.e. that there was a real gap the new offshore gambling duty closes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand gaming duty law as it stood before this bill (Gambling Act 2003 / Gaming Duties Act 1971 and IRD guidance on offshore online casino operators). True if offshore-based online casino operators taking bets from New Zealanders were not liable for the duties that domestic casino operators pay; false if they were already subject to equivalent duty.

veracity.statement: Again, this was an adjustment made during COVID, and we’re looking to return this back to what was the case previously.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the commercial building depreciation deduction now being removed was itself a COVID-era change, and that repealing it restores the pre-COVID position.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of commercial building depreciation: whether depreciation deductions for non-residential buildings were reinstated as a COVID-19 response measure in 2020 (COVID-19 Response (Taxation and Social Assistance Urgent Measures) Act 2020), having been set to zero from the 2011–12 income year. True if the deduction was reinstated in 2020 as a pandemic measure and the prior position was a zero rate; false if it predates COVID or the prior position was different.

civility.statement: I think this committee needs to understand from the Minister why he thought it was appropriate that the way we define some of our tax legislation is based on words that are put together by the OECD.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested constitutional criticism of the Minister's drafting choice, aimed entirely at the decision and the mechanism. No imputation of bad faith, no reflection on his competence or motives — the standard, met.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is multinational enterprises with consolidated revenues of above €750 million in any two of the proceeding four years.
specificity.explanation: A precise threshold with a stated figure, currency and lookback period — anyone could apply the test to a given enterprise.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I’m pleased to let the member know that the Inland Revenue Department will be providing the guidance and links to the OECD website, to the 25 entities that meet the criteria.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, the mechanism (guidance plus links to the OECD site) and the number of affected entities; no timeframe given.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is multinational enterprises with consolidated revenues of above €750 million in any two of the proceeding four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the revenue threshold and lookback period that bring a multinational group within the GloBE rules the bill incorporates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD Pillar Two GloBE Model Rules, Article 1.1 (scope), and the corresponding scope clause of the NZ Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill; true if the threshold is consolidated group revenue over €750 million in at least two of the four preceding fiscal years, false if the figure or the two-of-four test differs.

veracity.statement: But in terms of that, the 25 organisations that are headquartered in New Zealand that meet the definition of this are already case managed by Inland Revenue.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that 25 New Zealand-headquartered groups fall within the GloBE definition, and that all of them are already under Inland Revenue case management.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue / Regulatory Impact Statement estimates of the number of NZ-headquartered groups above the €750m GloBE threshold, and IRD's Significant Enterprises account-management coverage; true if the in-scope NZ-headquartered count is about 25 and those groups sit in IRD's case-managed population, false if the count is materially different or they are not case managed.

focus.statement: So another question for the Minister is: how many taxpayers do we think in New Zealand will be subject to these particular amendments in this clause 44?
focus.explanation: Names the specific clause before the committee and asks for a concrete number affected by it — squarely on the measure, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think if I quote—and I must say I haven’t heard this quote from a member on that side of the House for a long time—the “poor multinational organisations”, I mean, wow, a lot changes in a week in terms of that!
focus.explanation: Strip out the dig at what the other side supposedly says about multinationals and no policy point remains — no clause, figure or mechanism is engaged, only the opposition's supposed change of position.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So where can New Zealand taxpayers find the information that they need in order to comply with these global anti-base erosion rules?
focus.explanation: Goes directly to how the drafting approach in the bill will operate for those it binds — the substance of the measure, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is because there are a number of countries that have agreed that in terms of the global base erosion risk that exists for multinationals, we should be looking to ensure that there is a minimum taxation rule applied. I think that’s pretty sensible.
rigor.explanation: The ground offered for the policy being sensible is that a number of countries have agreed to it — an appeal to consensus. No mechanism or evidence about the base-erosion risk itself is supplied to carry the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But as soon as we incorporate something by reference, then, even if it’s by reference to another set of New Zealand legislation, it takes at least two steps for someone to find their way through the particular piece of law.
rigor.explanation: A supported inference: incorporation by reference necessarily adds a lookup step, and the accessibility cost she draws from it follows from that premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, that’s an interesting because that says that then, in fact, each of these 25 multinational enterprises (MNEs) has their own specialist tax advisor paid for by Inland Revenue.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: from 'each in-scope group has an IRD case manager' she concludes each has a publicly funded specialist tax adviser. A compliance relationship manager pointing to published guidance does not entail an advisory role, and nothing is offered to bridge the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: From what the Minister was saying about having a case manager who would be able to direct these multinational enterprises to particular pieces of OECD law, that sounds like advising, and I’m not quite sure why Inland Revenue would be in the business of providing advisers to large multinational enterprises.
civility.explanation: A sharp challenge to the administrative arrangement the Minister described, framed on the substance; no imputation of bad faith and no attack on the Minister.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the fact that this is a surprise and that they do this is not necessarily part of this bill, but I can assure the member that this is not a new concept.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the member asked what the case managers actually do (assess compliance, or advise on applying the law). Watts answers a different question — whether the unit is new — so the conclusion that the concern is misplaced does not follow from the premise that the team predates the bill.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Many medium-sized enterprises would quite like to be able to get hold of some easy advice from IRD too, and when we hear about the wait times on call lines—which, you know, happens; there are a lot of people who want to talk to IRD—it just seems to me that the way the Minister has described it and the way the Minister has described that these multinational enterprises will be informed about the OECD model rules does rather suggest that these large multinational enterprises are getting their own specialist tax adviser from Inland Revenue.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy — from the Minister's description of case managers to the conclusion that large MNEs receive a publicly funded specialist tax adviser others must pay for — but it rests on an impression of what the Minister implied rather than on the bill's text or IRD's stated service standards, and the call-wait contrast is anecdotal. Appropriately hedged, so a gap rather than a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the fact that this is a surprise and that they do this is not necessarily part of this bill, but I can assure the member that this is not a new concept.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee and on IRD's existing practice; the passing reference to the last Government is defensive context, not party-bashing. High focus with low rigor is the correct pairing here.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So this involves calculating its GloBE—global anti-base erosion—income and then deducting the amount of its substance-based income exclusion, which is a figure based on the tangible assets and payroll costs in that country.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the operation of the measure before the committee; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I’m conscious of the repetition, but, again, just for context for the member, this team has existed since 1994—right?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific founding date for the Inland Revenue unit that manages significant enterprises.
veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just in regards to the member’s questions in regards to case management, the Inland Revenue only case manage entities that are New Zealand - headquartered entities. rigor.statement: The first is that given that interest deductibility is already available for new builds under the changes that were made under the previous Government, has the Minister got any advice whatsoever or has he considered how making it deductible across the board will actually remove the relative incentive for investment in new supply—a really critical point there with regard to new builds.

rigor.subject: speaker
