veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement accompanying the offshore gambling duty provisions of the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill (Inland Revenue, 2023-24): true if it discusses offshore operators' readiness to collect the duty by the 1 July 2024 start date and rates that risk, false if the RIS contains no such discussion.

veracity.statement: Casinos in New Zealand currently pay a higher tax than online casinos based overseas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a comparative tax burden as at the date of the speech: domestic casinos taxed more heavily than offshore online casinos serving New Zealanders.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The gambling duty, casino duty and problem gambling levy rates payable by licensed New Zealand casinos (Gambling Act 2003 / Gambling Duties Act 1971) compared against the taxes payable by offshore online operators as at March 2024: true if the domestic total exceeds what offshore operators pay, false if offshore operators face equal or greater tax.

divination.statement: Depriving landlords of the ability to be able to claim mortgage interest deductions has made residential property less attractive as an investment, and this is simply a matter of supply and demand, as with more landlords offering properties, upward pressure on rents will resolve.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that upward pressure on rents will ease following the phased restoration of interest deductibility (80% from 1 April 2024, 100% from 1 April 2025).
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (annual growth, stock measure) and MBIE tenancy bond mean weekly rents: true if annual rent inflation by mid-2026 is materially below the rate recorded at March 2024, false if it is unchanged or higher.

specificity.statement: Under this coalition Government and as a result of this bill, from 1 July 2024, offshore operators will be required to pay a gambling duty of 12 percent of gross betting revenue.
specificity.explanation: Names the rate (12 percent), the base (gross betting revenue), the payer (offshore operators) and the start date (1 July 2024). Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: All of these measures, all of these amendments that have been added as a result of this paper, strengthen this bill, and New Zealanders, as a result, will be better off for the changes led by this coalition Government.
specificity.explanation: A summary claim carrying no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named beneficiary group. 'Strengthen this bill' and 'better off' commit to nothing checkable, in contrast to the detailed passages preceding it.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the last few years, where the brightline test was either five years or 10, we had the highest consents ever—the highest consents, applications for people to build homes—and now we are starting to see consents coming down, and yet they want to change this to two years.
rigor.explanation: Treats a temporal coincidence between the brightline setting and consent volumes as evidence that shortening it will not raise construction — a post hoc correlation-as-causation inference with no mechanism offered and no control for interest rates, migration or construction costs.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A house is not going to produce anything other than that house, and if a person, if an investor, doesn’t buy the house, the house doesn’t disappear; the house stays there—someone else can buy that house.
rigor.explanation: A real counter-inference against the Minister's productivity rationale: existing housing stock is fixed, so a transfer of ownership does not add output. Valid as far as it goes, but it quietly assumes the policy affects only existing stock and ignores any claimed effect on new build, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But yet that’s $2.9 billion—$2.9 billion—that cannot go into lunches in schools for children, $2.9 billion that cannot go to help the disabilities community have more access to reprieve, to help more with wheelchair services.
rigor.explanation: Presents the fiscal choice as a strict either/or: the sum is treated as unavailable for any of the named programmes solely because of this bill, with no showing that the alternatives were funded, costed at that amount, or foreclosed by this measure. A false-dichotomy framing of a genuine trade-off.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yet we received pretty opaque answers in response, which once again goes to show the mockery that this Government is making of this institution—this institution of Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: unsatisfying answers in one committee exchange are offered as sufficient to establish a general contempt for Parliament as an institution. Nothing connects the single observation to the sweeping conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is what we’re dealing with here: this Government is saying that they are taking a punt and putting a whole lot of weight on the potential of “could” and the notion of potential downward pressure, when they cannot guarantee us whatsoever that there will be a reduction in rents as a result of this $2.9 billion policy, which, as I have just demonstrated, comes at the trade-off of making those investments—and far, far better investments—in, for example, reducing inequality or poverty or paying to increase the public housing stock, for example.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the rent effect is unguaranteed — tracks the ministerial answer she has just quoted verbatim, which used 'could' and cited advice that tax changes would not significantly move rents in the short run. The inference is well grounded; the weaker half is the assertion that the alternatives are 'far, far better investments', which is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the last few years, where the brightline test was either five years or 10, we had the highest consents ever—the highest consents, applications for people to build homes—and now we are starting to see consents coming down, and yet they want to change this to two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that dwelling consents reached an all-time high during the period when the brightline test was set at five or ten years, and that consents are now declining.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued series (new dwellings, annual totals) for 2015–2024; true if the record annual total falls within the years the brightline test was 5 or 10 years (2015–2023) and the most recent annual totals are below it, false if the record predates that period or consents are not falling.

veracity.statement: At the first reading of this bill, we had members who are now on the Government side not supporting this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MPs now in Government voted against this taxation bill at its first reading, when they were in Opposition, because of the trust tax rate increase.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the first reading of the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023–24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill; true if National and/or ACT members voted against it, false if they voted in favour or the bill passed first reading unopposed.

veracity.statement: This House of Parliament has been asked in fewer than 48 hours to rubber stamp their will without the due scrutiny that we would expect of any Budget or any other piece of legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Parliament was given less than 48 hours between the introduction of the changes and being required to pass them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Order Paper and Hansard record for this bill: the date and time the Minister of Revenue's Amendment Paper was released or tabled, against the date and time of the committee of the whole House and third reading; true if the interval is under 48 hours, false if materially longer.

veracity.statement: We know that we have approximately 120,000 landlords, but we have approximately 1.5 million renters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts there are roughly 120,000 landlords and roughly 1.5 million renters in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Census/Household Economic Survey counts of people living in rented dwellings, and IRD or MBIE bond-lodgement-derived counts of residential landlords; true if both figures are within a reasonable margin of the official estimates, false if either is off by a large multiple. Note the speaker herself flags the landlord figure as uncertain.

focus.statement: A house is not going to produce anything other than that house, and if a person, if an investor, doesn’t buy the house, the house doesn’t disappear; the house stays there—someone else can buy that house.
focus.explanation: Engages the Minister's stated justification for the measure — that the change makes property more productive — rather than the character or record of the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But the issue that we have in front of us right now is that this Government is using the vehicle of an Amendment Paper at the committee of the whole House stage to drop fundamental structural changes to the intention of the legislation as was introduced, bypassing the opportunity for public consultation, engagement, and input, and the conventions of this place, not the least when it comes to something that has a price tag in excess of $3 billion, when we’re talking about those changes not only to tax deductibility but also to the brightline test.
focus.explanation: Names the specific legislative vehicle, the stage at which it was used, the two policy changes it carries and the cost — procedural scrutiny of a named measure, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But yet that’s $2.9 billion—$2.9 billion—that cannot go into lunches in schools for children, $2.9 billion that cannot go to help the disabilities community have more access to reprieve, to help more with wheelchair services.
specificity.explanation: Carries a costed figure and names concrete affected programmes (school lunches, disability support, wheelchair services), but attaches no timeframe, source for the $2.9 billion, or per-programme amounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the issue that we have in front of us right now is that this Government is using the vehicle of an Amendment Paper at the committee of the whole House stage to drop fundamental structural changes to the intention of the legislation as was introduced, bypassing the opportunity for public consultation, engagement, and input, and the conventions of this place, not the least when it comes to something that has a price tag in excess of $3 billion, when we’re talking about those changes not only to tax deductibility but also to the brightline test.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the instrument (Amendment Paper), the stage (committee of the whole House), the two substantive changes and an order-of-magnitude cost; short of exact figures or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that we have approximately 120,000 landlords, but we have approximately 1.5 million renters.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, checkable population figures with the sources for them named in the surrounding sentences (MBIE bond lodgement data, LINZ, the Companies Office); marked as approximate rather than exact.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think it’s shameful—absolutely shameful—that members of the Government want to support a bill that gives a bidding advantage to property investors when we have such low homeownership rates.
civility.explanation: Robust and pointed. The condemnation attaches to the bill and to the act of voting for it rather than to any individual's character or competence, but calling members' conduct 'shameful' edges toward the people rather than staying wholly on the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The other solution that I would put on the table is that we’ve heard a lot about these rock-solid figures, particularly from the now Prime Minister, saying throughout the campaign to “Just trust us because, you know, we’re the party ostensibly of economic management.”, despite the fact that that completely fell apart when any independent economist sought to put a lens over what was being proposed.
civility.explanation: Puts a mocking invented paraphrase in a named individual's mouth and uses 'ostensibly' to sneer at his claim to competence. It stops short of a direct insult and the underlying point is about costings, but the framing targets the person's credibility rather than the numbers.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It seems now that the Labour Party has finally woken up after six years and are in favour of supporting lots of groups that they decided to not fund properly in their time in Government. So we’re left to clean up the programmes, many of which she mentioned, that were underfunded or not funded at all: taxpayer school lunches, Pharmac, disability care.
focus.explanation: A real policy point — three named underfunded programmes (school lunches, Pharmac, disability care) — but the weight of the passage is party framing about Labour 'waking up after six years' rather than the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Parties opposite have continuously campaigned on wasteful spending, and it is bizarre to see that this Government says that wasteful spending is spending on something like the use of my own language, or even school lunches.
focus.explanation: Names two concrete spending areas — te reo Māori funding and school lunches — so there is genuine policy content, but it is framed as an inconsistency in what 'parties opposite' campaigned on rather than an engagement with the provisions at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And when was the last time a National Government did anything good for renters?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's general record. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — it is a rhetorical question about what National is like, not about what the bill does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But I do remember when the last Labour Government increased student allowances by $50, and all of a sudden, magically, my landlord put up my rent by $50 per person, just because they could. That is an example that landlords will find any old reason to lift our rents, and that there hasn’t been an awful lot of research into this particular bill to show the impacts that it will have on renters.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure at issue: whether the interest deductibility change will be passed through to rents. The reasoning is weak, but the subject is the policy, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are very pleased to see interest deductibility restored. It was a bad public policy to remove this from this type of investment class, and the previous Government was warned that this would lead to upward pressure on rents, and that is what occurred.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: rents rose after interest deductibility was removed, therefore the removal caused the rise. No mechanism, magnitude or control for the other drivers of rent inflation over the same period is offered; the fact that officials warned of a risk is treated as establishing that the risk materialised.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: GST on kai rolls in $3.4 billion, on average, per year to the Government, so it looks like the cost to eat is rolling straight to the landlords.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. Two unrelated fiscal figures — GST revenue on food and the cost of restoring interest deductibility — are placed side by side and the similarity in size is treated as showing that one funds the other. Nothing in the bill hypothecates GST on food to landlords, and no such link is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This clearly shows that we over-contribute to the system—the system that continues to suppress us, even after the fact that everything we’ve ever known has been taxed and axed from us: our natural resources, land, water, language, and culture.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. A gross tax contribution figure cannot establish over-contribution without the other side of the ledger — what the same population receives back, and what a proportionate contribution would be. The word 'clearly' carries the inference that the premise does not.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I do remember when the last Labour Government increased student allowances by $50, and all of a sudden, magically, my landlord put up my rent by $50 per person, just because they could. That is an example that landlords will find any old reason to lift our rents, and that there hasn’t been an awful lot of research into this particular bill to show the impacts that it will have on renters.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single personal anecdote about one landlord to a claim about landlord behaviour in general, and then couples it with an argument from absence of evidence — that little research exists is offered as support for the conclusion rather than as a reason to withhold one.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We are very pleased to see interest deductibility restored. It was a bad public policy to remove this from this type of investment class, and the previous Government was warned that this would lead to upward pressure on rents, and that is what occurred.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that the previous Government received official advice warning that removing interest deductibility on residential rental property would put upward pressure on rents, and (b) that rents subsequently rose.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement and Inland Revenue/Treasury advice accompanying the 2021 interest limitation rules: true if that advice explicitly warned of upward pressure on rents; false if it did not. Combined with the Stats NZ rental price index for 2021–2023: true if rents rose over that period, false if flat or falling.

veracity.statement: This 2 percent makes an average of $26 million—average—per year, and only pay 9.4 percent in tax.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the wealthiest 2 percent of New Zealanders have an average income of $26 million a year and pay an effective tax rate of 9.4 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue's High-Wealth Individuals Research Project (April 2023) and the associated Treasury Tax and Transfer Analysis: true if that research reports an effective tax rate of about 9.4 percent and average economic income of about $26 million for a group that constitutes roughly 2 percent of the population; false if the 9.4 percent figure applies to a materially narrower group (e.g. a few hundred families) or if the income figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s not just me who thinks that; it’s all of my friends who are renters, and even Treasury agrees with me that there’s no evidence that this bill will pass on any benefits to renters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury advised there is no evidence the restoration of interest deductibility will deliver benefits to renters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury/Inland Revenue Regulatory Impact Statement and departmental advice on restoring interest deductibility for residential investment property (2023–24): true if that advice states there is no clear evidence of pass-through of the tax change to renters; false if it forecasts rent reductions or pass-through to tenants.

specificity.statement: New Zealand First is committed to ensuring that our tax policies are equitable and transparent, and supportive of economic growth and social wellbeing.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — equitable, transparent, supportive of growth and wellbeing — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision of the bill. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This 2 percent makes an average of $26 million—average—per year, and only pay 9.4 percent in tax.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, checkable figures attached to a defined group: average annual income of $26 million and an effective tax rate of 9.4 percent for the wealthiest 2 percent.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In my recent research, I have found that 20 percent of the people in my rohe of Hauraki-Waikato that earn over $50k in income contribute $190 million of our tax to the system.
specificity.explanation: A named electorate, an income threshold, a population share and a dollar contribution. Precise enough that someone could go and test it against regional income tax data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Better solutions that we, the Greens, are constantly advocating for include more public housing to clear the public housing wait-list and bring down median rents across the country. We’re pushing for rent controls. We’re pushing for a rental warrant of fitness.
specificity.explanation: Three named mechanisms — public housing build, rent controls, a rental warrant of fitness — which is a real direction, but with no quantity, cost, design or timeframe attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yesterday, in question time, our Prime Minister said that this Government was unapologetically on the side of renters—well, that’s the joke of the year, isn’t it?
civility.explanation: Aimed at a claim rather than the Prime Minister's character, but 'the joke of the year' is mockery rather than rebuttal — it derides the sincerity of the statement instead of engaging why it is wrong. Pointed and sneering, short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’re doing it for themselves, knowing that most people in this House own multiple houses and make their living off people like me who are renting their houses. And they’re doing it to line the pockets of their rich landlord mates.
civility.explanation: Imputes corrupt motive to members opposite — that they legislated for their own property interests and those of their 'mates'. It stops short of naming and insulting an individual, but attributing self-dealing to colleagues is a genuine civility failure, not robust policy criticism.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Let’s not forget who is paying for this cash handout to landlords: it’s the kids at school who won’t be getting school lunches anymore, it’s disabled people and their carers, and it’s people on benefits, whose lives will get much worse so that landlords can get even richer.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that students currently receiving school lunches will lose them as a consequence of this Government's fiscal choices.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 and subsequent Ka Ora, Ka Ako | Healthy School Lunches Programme decisions: true if the programme is discontinued or its coverage reduced so that students who were receiving lunches no longer do; false if the programme continues to serve the same or a larger cohort.

civility.statement: Catherine Wedd in her contribution said this bill will improve the economy. No, it won’t. It will have the opposite effect. It will once again encourage over-investment by landlords in the residential property sector, sucking out investment from the productive economy and driving up house prices so that it will no longer be affordable by people who just want one home to live in.
civility.explanation: Names a member and directly contradicts her claim, but the disagreement is entirely about the economic effect of the bill; no attack on her person.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Catherine Wedd in her contribution said this bill will improve the economy. No, it won’t. It will have the opposite effect. It will once again encourage over-investment by landlords in the residential property sector, sucking out investment from the productive economy and driving up house prices so that it will no longer be affordable by people who just want one home to live in.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that restoring interest deductibility will increase investor purchasing of residential property and push house prices up beyond first-home-buyer affordability.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: REINZ House Price Index and RBNZ C31 new-lending-by-borrower-type series for the two years following the bill's commencement (1 April 2024); true if the investor share of new mortgage lending rises materially and the house price index rises in real terms, false if the investor share is flat or falls and real house prices do not rise.

divination.statement: They won’t be going up at that rate.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that following the restoration of interest deductibility, rent increases will run below the rate of increase seen under the previous government (which he put at $170/week over six years, roughly $28/week per year).
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE Tenancy Services bond-lodgement national median weekly rent for the two years from April 2024; true if the average annual increase is materially below ~$28 per week per year, false if it matches or exceeds that pace.

veracity.statement: Every year, every quarter, since this change was made in 2021, inflation has been higher than the increase in rents.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in every quarter from the 2021 interest-deductibility change to the date of speaking, annual CPI inflation exceeded the annual increase in rents.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI all-groups annual inflation compared with the CPI rentals-for-housing (or MBIE bond-lodgement mean rent) annual increase for each quarter from Q4 2021 to Q1 2024; true if CPI exceeded rent growth in every one of those quarters, false if rent growth exceeded CPI in any quarter.

veracity.statement: In fact, under the last Labour Government, the number of houses being built in Auckland doubled, because we got the settings right across both planning and other matters, like infrastructure financing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland dwelling construction roughly doubled over the 2017–2023 Labour Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ new dwelling consents (and code compliance certificates) for the Auckland region, 2017 calendar/year-ended figures versus 2022–2023; true if the annual count approximately doubled or more, false if the increase is materially less than double.

veracity.statement: Total lending to first-home buyers averaged 12 percent between 2014 and 2017, and 29 percent went to investors.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over 2014–2017 first-home buyers averaged 12 percent of new residential mortgage lending and investors 29 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ C31 new residential mortgage lending by borrower type, averaged over 2014–2017; true if the first-home-buyer share is approximately 12% and the investor share approximately 29%, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: Rents went up under the last Labour Government $170 a week. That’s nearly $9,000 a year that every rented house had to find under Labour.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that weekly rents rose by $170 over the term of the 2017–2023 Labour Government, equating to nearly $9,000 a year per rented dwelling.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Tenancy Services bond-lodgement national median/mean weekly rent, October 2017 versus late 2023; true if the increase is approximately $170 per week, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: Well, we know, as Nancy Lu said, that 80 percent of landlords own just one property.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 80 percent of New Zealand residential landlords own a single rental property.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD residential property owner data and/or MBIE bond-lodgement analysis of landlord portfolio size; true if approximately 80% of landlords hold exactly one rental property, false if the share is materially different.

rigor.statement: This had no effect on new supply, because the new supply was always exempt from the rule.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference given its premise: if new builds were carved out of the interest-limitation rule, the rule cannot directly have reduced new supply. The gap is that an exempt category can still be affected indirectly (e.g. via investor balance sheets), which is not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So rents didn’t go up higher than inflation, proving the point that rents are more determined by the marginal cost of new supply coming into the market, which was not changed by these rules.
rigor.explanation: Treats a single correlation as proof of a causal mechanism. That rents tracked below inflation is consistent with many explanations; no counterfactual or alternative cause is excluded, so the conclusion about what determines rents is not established by the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Total lending to first-home buyers averaged 12 percent between 2014 and 2017, and 29 percent went to investors.
specificity.explanation: Named data source, defined period and two precise percentage shares — directly checkable against the published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This taxation bill is sensible, it’s pragmatic, it’s fair and reasonable, and it will help our country get back on track.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues and a slogan; no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named effect that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They are serving the interests of the capital class, who pay lower rates of tax than working New Zealanders, once again—always have, always will.
focus.explanation: A characterisation of what the other party is fundamentally like and whose interests they always serve, rather than engagement with any measure, figure or mechanism in the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Labour tried to phase it out—they’d begun their phase-out period—and what happened? They failed, and failed badly, and renters were the loser.
focus.explanation: A real policy is named (the phase-out of interest deductibility) but the weight of the sentence is a verdict on the other party's failure rather than on the mechanism or its measured effects.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We will be looking for the evidence of rents coming down, because there is not a single economic commentator that agrees with the members opposite in terms of what the impacts are.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no economic commentator agrees with the claim that restoring interest deductibility will lower rents — an absolute claim about the state of published economic commentary in March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published NZ economic commentary (bank economists, Infometrics, NZIER, university economists, media commentary) around March 2024 on the rent effects of restoring interest deductibility; false if any identifiable economic commentator publicly agreed that the change would put downward pressure on rents, true if no such commentator can be found.

veracity.statement: If we take the gambling tax, for example, there were claims that there was going to be $176 million a year collected through this tax.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim she attributes to National's election campaign — that the offshore gambling duty would raise $176 million a year.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 fiscal plan / tax plan costings for the online casino gambling duty; true if the annual revenue figure published there is ~$176m, false if it is materially different.

veracity.statement: The problem that the Government now faces when putting together the Budget—with this taxation as the basis of it—is that the IRD’s regulatory impact statement for this bill tells us there’s going to be $35 million a year collected, or $155 million over a four-year period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the revenue figures contained in Inland Revenue's regulatory impact statement for this bill: $35m a year, $155m over four years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IRD regulatory impact statement accompanying the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill Amendment Paper; true if it forecasts ~$35m per year / ~$155m over the forecast period, false if the figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: What we do know is that this policy is going to cost $800 million more than what the National Party were on campaign telling New Zealanders that it would cost.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific $800 million gap between the official fiscal cost of restoring interest deductibility and the cost National published during the campaign.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the fiscal cost of interest deductibility restoration in National's 2023 tax plan against Treasury/IRD costings attached to the 2024 Amendment Paper; true if the difference is ~$800m, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Let’s look at the evidence. In the midst of a cost of living crisis, we saw rents consistently rising at less than the rate of inflation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that during the recent cost-of-living period rent increases consistently ran below CPI inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (flow and/or stock measure) compared with CPI annual inflation over 2021-2023; true if annual rent growth was consistently below CPI over that period, false if it exceeded CPI in a material part of it.

rigor.statement: We will be looking for the evidence of rents coming down, because there is not a single economic commentator that agrees with the members opposite in terms of what the impacts are.
rigor.explanation: The reason offered for expecting rents not to fall is the unanimity of commentators rather than any mechanism or evidence — an appeal to authority/consensus, with nothing shown about why the policy would not affect rents.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let’s look at the evidence. In the midst of a cost of living crisis, we saw rents consistently rising at less than the rate of inflation.
rigor.explanation: Offers a correlation (rents rising slower than inflation) as evidence that the previous government's interest deductibility settings worked, with no step connecting the policy to the observed rent path — post hoc reasoning.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The problem that the Government now faces when putting together the Budget—with this taxation as the basis of it—is that the IRD’s regulatory impact statement for this bill tells us there’s going to be $35 million a year collected, or $155 million over a four-year period.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document, an annual figure and a four-year total — directly checkable against the RIS.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we do know is that this policy is going to cost $800 million more than what the National Party were on campaign telling New Zealanders that it would cost.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named policy against a named campaign costing, with a figure attached — accountability, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a Government that is going to plunge us back into the days of the housing crisis with no solution, simply telling councils to go and zone land. A “build it and they will come” approach with no plan for how to turn that into build-ready or serviced land is putting us back a decade from where we need to be in addressing a housing crisis.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the government's housing approach — zoning directives to councils and the missing step of servicing land — rather than the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We will see the bad old days of mum and dad speculators getting into the burbs, competing with their kids on existing houses rather than doing what we as a country need them to do, and that is building new stock.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that reversing the interest deductibility rules will shift investor activity back toward buying existing dwellings rather than new builds.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: CoreLogic NZ buyer classification data on the investor share of purchases of existing dwellings versus new builds; true if the investor share of existing-dwelling purchases rises materially through 2025 relative to 2023-24 while the new-build share falls, false if the pattern does not shift or moves the other way.

civility.statement: The members opposite seem to have drunk the Kool-Aid and convinced themselves that this is going to solve the housing crisis, that this is something that they think is going to be.
civility.explanation: Mockery of opposing members as brainwashed believers rather than engagement with their argument; short of a direct insult but sneering.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This just reads code for tax breaks for their mates, because what we’re seeing is some kind of magical belief that these changes are going to lead to an increase in supply.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that the policy is a favour to the government's 'mates' — and derides their reasoning as magical belief.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If these members can lift their horizons beyond their desks for just a moment, they can see the kinds of policy measures that need to be put in place.
civility.explanation: Condescension toward other members' narrowness rather than engagement with what they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And we hear the howls from opposite, but some simple counting—and I suggest to those members that they do learn to count; it’s a very important political skill—of the gap between the number of people in the country and the number of houses we need closed for the first time in decades in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: 'Learn to count' is a jibe at other members' basic competence, inserted into an otherwise substantive point about the housing supply gap.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, I do, and the Minister has a very important job to do, fixing a system that is, frankly, not fit for purpose which she inherited from that member’s previous Government, and I am confident she’s going to do exactly that.
focus.explanation: There is a policy referent (the disability support system) but no mechanism, figure or measure is named; the weight of the answer is blame directed at the previous Government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we are committing to is FamilyBoost, which is a programme to give 100,000 low and middle income working families some relief so that they can put that towards their early childhood education centre costs, and we’re also committing to tax relief for low and middle income workers—a group, frankly, that the Labour Party and Te Pāti Māori used to care deeply about.
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme (FamilyBoost) and the number of families it targets, but closes with a content-free swipe about what the opposition parties 'used to care' about.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Could I ask the Prime Minister as to whether his Government is going to be guided by what may be described as the Roosevelt principle: that we’ll try our hardest but we may not always get it right, but we’ll keep on trying, rather than saying that we’re perfect, never apologise, and say that we’re the podium of truth?
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or figure is engaged; the question is entirely a contrast between the Government's posture and a jibe at the previous administration's 'podium of truth'.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As we have said, she didn’t bring it to Cabinet, and as a result there was no Cabinet discussion. That is something the Minister has apologised for, and she will do going forward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whaikaha changes to disability support entitlements were not taken to Cabinet and that Minister Simmonds has apologised for that.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous record (Hansard, Cabinet minutes summaries, Minister's public statements March 2024); true if Simmonds publicly apologised for not bringing the changes to Cabinet and the changes were not Cabinet-considered, false if she made no such apology or the matter went to Cabinet.

veracity.statement: But what I’d say to you is important is that this is a Minister that is actually making sure there is more money going in this year than there was last year under that previous Government, and—importantly—in Budget 2024, there’ll be even more money in place for people who need the disabled support and resource they need.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that disability support funding in the current financial year exceeds the previous year's funding under the last Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Health / Whaikaha—Ministry of Disable People appropriations in the 2023/24 Estimates and Supplementary Estimates compared with 2022/23 actuals; true if total disability support appropriation is higher in 2023/24, false if flat or lower.

veracity.statement: Does he believe the Minister for Disability Issues’ claim that “since 2018, the number of people accessing disability supports has increased by around 50 percent compared to population growth of 8.5 percent” is a sign that too many people are claiming disability support?
veracity.explanation: Relays Simmonds' figures: roughly 50 percent growth in people accessing disability supports since 2018 against 8.5 percent population growth.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whaikaha/Ministry of Health client numbers for disability support services 2018 vs 2023 and Stats NZ population estimates for the same period; true if the growth figures are approximately 50% and 8.5%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, what they need is a Government that’s going to have responsible financial management, rather than an 84 percent increase in Government spending, which drove up domestic inflation, which drove up interest rates, which put the economy into shrinking, into recession, and creates a rising risk of unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Government spending rose by 84 percent (under the previous Government).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenditure series comparing 2017/18 with 2022/23; true if total core Crown expenses rose by approximately 84%, false if materially different or if the figure only holds on a selectively chosen base.

veracity.statement: Our economy, for four of the last five quarters, has been shrinking and been in recession.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand GDP contracted in four of the five quarters up to March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP (production measure, seasonally adjusted) for the five quarters to December 2023; true if four of those five quarters recorded negative growth, false if fewer did.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by the Government’s decision to only increase the minimum wage by 2 percent when inflation is at 4.7 percent, which is a cut to the minimum wage in real terms?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the announced minimum wage increase is 2 percent and that inflation stands at 4.7 percent.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE minimum wage announcement for 1 April 2024 (dollar rates before and after) and Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the December 2023 quarter; true if the rise is ~2% and annual CPI is 4.7%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: What is his response to the fact that this effective cut to the minimum wage will increase child poverty rates, given that 64 percent of families in poverty are in work?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 64 percent of families in poverty have someone in work.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ household incomes / child poverty data or MSD analysis on the share of children in poverty living in working households; true if approximately 64%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I had a paper that was given to me by Whaikaha in February which noted, from providers, that the fund had been used for such expenses. I didn’t make any insinuation that those would be inappropriate; that was just stating what the fund had been used for at that time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existence of a February paper from Whaikaha recording provider reports that the flexible funding had been spent on things such as pedicures, massages and overseas travel.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whaikaha briefing paper of February 2024 (as tabled or released under OIA); true if such a paper exists and records those provider reports, false if no such document exists or it does not contain that content.

specificity.statement: This tax relief—and Mr Parker will be pleased to hear this—will be funded from within the operating allowance, and the operating allowance will be less than the $3.5 billion allowance indicated in the half-year update. This means the Government will not be borrowing extra to pay for tax relief, and it means tax relief will not be adding to inflationary pressures.
specificity.explanation: Names the funding mechanism, a specific dollar benchmark ($3.5 billion) and the document it comes from; checkable against the Budget Policy Statement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The legacy we inherited of elevated, lazy spending will take several Budgets to fix, but the first steps will be taken in Budget 2024.
specificity.explanation: A characterisation of past spending as 'elevated, lazy' with no figures, named programmes or mechanism, and 'several Budgets' gives no dated commitment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he stand by the Government’s decision to only increase the minimum wage by 2 percent when inflation is at 4.7 percent, which is a cut to the minimum wage in real terms?
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures and a named policy decision; anyone could check the minimum wage rate and the CPI print.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I had a paper that was given to me by Whaikaha in February which noted, from providers, that the fund had been used for such expenses. I didn’t make any insinuation that those would be inappropriate; that was just stating what the fund had been used for at that time.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (a Whaikaha paper), the month, and what it recorded, but gives no numbers, no title and no quantification of how often the fund was used that way.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This tax relief—and Mr Parker will be pleased to hear this—will be funded from within the operating allowance, and the operating allowance will be less than the $3.5 billion allowance indicated in the half-year update. This means the Government will not be borrowing extra to pay for tax relief, and it means tax relief will not be adding to inflationary pressures.
rigor.explanation: The step from 'funded within the allowance' to 'no extra borrowing' follows, but the further step to 'will not add to inflationary pressures' is a gap — reallocating spending toward tax cuts can still change demand; the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, what they need is a Government that’s going to have responsible financial management, rather than an 84 percent increase in Government spending, which drove up domestic inflation, which drove up interest rates, which put the economy into shrinking, into recession, and creates a rising risk of unemployment.
rigor.explanation: A single causal chain (spending → inflation → interest rates → recession → unemployment) is asserted without any evidence linking the links; the conclusion rests on unsupported mono-causal attribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Spending on front-line services will be reprioritised, despite some people practically fainting at the thought that the Government could do things differently and more effectively, and the Budget will deliver on Government policy commitments, including many of those in the coalition agreements.
civility.explanation: Mockery of unnamed opponents ('practically fainting') sneers rather than engaging their objection, though no individual is named or insulted directly.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she agree with her office, who told Newshub that they didn’t have any numbers but that the Minister had heard it anecdotally, and, if so, does this Minister make policy decisions based on hearsay?
civility.explanation: Pointed and grounded in a reported statement from the Minister's own office, but the closing 'decisions based on hearsay' edges from the evidence base toward the Minister's personal competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she accept that her statements and actions haven’t been evidence-based and have led to disability communities losing trust in her as their Minister and to the Prime Minister stripping her of her major decision-making ability in this portfolio and giving it to Cabinet?
civility.explanation: Goes beyond the decision to the Minister personally — her trustworthiness in the role and her loss of standing with the Prime Minister — rather than confining the attack to the policy or the process.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: What is his response to the fact that this effective cut to the minimum wage will increase child poverty rates, given that 64 percent of families in poverty are in work?
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a real-terms minimum wage cut will push child poverty rates up.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Child Poverty Statistics (material hardship and the below-50%-of-median after-housing-costs measures); true if child poverty rises for the year to June 2025 relative to the year to June 2024 beyond sampling error, false if it falls or is statistically unchanged.

specificity.statement: Well, thank you for the opportunity to speak on the third reading of this bill, which I support, because on this side of the House we are absolutely laser focused on strengthening this economy and ensuring that hard-working New Zealanders can keep more of what they earn.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general orientation — 'laser focused on strengthening this economy', 'keep more of what they earn' — with no figure, mechanism, threshold or date. She had the opportunity to name provisions of the bill (as she does later) and did not here.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our top income tax rate is 39 percent. Now, the top income tax rate in Australia is 45 percent, so we have comparatively low income-tax rates.
specificity.explanation: Two named jurisdictions with exact rates, offered as a checkable comparison rather than a general assertion of low taxation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A National-led Government is delivering positive changes in a timely manner.
specificity.explanation: A slogan: 'positive changes' and 'timely manner' carry no figure, mechanism, provision or date, in a speech where she does elsewhere name provisions.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is actually a “back to normal” brightline test requirement that brings greater flexibility for property owners, and, according to Stuff in 2021, the latest Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment data shows nearly 80 percent of residential landowners in New Zealand own just one rental property each—80 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names a source, a year, an agency dataset and a precise proportion, so a reader can go and check the figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But just another area where we are going to improve things is with interest deductibility, which will put downward pressures on rents and not keep adding costs to landlords, which are then passed on to renters. We need to put downward pressure on rents.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — the restoration of interest deductibility — and its claimed mechanism and effect on rents. No party framing, no characterisation of opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill gives tax breaks to people who already own a substantial asset in addition to their own home, while it still continues to tax workers for every single dollar they earn.
focus.explanation: Names the measure before the House and states who it claims the bill benefits and who it does not — a distributional claim about the bill itself, not about the other party's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But just another area where we are going to improve things is with interest deductibility, which will put downward pressures on rents and not keep adding costs to landlords, which are then passed on to renters. We need to put downward pressure on rents.
rigor.explanation: The inference is that removing a landlord cost lowers rents, resting on an unstated and contested assumption of full cost pass-through in a market-priced good. The chain is intelligible but nothing is offered to establish the pass-through step, so there is a real gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The changes that we put in place around interest deductibility were to try to curb this rampant trading in homes. And it worked—it worked. More homes were brought within the reach of first-home buyers. More people were able to buy homes, and this is critically important for all sorts of reasons.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the policy was introduced, an outcome is asserted to have followed, and causation is declared ('it worked') with no data, counterfactual or mechanism offered to rule out interest rates, supply, or the wider market cycle.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The evidence is really straightforward. Rents are not primarily driven by landlords’ costs; rents are driven by the market. That’s where rents come from. In fact, the rent increases in recent years have exactly matched inflation in recent years. And rents, where they have started to fall, have done so because more houses have been built.
rigor.explanation: An argument is genuinely advanced against cost pass-through and two supporting observations are offered (rents tracking inflation; falls where supply rose). But 'the evidence is really straightforward' substitutes assertion for citation, and the supply claim is a correlation presented as the cause, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The prospect of the shorter-term gains will stimulate economic activity in New Zealand and increase property transactions, which will lead to higher demand for related goods and services: construction, renovation, real estate agency services, repairs and maintenance, and everything that goes with maintaining a rental property.
rigor.explanation: A coherent chain — lower holding period requirement, more trading, more demand for related services — but each link is asserted rather than supported, and no estimate, evidence or offsetting factor (interest rates, supply) is offered to show the first step will actually bind.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: But just another area where we are going to improve things is with interest deductibility, which will put downward pressures on rents and not keep adding costs to landlords, which are then passed on to renters. We need to put downward pressure on rents.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that restoring interest deductibility for residential landlords will exert downward pressure on rents.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond data / Stats NZ rental price index for new tenancies: true if national median weekly rent growth decelerates materially or turns negative over the two years following the phased restoration of interest deductibility from 1 April 2024; false if rent growth continues at or above its pre-April-2024 pace.

divination.statement: The prospect of the shorter-term gains will stimulate economic activity in New Zealand and increase property transactions, which will lead to higher demand for related goods and services: construction, renovation, real estate agency services, repairs and maintenance, and everything that goes with maintaining a rental property.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that shortening the brightline test to two years will increase property transaction volumes and consequent demand in construction, renovation and real estate services.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: REINZ monthly residential sales volumes: true if national sales counts in the twelve months following the 1 July 2024 brightline reduction exceed the preceding twelve months by a clear margin, false if volumes are flat or lower.

veracity.statement: Our top income tax rate is 39 percent. Now, the top income tax rate in Australia is 45 percent, so we have comparatively low income-tax rates.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific statutory top marginal personal income tax rates: 39 percent in New Zealand and 45 percent in Australia, as at March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue personal income tax rate schedule and the Australian Taxation Office resident individual marginal rate schedule for the 2023-24 year; true if NZ's top rate is 39% and Australia's top marginal rate is 45%, false if either figure differs.

veracity.statement: Now, it’s a little bit ambiguous so we clarified that intention by picking up the brightline test that was introduced by the previous National Government and extending it to five years and then to 10 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a legislative history: the brightline test was introduced under a National-led government and subsequently extended by the Labour-led government first to five years and then to ten.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ statute book and Hansard: true if the brightline test was enacted under the National-led government (Taxation (Bright-line Test for Residential Land) Act 2015) and extended to five years and then to ten years under the Labour-led government; false if the introducing government or either extension step differs.

veracity.statement: The changes that we put in place around interest deductibility were to try to curb this rampant trading in homes. And it worked—it worked. More homes were brought within the reach of first-home buyers. More people were able to buy homes, and this is critically important for all sorts of reasons.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that after the previous government's interest deductibility restrictions, more first-home buyers were able to purchase homes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: CoreLogic/REINZ first-home buyer share and count of residential purchases: true if the first-home buyer share of buyers rose in the period following the October 2021 interest deductibility changes relative to the preceding period, false if it was flat or fell.

veracity.statement: In fact, the rent increases in recent years have exactly matched inflation in recent years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that recent rent increases have matched consumer price inflation over the same period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (or MBIE bond data median rents) compared with the Stats NZ CPI over the roughly three years to March 2024; true if cumulative rent growth is within about a percentage point of cumulative CPI growth, false if it diverges materially.

veracity.statement: This bill does nothing to help the lowest-income earners. It does nothing to help the marginalised. It does nothing to help anyone except for people who are already high paid.
veracity.explanation: An absolute claim that the Taxation (Annual Rates for 2023-24, Multinational Tax, and Remedial Matters) Bill contains no provision benefiting anyone other than high earners.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacted text of the named bill and its regulatory impact statements; false if it contains any provision benefiting non-high earners (for example the North Island weather event rollover relief, or the global anti-base erosion rules raising revenue), true only if no such provision exists.

veracity.statement: This is actually a “back to normal” brightline test requirement that brings greater flexibility for property owners, and, according to Stuff in 2021, the latest Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment data shows nearly 80 percent of residential landowners in New Zealand own just one rental property each—80 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, citing a 2021 Stuff report of MBIE data, that nearly 80 percent of residential landlords in New Zealand own only one rental property.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE tenancy bond / landlord ownership data as reported in 2021; true if approximately 80% of residential landlords are recorded as owning a single rental property, false if the share is materially different (e.g. below about 70%).

specificity.statement: We are deeply committed on delivering our net carbon zero 2050 goals, and one of the ways we’re going to do that is doubling the amount of renewable electricity in this country.
specificity.explanation: Names a dated target (net carbon zero 2050) and one concrete mechanism (doubling renewable electricity), but gives no baseline, cost, or date for the doubling.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to make sure that there are more jobs for people in the New Zealand economy, and what we’re doing is wanting to grow our economy. One of the ways we do that is by introducing fast-track consenting.
specificity.explanation: Mostly generic aspiration about jobs and growth; the only checkable content is the named fast-track consenting policy, with no figures, scope or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I can guarantee is that this is a Government that is working incredibly hard to deliver on our climate change commitments. That is what we’re doing. We’re also a Government that’s determined to grow our economy and deliver on our climate change commitments. We can do both those things at the same time.
specificity.explanation: A statement of effort and determination with no figure, mechanism, named commitment or timeframe; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My priorities to simplify and improve the Holidays Act, increase certainty for those in contracting relationships, reform health and safety, and put in place measures for the performance of front-line services will help increase labour market flexibility and improve business confidence, and I believe that these moves will be positive steps for both businesses and workers.
specificity.explanation: Names four policy areas including a specific statute (the Holidays Act), but supplies no mechanism, cost, timeframe or measurable target for any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But within Gloriavale, I am aware that the Minister for Education, for example, has members within the education portfolio working with Gloriavale to ensure that education standards are upheld. I am also aware that the Minister for community and social development has members of her officials who are working to ensure that members who leave the group also have support, and within my purview, which is workplace relations and safety, the labour inspectorate is continuing to do work to make sure that the rights of workers are upheld under the minimum standards that we expect of all people across New Zealand. It is not necessary for there to be added bureaucracy to ensure that all of these relations can happen within their respective purviews.
specificity.explanation: Names specific agencies and portfolios (Minister for Education, social development officials, the labour inspectorate) and what each is said to be doing, but gives no resourcing, coordination mechanism or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There will be two prizes: one prize of $100,000 will be awarded to someone who has demonstrated outstanding achievement and contribution to the New Zealand space sector, and a further prize will be awarded to a student in years 12 or 13 and the inaugural winner will receive a trip to visit Rocket Lab space facilities both here in New Zealand and in the United States.
specificity.explanation: Exact prize value, number of prizes, eligibility criteria and the named recipient organisation for the student prize's trip.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On 31 January, I welcomed an agreement with Australia that will benefit New Zealand researchers to participate in collaborative research projects through Australia’s SmartSat Cooperative Research Centre; on 5 March, together with the climate change Minister, the Hon Simon Watts, I welcomed the successful launch of MethaneSAT, a state-of-the-art satellite designed to accurately detect methane emissions and contribute to global efforts to combat climate change; and just last week, we announced New Zealand’s research being sent to the International Space Station.
specificity.explanation: Three named initiatives with specific dates, a named partner institution, a named satellite and a named co-Minister — each item is directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: For the benefit of the country and the House and the member asking the question, could the Prime Minister tell us: what on earth would a climate change job be?
civility.explanation: Framed as a question but functions as mockery of the questioner's premise; the sneering 'what on earth' ridicules rather than engaging the substance, though it stops short of a direct insult to the member.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For the benefit of the country and the House and the member asking the question, could the Prime Minister tell us: what on earth would a climate change job be?
focus.explanation: Names no policy, measure, figure or outcome; it is a rhetorical dismissal aimed at how the other side frames the issue rather than at the substance of climate-related employment.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But within Gloriavale, I am aware that the Minister for Education, for example, has members within the education portfolio working with Gloriavale to ensure that education standards are upheld. I am also aware that the Minister for community and social development has members of her officials who are working to ensure that members who leave the group also have support, and within my purview, which is workplace relations and safety, the labour inspectorate is continuing to do work to make sure that the rights of workers are upheld under the minimum standards that we expect of all people across New Zealand. It is not necessary for there to be added bureaucracy to ensure that all of these relations can happen within their respective purviews.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: each relevant portfolio is doing its own Gloriavale work, therefore a cross-government group is unnecessary. The premises support the conclusion only if the group's sole value was duplicating portfolio work — the coordination function the question asked about is assumed away rather than addressed, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There is a great opportunity for New Zealand to capture an even larger share of a sector projected to reach—and wait for this—US$1 trillion by 2040.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that published projections put the global space sector at around US$1 trillion by 2040. The checkable element is whether such a projection exists as described, not whether it comes to pass.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: industry forecasters cited by the Minister
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published industry/investment-bank forecasts of global space economy revenue (e.g. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, McKinsey, or MBIE/NZ Space Agency briefing material) for 2040; true if a recognised forecast puts the sector at approximately US$1 trillion by 2040, false if the mainstream forecasts for that date are materially different in magnitude or year.

veracity.statement: On 31 January, I welcomed an agreement with Australia that will benefit New Zealand researchers to participate in collaborative research projects through Australia’s SmartSat Cooperative Research Centre; on 5 March, together with the climate change Minister, the Hon Simon Watts, I welcomed the successful launch of MethaneSAT, a state-of-the-art satellite designed to accurately detect methane emissions and contribute to global efforts to combat climate change; and just last week, we announced New Zealand’s research being sent to the International Space Station.
veracity.explanation: Three dated factual claims: a 31 January 2024 NZ–Australia SmartSat CRC agreement, a MethaneSAT launch welcomed on 5 March 2024, and an announcement in the week before 27 March 2024 of NZ research going to the ISS.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Beehive.govt.nz ministerial releases and NZ Space Agency/MBIE records for January–March 2024, plus the MethaneSAT/SpaceX launch record; true if each of the three events occurred on or about the dates given, false if any date or event is materially wrong (e.g. no SmartSat agreement in January, or MethaneSAT launching outside early March 2024).

focus.statement: Does she accept, based on what her office has told Newshub, that her statements and actions haven’t been based on evidence and they have led to disability communities writing in droves, saying that they have lost their trust in her, and to the Prime Minister saying that Cabinet will be making major decisions on her behalf?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the Minister's handling of the disability portfolio, citing a named evidentiary basis and a specific reported consequence (Cabinet taking over decisions). This is named-policy scrutiny, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a Government that understands working people have done it tough for too long with the prolonged cost of living crisis that the previous Government presided over. Our Budget will make sure that they get relief in their bank accounts and back pockets, that we target additional spending carefully to the services they rely on, and that we won’t waste it like the people opposite did.
focus.explanation: A gesture at Budget priorities, but the weight of it is comparative party framing — who presided over the crisis and who wasted money — with no measure, figure or mechanism named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Does she accept, based on what her office has told Newshub, that her statements and actions haven’t been based on evidence and they have led to disability communities writing in droves, saying that they have lost their trust in her, and to the Prime Minister saying that Cabinet will be making major decisions on her behalf?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, within a question, that the Prime Minister said Cabinet will make major decisions on the Minister for Disability Issues' behalf.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon in March 2024 (press conference transcripts / contemporaneous media reports); true if he stated that Cabinet would be making or signing off major decisions in the disability portfolio in place of the Minister, false if no such statement exists.

specificity.statement: They deserve better than a Minister for Disability Issues who knew that Whaikaha had funding issues on 15 December, did absolutely nothing, did not alert that to her finance Minister or Prime Minister, didn’t ask for more money for Whaikaha, but, instead, on 14 March signed out a briefing approving changes that were announced and implemented with immediate effect on 18 March—changes that left our disability communities blindsided and, in their own words, “devastated”.

rigor.statement: He’s making sure the freshwater rules and the on-farm management is fixed up to be more realistic, and respect the fact that farmers actually want to look after their land; they’re not trying to destroy their own livelihood. And the people who suggested for too long that they’re that stupid have been insulting and, frankly, ignorant of how rural New Zealand actually works.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the case for freshwater regulation rests on the cumulative external effects of farming, not on a claim that farmers are stupid or want to wreck their own land. Refuting the invented position leaves the actual argument for the rules untouched, so the conclusion that the rules should be loosened does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s why that fund was always underutilised. When flexibility was brought in, it’s not that need miraculously increased; it’s that people could actually meet the needs that they had to be able to take respite, to be able to have capability to then care for the disabled person.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal argument with a stated mechanism: prescriptive rules blocked access, so uptake was low; loosening them raised uptake without any change in underlying need. The inference is coherent, though it rules out a rise in need by assertion rather than by evidence, which is the gap between what is shown and what is concluded.

focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question before the committee — the Government's transport decarbonisation commitment and its pathway to 2030. No party framing.
