specificity.explanation: States a named penalty mechanism and a maximum figure from the bill — someone could check it against the text of the legislation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There will be a new offence which will prohibit operating or engaging with any vessel that has been listed internationally as having engaged in illegal fishing.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism in the bill — a new offence tied to internationally listed vessels — which someone could check against the bill text. No figures or dates, so short of full precision.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This step is global best-practice approach. Actions like this showcase our commitment to being world leaders in fighting illegal fishing, as we are in so many different areas.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — 'best practice', 'world leaders' — with no benchmark, comparator country or measure named that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There will be a new offence which will prohibit operating or engaging with any vessel that has been listed internationally as having engaged in illegal fishing.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure before the House (what the bill actually does) rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Recent actions by the Government would lead us to believe there is a pattern of behaviour of not bothering to be concerned with what the ramifications for the Treaty partner may contain, so we move forward with caution to the Government to actively and continually respect Māori rights, Māori Tiriti rights in fishing, be they on the high sea or in the inshore waters.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's general 'pattern of behaviour' without naming any specific policy, decision or outcome; the only policy anchoring is the closing gesture at Māori fishing rights, so the weight of the statement is party framing rather than scrutiny of a named measure.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Last year, Pew Research stated that illegal fishing is one of the biggest threats to global ocean sustainability, with researchers estimating that one in five fish caught globally are caught illegally.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Pew: that a Pew publication in the year before March 2024 described illegal fishing as among the biggest threats to ocean sustainability, and that researchers estimate one in five fish caught globally are caught illegally.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Locate the Pew (Charitable Trusts / Pew Research) publication from 2023 on IUU fishing; true if it characterises illegal fishing as one of the biggest threats to global ocean sustainability and cites an estimate of roughly one in five (≈20%) of global catch being illegal, false if no such publication exists or the figure materially differs.

veracity.statement: One in five is no small drop in the ocean; it’s a whale of a problem, especially to our $2 billion a year seafood export industry.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's seafood export industry is worth about $2 billion per year as at March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries seafood export revenue for the year to June 2023/2024; true if roughly $2 billion (±10%), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: And, for sure, the precedent was set in 1992 at the conclusion of the first Treaty of Waitangi settlement process and the conclusion of the fisheries settlement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Treaty of Waitangi fisheries settlement was concluded in 1992 and that it was the first such settlement process to be concluded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Deed of Settlement of 23 September 1992 and the Treaty of Waitangi (Fisheries Claims) Settlement Act 1992, plus the Office of Treaty Settlements list of settlements by date; true if the fisheries settlement concluded in 1992 and no earlier full Treaty settlement was concluded, false if the date is wrong or an earlier settlement was concluded first.

rigor.statement: And consider that all changes—all and any changes—to fisheries legislation should have the active consent of tangata whenua, given our customary, proprietary, governance, and Tiriti-based rights.
rigor.explanation: An argument is offered: stated customary, proprietary and Tiriti rights are the premise for a consent requirement. The inference is reasonable but there is a real gap — holding rights in a domain does not by itself establish a veto or consent right over every legislative change in it, and no bridging principle is supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s about protecting our deepwater fisheries industry, which contributes $2.7 billion a year to the New Zealand economy, $1.6 billion to GDP, and employs almost 8,500 people.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete, checkable figures (economic contribution, GDP contribution, employment) attached to a named sector.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill strengthens the powers of high-seas fishing inspectors to investigate offending by foreign-flagged and even Stateless vessels, and it makes it an offence to operate, engage with, or assist a vessel recorded as having engaged in illegal, unreported, or unregulated fishing.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanisms the bill uses — expanded inspector powers over foreign-flagged and stateless vessels, and a new offence — though without clause references or penalty amounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s worth noting that the Ministry for Primary Industries reported, in September 2023, that as part of the special annual mission called Operation Nasse, fisheries compliance officers from New Zealand, Australia, Fiji, France, and the United States detected nearly 40 alleged breaches of high-seas rules during a major South Pacific patrol.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the date, the operation, the participating countries and the number of breaches — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It adjusts the administrative penalty regime for breaches of international fishing permit conditions for greater effectiveness and proportionality. It does this by increasing the maximum amounts for administrative penalties and by broadening the scope of the activities to which they apply.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the actual mechanism — higher maximum administrative penalties and a wider set of covered activities — but gives no amounts, thresholds or commencement dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s about protecting our deepwater fisheries industry, which contributes $2.7 billion a year to the New Zealand economy, $1.6 billion to GDP, and employs almost 8,500 people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's deepwater fisheries industry contributes $2.7b to the economy, $1.6b to GDP, and employs about 8,500 people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Deepwater Group / Seafood New Zealand and MPI economic contribution reporting for the deepwater sector around 2023; true if the published figures are approximately $2.7b total contribution, $1.6b GDP and ~8,500 jobs, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s worth noting that the Ministry for Primary Industries reported, in September 2023, that as part of the special annual mission called Operation Nasse, fisheries compliance officers from New Zealand, Australia, Fiji, France, and the United States detected nearly 40 alleged breaches of high-seas rules during a major South Pacific patrol.
veracity.explanation: Relays an MPI report that a September 2023 multinational South Pacific patrol, Operation Nasse, involving NZ, Australia, Fiji, France and the US, detected close to 40 alleged high-seas breaches.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI media release / Fisheries New Zealand reporting on Operation Nasse 2023; true if it records those five participating nations and roughly 38-40 alleged breaches, false if the participants or breach count differ materially.

veracity.statement: Operation Nasse was also significant as it was the first time the Royal New Zealand Air Force’s new Poseidon P-8A aircraft had been deployed, and it was from Ōhākea in the mighty Rangitīkei.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Operation Nasse was the first operational deployment of the RNZAF's new P-8A Poseidon aircraft, flying from Ōhākea.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZDF/RNZAF and MPI records of P-8A Poseidon deployments in 2023; true if Operation Nasse is documented as the aircraft's first operational deployment out of Ōhākea, false if an earlier operational deployment is recorded.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has one of the largest economic exclusion zones in the world, and we fish in several international fisheries.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand's exclusive economic zone ranks among the largest globally and that New Zealand vessels fish in multiple international fisheries.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published rankings of EEZ area (e.g. Sea Around Us / LOSC-based national EEZ area tables); true if New Zealand's EEZ is in the top ten by area, false if it is not.

focus.statement: This bill is about getting New Zealand back on track and firmly establishing New Zealand as a world leader in combatting illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and its purpose, but carries a governing-party slogan ('back on track') rather than pure policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It adjusts the administrative penalty regime for breaches of international fishing permit conditions for greater effectiveness and proportionality. It does this by increasing the maximum amounts for administrative penalties and by broadening the scope of the activities to which they apply.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the substance of the measure before the House: what the bill changes and how it operates. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As global citizens, we need to take our responsibilities seriously when it comes to IUU, illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing. And why is that? Because not doing so is a threat to sustainability of regional and global fisheries.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (act on IUU fishing) offered with a stated reason (it threatens fishery sustainability). The inference holds, but the link is asserted rather than evidenced — closer to an appeal to shared obligation than a demonstrated causal chain.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This conversation began in 2015 with an independent review of the Māori Fisheries Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the reform process traces to a 2015 independent review of the Māori Fisheries Act 2004.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Ohu Kaimoana / Ministry for Primary Industries records and the bill's explanatory note: true if an independent review of the Māori Fisheries Act 2004 was commenced in 2015, false if the review began in a materially different year or no such review exists.

veracity.statement: Ten submissions were received on the bill from iwi, the settlement trustee Te Ohu Kaimoana, and individuals. Six submitters presented their views in person.
veracity.explanation: Two countable claims about the Māori Affairs Committee's consideration of the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill: ten written submissions and six oral submitters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Māori Affairs Committee's report on the Māori Fisheries Amendment Bill and the committee's published submissions list: true if ten submissions were received and six submitters were heard, false if the counts materially differ.

veracity.statement: These changes have been taken on board and a total of 21 changes were recommended by officials, that were all accepted by the select committee.
veracity.explanation: Claims officials recommended 21 changes to the bill and that the select committee accepted every one of them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Māori Affairs Committee report on the bill and the departmental report to the committee: true if 21 official recommendations are listed and all were adopted, false if the number differs materially or any recommendation was declined.

specificity.statement: On this basis, a change has been made to require the Crown to take all reasonable steps within its authority to introduce a bill to the House within three years of Te Ohu Kaimoana presenting iwi recommendations to the Minister.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete drafting change with a defined trigger (Te Ohu Kaimoana presenting iwi recommendations) and a defined deadline (three years); someone could check the clause. The 'all reasonable steps' qualifier keeps it short of fully enforceable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I also intend to make minor amendments to the bill to extend the framework policing the annual catch entitlements from five to 10 years.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact parameter being changed and the before-and-after figures (five years to ten), though the amendment itself is not yet drafted or dated.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Some submitters expressed concern that the proposed changes would diminish the role of representative Māori organisations, or RMOs. Select committee responded to these concerns and updated the bill to provide RMOs with voting rights.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — a specific concern raised in submissions and the specific amendment made in response. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Independent reviews are important to ensure the governance arrangements remain fit for purpose and continue to deliver benefits to Māori. Given their importance, a change has been made to make independent reviews mandatory unless iwi pass a special resolution not to hold a review.
rigor.explanation: Premise (independent reviews keep governance fit for purpose) supports the conclusion (default them on, with an iwi opt-out). The inference tracks, though the step from 'important' to 'mandatory by default rather than by request' is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I speak in support of the Fisheries (International Fishing and Other Matters) Amendment Bill as we need to protect our $2 billion seafood export industry in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's seafood export industry is worth $2 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries / Stats NZ seafood export revenue for the year to mid-2023 or mid-2024; true if annual seafood export revenue is approximately $2 billion (say $1.8-2.2b), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s fantastic to have a bill which looks to protect our seas, protect against illegal activity, and also has such an abundance of information as to the effectiveness of the bill: an amazing regulatory impact statement, 48 pages long, going through all of the aspects that the parliamentarian could want to know around this particular bill; also a departmental disclosure statement; a legislative statement—all of the things that we have got used to not seeing on the Table.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement accompanying the Fisheries (International Fishing and Other Matters) Amendment Bill runs to 48 pages, and that a departmental disclosure statement and legislative statement were also presented.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement published by MPI/Treasury for the Fisheries (International Fishing and Other Matters) Amendment Bill; true if it is approximately 48 pages and a disclosure statement and legislative statement were tabled, false if the page count is materially different or those documents were absent.

veracity.statement: Anywhere between 18 and 14 million tonnes annually are alleged to be from illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a global annual IUU fishing catch in the range of roughly 14-18 million tonnes (the range is stated in inverted order in live speech).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FAO and published peer-reviewed estimates of annual global IUU catch; true if mainstream estimates centre on roughly 14-18 million tonnes, false if the accepted range is materially different (e.g. the commonly cited 11-26 million tonne band would make the stated band unrepresentative).

veracity.statement: Well, closer to home, we’ve heard that, actually, in our own backyard in the Pacific, illegal and unregulated and unreported fishing is in the estimated range of around $300 million per annum—that’s US dollars.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that IUU fishing in the Pacific is estimated at around US$300 million per year.
veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.explanation: Asserts as a premise that the Iwi Chairs Forum withdrew from the national plan of action against racism.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Iwi Chairs Forum statements and contemporaneous media reporting (early 2024) on participation in the National Action Plan Against Racism. True if the Forum publicly withdrew; false if it did not, or if the withdrawal was by a different body.

veracity.statement: What will he do to alleviate the concerns of the acting Race Relations Commissioner, who has stated that his justice Minister’s attempt to remove some Māori experiences from the action plan would deny many Māori’s lived experiences with racism, which studies show occur daily for 93 percent of Māori?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that studies show 93 percent of Māori experience racism on a daily basis, and that the acting Race Relations Commissioner made the stated criticism of the Minister of Justice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The cited research (e.g. Human Rights Commission / Ministry of Justice or academic survey work on experiences of racism in Aotearoa) and public statements by the acting Race Relations Commissioner in early 2024. True if a published study reports approximately 93% of Māori respondents experiencing racism daily and the Commissioner made that criticism; false if the figure is for a different frequency, population or measure.

rigor.statement: Well, it’s something that we’ve talked about in Opposition for some time, it’s something that we’ve campaigned on, and all we’re saying is we’re making sure we’ve got complementary work going on to make sure we have the latest knowledge around methane science.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason for the second review, but the reason is an appeal to mandate ('we campaigned on it') rather than anything bearing on the question of why a duplicate review is needed; 'complementary' is asserted, not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We can’t just shut down the world’s best farmers and send agricultural production offshore, making global greenhouse gas emissions worse in the process.
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: treats the alternative to 'no additional warming' as shutting down farming entirely. The emissions-leakage step is asserted rather than supported, so the conclusion outruns what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d just say to the member I really look forward to her adjusting the Green Party website to come out in support of our GE policy so that we can actually drive emissions down.
focus.explanation: Pivots from the Climate Change Commission question to the other party's website and general positioning; GE policy is named but nothing about it is engaged — the weight is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Your Government had six years. You did very little; you failed at it.
focus.explanation: Answering a direct question about Cabinet approval of a truancy announcement, this names no policy, figure, target or outcome — it is a blanket verdict on the other side's time in office.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I mean, I reject the premise of the question. We have a fantastic plan to tackle school attendance in New Zealand—something the previous administration, the previous Minister for 5½ years, didn’t seem to care about. We care about it.
civility.explanation: Moves off the record and onto motive: imputes to a named individual (the previous Minister, the questioner) indifference to children's schooling rather than a policy failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, does he agree with Matt Doocey, “I’m responsible for the $2.5 billion that we spend for mental health and addiction ring-fenced funding—I’m going line by line, by line, by line, through that”, and, if so, how did the Suicide Prevention Office almost close without its Minister even noticing?

civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In addition to improving competition for building products, we are also putting the spotlight on building consent delays by requiring councils to supply building consent time frames, lowering the building levy threshold, meaning Kiwis doing small renovations don’t have to pay it.
specificity.explanation: Names several concrete mechanisms (consent time-frame reporting requirement, levy threshold change) but supplies no figures, thresholds or dates for them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ll be rolling out a communications plan to improve awareness of the importance of attendance from term 2 this year onwards.
specificity.explanation: Names an action and a start point (term 2) but gives no content, cost or measure of the communications plan.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is he aware that the rest of the economy will pay a higher price than otherwise if agricultural methane emissions are not required to assist with reducing the rise in global temperatures—a price that one report has estimated equates to a 1 percent change in our methane targets and will require 40 megatons of extra reductions or removals in long-lived gases, and that will put an undue strain on our economy?
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete, checkable quantity (a 1 percent change in methane targets equating to 40 megatons of additional long-lived gas reductions) attributed to a report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m not going to pre-empt a review that hasn’t actually started yet, but what I can be clear about is this review will be comprehensive, it will have integrity, and the results, once received, will be in addition to the work undertaken by the Climate Change Commission, and we’ll go from there.
specificity.explanation: Offers generic virtues for the review — 'comprehensive', 'integrity' — with no terms of reference, membership, timeframe or deliverable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Resources will play a critical role in our export-led recovery, and as part of my strategy as the climate-smart mining Minister, I have announced that settings will be developed to enable investors and other stakeholders to explore the potential of naturally occurring hydrogen as a contribution to lessening our reliance on overseas hydrocarbon fuels, boosting our resilience, and ensuring that there is a suitable framework enabling people to find this potential sooner rather than later.
specificity.explanation: Names a subject (regulatory settings for naturally occurring hydrogen exploration) but no instrument, cost or date — 'sooner rather than later' carries no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are open for business. We will have a legislative framework that rewards risk taking, rewards investment, and restores the place of the extractive sector to a place of pride that it enjoyed with the development, originally, of the party sitting on the other side of the House.
specificity.explanation: Slogan plus a string of generic aspirations for an unnamed legislative framework; no mechanism, measure or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Will the Minister match the $750 million targeted investment for Māori housing that was delivered under the previous Government, and, if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable ask — a named dollar figure for a named programme area, with a direct request to match it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Finally, we have provided relief to rural New Zealand by exempting dams from under 4 metres from additional compliance costs, and there is still much more to come.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has exempted dams under 4 metres in height from additional dam-safety compliance requirements/costs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Amendments to the Building (Dam Safety) Regulations 2022 and associated Ministerial announcements as at April 2024; true if a height threshold of 4 metres was adopted exempting smaller dams from the regime, false if no such exemption was made.

veracity.statement: The review that the member is citing was undertaken nearly five years ago. It is an imperative for this coalition Government to use the latest science available, and that’s what our review will undertake.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment work Megan Woods cited was undertaken nearly five years before April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Publication date of the PCE report on methane/agricultural emissions being cited (e.g. 'Farms, forests and fossil fuels', 2019); true if published around 2019, false if published materially more recently (e.g. 2022–2023).

veracity.statement: As you have heard through the last few months, we are ruthlessly focused on delivering on the genuine needs of Māori: education, health, and housing, particularly the over 1,500 Māori whānau who are living in the emergency housing disaster that the malfeasance of the previous Government created.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 1,500 Māori whānau were living in emergency housing at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD emergency housing special needs grant data by ethnicity for the quarter to March 2024; true if households with a Māori primary applicant exceed 1,500, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: What we will have are targets that reduce the number of children and whānau in emergency housing. We’ve established that target and announced it yesterday through the Prime Minister, rather than sitting by and talking about how we’re going to help whānau Māori in emergency housing and to see those numbers go up by several hundred.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an emergency-housing reduction target was established and announced by the Prime Minister on 8 April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Beehive releases and media coverage dated 8 April 2024; true if a Government target to reduce households/children in emergency housing was announced by the Prime Minister that day, false if no such announcement was made then.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister stand by his statement that he will deliver for Māori communities, and, if so, how will he deliver more homes for Māori when his Government disestablished the ministerial Māori associate housing role?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming Government abolished the associate ministerial portfolio responsible for Māori housing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministerial List of 27 November 2023 compared with the previous list; true if no Associate Minister of Housing (Māori Housing) portfolio exists in the new list where one previously did, false if the portfolio was retained under any name.

veracity.statement: Will the Minister match the $750 million targeted investment for Māori housing that was delivered under the previous Government, and, if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government delivered $750 million of targeted investment in Māori housing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2021/2022 appropriations for the Whai Kāinga Whai Oranga Māori housing programme; true if the targeted Māori housing package totals approximately $750m, false if materially different (e.g. $380m or $730m under a different scope).

civility.statement: I’ve just heard from Willow-Jean Prime, the member for Northland, that somehow we don’t trust the parents—this from a member who was in a Government that propagandised and blasted New Zealanders and didn’t trust them even to go outside for weeks at a time. That is not a member who should be heckling about trust.
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy to the individual member, imputing bad faith to her personally and telling the House she is not fit to raise the subject.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’ve just heard from Willow-Jean Prime, the member for Northland, that somehow we don’t trust the parents—this from a member who was in a Government that propagandised and blasted New Zealanders and didn’t trust them even to go outside for weeks at a time. That is not a member who should be heckling about trust.
focus.explanation: Once the characterisation of the previous Government and the member is removed there is no policy content left — it is entirely about the other side's record and standing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As you have heard through the last few months, we are ruthlessly focused on delivering on the genuine needs of Māori: education, health, and housing, particularly the over 1,500 Māori whānau who are living in the emergency housing disaster that the malfeasance of the previous Government created.
focus.explanation: Names a real cohort and figure (over 1,500 Māori whānau in emergency housing) but the weight of the answer is blame framing of the previous Government rather than the policy asked about.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, let me help Willow-Jean Prime: actually, the Ministry of Education has been upgrading its IT software so that the student management systems from the school can automatically push the data each day. This is an object lesson for the Labour Party. You see, we’re actually going to able to do more with less money, using innovation and technology.
rigor.explanation: A single IT upgrade in one ministry is generalised into the broad conclusion that the Government will 'do more with less money' — hasty generalisation, with no cost or output evidence connecting the instance to the claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The review that the member is citing was undertaken nearly five years ago. It is an imperative for this coalition Government to use the latest science available, and that’s what our review will undertake.
rigor.explanation: The inference — the cited work is old, therefore a fresh review is needed — is coherent but leans on an implicit premise (that the science has materially moved since) which is asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We are absolutely committed to delivering on the genuine needs of all New Zealanders, to ensure that there are sufficient houses to accommodate people, unlike the previous Government, which curated a situation where there are now five times as many whānau on the social housing wait-list as there was when they started.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the social housing register grew fivefold between the start of the previous Government (Oct 2017) and now (April 2024).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly series: compare the number of applicants on the social housing register for the quarter ending September/December 2017 with the most recent quarter before April 2024; true if the later figure is approximately five times the earlier, false if materially lower (e.g. around four times or less).

veracity.statement: Can the Minister confirm that between 2017 and today, billions upon billions of dollars have been borrowed to put into Kāinga Ora and, despite that, the number of New Zealanders waiting for a State house today is four times as many as it was in 2017?
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that billions were borrowed for Kāinga Ora since 2017, and that the state house waiting list in April 2024 is four times its 2017 level.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register applicant numbers for the December 2017 and December 2023/March 2024 quarters (true if the ratio is approximately 4:1, false if materially different), plus Kāinga Ora annual reports / Treasury borrowing figures showing whether multiple billions of debt were raised for Kāinga Ora over that period.

veracity.statement: Does he agree with the Salvation Army’s Greg Foster, who said that they are having to pause future social housing developments because “we’ve been told that there’s no funding for us to build”?
veracity.explanation: Relays a named third party's statement that the Salvation Army has paused future social housing developments because it was told no build funding was available.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements or media reporting attributable to Greg Foster of the Salvation Army around March/April 2024; true if he said the Salvation Army was pausing social housing developments for lack of build funding, false if no such statement exists or he said something materially different.

veracity.statement: Can he confirm that advice provided to the incoming Government in December 2023 from Treasury said that on the current track, Kāinga Ora is forecast to sell over 10,000 public houses in the next few years?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of a dated Treasury briefing to the incoming Government — that Kāinga Ora was forecast on current settings to sell over 10,000 public houses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury Briefing to the Incoming Minister / incoming Government advice of December 2023 as released; true if it contains a forecast of Kāinga Ora selling more than 10,000 public houses on the current track, false if it contains no such forecast or a materially different number.

veracity.statement: I acknowledge the Hon Chris Finlayson, who signed the terms of negotiation with Ngā Iwi o Taranaki in 2017 and began the process of negotiation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Chris Finlayson, as Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations, signed the terms of negotiation with Ngā Iwi o Taranaki over the maunga in 2017.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The signed terms of negotiation for the Taranaki Maunga collective redress held by the Office for Māori Crown Relations – Te Arawhiti; true if dated 2017 and signed by Finlayson, false if signed in a different year or by a different Minister.

focus.statement: We are absolutely committed to delivering on the genuine needs of all New Zealanders, to ensure that there are sufficient houses to accommodate people, unlike the previous Government, which curated a situation where there are now five times as many whānau on the social housing wait-list as there was when they started.
focus.explanation: Engages a named policy area and cites a specific outcome measure (the social housing wait-list), but a substantial share of the weight is the 'unlike the previous Government' framing rather than the mechanism or funding.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As we are all aware, we have inherited a significant fiscal cliff, left behind for us by the previous Government. But we are absolutely committed to actually delivering on the housing needs of Māori and all New Zealanders, unlike the development aspirations of the previous Ministers.
focus.explanation: Asked a specific question about Kāinga Ora funding and house sales; the answer names no policy, figure or timeframe and rests largely on characterising the previous Government and its Ministers.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why, then, with community housing providers stating they are cancelling or pausing housing developments due to no funding certainty, won’t he simply announce the funding they need so that community housing providers can get on with building the houses that that Minister promised?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: names community housing providers, the funding-certainty mechanism, the consequence (cancelled or paused developments) and the Minister's own commitment to build houses.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he agree with Kāinga Ora interim board chair John Duncan that if the Government doesn’t provide the required funding past 2025, up to 10,000 houses may need to be sold?
specificity.explanation: Names a source, a funding date (past 2025) and a quantified consequence (up to 10,000 houses sold) — precise enough that the Minister could confirm or deny it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As we are all aware, we have inherited a significant fiscal cliff, left behind for us by the previous Government. But we are absolutely committed to actually delivering on the housing needs of Māori and all New Zealanders, unlike the development aspirations of the previous Ministers.
specificity.explanation: 'Significant fiscal cliff' and 'absolutely committed to delivering on the housing needs' carry no amounts, mechanisms or dates; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the Minister confirm that between 2017 and today, billions upon billions of dollars have been borrowed to put into Kāinga Ora and, despite that, the number of New Zealanders waiting for a State house today is four times as many as it was in 2017?
specificity.explanation: Gives a defined baseline year, a defined comparison point and a quantified multiple for the waiting list; the borrowing side is left as 'billions upon billions' rather than a figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But what I can confirm is that we are committed to ensuring that the housing that we tautoko—support—both public and private housing, will accommodate Māori and all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A general statement of commitment with no funding amount, build number, mechanism or date; nothing checkable is offered.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This board will be made up of 50 percent Crown and 50 percent iwi appointees.
specificity.explanation: States the exact composition of Te Tōpuni Kōkōrangi as a proportion; a concrete, checkable feature of the arrangements before the House.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, some of us are working very hard on our ministerial portfolios at 6 o’clock.
civility.explanation: A sneer implying the questioner does not work hard; it targets the member personally rather than anything in the question about social housing funding.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Passive resistance, Parihaka, and the kōrero of “patua te hē ki te rangimārie”, or “let peace combat the errors of our ways”—1.2 million acres were stolen; our language, our marae, our culture.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 1.2 million acres of land were confiscated/taken from Taranaki iwi.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal Taranaki Report and Crown/Office of Treaty Settlements historical accounts of the area confiscated in Taranaki under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863; true if the confiscated area is recorded as approximately 1.2 million acres, false if materially different (e.g. an order of magnitude off).

veracity.statement: The love and the compassion and the generosity that the people above us and the people at home in Taranaki have for this nation is so huge that eight iwi agreed to 1 to 2 percent as settlement in recognition of the hē that the Government had done to them because they wanted this nation to grow, they wanted their mokopuna to prosper, and they wanted to live as one.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that eight Taranaki iwi accepted settlement redress amounting to only 1 to 2 percent of what was lost.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Deeds of settlement for the Taranaki iwi held by the Office of Treaty Settlements/Te Arawhiti, plus Waitangi Tribunal valuations of confiscated land; true if quantum redress is on the order of 1-2 percent of the assessed value of the losses for the eight iwi, false if the recorded proportion is materially higher.

veracity.statement: Generation after generation, our grandparents of the negotiators today have walked across the threshold in Parliament seeking the Crown’s honour, seeking the Crown—even though we had our maunga named after an Englishman who had never set foot in Taranaki.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the mountain's colonial name honoured an Englishman who never visited Taranaki.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical record of the naming of Mount Egmont by James Cook in 1770 after John Perceval, 2nd Earl of Egmont; true if that person never travelled to New Zealand/Taranaki, false if there is evidence he visited.

specificity.statement: The love and the compassion and the generosity that the people above us and the people at home in Taranaki have for this nation is so huge that eight iwi agreed to 1 to 2 percent as settlement in recognition of the hē that the Government had done to them because they wanted this nation to grow, they wanted their mokopuna to prosper, and they wanted to live as one.
specificity.explanation: Names a count of iwi and a numeric proportion of redress, both checkable against settlement records, though the base for the percentage is left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They love you all so much; even you, David Seymour, who’s not here.
civility.explanation: Singles out a named member and pointedly notes his absence from the ceremony. Barbed and personalised, but stops well short of an insult to his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is the opportunity that the coalition’s partners are missing with us.
focus.explanation: Framed around what the coalition partners are collectively getting wrong rather than any provision, cost or mechanism of the settlement before the House; a real relational point, but carried entirely in party framing with no named policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Taranaki maunga was first confiscated in 1865 by the Crown as a punishment for the so-called rebellion of Māori during the Land Wars.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a date (1865) and a legal basis (confiscation by the Crown as punishment for alleged rebellion during the New Zealand Wars) for the taking of Taranaki maunga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal Taranaki Report (Wai 143) and the Taranaki deed of settlement historical account: true if the maunga was confiscated by the Crown in 1865 under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863 on the stated rebellion ground; false if the year or the mechanism is materially different.

veracity.statement: This national park is the first and only one in Aotearoa to have a full te reo Māori name, and I hope that we will see more of that in the future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the national park covered by this bill is the only national park in New Zealand carrying an entirely te reo Māori name.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC's list of New Zealand's national parks and their statutory names at the date of the statement: true if this is the only park whose official name is wholly te reo Māori; false if another national park (e.g. Te Urewera's status, or any other) also carries a full te reo name.

veracity.statement: The first oil well was drilled on confiscated land in the 1860s in Taranaki.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's first oil well was drilled in Taranaki in the 1860s and that it sat on land confiscated from Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Ara / Ministry for Culture and Heritage records of the Alpha well at New Plymouth and Taranaki raupatu boundary maps: true if the first well was drilled in the 1860s and its site fell within the 1865 confiscation area; false if the drilling date is outside the 1860s or the site lay outside confiscated land.

veracity.statement: I acknowledge the horrendous injustices when in 1865, the Crown unfairly punished Māori by confiscating 1.2 million acres of Taranaki land, including Taranaki maunga.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantum — 1.2 million acres of Taranaki land confiscated by the Crown in 1865, including the maunga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Waitangi Tribunal Taranaki Report (Wai 143) and the Taranaki collective deed of settlement Crown acknowledgements: true if the confiscated area is stated at approximately 1.2 million acres and includes the maunga; false if the accepted figure differs materially.

specificity.statement: What we have in the redress today is unique: recognising the maunga as a legal personality having personhood, and setting up a rōpū who will be responsible for its care and its administration.
specificity.explanation: Names two concrete mechanisms in the bill — legal personhood for the maunga and a governance body responsible for care and administration — but supplies no composition, powers, funding or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Te Tōpuni Kōkōrangi will function as a statutory body with the purpose of being the human face and voice of Te Kāhui Tupua, consisting of four members appointed by Te Tōpuni Ngārahu, the collective governance entry for Ngā Iwi o Taranaki, for any matters pertaining to the collective redress and arrangements, and four members appointed by the Department of Conservation.
specificity.explanation: Names the statutory body, its function, its exact composition (four members from each of two named appointing entities) and the scope of matters it covers — all checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The fracking and the mining and the drilling and the proposed reopening of seabed mining and of offshore oil and gas drilling by this Government—these are continuations of that desecration of nature that goes against what is in the best interests of the people, and it is certainly what has caused the most harm long term to tangata whenua Māori.
focus.explanation: Names specific extractive policies — seabed mining and offshore oil and gas drilling — and engages the Government's position on them rather than characterising the parties opposite.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The fracking and the mining and the drilling and the proposed reopening of seabed mining and of offshore oil and gas drilling by this Government—these are continuations of that desecration of nature that goes against what is in the best interests of the people, and it is certainly what has caused the most harm long term to tangata whenua Māori.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that these named activities are 'what has caused the most harm long term to tangata whenua Māori' is a superlative causal claim offered with no supporting evidence or comparison; the inference rests on assimilating present-day extraction to nineteenth-century raupatu by analogy alone.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The fracking and the mining and the drilling and the proposed reopening of seabed mining and of offshore oil and gas drilling by this Government—these are continuations of that desecration of nature that goes against what is in the best interests of the people, and it is certainly what has caused the most harm long term to tangata whenua Māori.
civility.explanation: Sharp, unqualified criticism of the Government's resource policy that lands entirely on the policy; no individual is impugned and no bad faith is imputed to any person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The idea of personhood for Taranaki is a really, really important one, and it’s the personhood, in a sense, that goes after the personhood and the recognition that was granted to the Whanganui River, because it was Taranaki that made that long journey from the central North Island, down the Whanganui River, to be where Taranaki stands today.
rigor.explanation: An argument is offered: the appropriateness/ordering of granting legal personhood to Taranaki is justified by the traditional account of the maunga's journey down the Whanganui River. The conclusion (that this sequencing is fitting) rests on an appeal to tradition and narrative resonance rather than on anything connecting the precedent to the legal mechanism; a real inference about the measure, but a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill establishes and recognises Te Kāhui Tupua as a legal person, giving it rights, powers, and duties, and giving it the ability for those to be exercised and performed on its behalf and in its name by the joint governance entity Te Tōpuni Kōkōrangi.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific legal entity created, the legal status conferred, and the named body that exercises the rights on its behalf — a mechanism a reader could check against the bill rather than a general endorsement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The third aspect is the protection against commercial mining, which is clearly important to the eight iwi. The fourth area is around the acknowledgment of the historical injustice that has been forced upon these iwi over many generations.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete provisions of the bill (a protection against commercial mining, an acknowledgment of historical injustice) as part of an enumerated list, but gives no clause references, scope or mechanism for how the mining protection operates.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The bill establishes and recognises Te Kāhui Tupua as a legal person, giving it rights, powers, and duties, and giving it the ability for those to be exercised and performed on its behalf and in its name by the joint governance entity Te Tōpuni Kōkōrangi.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the specific legal effect of the bill before the House — creation of Te Kāhui Tupua as a legal person and Te Tōpuni Kōkōrangi as the entity acting for it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Taranaki Maunga Collective Redress Bill as introduced: true if the bill declares Te Kāhui Tupua a legal person with rights, powers and duties, and provides for those to be exercised in its name by Te Tōpuni Kōkōrangi; false if the bill contains no such provisions or assigns them differently.

veracity.statement: It’s also a historic moment because this is the 100th deed that successive Governments have signed as part of the Treaty of Waitangi redress negotiations.
veracity.explanation: A precise ordinal count claim: that this deed is the hundredth Treaty settlement deed signed by the Crown.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations published register of signed deeds of settlement: true if the Taranaki maunga deed is recorded as the 100th deed of settlement signed by the Crown, false if the tally at that date is materially different.

veracity.statement: Not when you hear that they wanted to get rid of the reo in Government departments.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming coalition parties sought to remove te reo Māori from government department naming/usage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 National–NZ First and National–ACT coalition agreements and associated public service directives: true if they require removal or replacement of te reo Māori department names/communications; false if they contain no such provision. divination.falsification_criterion: Outcome of the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act polls held with the October 2025 local elections; true if a majority of councils with Māori wards, including Far North District Council, lose them, false if Māori wards are retained across most affected councils.

veracity.statement: They just opened a $10 million freshwater storage project, which will unlock the potential for 300 hectares of horticultural land and provide ongoing diversified income for that iwi, Te Whānau-ā-Apanui, and jobs for the future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a freshwater storage project costing $10 million has just opened at Raukokore, and that it services the potential of 300 hectares of horticultural land for Te Whānau-ā-Apanui.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kānoa / Provincial Growth Fund project records and Te Whānau-ā-Apanui / regional council announcements for the Raukokore water storage scheme; true if a water storage project of approximately $10 million opened there in early 2024 and is documented as unlocking about 300 hectares of horticultural land, false if the cost or the hectarage is materially different or the project had not opened.

veracity.statement: In Kawerau, the mayoral task force is doing incredible work getting our rangatahi and young people into work: 260 placements in three years of young people into jobs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Kawerau Mayors Taskforce for Jobs has placed 260 young people into jobs over three years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Mayors Taskforce for Jobs / Kawerau District Council placement reporting for the three years to 2024; true if cumulative placements are approximately 260, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: Kawerau is the industrial heartland of the country, and we look forward to the new development from Forrester: $300 million investment into geothermal and renewable energy sources.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a company named Forrester is investing $300 million in geothermal and renewable energy at Kawerau.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Company announcements, resource consent applications or Bay of Plenty regional / Kawerau District Council records for a Forrester geothermal-renewables development at Kawerau; true if a project of approximately $300 million is documented as of April 2024, false if no such investment exists or the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The East Coast has much to offer, but I can’t go past Whakatāne, voted best small town for 2023; and Ōhope Beach, the best beach in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Whakatāne won a 'best small town' vote for 2023 and that Ōhope Beach holds a title as New Zealand's best beach.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published 2023 award results (e.g. Keep New Zealand Beautiful / national travel or media polls) naming a best small town, and the poll or award (e.g. TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice) naming New Zealand's best beach; true if Whakatāne was so named for 2023 and Ōhope holds a documented best-beach title, false if either award went elsewhere or no such vote exists.

veracity.statement: The Government, under my predecessor the MP for Christchurch Central and Megan Woods, have put $25 million into this project, which is now going to cost $248 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Crown has contributed $25 million to the Christ Church Cathedral reinstatement and that the project's current cost estimate is $248 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown funding records for the Christ Church Cathedral reinstatement (Ministry for Culture and Heritage / Budget documents) and the Christ Church Cathedral Reinstatement Ltd cost estimate current in early 2024; true if Crown contribution is approximately $25 million and the estimate is approximately $248 million, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: We thought that when State Highway 25A was closed for almost a year and reopened quickly, thanks to the great work of the New Zealand Transport Agency’s (NZTA) contractors ahead of the time frame that NZTA had set and under budget, it would be the end of our major issues from Cyclone Hale and Cyclone Gabrielle.
veracity.explanation: Asserts SH25A was closed for close to a year and reopened both ahead of NZTA's stated timeframe and under budget.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA records for the SH25A Taparahi slip repair: closure date (early 2023), reopening date, the publicly stated target reopening date, and final cost against budget; true if reopening preceded the announced target date and final cost was below the announced budget, false if it opened on or after target or over budget.

specificity.statement: They just opened a $10 million freshwater storage project, which will unlock the potential for 300 hectares of horticultural land and provide ongoing diversified income for that iwi, Te Whānau-ā-Apanui, and jobs for the future.
specificity.explanation: Names the project, its cost, the hectarage unlocked and the iwi beneficiary — concrete enough for someone to check or follow up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government, under my predecessor the MP for Christchurch Central and Megan Woods, have put $25 million into this project, which is now going to cost $248 million.
specificity.explanation: Gives named funders, the Crown contribution and the total project cost — precise and directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In my view, the church will hold it on trust for the people of Christchurch, and when it is rebuilt, because it will be rebuilt, it needs to be an open and community space.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Christ Church Cathedral reinstatement will in fact be completed, rather than the building being left unrestored or demolished.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Status of the Christ Church Cathedral reinstatement project; true if the cathedral is reinstated and reopened, false if the project is abandoned, the building demolished, or the reinstatement remains permanently mothballed with no funded path to completion.

rigor.statement: Now, I’m not suggesting that the Government should bear the lion’s share of that burden, but I think the funding ratios that have gone on in the past are a good way to look forward.
rigor.explanation: An argument from precedent: the conclusion that past funding ratios should guide future contributions rests on the ratios' existence alone, with no reason offered as to why they were the right proportions or why they transfer to a cost that has grown roughly tenfold. A real inference, but with a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, yes, there was some cyclone damage to the pathway that takes people down to the beach from the lookout, down quite a long and windy walk, and some damage has occurred, but, by engineering standards and by any other measure, it’s not that big a job to get it fixed.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the repair is a small job rests on a bare appeal to unnamed authority — 'by engineering standards and by any other measure' — with no engineering assessment, cost, or geotechnical finding offered to support it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I want to talk today about why it is that the Department of Conservation, in my view, has been so slack, so slow to get that track open.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism aimed at an agency's performance rather than at any individual; 'slack' edges toward imputing indifference, but no person is attacked and the complaint is anchored to a specific failure to reopen a track.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, thanks to the good work of Tama Potaka, the new Minister of Conservation, I was delighted, on behalf of local businesses, tourist operators, and also the hundreds of thousands of visitors who want to come and see Cathedral Cove, that he has now committed to ensuring that his Department of Conservation officials have on his desk, in June, their plan for getting the track reopened for the coming summer season.
specificity.explanation: Names the Minister, the agency, a month (June) for delivery of the plan, and the target (track reopened for the coming summer season) — checkable detail rather than a general intention.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Well, thanks to the good work of Tama Potaka, the new Minister of Conservation, I was delighted, on behalf of local businesses, tourist operators, and also the hundreds of thousands of visitors who want to come and see Cathedral Cove, that he has now committed to ensuring that his Department of Conservation officials have on his desk, in June, their plan for getting the track reopened for the coming summer season.
divination.explanation: Relays the Minister's commitment as a forecast that a DOC plan will be on the Minister's desk in June and the track reopened for the coming summer.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: DOC/ministerial records or media reporting on the Cathedral Cove track: true if DOC officials delivered a reopening plan to the Minister in June 2024 and the track was open for the 2024/25 summer season; false if no June plan was delivered or the track remained closed through that summer.

veracity.statement: It wasn’t going to be until September of this year that they were even going to make a decision about what might eventually happen at the cove.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that DOC's original timetable put any decision about Cathedral Cove no earlier than September 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC's published Cathedral Cove/Mautohe work programme or timeline as at early 2024: true if DOC's stated decision point on the future of the site was September 2024, false if a decision was scheduled materially earlier.

veracity.statement: There are literally tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of people who want to come and walk that track and experience the beautiful Cathedral Cove experience, who currently cannot do it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the scale of foregone visitation to the closed Cathedral Cove track.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC visitor-count data for the Cathedral Cove track in the years before the 2023 cyclone closure, plus regional tourism figures: true if annual visitation was in the tens to hundreds of thousands, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: What transpired was that there are many community groups there working with youth; that the Invercargill Initiative has shown that 23 percent of youth in Invercargill live in deprivation, which is much higher than the national average; that there are parents who work multiple jobs who find it very difficult to be at home; and that there are intergenerational issues around parenting, around violence, around poverty.
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific statistic attributed to the Invercargill Initiative about the youth deprivation rate in Invercargill relative to the national average.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Invercargill Initiative published research and Stats NZ / NZ Deprivation Index youth deprivation figures: true if that work reports approximately 23% of Invercargill youth living in deprivation and that this exceeds the national rate, false if the figure or the comparison is materially different.

veracity.statement: The council has said it is spending $2.2 million on security cameras.
veracity.explanation: Relays the council's own stated spending figure on security cameras.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Invercargill City Council budget or council resolutions on CCTV/security camera spending around 2024: true if a commitment of about $2.2 million is recorded, false if the figure is materially different or no such commitment exists.

rigor.statement: Well, it’s important because many of those local businesses have to do sometimes up to about 80 percent of their annual turnover over a summer period. When we don’t have a good summer period, there isn’t an opportunity for those businesses to make that revenue up any other way. So having the track closed is a real problem.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: seasonal revenue concentration plus no substitute earning period yields the conclusion that closure over summer materially harms the businesses. No gap between premises and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think it’s beholden upon the Department of Conservation to actually get their act together, to pull finger, and to actually get ahead of the Minister’s timetable and see if we can get the track open sooner.
civility.explanation: Blunt, colloquially impatient criticism of an agency's pace of work, but it targets institutional performance rather than any individual; edges toward disparagement without landing on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And, indeed, when people stood up, there was a whole parade of people appointed from the panel, handpicked in the audience, to vindicate the mayor’s stance that this is a very dangerous city and that these youth need real consequences.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the mayor personally — that he stage-managed the meeting with handpicked speakers to validate his own position. Short of insult, but an attack on the person's honesty rather than on his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Queenstown Lakes District, between 1996 and 2020, had an average annual population growth of 5.3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific average annual population growth rate for the Queenstown Lakes District over a defined 24-year window.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for Queenstown-Lakes District, 1996 to 2020; true if the compound average annual growth rate over that period is ~5.3% (± rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I was very proud to see the Minister Simeon Brown down in Queenstown last week to announce a $250 million transport package, that the coalition Government had agreed, to up the funding by $120 million to address some of those needs, although I would say that there is a lot more that needs to be done in that region, but I appreciate that we are in a challenging fiscal time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Transport Minister announced a $250 million transport package for Queenstown in early April 2024, including a $120 million funding increase.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial press releases / NZTA announcements dated late March–April 2024 for the Queenstown transport package; true if a package of ~$250m including an uplift of ~$120m was announced by Simeon Brown in Queenstown in that week, false if no such announcement or materially different figures.

veracity.statement: That has been confirmed by the latest Beef + Lamb report, which said the updated forecasts for profits will be down 54 percent, to an average of $62,600 per farm.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to a Beef + Lamb New Zealand forecast a 54 percent fall in average sheep and beef farm profit to $62,600 per farm.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Beef + Lamb New Zealand New Season Outlook / mid-season update for 2023-24; true if it forecasts average farm profit before tax of ~$62,600, down ~54%, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: There has been no real recovery from China in terms of our demand for our products and the exports of red meat out of Australia have been bigger than forecast.
veracity.explanation: Two factual claims about the state of the red meat market in early 2024: weak Chinese demand recovery, and Australian red meat export volumes exceeding forecasts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Beef + Lamb NZ / MPI Situation and Outlook export data and Meat & Livestock Australia export statistics for 2023-24; true if Chinese import demand for NZ red meat remained flat or falling and Australian red meat exports exceeded prior forecasts, false if either series shows the contrary.

veracity.statement: We have a roading network that is a total of 4,969 kilometres in length. Just under 2,000 kilometres of those are sealed, and just under 3,000 kilometres are unsealed. We have 1,121 bridges, and, of those, at present, 68 bridges are either closed or weight restricted, and 134 of those bridges will require replacing by 2034.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Southland's roading network length, sealed/unsealed split, bridge count, and that 68 bridges are currently closed or weight restricted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Southland District Council / Waka Kotahi road asset management data for 2023-24; true if total network is ~4,969 km with ~1,121 bridges and ~68 closed or weight restricted, false if the asset registers show materially different counts.

veracity.statement: We have 2,395 people waiting for a home on the public housing wait-list, and homelessness is increasing, particularly at both ends of the age spectrum where you see more young people, more rangatahi sleeping on our streets, on Lambton Quay and Courtenay Place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific Wellington public housing register figure of 2,395 applicants and that homelessness in the city is rising.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Housing Register quarterly data for the Wellington region as at the December 2023 / March 2024 quarter; true if the register total is ~2,395, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The average house price in Wellington is about $1 million, far out of reach for most people who live here.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the average Wellington house price was approximately $1 million as at April 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: REINZ / QV Wellington city average or median dwelling value for early 2024; true if approximately $1 million (within ~10%), false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: We have the Granville Flats, owned by council and operated by Kāinga Ora, home to 144 tenants; that has been closed and soon to be demolished.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Granville Flats are council-owned, Kāinga Ora-operated, housed 144 tenants, and have been closed pending demolition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington City Council housing records and news reporting on the Granville Flats; true if the block was council-owned, held ~144 tenancies, and was closed with demolition planned as at April 2024, false if the ownership, tenant count or status differ.

specificity.statement: The Queenstown Lakes District, between 1996 and 2020, had an average annual population growth of 5.3 percent.
specificity.explanation: Named district, named date range, and a precise percentage figure — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That has been confirmed by the latest Beef + Lamb report, which said the updated forecasts for profits will be down 54 percent, to an average of $62,600 per farm.
specificity.explanation: Named source, a percentage change and a dollar figure per farm; someone could look the report up and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have a roading network that is a total of 4,969 kilometres in length. Just under 2,000 kilometres of those are sealed, and just under 3,000 kilometres are unsealed. We have 1,121 bridges, and, of those, at present, 68 bridges are either closed or weight restricted, and 134 of those bridges will require replacing by 2034.
specificity.explanation: Network length, seal split, bridge count, current restrictions and a replacement timeframe — all concrete and checkable against council asset data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have 2,395 people waiting for a home on the public housing wait-list, and homelessness is increasing, particularly at both ends of the age spectrum where you see more young people, more rangatahi sleeping on our streets, on Lambton Quay and Courtenay Place.
specificity.explanation: Carries an exact wait-list count and named locations, though the homelessness trend claim is stated without figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We can be the first city to end homelessness and to not have it in our streets, but, in order to do that, we need more public housing, we need to have the wraparound care that people need to live the best lives possible, and that is something that I know we’ll be very proud of into the future.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no numbers, no mechanism, no cost and no timeframe — 'more public housing' and 'wraparound care' commit to nothing checkable, in contrast to the figures she supplied earlier.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s an annual average growth of 5.3 percent. To put that in perspective, that means the population doubles in just over 13 years.
rigor.explanation: The inference is a correct compounding calculation: at 5.3% per annum, doubling time is ln2/ln(1.053) ≈ 13.4 years. The conclusion follows exactly from the stated premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But we realise that there is money to be made in the absence of public housing, which is why there has been such a degradation of our public housing offering here in Wellington.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion — that the decline of Wellington public housing was caused by private profit motive — asserted from a bare motive claim with no mechanism, decision or evidence linking the two. The inference does not follow from what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In February 2021, the previous Minister of Local Government—oh, a few ago—was Nanaia Mahuta. She installed four commissioners.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Nanaia Mahuta, as Minister of Local Government, appointed four commissioners to Tauranga City Council in February 2021.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DIA/Ministerial announcement and the Local Government Act appointment record for Tauranga City Council; true if four commissioners were appointed by the Minister of Local Government (Nanaia Mahuta) in February 2021, false if the number, date or Minister differs.

veracity.statement: But she extended their term, cancelling local government elections in 2022 for the people of Tauranga.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the commissioners' term was extended by the Minister, with the effect that Tauranga did not hold local body elections in the 2022 nationwide round.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tauranga City Council / DIA records and the relevant legislation or ministerial decision; true if the commissioners' term was extended and no Tauranga local election was held in October 2022, false if Tauranga voted in 2022 or the extension came from another source.

veracity.statement: The people of Christchurch, God bless them—a highly indebted council, unfortunately; I think it’s about $9,300 per ratepayer. Well, in Tauranga, we’re at $17,000 per ratepayer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Christchurch City Council debt is about $9,300 per ratepayer and Tauranga City Council debt about $17,000 per ratepayer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Christchurch and Tauranga City Council long-term plan / annual report debt figures divided by rateable properties as at 2024; true if both figures are within rounding of the stated amounts, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: We have the highest city rates for residential property and our commercial rates are growing rapidly.
veracity.explanation: Claims Tauranga has the highest residential rates of any New Zealand city council, and that its commercial rates are rising rapidly.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparison of average residential rates across NZ city councils for 2023/24 (e.g. Taxpayers' Union Ratepayers' Report or council annual plans); true if Tauranga's average residential rates are the highest of the city councils, false if another city council is higher.

veracity.statement: We in this Government have voted to give councils the chance to repeal or have a referendum on local government having a Māori ward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, as at 9 April 2024, the governing parties had already voted in the House on a measure allowing councils to repeal Māori wards or put them to a referendum.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard division records up to 9 April 2024 for any bill on Māori wards/constituencies; true if such a vote had been taken by that date, false if the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill had not yet been introduced or voted on.

veracity.statement: That is based off the Limited Services Volunteer programme that is actually in my colleague the Hon Chris Penk’s electorate up in Whenuapai.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Limited Service Volunteer programme runs at Whenuapai and that Whenuapai falls within Chris Penk's electorate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZDF/MSD documentation of LSV course locations and the Electoral Commission's 2023 boundary for Kaipara ki Mahurangi; true if LSV operates at Whenuapai and Whenuapai lies in Penk's electorate, false if either is wrong.

specificity.statement: The people of Christchurch, God bless them—a highly indebted council, unfortunately; I think it’s about $9,300 per ratepayer. Well, in Tauranga, we’re at $17,000 per ratepayer.
specificity.explanation: Gives two concrete per-ratepayer debt figures with named councils, allowing a direct comparison someone could check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, two initiatives I wish to speak about: the young offender military academy programme, which is going to start later on this year and it’s going to be trialled in Auckland.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific programme, an approximate start timeframe and the trial location, though without numbers, cost or provider.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We saw this go to the head of some of the commissioners.
civility.explanation: Rather than criticising the commissioners' decisions, this imputes arrogance to them personally — a sneer at character rather than at the substance of their governance.
civility.subject: speaker
