rigor.statement: Yeah, well, you might say that, Arena, but she also thought hybrid democracy was something that the people of Tauranga would want—unelected commissioners governing in a co-governance between unelected and elected decision-makers. Now, I would have to say that is an admission of failure. One of the terms of reference was to work with council to encourage quality candidates to stand.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the chair proposing a transitional mix of elected and unelected decision-makers is offered as proof that a separate term of reference — encouraging quality candidates to stand — was not met. Nothing is supplied to connect the proposal to that conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So it’s all very well for them to go on and get this great training and mentoring, but when they get placed back into their home environment they’re often back reoffending. So we need to make sure that there’s actually good pastoral care to help these kids as well.
rigor.explanation: A stated premise (reoffending on return to the home environment) supports the conclusion that post-programme pastoral care is needed; the inference tracks, though the premise rests on unsourced report rather than evidence offered here.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I see them as a divisive and very unfortunate thing in a 21st century democracy.
focus.explanation: Directly addresses the policy question at issue — Māori wards in local government — rather than the other party, though it carries no detail about mechanism or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But there’s also some proactive measures that we can focus on, and I think the biggest one we can focus on a proactive way is offering youth a way out of their current predicament, and that is by encouraging apprenticeships and encouraging further training opportunities.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of crime-prevention policy — naming apprenticeships and training as the proactive lever — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Reactive ones include restoring consequences for crime, making sure there are, in fact, tougher sentences—we’ve got the Minister of Justice here who will be introducing laws to limit the amount judges can deduct from offenders when they’re sentenced.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Minister of Justice will introduce legislation capping the sentencing discounts judges may apply.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills register; true if a Government bill limiting sentencing discounts was introduced by the Minister of Justice after 9 April 2024, false if no such bill was introduced by the resolve-by date.

specificity.statement: There’s a huge development going up in Morningside Drive; I think it’s 256 houses going in there, and there’s another one further in the electorate of 56 houses.
specificity.explanation: Names a location and two concrete dwelling counts (256 and 56); someone could go and check the consent records, though the developer's timeframe and cost are absent.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We had a whole lot of things when the Labour Party was part of the Government which were to incentivise this, and I’d urge the new Government to keep on thinking about new incentives, because some of those incentives have been taken away because of recent changes.
specificity.explanation: Refers to 'a whole lot of things', 'new incentives' and 'recent changes' without naming a single incentive, mechanism, figure or date; the direction is clear but nothing here is checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So National promised—indeed, committed—to reinstate the PET scanner, to replace the cut aged-care beds, to build the original number of operating theatres. National promised at least an additional $30 million on top of the $1.6 billion.
specificity.explanation: Names four discrete commitments — PET scanner, aged-care beds, original theatre count — and attaches precise figures ($30 million on top of $1.6 billion), all of which can be checked against the election commitment.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There’s a huge development going up in Morningside Drive; I think it’s 256 houses going in there, and there’s another one further in the electorate of 56 houses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Simplicity Living long-term rental development of about 256 homes is under construction on Morningside Drive, plus a further development of 56 homes in the same electorate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council resource consent / Simplicity Living project records for the Morningside Drive development in Mt Albert as at April 2024; true if the consented dwelling count is approximately 256 with a second Simplicity development of about 56 dwellings in the Mt Albert electorate, false if the counts are materially different or no such developments exist.

veracity.statement: The old hospital, still in use, has a clinical services building in a parlous state, with leaks, asbestos, and it’s beyond end of life—an actual trigger for the Dunedin Hospital.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual condition assessment of the existing Dunedin Hospital clinical services building — leaks, asbestos, past end of life — and that this drove the rebuild decision.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Southern DHB asset condition reports and the Dunedin Hospital rebuild business case; true if the existing clinical services building is documented as containing asbestos, having water ingress, and being assessed at or beyond end of economic life, false if condition assessments show otherwise.

veracity.statement: My father-in-law, who’d retired from an illustrious career in surgery, was part of a working group looking at final detailed design—how many sinks, how many doors, where they should be placed—right up until Labour began trimming the budget and causing a major redesign.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Labour government cut the Dunedin Hospital budget, which interrupted detailed design work and forced a major redesign.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health / Te Whatu Ora records and contemporaneous reporting on the New Dunedin Hospital programme in 2022–23; true if the then-Labour government required cost reductions that forced a redesign of the detailed design, false if no such budget-driven redesign occurred under Labour.

veracity.statement: So National promised—indeed, committed—to reinstate the PET scanner, to replace the cut aged-care beds, to build the original number of operating theatres. National promised at least an additional $30 million on top of the $1.6 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content and dollar value of National's pre-election commitment on the Dunedin Hospital rebuild.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National's 2023 election policy documents and campaign statements on the New Dunedin Hospital; true if National publicly committed to reinstating the PET scanner, restoring the cut aged-care beds and the original number of operating theatres, and to at least $30 million on top of the $1.6 billion, false if any of those commitments were not made or the figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: The PM has said that people need to live better lives and that he’s going to get things done and deliver better outcomes, yet I have submitted many questions to Minister Reti seeking a response on whether National will honour its pre-election commitment, and the Minister will not give a straight answer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker lodged many written questions to Minister Reti on the Dunedin Hospital commitment and received no direct answer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary written questions register for 2024; true if Scott Willis lodged multiple written questions to Shane Reti about the Dunedin Hospital funding commitment and the replies did not state whether the commitment would be honoured, false if few or no such questions exist or the replies gave a direct answer.

rigor.statement: It’s actually really, really helpful for our economy too, because it is allowing people to spend their money in the productive sector.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference — long-term rental frees household capital, which is then directed to productive investment — but the causal step from 'renting instead of buying' to 'money flows to the productive sector' is asserted rather than shown; no evidence or mechanism is offered that renters redirect savings that way.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: After all, they have given a massive tax break to the landlords of student flats in north Dunedin. So why can’t they just fund a decent hospital, which they promised in the election campaign?
rigor.explanation: A real argument about a real policy — fiscal capacity — but it is a false-equivalence step: nothing is offered to show the value of restored interest deductibility for landlords is of a scale that would cover the hospital shortfall, so the conclusion does not follow from the premise as stated.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We had a whole lot of things when the Labour Party was part of the Government which were to incentivise this, and I’d urge the new Government to keep on thinking about new incentives, because some of those incentives have been taken away because of recent changes.
focus.explanation: Squarely about a policy question — incentives for long-term rental housing supply — and addressed as a request to the incoming Government rather than as party attack, despite the passing party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s tragically true that this Government is all about slogans over action.
focus.explanation: A blanket characterisation of the other side with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named; strip out the claim about what the Government is 'really like' and nothing about the hospital or any other policy remains in this sentence.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The PM has said that people need to live better lives and that he’s going to get things done and deliver better outcomes, yet I have submitted many questions to Minister Reti seeking a response on whether National will honour its pre-election commitment, and the Minister will not give a straight answer.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of a Minister's conduct in office — evasiveness in answering questions — which edges toward the person but stays on his official record rather than his character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is the Minister simply as hollow as the Prime Minister?
civility.explanation: A direct personal attack on the character of two named individuals — calling both the Minister and the Prime Minister 'hollow' — rather than any criticism of a policy or decision.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: A Government that has given tax breaks to landlords, that’s mislaid their cast-iron promise to fund our hospital, and that’s repealed three waters, leading to looming massive rises to rates.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that repealing the Three Waters reforms will push council rates sharply upward for ratepayers such as those in Dunedin.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Dunedin City Council adopted annual plan rates increases for 2024/25 and 2025/26; true if average residential rates rises materially exceed the pre-2024 historical norm (say above 10% per year) with water infrastructure costs cited as a driver following the Three Waters repeal, false if rates rises stay near historical levels.

specificity.statement: We have 21 schools in our rohe. We have 11 primary schools, three intermediates, and the rest are our high schools and our kura.
specificity.explanation: Gives a precise count and a breakdown by school type for a named area — checkable against the Ministry of Education school directory.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My plea: the Government needs to consider that the policies that you are making, these tax cuts, the flow-on effect to our tamariki in Māngere—this a really serious problem.
specificity.explanation: Names tax cuts and an affected community but supplies no figure, mechanism, or requested action — a general appeal to consider consequences.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, you can say what you like about whether we do a review of the rebuild of all the schools that we need to do, but there should have been ring-fencing for students with severe intellectual and physical disabilities.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (ring-fencing) and the cohort it should cover, but no amount, threshold or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So I want to help highlight the problem for the members right across the House, because it’s actually quite timely that in today’s Dominion Post, the Minister, Minister Costello, talks about—it’s reported in this article that there has been a reduction of staff who know the business in terms of regulatory and compliance.
veracity.explanation: Relays a media report that regulatory and compliance staff dealing with vaping/tobacco have been reduced.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Dominion Post / Stuff article published 9 April 2024 on vaping and tobacco regulation, plus Ministry of Health / Health NZ staffing records for the regulatory and compliance function; true if the article reports a reduction in such staff, false if no such reporting or no such reduction is documented.

veracity.statement: These vaping devices, they’re poison. It’s really poisoning our tamariki’s brain development.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that vaping devices are poisonous and damage children's brain development.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed literature and NZ Ministry of Health / WHO advice on nicotine exposure and adolescent brain development; true if authoritative health evidence holds that adolescent nicotine exposure harms brain development, false if the evidence does not support a developmental harm claim.

veracity.statement: We had some good news that one of our kura is the highest-achieving kura in the country with regards to NCEA results—highest-achieving kura for 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a kura in the Māngere electorate recorded the highest NCEA achievement of any kura nationally for 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZQA / Education Counts NCEA attainment data by school for 2023 restricted to kura kaupapa Māori and wharekura; true if a Māngere kura tops that ranking, false if another kura ranks higher.

veracity.statement: So, in 2019, the Labour Government announced a rebuild of Salisbury School and Maitai School on the site of Salisbury School.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 2019 government announcement of a co-located rebuild of Salisbury School and Maitai School on the Salisbury site.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education and Beehive announcements from 2019 on the Salisbury School site; true if a rebuild of both schools on that site was announced in 2019, false if no such announcement exists or it was made in a different year or covered different schools.

veracity.statement: In November last year, the school submitted a Budget bid. That rebuild is now on hold. That’s appalling. It is about the Government’s choices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Maitai School lodged a Budget bid in November 2023 and that the rebuild has since been placed on hold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education school property records / OIA responses on the Maitai School rebuild status as at April 2024; true if the project was paused or unfunded at that date, false if it remained active and funded.

rigor.statement: But when a former senior health ministry staffer says that there’s going to be cuts—and I know that this Government has talked about tax cuts—this Government is making choices that is harming the flow-on effect.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that government choices are causing harm is asserted from two loosely linked items — a former official's statement about cuts and the existence of tax cuts — with no connection shown between the tax policy and the regulatory staffing reduction. A non sequitur resting on an unstated causal chain.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But when a former senior health ministry staffer says that there’s going to be cuts—and I know that this Government has talked about tax cuts—this Government is making choices that is harming the flow-on effect.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of the Government's fiscal and regulatory choices; no individual is attacked and no bad faith is imputed.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My plea: the Government needs to consider that the policies that you are making, these tax cuts, the flow-on effect to our tamariki in Māngere—this a really serious problem.
focus.explanation: Directed at a named government policy and its consequences for a named community, but the link is asserted as party framing rather than developed as a policy point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In November last year, the school submitted a Budget bid. That rebuild is now on hold. That’s appalling. It is about the Government’s choices.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named school rebuild, its Budget bid and its current status — a specific policy commitment and outcome, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, you can say what you like about whether we do a review of the rebuild of all the schools that we need to do, but there should have been ring-fencing for students with severe intellectual and physical disabilities.
focus.explanation: Concedes the general policy question and argues a specific mechanism — ring-fencing capital funding for a defined group of students.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I’m calling on the Minister to come to the meeting on Thursday in Nelson so that we, instead of tax cuts for landlords, can rebuild Maitai School.
focus.explanation: A concrete ask about a named school and a named meeting, but the framing sets it against 'tax cuts for landlords' rather than developing the funding trade-off.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know that has been discussed regarding the risk of reintroducing or reclassifying this medicine back into the market, but I think that as we’ve learnt as time has gone by, the manner in which we receive methamphetamine into our criminal elements in New Zealand has changed so markedly and methamphetamine has become so cheap to produce and so prevalently produced that the risk presented by pseudoephedrine bought legitimately or obtained legitimately from the markets to be used to manufacture methamphetamine really isn’t the risk that it would be.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: if the meth supply chain has shifted to cheap, prevalent supply (largely importation) rather than domestic pseudoephedrine-based manufacture, then the diversion risk from pharmacy pseudoephedrine is correspondingly reduced. The conclusion tracks the premises offered; the gap is that no evidence beyond assertion is supplied for the shift.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This legislation allows it to be even more accessible and puts it into the hands of our whānau who don’t need this drug.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation: the preceding sentences are about methamphetamine ('P... available on every street corner'), and the conclusion that 'this legislation allows it to be even more accessible' transfers that to a bill reclassifying pseudoephedrine as a pharmacy medicine. Nothing is offered to connect the pharmacy sale of a decongestant to increased meth availability.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I know that has been discussed regarding the risk of reintroducing or reclassifying this medicine back into the market, but I think that as we’ve learnt as time has gone by, the manner in which we receive methamphetamine into our criminal elements in New Zealand has changed so markedly and methamphetamine has become so cheap to produce and so prevalently produced that the risk presented by pseudoephedrine bought legitimately or obtained legitimately from the markets to be used to manufacture methamphetamine really isn’t the risk that it would be.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand methamphetamine supply has changed markedly, that meth is now cheap and prevalently produced, and that pseudoephedrine diversion is therefore no longer a material source.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police/Customs and NZ Drug Foundation data on methamphetamine supply 2010-2024 (clandestine lab seizures, border interceptions, wastewater consumption and street price), plus the Regulatory Impact Statement for the pseudoephedrine reclassification: true if lab detections based on pseudoephedrine extraction have fallen sharply while imported supply and consumption rose and price fell; false if domestic pseudoephedrine-based manufacture remains a significant supply source.

focus.statement: We are introducing it, or reclassifying it, with supports around how it will be used, how it will be managed, and how it will be regulated for importation to prevent those large-scale importations getting into the wrong hands.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — what the reclassification does and the controls attached to it — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This legislation allows it to be even more accessible and puts it into the hands of our whānau who don’t need this drug.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly, claiming what the reclassification will do to availability in her community; the framing is about the legislation, not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, it’s hypocritical, really, from this Government—to know that they’re lowering the class of this drug so it’s more accessible for medication during the winter wellness.
focus.explanation: Names the actual mechanism (lowering the drug's classification to make it available as winter cold medication), but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the Government rather than the policy consequence.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are introducing it, or reclassifying it, with supports around how it will be used, how it will be managed, and how it will be regulated for importation to prevent those large-scale importations getting into the wrong hands.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at controls on use, management and importation but names no classification, no purchase limit, no record-keeping requirement and no import threshold; a direction without the how or how much.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This is just going to allow more things to come—increased crime. It’s another avenue for the ram raids to happen.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that reclassifying pseudoephedrine to a pharmacy medicine will drive an increase in crime, specifically ram raids on premises stocking it.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded crime statistics for burglary/ram-raid offences against pharmacies in the 12 months after pseudoephedrine returned to pharmacy sale, compared with the preceding 12 months: true if pharmacy ram raids/burglaries rose materially over that period; false if they were flat or fell.

veracity.statement: Firstly, just to get on the Hansard record what this bill is actually doing, it is changing pseudoephedrine to a class C controlled drug instead of a class B—a downgrading, if you like. And so, as a class C controlled drug, pseudoephedrine will then be available without prescription but will have significant restrictions, such as at the import and export control level.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill reclassifies pseudoephedrine from a class B to a class C controlled drug, making it available without prescription while retaining import/export controls.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill as reported back by the Health Committee in 2024; true if it moves pseudoephedrine from Schedule 2 (class B) to Schedule 3 (class C) and removes the prescription requirement while retaining import/export controls, false if the reclassification or the prescription change is otherwise.

veracity.statement: We had submissions from 169 individuals and nine organisations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a precise count of submissions received by the Health Committee on this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill, submissions section; true if it records 169 individual and 9 organisational submissions, false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: I’d also like to point out that this is not something that’s unique to New Zealand; there’s a number of countries where it is available—the likes of Australia, the UK, Canada.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that pseudoephedrine-containing cold and flu medicines are available in Australia, the United Kingdom and Canada.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Medicines scheduling registers in each named country as at April 2024 (Australian Poisons Standard Schedule 3 'Pharmacist Only', UK MHRA pharmacy (P) medicine list, Health Canada behind-the-counter scheduling); true if pseudoephedrine products are lawfully supplied without prescription in all three, false if any of the three requires a prescription or prohibits it.

veracity.statement: Since the ban of pseudoephedrine, we’ve actually seen the availability of methamphetamines increase. We’ve seen the price absolutely decrease, making it kind of not an economically viable approach to make drugs from pseudoephedrine.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that since pseudoephedrine was restricted in New Zealand (2011), methamphetamine availability has increased and its price has fallen.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police/ESR national wastewater testing programme meth consumption estimates and NZ Drug Foundation / Massey Illicit Drug Monitoring System retail price series from 2011 to 2024; true if availability indicators rose and street price per gram fell over the period, false if availability fell or price rose.

veracity.statement: I will just bring the House’s attention to a press release by the Minister of Health that came out on 2 April—it was a week ago today—and that was reinforcing the importance of vaccination against flus.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Health issued a press release dated 2 April 2024 urging influenza vaccination.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: beehive.govt.nz releases by the Minister of Health (Shane Reti) for 2 April 2024; true if a release of that date concerns influenza vaccination, false if no such release exists on that date or it concerns another subject.

specificity.statement: Firstly, just to get on the Hansard record what this bill is actually doing, it is changing pseudoephedrine to a class C controlled drug instead of a class B—a downgrading, if you like. And so, as a class C controlled drug, pseudoephedrine will then be available without prescription but will have significant restrictions, such as at the import and export control level.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact legal mechanism — the schedule change from class B to class C — and the practical consequence (no prescription, retained import/export controls). Checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Therefore, that does mean we have to make sure that we have got adequate, quality, affordable housing; incomes; health services—at the very least.
specificity.explanation: Names three broad domains but supplies no figures, mechanisms, thresholds or timeframes; 'adequate, quality, affordable' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I understand, in the speeches from the Government and the honourable member whose bill this is—the speeches have put up and have communicated the driver behind this bill as being more about lessening the restrictions and about accessibility. What the Greens are supporting in this bill is the consistency with taking a harm reduction approach, and consistency with previous positions that we have held.
civility.explanation: Genuinely contests the Government's stated rationale for the bill and distinguishes her own party's reasoning, entirely on the substance, with no imputation of motive or attack on any member.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It has been shown, time and time again, that a criminalisation approach does not support harm reduction and does not support addiction becoming less harmful for people.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on a bare appeal to unnamed evidence — 'it has been shown, time and time again' — with no study, jurisdiction or data point offered to connect criminalisation to the stated outcomes. Appeal to unspecified authority.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think statistics would tell us we’d have, on average, two to four colds or flus a year, and since it’s been about 10 years since pseudoephedrine was available in New Zealand—I was just doing a bit of rough calculation as some of the previous speakers were speaking—I actually calculated that that would probably put us at about 52 weeks over those 14 years.
rigor.explanation: The arithmetic is internally inconsistent — the premise says 'about 10 years' and the conclusion is drawn 'over those 14 years' — and no duration-per-cold is supplied to get from two-to-four colds a year to 52 weeks. The stated figure does not follow from the stated premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They all have these medications available in a similar sort of regime, and they can manage some of the negative side effects; so I think we can too.
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy to comparable jurisdictions. Reasonable in form, but nothing is offered to show the regimes or the diversion risks are relevantly similar, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But, look, there’s a number of studies and probably a lot of expert opinion, and actually personal opinion, that this medication is probably one of the most effective medications to release nasal congestion and cold symptoms.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on unnamed studies plus 'expert opinion' and explicitly 'personal opinion' — an appeal to authority and anecdote, with no trial, comparator or effect size given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Since the ban of pseudoephedrine, we’ve actually seen the availability of methamphetamines increase. We’ve seen the price absolutely decrease, making it kind of not an economically viable approach to make drugs from pseudoephedrine.
rigor.explanation: Valid economic inference given the premises: if imported methamphetamine is cheap and plentiful, domestic manufacture from pharmacy pseudoephedrine is less attractive. The step from cheap supply to 'not economically viable' is asserted rather than quantified, but the conclusion tracks the evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I concur with the comments that have been expressed by colleagues around the fact the that there is no rush around this, although, given that members opposite seem to be taking lengthy calls, well, they wouldn’t seem to be in any hurry to actually get this piece of legislation passed this evening.
focus.explanation: A debate-chamber jibe about how long Government members are speaking; the only policy hook is the timing of the bill's passage, with no engagement of the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think about the cutting exercise, that the current Government seems to be under, around reducing access to the flu vaccine as we head into a time of winter months and winter ailments, and I challenge members opposite to align that fact with the comments that the Minister had made.
focus.explanation: Names a specific area of government policy (funded influenza vaccine access) and puts it against the Minister's stated position; substantive scrutiny, though partly framed as a challenge to 'members opposite'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are some concerns that have been raised, such as the safe care and custody of any controlled or restricted medication, that don’t seem to have been addressed through the committee stage and don’t seem to have been addressed in what is the final part of the bill, and that is only because of the rushed nature that this piece of legislation seems to be following through, in terms of its passage this evening.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the bill: names a substantive concern (safe care and custody of restricted medicines) and the stage at which it should have been dealt with.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Oh, colleagues across the House are telling me to get on with it and rush. That’s a change of tune—that’s a change of tune from the other side.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's inconsistency in the chamber; no policy, figure or measure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this is a piece of legislation that, effectively, will change the classification of pseudoephedrine but will still maintain some oversight at a pharmacy level.
specificity.explanation: Names the substance and the general mechanism (reclassification with continued pharmacy oversight) but gives no classes, statute or conditions of sale — a direction with partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We support it because the change of classification for pseudoephedrine as a controlled drug—this bill reclassifies it from a class B2, which it was changed to in 2011, to a class C3 controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 so that cold and flu products containing pseudoephedrine can be sold in pharmacies without a prescription.
specificity.explanation: Gives the exact classifications, the governing statute, the year of the previous change and the practical effect on sale — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I think about the cutting exercise, that the current Government seems to be under, around reducing access to the flu vaccine as we head into a time of winter months and winter ailments, and I challenge members opposite to align that fact with the comments that the Minister had made.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Government is reducing access to the influenza vaccine heading into winter 2024.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Pharmac / Ministry of Health decisions on funded influenza vaccination eligibility and funding for the 2024 season compared with 2023; true if funded eligibility or access was narrowed by a Government decision, false if eligibility was unchanged or widened.

veracity.statement: We support it because the change of classification for pseudoephedrine as a controlled drug—this bill reclassifies it from a class B2, which it was changed to in 2011, to a class C3 controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975 so that cold and flu products containing pseudoephedrine can be sold in pharmacies without a prescription.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that pseudoephedrine was moved to class B2 in 2011 and that this bill reclassifies it to class C3 under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, permitting pharmacy sale without prescription.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill and the schedules of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1975, plus the 2011 amendment reclassifying pseudoephedrine; true if the classes and the 2011 date match, false if either differs.

veracity.statement: Patients are currently unable to access over-the-counter medicines containing pseudoephedrine medicines for the self-treatment of cold symptoms in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at April 2024 no pseudoephedrine-containing cold medicine could be obtained in New Zealand without a prescription.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Medsafe classification of pseudoephedrine and the regulatory impact statement for the bill as at April 2024; true if pseudoephedrine products were prescription-only, false if any over-the-counter pseudoephedrine product was legally available.

veracity.statement: Australia, prescription required? No. Canada, prescription required? No. United Kingdom, prescription required? No. What about the United States? No.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that none of Australia, Canada, the UK or the US require a prescription for pseudoephedrine-containing cold medicines.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement for the bill and each jurisdiction's medicines scheduling (Australian Poisons Standard, Health Canada, UK MHRA, US Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act); true if pseudoephedrine is obtainable without prescription in all four, false if any requires a prescription.

veracity.statement: Just to relay some of the comments made earlier in this debate, relief is on the way for those New Zealanders who have battled through 14 winters without strong cold and flu medicine.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealanders have gone 14 winters without access to strong (pseudoephedrine-based) cold and flu medicine.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Date of the 2011 reclassification of pseudoephedrine to prescription-only, counted against the winters elapsed to April 2024; true if 14 winters fell within the restricted period, false if the count is materially different (e.g. 13).

veracity.statement: This bill gives effect to the deed of settlement signed by Ngāti Hei and the Crown in August 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Ngāti Hei deed of settlement with the Crown was signed in August 2017.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Arawhiti / Office for Māori Crown Relations record of the Ngāti Hei deed of settlement signing date; true if signed in August 2017, false if signed in another month or year.

veracity.statement: The committee received and considered 11 written submissions and heard oral evidence from two submitters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Māori Affairs Committee received 11 written submissions on the bill and heard two oral submitters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Māori Affairs Committee report on the Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill; true if it records 11 written submissions and two oral submitters, false if the numbers differ.

rigor.statement: There are some concerns that have been raised, such as the safe care and custody of any controlled or restricted medication, that don’t seem to have been addressed through the committee stage and don’t seem to have been addressed in what is the final part of the bill, and that is only because of the rushed nature that this piece of legislation seems to be following through, in terms of its passage this evening.
rigor.explanation: Identifies an unaddressed concern and then attributes it entirely ('only because') to the truncated process — a post hoc causal leap; nothing is offered to rule out the concern simply having been considered and rejected.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Pseudoephedrine is an effective medicine. Allowing New Zealanders access to effective cold and flu medicine will help to improve people’s welfare when they are unwell.
rigor.explanation: The welfare conclusion follows loosely from the efficacy premise, but the inference is asserted rather than supported — nothing is offered on effect size or on the harms the restriction was meant to prevent, so the trade-off side of the argument is simply absent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So this is simply bringing New Zealand back into line with many other countries that we compare and contrast ourselves to across the world.
rigor.explanation: The comparative conclusion tracks the four jurisdictions just enumerated from the regulatory impact statement; the weakness is a mild appeal to consistency — that others allow it is offered as sufficient reason, without addressing why New Zealand diverged.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We fully expect that we’ll have many representatives from Ngāti Hei in the third reading, but I’m sure there will be many tuning in on their computer screens and maybe listening in on the radio to this speech.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a substantial delegation of Ngāti Hei will attend Parliament for the bill's third reading.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the third reading of the Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill; true if members of Ngāti Hei are acknowledged as present in the gallery, false if the third reading proceeds without any Ngāti Hei representatives present.

civility.statement: It’s great to hear that the previous member, Dr Hamish Campbell, has so much concern for all New Zealanders about cold and flu symptoms. I really have to question, though: which New Zealanders is he concerned for?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic framing ("It's great to hear that... has so much concern") followed by a rhetorical question imputing that the named member's concern is insincere or selective. Short of a direct insult, but it targets the person's good faith rather than his argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m a little concerned at the cavalier approach of the Minister.
civility.explanation: Characterises the Minister personally as "cavalier" — a judgement about his attitude rather than about the policy — but mildly phrased and not an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t wish for any harm to come to anyone, but if there are ram raids, then that is on his shoulders.
civility.explanation: Assigns personal blame in advance to a named Minister for potential violent crime against pharmacies. It goes beyond criticising the decision to placing future harm on the individual, though it stops short of abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s great to hear that the previous member, Dr Hamish Campbell, has so much concern for all New Zealanders about cold and flu symptoms. I really have to question, though: which New Zealanders is he concerned for?
focus.explanation: A real policy hook exists (flu vaccine access, developed in the following sentences), but this passage itself is framed as a challenge to which people the member and the Government care about rather than engaging the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Make no mistake: the National-led coalition Government is committed to improving the health outcomes of all New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: Party-branding rather than policy content: it asserts his own side's general virtue instead of engaging the reclassification before the House. The following sentences supply policy; this one does not.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: He mentioned 2 April as a date when the flu vaccine would be available to New Zealanders; actually, under the previous Labour Government, the most vulnerable group—Māori aged 55 to 64—were able to get that flu vaccine for free. This is no longer available.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that free (publicly funded) influenza vaccination was available to Māori aged 55–64 under the previous Labour Government and that this eligibility has since been withdrawn.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Pharmac/Health New Zealand funded influenza immunisation eligibility criteria for the 2022–2023 seasons compared with the 2024 season; true if Māori aged 55–64 were a funded group previously and are not a funded group in 2024, false if that eligibility continued in 2024.

veracity.statement: If that is the case, we should not be cutting the Government expenditure for Customs officers by 7.5 percent, making it easier for methamphetamine to come in, as has been reported by the Public Service Association, who are saying that this puts New Zealand at risk.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Government expenditure on Customs is being cut by 7.5 percent, and that the Public Service Association has reported this as putting New Zealand at risk.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 / Treasury baseline savings target documents for the New Zealand Customs Service, plus PSA public statements in early 2024; true if Customs was set a 7.5 percent baseline savings target and the PSA publicly warned it increases border risk, false if the target was a different figure or the PSA made no such statement.

veracity.statement: Also, we got more feedback during the select committee stage as well, with 169 submissions received from individuals and nine from organisations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a precise count of submissions to the select committee on the bill: 169 from individuals and nine from organisations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Misuse of Drugs (Pseudoephedrine) Amendment Bill and the published submissions list on parliament.nz; true if the counts match 169 individual and nine organisational submissions, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The price of meth or P dropped by 28 percent from $563 per gram in 2017 to, now, $406 in 2022-23.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the New Zealand retail methamphetamine price fell from $563 per gram in 2017 to $406 per gram in 2022-23, a 28 percent decline.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Massey University SHORE/NZ Drug Trends Survey (Wilkins et al.) reported median methamphetamine gram prices for 2017 and 2022-23; true if the figures match within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The bill actually reflects international best practice and matches similar settings in the range of other countries we like to compare ourselves to, including the United Kingdom, United States, Canada, and Australia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the pharmacist-supervised, non-prescription setting for pseudoephedrine created by the bill matches the regulatory settings in the UK, US, Canada and Australia.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Current medicines scheduling for pseudoephedrine in each named jurisdiction (UK MHRA pharmacy medicine, Australia TGA Schedule 3, US Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act behind-the-counter rules, Health Canada behind-the-counter); true if all four allow supply without prescription under pharmacist control, false if any require a prescription.

veracity.statement: In my previous contribution, I spoke about some of the evidence for pseudoephedrine as being the only effective treatment that is available, which, in the context of nasal congestion or sinus congestion, prevents barotrauma of the tympanic membrane. The other medications that we have to treat cold and flu congestion, such as nasal sprays, are actually not effective for that outcome.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that oral pseudoephedrine is the only available effective treatment for preventing barotrauma of the eardrum arising from nasal or sinus congestion, and that topical nasal sprays are not effective for that outcome.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed evidence on decongestants and otic barotrauma (e.g. Cochrane reviews and aviation-medicine trials of oral pseudoephedrine versus topical decongestants such as oxymetazoline); true if the literature shows oral pseudoephedrine effective and topical decongestants ineffective for barotrauma prevention, false if topical decongestants also show benefit or if pseudoephedrine's benefit is not established.

rigor.statement: We had a revelation from one of the officials that that could be any number between two and 10. So I don’t think that’s indicative of the whole pharmacy profession.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference: a consultation sample that may have been as few as two pharmacists cannot support a generalisation about the profession. The conclusion follows directly from the stated sample size; no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We heard a dismissive response about people shopping around to buy pseudoephedrine in an orchestrated way to make it for communities that might be wanting to make methamphetamine; he said, “Oh, I’m going to keep a close eye on it.” But there is no mechanism by which to do that, unless there is a register, so that was nonsensical.
rigor.explanation: The inference holds given its premise: monitoring bulk purchasing requires a record of purchases, so an undertaking to "keep a close eye" without a register is unsupported. The gap is that she asserts rather than establishes that no other monitoring mechanism exists.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the past few months, I have been visiting medical centres, having a chat, having a conversation with a lot of GPs, especially in Mount Roskill. The common feedback I receive is that they are reaching their maximum capacity and are no longer taking any new patients. So this bill means that New Zealanders will have an effective option, rather than picking up the phone to their overloaded GP.
rigor.explanation: A real argument about the measure, but the evidential base is anecdote from unstructured conversations in one electorate, and it does not establish that people currently consult GPs for pseudoephedrine or that OTC access would displace those visits.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, this Government is committed to tackling gangs and organised crime, including banning gang patches and seizing unlawfully obtained assets, so the concern that it will be used in unlawful drugs will be minimised.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: gang patch bans and asset seizure do not bear on whether pharmacy-supplied pseudoephedrine is diverted into methamphetamine manufacture. Nothing is offered to connect the stated measures to the stated conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think the theme of this third reading really has been that the Government has certainly, I think, overstated the protections that are in this bill, because none of the things that have been talked about as protective factors tonight is actually in the legislation, in the bill.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premise offered: if the safeguards cited in debate are not enacted in the bill's text, describing them as protections the bill provides overstates it. The premise is asserted rather than demonstrated, which is the only gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If that is the case, we should not be cutting the Government expenditure for Customs officers by 7.5 percent, making it easier for methamphetamine to come in, as has been reported by the Public Service Association, who are saying that this puts New Zealand at risk.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency, a precise percentage cut and the source of the claim — checkable and actionable, though the base the 7.5 percent applies to is not stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Make no mistake: the National-led coalition Government is committed to improving the health outcomes of all New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: A commitment slogan with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named action — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We recently announced five health targets: a focus on faster cancer treatment, improved immunisation rates, shorter stays in emergency departments, shorter wait times for first specialist assessments, and shorter times for elective treatment.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific policy and enumerates all five target areas, but supplies no numeric thresholds or dates for any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The price of meth or P dropped by 28 percent from $563 per gram in 2017 to, now, $406 in 2022-23.
specificity.explanation: Two dated price points, a percentage change and an attributed research source — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In my previous contribution, I spoke about some of the evidence for pseudoephedrine as being the only effective treatment that is available, which, in the context of nasal congestion or sinus congestion, prevents barotrauma of the tympanic membrane. The other medications that we have to treat cold and flu congestion, such as nasal sprays, are actually not effective for that outcome.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific clinical mechanism and outcome (prevention of tympanic membrane barotrauma) and a specific comparator (nasal sprays), so the claim is concrete enough to check against the clinical literature, though no study or figure is cited.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Eleven groups presented before the committee with the majority agreeing with the actions discussed in the bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that eleven groups made submissions to the Māori Affairs Committee on the Ngāti Hei claims settlement bill and that most of them supported the bill's provisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Māori Affairs Committee report and submission list for the Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill; true if eleven submitters are recorded and the report characterises a majority as supportive, false if the submitter count is materially different or most submissions opposed.

veracity.statement: Between 1859 and 1865, the Crown acquired 20,000 acres.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure for Crown land acquisition in the Ngāti Hei rohe over 1859-1865.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The historical account in the Ngāti Hei deed of settlement and the associated Waitangi Tribunal record; true if approximately 20,000 acres are recorded as Crown-acquired in that period, false if the recorded area or dates differ materially.

veracity.statement: In 1888, a Melbourne company bought all the cutting rights to standing kauri on the peninsula, and its production peaked in 1902.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an Australian company purchased all kauri cutting rights on the Coromandel Peninsula in 1888 and that its output peaked in 1902.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Documented Coromandel kauri-milling history (e.g. Te Ara / DOC / regional histories of the Kauri Timber Company); true if a Melbourne-based company acquired peninsula-wide cutting rights in 1888 with peak production around 1902, false if the year, the company's origin, or the peak year differ materially.

divination.statement: So, to Ngāti Hei at home watching, I want to reiterate this bill continues with the support of the Minister, and soon, will be read a third time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Ngāti Hei settlement bill will reach and pass its third reading in the near future.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary records for the Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill; true if the bill is read a third time within roughly a year of this speech, false if it is still awaiting third reading or is not passed by then.

focus.statement: This notion of full and final Treaty settlements troubles us greatly because, like all settlements, the redress in these settlement bills will reflect only a fraction of the economic and social losses suffered by iwi because of Crown actions—perhaps 1 to 2 percent reparation; a tiny fraction and yet we stamp an obligation that that must mean the end of future claims prior to 1992.
focus.explanation: Engages directly with the substance of the measure before the House — the redress quantum and the finality clause of Treaty settlements — naming the mechanism and the 1992 cut-off rather than attacking another party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This notion of full and final Treaty settlements troubles us greatly because, like all settlements, the redress in these settlement bills will reflect only a fraction of the economic and social losses suffered by iwi because of Crown actions—perhaps 1 to 2 percent reparation; a tiny fraction and yet we stamp an obligation that that must mean the end of future claims prior to 1992.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: if redress is only a small fraction of the loss, extinguishing future claims is disproportionate. The premise linking proportion of loss to the legitimacy of finality is asserted rather than shown, and the '1 to 2 percent' figure is offered without support, leaving a gap between evidence and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This notion of full and final Treaty settlements troubles us greatly because, like all settlements, the redress in these settlement bills will reflect only a fraction of the economic and social losses suffered by iwi because of Crown actions—perhaps 1 to 2 percent reparation; a tiny fraction and yet we stamp an obligation that that must mean the end of future claims prior to 1992.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of the settlement policy and the Crown's negotiating posture, with no attack on any individual member.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, to be clear, even the land which has been returned, and that of which may be conservation estate, could still be mined for gold, and we know there’s a lot of gold mined in the Coromandel.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete mechanism — the nationalised-minerals carve-out in the deed means returned land, including conservation estate, remains open to gold mining — and locates it geographically, though no figures or areas are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal found that the people of Hauraki, Ngāti Hei, only retain 2.6 percent of their tribal territories, e tātou mā, being one of the largest groups in Aotearoa to have such grave land loss within their tribal territories.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific Waitangi Tribunal finding: that Hauraki/Ngāti Hei retain only 2.6 percent of their tribal territories, and that this is among the largest proportional land losses in the country.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's Hauraki Report (Wai 686) and associated Tribunal findings; true if the Tribunal records retention of roughly 2.6 percent of tribal lands for Hauraki/Ngāti Hei, false if the Tribunal figure is materially different or no such finding exists.

veracity.statement: This is something that was experienced by the people of Ngāti Hei, with over 81,000 acres of land lost through Crown purchases.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ngāti Hei lost more than 81,000 acres specifically through Crown purchases (as distinct from confiscation).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ngāti Hei deed of settlement historical account and the Waitangi Tribunal Hauraki Report land-loss tables; true if Crown purchases from Ngāti Hei total more than 81,000 acres, false if the recorded figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: This has been 24 years in the making, but 180 years in the waiting.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ngāti Hei settlement process has run for about 24 years, and that the grievances date back roughly 180 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ngāti Hei deed of settlement and Wai claim registration records; true if the claim/negotiation process began around 2000 (roughly 24 years before April 2024) and the raupatu-era grievances date to the 1840s–1860s, false if the process began materially later or earlier.

veracity.statement: That select committee process yielded 11 submissions, and we only heard evidence of two submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Māori Affairs Committee received 11 submissions on the Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill and heard oral evidence from two of them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report on the Ngāti Hei Claims Settlement Bill and the committee's submissions record on parliament.nz; true if 11 submissions were received and two heard, false if the counts differ.

specificity.statement: The Waitangi Tribunal found that the people of Hauraki, Ngāti Hei, only retain 2.6 percent of their tribal territories, e tātou mā, being one of the largest groups in Aotearoa to have such grave land loss within their tribal territories.
specificity.explanation: Names a source (Waitangi Tribunal), a precise figure (2.6 percent) and the group it applies to — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Part 3 talks about the commercial redress, which is about $8.5 million, plus contractual memorandums of understanding to enter into relationships with the Department of Conservation and to facilitate relationships with local authorities as well.
specificity.explanation: Names the part of the bill, the redress figure and the specific relationship instruments and agencies involved.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The proviso of “full and final settlement” makes it unjust for the people of Ngāti Hei and Pare Hauraki to accept—to accept—$8.5 million in commercial redress; $8.5 million, e tātou mā, for 184 years of losses.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly — the full-and-final clause and the quantum of commercial redress in this bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Part 3 talks about the commercial redress, which is about $8.5 million, plus contractual memorandums of understanding to enter into relationships with the Department of Conservation and to facilitate relationships with local authorities as well.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the provisions of the bill before the House; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The proviso of “full and final settlement” makes it unjust for the people of Ngāti Hei and Pare Hauraki to accept—to accept—$8.5 million in commercial redress; $8.5 million, e tātou mā, for 184 years of losses.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the settlement's terms and the Crown's offer; no individual is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So Whenuakite Station, a Landcorp farm, is now a part of the redress for 85 percent—85 percent available for Ngāti Hei, and acknowledging Ngāti Tamaterā—but these whenua, they have to buy it back. They have to buy it back, and yet it was taken.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the redress mechanism: if land was wrongfully taken, requiring the iwi to purchase it back does not constitute restitution. The premise (deferred purchase rights rather than transfer) supports the conclusion, though the argument does not address that the purchase is funded from the settlement quantum.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But this is a start. And that’s something that, actually, both sides of this House have signed up to, and iwi have also signed up to this process.
rigor.explanation: Defends the adequacy of the settlement framework by pointing to who has agreed to it — an appeal to consensus/agreement, which does not address the objection that the redress is disproportionate to the loss.
rigor.subject: speaker
